Its first verse, *ud u tyaṃ jātavedasam*, and its tenth, *ud vayaṃ tamasas pari*, both stand in the *sūryopasthāna* — the standing address to Sūrya at the close of sandhyāvandana, after the arghya has been offered. Anyone who performs sandhyā has said the tenth verse facing the sun and has therefore already made its claim in the first person: *aganma jyotir uttamam*, we have gone to the highest light. The hymn is not being described here so much as identified.

Sūrya's own hymns are scarcer than that prominence suggests. Across all 1,028 sūktas only six are ascribed to Sūrya alone — this one, [[1.115]], and four in the tenth maṇḍala. What he has instead is placement. He stands inside the daily rite rather than inside a large body of hymns, which is a different and more durable kind of presence.

The place of this sūkta in its own neighbourhood is deliberate. Praskaṇva Kāṇva, who is given this hymn, has seven consecutive sūktas here, and they run in the order of a morning: [[1.44]] and 1.45 to Agni, 1.46 and 1.47 to the Aśvins, [[1.48]] and 1.49 to Uṣas, and then this one to Sūrya. The kindled fire, the twin riders who come before dawn, the dawn, the sun. A reader who takes the seven in sequence is walking through the hours of a sandhyā rather than through a list.

The last three verses are where the hymn touches an ordinary life. They ask Sūrya to take away *hṛdroga*, the trouble in the heart, and *harimān*, the yellowness — and then, rather than leaving the affliction nowhere, they place it somewhere: in the parrots, in the yellow birds, in the yellow-sapped trees. That is the logic of a great deal of later domestic ritual, in which what is removed must be given a place to go. Whatever one makes of it medically, the structure is honest about something. A thing taken out of a person has to be put down.

One word carries the whole sūkta and is worth keeping: *jyotis*, light. It appears in the tenth verse three times over — light seen, the higher light, the highest light — and the tradition has never stopped using that ladder.
50.disagreements:
Sāyaṇa reads the second verse's *nakṣatras* as more than stars. Citing the Brāhmaṇa maxim *devagṛhā vai nakṣatrāṇi*, the constellations are the houses of the gods, he takes them as the visible forms of those who performed rites here and attained the higher world. Neither translator carries this into the English.

Verse 5's *devānāṃ viśaḥ* divides them. Sāyaṇa identifies the "clans of the gods" as the Maruts, on the standing equation *maruto vai devānāṃ viśaḥ*, and Wilson prints "in the presence of the Maruts"; Griffith keeps the general "hosts of Gods". Verse 6 divides them more sharply: *varuṇa* is a plain vocative in the morphology, so Sūrya is being addressed by Varuṇa's name. Griffith keeps the name — "brilliant Varuna" — while Wilson dissolves it into an epithet, "defender from evil".

On the seven *haritaḥ* Sāyaṇa offers three answers and settles on none: seven rays, or the seven days of the week, or — he raises it as a question — the scattered prismatic rays.

Verse 10 is where he is most expansive. He reads the darkness as sin and the approach to Sūrya as reunion with the supreme spirit, glossing *aganma jyotir uttamam* as *sāyujyaṃ gacchāmaḥ*, we go to union, and citing the principle that one becomes what one worships. On verse 11 he preserves the tradition that Praskaṇva himself was cured of a skin affliction by this praise, and records Śaunaka's use of the hymn against sin, disease and poison alike.

51.title: Indra as Ram — the Rescues Named, Ārya from Dasyu
51.synthesis:
The hymn opens on an image the collection uses only rarely: *abhi tyaṃ meṣam*, that ram. {{indra}} is greeted under an animal form, called *puruhūta* — invoked by many — and *vasvo arṇavam*, an ocean of wealth, and the singers are told to gladden him with songs. The second verse has the {{ṛbhu}}s coming to his side as helps, and something moves toward him at the same moment: *javanī sūnṛtā ā aruhat*, a swift and generous word climbed up to him. Praise is described as travelling, and arriving.

Then four verses beginning *tvam*, you, and each one is a rescue with a name attached. You opened the *gotra* — the pen, or the cloud — for the Aṅgirasas; you found the way out for Atri behind a hundred doors; you carried wealth with food to Vimada. You opened the covering of the waters; you held the treasure in the mountain; and when you slew Vṛtra with force you *made Sūrya climb the sky to be seen*. That last clause is the same claim [[1.32]] makes in its fourth verse: the killing is also a cosmogony. You blew away the *māyins*, the wielders of illusion, who poured offerings only into their own mouths; you broke Pipru's forts and stood by Ṛjiśvan. You stood by {{kutsa}} when Śuṣṇa was killed, gave Śambara to Atithigva, trod down the great Arbuda — *sanād eva dasyuhatyāya jajñiṣe*, from of old you were born for that work.

The seventh verse gathers it: all *taviṣī*, all vigour, is set in you together; your bounty rejoices toward the soma-drinking; the *vajra* is known to be lodged in your arms. And then the eighth, the hymn's most argued line: *vi jānīhy āryān ye ca dasyavaḥ* — discriminate the āryas and those who are dasyus. The verse supplies its own criterion in the next breath: subdue them *barhiṣmate*, for the man whose grass is strewn, and chastise the *avratāḥ*, those without observance. What is being asked for is discernment between one who keeps the rite and one who does not.

The ninth continues it — he hands the *apavratāḥ* over to the *anuvrata* — and closes with a small strange story: Vamra, praising, broke through the heaped piles. The tenth and eleventh bring in Uśanā Kāvya, who sharpened his force against his own, so that his *śavas* pressed apart both worlds; when Indra takes delight beside Uśanā he mounts steeds that swerve ever wider, releases the waters in a torrent, and scatters Śuṣṇa's built forts. The twelfth puts him in the chariot at Śāryāta's pressings. The thirteenth gathers three human debts in one verse: Vṛcayā given to the aged Kakṣīvat, and — flatly, without apology — *menā abhavo vṛṣaṇaśvasya*, you became Menā, the daughter of Vṛṣaṇaśva; all these deeds of yours are to be recited at the pressings.

The fourteenth changes register. Indra has been resorted to in a strait, and the praise among the Pajras stands *duryo na yūpaḥ*, firm as the post at a door. Then the fifteenth ends not with a deed but with a bow: *idaṃ namo vṛṣabhāya svarāje satyaśuṣmāya tavase avāci* — this *namas* has been spoken to the bull, the self-ruling, whose vehemence is true. And the last thing asked for is company: in this strait, with our patrons, may we be under your shelter.
51.practice:
This is the first of a set of seven, and the set is worth knowing as a set. Savya Āṅgirasa has exactly seven sūktas in the whole Ṛgveda — 1.51 through 1.57 — and every one of them is to Indra. Whatever else a reader takes from this stretch, it is one poet's complete surviving work on one god, laid out in order. The seven are also tied at the ends: the phrase *satyaśuṣmāya tavase*, "to him of true vehemence, the strong", closes this hymn's last verse and opens the first verse of [[1.57]], the last of the seven. The phrase occurs four times in the whole collection and two of those four are these two positions.

The eighth verse is the one a reader will meet quoted, usually stripped of its second half, and the second half is what matters. *Vi jānīhy āryān ye ca dasyavaḥ* is followed immediately by *barhiṣmate randhayā śāsad avratān* — for the man whose *barhis* is strewn, chastising the *avratāḥ*. The distinction the verse itself draws is between the one who has laid the grass and made the offering and the one who keeps no *vrata*. In this sūkta *ārya* appears once and *dasyu* twice, both times inside the compound *dasyuhatya*; the words are used, not defined, and readers have taken them in more than one direction ever since. What can be said from the text here, and only this, is that the criterion named in the line is observance.

*Vrata* is the word to carry out. It is still the ordinary Hindu word for an undertaking kept — Ekādaśī vrata, Satyanārāyaṇa vrata — something one binds oneself to and performs on time. Here it is already the dividing line, and its negative, *avrata*, already means the one who is bound to nothing.

The other thing to take is the hymn's method. Nine of its fifteen verses do nothing but name people Indra helped: the Aṅgirasas, Atri, Vimada, Ṛjiśvan, Kutsa, Atithigva, Śāryāta, Kakṣīvat. A god is being praised entirely by a list of the people he stood beside. That is a recognisable model for how one is expected to remember help — specifically, with names.
51.disagreements:
The ram in verse 1 has two explanations in Sāyaṇa and he keeps both. There is a legend that Indra took the form of a ram and came to Medhātithi's sacrifice to drink soma; and there is a plain derivation, *meṣa* as the one who prevails over foes. He adds a second legend attached to this hymn's poet — that Aṅgiras worshipped for a son resembling Indra, and Indra was born as that son, named Savya. The word occurs five times in the whole Ṛgveda; two of the five open this hymn and the next.

At verse 2 Sāyaṇa takes the *ṛbhus* to be the Maruts, and supplies the words they shouted — *prahara, bhagavan, vīryasva*: strike, lord, be valiant. Griffith keeps them as the Ṛbhus, "strong to save".

On verse 8 Sāyaṇa is explicit and narrow: āryas are those who practise the rites, dasyus those who do not observe them and are hostile to those who do. Wilson follows him closely; Griffith renders *avratān* as "the lawless".

Verse 13 is where the translators are least comfortable. Both render *menā abhavo vṛṣaṇaśvasya* as Indra becoming Menā; Sāyaṇa states it and adds that he afterwards fell in love with her, and notes the separate Menā who is Himavat's wife. Verse 12's Śāryāta he attaches to the Kauśītaki legend of Cyavana taking the Aśvins' share, which angered Indra.

52.title: Indra Fills the World, Then Splits Vṛtra's Jaw
52.synthesis:
The ram returns in the first verse — *tyaṃ su meṣam mahaya svarvidam*, magnify that ram who finds the light of heaven — and a hundred good ones go out with him. The singer asks to turn {{indra}} back toward him with well-turned praises, as one would turn a chariot that runs to the call like a fast horse. That is the frame: a hymn trying to bring something enormous within reach.

The second verse sets him standing. Unshaken as a mountain on its foundations, thousandfold in his helps, he grew in his vigours when he slew {{vṛtra}} who had penned the rivers, and forced the floods out, exhilarated by the pressing. The third calls him *candrabudhna*, whose base is bright, grown great in rapture — and says how he is reached: *suapasyayā dhiyā*, with a {{dhī}} bent on good work. The fourth has the offerings poured on the strewn grass filling him as rivers fill the sea, and it names the company: the {{marut}}s stood by him at the Vṛtra-killing, unswerving, of undistorted form. In the fifth the helps run down to him as streams run down a slope, and he splits {{vala}} open *paridhīn iva tritaḥ*, as Trita broke through the coverings — a passing comparison to another and older escape.

Then the killing itself, and it is placed exactly. The sixth: heat played about him, his *śavas* flashed out, and Vṛtra lay at the bottom of the region having penned the waters — *nijaghantha hanvor indra tanyatum*, you struck the thunder down upon his jaws. The seventh turns from the deed to the praise: the *brahman*s that magnify you reach you as waves reach a lake, and Tvaṣṭṛ increased the *śavas* proper to you and forged the *vajra* of overwhelming might. The eighth restates the outcome in the older order — having slain Vṛtra with your tawny horses, you made a path for man, you held the metal bolt in your arms, and you set Sūrya in the sky to be seen. The ninth records what the worshippers did while it happened: in fear they raised the *bṛhat*, the high self-shining chant that climbs to heaven, and the Maruts, fighting for men, sang him on.

The tenth is the loudest verse in the hymn. Dyaus himself, mighty as he is, shrank back in fear at the *ahi*'s roar — and in that same moment your bolt, in the rapture of the pressing, struck off the head of the Vṛtra who had been crowding both worlds.

What follows is not more battle but measurement, and it is the hymn's real subject. Verse eleven: if the earth were tenfold and men multiplied every day, your *sahas* would still be famous here, Maghavan, and would spread as wide as heaven. Verse twelve: standing beyond the limit of this open region, of your own strength, you made the earth *pratimānam ojasaḥ*, the counter-measure of your force, and reached all the way to heaven. Verse thirteen presses it further: you became the counter-measure of earth, lord of the great sky where the gods dwell; you filled the whole *antarikṣa* with your greatness; and — *satyam addhā nakir anyas tvāvān* — truly, in fact, there is no other like you. Verse fourteen makes the point negatively: heaven and earth have not reached your breadth, the waters of the region have not reached your limit; alone, you made all the rest in its order.

The fifteenth ends where a rite ends, with the company singing. In that encounter the Maruts sang, and all the *deva*s took delight in you, when you struck the face of Vṛtra with the many-edged weapon.
52.practice:
This hymn and [[1.32]] tell one story, and the difference between them is instructive. [[1.32]] narrates: the drinking, the striking, the corpse, the fear, the kingship. This one narrates the same act in five verses and then spends five more asking how large the actor is — earth as his counter-measure, heaven not reaching his breadth, no other like him. It is the earlier hymn's event turned into a question about scale. A reader who wants the story goes to [[1.32]]; a reader who wants to know what the tradition made of the story comes here.

The instrument in verse 15 is worth a moment. The weapon that strikes Vṛtra's face is *bhṛṣṭimatā vadhena*, the weapon that has points or edges, and the received tradition counts them: the *vajra* has eight edges. That is why the word survives in ordinary Hindu speech for anything unbreakable — *vajra* in a body posture, in a name, in the vajra held in later iconography. The Ṛgveda's own account of it is that it was made: Tvaṣṭṛ, the artificer, forged it (verse 7), which is also how [[1.32]] tells it. The most powerful thing in the hymn is a manufactured object handed to the god by a craftsman.

Verse 9 records something small and easy to miss: what people were doing while the fight was on. They raised the *bṛhat*, the high chant, in fear. The hymn does not describe them watching. It describes them singing, and it names the Maruts as fighting alongside — help that arrives in two forms, one martial and one vocal, treated as the same kind of help. Anyone who has chanted through a crisis rather than merely waited through it will recognise the claim being made about what singing is for.

And the ninth verse's word for what they were feeling is *bhiyasā*, out of fear. The Ṛgveda is not embarrassed by it. Fear appears here as the thing that produces the chant, and in [[1.32]].14 as the thing that enters the victor's own heart after the killing.
52.disagreements:
The Trita simile in verse 5 draws Sāyaṇa's fullest note here. *Trita* can simply mean triple, so "as through threefold defences" — but he also gives the legend: Ekata, Dvita and Trita produced in the waters by Agni, and Trita falling into a well over which the asuras heaped coverings, which he broke through. Indra's breaking of Vala's enclosures is being compared to that escape. Griffith prints the name and no legend.

Verse 15's *bhṛṣṭimatā vadhena* Sāyaṇa glosses as the weapon possessed of angles, citing the Aitareya Brāhmaṇa's *aṣṭāśrir vai vajraḥ* — the thunderbolt has eight edges. Wilson prints "angular and fatal"; Griffith, "spiky weapon".

On verse 9 Sāyaṇa supplies what the text leaves as a bare adjective: *bṛhat* is the Bṛhat-sāman, and he notes that a sāman is the singing of a ṛc. Wilson accordingly writes "the suitable hymn of the Bṛhat (Sāma)"; Griffith keeps it as "the lofty self-resplendent hymn" and lets the technical sense go.

At verse 13 Sāyaṇa reads *ṛṣvavīrasya bṛhataḥ patiḥ* as lord of the great region in which the pleasant heroes — the gods — reside, and *pratimānaṃ bhuvaḥ* as being of the same magnitude as the earth and of the same inconceivable power. Wilson follows; Griffith gives "counterpart of earth", which keeps the arithmetic and loses the gods.

53.title: Indra the Opener — of Horses, Cattle, Barley, Kings
53.synthesis:
The first verse states a rule about praise before it offers any. We bring speech forward to the great one, songs to {{indra}} in Vivasvat's seat — and then, without softening it, *na duṣṭutir draviṇodeṣu śasyate*: badly made praise is not thought well of among the wealth-givers. The hymn puts its own standard on the table in its first line, and everything after has to meet it.

The second verse meets it with one word said three times. *Duro aśvasya, duro gor asi, duro yavasya* — you are the opening of the horse, the opening of the cow, the opening of the barley. Horse, cow, barley: transport, milk, food, in that order, and one word for what Indra is to each. Then a run of titles that are all about reliability rather than power: lord of wealth, *akāmakarśana*, one who does not wear down a desire, and *sakhā sakhibhyaḥ*, a friend to his friends.

The third verse asks him to act on it. The wealth spread around here is known to be yours; having gathered it, bring it — *mā tvāyato jaritur kāmam ūnayīḥ*, do not leave short the desire of the singer who trusts you. The fourth turns to the assembly's own wish: with these days and these drops, drive off *amati*, want, with cattle and horses; with Indra scattering the {{dasyu}}, freed from those who hate us, may we together take hold of nourishment. The fifth repeats the taking-hold twice over — *sam indra rāyā sam iṣā rabhemahi* — and asks for divine *pramati*, forethought, that has heroic force in it and cattle and horses at its head.

From the sixth the hymn turns backward to what has already been given. Those raptures and those pressings gladdened you at the Vṛtra-killings, lord of the good, when for the singer with strewn grass you laid low ten thousand obstructions, unresisted. The seventh has him going from fight to fight without hesitating, breaking fort after fort, and killing far off the deceiver named Namuci with his bowing friend. The eighth: you struck down Karañja and Parṇaya on Atithigva's most brilliant course; unyielding, you broke the hundred forts of Vaṅgṛda when Ṛjiśvan had them under siege.

The ninth is the hymn's oddest and most concrete verse, and its numbers are exact: twenty kings of men who had come against friendless Suśravas, and sixty thousand and ninety-nine of their followers, overturned with the chariot wheel. Whatever this refers to, the poet expects it to be recognised. The tenth names the beneficiaries in a row — you protected Suśravas with your helps and Turvayāṇa with your defences; you made {{kutsa}}, Atithigva and Āyu subject to that great and young king. Two verses of names, from opposite sides of the same events.

Then the eleventh, and the hymn does not end on a battlefield. *Ye ṛci deva-gopāḥ* — may we, guarded by the gods at the recitation, be your most fortunate friends; may we praise you, having good heroes through you, holding a longer life and one that carries further. The last thing asked for after twenty kings and sixty thousand men is a longer life and the right to keep singing.
53.practice:
Verse 2 is the one to keep, and it is unusually plain about what wealth means here. Horse, cow, barley — movement, milk, grain. Not gold, not land, not rank. The Ṛgveda's *rayi* is repeatedly this: the things that keep a household running from one season into the next. When a Hindu today prays for prosperity in a pūjā saṅkalpa, the older content of the word is exactly this list, and it is worth knowing that the tradition's first vocabulary for wealth is a vocabulary of livelihood.

The same verse gives Indra a title that is ordinary Sanskrit for friendship: *sakhā sakhibhyaḥ*, a friend to friends. The phrase occurs seven times in the whole Ṛgveda, and two of the seven are here and at [[1.75]].4, where it is said of Agni instead. Two different gods, the same formula. What both hymns are doing with it is refusing a purely hierarchical relation — the god is being addressed as one of a set that includes the worshipper.

The first verse is a standard, and it should be read as one. *Na duṣṭutir draviṇodeṣu śasyate* — poorly made praise is not commended among the givers. The Ṛgveda repeatedly assumes that a hymn can be well or badly made, and that the difference matters to its addressee. This is the ground of the whole Vedic discipline of exact recitation: not superstition about sound, but the older conviction that an offering made carelessly is a different offering. A reader who wonders why the tradition spent three thousand years on accent and metre has the reason in this line.

The last verse is the practical one. After a hymn full of forts and kings, what is asked is *drāghīya āyuḥ prataraṃ dadhānāḥ* — holding a longer life that carries further — and the standing that lets one keep praising. The Ṛgveda's requests are almost always for continuation rather than for conquest, even in its most warlike hymns, and this verse is where the seam shows.
53.disagreements:
The word repeated three times in verse 2, *duraḥ*, is unsettled. Both translators take it as "giver" — Wilson's "giver of horses, of cattle, of barley", Griffith's the same. The stem is more naturally the door or opening, which would make Indra the aperture through which these come rather than the hand that hands them over. The morphology supports either; the hymn does not decide.

Sāyaṇa's contribution here is mostly onomastic and cautious. He identifies Namuci in verse 7 as an asura and a Dānava, descendant of Danu; Vaṅgṛda in verse 8 as an asura and Ṛjiśvan as a king; and on the great numbers of verse 9 he offers only a guess, that the reference may be to Āyus, son of Purūravas. On verse 6's *daśa sahasrāṇi vṛtrāṇi* he takes *vṛtra* in its plain sense of coverings or obstructions, *āvarakāni* — which supports reading the name itself as descriptive.

Verse 1 divides the two translations at its simile. Wilson, following Sāyaṇa, supplies a thief: Indra has quickly taken wealth "as a thief carries off the property of the sleeping". Griffith reverses the sense entirely — "he hath ne'er found wealth in those who seem to sleep" — making the sleepers the negligent worshippers rather than the victims.

54.title: Do Not Set Us in This Fight — Indra Asked, Then Sung
54.synthesis:
The hymn begins with a refusal, which is rare. *Mā no asmin maghavan pṛtsu aṃhasi* — do not set us, Maghavan, in this narrow place, in these battles; for the far end of your force is not to be reached. And then, as though to show what that unreachable force looks like, the same verse remembers the rivers made to roar and the woods bellowing, and asks how the settlements did not huddle together in fear. The opening move of the sūkta is to ask {{indra}} not to bring his strength near, and then to describe it.

Two verses answer that fear with singing, and both begin with the same imperative. *Arca* — sing to the acting one, the strong, the one whose *śacī*, whose effective skill, is his own; magnify Indra who listens. *Arca* again — sing a strengthening word to great Dyaus, whose bold mind holds its own dominion; the *asura* of great renown, made forceful, drawn by two tawny horses. Told not to be afraid, the hymn does not argue; it starts to chant.

Then the deeds, which are the reason the first verse was afraid. The fourth: you shook the ridge of the high heaven and by your own resolve split {{śambara}} through, when, bold with the exhilarating drink, you fought with a sharpened bolt against the banded wielders of *māyā*. The fifth: when you press down on the head of the blowing wind and on the roaring woods of {{śuṣṇa}} — who then, with a mind set forward and full of force, could hold you back from doing today what you did before? The sixth is the roll of names: you helped Narya, Turvaśa, Yadu, Turvīti son of Vayya; you helped horse and chariot in the decisive stake; you broke down ninety-nine forts.

The seventh turns from war to a household, and this is the hymn's hinge. That man becomes a king and a lord of the good, and his people thrive, who gives his offering freely, who sets the recitation going in reply, who welcomes hymns along with his gift — *for him the bounteous rain swells beneath the sky*. Nothing has been said about fighting. What produces rain is a man who both gives and sings.

The eighth measures him against Indra: unequalled is his *kṣatra*, unequalled his *manīṣā*, thought — and may some of these soma-drinkers become his equals by their work, for those who give increase his great, firm, manly power. The ninth is simply the offering held out: these many cups pressed with the stones, seated in the vessels, are Indra's drink — take them, fill your desire with them, and then turn your mind to giving.

The tenth returns once more to the old event, and states it as a physical fact rather than a battle. Darkness stood, the crooked support of the waters; the mountain was within {{vṛtra}}'s belly; and all the rivers that the encloser had held, Indra drove down the slopes one after another. Then the eleventh asks, at last, for what the first verse was really about — not victory but security. Lay on us a glory that increases wellbeing, a great and strong *kṣatra* that overcomes peoples; guard us in our wealth, protect our patrons, and set us in riches with good offspring and food.
54.practice:
The first verse is the honest one, and it is the reason to read this hymn. It asks Indra not to place us in the fight. The Ṛgveda is often read, from outside, as unbroken martial enthusiasm; here the poet's first request of the war-god is to be kept out of a war, and the reason given is not cowardice but proportion — *nahi te antaḥ śavasaḥ parīṇaśe*, the far edge of your force cannot be reached. A power that has no measurable limit is not something to stand next to. That is an observation about the god, not a strategic one.

The second and third verses answer it with an instruction — *arca*, sing — repeated at the head of both. Fear is not argued away. It is given something to do. Anyone who has been taught to chant when frightened rather than to reason themselves out of fear knows this sequence, and it is set out here in three verses.

Verse 7 is the one to sit with. It describes what makes a man prosper, and the description has three parts: he gives his offering freely (*rātahavya*), he answers the recitation, and he greets hymns together with his gift. Not one of them is a military qualification. The reward named is rain — the thing a whole settlement needs and no individual can produce. The Ṛgveda's picture of a good man is here: someone whose generosity and whose praise are the same gesture, and whose reward arrives for everybody.

*Kṣatra* is the word that binds the hymn's two halves and is worth keeping. In verse 8 it is what Indra has beyond comparison; in the last verse it is what is asked for us — *mahi kṣatraṃ janāṣāṭ*, a great *kṣatra* that prevails among peoples. It is the older, wider word behind *kṣatriya*: not a caste but a capacity, the power to hold and protect. The hymn asks for it in the same breath as it asks for food and offspring, which is a fair statement of what it is for.
54.disagreements:
Verse 1 splits the translators at its first word. Wilson reads *mā naḥ ... aṃhasi* as "urge us not to this iniquity, to these iniquitous conflicts" — the poet asking not to be pushed into wrongdoing. Griffith reads *aṃhas* as straits rather than sin: "urge us not to this distressful fight". The word carries both, and the whole tone of the verse turns on which is chosen.

Verse 3 divides them more sharply still. Wilson takes the whole verse as praise of Indra; Griffith addresses it to Dyaus — "Sing forth to lofty Dyaus a strength-bestowing song" — and keeps *asura* as a title of honour, "high glory hath the Asura". Since the Anukramaṇī assigns the sūkta to Indra throughout, Wilson's reading is the traditional one, but the vocabulary of the verse is genuinely Dyaus's.

On verse 5 Wilson, following Sāyaṇa, turns Śuṣṇa into a natural process — the drying, absorbing sun, upon whose head the rain is poured; Griffith keeps Śuṣṇa as a being who "kept confined" the stores. This is the same fork that runs through [[1.32]], where Sāyaṇa reads Vṛtra as accumulated vapour and Griffith as a dragon.

Sāyaṇa's note on verse 6 is genealogical: Turvaśa is likely Turvasu, son of Yayāti, since Yadu, another son of Yayāti, is named beside him; Turvīti he takes for a ṛṣi, and *etaśa* simply as a horse.

55.title: Indra Wider Than Heaven, Whetting the Vajra
55.synthesis:
The hymn opens by trying two measurements and abandoning both. The width of heaven has spread out — and even so, *indraṃ na mahnā pṛthivī cana prati*, not even the earth matches {{indra}} in greatness. Then, having failed to size him, the verse shows him doing something small and precise: *śiśīte vajraṃ tejase na vaṃsagaḥ*, he whets the *vajra* to sharpness the way a bull whets his horns. The unmeasurable thing is caught in the act of getting ready.

The second verse gives him the ocean's behaviour: like the sea, he takes in the rivers that have spread out in every direction — he receives rather than seizes. And then in the same verse he *bulls himself up* for the soma-drinking, and, a fighter from of old, is admired for his force. Taking in and going out, in one breath.

The third verse makes a claim that is easy to read past. *Tvaṃ taṃ indra parvataṃ na bhojase* — you rule over the great manly power's ordinances, and among the gods you are known to exceed by heroism; *viśvasmai ugraḥ karmaṇe purohitaḥ*, the fierce one is set in front for every work. *Purohita*, the one placed in front, is the title given to {{agni}} in the very first line of the collection. Here it is given to Indra, and given for a reason: not for priestly office but because he is the one you put at the head of any difficult undertaking.

The fourth is quieter and more surprising. He is praised *vane*, in the wood, by those who bear *namas*; he proclaims his *indriya*, his own proper power, among the peoples in a manner that is *cāru*, beautiful; he is a bull, and one to be wished for, when the wealthy giver, secure in his protection, sends his speech out. Praise is happening in an ordinary place, out among the trees, not only at an altar.

The fifth verse contains one of the collection's most consequential words. The warrior makes great encounters for the peoples with his force — *adha cana śrad dadhati tviṣīmate indrāya vajraṃ nighanighnate*, and only then do they place their trust in the glittering Indra as he hurls the weapon down. *Śrat* set into place with √dhā: the phrase that becomes *śraddhā*. The hymn says plainly what earns it — people trust him when they have seen him strike.

The sixth turns that force outward for others. Eager for renown, growing on the earth by his force, he destroys the dwellings that were made by craft, makes the lights of heaven shine free of concealment, and — *sukratuḥ*, of good effective power — releases the waters to run for the man who sacrifices. The seventh asks him to turn it toward giving: soma-drinker, let your mind incline to the gift; let the two tawny horses come this way, hearer of praise; your charioteers rein best, and no cunning designs overpower you.

The eighth ends by looking at his hands and his body rather than at the sky. You carry in both hands wealth that is never used up; in your body, famed one, an unconquerable *sahas* is lodged; and your limbs are covered over with *kratu*s, effective powers, *āvṛtāso avatāso na kartṛbhiḥ* — as wells are surrounded by those who draw from them. After eight verses of a god too big to measure, the closing image is people standing round the edge of a well with their vessels.
55.practice:
The fifth verse is where this hymn matters most, and it matters because of one word. *Śrad dadhati* — they place *śrat*, they set their trust — is the phrase from which *śraddhā* comes, the word that later carries an enormous weight: the śraddhā the Gītā says a person is made of, the *śrāddha* rite named from the same root. The construction occurs nineteen times in the Ṛgveda, and this is its first appearance in the order of the collection. What the verse says about it is worth attending to. Trust is placed in Indra *when he hurls the bolt* — after the demonstration, not before it. *Śraddhā* here is not credulity. It is what people extend to a power they have watched act.

The third verse hands Indra the word *purohita*, the one placed in front. That is Agni's title in the first line of [[1.1]], and it is the ordinary Sanskrit word still used for a household's priest. Read against each other, the two uses tell you what the word originally meant: not a rank but a position — whoever goes at the head. Agni goes in front because the offering passes through him; Indra goes in front because he is the one you want ahead of you in a hard undertaking.

The closing image is the one to carry. Indra's limbs are said to be covered with *kratu*s as wells are ringed by those who draw water. *Kratu* is resolve and effective intelligence together — the capacity to determine what to do and to do it — and the picture is not of a hoard but of a source with people standing round it. A well is inexhaustible only in the sense that it keeps giving to whoever comes with a vessel. The hymn has spent seven verses saying that Indra cannot be measured, and ends by saying he can be drawn from.

*Namas* appears in verse 4 in an unexpected place: he is praised *vane*, in the wood, by those bearing *namas*. Reverence in the Ṛgveda is not confined to the enclosure where the fire is laid.
55.disagreements:
Verse 3 is where Wilson and Griffith part most visibly, and Sāyaṇa is the reason. Wilson has "you have not struck the cloud for your own enjoyment", reading a denial that Indra's acts are self-serving; Griffith reads the same words as an act, "so as to bend, as it were, even that famed mountain down". One makes the verse about motive, the other about a mountain.

Sāyaṇa's own notes on this sūkta are brief and technical. At verse 2 he glosses *gṛbhṇāti varīmabhiḥ* two ways without deciding: he grasps by his powers of comprehending, *saṃvaraṇaiḥ*, or by his vastnesses, *urutvaiḥ*. At verse 8 he confirms that the closing comparison is to wells.

Verse 7's *ketāḥ* divides them. Wilson makes them crafty enemies bearing arms who cannot prevail; Griffith makes them Indra's own — "the rapid sunbeams, Indra, lead thee not astray" — turning a line about hostile designs into one about his charioteers.

Verse 4's *vane* is left alone by both, and worth noting for that reason: neither translator explains why Indra is being praised in the wood, and the text does not say.

56.title: Indra Drinks, Then Props the Sky's Support
56.synthesis:
Six verses, and they move in one direction: from a god arriving at a cup to a god holding up the sky. The first verse is the arrival, and its comparison is frank. He has raised himself eagerly toward the many libations held in the vessels *atyo na yoṣām*, as a stallion toward a mare; then he stops his golden chariot with its tawny team and drinks — and what he drinks is called *dakṣam*, the effective skill, *mahe*, for a great work. Even the drinking is described by what it is for.

The second verse is about the people, not the god. The praises and the demands for help come thronging to him as men crowd toward the sea when they are after gain; and they climb him — *girim na venāḥ adhi roha tejasā*, as the loving ones climb a mountain — for he is *patir dakṣasya*, lord of that same effective skill, and the strength of the assembly. The image is deliberately domestic beside the one before it. A god who came like a stallion is approached like a hillside people walk up.

The third verse holds the hymn's clearest picture. He is *turvaṇi*, overpowering, and great, and in manly action his force shines *areṇu*, without dust — *girer bhṛṣṭir na*, like the point of a mountain. A peak is visible from far off precisely because nothing is raised around it; force here is bright because it is unclouded. And with that force, hard to withstand and in his rapture, he brought {{śuṣṇa}} the deceiver to rest in fetters.

The fourth is the strangest and the finest. *Devī yadi taviṣī tvāvṛdhā ūtaye* — when the goddess Strength, made greater by you, attends {{indra}} for help, *uṣasaṃ na sūryaḥ*, as {{sūrya}} attends {{uṣas}}. Strength is feminine here, and she does not obey; she accompanies, in the way the sun accompanies the dawn — always behind her, never separate, arriving because she has arrived. And the verse ends with him beating down the darkness and raising the dust with a great roar.

The fifth and sixth are one act stated twice, and they are the hymn's destination. In the fifth: when across the frame of heaven you set the unshaken *dharuṇa*, the support of the region, firmly in place — then in the light-winning battle, in rapture, exulting, you slew {{vṛtra}} and let the flood of the waters out. In the sixth the same word comes back and the subject changes: *tvaṃ divo dharuṇaṃ dhiṣe ojasā*, you place the support of heaven by your force, and you are the great one in the seats of the earth; gladdened by the pressing, you set the waters running and broke Vṛtra's stony enclosures through and through.

That repetition is the point. The propping of the sky and the killing are not two deeds placed side by side; each verse states them together, in that order, as one motion. The hymn that opened with a horse at a mare ends with the roof of the world staying up.
56.practice:
*Dakṣa* is the thread here, and it is a word worth taking home. It appears in the first verse as what Indra drinks — not merely a drink that pleases, but *dakṣam mahe*, effectiveness for a great work — and in the second as what he is lord of. The tradition's later use holds the same sense: *dakṣa* is competence, the capacity that actually gets something done, and it stands beside *kratu*, resolve, in the Ṛgveda's short list of what a person needs. [[1.2]] ends by asking Mitra and Varuṇa for exactly this, *dakṣam apasam*, skill that works. Here Indra is not asked for it; he consumes it. A god drinking his own competence before acting is a picture of preparation, and the hymn thinks the preparation is worth a whole verse.

The fourth verse carries something the later tradition made central. *Taviṣī*, strength, is a goddess, and she attends Indra as Sūrya attends Uṣas — behind, inseparable, arriving because she has arrived. This is the Ṛgvedic seed of what becomes an entire way of thinking: that a god's power is itself a person, feminine, standing with him and not under him. Anyone who has stood before a mūrti of a god with his śakti beside him is looking at what this verse states in a single comparison.

*Dharuṇa*, in the last two verses, is the word for what holds a thing up — the prop, the support. The hymn's claim is that the same act by which the waters were released is the act by which the sky is kept up: not two divine functions, breaking and upholding, but one. It is the older form of an idea a Hindu meets everywhere later — that the god who destroys is the god who sustains, and that these are descriptions of a single motion rather than a division of labour.

And the second verse offers the plainest instruction in the sūkta about how to approach: the praises go to Indra the way traders go to the sea, and people climb him the way they climb a hill. Both comparisons assume effort on the human side.
56.disagreements:
Sāyaṇa's note on verse 2 is domestic and unexpected. Where the text has the loving ones climbing a mountain, he explains simply that women climb a hill to gather flowers. Wilson prints "as women climb a mountain"; Griffith turns the comparison abstract — "as to a hill, with speed, ascend the loving ones" — and loses the errand.

At verse 3 Sāyaṇa glosses *āyasaḥ*, of metal, as meaning that Indra's body is defended by metal armour, and adds a remark that reaches beyond philology: he takes it as an intimation of Indra as an image, a mūrti. Wilson keeps "clothed in metal armour"; Griffith renders "the iron one".

Verse 4's *devī taviṣī* is handled differently by the two. Griffith keeps Strength as a goddess in her own right — "when Strength the Goddess, made more strong for help by thee" — while Wilson turns her into an attribute, "divine strength waits ... upon that Indra who is made more powerful by you, his worshipper", shifting the increase from the goddess to the god.

On verse 6's *samayā pāṣyā* Sāyaṇa is openly uncertain, taking *sama* as whole or entire and allowing that *pāṣya* may be a stone or possibly a spear. Wilson chooses "a solid rock"; Griffith avoids the question with "Vṛtra's stony fences".

57.title: Indra's Bounty Runs Downhill — Savya's Last Hymn
57.synthesis:
*Pra maṃhiṣṭhāya bṛhate bṛhadraye satyaśuṣmāya tavase matim bhare* — I carry forward a thought to the most liberal, the lofty, rich in loftiness, whose vehemence is true, the strong. The opening line is a chain of titles and one verb; and the comparison that follows tells you how the poet imagines what {{indra}} gives. His *rādhas*, his bounty, is *duṣṭharam*, not to be held back, *apām iva pravaṇe*, like waters down a slope, and it lies open for the whole span of life so that men may have strength. Not a gift handed down but a gradient. Water goes downhill whether or not anyone asks.

The second verse turns the whole world toward the rite: all this shall follow after you for the seeking, and the libations of the man with the offering come like floods to a depth. Then it names the weapon and denies it a rest: when the beloved bolt of Indra, the golden shatterer, lay against the mountain, it did not sleep there. The image is of a weapon on a slope, holding, not yet released — and it is a picture of the moment before [[1.32]].

The third verse hands the offering to someone unexpected. *Asmai bhīmāya namasā sam adhvare uṣo na śubhre ā bhara panīyase* — bring the offering to this fearful and praiseworthy one with *namas* in the rite, O bright one, like {{uṣas}}. Whoever is being addressed is being told to bring it as the dawn brings, and the verse ends by saying what has been made for Indra: his *dhāman* and his name and his *indriya* were fashioned for renown, and light was made *haritaḥ na āyase*, as the tawny mares were made for going. Even his name is described as manufactured for a purpose.

The fourth verse is the plainest in the seven hymns of this poet. *Ime te indra te vayam puruṣṭuta* — these are yours, Indra, and we are yours, much-praised one, we who go about having taken hold of you. There is no other than you, lover of song, who can receive our songs; be pleased with this speech of ours as the earth is with her creatures. The relation is stated twice in one line — *te ... te* — with nothing between the two possessives.

The fifth continues without a break: great is your heroism, Indra, and we are yours; fill the desire of this singer, Maghavan. The high heaven has measured itself against your heroism, and this earth has bowed down to your force. Two enormous things are named only in order to be used as a scale, and the scale is being applied on behalf of one man's request.

The sixth ends the sūkta, and the poet's whole surviving work, with the deed the seven hymns keep returning to. You, wielder of the bolt, cut that broad and massive mountain apart joint by joint; you released the waters that had been held back, to run; and *satrā viśvaṃ dadhiṣe kevalaṃ sahaḥ* — wholly and alone you hold all force, and hold it as your own. The last word of the last hymn is *sahaḥ*, force; but the last claim is *kevalam*, that it belongs to one and to no other.
57.practice:
This is the seventh and last of Savya Āṅgirasa's hymns — his entire surviving work is 1.51 through 1.57, all of it to Indra — and it is tied to the first by a phrase. *Satyaśuṣmāya tavase*, "to him of true vehemence, the strong", stands in the closing verse of [[1.51]] and again in the opening line of this one. The phrase occurs four times in the whole Ṛgveda; two of those four are these two positions. Whether the poet or a later arranger put them there, the seven hymns are held between the same words at both ends, and a reader who begins at [[1.51]] and finishes here hears the ring close.

The image to keep is the first one. Indra's *rādhas* is like water down a slope — *apām iva pravaṇe*. The Ṛgveda has many pictures of divine giving, most of them transactional: the offering goes up, the gift comes down. This one is not transactional at all. Water on a gradient does not decide; it goes where the ground takes it. The same picture returns in the second verse from the human side — the libations of the offerer come "like floods to a depth". Both directions of the rite are described as flow rather than exchange, and the poet plainly liked the picture enough to use it twice in two verses.

The fourth verse is the one for a person rather than for the cosmos. *Ime te indra te vayam* — these are yours, and we are yours. Nothing is asked in that line. It is the sentence that a great deal of later devotional Sanskrit will spend itself elaborating, and it is here in four words, in the middle of a battle hymn, with no elaboration at all.

And the last verse is worth reading for its restraint. After seven hymns of forts broken and rivers freed, the poet's final claim is not that Indra won but that the force is *kevalam*, his own alone. It is a statement about ownership, not about victory — which is the harder and more interesting thing to say.
57.disagreements:
Sāyaṇa's surviving note here is a single sharp gloss on verse 2: the bolt that "did not sleep upon the mountain" means it did not rest against the side of Vṛtra. That converts a landscape into a body, and it is the reading Wilson prints — "the fatal golden thunderbolt did not sleep upon the mountain" understood of the enemy. Griffith keeps the landscape and adds a hesitation: "when the well-loved one seems to rest upon the hill".

Verse 3 divides them over who is being addressed. Wilson makes Uṣas the addressee outright — "Beautiful Uṣas, now present the oblation" — so that the dawn is told to bring the offering. Griffith reads *uṣo na śubhre* as a comparison rather than a vocative: "like bright Dawn, now bring gifts with reverence in this rite". The difference decides whether a goddess is being commanded or a worshipper is being compared to one.

The same verse's close is unsettled in both. Wilson supplies a charioteer driving horses in various directions in quest of sacrificial food; Griffith has Indra's being and light "created, like bay steeds, to move with speed". Neither is confident, and the text gives little to decide with.

Verse 4's closing simile is read two ways: Wilson's earth cherishes her creatures, Griffith's earth loves them. The verb is the same; what changes is whether the relation is maintenance or affection.

58.title: Agni Eats the Forest, and Is Asked for a Shelter
58.synthesis:
Nine verses, and they divide cleanly. Five of them describe a fire that nothing standing or moving can face, and four ask that fire to be a place to hide. The hymn's whole force is in that turn.

It begins with what {{agni}} became. *Nū cit sahojā amṛto ni tundate* — the son of strength, the immortal, does not slacken, since he became *hotā* and the messenger of Vivasvat; by the most effective paths he measured out the *rajas*, the middle region, and with the offering he seeks to serve the gods. The god who carries is introduced by the work of carrying.

The second verse turns to the burning. Undecaying, taking his own food to himself, eager, he moves greedily among the dry sticks; his back gleams like a sprinkled horse's; and he cried out — *divo na sānu stanayan acikradat* — thundering like the height of heaven. In the third he is seated: honoured in front among the {{rudra}}s and the Vasus, set down as *hotā*, conqueror of wealth, immortal; and like a chariot among the settlements, straining toward men, the god delivers what is desirable in due order. The fourth returns to Agni itself with the wind behind it: driven by the wind he spreads through the dry wood at will, with his tongues for sickles, loud-roaring — and when you rush like a bull among the trees, *kṛṣṇaṃ te ema*, your path is black, you of the gleaming wave, you who do not age.

The fifth is the last and worst of them. Flame-toothed, wind-urged, he comes into the wood like a bull that has beaten the herd; advancing with his mass into the unwasting region, *sthātuś caratham bhayate patatriṇaḥ* — the standing and the moving, and the winged, are afraid of him. Everything in three categories, and all of it afraid.

Then the sixth verse, and the hymn changes hands. *Dadhus tvā bhṛgavo mānuṣeṣu* — the Bhṛgus set you among men, *rayiṃ na cārum*, like a beautiful treasure, easy to call, for the peoples: as *hotā*, as *atithi*, the chosen guest, as kindly as a friend, for the divine birth. Agni that everything fled from in the previous verse is now a guest in the house. Nothing explains the transition; the poet simply performs it, and the placement is exact.

The seventh names the office again: the *hotā* whom seven ladles and the priests choose at the rites, the Agni who is the steward of all good things — him I attend with the offering, and I ask him for treasure. The eighth is the request the whole hymn has been building toward: *acchidrā sūno sahaso no adya stotṛbhyo mitramahaḥ śarma yaccha* — son of strength, great as a friend, hold out to your praisers today a *śarman*, a shelter, that has no crack in it; guard the singer from *aṃhas*, from the strait, *pūrbhir āyasībhiḥ*, with forts of metal.

And the ninth: be a *varūtha*, a covering, for the singer, you of wide light; be a shelter, Maghavan, for the generous; guard the singer from the strait. Then the line that will close five more of this poet's hymns: *prātar makṣu dhiyāvasur jagamyāt* — may he who is rich through *dhī* come quickly, early in the morning. Agni that everything on earth ran from is asked, in the last four verses, to be a roof.
58.practice:
The shape of this hymn is its teaching, and it is a shape a Hindu already lives with. Agni that eats the forest and Agni kept in the house are the same Agni. Verses 2 through 5 describe a wildfire — black path, tongues like sickles, everything standing and moving afraid — and verse 6 says the Bhṛgus set that same being among men, *rayiṃ na cārum*, like a lovely treasure, and *atithi*, the guest. The domestic fire is not a tame relative of the wild one. It is the wild one, seated.

That is why the request in verse 8 is worded as it is: *acchidrā śarma*, a shelter without a crack in it, and *pūrbhir āyasībhiḥ*, forts of metal. One asks for shelter of that grade from something one has just seen behave that way. Anyone who has kept a lamp burning in a house through the night, or carried Agni round at a wedding, is handling what these five verses describe.

The last line is the signature of the poet, Nodhas Gautama, and it is worth recognising because it will keep returning. *Prātar makṣu dhiyāvasur jagamyāt* closes this hymn and five more — [[1.60]], [[1.61]], [[1.62]], [[1.63]] and [[1.64]] — six of his seven sūktas in this book. In the whole Ṛgveda the line occurs eight times; six of the eight are here. A reader moving through 1.58 to 1.64 will hear the same closing cadence at the end of hymn after hymn to three different deities, and that repetition is a poet's seal rather than an accident.

The word inside it is the one to carry. *Dhiyāvasu* means one who is wealthy by means of *dhī* — thought, insight, the mind at work. It is the same word that binds [[1.3]] together, where Sarasvatī is called *dhiyāvasu* in the tenth verse. The form occurs ten times in the collection; seven of the ten are in this maṇḍala, and six of those seven are this poet's closing line. What he asks for, at the end of every hymn, is not that the god be rich, but that he come early and be rich in a particular way — by mind.
58.disagreements:
Sāyaṇa reads the first verse cosmologically. Because the firmament stood in darkness and Agni made it visible, he takes *rajo mame* to mean that Agni created, *nirmame*, the middle region — identifying Agni with light and making the measuring an act of making. Wilson prints "he has made the firmament"; Griffith keeps the plainer "on paths most excellent he measured out mid-air".

At verse 2 Sāyaṇa keeps the vocabulary domestic: *adma*, food, he explains as straw and shrubs, *tṛṇagulmādi*, and *atasa* as timber. Both translators follow into "dry wood".

Verse 3's *purohita* he takes as *puraskṛtaḥ*, honoured or placed in front, which lets Wilson write "honoured by the Rudras and the Vasus" where Griffith has "set high in place o'er all that Vasus, Rudras do" — an honour in one reading, a rank in the other.

Verse 9's *maghavan* is the point of most interest, because it is Indra's standing title. Sāyaṇa notes it here as an epithet of Agni in its literal sense, possessor of riches, rather than a slip. Wilson accordingly addresses Agni as Maghavan; Griffith avoids the name entirely and renders "Bounteous Lord".

59.title: Vaiśvānara — Every Other Fire a Branch of Him
59.synthesis:
Seven verses, and the name {{vaiśvānara}} stands in every one of them. That is not ornament. The hymn exists to argue that the many fires burning in many houses are one thing, and it makes the argument by refusing to say anything without the name attached.

The first verse states it outright. *Vayā id agne agnayas te anye* — the other fires, Agni, are your branches; in you all the immortals take their delight. *Vaiśvānara nābhir asi kṣitīnām*, you are the navel of the settlements, and *sthūṇeva janān upamid yayantha*, you have held the peoples up as a prop holds, like a post. Two images in one line, and they are structural: the navel is where a body is joined, and the post is what keeps a roof from coming down.

The second gives him the two ends of the world at once. *Mūrdhā divo nābhiḥ pṛthivyāḥ* — the head of heaven, the navel of earth — and then he became the *arati*, the wheel or the manager, of both. And the verse closes with something the gods did: they engendered you, Vaiśvānara, as *jyotir id āryāya*, light for the man who observes. Agni that joins earth and sky was made, deliberately, for the use of a person keeping a rite.

The third holds the treasure. As fixed rays are set in {{sūrya}}, so goods are set in Vaiśvānara; and then the inventory, which is the widest in the hymn: whatever is in the mountains, in the plants, in the waters, among men — of that you are king. Every place a thing can be hidden, and one owner for all of it.

The fourth is about the singing rather than the god. Heaven and earth are like two great ones for their son; the *hotā*, skilled as a man is skilled, sends many and young songs to Vaiśvānara — to him who has the light, whose vehemence is true, the most manly. That phrase, *satyaśuṣmāya*, is the one that closes [[1.51]] and opens [[1.57]]; here it crosses over from {{indra}} to Agni, one hymn after the seven Indra hymns end.

The fifth is the measurement. Even the high heaven, Jātavedas, has not exceeded your greatness; you are the king of the settlements descended from Manu; and *yudhā devebhyo varivaś cakartha* — by fighting you made room for the gods. That is Indra's work, and the hymn hands it to Agni without comment.

The sixth goes further and says it in Indra's own words. *Pra nu mahitvaṃ vṛṣabhasya vocam* — now I will proclaim the greatness of the bull whom the Pūrus attend as *vṛtrahan*, the Vṛtra-slayer; Agni Vaiśvānara, having killed the {{dasyu}}, shook the boundaries down and split {{śambara}} apart. The epithet, the enemy, the fort: all three belong elsewhere in the collection, and all three are given here to Agni.

The seventh comes back to earth and to a household. Vaiśvānara by his greatness belongs to all peoples, far-shining, to be worshipped among the Bharadvājas; with hundreds of songs Agni, holding true and generous speech, is praised by Purunītha Śātavaneya. The hymn that began with the navel of the settlements ends by naming one family and one man.
59.practice:
*Vaiśvānara* is one of the few Ṛgvedic epithets a Hindu still meets in daily language, and this is its densest hymn. The word occurs sixty times in the whole Ṛgveda; seven of those sixty are here, one in each of seven verses — a concentration matched only twice elsewhere, in the sixth and seventh maṇḍalas. If a reader wants to know what the tradition means by the name, this is where to look.

The name is *viśva* + *nara*: belonging to all men. The first verse says what follows from it — the other fires are *vayāḥ*, branches, of this one. That claim is the reason the word travelled. It reappears in the Gītā, where Kṛṣṇa says *ahaṃ vaiśvānaro bhūtvā prāṇināṃ dehamāśritaḥ*, having become Vaiśvānara I abide in the bodies of the living and digest the fourfold food. The hearth fire, Agni of the rite, and Agni in the belly are being treated as branches of one thing, and the identification is not a later invention laid over the Veda; the Ṛgvedic verse already calls this Agni the navel of the settlements and lists what is in the mountains, the plants and the waters as his.

The second image is worth as much as the first. *Sthūṇeva janān upamid yayantha* — you have held the peoples up as a post holds. A *sthūṇā* is the pillar that carries the ridge-beam of a house. What is being said is not that Agni is grand but that people are standing on him, and would come down without him. It is the least ornamental claim about a god in this stretch of the collection.

Then the fifth and sixth verses do something a reader should notice rather than smooth over. Agni is given Indra's title *vṛtrahan*, Indra's enemy the dasyu, and Indra's fort Śambara. The Ṛgveda does not keep its gods in separate compartments; a god is described by the work he does, and when Agni does Indra's work he is given Indra's names. Anyone puzzled by the later tradition's freedom in identifying one deity with another can see the practice already at work here, seven hymns into a poet's output.
59.disagreements:
Sāyaṇa gives the etymology twice over and keeps both senses: *vaiśvānara* from *viśva* and *nara*, the fire common to all mankind — and, without choosing against it, the natural heat of the stomach. On the first verse's *sthūṇā* he is concrete: a post fixed firmly in the ground that supports the main beam of a house.

His note on verse 2 records a ritual placement that neither translation carries: this verse begins a *tṛca*, a group of three, recited on the day of the equinox. He also leaves *āryāya* open — it may mean Manu, who instituted the first sacrifice, or simply the *yajamāna* of the present rite.

Verse 6 is where he is most interesting and least tidy. He first says flatly that Vaiśvānara here is Indra; then he offers the reading he prefers, that Vaiśvānara is the Agni of the middle region, lightning, from which the terrestrial fire is born when it falls to earth, and from which rain is generated as the burnt offering rises to the sun. He notes separately that a Vaiśvānara appears in the purāṇic accounts as a Dānava. Wilson prints the lightning reading; Griffith translates *pūravaḥ* as "Prarti's sons" and keeps the deity unexplained.

At verse 7 Sāyaṇa allows *bharadvājeṣu* to be either sacrifices offering nourishing oblations or the Bharadvāja ṛṣis. Wilson prints the first, Griffith the second.

60.title: Mātariśvan Brings Agni to Bhṛgu — Twice-Born
60.synthesis:
Five verses, and the first of them is a delivery. *Bharad bhṛgave mātariśvā* — Mātariśvan brought him to Bhṛgu: the *vahni*, the one who conveys; glorious; *vidathasya ketum*, the banner of the assembly; a good protector; the messenger whose errand is done the same day; and — the word this hymn is remembered for — *dvijanmānam*, of two births, *rayim iva praśastam*, praised like a treasure, *rātim*, a gift. {{agni}} does not appear here; he is handed over.

The second verse says who serves him and adds a detail about the hour. Both kinds attend this ruler's command — the *uśijaḥ*, those who long, and the mortals who bring the offering. And then: *divaś cit pūrvo ni asādi hotā* — earlier even than the day he was seated as *hotā*, the one to be consulted, lord of the settlements, the ordainer among the peoples. He is in place before there is light to see him by.

The third is the most inward verse in the sūkta. May our newest good praise reach him as he is being born — *hṛdo ā jāyamānam*, born out of the heart — the honey-tongued one, whom the *ṛtvij*s, the men descended from Manu, bringing their offerings, engender in the enclosure. Two births are being described in the same breath: he is kindled out of the wood by human hands, and he is born out of the heart of the man who praises him. Neither is presented as a figure for the other.

The fourth is the household verse. *Uśik pāvako vasur mānuṣeṣu* — longing, purifying, good, choiceworthy, he has been set among men as the *hotā* in the settlements; *damūnā*, at home in the house, and *gṛhapatiḥ*, master of the house, may Agni be in the dwelling — *rayipatī rayīṇām*, lord of riches over riches. A god who was carried in from outside in the first verse now owns the house he was carried into.

Between those two verses the hymn has quietly changed the terms of the relationship three times, and it is worth counting them. In the first verse Agni is an object carried and given. In the third he is an event that happens inside a person praising. In the fourth he is the owner of the building. Nothing in the sūkta announces these shifts; they simply happen in order, one verse apart, and the effect is that a reader who started out watching a delivery arrive finds by the fourth verse that the recipient has become the host.

The fifth is the Gotamas signing their work. We, of Gotama's line, praise you with our thoughts as the lord of riches, *āśuṃ na vājam-bharam marjayantaḥ* — grooming you, the prize-bearer, as one rubs down a swift horse. And then the poet's closing line, which will end five more of his hymns: *prātar makṣu dhiyāvasur jagamyāt*, may he who is rich by *dhī* come quickly, early in the morning. The last picture in a hymn about carrying, birth and lordship is a man's hands on an animal's back before dawn.
60.practice:
*Dvijanman*, twice-born, appears exactly once in the whole Ṛgveda — in the first verse of this hymn, of Agni. That single occurrence is worth knowing, because the word is the *dvija* of the upanayana, born once of parents and again of the veda. Its first use is not about a human being at all. It is about fire, and the two births in question are read in two ways in the tradition: from heaven and earth, or from the two *araṇi*s, Agni-drills rubbed together to produce a flame. Whichever is meant, the pattern is set here — a second birth is one that comes about through a rite performed by others.

The third verse gives a third birth and does not rank it: *hṛdo ā jāyamānam*, born out of the heart. The *ṛtvij*s, it says, engender him. The word *ṛtvij* is *ṛtu* + √yaj, one who sacrifices at the right season, and it is the word every saṅkalpa still turns on. Here the men who act at the right time are described as generating the god, which is a bold sentence, and the hymn lets it stand.

The fourth verse names Agni *gṛhapati*, master of the house — a title that occurs twelve times in the collection and that has never left Hindu usage. The *gārhapatya*, the householder's fire, is named from it; the man who maintains it is the *gṛhapati*; the word is still used for the head of a household in ritual contexts. This verse is where a reader can see why the household fire is the one that must not go out: Agni is not the householder's property but the householder of the house.

The closing line of the fifth verse is the poet's signature, shared with [[1.58]] and four hymns after it; the word inside it, *dhiyāvasu*, wealthy by thought, is the same word given to Sarasvatī at [[1.3]].10.

The last image is the practical one. The Gotamas say they groom Agni as one rubs down a fast horse before the race. Praise here is described as physical work done on the god — currying, preparing, making him fit to run. It is a corrective to the idea that praise is a report of feeling. In this hymn it is maintenance.
60.disagreements:
*Dvijanman* draws Sāyaṇa's only real hesitation here, and he keeps both readings: born of heaven and earth, or born of the two pieces of wood. Neither translator chooses either — Wilson prints "the offspring of two parents", Griffith "child of two births", both leaving the question where the text leaves it.

The word *rāti* in the same verse divides them further. Sāyaṇa allows it to be Agni as the gift brought to Bhṛgu, or as the friend — noting the negative *arāti*, one who is not a friend, as the ground for the second. Wilson takes the friendship reading, "brought as a friend to Bhṛgu"; Griffith takes the gift, "as a gift, the glorious Priest".

Verse 2 gets Sāyaṇa's most specific ritual note, and it explains the phrase about earliness: the priests conduct the *yajamāna* to the place where the fire has been prepared by the adhvaryu before daybreak. He also reads *ubhayāsaḥ*, "both", two ways — gods and men, or the officiating priests and their employer.

On verse 3 he glosses the birth from the heart physiologically: Agni is generated from air, and that air is the vital breath, so he is produced in the interior of the body. He also takes *vṛjane* as meaning in battle, the offerings being made to secure success — where both translators keep the sacrificial enclosure.

At verse 5 Sāyaṇa expands the bare verb "rubbing" into the sweeping of the fire-altar, and offers the comparison with a rider who rubs down a horse's back before mounting.

61.title: For Him, For Him — Nodhas Builds Indra a Hymn
61.synthesis:
Sixteen verses, and fifteen of them begin the same way: *asmā id u* or *asya id u* — to him, of him. To him I offer, of him I proclaim, for him Tvaṣṭṛ forged. The hymn is held together by a pointing finger that never lowers, and only the last verse breaks the pattern, to name the singers.

The first five verses are about making the hymn, and each gives a different picture of what making it is like. In the first, praise is set out as food is set out: *prayo na harmi stomam*, I present the *stoma* as one presents a meal to {{indra}} who is strong, swift, unstoppable. In the second, the praise is aimed — a shout meant to press hard on an adversary — and is offered *hṛdā manasā manīṣā*, with heart, with mind, with understanding, while others polish their {{dhī}}s for the ancient lord. The third has him bringing it out with his mouth. The fourth is the one that has stayed in the tradition: *stomaṃ saṃ hinomi rathaṃ na taṣṭeva* — I put a praise together the way a wright puts together a chariot for the man who needs it. The fifth changes the craft: I anoint the song *saptim iva*, as one grooms a racehorse, out of desire for renown.

Then the deeds. The sixth: for him Tvaṣṭṛ fashioned the *vajra*, most skilfully wrought, heavenly, for the fight, with which the holder of much found {{vṛtra}}'s vital part. The seventh is the collection's densest verse in this range: having drunk the great draught at his mother's pressings, {{viṣṇu}} stole the cooked food, and the archer shot the boar clean through the mountain. Three obscure things happen in three lines, and the hymn does not slow down. The eighth: for him even the *gnāḥ*, the wives of the gods, wove a song at the killing of the *ahi*; he encompassed heaven and earth, and the two of them together do not exceed his greatness.

The ninth and tenth do the measuring. His greatness exceeds earth, sky and the middle region; self-ruling, praised by all, he grew great in his own house for the battle. And by that same force he cut Vṛtra apart with the bolt and *released the rivers as one releases penned cattle*, of one mind with the giver. The eleventh has the rivers already running: at his flashing they played, once he had encircled them with the bolt — and, making a lord of the man who gave, the swift one made a ford for Turvīti.

The twelfth is the hymn's most physical line and its most disquieting: hurl the bolt at this Vṛtra, and *gor na parva vi rada*, split his joints apart as one splits the joints of an ox, so that the floods of the waters may go. The thirteenth then asks for the old deeds to be told *navyaḥ ukthaiḥ*, with new hymns — the hymn is aware that it is doing this. The fourteenth is where the poet appears: through fear of him the firm mountains and heaven and earth shake at his coming — and may Nodhas, praising again and again the help of that dear one, quickly have heroic strength. He names himself in the middle of the sentence about fear.

The fifteenth records a contest: Indra helped Etaśa, the presser, when he strove with {{sūrya}} in the matter of Svaśva's horses. And the sixteenth closes the pattern by breaking it. *Evā te hāriyojana suvṛkti indra brahmāṇi gotamāso akran* — thus, yoker of the tawny pair, the Gotamas have made these *brahman*s for you; set among them a thought fitted with every ornament. And then the line that ends five more of this poet's hymns: may he who is rich by *dhī* come quickly, early in the morning.
61.practice:
This is the hymn to read when the question is what the Ṛgveda thinks a hymn is. Five consecutive verses answer it with five images, and all five are trades. Praise is food set before a guest. Praise is a shout aimed at an opponent. Praise is spoken out with the mouth. Praise is *rathaṃ na taṣṭeva*, a chariot built by a wright for a man who needs one. Praise is a racehorse groomed for a prize. The verb in the fourth of these is √takṣ, to hew or fashion — the root behind *takṣan*, carpenter, and *takṣaśilā*. The same poet uses it again at the end of [[1.62]]: *navyam atakṣad brahma*, he fashioned a new *brahman*. A hymn is a manufactured article, made to specification, for a purpose, by someone with a skill.

That is a workable idea for a person who recites without composing. It says that the thing in one's mouth was built, that it was built well, and that its quality is part of the offering. It also explains why the tradition guards the text to the syllable: one does not improve a chariot by loosening its joints.

The thirteenth verse states the paradox the hymn lives inside. *Pra brūhi pūrvyāṇi ... navyaḥ ukthaiḥ* — proclaim the ancient deeds with new hymns. The deeds do not change; the hymns are made fresh. That is exactly the relation a reciter today stands in: the words are three thousand years old and the saying of them is happening now, this morning, for the first time.

And the fourteenth verse has something rarer. The poet gives his own name, Nodhas, inside the verse about everything shaking with fear of Indra. The Ṛgveda's poets are not anonymous and did not wish to be; they sign their work, usually near the end, and the signature is part of the offering rather than a claim on it.

One verse to hold lightly and not smooth over: the twelfth, which asks Indra to cut Vṛtra's joints as a butcher cuts an ox's. The tradition kept it. It is a war hymn, and it does not soften what it is asking for.
61.disagreements:
Verse 7 is the hardest in the hymn and Sāyaṇa's reading is the most elaborate note in this stretch of his commentary. He takes *viṣṇu* as an epithet of Indra, the pervader of the whole world, and *varāha*, the boar, as the cloud. He then supplies a legend: Viṣṇu as the personified sacrifice carried off the asuras' wealth and hid behind seven difficult passes — or the seven days of initiatory preparation — which Indra crossed and pierced. He cites the Taittirīya version in which the boar keeps the asuras' treasure beyond seven hills, and Indra takes up a tuft of darbha grass, splits the hills and kills him. Griffith keeps Viṣṇu as Viṣṇu and lets "One stronger" do the shooting; Wilson follows Sāyaṇa and makes the whole verse Indra's.

At verse 8 Sāyaṇa identifies the *gnāḥ*, the wives of the gods, as the personified Gāyatrī and the other metres — deriving *gnā* from a root of motion, females whose nature is to move. Neither translator carries this; both keep "the wives of the gods" or "the Dames".

Verse 12's simile Sāyaṇa expands rather than softens: as the carvers of flesh in this world divide the limbs of animals, so the joints of Vṛtra. Wilson prints the butchers; Griffith leaves the ox and drops the trade.

On verse 15 he gives the only account of Etaśa's race — a king Svaśva who worshipped Sūrya for a son, a dispute between that son and the ṛṣi Etaśa, and Indra taking Etaśa's side.

62.title: Saramā Finds the Cattle; Then Six Verses on 'Of Old'
62.synthesis:
The hymn has two halves and you can hear the join. The first six verses look back at one event; the last six all begin with the same word for antiquity, and turn that event into a claim about how old the friendship is.

It opens by naming its model. *Pra manmahe śavasānāya śūṣam āṅgūṣaṃ girvaṇase aṅgirasvat* — we think out a strengthening shout for the mighty one, in the manner of {{aṅgiras}}. The second verse tells the priests to bring the great *namas* and *āṅgūṣyaṃ sāma*, a chant fit to be sung aloud — *the very chant by which our forefathers, the Aṅgirasas, singing, and knowing the tracks, found the cattle*. The hymn is not describing an old rescue. It is claiming to be performing the piece of music that accomplished it.

The third verse is the rescue itself, in four clauses and no ornament. When {{indra}} and the Aṅgirasas made their search, Saramā found sustenance for her offspring; Bṛhaspati split the rock and found the cows; and the men shouted together with the cattle. The fourth fills in the searchers: with the well-shouting and the shouting, with seven singers, with the Navagvas and the Daśagvas, with a roar, you tore the rock and split {{vala}} open. The fifth widens the outcome enormously: praised by the Aṅgirasas, you uncovered the darkness *with {{uṣas}}, with {{sūrya}}, with the cattle* — the dawn, the sun and the recovered herd all released by one act; and you spread out the earth's high ground and propped up the region beneath the sky. The sixth names the deed the poet considers finest: near where heaven bends down, he filled four rivers full of sweet water.

Then the second half begins, and six consecutive verses open on the syllable *sanā-*, from of old. The seventh has him parting the twinned pair, born together, ever united — heaven and earth — and holding them apart like Bhaga in the highest vault. The eighth: from of old the two young women of unlike colour, born again and again, travel round earth and heaven by their own courses, one anointed with black limbs, the other with shining — night and dawn, alternating. The ninth: from of old the son, skilled in work, has held his friendship by force; and *you put ripe milk inside the raw cows*, white inside the black and the red. The tenth: from of old the kindred streams, unresting, keep the *vrata*s with their strengths, and, like wives to husbands, the sisters serve him. The eleventh: from of old, seeking wealth with *namas* and with new songs, our thoughts have run to you; *patiṃ na patnīr uśatīr uśantam*, as loving wives cleave to a loving husband, so our understandings touch you. The twelfth: from of old the riches in your hand have neither wasted nor run out; you are bright, possessed of *kratu*, steady — help us with your skills.

The thirteenth ends it and, in ending, states the paradox the second half has been circling. *Sanāyate gotama indra navyam atakṣad brahma* — for the ancient one, Gotama fashioned a new *brahman*; Nodhas made it, for the yoker of tawny horses, our sure guide. And then the closing line that seals five more of this poet's hymns: may he who is rich by *dhī* come quickly, early in the morning.
62.practice:
The two halves of this hymn are two ways of being old, and the difference is the thing to take away. The first half is memory: a specific search, specific searchers, a rock split, cattle brought back. The second half is not memory but continuity — six verses each beginning "from of old", about night and dawn still alternating, rivers still keeping their courses, milk still white inside a black cow, and wealth in a hand that has not run out. The event is finished; the ordinance is not.

This is what the tradition means when it distinguishes what happened once from what holds always, and a Hindu meets both in the same rite. The saṅkalpa recites a lineage and a date. The mantra it introduces is said to be without a date. This hymn puts the two side by side and lets the second half absorb the first.

The last verse states the position exactly: *sanāyate ... navyam atakṣad brahma* — for the ancient one, a new *brahman* was fashioned. Not a new god, not a new claim; a newly built utterance for an addressee who has not changed. That is a working description of every hymn ever composed inside a living tradition, and of what a person does who takes up an old text this morning with their own attention.

The third verse holds a figure worth knowing. Saramā, sent ahead in the search, finds sustenance *tanayāya*, for her offspring — the errand and the reward are stated in the same line. The tradition keeps her as the hound of the gods and the ancestress of dogs, and she reappears in the Aṅgirasa story wherever it is told, including in [[1.72]].8 of this same book, where it is she who finds the firm-built pen. What the Ṛgveda gives her is the finding, and it never gives it to Indra.

One phrase from the eleventh verse travels forward. *Uśatīr uśantam*, the loving ones toward the loving one, occurs three times in the whole collection; two of the three are here and in the opening line of [[1.71]], a hymn to Agni by a different poet ten sūktas later. Whichever way the borrowing ran, the same picture of approach — desire meeting desire, not petition meeting power — was in use across two poets in this book.
62.disagreements:
Sāyaṇa's fullest note here is on the Aṅgirasas of verse 4. He takes the seven *vipras* to be Medhātithi and other ṛṣis of the Aṅgiras line, and the Navagvas and Daśagvas to be those who conduct sacrifices for nine months and for ten. On *phaligam* he keeps two senses, that which yields fruit and a cloud; *adri* he glosses both as the mountain and as that which is to be split by the bolt; and *vala* as cloud in one reading and an asura in another. The two translations follow the fork exactly — Wilson's "divisible fructifying cloud", Griffith's "obstructive Vala".

At verse 2 he identifies *āṅgūṣyaṃ sāma* as a chant fit to be sung aloud, such as the Rathantara, and adds the definition that a *sāman* is the singing of a ṛc. Wilson prints the technical sense, Griffith only "a chant with praise".
