Verse 3 divides them over Bṛhaspati. Sāyaṇa reads him as Indra himself, lord of the great ones, and Wilson's rendering makes Bṛhaspati "slay the devourer"; Griffith keeps Bṛhaspati as a separate god who cleaves the mountain.

At verse 10 Sāyaṇa takes the *avanīs* not as rivers but as the fingers, the sisters who work at the pressing, and Wilson prints "fingers". Griffith keeps them as paths. The same choice governs the opening line of [[1.71]], where the flames and the fingers are again both available.

63.title: You, and You — Indra for Kutsa, Purukutsa, Sudās
63.synthesis:
Nine verses, and eight of them begin by pointing: *tvam*, you. Four consecutive verses in the middle open with the same three words, *tvaṃ ha tyat*, you indeed that — as though the poet were laying down one instance after another with the same gesture of the hand. It is the plainest structure in this poet's work.

The first verse is a birth and its effect. You are the great one, {{indra}}, who, being born, terrified heaven and earth with your vehemences; and through fear of you all the mountains, firm as they are, and the monstrous things, shook like specks of dust. Nothing has been done yet; the being has merely arrived.

The second verse gives him a weapon, and gives it in a startling way. When you draw your two tawny horses this way, *ā te vajraṃ jaritā bāhvor dhāt* — the singer places the bolt in your arms. Not Tvaṣṭṛ, who forges it in [[1.61]].6, but the man singing. With it, you of undesired resolve, invoked by many, you drive down enemies and many forts.

The third names the beneficiary the hymn cares most about: you are the true one, the daring, the *ṛbhukṣā*, lord of the Ṛbhus, manly, the overcomer — and at his side, in the close and hard-pressed fight, you killed {{śuṣṇa}} for young and shining {{kutsa}}. The fourth: as a friend you urged that on, when, wielder of the bolt, of bull-like work, you crushed {{vṛtra}}; and when, great-souled hero, you tore the {{dasyu}}s apart far off in their own place, conquering easily. The fifth turns from the past to the present need: you do this and take no hurt from it, even in the anger of the firmest of mortals — so open the running-ground for our horses, and strike our enemies down as with a club. The sixth places him where he is actually wanted: men call on you in the seizing of waters, in the light-winning contest, in the fray; may this help of yours, self-sustaining one, always be the thing sought after in trials of strength.

The seventh is the verse of names. Fighting for Purukutsa you broke the seven forts; for Sudās you tore them *barhir na*, as easily as one strews the sacred grass; and out of a strait, O king, you made room for Pūru. Three men, three deeds, one line each, and the middle comparison — breaking forts as easily as laying out grass for a rite — is the hymn's coolest moment.

The eighth changes the request entirely. Divine Indra, swell for us that bright *iṣ*, nourishment, as you swell the waters all around — the nourishment by which, hero, you extend to us the strength that flows out on every side. After seven verses of forts, the eighth asks for food, and the image for food is water rising.

The ninth is the Gotamas' signature: praises have been made for you by the Gotamas, *brahmāṇi* uttered with *namas*, for you and the tawny pair; bring us a well-shaped {{vāja}}, the prize. And then the closing line this poet uses six times over: may he who is rich by *dhī* come quickly, early in the morning.
63.practice:
The second verse is the one that repays sitting with. *Ā te vajraṃ jaritā bāhvor dhāt* — the singer places the bolt in your arms. Elsewhere in this same poet's work the *vajra* is forged by Tvaṣṭṛ, the artificer of the gods ([[1.61]].6). Here it is handed over by the man doing the praising. The Ṛgveda does not treat these as competing accounts; it says both, ten verses apart, and lets the reader hold them. What the second says is that praise is not commentary on the god's power but part of its arming. Anyone who has been asked why recitation should matter to a deity who lacks nothing has a Vedic answer here, and it is not a comfortable or a modest one.

The seventh verse names Sudās, and that name is worth recognising because it carries a great deal elsewhere. Sudās is the king of the Battle of the Ten Kings in the seventh maṇḍala, one of the very few historical-seeming events the Ṛgveda records. Here he appears in a single line, receiving help, with no story attached — which is how most of the Ṛgveda's persons appear. The tradition remembered names long after it stopped explaining them.

Kutsa is named in the third verse, and he is named again at [[1.51]].6 and [[1.53]].10 in this same stretch of the book. He is not the poet of any of these hymns; he is the man on whose behalf Śuṣṇa is killed, over and over, by different poets. A reader working through maṇḍala 1 will meet him repeatedly in that one role.

The eighth verse is where the hymn touches an ordinary want. After the forts and the kings, what is asked for is *iṣ*, nourishment, and the verb is *pīpayaḥ*, make it swell — the word used of udders filling and rivers rising. Abundance in the Ṛgveda is almost never counted; it is described as swelling. That is a different picture of enough from the one most of us carry, and it is worth noticing what it implies: not a quantity reached, but a thing still filling.
63.disagreements:
Sāyaṇa reads the dasyus of verse 4 narrowly and locally: they are the enemies of Kutsa, *kutsasyopakṣayitāraḥ*, those who were destroying him — which ties the word here to a particular quarrel rather than to a class. Griffith keeps them general, "the Dasyus in their distant dwelling".

At verse 3 he glosses *ṛbhukṣā* two ways: lord of the Ṛbhus, or the one who dwells among them — and he defines *ṛbhu* itself as *medhāvin*, a wise man. Wilson takes "chief of the Ṛbhus"; Griffith the same, without the second sense.

Verse 2's *aviharyatakratu* he explains as one whose acts are undesired by his foes. Wilson turns this into "accomplisher of undesired acts", which reads oddly in English; Griffith gives "in will resistless", which loses the enemies but keeps the sense.

Verse 7 is where the two translations diverge most. Sāyaṇa takes *aṃhoḥ* as the name of an asura, and Wilson accordingly has Indra cutting off "wealth of Aṅhas" for Sudās as if it were a tuft of grass. Griffith reads the same word as the ordinary noun for a strait — "out of need, King, broughtest gain to Puru" — which makes the line about deliverance rather than plunder. The morphology allows both, and the choice changes whether a person or a predicament is being named.

64.title: The Maruts, Rudra's Sons, Milking the Sky's Udder
64.synthesis:
The poet begins by naming himself and by describing his own labour. *Vṛṣṇe śardhāya sumakhāya vedhase nodhaḥ suvṛktiṃ pra bhara marudbhyaḥ* — Nodhas, bring forward a well-turned praise for the bull-like troop, the ordainers, for the {{marut}}s. And then: *apo na dhīro manasā suhastyaḥ giraḥ sam añje* — I anoint my songs as a skilled and deft-handed man handles the waters, songs that come to be present at the rites. Making a hymn is put beside handling water with clean hands.

The second verse is their birth certificate. They were born from Dyaus, the lofty bulls; the *maryas*, the young men, of {{rudra}}; *asurāḥ*, lords; *arepasaḥ*, without a stain; purifying, bright, *sūryā iva*, like suns — and, in the same breath, *ghoravarpasaḥ*, of terrible form. Spotless and terrifying at once, and the hymn will not choose between the two. The third: young, ageless, striking down the one who does not give, they have grown *adhrigāvaḥ parvatā iva*, unstoppable as mountains, and by their greatness they shake every settled thing on earth and in heaven.

The fourth dresses them. They anoint themselves with bright ornaments for beauty; they have fixed gold discs on their chests for splendour; the lances on their shoulders grind as they go; and they were born together *svadhayā*, of their own nature, the men of heaven. The fifth is the first of the rain verses and the finest: they make the winds and the lightnings with their strengths — *duhanti ūdhaḥ divyāni*, they milk the heavenly udders — and, ranging round, they swell the earth with milk. The sixth continues the milking and adds a stranger picture: the bountiful Maruts swell the waters with ghee-rich milk; they lead the strong one out *mihe*, for the raining, as one leads a stallion out; and they milk the thundering, unfailing spring.

Then four verses of pure animal comparison, which is what this hymn is chiefly made of. The seventh: buffaloes, wielders of *māyā*, bright-rayed, self-strong as mountains and swift as deer — *mṛgā iva hastinaḥ*, like elephants you devour the woods when you have yoked your strength among the ruddy ones. The eighth: they roar like lions, all-knowing, ornamented as antelopes are dappled, stirring the darkness with their spotted deer and their spears, crowding together, *ahimanyavaḥ*, with the fury of serpents. The ninth: you make heaven and earth resound, glorious in your troop, following men, heroes; and on your chariot-seats, {{marut}}s, a form stands visible — *vidyun na tasthau*, like lightning that has stopped. The tenth: possessing everything, at home with riches, mixed with strengths, loudly singing, unlimited in vehemence, wearing the bull-rings, the archers have laid the arrow on their arms.

The eleventh returns them to the sky: with golden felloes, swelling the rain, they drive up the mountains as things on a road are driven; makers, unwearied, self-moving, shakers of the fixed, the Maruts with their blazing spears. The twelfth is the invocation proper: we call with our cry upon Rudra's son — eager, purifying, and of the woods — and cleave, for prosperity, to the strong *mārutaṃ gaṇam*, the Marut troop.

The last three ask. The thirteenth: the mortal you have helped goes past all men in force; with his horses he wins the prize, with his men the stakes; he attains an enviable *kratu* and thrives. The fourteenth: set upon our patrons a splendid vehemence, unsurpassable in battles, prize-winning, worth praising, known to all — *tokaṃ puṣyema tanayaṃ śataṃ himāḥ*, may we nourish son and grandson for a hundred winters. The fifteenth: set among us firm wealth, full of heroes, withstanding attack, thousandfold, hundredfold, ever swelling — and then the poet's closing line: may he who is rich by *dhī* come quickly, early in the morning.
64.practice:
The Maruts are a *gaṇa*, and this hymn is the best short introduction to what that means. They are never counted, never given individual names here, never addressed singly. They arrive together, dress alike, roar together, and are asked for as a troop — *mārutaṃ gaṇam*, in the twelfth verse. Thirty-one sūktas in the whole Ṛgveda are addressed to them alone, eleven of those in this maṇḍala, and this is Nodhas Gautama's only hymn to them; his six others in this book go to Agni ([[1.58]]–[[1.60]]) and Indra ([[1.61]]–[[1.63]]). The tradition's later fondness for divine hosts rather than solitary gods — the gaṇas of Śiva, the very word *gaṇapati* — has its Vedic ground here.

Their parentage matters. They are *rudrasya maryāḥ*, Rudra's young men, and the epithets given them in the second verse are the ones Rudra keeps: *pāvaka*, purifying; *arepas*, stainless; and *ghoravarpas*, of terrible form, in the same line. A god who is at once purifying and frightening is not a later theological complication. It is stated here in one verse, of Rudra's sons, in the second maṇḍala-one hymn a reader is likely to reach.

The image to keep is the fifth verse: *duhanti ūdhaḥ divyāni*, they milk the heavenly udders. Rain is not poured or sent; it is drawn out, the way milk is drawn out — by hand, patiently, from something living that has to be willing. That single verb governs the whole picture of the monsoon in this hymn, and it explains why the Maruts are described as attendants rather than as rulers of the storm. Milking is service.

The fourteenth verse ends with the formula every Hindu has heard at a blessing: *śataṃ himāḥ*, a hundred winters, with sons and grandsons flourishing. It is one of the oldest well-wishes in the language and is still what is said over a child. Nothing in it has needed updating in three thousand years.
64.disagreements:
Sāyaṇa takes *rudrasya maryāḥ*, literally Rudra's mortals or young men, as necessarily meaning sons, since the Maruts are immortal and are elsewhere called *rudrasya sūnavaḥ*. On the same verse's *satvāno na* he gives a reading neither translator quite accepts: *satvānaḥ* as the troops of beings attendant on Parameśvara — that is, on Śiva. Wilson prints "powerful as evil spirits"; Griffith, "awful of form like giants".

At verse 8 he glosses *pṛṣatībhiḥ* as the spotted deer that are the Maruts' mounts, which both translators keep. The two diverge instead on *piśā iva supiśaḥ*: Wilson makes them graceful as spotted deer, Griffith beauteous as antelopes, and neither is certain what animal is meant.

Verse 11's *āpathyo na* is left unresolved by Sāyaṇa himself. He offers "like that which occurs on the road" and then two expansions — like elephants breaking what is in their way, or like a chariot crushing the sticks and straw beneath it. Wilson chooses the elephants; Griffith chooses neither and gives "like wanderers on the way".

At verse 12 he reads *ṛjīṣiṇam* through the ritual vessel: *ṛjīṣa* is a pan, and in context any sacrificial vessel, so the Maruts are those into whose vessels the soma is poured. Wilson prints this; Griffith renders "impetuous", taking the word from a different root altogether.

71.title: Agni Approached as Wives Approach a Husband
71.synthesis:
The first line is one of the most compressed in the collection, and everything in the hymn grows out of it. *Upa pra jinvann uśatīr uśantam patiṃ na nityaṃ janayaḥ sanīḷāḥ* — the longing ones quickened the longing one, as wives their own husband; sisters of one nest. Who they are is not said. They may be the flames, or the fingers at the kindling, or the ten *dhītis* of the reciter; the grammar allows all three and the hymn does not settle it. And then a second comparison stacked on the first: they welcomed him, the dark one and the ruddy one, *citram ucchantīm uṣasaṃ na gāvaḥ*, as cattle welcome the bright dawn breaking. Desire meeting desire — that is the picture of approach {{agni}} gets here, not petition meeting power.

The second verse goes back to the ancestors. Our fathers, the Aṅgirasas, broke the firm, hard things with their *ukthas*; with a roar they split the rock; they made a path for us to the high heaven — *ahaḥ svar vividuḥ ketum usrāḥ*, they found day, the light of heaven, its banner, and the ruddy cows. The third says what came of it: they set {{ṛta}} in place, they made his *dhīti*, his thought, bear fruit; and from then on the men of substance, holding him distributed among them, thirsting after nothing else, go toward the gods, strengthening the divine birth with their offering.

The fourth is the churning. When Mātariśvan, spread abroad, churned him out, he became bright and noble *gṛhe-gṛhe*, house by house — and then, staying beside as a companion, he went on the errand of a messenger *bhṛgavāṇaḥ*, in the manner of Bhṛgu, as though to a stronger king. The fifth is the hardest verse in the hymn and should be left hard. When he made the sap for the great father, the heaven — the one who had crept close, who knew, was recognised; the archer boldly loosed his shaft at him; and *svāyāṃ devo duhitari tviṣiṃ dhāt*, the god set his brilliance on his own daughter. What is being told here is told nowhere completely, and the text does not explain itself.

The sixth returns to the house and to plain benefit: for whoever kindles you in his own dwelling and gives *namas*, longing, day after day — increase his *vayas*, his vigour, you who are doubled in strength; and may the man you urge on come back with wealth on the same chariot. The seventh gives the picture of everything running to one place: all nourishments attend Agni as the seven great rivers run to the sea; and then, quietly, a domestic grievance — *na jāmibhir vi cikite vayo naḥ*, our vigour was not discerned by our own kinsmen; so you who know, find us regard among the gods.

The eighth is about generation. When brilliance reached the lord of men for the increase, when the pure seed was poured down at the meeting of heaven, Agni brought forth and set going a blameless, youthful, well-intentioned host. The ninth widens once more and names three others: he who goes his road in a single day like thought — {{sūrya}} — is alone lord of the goods; and the two kings {{mitra}} and {{varuṇa}}, with their fair hands, guard the dear immortal thing in the cattle.

Then the tenth, which is why the hymn is remembered. *Mā no agne sakhyā pitryāṇi pra marṣiṣṭhāḥ* — do not forget, Agni, the friendships that come from our fathers, since you are a *kavi* and know them. *Nabho na rūpaṃ jarimā mināti* — old age wears the form away as cloud wears the sky. And then: *purā tasyā abhiśaster adhīhi*, think on me before that ruin arrives. The hymn that began with wives running toward a husband ends with a man asking to be remembered before he is unrecognisable.
71.practice:
The tenth verse is the one to take away, and it is unusually direct about a thing the tradition does not often say out loud. *Jarimā mināti* — ageing diminishes; the form goes the way a shape goes in cloud. There is no consolation offered, no doctrine of the imperishable self applied, no promise about what follows. There is a request: remember the friendships that came down from my fathers, and attend to me *before* that. It is a prayer made by someone who can see what is coming and wants the relationship secured while he is still himself. Anyone caring for an ageing parent, or ageing, has this verse.

What it asks Agni to remember is *sakhyā pitryāṇi*, the friendships of the fathers — not the man's own merit. The claim being made is inherited. That is the logic of every śrāddha and every tarpaṇa a Hindu performs: one stands before Agni in a position established by people who are gone, and the standing is real because the relation was theirs first. This verse is where that logic is stated most plainly in the first maṇḍala.

The opening line has travelled further than the hymn. *Uśatīr uśantam*, the longing ones toward the longing one, occurs three times in the whole Ṛgveda, and one of the other two is in [[1.62]].11, where Nodhas uses the same words of thoughts cleaving to Indra. Two poets, ten sūktas apart, describing approach to a god as mutual wanting rather than as request. Whichever borrowed, the picture was current.

And the second verse states the tradition's own account of why the words matter. The Aṅgirasas split the rock *ukthaiḥ* and *raveṇa* — with recited verses, with a roar — and what they found was not only cattle but *svar* and its banner, the daylight. The Ṛgveda's most repeated origin story is a story about sound doing work. A reader who wonders why recitation was preserved with such ferocity is being told here: the fathers got the light out of the rock by saying something correctly.

The fourth verse gives Agni's ordinary location: *gṛhe-gṛhe*, house by house. Not in one temple, one shrine, one place. In every house separately, and the same fire in each.
71.disagreements:
The opening line's *janayaḥ sanīḷāḥ svasāraḥ* is where the readings part hardest. Wilson, following Sāyaṇa, makes them the fingers of the priest — "the contiguous fingers, loving the affectionate Agni, as wives love their own husbands". Griffith keeps them as the flames themselves, "the sisters of one home". The morphology gives only feminine plurals — wives, of one nest, sisters — and settles nothing. Sāyaṇa reads the same word as fingers at [[1.62]].10, so his choice here is consistent rather than local.

Verse 5 is unresolved in every witness. Sāyaṇa reads a *rākṣas* who creeps up, is recognised and retreats, with Agni shooting an arrow after him, and refers the verse to a Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa passage. Wilson prints that. Griffith reads a different scene entirely — the Father who "knew and freed himself from close embracement", the archer shooting at him, and the god casting his splendour on his daughter — which points toward the account of Prajāpati and his daughter told in the tenth maṇḍala. The Sanskrit supports the sentence but not the story; what happened here is not recoverable from this evidence.

At verse 4 Sāyaṇa gives Mātariśvan as Vāyu and, more narrowly, as the chief vital breath, and cites the Taittirīya legend of the gods entering fire during the war with the asuras and putting Agni in front of them.

Verse 10's close he reads as a request for immortality outright — *amṛtatvaṃ prayacchati yāvat* — where both translators keep the plainer sense, protect me before that ruin comes.

72.title: The Gods Lose Agni and Track Him to His Seat
72.synthesis:
This is a hymn about looking for something, and the verb of finding runs through six of its ten verses. What is lost is {{agni}}; who loses him is the gods; and what they do to get him back is exactly what a human search would be — they get tired, they follow tracks, and eventually somebody spots him.

The first verse sets him up as the holder. Holding in his hand many manly things, he brings the poetic powers of the eternal ordainer to himself; Agni is the lord of riches over riches, having wholly made all immortal things his own. The second begins the search and states its absurdity plainly: *asme vatsaṃ pari santaṃ na vindan* — seeking him, all the immortals, undeluded, did not find the calf who was right there around us. Worn out with effort, tracking, holding their *dhī*s, they stopped at the highest lovely station of Agni.

The third is what they did once they got there: because the pure ones served you, the pure one, with ghee for three autumns, they took to themselves names fit for the sacrifice, and, well-born, they made their bodies sweet. The verse is quietly enormous — the gods acquire their sacrificial names and their bodies by serving Agni for three years. The fourth continues the hunt: making themselves known between the two wide worlds, those fit for worship brought forward the songs belonging to {{rudra}}; and *vidan martaḥ nemadhitā cikitvān* — a mortal, discerning, in the division, found Agni standing in the highest station. A man finds what the gods could not.

The fifth is the finding's aftermath and the hymn's tenderest verse. Of one mind they sat down close to him, on their knees, with their wives, doing *namas* to the one who deserves it; and, having given up their own bodies, they made them theirs again — *sakhā sakhyur nimiṣi rakṣamāṇāḥ*, friend guarding friend in the blink of an eye. The sixth is the hymn's most cited line: when those fit for sacrifice found the thrice seven hidden steps set down in you, with those, of one accord, they guard the immortal — *paśūṃś ca sthātṝṃś carathaṃ ca pāhi*, and you, guard the cattle, the standing and the moving.

The seventh turns the finding outward. Knowing the ways of the settlements, Agni, you set down nourishment in due order for living; knowing between them the paths that the gods travel, you became the tireless messenger, the carrier of the offering. The eighth is the widest verse in the sūkta: the seven great streams from heaven, well-intentioned, *ṛtajñāḥ*, knowers of {{ṛta}}, knew the doors of wealth; and Saramā found the firm-built pen of the cattle, by which the human clan still eats. Rivers finding their doors and a hound finding a pen, in one verse, as two instances of the same thing.

The ninth gives the reason all this searching was worth doing: those who took up all the good works, making a path to immortality — and Aditi, the mother, with her great sons, stood spread out to sustain. The tenth ends with what they did to him once found. They set beautiful splendour on him, and the immortals made the two eyes of heaven; then the rivers run down as if released, and they knew the ruddy ones, Agni, coming down. The hymn that began with a search ends with everything moving again.
72.practice:
The sixth verse is the reason a Hindu should know this hymn. *Triḥ sapta yad guhyāni ... padā* — the thrice seven hidden steps set down in Agni, which those fit for worship found, and by which they guard the immortal. Twenty-one hidden things: the phrase occurs eleven times in the Ṛgveda and it has never been fully explained by anyone. The received traditional account divides the Vedic rites into three classes of seven: the seven *pāka-yajña*s in which cooked food is offered, including the daily *aupāsana* and *vaiśvadeva*; the seven *havir-yajña*s, including *agnyādheya* and the new- and full-moon rites; and the seven *soma-yajña*s, of which the *agniṣṭoma* is first. Twenty-one rites, all of them involving Agni, hidden in the sense that they must be learnt rather than seen. Whether or not that is what the poet meant, it is what the tradition made of it, and it is the reason the verse is quoted whenever the number of the rites is being taught.

The hymn's second verse is worth more than its obscurity suggests. The gods search for Agni and cannot find him *pari santam*, though he is right around them. That is a description of the difficulty of noticing what is everywhere, and the Upaniṣads will spend themselves on it. What this verse adds is a detail those later texts drop: the searchers get tired. *Śramayuvaḥ*, worn with effort, they follow tracks on foot. The Ṛgveda's gods are not spared the work.

And the fourth verse gives it to a human being. *Vidan martaḥ* — a mortal, discerning, found him. After the immortals failed. The Veda does not usually flatter its reciters, and this is not flattery; it is a claim about what attention can do that power cannot.

The eighth verse names Saramā, whose finding of the cattle is told at greater length by another poet at [[1.62]].3, and puts two finders side by side — the seven rivers, who *knew the doors of wealth*, and Saramā, who found the pen. Both are called knowers of *ṛta* or act on its behalf. The hymn's whole theology is in that pairing: what is hidden is found by those who know the order of things, and knowing the order is what makes finding possible.
72.disagreements:
Sāyaṇa's note on verse 6 is the fullest account of *triḥ sapta* in the commentary tradition and the source of the standard teaching. He glosses the *guhyāni padāni* as the secret steps by which heaven is obtained, and enumerates three classes of seven yajñas each — the *pāka-yajña*s such as aupāsana, homa and vaiśvadeva; the *havir-yajña*s such as agnyādheya and darśapūrṇamāsa; and the *soma-yajña*s beginning with agniṣṭoma. Neither translator supplies this; Wilson writes only "the thrice seven mystic rites", Griffith "the thrice-seven mystic things".

At verse 3 he identifies the "pure ones" as the {{marut}}s, connects them with the seven plates placed at the Agnicayana, and draws the conclusion that the Maruts are deified mortals, like the Ṛbhus, who exchanged perishable bodies for immortal ones. Wilson prints the Maruts throughout; Griffith keeps the vaguer "the pure Ones".

Verse 4's *rudriyā* he explains by identifying Rudra with Agni, citing the Taittirīya legend in which Agni carried off the gods' hidden wealth, was pursued, and wept — *arodīt* — and was thereafter called Rudra. He reads *nemadhitā* as the half-share, and reports the rule that Indra takes one half of all sacrifice and the remaining gods the other.

At verse 8 Sāyaṇa supplies Agni as the hidden agent of everything named: the sun fed by offerings sends the rain that fills the rivers, and Indra sent Saramā only because he had been propitiated with oblations in fire. Griffith leaves the verse without an agent.

73.title: Agni Like Wealth, Like a Guest, Like a Faithful Wife
73.synthesis:
The first three verses of this hymn contain twelve comparisons — four in each — and nothing else. No request, no deed, no history. {{agni}} is presented entirely by what he is like, and the comparisons are all drawn from ordinary life, not from the sky.

The first verse: like inherited wealth that gives vigour; like the direction of one who knows, a good guidance; like a guest well seated and pleased; and *hoteva sadma vidhato vi tārīt*, like a *hotā* he extends the house of the man who serves. Property, instruction, hospitality, priesthood — four relations, and Agni stands in all of them.

The second: like the god {{savitṛ}}, whose thought is true, he guards all enclosures with his *kratu*; praised by many; *amatir na satyaḥ*, true as a form is true; and *ātmeva śevaḥ*, kindly as the self is, and to be sought after. The third: like a god who sustains all, he dwells beside the earth; like a king who has good friends about him; men sit before him as heroes sit in a shelter; and *anavadyā patijuṣṭeva nārī*, like a blameless woman cherished by her husband.

Only in the fourth does the hymn stop comparing and describe. Such as you are, Agni, men keep you at home constantly kindled, in settled dwellings, and they have laid abundant *dyumna*, brilliance, upon you. Be for us, you in whom all life is, the holder of riches.

From here the hymn asks and then observes. The fifth: may our patrons obtain nourishments, may our *sūri*s obtain a whole life; may we win the prize in encounters, setting the stranger's portion among the gods for renown. The sixth is the loveliest observation in the sūkta: *ṛtasya hi dhenavo vāvaśānāḥ*, the milk-cows of {{ṛta}}, lowing, with their udders full, apportioned by heaven, have swelled — and the rivers, begging his good will from far off, have run right across to the rock. Two natural facts, rain and river, described as creatures asking.

The seventh: those fit for worship, begging your good will, have set their renown in heaven; and they made night and dawn of unlike form, and joined the black colour and the ruddy together. The eighth is the hymn's most memorable image: may we be those mortals whom you have sped to wealth, and our patrons with us — for *chāyeva viśvaṃ bhuvanaṃ sisakṣi*, you attend the whole world like a shadow, having filled heaven and earth and the middle air.

The ninth is the plain human request, three parallel clauses long: aided by you, Agni, may we overcome horses with horses, men with men, heroes with heroes; may our *sūri*s, lords of what our fathers found, live a hundred winters. The tenth ends where such hymns end: may these *ucthas* of ours be welcome to your mind and to your heart, ordainer; may we be able to hold your well-yoked riches, laying upon you the renown that the gods have apportioned.

The hymn has moved from twelve similes to a hundred winters, and the distance is short. Its argument, if it has one, is that a god best described by household comparisons is the right god to ask about a household's length of days.
73.practice:
This is the last of the nine hymns ascribed to Parāśara Śāktya — [[1.65]] through 1.73, every one of them to Agni — and it is the sūkta to give someone who asks what Agni actually is to a Hindu family, because it answers only by comparison and every comparison is domestic. Inherited wealth. The instruction of someone who knows. A guest, seated and content. A king with loyal friends. A blameless wife cherished by her husband. The self. Not one image comes from the sky, and the god of the rite is described entirely in the vocabulary of a house.

The comparison in the third verse deserves to be read as it stands, because it runs against expectation. Agni is not compared to a husband but to a *wife* — *anavadyā patijuṣṭeva nārī*, a blameless woman dear to her husband. The point of comparison is constancy and welcome, and the hymn is untroubled about applying it to a male deity. The Veda's similes go where the resemblance goes.

The image most worth carrying is in the eighth verse: *chāyeva viśvaṃ bhuvanaṃ sisakṣi*, you attend the whole world like a shadow. A shadow does not lead or push; it accompanies, exactly, and cannot be shaken off. That is a different account of divine presence from either surveillance or protection, and it is the one this hymn chooses after seven verses of intimacy.

The sixth verse gives *ṛta* its most physical form anywhere in this stretch of the book. *Ṛtasya dhenavaḥ* — the milk-cows of ṛta, with full udders, lowing. Ṛta is the order by which things come round on time; here that order is not an abstraction but a herd that has to be milked and that complains when it is not. Anyone who has kept animals knows that a full udder is a deadline. The order of the world, in this verse, has one.

And the last verse says what the hymn wants done with itself: *etā te agne ucathāni ... juṣṭāni santu manase hṛde ca* — may these utterances be welcome to your mind and to your heart. Both are named, separately. The tradition's insistence that a mantra be understood as well as said has this verse behind it.
73.disagreements:
Sāyaṇa's most consequential note is on the second verse's *ātmeva śevaḥ*. He takes *amati* as *rūpa*, the peculiar form or nature of a thing, and reads the *ātman* comparison philosophically: as the self is the seat and source of all happiness, so Agni, the chief agent of the sacrifice, is the cause of felicity here and hereafter — and he cites the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad for it. Wilson prints the reading, "like nature, he is unchangeable, and like soul, is the source of happiness". Griffith takes both words physically instead — "truthful, like splendour ... like breath joy-giving" — which turns a verse about the self into a verse about light and air.

The sixth verse divides them completely. Wilson reads literal cattle who love Agni and bring their milk; Griffith reads *ṛtasya dhenavaḥ* as "the cows of holy law, sent us by Heaven", making them a figure for the rains. The Sanskrit says only that they belong to ṛta, and the two translators have taken that in opposite directions — one toward the byre, the other toward the sky.

Verse 3's fourth simile is likewise split. Wilson supplies a comparison the text does not make, adding "in purity he resembles" before the blameless wife, as though embarrassed; Griffith prints the simile bare, "like as a blameless dame dear to her husband". The padapāṭha supports Griffith here: the comparison stands without qualification.

Sāyaṇa's gloss on verse 1's *pitṛvitta* — found by the fathers — is left implicit by both translations, which give simply "patrimonial".

74.title: A Mantra Spoken on the Way to the Rite — Agni
74.synthesis:
Nine short gāyatrī verses, and the first of them says where the speaker is standing. *Upaprayanto adhvaraṃ mantraṃ vocemāgnaye* — as we go up toward the rite, let us speak a *mantra* to {{agni}}, *āre asme ca śṛṇvate*, who hears both far off and here among us. The hymn is spoken on the way. Not at Agni, not after the offering: while walking toward it. And the first thing said about the god is that distance makes no difference to his hearing.

The second verse gives the reason he is worth addressing, and it is a memory of protection rather than of conquest: he who from of old, when the peoples had clashed together, kept safe the *gaya*, the household and its goods, of the man who gave. The third is what the hymn wants people to say: *uta bruvantu jantavaḥ*, and let the creatures say — Agni has been born, the {{vṛtra}}-slayer, the winner of wealth *raṇe-raṇe*, in fight after fight. Agni is given Indra's own standing epithet here without apology, as he is at [[1.59]].6.

The fourth and fifth describe the household he attends. In whose dwelling you are the messenger, whose offerings you seek out for the eating, whose rite you make wonderful — him, {{aṅgiras}}, son of strength, men call *suhavya*, good in his offering; *sudeva*, well provided with his god; *subarhis*, well laid with grass. Three compounds, all beginning the same way, all describing the same man from three angles: what he gives, whom he has, and how carefully he prepared the place.

The sixth is the errand: bring these gods here, you of fair light, for our praise and for the eating of the offerings. It is the whole business of Agni in one verse, and the hymn spends only one verse on it.

The seventh is the finest thing in the sūkta and one of the quietest images in the collection. *Na yoḥ upabdir aśvyaḥ śṛṇve rathasya kac cana* — no sound of horses is heard, nor any sound of a chariot at all, when you go, Agni, on your errand. Every other divine journey in the Ṛgveda is loud: hooves, wheels, thunder, roaring. This one makes no noise whatever. The god who carries between earth and heaven travels in silence, and the poet noticed.

The eighth records a change in a man's standing. Helped by you, unharmed, the prize-winner who is not shy — *abhi pūrvasmād aparaḥ pra dāśvān agne asthāt* — the later giver has come to stand ahead of the earlier one. Someone who was behind is now in front, and the hymn attributes it to Agni without further comment. The ninth closes by naming what he brings across: and you shine forth to the giver, god, from the gods, a brilliant and lofty *suvīrya*, the strength that consists in good men. The hymn began on a road and ends with what is carried back down it.
74.practice:
The first verse is unusual and useful: the Ṛgveda here calls its own utterance a *mantra*. The word occurs nineteen times in the whole collection, which is remarkably few for a body of text the tradition will later refer to entirely by that name. What this verse tells us is what the word originally described — something spoken, deliberately, on the way to a rite, to a god who hears at any distance. Not a formula with power of its own, but an address made by people in motion.

That setting is the practical gift of this hymn. *Upaprayantaḥ*, going up toward the rite: the speaking begins before the arrival. Anyone who has said something under their breath walking to a temple, or begun a stotra in the car before reaching it, is doing precisely what this verse describes, and the Ṛgveda gives that in-between speech a name and a first line.

The third verse gives Agni the title *vṛtrahan*, the Vṛtra-slayer, which is Indra's above all others', and *dhanaṃjaya*, winner of wealth, in fight after fight. This happens twice in the space of fifteen sūktas — here and at [[1.59]].6. It is worth taking as instruction about how the tradition uses names: an epithet marks the work being done, and the same work done by a different god carries the same title over. A reader who finds the later tradition's identifications between deities bewildering can see the practice starting here.

The seventh verse is the one to keep for its own sake. Agni's journey makes no sound. In a collection full of thundering chariots, roaring winds and shouting hosts, the god who actually makes the connection between a household and the gods travels without being heard at all. Nothing is drawn from this in the hymn; it is simply observed. What can be said is that the tradition's own picture of the most constant divine activity is a silent one, and that Agni on a hearth is exactly what that looks like.

The eighth verse is a small social observation with a long life: the giver who came later now stands ahead of the one who came first. Precedence in the Ṛgveda's world is not fixed by arrival, and generosity is what moves a man up.
74.disagreements:
Sāyaṇa's one surviving note here goes to the heart of the third verse. *Vṛtra*, he says, means an enemy in general — and on that basis he identifies Agni with {{indra}} for the purposes of this verse. That is the traditional way of managing the transferred epithet: not two gods confused but one title earned. Wilson prints the epithet flatly, "the slayer of Vṛtra"; Griffith likewise, "e'en he who slayeth Vrtra", and neither comments on the transfer.

Verse 2's *snīhitīṣu* is genuinely obscure and the translators disagree about what kind of event is meant. Wilson reads a gathering of malevolent men; Griffith reads "in carnage, when the people gathered". The word is rare, and what is preserved from it in both is only that something violent was happening when the peoples came together.

The same verse's *gaya* divides them: Wilson has Agni preserving wealth for the sacrificer, Griffith "his household". Both are within the word's range, and the difference is whether what was saved was property or people.

At verse 8 Wilson supplies a social situation the Sanskrit only implies — a man "formerly subject to a superior" who now stands unashamed and supplied with food. Griffith declines to supply it and gives only "one after other, goes he forth". The comparative in the verse is clear; who is being compared to whom is not.

75.title: Who Is Your Kinsman, Agni? — the Question Answered
75.synthesis:
Five gāyatrī verses, and they are built as a small catechism: two verses of approach, one of questions, one of answers, one of instruction. Nothing in this maṇḍala is tighter.

The first asks {{agni}} to take what is being offered. *Juṣasva saprathastamaṃ vaco devapsarastamam* — accept this word, the most far-reaching, the most delightful to the gods — *havyā juhvāna āsani*, you who pour the offerings in your mouth. The offering and the speech arrive in the same line, and the mouth that takes the one takes the other.

The second names him twice with superlatives and asks for permission to speak. *Atha te aṅgirastama agne vedhastama* — then, most Aṅgiras-like, most ordaining of ordainers, may we speak a dear *brahman* that avails. The two epithets are not decorative. *Aṅgirastama* places him at the head of the line the poets of these hymns claim descent from; *vedhastama* makes him the most competent arranger of the rite. The speaker asks the best practitioner for leave to practise.

Then the third verse, which is why this sūkta is remembered. Three questions in three lines, with no answer offered. *Kas te jāmir janānām agne, ko dāśvadhvaraḥ, ko ha kasminn asi śritaḥ* — who among men is your kinsman, Agni? who is fit to make the offering? who indeed are you, and in whom do you rest? The last question is the one that will occupy the Upaniṣads. It is asked here in three words, in a gāyatrī, and the hymn does not treat it as difficult.

The fourth answers, and it answers only the first question — deliberately, one suspects. *Tvaṃ jāmir janānām agne mitro asi priyaḥ, sakhā sakhibhya īḍyaḥ* — you are the kinsman of men, Agni; you are the dear {{mitra}}; a friend to friends, worthy of praise. Three words for relation in one verse, and they climb: *jāmi*, kin by blood or household; *mitra*, the ally bound by agreement; *sakhā*, the companion one chooses. The question asked who Agni's relative among men might be, and the answer reverses it: he is the relative, of all of them. The two other questions — who is fit to offer, and in whom does Agni rest — are left standing.

The fifth stops asking and gives orders, three of them. *Yajā no mitrāvaruṇā, yajā devān ṛtaṃ bṛhat, agne yakṣi svaṃ damam* — sacrifice for us to {{mitra}} and {{varuṇa}}; sacrifice to the gods, and to the great {{ṛta}}; Agni, offer to your own house. The verb is the same three times and the object widens each time: two named gods, then all the gods with the order of things beside them, and then — smallest and strangest — his own dwelling. The hymn that opened by asking who Agni is closes by telling him to make an offering at home.
75.practice:
This is one of the shortest sūktas in the maṇḍala and one of the most useful, because it does in five verses what a great deal of later Hindu literature does at length: it asks who the god is, and answers in terms of relationship rather than of attributes.

The third and fourth verses should be read together and, if possible, learnt together. *Kas te jāmir janānām* — who is your kinsman among men? *Tvaṃ jāmir janānām* — you are the kinsman of men. The same three words, question and answer, in consecutive verses. *Jāmi* occurs seven times in the whole Ṛgveda and two of those seven are these two lines. What the answer does is refuse the premise: the question looked for one qualified person, and the reply says the relation runs the other way and covers everyone.

The three words for relation in the fourth verse are the practical content. *Jāmi* is kin — given, not chosen. *Mitra* is the ally bound by an agreement, and it is also the name of the god of agreements, so the word is doing double work. *Sakhā* is the companion one keeps by choice; *sakhā sakhibhyaḥ*, friend to friends, occurs seven times in the collection and is used of {{indra}} at [[1.53]].2 in exactly the same form. A Hindu standing before the household fire is being told here that all three kinds of bond are available, and that none of them is the bond of a subject to a ruler.

The fifth verse contains an instruction that repays thought. Agni is told *yakṣi svaṃ damam*, offer to your own house. The one who carries every offering to every god is told to make an offering at home. Whether that means Agni is to sacrifice for its own dwelling, or for the household in which it burns, the two are not clearly separable, and the tradition has never fully separated them: the household fire is the household's, and it is also its own.

And the second verse is worth keeping for its manners. Before saying anything, the poet asks whether he may — *priyaṃ vocema brahma sānasi*, may we speak a dear and availing utterance. The request precedes the speech.
75.disagreements:
This sūkta has no surviving gloss in the Sāyaṇa material available here. That is a gap in this witness and not a statement about the commentator, who wrote on the maṇḍala continuously; readings attributed to him elsewhere in this stretch are simply not recoverable for these five verses from what we hold.

The translators diverge chiefly on verse 4's *mitraḥ*. Wilson takes it as a common noun and expands it into a function — "you are the protector of sacrificers ... since you are the friend of all" — while Griffith keeps it as the ordinary word for friend, "their well beloved Friend art thou". Neither reads it as the god Mitra, though the word is the same and the very next verse addresses Mitra and Varuṇa by name. That juxtaposition is left unexplained by both.

Verse 5 divides them over what *ṛtaṃ bṛhat* is doing. Wilson makes it a description of the rite — "celebrate a great sacrifice" — so that ṛta means the ceremony itself; Griffith takes the phrase as the object of worship alongside the gods, "bring the Gods to mighty sacrifice". Both are inside the word's range, since in this vocabulary the order of things and the correct performance of the rite are not two separate objects.

At verse 3 the two agree on the questions but not their weight. Wilson gives "who indeed are you and where do you abide?" as one question in two parts; Griffith splits it — "On whom dependent? who art thou?" — making dependence the prior issue.

76.title: Four Questions to Agni, Then Sit Down as Hotā
76.synthesis:
Five verses, and the first of them is nothing but questions. Not rhetorical ones — the hymn genuinely does not know what to bring, and says so before it says anything else.

*Kā te upetiḥ manaso varāya bhuvad agne śaṃtamā* — what approach of the mind would be most benign, for the choosing? Then: *kā manīṣā* — what insight? Then: who has ever compassed your *dakṣa*, your effective power, by means of *yajña*s? And last: *kena vā te manasā dāśema* — with what mind, then, shall we give to you? Four questions in one verse, and two of them turn on the same word. The verse opens on *manasaḥ* and closes on *manasā*: what is being asked is not what to place in Agni but what state to be in while placing it. The second verse answers by changing the subject, and the answer is hidden in a word. Come here, {{agni}}, sit down as *hotā* — the one who offers and who calls the gods by name — *adabdhaḥ*, undeceived and undeceivable; be our *supuraetā*, our good forerunner. May the two world-halves, all-pervading, favour you. And then the purpose: *yaja mahe saumanasāya devān* — sacrifice to the gods for great *saumanasa*, good-mindedness. The worshipper asked with what *manas* he should give; the rite is performed so that *manas* may come out well. That is the whole hymn in miniature, and it is stated three words at a time across two verses.

The third verse turns outward. Burn up all the *rakṣas*es; become the *abhiśastipāvā* of the sacrifices — the one who cleanses them of curse and imprecation, the officer whose job is to keep the rite from being spoiled by hostile speech. And then bring here the lord of {{soma}} with his two tawny horses: *ātithyam asmai cakṛma sudāvne*, we have made the guest-welcome ready for the generous one. The guest is not named. He does not have to be; the two bays name him.

The fourth verse gives Agni the offices themselves. He is *vahni*, the conveyor, called with his mouth and with *prajāvatā vacasā*, speech that brings offspring. Sit here with the gods, the verse says, and then: *veṣi hotram uta potram* — you perform the *hotra* and the *potra*, the calling office and the cleansing office both. In a full rite these belong to two different men. Here one god holds both, which is the practical form of the claim that Agni is where the whole rite converges. He is addressed at the close as *prayantaḥ janitaḥ vasūnām*, the giver and begetter of goods, and asked simply to be awake.

The fifth verse finally answers the first. What approach works? The one that has worked. *Yathā viprasya manuṣo havirbhir devān ayajaḥ kavibhiḥ kaviḥ san* — as, with the oblations of the wise Manu, you sacrificed to the gods, a seer among seers, so today, O *hotar satyatara*, most true of callers, sacrifice with the gladdening ladle. The question of verse 1 was answered not by a rule but by a precedent. Nobody has to invent the right approach; it was found once, and Agni that carried it is the same fire.
76.practice:
This is the hymn for the moment before the rite, when the question is not what to do but how to be while doing it. A worshipper who has ever sat down before the lamp and wondered whether the mind he has brought is fit for it is standing exactly where verse 1 stands. The Ṛgveda's answer is not reassurance. It is that the mind is what the rite works on — *yaja mahe saumanasāya*, sacrifice for great good-mindedness. You do not need to arrive with the right *manas*; the offering is how it is acquired.

Two of the offices named here still structure a śrauta rite. The *hotā* calls and offers; the *potṛ* purifies. In the classical sixteen-priest arrangement these are separate men serving separate deities, and the hymn's claim that Agni does both is a claim about where authority in the rite actually sits. [[1.94]].6, by the same collection's arrangement only eighteen sūktas later, extends the same list further — *adhvaryu*, *hotā*, *praśāstā*, *potā*, *purohita* — and gives Agni all of them.

The third verse names a fear that has not gone away. *Abhiśasti* is hostile speech, the curse or the accusation, and Agni is asked to be the one who cleanses a rite of it. Anyone who has performed something carefully while knowing it was being spoken against has that verse.

This is the third of Gotama Rāhūgaṇa's sūktas, and the run he holds is unusual. The Anukramaṇī gives him 1.74 through 1.93 without a break — twenty consecutive sūktas, the second-longest unbroken stretch under one name in maṇḍala 1, behind Dīrghatamas at 1.140–1.164 — plus one more at 9.31. Reading 1.76 with [[1.77]] and [[1.78]] beside it is reading one man's sustained work on one god, not three unrelated hymns; the same Agni is addressed, the questions accumulate, and the family name closes them.
76.disagreements:
Verse 1's *kā manīṣā* divides the translators, and one of them appears to have slipped. The padapāṭha reads *kā manīṣā* — what insight, what considered thought — which Griffith renders "What hymn of praise shall bring us greatest blessing?" Wilson prints "what can a hundred encomiums (effect)", which corresponds to nothing in the word-division and looks like a misreading rather than a variant.

On verse 2, Sāyaṇa is concrete where the translators are general: *ni sīda*, sit down, means sit down in the chamber where the burnt offerings are presented — the hymn is telling Agni where in the enclosure to be, not merely inviting him.

Verse 3's guest is unnamed in the Sanskrit, and Sāyaṇa supplies the identification: *somapati*, lord of soma, is a remarkable epithet for {{indra}}, indicated not by the name but by *haribhyām*, the two bays, which belong to Indra alone. Wilson accordingly prints "( Indra )" in brackets; Griffith leaves "the Lord of Soma" unglossed and lets the reader make the inference the Sanskrit intends.

Verse 4's *bodhi* is read by Wilson as transitive — "awaken us" — and by Griffith the same way. The form is more naturally an imperative of √bhū or √budh addressed to Agni himself, which would make it "be aware", and the ambiguity is not resolved by the witnesses here.

77.title: What Do We Give Agni? — Ṛtāvan Said Three Times
77.synthesis:
This sūkta begins where [[1.76]] began, with a question about giving, and then does something the previous hymn did not: it answers by repeating one epithet until the answer is unmistakable.

*Kathā dāśema agnaye* — how shall we give to {{agni}}? What speech, loved by the gods, is spoken to the shining one? The first verse gives its own reply in the second half: he who among mortals is *amṛta*, deathless, *ṛtāvā*, possessed of {{ṛta}} — the order by which things run true — and *hotā yajiṣṭhaḥ*, the caller who sacrifices best. That is the answer. You give to the one who keeps the order, and what you give is the giving itself.

The second verse repeats *ṛtāvā* and adds what it is for. Him who is *śaṃtama* in the rites, most benign, and *ṛtāvā hotā* — bring him near with *namas*, with the homage that bends. And then the reason, stated as a piece of information rather than praise: when Agni goes to the gods on a mortal's behalf, *sa ca bodhāti manasā yajāti*, he knows them, and he sacrifices with mind. The intermediary is not a conveyor belt. He understands the parties on both sides, which is why he can be trusted with the errand.

The third verse piles up what Agni is, in short clauses that do not connect grammatically so much as accumulate. *Sa hi kratuḥ sa maryaḥ sa sādhuḥ* — he is *kratu*, the resolve that gets things done; he is a young man; he is one who brings things to completion. He becomes like a *mitra*, a friend and ally, and is *rathīḥ adbhutasya*, charioteer of the wondrous. Then the social fact: *taṃ medheṣu prathamaṃ devayantīḥ viśaḥ upa bruvate dasmam ārīḥ* — at the rites, the god-seeking Ārya clans speak to him first, to him the wonder-worker. First, before any other god. That is not a claim about rank; it is a description of what people actually do, and it is the same practice that put Agni at the head of the collection.

The fourth verse asks for the reception of the offering and then widens. May Agni, *nṛtamaḥ* — most manly among men — and *riśādāḥ*, destroyer of hostility, come to our songs and to our *dhīti*, our formed thought, with help. And with him: those *maghavānaḥ*, the liberal patrons, strongest, *vājaprasūtāḥ*, impelled by *vāja*, the strength that a rite generates — may they too take pleasure in the *manman*, the composed hymn. The patrons are inside the prayer, not outside it. A rite has people who pay for it, and this verse asks that they be moved as well.

The fifth verse signs the work. *Evā agnir gotamebhir ṛtāvā viprebhir astoṣṭa jātavedāḥ* — thus Agni, *ṛtāvā*, Jātavedas, has been praised by the Gotamas, the inspired ones. Third and last occurrence of *ṛtāvā*, and it is now the settled name of the one who has been described. What follows is the return: may he swell *dyumna*, brilliance, in them; he goes to *vāja*, to *puṣṭi*, to nourishment, *joṣam ā cikitvān* — perceiving, and taking pleasure. The hymn that opened not knowing what to give ends by describing the giver enjoying what came back.
77.practice:
The question in the first line is the ordinary one: *kathā dāśema* — how are we to give? Not what to give. The hymn assumes the materials are available and doubts the manner, which is where most people actually stand.

What it settles on is *ṛtāvan*, three times: verse 1, verse 2, verse 5. The word is a possessive — one who has *ṛta*, who holds the order of things. Agni is worth giving to because he keeps that order, and by extension the giving is worth doing because it participates in the same order. This is the vocabulary a reciter already carries: *ṛta* is the truth of a thing, the regularity of the seasons, and the correct performance of a rite, all under one word, and the Ṛgveda does not treat these as three meanings. [[1.2]].8 puts three forms of it in a single line about Mitra and Varuṇa; here one form does the same work three times across a short hymn.

Verse 3 records something about ordinary observance that no doctrine states: the clans *speak to Agni first*. Before Indra, before Varuṇa, before whoever the day's rite is for. That habit is why the Anukramaṇī names Agni in the dedication of 230 of the Ṛgveda's 1,028 sūktas, why eight of the ten maṇḍalas open with him, and why in a modern pūjā the lamp is lit before anything else is offered. The verse describes the practice; the arrangement of the collection reflects it.

Verse 4 is the one worth carrying into a household. It asks for the offering to be received, and in the same breath asks that the *maghavānaḥ*, the people whose generosity paid for the rite, be stirred by the hymn. A rite is not only between a worshipper and a god. Somebody bought the ghee. The Ṛgveda puts them inside the prayer rather than thanking them afterward, and a family that supports a temple, a teacher or a recitation is standing where those patrons stand.

The closing verse names the singers as *gotamāḥ*, plural. Whatever the individual authorship, the tradition transmits these as a family's work, and the last verse of a Gotama hymn regularly says so.
77.disagreements:
Verse 3 is where the readings diverge most sharply, on three short words: *sa hi kratuḥ sa maryaḥ sa sādhuḥ*. Sāyaṇa takes *marya* and *sādhu* as a paired opposition — destroyer and reviver, "killer or extirpator of all and the producer" — and Wilson prints exactly that: "he is the destroyer and reviver (of all things)." Griffith reads the words at face value: "he is mental power, a man, and perfect." The Sanskrit supports Griffith more easily; *marya* is a common word for a young man. But Sāyaṇa's reading is not arbitrary, and it makes verse 3 a statement about Agni's double capacity rather than a list of compliments.

The last verse divides them almost as far. Wilson has Agni giving the singers "the bright Soma to drink, along with the sacrificial food"; Griffith has him augmenting "splendour and vigour" in them. The padapāṭha reads *saḥ eṣu dyumnam pīpayat*, he shall make *dyumna* swell in them, which is closer to Griffith; Wilson's soma appears to come from Sāyaṇa's expansion rather than from the words.

On verse 2, Sāyaṇa notes that *manasā*, with the mind, is read by some as *namasā*, with reverence, assuming a transposition of syllables — a genuine textual observation, and one he records without choosing.

78.title: Gotama's Five-Verse Refrain to Agni Jātavedas
78.synthesis:
Five gāyatrī verses, each two lines of address and one line that never changes: *dyumnair abhi pra ṇonumaḥ* — with brilliances we shout our praise again and again. The verb is intensive; *nonumaḥ* is not "we praise" but "we praise over and over", and the form itself says what the hymn is doing. Whatever else changes across the five verses, that line comes back, and the reciter says it five times in about a minute.

The first verse sets the addressee and the singers. *Abhi tvā gotamā girā jātavedo vicarṣaṇe* — to you, {{agni}} Jātavedas, keen-seeing, the Gotamas come with song. *Jātavedas* is the name that will hold the whole hymn: the one who knows all that is born, or in whom all that is born is known. Then the refrain.

The second verse narrows from the family to one man and states his motive without embarrassment. *Tam u tvā gotamo girā rāyaskāmo duvasyati* — you, that same one, Gotama, desiring *rayi*, honours with song. The wanting is named. There is no pretence that the singer approaches with an empty motive, and the tradition kept the line as it stands.

The third verse changes the ancestor. *Tam u tvā vājasātamam aṅgirasvad havāmahe* — you, best winner of *vāja*, the substance of strength, we call *aṅgirasvat*, in the manner of Aṅgiras. The singer's own family name has just been used twice; now he reaches past it to the older lineage of fire-priests, and says that this is how they did it. A recitation is being placed in a line rather than invented.

The fourth verse is the only one that names an enemy, and it does so with a word that ordinarily belongs to another god. *Tam u tvā vṛtrahantamam yo dasyūn avadhūnuṣe* — you, most Vṛtra-slaying, who shake off the {{dasyu}}s. *Vṛtrahan* is {{indra}}'s standing epithet, fixed by [[1.32]]; here it is given to Agni in the superlative. Agni that clears an obstruction and the bolt that clears one are being described with the same word, and the hymn does not pause to justify it.

The fifth verse signs and closes. *Avocāma rāhūgaṇā agnaye madhumad vacaḥ* — we, the Rāhūgaṇas, have spoken to Agni a speech containing honey. Then the refrain, for the fifth and last time. The song is described as *madhumat*, sweet — an assessment of its own quality that is also a description of what it is for, since sweetness is what one brings to a guest.

What the five verses actually do is name four things a hymn can rest on, one per verse: the family that sings, the wealth that is wanted, the ancient lineage the manner is borrowed from, and the enemy that needs removing. The fifth verse says the naming is finished. The refrain does not develop or resolve; it simply returns, and the returning is the point. This is a hymn built to be said, not to be followed — the shortest and plainest thing in Gotama's long series, and placed immediately after two sūktas that spent themselves on questions.
78.practice:
This is one of the easiest sūktas in the Ṛgveda to learn by heart, and that is not an accident of its size. Five gāyatrī verses with an identical third line means a reciter holds only ten unfamiliar lines; the eleventh through fifteenth are the same as the first refrain. Anyone beginning Ṛgvedic recitation could take this hymn on in an afternoon, and the tradition's habit of building a hymn around a returning line — visible here, at [[1.80]] with *arcann anu svarājyam* sixteen times, at [[1.94]] with *agne sakhye mā riṣāma vayaṃ tava* fourteen times, at [[1.97]] and [[1.100]] — is in the first place a transmission technology. Repetition is what let a text survive three thousand years without writing.

*Jātavedas* is the name worth carrying. It is Agni under the aspect of knowing — *jāta* + *vedas*, the one who knows what is born, or to whom all births are known. This is the name a Hindu meets most often outside the Ṛgveda itself, because it is the name in the Durgā Sūktam, whose first verse is [[1.99]], sixteen sūktas further on in this same maṇḍala. Reciting 1.78 is preparation for recognising what 1.99 is saying.

The second verse deserves note for its plainness. *Rāyaskāmaḥ* — desiring wealth — is said of the singer, by the singer, in a hymn of praise. The Ṛgveda does not treat the wish for *rayi* as something to be concealed or apologised for; *rayi* is sustenance, cattle, sons, standing, the material basis of a household able to keep a rite going at all. A tradition that later developed elaborate vocabulary for renouncing wealth began by asking for it out loud.

And the fourth verse is a reminder that the epithets move. *Vṛtrahantama* belongs to Indra everywhere else; given to Agni here, in the superlative, it says that what the tradition means by "obstruction-slayer" is a function before it is a person, and any god who performs it can be called by the name.
78.disagreements:
The first verse's *dyumnaiḥ* is the hinge of the refrain, and Sāyaṇa flags exactly where the translations go beyond the text. He notes that *gotamaḥ* is singular though rendered as a plural honorifically, that the word "mantras" is supplied by the commentator, and that the text has *only dyumnaiḥ* — "with brilliances", either the bright hymns themselves or the things that manifest Agni's worth. Wilson accordingly prints "commendatory (hymns)" with the bracket showing the addition; Griffith writes "for thy glories' sake", making *dyumnaiḥ* Agni's splendours rather than the singers' songs. The word can carry either, and neither witness resolves it.

Verse 4 divides them on *avadhūnuṣe*. Wilson has Agni "put the Dasyus to flight"; Griffith has him "shakest off our Dasyu foes". The verb is from √dhū, to shake, and both are within it — the difference is whether the Dasyus are driven away or shaken loose, which is small in English and not small in tone.

Wilson translates the fifth verse's authors as "the descendants of Rāhugaṇa", making them a family; Griffith writes "sons of Rahugana". The Anukramaṇī names the ṛṣi as Gotama Rāhūgaṇa, Gotama son of Rāhūgaṇa, so the hymn's plural is the family speaking in his name.

79.title: Agni Golden-Haired in the Storm, Then Asked for Rayi
79.synthesis:
Twelve verses in three metres, and the hymn changes character twice. It opens as weather and ends as household prayer, and the seam between them is one of the more abrupt in maṇḍala 1.

The first three verses are storm. *Hiraṇyakeśaḥ rajaso visāre* — golden-haired, in the spreading of the mid-region; *ahir dhuniḥ*, a roaring serpent; *vāta iva dhrajīmān*, sweeping like the wind; *śucibhrājāḥ*, blazing pure, and *uṣaso navedāḥ*, knowing the dawns. The dawns themselves are compared to women of good repute who are *apasyuvaḥ*, intent on their work, and *satyāḥ*, true. That is {{agni}} as lightning, and the picture is of a sky in motion, not a hearth. The second verse continues it: your well-winged flashes are unhindered; the black bull has bellowed; then it comes with drops that are *śivābhiḥ*, kindly, and seeming to smile — *patanti mihaḥ stanayanti abhrā*, the mists fall, the clouds thunder. The third verse tells what the falling water is: it is *ṛtasya payasā*, the milk of {{ṛta}}, led along *ṛtasya pathibhiḥ rajiṣṭhaiḥ*, the straightest paths of ṛta. Aryaman, Mitra, Varuṇa and the circling one fill the hide at the lower stone's seat. Rain arrives as an act of order keeping to its road. The word *ṛta* stands twice in that one verse, and it is the reason the storm belongs in a hymn at all.

Then the register drops, and stays down. The fourth verse asks flatly: Agni, *sahaso yaho*, child of strength, lord of the *vāja* that comes with cattle, place great renown in us, Jātavedas. The fifth: kindled, good, a *kavi* — a seer in whom insight and making are one — Agni is to be praised with song; *puruaṇīka*, many-faced, shine richly for us. The sixth is protective and blunt: king of the nights and of the daybreak, *tigmajambha*, sharp-toothed, burn against the *rakṣas*es.

Verses seven to nine are three short petitions, each one line of address and one of request. Guard us with your helps, you who are to be praised *viśvāsu dhīṣu*, in all our thoughts, at the bringing-forth of the gāyatra chant. Bring us *rayi* — wealth as sustenance — that is *satrāsaham*, altogether overcoming, choiceworthy, *dustaram* in all encounters. Grant us, with good understanding, wealth that nourishes a whole lifetime, *mārḍīkam*, merciful, *jīvase*, for living. Three verses, three things: protection, wealth that holds under pressure, wealth that lasts a life.

The tenth verse names the singer. *Pra pūtā tigmaśociṣe vāco gotama agnaye bharasva* — Gotama, bring purified speech to sharp-flamed Agni, *sumnayuḥ*, desiring favour. The speech has to be *pūtā*, clean, before it goes; that is a condition, not a compliment.

The eleventh asks that whoever attacks us, near or far, fall — and then, in the same breath, *sa asmākam id vṛdhe bhava*, be you for our increase. The hymn does not pretend the two wishes are the same wish. The twelfth closes on the god's own capacity: *sahasrākṣaḥ vicarṣaṇiḥ*, thousand-eyed and keen-seeing, Agni drives off the *rakṣas*es; as *hotā*, the calling priest, he is himself praised, worthy of the *uktha*. The lightning of verse 1 and the officiant of verse 12 are one person, and the hymn has spent twelve verses getting from one to the other without ever saying they are the same.
79.practice:
What this hymn gives a reader is a way of holding together two things that modern habit separates: weather and worship. Verses 1 to 3 are unmistakably a thunderstorm — the flash, the black bull's bellow, mist falling, clouds thundering. Verse 3 then calls the rain *ṛtasya payaḥ*, the milk of ṛta, moving along ṛta's straightest paths. Rain is not a metaphor for order here and order is not a poetic name for rain. The same word covers the regularity of the monsoon, the correctness of a rite, and the truth of a statement, and a tradition that says *ṛtaṃ vadiṣyāmi* in its recitation vow is using the word the storm verse uses.

The three petitions at verses 7, 8 and 9 are worth memorising as a set, because they distinguish things that a hurried prayer runs together. Verse 7 asks for protection *viśvāsu dhīṣu*, in all thoughts — the mind's work, the same *dhī* that stands behind *dhyāna*. Verse 8 asks for *rayi* that is *dustara*, not to be got past, in every contest: wealth that survives challenge. Verse 9 asks for *rayi* that is *viśvāyupoṣas*, nourishing a whole span, and *mārḍīka*, merciful, *jīvase* — for living. Strength that holds and sufficiency that lasts are separate requests, and the hymn makes them separately.

Verse 10 states a condition on speech that is easy to pass over. The words brought to Agni must be *pūtā*, purified. The later insistence on *śuddhi* before recitation, on rinsing the mouth, on not reciting in an unfit state, has its root in lines like this one — not as ritual fussiness but as the plain claim that what is carried up must be clean before it is carried.

And verse 11 is honest in a way devotional literature usually is not. It asks for an enemy's fall and for one's own increase, in the same verse, without harmonising them. The Ṛgveda records what people actually pray, including the part of it that is not generous.
79.disagreements:
The first three verses are where the readings split hardest, and the split is the familiar one. Sāyaṇa reads the storm naturalistically and Wilson follows him into English: the golden-haired Agni is "the agitator of the clouds when the rain is poured forth", the dawns "know not of the showers", and verse 3's actors "pierce through the (investing) membrane into the womb of the cloud." Griffith keeps the strangeness: "a raging serpent, like the rushing tempest", and for verse 3, "fill the hide full where lies the nether press-stone" — an image he leaves unexplained rather than dissolve. Sāyaṇa does gloss verse 3's "straightest paths" concretely, as the uses water is put to: drinking, washing, bathing.

Verse 5's *puruaṇīka* Sāyaṇa derives as *puru*, many, plus *anīka*, face or mouth, and connects it to Agni as *jvālā-jihvā*, flame-tongued; Wilson prints "whose mouth (glows) with many (flames)", Griffith flattens it to "thou of many forms."

Verse 12's *sahasrākṣa*, thousand-eyed, Sāyaṇa explains as *asaṃkhyātā jvālāḥ*, countless flames — the eyes are the flames. Both translators keep "thousand-eyed" and leave the identification out.

80.title: Indra Slays Vṛtra — Sixteen Times, His Own Sway
80.synthesis:
Sixteen verses, and every one of them ends *arcann anu svarājyam* — singing along with, or making manifest, his own sovereign rule. Nothing else in maṇḍala 1 hammers a line this many times. The effect is not decoration; it is a verdict passed at the end of each verse, and by the sixteenth the reciter has pronounced it sixteen times.

The first verse names the two things that made the deed possible: *itthā hi some it made brahmā cakāra vardhanam* — thus, in the {{soma}}, in the exhilaration, the *brahman*-priest performed the strengthening. Praise and drink together increase {{indra}}, and then, mightiest wielder of the bolt, by your *ojas* you shook the *ahi* off the earth. The second verse gives the soma its history — it was *śyenābhṛta*, brought by the hawk — and moves the killing: by it you struck Vṛtra out of the waters. The third is pure urging, three imperatives in a row: *pra ihi abhi ihi dhṛṣṇuhi* — go forth, go at him, dare. Your bolt will not be checked; slay Vṛtra, win the waters. The fourth locates the blow in both worlds — from the earth, from the sky — and asks for the release of the waters that are *marutvatī*, attended by the {{marut}}s, and *jīvadhanya*, rich with life.

Verses five to eight are the striking itself, seen four ways. Angered, he steps up and strikes the crest of the raging Vṛtra with the bolt, urging the waters to run (v5). He strikes on that crest with the hundred-jointed bolt, and — exhilarated by the juice — *sakhibhyo gātum icchati*, seeks a passage for his friends (v6): the whole violence is for someone else's road. The seventh introduces the strangest detail: your prowess is unsurpassed, and *tyaṃ māyinaṃ mṛgam tam u tvaṃ māyayā avadhīḥ* — that beast of *māyā*, him you slew by *māyā*. Craft answered with craft. The eighth counts the aftermath: your bolts lay scattered over ninety-nine streams; strength is deposited in your two arms.

The ninth verse steps out of the battle to the people singing about it — a thousand together, twenty shouting, hundreds roaring after him, and to Indra the *brahman* raised up. The tenth returns and states the exchange plainly: he struck away Vṛtra's *taviṣī*, force, with *sahas*, overcoming force; that was his manhood, and having slain, he loosed. The eleventh has the two world-halves shaking with fear at his *manyu*, his fury. The twelfth denies the enemy any credit: not by trembling, not by thundering, did Vṛtra frighten Indra; the iron bolt of a thousand points came at him. The thirteenth sets the outcome in place — when you made Vṛtra and his own missile fight against the bolt, your *śavas* was fixed fast in heaven.

Then the last three turn from event to standing. At his roar everything that stands and moves shakes, and even Tvaṣṭṛ, who made the bolt, quakes at his fury (v14). We know of none who surpasses him in *vīrya*; in him the gods concentrated *nṛmṇa*, *kratu* — effective resolve — and all their strengths (v15). And the sixteenth, which is why the refrain has been said fifteen times already: the *dhī*, the formed thought, that Atharvan, father Manu and Dadhyañc stretched out — in that Indra the *brahman*s and the *uktha*s came together, as of old. The hymn ends not on the corpse but on the convergence of everyone's speech in one place. The refrain has been saying that all along.
80.practice:
What this hymn is for is not the story. [[1.32]] tells the Vṛtra killing once, at length, and ends with fear and a wheel. This one tells it sixteen times and ends with a refrain. The difference is the difference between a narrative and a recitation, and 1.80 exists to be said.

That has a practical consequence a reciter feels immediately. A verse of paṅkti here is four lines of new matter and one line already known. Sixteen verses means sixteen returns to the same cadence, and the mind that recites it settles into a rhythm rather than following a plot. This is how Vedic memory works — the refrain is a rest point, and it is also the meaning: *arcann anu svarājyam*, praising in accordance with his own rule. The act of reciting and the thing recited about are named by the same phrase.

Verse 6 is the one to keep. Indra strikes with a hundred-jointed bolt, and in the same verse *sakhibhyo gātum icchati* — he wants a way through for his friends. The whole apparatus of force in this hymn is oriented at a passage being opened for somebody else. A reader looking for what authority is for in the Vedic imagination has it in half a line.

Verse 7 is the one to be careful with. Indra kills a creature of *māyā* by *māyā*. The word later hardens into "illusion" in Vedāntic usage, but here it means craft, contrivance, the capacity to make appearances — and it belongs to both sides. The gods are not exempt from it. Whatever *māyā* becomes later, it starts as a neutral skill.

And verse 16 names three figures a Hindu reader will meet again: Atharvan, from whom the Atharvaveda takes its name; Manu, called *pitā* here, the ancestor; and Dadhyañc, whose bones become Indra's weapon in the very next Gotama hymn, [[1.84]].13. Sixteen verses about a single killing close by saying that the point of the killing was that hymns could converge on the killer — that the *dhī* those three stretched out ends up here. The last verse gives the recitation its pedigree.
80.disagreements:
The refrain itself is the first thing the readings differ on. Sāyaṇa parses *arcann anu svarājyam* as *prakaṭayan* — making manifest his own mastership — so the participle describes Indra displaying his sovereignty. Wilson follows: "manifesting your own sovereignty." Griffith takes the participle of the singer instead: "lauding thine own imperial sway." One reading has the god displaying, the other the priest praising; the Sanskrit permits both, and the ambiguity is arguably the point, since the hymn's last verse is about hymns converging on Indra.

Sāyaṇa's smaller glosses are where the ritual detail sits. On verse 2 he explains *śyenābhṛta*, hawk-brought: soma was carried from heaven by Gāyatrī in the form of a hawk. On verse 8 he declines to take "ninety-nine" literally, offering 9,000 or simply an indefinite number. On verse 9 he reads the numbers as personnel — the "twenty" being the sixteen priests employed at a sacrifice, the *yajamāna*, his wife, and two functionaries, the *sadasya* and *śamitṛ*. On verse 7 he supplies the legend the text only gestures at: Vṛtra had assumed the form of a deer.

Verse 6's *gātum icchati* Wilson renders "wishes to provide means of sustenance for his friends"; Griffith has "seeketh prosperity for friends". *Gātu* is a path or passage, and both have moved it toward provision.

81.title: Indra in Great Fights and Small — Divide the Wealth
81.synthesis:
Nine verses about what a strong god is actually for, and the answer this hymn keeps giving is: distribution.

The first verse establishes the relation before anything is asked. *Indro madāya vavṛdhe śavase vṛtrahā nṛbhiḥ* — {{indra}}, the Vṛtra-slayer, has been made to grow by men, for exhilaration and for *śavas*. Men increase him. Then the range: we call him *mahatsu ājiṣu*, in the great contests, *uta īm arbhe*, and also in the small one. Both. The god of the cosmic combat is invoked over a village quarrel, and the hymn says so in its opening verse without any sense of incongruity.

The second verse turns the strength toward those who have none. You are a host in yourself; you are a great surrenderer of spoils; and — the phrase that matters — *asi dabhrasya cit vṛdhaḥ*, you are the increaser of even the small, the slight, the one with little. You teach the *yajamāna*, you give to the presser. Abundant is your *vasu*.

The third verse is the hymn's hard centre. When battles arise, *dhṛṣṇave dhīyate dhanā* — the stakes are set for the bold. Yoke your two bays that reel with exhilaration.
