And then two questions and an answer: *kaṃ hanaḥ kaṃ vasau dadhaḥ* — whom will you slay, whom will you place in wealth? *Asmān indra vasau dadhaḥ* — place us in wealth. The prayer does not pretend that one man's gain is nobody's loss. It asks to be on the receiving side of a distribution it knows has two sides.

The fourth verse describes the giver's own bearing: great by *kratu*, effective resolve, terrible according to his own nature, his *śavas* grown for splendour; lofty, *śiprin*, lord of the bays, he has set the iron bolt in his two hands. The fifth widens it as far as it goes: he filled the earthly region, he pressed against the lights in heaven; none like you was born, none will be born; you have grown past everything. Then, immediately, the sixth verse brings that unlimited magnitude back down to a household ledger — he who hands over the enemy's *martabhojana*, the food fit for a man, to the giver: may Indra be liberal to us. *Vi bhaja bhūri te vasu, bhakṣīya tava rādhasaḥ* — distribute; abundant is your wealth; may I have a share of your bounty.

The seventh verse names the quality the giving needs: *ṛjukratuḥ*, of straight resolve. At each exhilaration he gives us herds; gather up with both hands many hundreds of goods; *śiśīhi rāya ā bhara* — sharpen us, bring wealth. Sharpening and bringing in one breath: the request is for capacity as well as goods. The eighth is the invitation itself — rejoice with us in what has been pressed, hero, for *śavas* and for *rādhas*; we know you as *puruvasu*, and we have released our desires toward you; therefore be our protector.

The ninth verse ends somewhere uncomfortable and does not soften it. These your creatures cherish everything choiceworthy; you have looked inside men; *aryo vedo adāśuṣām teṣāṃ no veda ā bhara* — the wealth of the non-givers, of those who make no offering: bring theirs to us. Nine verses that began by calling Indra the increaser of the small end by asking him to move property from those outside the rite to those inside it. The Ṛgveda preserves the request exactly as it was made.
81.practice:
The first verse is the reason to keep this hymn. *Mahatsu ājiṣu uta īm arbhe* — in the great contests and also in the small one. The Vṛtra-slayer of [[1.32]] and [[1.80]] is called on here for whatever is in front of the speaker, of whatever size. A tradition that had cordoned its highest god off for cosmic emergencies would not have written that line. The same god is available for the small thing, and asking him for it is not a diminishment.

Sāyaṇa preserves an occasion for the hymn, and it is a specific one: Gotama Rāhūgaṇa was *purohita* to the Kuru and Sṛñjaya princes, and propitiated Indra with this sūkta during an engagement with rival kings, who consequently gave the victory to his patrons. That story cannot be verified from the text — the hymn names no king and no battle — but it is what the tradition transmits about why 1.81 exists, and it fits verse 3's frank question about who is slain and who is enriched.

Verse 2's phrase is worth carrying alone: *dabhrasya cit vṛdhaḥ*, increaser of even the small. Power that only augments what is already large is not what is being praised. And verse 7 asks for two different things in one line — *śiśīhi*, sharpen us, and *rāya ā bhara*, bring wealth. Sharpening first. A person who receives goods without the capacity to use them has received less than the hymn is asking for.

Verse 9 should not be smoothed over. It asks Indra to bring the singers the wealth of *adāśvāṃsaḥ*, those who do not give. This is a real feature of the collection: the community that sacrifices understands itself as standing in a different relation to prosperity than the community that does not, and it prays accordingly. Reading the Ṛgveda as a living manual means noticing where its assumptions are not ours, rather than translating them away.
81.disagreements:
Sāyaṇa supplies this hymn's only narrative frame, and it is his alone: Gotama, son of Rāhūgaṇa, was the *purohita* of the Kuru and Sṛñjaya princes and propitiated Indra by this hymn in an engagement with other kings, who accordingly received the victory. Neither Wilson nor Griffith adds anything to it, and nothing in the padapāṭha confirms or denies it.

On verse 1's *vavṛdhe*, Sāyaṇa states the principle behind the grammar: "a deity acquiring vigour by praise increases" — the passive is real, and men actually augment the god. Wilson prints it as "augmented in strength and satisfaction by (the adoration of) men"; Griffith renders "The men have lifted Indra up", which keeps the agency but loses the growth.

Verse 3's *kam* Sāyaṇa explains as *kañcit*, anyone — Indra gives victory to whomever he is pleased with, so the question is genuinely open rather than rhetorical. Wilson follows with "that you may destroy one and enrich another"; Griffith keeps the interrogative: "Whom wilt thou slay and whom enrich?"

Verse 9's *aryaḥ* is the sharpest divergence. Wilson makes it Indra himself — "you, lord of all, know what are the riches of those men who make no offerings" — while Griffith reads it as an address, "Discover thou, as Lord, the wealth of men who offer up no gifts". Either way the request is the same.

82.title: Yoke Your Bays Now, Indra — Then Go to Your Wife
82.synthesis:
Six verses, five of which end with the same imperative — *yoja nv indra te harī*, yoke now, Indra, your two bays — and a sixth that answers it in a way the first five do not prepare you for.

The first verse opens with an unusually direct piece of speech. Listen well to our songs, *maghavan*, bountiful one; *mā atathā iva*, do not be as though you were not-such — do not, that is, be other than what you have always been to us. Then the ground for the request: *yadā naḥ sūnṛtāvataḥ karaḥ*, since you have made us possessed of *sūnṛtā*, true and generous speech, therefore you are indeed being asked. The logic is a household's: you have already given us the words; the words are now being used on you.

The second verse describes what has already happened at the rite. *Akṣan amīmadanta hi* — they have eaten, they have taken their fill; the dear ones have shaken down (the drops); the *vipra*s, self-shining, have praised with the newest thought, *naviṣṭhayā matī*. The offering is finished, the singing is finished, and the god's horses are still unyoked. That is the tension the refrain keeps stating.

The third verse asks for the sight of him: may we praise you well-seen, *maghavan* — and now, praised, come *pūrṇavandhuraḥ*, with your chariot-seat full, *vaśān anu*, according to (our) wishes. The vehicle is asked to arrive loaded. The fourth turns to whoever will get the benefit: he indeed will mount that bull-like, cow-finding chariot who takes notice of the full vessel of *hāriyojana* — the mixture set out specifically for the moment of yoking. A rite has a dish whose name means "for harnessing the bays." The invitation is not abstract.

The fifth verse yokes both sides — let your right one be yoked and your left too, *śatakrato*, you of a hundred resolves — and then says where he is to drive. *Tena jāyām upa priyāṃ mandāno yāhi andhasaḥ*: with that team, exhilarated by the juice, go to your beloved wife. The most-invoked god in the collection is being sent home.

And then the sixth verse breaks the refrain, and the break is the whole point. For five verses the singers have said *yoja*, yoke — imperative, addressed to {{indra}}. The sixth says *yunajmi te brahmaṇā keśinā harī* — **I** yoke your long-maned bays, with *brahman*, with the formed sacred word. The priest turns out to be the one doing the harnessing, and the instrument is the hymn itself. Then: come near; you have taken them in your two hands; the pressed, impetuous drops have gladdened you; and *pūṣaṇvān vajrin sam u patnyā amadaḥ* — with Pūṣan beside you, wielder of the bolt, you have rejoiced together with your wife.

The hymn thus ends twice over in domesticity: the god goes to his wife, and the last thing said of the thunderbolt-bearer is that he was glad with her. Nothing is asked for in that verse. After five verses of urging, the sixth simply reports that the yoking was done, by the singer, with a hymn, and that the god went home content. [[1.84]].3 uses the same phrase — *yuktā te brahmaṇā harī*, your bays have been yoked by *brahman* — which confirms that this is not a flourish but the standing description of what a hymn does to a god's horses.
82.practice:
The turn at verse 6 is the teaching, and it is compressed into a change of person. Five verses say "yoke your horses"; the sixth says "I yoke your horses, with *brahman*." What moves the god is not the request but the recitation. *Brahman* here is the formulated sacred utterance — the word before it became the name of the Absolute — and the claim is that it is instrumentally effective: it is the harness. Anyone who has wondered what a mantra is supposed to *do* has the Ṛgveda's own answer in half a line of 1.82.6, and it is repeated at [[1.84]].3.

The other thing worth taking is where the hymn sends Indra. Verse 5: go to your beloved wife. Verse 6: you rejoiced with your wife. There is no petition attached, no benefit sought from it. The collection's most martial deity is dismissed from the rite into his household, and that is how the sūkta ends. A tradition that would later build a large literature on the householder's life as a legitimate and complete path has this verse behind it. Indrāṇī is not named here, and the hymn does not need her to be; *patnī* is the ritual word for the wife who is present at and required for the rite, the one without whom a *yajamāna* cannot offer.

Verse 4 preserves a ritual detail that would otherwise be lost: *hāriyojana*, which Sāyaṇa describes as a mixture of fried barley or other grain with soma, set out in its own vessel. The name means "for the yoking of the bays." A dish exists in the rite whose entire purpose is the moment when the god's horses are harnessed, and verse 4 says that the man who notices it is the one whose chariot arrives.

And verse 1's *mā atathā iva* is a phrase for a long relationship: do not be unlike yourself. It is what one says to someone who has always been reliable, at the moment when one needs them to be reliable again — not flattery, and not quite a request. The Ṛgveda's register with Indra is often this: familiar, faintly impatient, and confident of the history.
82.disagreements:
Verse 1's *mā atathā iva* is where Sāyaṇa does the most work and the translators do the least. He parses it as "be not, as it were, non-such" — be not the contrary of the propitious divinity you have always been to us — and explains the second half as: since you make us possessed of *sūnṛtā*, therefore you are asked, *arthayase eva*, to accept our praises. Wilson prints the paraphrase, "be not different (from what you have hitherto been)"; Griffith reduces it to "be not negligent", which loses the relationship the phrase depends on.

Verse 2 divides them completely. Wilson has the worshippers eating, rejoicing and trembling "through their precious (bodies)"; Griffith has "the friends have risen and passed away" — one reading has the singers still present and shaking, the other has them gone. The padapāṭha's *ava priyāḥ adhūṣata* supports shaking down rather than departing.

Verse 4's *pātraṃ hāriyojanam* Sāyaṇa identifies precisely as a plate or vessel filled with a mixture of fried barley or other grain and soma; Wilson repeats him, Griffith gives only "the well-filled bowl".

On verse 6 Wilson supplies "(sacred prayers)" for *brahmaṇā* in brackets, treating it as an addition; Griffith prints "With holy prayer I yoke thy long-maned pair" without hesitation, and the padapāṭha supports him — *brahmaṇā* is in the text.

83.title: Indra and the Aṅgirases — Where the Stone Speaks
83.synthesis:
Six jagatī verses that begin with one protected man and end with three sounds, and in between recover the oldest story the Aṅgirases tell about themselves.

The first verse describes the beneficiary. The mortal who is *supravīḥ*, well-protected by {{indra}}'s helps, goes first among horses and among cows — first, that is, to the wealth. And then the simile that gives the verse its size: *taṃ id pṛṇakṣi vasunā bhavīyasā sindhum āpo yathābhitaḥ vicetasaḥ* — you fill him with more and more goods, as the waters, *vicetas*, fill the {{sindhu}} from every side. Discerning waters, converging on one river from all directions. Wealth is being described as a watershed rather than a gift.

The second verse moves the waters into the rite. The divine waters come to the *hotriya*, the vessel of the offering priest; they look down as the region is spread out; the gods lead forward the god-seeking, *brahmapriya*, the one who loves the sacred word — and they take pleasure in him, *varāḥ iva*, like suitors. The gods court the worshipper. The direction of desire has been reversed, quietly, in one word.

The third verse is the most domestic thing in the Indra hymns. *Adhi dvayor adadhāḥ ukthyaṃ vacaḥ* — upon the two you have laid the speech worthy of praise, *yatasrucā mithunā yā saparyataḥ*, the pair who serve together with the ladle held out. Husband and wife, ladle between them; and the consequence: *asaṃyattaḥ vrate te kṣeti puṣyati*, unimpeded he dwells in your *vrata*, your observance, and prospers; auspicious is the power granted to the sacrificer who presses. The blessing is not on the man. It is on the two of them, jointly, and the Sanskrit word for them is *mithuna*, the couple.

Then the fourth verse reaches back. *Ād aṅgirāḥ prathamaṃ dadhire vayaḥ* — then first the {{aṅgiras}}es obtained vigour, *iddhāgnayaḥ*, having kindled their fires, by *śamī* and by good work; and *sarvaṃ paṇeḥ sam avindanta bhojanam* — they found the whole store of the {{paṇi}}, with horses, with cows, with the herd. This is the cattle-recovery that runs beneath so much of maṇḍala 1: something was hoarded, and Agni-kindlers got it back. Notice what the verse credits it to — kindled fires, *śamī* (ritual labour), *sukṛtyā* (good doing). Not weapons.

The fifth verse continues the same recovery with different actors and adds a birth. *Yajñair atharvā prathamaḥ pathas tate* — by sacrifices Atharvan first stretched out the paths; then Sūrya was born, *vratapā*, keeper of the observance, *vena*, longing. Uśanā Kāvya drove the cows hither. And the verse ends: let us worship the deathless birth of Yama. Four figures from four different corners of the tradition — Atharvan, Sūrya, Uśanā, Yama — in one verse, and the connective is the path that sacrifice opened.

The sixth verse comes back to the enclosure and ends on sound. Whether the *barhis* is trimmed *svapatyāya*, for good offspring; or the *arka*, the chant, sends its *śloka* ringing in the sky; or where the pressing-stone speaks like a singer worthy of the *uktha* — *tasyed indraḥ abhipitveṣu raṇyati*, in that man's rites Indra takes his delight, at the times of coming together. Three sounds: grass being cut, a chant going up, a stone knocking. Not one of them is a request. The hymn's last word on what pleases the greatest god is the noise a rite makes when it is being properly done.
83.practice:
Verse 3 is the reason a household should know this hymn. *Yatasrucā mithunā yā saparyataḥ* — the pair who serve together with the ladle held out. Both are holding it; the praise-worthy speech is laid on both; and the prosperity that follows is theirs jointly. This is stated as rule elsewhere in the Veda: the *yajamāna* cannot offer without his *patnī*. A man performing alone is not performing. Anyone who has stood at a homa and wondered why the wife's hand rests on the husband's during the offering is looking at verse 3 of 1.83.

Verse 6 is the one to carry into an ordinary day. It lists three ways a rite becomes audible — the barhis being cut, the *arka* sounding, the stone knocking — and says Indra delights in the man in whose place these are heard. Not in his eloquence, not in the size of his offering. In the sounds of the work being done. A house where the grass is being trimmed and the stone is being struck is a house the god comes to.

Verses 4 and 5 preserve the Aṅgirases' own charter. They kindled fires, they did *śamī* — the ritual labour, the same root that gives *śamī* the sacrificial wood and *śānti* — and by that they recovered everything the Paṇi had shut away. The Vedic imagination has two ways of getting what is held back: [[1.32]] breaks it out by force, and 1.83.4 works it out by kindling fires and doing the labour properly. Both are in the collection, and both are Indra's.

Verse 5 names Yama, and the mention is easy to miss because it is a single phrase — *yamasya jātam amṛtaṃ yajāmahe*. Yama is the deity of the *śrāddha* and of the last rite, met by every Hindu family, and here he appears in his oldest surroundings, alongside Atharvan and Uśanā Kāvya, in a verse about the paths that sacrifice first opened.

Verse 1's image is worth keeping for its own sake: the waters filling the Sindhu from every side, *vicetasaḥ* — discerning, knowing the way. Prosperity in this hymn is a convergence, not a windfall.
83.disagreements:
Verse 1's *vicetasaḥ* is where Sāyaṇa parts company with the plain sense. Wilson prints "the unconscious rivers", reading *vi-cetas* privatively, but Sāyaṇa explains it the other way — *viśiṣṭajñānahetubhūtāḥ*, the sources of excellent knowledge — so the waters are discerning rather than mindless. Griffith sidesteps with "the waters clearly seen afar". Given the compound, Sāyaṇa's reading is the stronger one and Wilson's own commentary contradicts his translation.

Verse 2 is the most heavily supplemented verse in the hymn, and Sāyaṇa is candid about it. He notes that *devāḥ*, the gods, is supplied; that "descends on earth" is added; and that what is being led — the ladle, the altar, or the maiden — is filled in by the commentary rather than found in the text. Wilson prints the whole expanded reading, bridegrooms and all. Griffith translates the bare words and produces something quite different: "The heavenly Waters come not nigh the priestly bowl."

On verse 5 Sāyaṇa identifies Kāvya with Uśanas and Uśanas with the family of Bhṛgu, and explains *yamasya* not as the god but as *asurāṇāṃ niyamanārtham*, for the restraint of the asuras — which is why Wilson prints "who was born to restrain (the asuras)" where Griffith has "Yama's deathless birth". The name and the verb are the same root, and the tradition kept both.

84.title: Indra in Six Metres — Dadhyañc's Bones, and "Who?"
84.synthesis:
Twenty verses in six metres, and the metre changes exactly where the subject changes: anuṣṭubh for 1–6, uṣṇih for 7–9, paṅkti for 10–12, gāyatrī for 13–15, triṣṭubh for 16–18, bṛhatī for 19–20. Read it as six short pieces, not one long one.

The first six are the invitation. The {{soma}} has been pressed for you, {{indra}}, mightiest, bold one — come; may *indriya*, your own force, fill you as Sūrya fills the mid-region with rays (v1). The two bays bring him, of unresisted *śavas*, to the ṛṣis' praises and men's *yajña* (v2). Mount the chariot, Vṛtra-slayer: *yuktā te brahmaṇā harī*, your bays have been yoked by the sacred word, and may the pressing-stone with its noise turn your mind toward us (v3) — the same claim [[1.82]].6 makes when the priest says *I* yoke them. Drink this pressed, deathless exhilaration; the bright streams have flowed to you *ṛtasya sādane*, at the seat of {{ṛta}} (v4). Sing to Indra, speak the *uktha*s; the drops have gladdened him; do *namas* to his supreme *sahas* (v5). And: when you rein the bays there is no better charioteer, none has equalled you, none however well-horsed has overtaken you (v6).

Verses 7 to 9 end on a single syllable — *indraḥ aṅga*, Indra, indeed! — and each states a different relation. He alone distributes wealth to the mortal who gives, the ruler unopposed (v7). Then a complaint, and it is a complaint: *kadā martam arādhasam padā kṣumpam iva sphurat, kadā naḥ śuśravad giraḥ* — when will he kick aside with his foot the man who makes no gift, as one kicks a *kṣumpa*; when will he hear our songs? (v8). And: whoever, with soma pressed, seeks to win him from among many — that fierce *śavas* becomes his (v9).

Verses 10 to 12 change the worshipper entirely: the cows. They drink of this sweet, pervading honey, the tawny ones who go with Indra, and rejoice for splendour (v10). Craving his touch, the dappled ones mix the soma with their milk, and the milch-cows dear to Indra *vajraṃ hinvanti sāyakam*, speed the bolt as a missile (v11). With *namas* they honour his *sahas* and follow his many *vrata*s (v12). Each of the three ends *vasvīr anu svarājyam* — good ones, in accordance with his own sovereignty.

Verses 13 to 15 are three gāyatrī lines of pure legend, told at speed and unexplained. With the bones of Dadhyañc, Indra, unopposed, slew ninety-nine Vṛtras (v13). Seeking the horse's head hidden among the mountains, he found it at Śaryaṇāvat (v14). And there indeed they thought out the hidden name of the cow, of Tvaṣṭṛ, in the house of the moon (v15). The Ṛgveda assumes its audience knows the story; it supplies only the three points at which the story turns.

Verses 16 to 18 are questions — ten of them. Who yokes today to the pole the bulls of *ṛta*, fierce, hard-tempered, arrows in their mouths, piercing hearts, making well-being? He who pays their service shall live (v16). Then seven *kaḥ* in a single verse: who flees? who is hurt? who fears? who thinks Indra is really here? who thinks him near? who speaks for offspring, for retinue, for wealth, for his own body, for the people? (v17). And: who kindles Agni, who offers ghee with the ladle *ṛtubhir dhruvebhiḥ*, at the fixed seasons? To whom do the gods swiftly bring? What offerer truly knows him? (v18). None is answered.

The last two verses answer them by declining to. You, indeed, a god, will bless a mortal; *na tvad anyo maghavann asti marḍitā* — there is no comforter but you; Indra, I speak my word to you (v19). Let not your bounties, let not your helps ever fail us; measure out to us all goods from the peoples (v20). After ten unanswered questions, a man simply says: there is nobody else.
84.practice:
Three verses in this sūkta are the seed of something a Hindu reader meets much later, and it is worth knowing they are here.

Dadhyañc — Dadhīci in the later name — is the sage whose bones become Indra's weapon. Sāyaṇa preserves the whole legend attached to these three verses: Dadhyañc son of Atharvan overawed the asuras by his mere presence; when he went to svarga they overran the earth; Indra, told that the horse's head through which Dadhyañc had once taught the *madhu-vidyā* to the {{aśvin}}s still existed somewhere, searched and found it in the lake Śaryaṇāvat near Kurukṣetra, and with the bones of that skull destroyed the asuras' contrivances. The *madhu-vidyā* is not a footnote: it is the "honey-teaching" that the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad expounds at length, attributing it to Dadhyañc and the Aśvins, and the reason a horse's head is involved is the story compressed into 1.84.14. The Vedānta's honey doctrine and this gāyatrī verse are the same tradition at two ends of its life.

Verse 18 hands the reader a word from every saṅkalpa. *Ṛtubhir dhruvebhiḥ* — with the fixed seasons — is the standard for offering ghee correctly: not whenever moved to, but at the appointed time. The same *ṛtu* is named aloud when the occasion of any rite is declared, and it is the same root behind *ṛtvij*, the priest of [[1.1]].1 who is named for timeliness rather than knowledge.

Verse 17 is the one to sit with. Seven times *kaḥ* — who? Who flees, who is hurt, who is afraid, who knows that Indra is actually present? The verse is not asking for names. It is asking whether anyone, in fact, behaves as though the god were there. That is a question a devout person can put to themselves in any century, and the hymn's own answer comes two verses later and is not an argument: *na tvad anyo marḍitā* — there is no comforter but you.

And verses 10 to 12 give the cattle their own three verses of worship, with their own refrain, mixing the soma with their milk and honouring his *sahas* with *namas*. The reverence a Hindu household extends to the cow does not begin with a doctrine; it begins with texts in which she is a participant in the rite rather than its property.
84.disagreements:
Sāyaṇa carries almost all the material here.

On verse 13 he supplies the Dadhyañc legend in full — Atharvan's son, the horse's head with which he taught the *madhu-vidyā* to the Aśvins, the search, the lake Śaryaṇāvat near Kurukṣetra — and then explains the number. "Ninety times nine" is 810: the *āsurī māyā* practised in three worlds for three times is nine; each with three *śakti*s, twenty-seven; each modified by three *guṇa*s, eighty-one; displayed in the ten regions, 810. The arithmetic is his, not the text's. Wilson prints "ninety times nine Vṛtras", Griffith "nine-and-ninety Vrtras", neither with comment.

On verse 17's *kaḥ* he gives a one-word gloss with a long history: *kaḥ = prajāpati*. Read that way "who?" is not a question but a name: Prajāpati flees, Prajāpati fears, Prajāpati knows Indra present. Neither translator takes it up; both keep the interrogatives. The identification of Ka with Prajāpati is old, and the Brāhmaṇas develop it.

Verse 15 divides them completely. Wilson follows Sāyaṇa's astronomical reading — "the (solar rays) found the light of Tvaṣṭā concealed in the mansion of the moving moon", with the note that the moon's light derives from the sun's ray *suṣumṇā*, citing the Nirukta. Griffith translates the words: "they recognized the essential form of Tvastar's Bull, here in the mansion of the Moon." The padapāṭha has *goḥ nāma tvaṣṭuḥ apīcyam*, the hidden name of the cow, of Tvaṣṭṛ, and does not settle it.

On verse 8's *kṣumpa* Sāyaṇa gives *ahicchatraka*, a plant whose coil suggests a sleeping snake; Wilson prints "a coiled-up snake", Griffith "a weed".

85.title: Maruts Adorn Themselves, and Bring Gotama a Well
85.synthesis:
Twelve verses on the {{marut}}s, and the hymn spends most of its length on how they look before it says what they did.

*Pra ye śumbhante janayo na saptayaḥ* — they who adorn themselves like women, swift as coursers, on their journey; sons of Rudra, *sudaṃsasaḥ*, of good works; they have made the two world-halves grow, and they take delight in the *vidatha*s, the assemblies, *ghṛṣvayaḥ*, exuberant (v1). Sprinkled and grown, they have reached greatness; the Rudras have made their seat above the sky; singing the *arka* and generating *indriya*, they have put splendour on, the sons of Pṛśni (v2). When the sons of the cow adorn themselves with ornaments, the bright ones set gleaming things on their bodies; they thrust off every adversary, and *anu rīyate ghṛtam*, richness runs along their tracks (v3).

Then the equipment. They shine with their spears, *sumakhāsaḥ*, good fighters, shaking even what cannot be shaken by their *ojas*; swift as thought, Maruts, in your chariots you have yoked the dappled mares (v4). And when you have yoked them, urging the stone toward the *vāja*, then the streams of the ruddy one break loose, and they drench the earth with waters as one soaks a hide (v5). The sixth verse invites them down: let your swift-gliding teams bear you; come forward with your arms; sit on the *barhis* — a wide seat has been made for you — and take your fill of the sweet draught.

The seventh verse states their standing: strong of themselves, they have grown by greatness, they have stood in the vault and made a wide seat, and when Viṣṇu helped the exhilarating bull, they sat down like birds on the dear *barhis*. The eighth describes the effect they have: like heroes, like men eager for fame, they contend in the fights; all beings fear the Maruts; they are men who look like kings, *tveṣasandṛśaḥ*, terrible to see.

The ninth verse hands the credit elsewhere for a moment. When Tvaṣṭṛ, the skilled worker, turned the well-made golden bolt with a thousand edges, {{indra}} took it up to do heroic deeds — *ahan vṛtraṃ nir apām aubjat arṇavam*, he slew Vṛtra and forced out the flood of waters. The Maruts' hymn pauses to record whose weapon it was and who used it, because what comes next is the Maruts doing something of the same kind on a smaller scale.

The tenth verse: by their strength they pushed the well upward, and split the mountain though it stood firm; blowing on the *vāṇa*, the Maruts, good givers, in the exhilaration of {{soma}} did their delightful deeds. The eleventh makes it personal and local. *Jihmaṃ nunudre avataṃ tayā diśā* — they pushed the slanting well in that direction, and *asiñcann utsaṃ gotamāya tṛṣṇaje*, they poured out the spring for Gotama who was thirsty. They come to him with help, of many-coloured brilliance, and satisfy the sage's desire with their *dhāman*s. Everything the hymn has been describing — the ornaments, the spears, the shaking of what cannot be shaken — comes down in the end to water reaching one thirsty man.

The twelfth verse asks for the same on the reciter's behalf. The *śarman*, the shelters, that you have for the one who has laboured and given, *tridhātūni*, threefold — extend these to us as well, and grant us *rayi* with good offspring. The hymn that opened with gods dressing for a journey ends by asking for the same shelter the thirsty sage received.
85.practice:
The Maruts are the storm troop — Rudra's sons, Pṛśni's sons, riding the dappled mares — and the reason to know them is verse 11. A sage was thirsty. They pushed a well over to where he was.

That is the whole event, and it is preserved as legend: Sāyaṇa records that Gotama, being thirsty, prayed to the Maruts, and they brought a well from a distance to his hermitage. The same episode surfaces again at [[1.88]].4, where the Gotamas "pushed up the well's lid to drink" — two hymns of the same family, four sūktas apart, on the same rescue. A family transmits its own history in its hymns, and this is the piece of it they kept.

What that means for a reader is a correction of scale. The Maruts break mountains in verse 10 and drench the earth in verse 5; in verse 11 they fetch water for one man. The Ṛgveda does not treat these as different orders of act. The powers that split rock are the same powers that answer a thirst, and there is no register-change between the verses.

Verse 12 gives the request to make of them: *śarman*, shelter — the word behind *śaraṇa*, refuge — described as *tridhātu*, threefold, and asked for on behalf of the man who has both laboured (*śaśamāna*) and given (*dāśvān*). Both. Effort and offering, and then shelter.

The Maruts are also more present in the collection than a reader might guess. The Anukramaṇī names them in the dedication of 46 sūktas and gives 31 to them alone — a larger share than Sarasvatī, Viṣṇu or Pūṣan receive, and second among the maṇḍala's storm-and-sky powers only to Indra himself. Four consecutive sūktas here, this one through [[1.88]], are theirs, which is Gotama's block turning as a whole from Indra to Indra's companions.

And verse 1's image should not be tidied away. *Pra ye śumbhante janayo na* — they adorn themselves like women. Gods who dress before they go out, who fix gleaming things on their bodies, who are described three times in three verses as making themselves beautiful before they do anything at all. Preparation is part of the power, not a preface to it.
85.disagreements:
Verse 3's *gomātaraḥ* is where the readings diverge most. Sāyaṇa glosses it "having for their mother the cow", which Wilson renders as "the sons of earth"; Griffith keeps the literal "Children of the Cow". Since verse 2 has called them *pṛśnimātaraḥ*, sons of Pṛśni — and Pṛśni is a dappled cow — the two epithets are probably one claim, but the witnesses do not connect them.

Verse 5's *aruṣa* Sāyaṇa explains as "radiant", applied either to the sun or to the Agni of lightning as a harbinger of rain; Wilson accordingly writes "the radiant (sun)", Griffith "the dark red stormy cloud". The same word has become two different things in the sky.

Verse 10's *dhamanto vāṇam* Sāyaṇa reads as blowing on a wind instrument, and identifies *vāṇa* as a lute or *vīṇā* of a hundred strings — an odd pairing, blowing on a stringed instrument, which he does not resolve. Wilson prints "blowing upon their pipe"; Griffith avoids it with "sending forth their voice." He also glosses *avata* as *kūpa*, a well, citing the Nirukta, which is what makes verses 10 and 11 a single episode rather than two images.

Verse 7 divides them entirely. Wilson has Viṣṇu defending the sacrifice; Griffith has "When Visnu saved the Soma bringing wild delight." The padapāṭha's *viṣṇur yad hāvat vṛṣaṇaṃ madacyutam* supports Griffith's object.

86.title: Maruts, Hear — Ten Short Verses, Ending in Light
86.synthesis:
Ten gāyatrī verses, the shortest of Gotama's four {{marut}} hymns, and the plainest. There is almost no description in it. Where [[1.85]] spent six verses on how they look, this one spends all ten on the relation between them and a household, and it ends by asking for one thing.

*Maruto yasya hi kṣaye pātha divo vimahasaḥ, sa sugopātamo janaḥ* — Maruts, greatly powerful, from the sky: the man in whose dwelling you drink, that man has the best of guardians (v1). The claim is stated first and everything after it follows from it. The second verse asks to be heard on either of two terms: *yajñair vā yajñavāhasaḥ, viprasya vā matīnām* — whether by sacrifices, you who are carried by sacrifice, or by the thoughts of an inspired man, hear the call. Offering or thought; either channel is open, and the hymn does not rank them.

The third verse describes the outcome for the strong man to whom they have granted an inspired singer: *sa gantā gomati vraje*, he shall go among a pen full of cattle. The fourth locates the whole thing in an actual observance: for this hero the {{soma}} is pressed on the *barhis* *diviṣṭiṣu*, at the daily quests, and the *uktha* is recited and the exhilaration sung. The rite is not occasional; it recurs.

The fifth verse widens the audience: may all beings hear him — the one who surpasses men — and may his food reach as far as the sun. The sixth speaks in the family's own voice and puts a number on the relationship: *pūrvībhir hi dadāśima śaradbhir marutaḥ vayam* — for many autumns we have given to you, Maruts, under the protection of you who watch over the peoples. Not a first approach; a long account.

The seventh states the exchange from the other side: *subhagaḥ sa prayajyavaḥ marutaḥ astu martyaḥ, yasya prayāṃsi parṣatha* — fortunate be that mortal, O Maruts worthy of first worship, whose offerings you carry across. The eighth asks for something more intimate than acceptance: *satyaśavasaḥ*, you of true strength, know the *sveda*, the sweat, of the man who has laboured — know his desire, his longing. The god is asked to be aware not of the offering but of the effort that produced it, and of the wanting behind it.

The ninth turns outward and hard. *Yūyaṃ tat satyaśavasaḥ āviḥ karta mahitvanā* — you of true strength, make this manifest by your greatness: *vidhyata vidyutā rakṣaḥ*, pierce the *rakṣas* with the lightning. The epithet *satyaśavas* is repeated from the previous verse, and the repetition binds the two requests: the strength that knows a man's sweat is the same strength that strikes.

And the tenth is the whole hymn's destination. *Gūhata guhyaṃ tamaḥ, vi yāta viśvam atriṇam, jyotiḥ karta yad uśmasi* — cover up the hidden darkness; drive away every devourer; make the light that we long for. Three imperatives, and the last of them is the only thing the sūkta has asked for on its own account. Ten verses of relationship, protection, long service and mutual knowing, and what they are all for is stated in four words at the end: make the light we want.
86.practice:
The last verse is the one to keep, and it is short enough to keep exactly. *Jyotiḥ karta yad uśmasi* — make the light that we long for. It is the ancestor of a request the tradition never stops making, from *tamaso mā jyotir gamaya* in the Bṛhadāraṇyaka to the *dhiyo yo naḥ pracodayāt* of the Gāyatrī. Here it is asked of the {{marut}}s, the storm troop, and asked at the end of ten verses that were about something else entirely.

Verse 2 is the theologically generous one. *Yajñair vā... viprasya vā matīnām* — by sacrifices, or by the thoughts of an inspired man. The Maruts may be reached either way. Sāyaṇa notices the *vā* and observes that it can also mean *without* sacrifices. A householder who cannot perform the full rite, and a person whose practice is mental rather than material, are both inside verse 2, and the hymn puts them there without argument.

Verse 6 is the one that describes what a family's relationship to a deity actually looks like over time: *pūrvībhiḥ śaradbhiḥ* — for many autumns we have given. Not a transaction but a history, with a count of years behind it. That is the register a family shrine works in.

Verse 8 asks the gods to know a man's *sveda* — his sweat. Not his gift, not his hymn. The physical labour that went into producing them, and the *kāma*, the wanting, that lies under it. This is the Ṛgveda's most economical statement of what it thinks a deity attends to, and it is worth setting against the frequent claim, made from outside, that the Veda's dharma is an exchange and nothing more. Verse 7 has the Maruts carrying a man's offerings across; verse 8 has them knowing what it cost him.

And verse 4 records something about frequency. The soma is pressed *diviṣṭiṣu* — at the recurring daily rites — and the *uktha* is recited each time. The Maruts here are not summoned for storms. They are part of an ordinary schedule.
86.disagreements:
Verse 2's *yajñair vā* draws Sāyaṇa's most consequential note in this hymn: the particle, he says, will also mean *without* sacrifices. That single observation opens the verse to a reading in which the inspired man's thoughts substitute for the rite rather than accompanying it. Neither translator follows him — Wilson prints "with or (without) sacrifices" with the alternative in brackets, Griffith gives simply "Honoured with sacrifice or with the worship of the sages' hymns."

Verse 3's *atakṣata* Sāyaṇa glosses as "have sharpened, i.e. have animated by their offerings", making the priests the agents who whet the Maruts. Wilson follows: "for whom ministrant priests have sharp-ended the sapient (troop)." Griffith reverses the direction entirely — "the strong man to whom ye have vouchsafed to give a sage" — so that the Maruts grant the singer rather than being sharpened by him. The grammar is genuinely unsettled here.

Verse 5 divides them the same way. Wilson has the Maruts hearing the worshipper's praises; Griffith has all beings hearing the worshipper. And verse 8's *venataḥ*, from √ven, to long for, Wilson renders "desirous of (your favour)" and Griffith "him who loves" — the same word applied to Sūrya at [[1.83]].5, where Wilson drops it and Griffith gives "the loving Sun".

87.title: How the Maruts Earned Their Sacrificial Names
87.synthesis:
Six jagatī verses, dense with epithets, and the fifth of them says something the other five have been building toward: the {{marut}}s acquired their ritual names by what they did.

The first verse is one long string of descriptions with no main clause until the end. *Pratvakṣasaḥ pratavasaḥ virapśinaḥ* — of surpassing force, surpassingly strong, overflowing; *anānatāḥ*, unbowed; *avithurāḥ*, unshaking; *ṛjīṣiṇaḥ*, entitled to the *ṛjīṣa*, the residue of the pressing that falls to them at the third service of the day; *juṣṭatamāsaḥ*, most welcome; *nṛtamāsaḥ*, most manly. And then the verb: they have made themselves visible with their ornaments, some few of them, like the sky with its stars. Eight epithets and one act, and the act is being seen.

The second verse gives them their work. When on the slopes you pile up the moving cloud, Maruts, like birds on whatever path — then the buckets pour, wherever they are, upon your chariots; *ghṛtam ukṣata madhuvarṇam arcate*, sprinkle richness, honey-coloured, upon the one who sings. The rain is asked for by the man who is singing about it, and the request is the second half of the verse that describes it.

The third verse is what the ground does. *Pra eṣām ajmeṣu vithurā iva rejate bhūmiḥ* — at their onsets the earth trembles as though unsteady, when on their journeys they yoke for splendour. They are *krīḷayaḥ*, playful; *dhunayaḥ*, roaring; *bhrājadṛṣṭayaḥ*, of gleaming spears; *dhūtayaḥ*, shakers — and *svayaṃ mahitvaṃ panayanta*, they themselves admire their own greatness. The Ṛgveda is not embarrassed by this. The storm's self-delight is part of the description.

The fourth verse turns from spectacle to office. That troop is *svasṛt*, self-moving, *pṛṣadaśva*, borne by dappled mares, *yuvā*, young, lordly, girt with strength — and then: *asi satyaḥ ṛṇayāvā anedyaḥ*, you are true, a pursuer of debt, blameless, *asyāḥ dhiyaḥ prāvitā*, the furtherer of this {{dhī}}, this formed thought. The band that shook the earth two verses ago is now the guarantor of a hymn and a settler of debts.

The fifth verse is the hymn's centre. *Pituḥ pratnasya janmanā vadāmasi* — we speak by the birth from our ancient father; the tongue moves forward at the sight of the {{soma}}. And then the claim: *yad īm indraṃ śamy ṛkvāṇaḥ āśata, ād it nāmāni yajñiyāni dadhire* — when the singers, in the labour of the rite, reached {{indra}}, then and only then did they take on names fit for sacrifice. The Maruts became worth naming in a rite because they stood by Indra when the work was done. A name in the liturgy is earned, not possessed, and this verse says so about gods.

The sixth verse describes the state that follows. For splendour they have been joined with rays, with beams, with singers; *sukhādayaḥ*, well-ringed; *vāśīmantaḥ*, carrying axes; *iṣmiṇaḥ*, impetuous; *abhīravaḥ*, fearless — and *vidre priyasya mārutasya dhāmnaḥ*, they know their own dear Marut station. The hymn ends where a name ends: in a place that belongs to the one who holds it. Six verses of noise and ornament, and the settled point of them is that these gods have a station in the rite, and it was worked for.
87.practice:
The fifth verse is why this hymn matters outside a study of storm gods. *Ād it nāmāni yajñiyāni dadhire* — then indeed they took on names fit for sacrifice. Before that, the {{marut}}s are a band of powers; after it, they are a deity with a place in the liturgy. What made the difference was *śamī*, the labour of the rite, and standing with {{indra}} while it was done.

That is a claim about how anything gets into a liturgy, and it holds for people too. The name a person is called by in a rite — the *gotra*, the *nakṣatra* name, the name given at the *nāmakaraṇa* — is not simply an identifier; it is a standing in a shared work, and the Ṛgveda's account of how even gods acquired theirs runs through participation rather than birth.

Verse 1 preserves an exact ritual fact worth knowing. *Ṛjīṣin*, a standing epithet of the Maruts, means they are entitled to the *ṛjīṣa*, the residue left after the soma has been pressed, and Sāyaṇa specifies when: at the third daily service, the evening pressing. The Maruts have a slot. Their portion is not the first and best of the offering but what remains at the day's last pressing, and they are named for it. A deity's epithet turns out to be a line in a schedule.

Verse 4 gives them a title a modern reader will not expect from a storm: *ṛṇayāvan*, pursuer of debt. Sāyaṇa reads it as freeing the worshipper from debt by making him wealthy. Either way the storm troop is described in the vocabulary of obligations settled, and in the same breath as *asyāḥ dhiyaḥ prāvitā*, furtherer of this thought — the same {{dhī}} that stands behind *dhyāna*. The Maruts advance a man's thinking and clear his debts.

And verse 2 asks for something specific: *ghṛtaṃ ukṣata madhuvarṇam arcate*, sprinkle honey-coloured richness on the one who sings. Sāyaṇa glosses *madhuvarṇa* as *svaccha*, clear, so the colour names a purity rather than a shade. The rain that falls on fields and the reward that falls on a singer are asked for with one verb.
87.disagreements:
Sāyaṇa's note on *ṛjīṣin* in verse 1 is the most substantial ritual detail in the hymn, and it is entirely his. *Ṛjīṣa*, literally a frying-pan, is here a name for the soma residue, and the {{marut}}s are called *ṛjīṣiṇaḥ* because they are entitled to a share of it at the third daily ceremony, the evening worship. He offers an alternative derivation as well — *prārjayitāraḥ rasānām*, acquirers of the juices, from √ṛj, to acquire — and does not choose between them. Wilson prints "inseparable partakers of the evening oblation", folding both in; Griffith gives "impetuous", losing the ritual reference entirely.

The same verse's closing simile divides them. Wilson has the Maruts "conspicuous (in the sky) like certain rays of the sun", following Sāyaṇa, who reads *stṛbhiḥ* as coverings, from √stṛ, to cover — ornaments covering their own persons. Griffith reads *stṛbhiḥ* as stars: "a few in number only, like the heavens with stars." The two produce quite different pictures, and the second is the more natural reading of the word.

Verse 3's *vithurā iva* Wilson expands with an image the padapāṭha does not supply — the earth trembles "like a wife (whose husband is away)" — where Griffith has only "as if weak and worn". Verse 6 divides them as far: Wilson's Maruts obtain "a station agreeable and suitable"; Griffith's "have possessed the Maruts' own beloved home."

88.title: Maruts on Lightning Cars — Gotama's Unmatched Song
88.synthesis:
Six verses, and the last of Gotama's four {{marut}} hymns. It begins as an invitation and ends as a claim about itself, and the two middle verses hold the family's own history.

*Ā vidyunmadbhir marutaḥ svarkair rathebhir yāta ṛṣṭimadbhir aśvaparṇaiḥ* — come, Maruts, on chariots that carry lightning and good chants, armed with spears, winged with horses. Then the simile: *vayo na paptata sumāyāḥ*, fly to us like birds, you of good craft, bringing the most abundant food. Two things arrive in one verse, weather and provisions, and the word for what the Maruts have is *māyā* — skill, contrivance, the making of appearances — used here entirely without suspicion.

The second verse is their approach seen from the ground. With ruddy and tawny horses that speed the chariot they go for splendour; bright like burnished gold, *svadhitivān*, axe-bearing — and *pavyā rathasya jaṅghananta bhūma*, they beat the earth with the felly of the chariot. The rim strikes the ground. Whatever the Maruts are, they are the noise a storm makes when it lands.

The third verse asks for something odd and precise. The *vāśī*, the axe or blade, is on your bodies for splendour — and then: *medhā vanā na kṛṇavante ūrdhvā*, may they stir up our insight as they stir the trees upright. The blade that fells wood is asked to do to a man's *medhā*, his mental grip, what a storm does to a forest. And for you, well-born Maruts, greatly brilliant, the wealthy set the pressing-stone in motion.

The fourth verse turns to the family. *Ahāni gṛdhrāḥ pari ā vaḥ ā aguḥ* — the days, eager ones, have come round to you again, to this *dhī* and to the divine Vārkāryā chant; and *brahma kṛṇvantaḥ gotamāsaḥ arkaiḥ ūrdhvaṃ nunudre utsadhim pibadhyai*, the Gotamas, making the sacred word with their chants, pushed up the covering of the well, to drink. This is the same rescue [[1.85]].11 records — the Maruts pouring out a spring for the thirsty Gotama — told here from the family's side, with the men doing the pushing and a hymn as the lever.

The fifth verse makes the boldest statement in the sūkta. *Etat tyat na yojanam aceti* — no such harnessing was ever known as that which Gotama sang for you, Maruts, when he saw you with golden wheels, iron-tusked, *vidhāvataḥ varāhūn*, boars rushing about. The word for what Gotama made is *yojana*, a yoking — a hymn is described as the harness, the same claim [[1.82]].6 makes when the priest says *I* yoke the bays. And the vision he had is not decorous: gold-wheeled gods with iron tusks charging like wild boar.

The sixth verse closes on the sound the hymn makes. *Eṣā syā vaḥ marutaḥ anubhartrī prati stobhati vāghato na vāṇī* — this is that voice of yours, Maruts, which sustains, which answers back like the voice of a priest; it has resounded freely, according to their own nature, in their two hands. The hymn has become the thing it describes. It began by asking the Maruts to come like birds and ends by saying that the sound now in the air is theirs, given back through a man's mouth and held in the hands that pour.
88.practice:
Verse 3 is the request to make of the {{marut}}s if you make only one. The axes are on their bodies for splendour, and the hymn asks: *medhā vanā na kṛṇavante ūrdhvā* — let them raise our *medhā* as they raise the trees. *Medhā* is mental grip, retentive intelligence, the faculty a student prays for at the beginning of study; the Taittirīya's *medhā-sūkta* and the *medhājanana* rite are built on the word. Here it is asked of a storm, and the image is exact: whatever a gale does to a forest, do that to my thinking.

Verses 4 and 5 are the Gotamas' own record. The well that the Maruts pushed toward the thirsty sage in [[1.85]].11 appears here from the human side — the men pushed up the well's cover, and they did it *brahma kṛṇvantaḥ arkaiḥ*, by making the sacred word with their chants. That is the family's account of what a hymn is for. It moved a lid.

And verse 5 records a claim a modern reader may find surprising in a liturgical text: *etat tyat na yojanam aceti* — no such song was ever known before. The Ṛgveda's poets thought of themselves as making something new. [[1.82]].2 asks the gods to hear a praise offered *naviṣṭhayā matī*, with the newest thought; here Gotama says outright that nothing like his hymn had been heard. Fidelity of transmission is the tradition's later virtue; making something not made before is what these poets thought they were doing.

The vision in that same verse deserves not to be tidied. The Maruts appear to Gotama as *ayodaṃṣṭrān vidhāvato varāhūn*, iron-tusked boars rushing about, on golden wheels. It is the sort of image a person actually sees in a storm, and the tradition kept it exactly as reported.

Four consecutive sūktas, [[1.85]] to 1.88, are given to the Maruts here, and the Anukramaṇī gives them 31 sūktas of their own across the collection and names them in 46. They are not minor.
88.disagreements:
Verse 3 is where the readings diverge furthest, and the divergence is total. Wilson takes the verse as being about weapons and worship: "the threatening (weapons) are upon your persons... (to you) they praise lofty sacrifices, like (tall) trees." Griffith reads *medhā vanā na kṛṇavante ūrdhvā* as a prayer: "As they stir woods so may they stir our spirits." The padapāṭha has *medhā*, insight, and *vanā*, trees, side by side, which supports Griffith; Wilson appears to have taken *medhā* as the sacrifice rather than the faculty.

Verse 4 divides them equally. Wilson has "fortunate days have befallen you, (sons of Gotama), when thirsty"; Griffith has "The days went round you and came back, O yearners". The word *gṛdhrāḥ* — eager, greedy — is applied by Wilson to the Gotamas and by Griffith to the days, and the Sanskrit does not decide it. Both agree on the well and the Gotamas pushing.

Verse 6 divides them most of all. Wilson has the priest's speech glorifying the Maruts "since (you have placed) food in our hands"; Griffith has a Soma draught rushing "like the voice of one who prayeth... freely from our hands". They have read the same sentence as two different subjects.

Sāyaṇa's long note here is on the name rather than any verse. He gives four derivations of *marut* — they sound (*ru*) having reached the middle heaven (*mita*); they sound without measure (*amita*); they shine (*ruc*) in clouds of their own making; they run (*dravanti*) in the sky — and cites the legend of forty-nine Maruts born in seven troops as sons of Kaśyapa.

89.title: Ā No Bhadrāḥ — the Śānti Verses to Viśvedevāḥ
89.synthesis:
Ten verses to the {{viśvedevāḥ}}, and four of them are among the most recited lines in the whole collection. The hymn asks for nothing that could be called a possession. It asks for good thoughts, long life, health, hearing, seeing, and a hundred autumns.

*Ā no bhadrāḥ kratavo yantu viśvataḥ* — may auspicious *kratu*s, resolves that get things done, come to us from every side; *adabdhāsaḥ*, undeceived; *aparītāsaḥ*, unopposed; *udbhidaḥ*, breaking through. And the reason: so that the gods may always be for our increase, unremitting, guardians *dive-dive*, day upon day (v1). What arrives from every side is not wealth but capacities of mind, and the verb is *yantu*, let them come — they are not made, they are received.

The second verse asks for the gods' *sumati*, their good thinking toward us, and their *rāti*, their giving; then something more than either: *devānāṃ sakhyam upa sedima vayam*, we have sat down close to the friendship of the gods. And the request that follows from sitting there — may the gods extend our *āyus* for living. The third calls the roll with an old formula, *pūrvayā nividā*: Bhaga, Mitra, {{aditi}}, Dakṣa, Asridh, Aryaman, Varuṇa, {{soma}}, the {{aśvin}}s — and closes, *sarasvatī naḥ subhagā mayaḥ karat*, may Sarasvatī the fortunate make us joy.

The fourth verse is a healing verse and it names its pharmacy: may Vāta blow to us the *mayobhu bheṣaja*, the medicine that makes wellbeing; may mother Pṛthivī, may father Dyaus, may the soma-pressing stones bring it; Aśvins, on whom the mind rests, hear this. Wind, earth, sky and stone are the sources of the remedy, and the physicians of the gods are asked to listen. The fifth invokes the lord of what moves and what stands, *dhiyaṃjinva* — the quickener of {{dhī}}, of formed thought — and asks that Pūṣan be an undeceived guardian *svastaye*, for wellbeing.

The sixth verse repeats one word four times. *Svasti naḥ indro vṛddhaśravāḥ, svasti naḥ pūṣā viśvavedāḥ, svasti nas tārkṣyo ariṣṭanemiḥ, svasti no bṛhaspatir dadhātu* — may Indra of grown fame, Pūṣan who knows all, Tārkṣya of unbroken felly, and Bṛhaspati establish *svasti* for us. Four gods, four times *svasti*, one verb at the very end holding all of them.

The seventh brings the {{marut}}s in: dappled-horsed, sons of Pṛśni, going in splendour, frequenters of the assemblies, *agnijihvāḥ*, Agni-tongued, wise, sun-eyed — may all the gods come here with help. The eighth is the hymn's most famous line and it asks for the senses. *Bhadraṃ karṇebhiḥ śṛṇuyāma devāḥ, bhadraṃ paśyema akṣabhir yajatrāḥ* — may we hear what is good with our ears, may we see what is good with our eyes; and with firm limbs and bodies, having praised, may we attain the span of life the gods appointed. *Bhadra*, twice, the same word that opened verse 1 as the quality of the *kratu*s. What comes from every side in verse 1 is what the ears are asked to catch in verse 8.

The ninth verse is unusually specific about the shape of a life: a hundred autumns stand before us, in whose course you bring our bodies to age and in whose course our sons become fathers in turn — *mā naḥ madhyā ririṣata āyur gantoḥ*, do not injure our life in mid-passage. Not a plea against death; a plea against interruption.

And the tenth dissolves into a single name. *Aditir dyaur aditir antarikṣam, aditir mātā sa pitā sa putraḥ, viśve devā aditiḥ pañca janāḥ, aditir jātam aditir janitvam* — Aditi is the sky, Aditi the mid-region; Aditi is mother, father, son; Aditi is all the gods and the five peoples; Aditi is what has been born and what is to be born. Ten verses that asked for good thoughts, health and length of days end by naming one goddess as everything that was asked from.
89.practice:
This is one of the most widely recited sūktas in the Ṛgveda, and a Hindu reader almost certainly knows parts of it already without knowing where they come from.

Verse 8 — *bhadraṃ karṇebhiḥ śṛṇuyāma devāḥ* — is the *śānti* attached to the study of the Atharvavedic Upaniṣads, recited before and after the Praśna, Muṇḍaka and Māṇḍūkya. Verse 6, *svasti na indro vṛddhaśravāḥ*, is recited alongside it and independently as a *svasti-vācana*. Verse 1, *ā no bhadrāḥ kratavo yantu viśvataḥ*, is quoted more often than any other line of the Ṛgveda in modern Indian public speech. All three are in this one hymn, which is Gotama Rāhūgaṇa's, and which the Anukramaṇī assigns to no single deity but to the Viśvedevāḥ.

What verse 8 asks for is worth noticing precisely, because it is often loosely quoted. It does not ask to hear well. It asks to hear *bhadram*, what is good — and to see what is good, and to have limbs firm enough to last the appointed span. The prayer is about what the senses are turned toward, not their acuity.

Verse 9 gives the frame that the whole tradition afterwards uses for a lifetime: *śataṃ śaradaḥ*, a hundred autumns, with the natural handover in the middle — *putrāso yatra pitaro bhavanti*, where sons become fathers in turn. The blessing *jīvema śaradaḥ śatam* said at saṃskāras rests on this verse. What it asks is not immortality but an uninterrupted arc: do not break us in mid-passage.

Verse 4 is the one to know when illness is the reason for opening the book. It asks Vāta, Pṛthivī, Dyaus and the pressing-stones for *bheṣaja*, medicine, and it addresses the request to the Aśvins, whom the tradition keeps as *devānāṃ bhiṣajau*, physicians of the gods. Āyurveda's self-understanding as a Vedic science begins in verses like this one.

And verse 10 is the collection's fullest statement about Aditi — sky, mid-region, mother, father, son, all the gods, the five peoples, what is born and what will be born. The Anukramaṇī gives no sūkta in the Ṛgveda to Aditi alone. She is named inside other people's hymns, and this is the verse in which the naming becomes total.
89.disagreements:
The names in verse 3 are where Sāyaṇa supplies the most, and his identifications are not all obvious from the words. Bhaga and Mitra are Ādityas, Mitra the lord of the day; *dakṣa* is a Prajāpati, and he cites the Taittirīya Saṃhitā's *prāṇo vai dakṣaḥ*, dakṣa is verily breath; *asridh* he derives from √sridh, to dry up, hence undrying, and takes as the class of {{marut}}s — where both translators keep it as an epithet of Dakṣa or leave it standing alone. Aryaman he identifies with the sun on the authority of the Taittirīya Saṃhitā. On the {{aśvin}}s he records the whole range without choosing: named from having horses, or from pervading with moisture and with light; they are heaven and earth, day and night, sun and moon; and the *aitihāsika*s hold they were two virtuous princes, citing the Nirukta.

Verse 6's Tārkṣya draws his most specific note: son of Tṛkṣa, he is Garuḍa, and *ariṣṭanemi* means one whose weapons — or whose wheel-rim — are unbroken; he adds that Ariṣṭanemi is a Prajāpati in the Vāyu Purāṇa, and that Tārkṣya may be Aruṇa, the personified dawn. Wilson prints only "Tārkṣya, with unblemished weapons"; Griffith gives "Tarksya with uninjured fellies."

Wilson's verse 6 omits Bṛhaspati from the English altogether, though he stands in the padapāṭha and Griffith renders him. On verse 10's "five peoples" Sāyaṇa lists gandharvas, pitṛs, gods, asuras and rākṣasas; the phrase is more usually taken of human tribes, and neither translator commits.

90.title: Madhu Nine Times, and Śaṃ No Mitraḥ to Close
90.synthesis:
Nine short verses to the {{viśvedevāḥ}}, and the hymn arrives twice at a formula that outlived it. It opens on straight paths and ends on peace, and between them are three verses that say *madhu*, honey, nine times.

*Ṛjunītī no varuṇo mitro nayatu vidvān, aryamā devaiḥ sajoṣāḥ* — may Varuṇa lead us by straight guidance, and Mitra who knows, and Aryaman in accord with the gods (v1). Straightness is the first request, and it is a request about the road rather than the destination. The second verse says why these three can be asked: they are *vasvaḥ vasavānāḥ*, dispensers of what is good, *apramūrāḥ*, never confused, and *vratā rakṣante viśvāhā*, they guard the observances every day. Not occasionally. Every day, and without losing track.

The third verse asks what follows from that: may they, the immortals, hold out *śarman*, shelter, to us mortals, driving away hostilities. The fourth widens the list — may {{indra}}, the {{marut}}s, Pūṣan and Bhaga, worthy of praise, mark out our paths *suvitāya*, for good going. The road of verse 1 is being asked for again with different gods. And the fifth makes the request domestic: *uta no dhiyo goagrāḥ*, and may our thoughts have cattle at their head — Pūṣan, Viṣṇu, you who go swiftly, make us possessors of *svasti*. A *dhī* with cows at its head is a thought that arrives with the herd behind it; the word for wellbeing here is the one the tradition never lets go of.

Then the hymn stops asking and starts declaring. *Madhu vātā ṛtāyate madhu kṣaranti sindhavaḥ, mādhvīr naḥ santu oṣadhīḥ* — the winds are honey for the one who keeps {{ṛta}}, the rivers run honey; may the plants be honey for us (v6). *Madhu naktam uta uṣasaḥ, madhumat pārthivaṃ rajaḥ, madhu dyaur astu naḥ pitā* — honey the night and the dawns, honeyed the earthly region, honey be Dyaus our father (v7). *Madhumān no vanaspatir madhumān astu sūryaḥ, mādhvīr gāvo bhavantu naḥ* — honeyed be the lord of the forest, honeyed the sun, honeyed our cows (v8). Nine occurrences of the word in three verses, three to a verse, and the list runs through wind, river, plant, night, dawn, earth, sky, tree, sun and cattle. Nothing is left out. And it is not a wish for sweetness in the ordinary sense: verse 6 says the winds are honey *ṛtāyate*, for the man who acts in accordance with ṛta. The condition is stated once and then not repeated, and it governs all nine.

The ninth verse closes with five instances of another single syllable. *Śaṃ no mitraḥ śaṃ varuṇaḥ, śaṃ no bhavatv aryamā, śaṃ na indro bṛhaspatiḥ, śaṃ no viṣṇur urukramaḥ* — may Mitra be *śam* to us, and Varuṇa; may Aryaman be *śam*; may Indra and Bṛhaspati; may wide-striding Viṣṇu. *Śam* is not quite "peace" and not quite "wellbeing"; it is the state in which nothing is working against you. The hymn's first verse asked three gods for a straight road; its last asks six for the condition of being unharmed, and the last name in it is Viṣṇu *urukrama*, of the wide stride.
90.practice:
Two things in this hymn are recited daily by people who may not know they come from the Ṛgveda.

Verses 6 to 8 are the *madhu* verses — *madhu vātā ṛtāyate* — among the best-known lines in the collection, recited in auspicious contexts across many traditions. The precise placement differs by śākhā and by family usage, and this text does not determine it, so no single liturgical home should be claimed for them. What can be said from the words themselves is the condition attached in verse 6: the winds are honey *ṛtāyate*, for the one who is acting in accordance with {{ṛta}}. The sweetness of the world is not promised unconditionally. It is described as what the world is like for a person who is in order with it, and there are three verses of it because the claim covers everything — wind, water, plants, night, dawn, ground, sky, tree, sun, cattle.

Verse 9 is more precisely traceable. *Śaṃ no mitraḥ śaṃ varuṇaḥ* is the opening of the *śānti* recited before and after the Taittirīya Upaniṣad, where these lines stand at the head of the Śīkṣāvallī with the *namo brahmaṇe* continuation added. A student beginning the Taittirīya begins with this verse of Gotama's.

The word *śam* is worth pausing on, since it is in every *śānti-pāṭha* a Hindu will ever recite. It is not the absence of conflict; it is the condition in which what surrounds you is not working against you — the same root that gives *śānti*, and the same idea behind the closing *oṃ śāntiḥ śāntiḥ śāntiḥ*. Verse 9 asks it of six named gods in five clauses, and the syllable itself is what the verse is made of.

Read with [[1.89]] immediately before it, the pair form a single movement: 1.89 asks for good thoughts, health, hearing, seeing and a hundred autumns; 1.90 asks for a straight road, a sweet world, and the state of being unharmed. Between them they supply a large share of the *śānti* verses in living use, and both are Gotama Rāhūgaṇa's.
90.disagreements:
This hymn attracts less commentary than its fame would suggest, and where Sāyaṇa does speak he is glossing single words rather than settling disputes. On verse 5 he explains *evayāvaḥ* as the winds, that is the troops of {{marut}}s, because they go with horses, *evaiḥ* — so the "swift-goers" whom Wilson names as Maruts and Griffith leaves as an epithet of Pūṣan and Viṣṇu are, on his reading, a third party. He glosses Viṣṇu simply as the pervading deity. On verse 7 he cites the Nirukta for *rajas* meaning the worlds, which is why Wilson prints "the region of the earth" with the citation in his note.

Verse 2 divides the translations mildly but instructively. Wilson has Mitra and Varuṇa "discharge their functions every day"; Griffith has them "Guard evermore the holy laws". The padapāṭha reads *vratā rakṣante viśvāhā*, they guard the *vrata*s always — the observances, which are both the gods' own fixed courses and the rites men perform. Griffith's "laws" narrows it one way and Wilson's "functions" the other.

Verse 5's *dhiyo goagrāḥ* is rendered by Wilson as "make our rites restorative of our cattle" and by Griffith as "enrich our hymns with kine". The compound is *go-agra*, having cows at the head, and it is applied to *dhī*, thought — an image neither translation quite keeps.

91.title: Soma as King, Healer, and Friend in the Heart
91.synthesis:
Twenty-three verses, and seven of them begin with the same word: *tvam*, you. Verses 1, 2, 5, 6, 7, 8 and 22 open by pointing. This is the longest sustained second-person address in maṇḍala 1, and what it addresses is a plant that has been crushed, strained and poured.

The first four are large. *Tvaṃ soma pra cikito manīṣā* — you, {{soma}}, are pre-eminent by insight; you lead along the straightest path; by your leading our fathers, the wise, obtained the treasure among the gods (v1). You are *sukratu* by *kratu*s, *sudakṣa* by *dakṣa*s, all-knowing, *nṛcakṣas*, watching over men (v2). Then three gods in one verse: yours are the *vrata*s of king Varuṇa; lofty and deep is your *dhāman*, your standing place; you are pure like beloved Mitra, worth honouring like Aryaman (v3). The fourth locates him physically: the *dhāman*s you have in heaven, on earth, in the mountains, in the plants, in the waters — with all of these, well-minded and without anger, king Soma, receive our offerings.

Verses 5 to 16 are short and come quickly. You are *satpati*, lord of the true; king; Vṛtra-slayer; the auspicious *kratu* (v5). If you will it, *jīvātuṃ na marāmahe* — you are our living, we shall not die; lord of the plants, lover of praise (v6). You give *bhaga* and *dakṣa* for living, to the great man and to the young one who keeps {{ṛta}} (v7). Guard us on every side from the malicious; *na riṣyet tvāvataḥ sakhā*, the friend of one like you comes to no harm (v8). Be our protector with those helps that make wellbeing for the giver (v9). Taking pleasure in this *yajña* and this speech, come near and be for our increase (v10). Knowing speech, we make you grow with our songs; enter into us (v11). Then four names in a line: *gayasphāna*, expander of the household; *amīvahā*, slayer of sickness; *vasuvid*, finder of goods; *puṣṭivardhana*, increaser of nourishment — be a good friend to us (v12). And then the verse people remember this hymn for: *soma rarandhi no hṛdi gāvo na yavaseṣu ā, maryo iva sve okye* — Soma, be at ease in our heart, as cattle in fresh pasture, as a young man in his own house (v13). The mortal who delights in your friendship — him *dakṣa* the seer attends (v14). Deliver us from calumny, protect us from *aṃhas*, distress; be a kind friend (v15). Swell; may vigour come to you from every side; be present at the gathering of *vāja* (v16).

The last seven return to the long metre and to growth. Swell, most gladdening, with all your stalks; be a friend of highest fame (v17). May your milks and strengths come together, and the powers that overcome enemies; swelling toward immortality, set the highest renown in heaven (v18). Whatever *dhāman*s of yours men honour with the offering, may they all encompass our sacrifice; expander of the household, carrier-across, no killer of heroes — come to our dwellings (v19). Soma gives a milch-cow, a swift horse, a son able in work — fit for the household seat, the assembly, the council, a credit to his father — to the man who gives (v20). Unconquered in fights, winner of the sun and of the waters, guardian of the community, born in battles, renowned, victorious: after you we would rejoice (v21). *Tvam imā oṣadhīḥ soma viśvāḥ, tvam apo ajanayas tvaṃ gāḥ* — you generated all these plants, the waters, the cattle; you stretched the wide mid-region; you rolled back the darkness with light (v22). And last: with a divine mind, divine Soma, fight for us a share of wealth; let none hold you back; you rule over valour; look ahead for us in the quest for cattle (v23).

Between verse 13, where he is asked to settle in the heart, and verse 22, where he made the plants and the waters, the hymn does not choose. Both are said to the same *tvam*.
91.practice:
Verse 13 is the one to keep. *Soma rarandhi no hṛdi* — Soma, be at ease in our heart — with two similes for what "at ease" means: cattle in fresh pasture, a young man in his own house. Not possession, not visitation. Settledness. It is the most domestic thing said to a god in maṇḍala 1, and it is said to a drink.

Verse 12 is the practical one, and it explains why {{soma}} survives in the tradition's medical vocabulary: *amīvahā*, slayer of sickness; *gayasphāna*, expander of the household; *vasuvid*; *puṣṭivardhana*. Verse 6 goes further — *tvaṃ ca soma no vaśo jīvātuṃ na marāmahe*, if you will it, you are our living and we shall not die — and calls him *vanaspati*, lord of the plants. Sāyaṇa cites the Taittirīya Saṃhitā's *somo vai oṣadhīnāṃ rājā*, Soma is the king of plants, which is the sentence behind every later use of *soma* for the herb-king and for the moon that ripens herbs.

What the plant actually was is one of the genuinely contested questions in the study of the Veda, and this hymn does not settle it. What it does establish is that Soma was addressed as a person — king, friend, healer, guardian of a community, and in verse 22 the generator of plants, waters and cattle.

Verse 20 is worth reading to anyone who thinks the Ṛgveda's requests are vague. It asks for a son who is *karmaṇya*, capable at work; *sadanya*, fit for the household seat; *vidathya*, fit for the assembly; *sabheya*, fit for the council; and *pitṛśravaṇa*, a credit to his father. Five specific competences, three of them public. The Vedic household's idea of a well-raised child included his standing in the assembly.

Soma has the Ṛgveda's ninth maṇḍala nearly to himself: the Anukramaṇī names him in 113 of its 114 sūktas. Outside it he is named in only seventeen more across the whole collection, and just four of those are in maṇḍala 1 — this one, [[1.28]], [[1.43]] and [[1.164]]. Reading it before entering maṇḍala 9 is the right order.
91.disagreements:
A textual fact first: Griffith's Ṛgveda has twenty-two verses here against the twenty-three of the padapāṭha and Wilson. His verse 17 runs two together, and from that point his numbering is one behind, so his "18" answers Wilson's 19 and so on to the end. A reader comparing translations verse by verse in this sūkta will go wrong unless they know it.

Sāyaṇa carries the ritual identifications. On verse 3 he explains *rājño varuṇasya* by way of the soma purchased for a sacrifice and wrapped in cloth, and cites the Taittirīya Saṃhitā's *somo brāhmaṇānāṃ rājā*, soma is the king of the brāhmaṇas — which is why verse 5's *satpati* he glosses twice over, since *sat* may mean the true or may mean the brāhmaṇa. On verse 5 he also identifies Soma with the sacrifice itself, "since sacrifices are accomplished through him", which is a stronger claim than either translation makes. On verse 15 he cites the Nirukta for *uruṣyati* as an act of protection, and on verse 17 the Nirukta for *śravas* meaning food — which is why Wilson's "well supplied with food" stands where Griffith has "most illustrious fame".

On verse 23 Sāyaṇa notes that the hymn alludes both to Soma the product of the earth and to Soma the moon, which is his standing position and the reason the two are one word in later usage. Griffith's text lacks this verse entirely.

92.title: Uṣas Wears Down Our Days — Then the Aśvins Come
92.synthesis:
Eighteen verses, fifteen to {{uṣas}} and three to the {{aśvin}}s, and somewhere in the middle the hymn says something that changes how the first half reads.

The opening is all arrival. These Uṣases have raised their banner; in the eastern half of the region they anoint the light; making ready like bold men burnishing their weapons, the ruddy cows, the mothers, come on (v1). The purple rays have flown up readily; they have yoked the easily-yoked ruddy cows; the Uṣases have made the *vayunāni*, the marks by which things are told apart, as they did before, and set up a shining beam (v2). They sing like women at their work, with one common harnessing, coming from far off, bringing refreshment to the man who does well, who gives, who presses (v3).

Then five verses of her appearing and her effect. She puts on ornaments like a dancer; she bares her breast as a cow yields her udder; making light for the whole world of the living, she has opened the darkness as cattle open their pen (v4). Her white ray has been seen; it spreads and pushes away the black formlessness; like the ornament anointed on the sacrificial post, the daughter of Dyaus has set up her wondrous beam (v5). *Atāriṣma tamasaḥ pāram asya* — we have crossed to the far shore of this darkness; shining out, she makes the marks again; she smiles like a flatterer, for glory, and fair-faced she has woken us to gladness (v6). Shining, leader of *sūnṛtā*, true and generous speech, she is praised by the Gotamas; measure out to us *vāja* with offspring and men, founded on horses, headed by cattle (v7). And: may I obtain that renowned wealth, with heroes and a following, which you shine forth, impelled by strength (v8).

The ninth verse is the turn, and it turns quietly. Having looked over all beings, the goddess shines facing us, wide with her eye; waking every living thing to move, *viśvasya vācam avidat manāyoḥ*, she has found the speech of everyone who thinks. Then the tenth says the other thing. *Punaḥ punar jāyamānā purāṇī, samānaṃ varṇam abhi śumbhamānā* — born again and again, ancient, adorning herself in the same colour — *śvaghnīva kṛtnur vijaḥ āminānā, martasya devī jarayantī āyuḥ*: like a skilled gambler cutting the stakes, the goddess wears away the life of a mortal, ageing it. The dawn that woke everything is the dawn that is spending it.

The eleventh presses it. Uncovering the ends of the sky, she has awoken; she drives her sister far off; *praminatī manuṣyā yugāni*, diminishing the generations of men, the young woman shines with her lover's look. The twelfth restores the balance without cancelling the claim: bright as cattle, fortunate, spreading; like the {{sindhu}} rolling its flood, she has shone out wide; *aminatī daivyāni vratāni*, not injuring the divine observances, she is seen along with Sūrya's rays. She diminishes men's generations and does not diminish the gods' observances; the same verb, twice, three verses apart.

Verses 13 to 15 are three short petitions after all that: bring the wondrous thing by which we may sustain son and grandson (v13); shine richly on us here today, true of speech (v14); yoke your ruddy horses and bring us every good fortune (v15).

Then the Aśvins, and the join is the hour. Turn your chariot toward our house, rich in cattle and gold, of one mind (v16). You two who made the *śloka* out of heaven, a light for men — bring us vigour (v17). And may the *uṣarbudhaḥ*, those awake at dawn, bring here the two gods, makers of wellbeing, wonder-workers, of the golden path, to drink the {{soma}} (v18). The hymn ends by naming the moment it has been describing: the point at which the light has come and the first offering is poured.
92.practice:
Verse 10 is what this hymn is for. *Martasya devī jarayantī āyuḥ* — the goddess, ageing the life of a mortal. Every dawn that arrives is one taken off the count, and the Ṛgveda says it in the middle of a hymn of praise, without resolving it, and then goes on praising. The image is exact and unsentimental: like a skilled gambler cutting the stakes, she takes her share each time. Verse 11 adds the same thought about generations rather than individuals.

That is worth holding beside the fact that {{uṣas}} is the deity of the eastern *sandhyā*. A Hindu who performs *prātaḥ sandhyāvandana* is addressing this hour daily; the *arghya* offered as the sun rises is offered into exactly the interval verse 18 describes, when those awake at dawn bring the gods to drink. What 1.92 adds is that the hour is not only an opportunity. It is also a subtraction, and the tradition placed the recognition of that inside the daily observance rather than outside it.

Uṣas is the Ṛgveda's most substantial goddess by volume. The Anukramaṇī gives twenty sūktas to her alone and names her in thirty-three — against sixteen naming Sarasvatī and one to Sarasvatī alone. Whatever the later tradition did with its goddesses, the Ṛgveda's own largest body of hymns to a feminine deity is to the dawn.

Verse 9 gives her an office worth knowing: *viśvasya vācam avidat manāyoḥ*, she found the speech of everyone who thinks. The dawn is when speech becomes possible again, and the hymn treats that as a discovery she makes rather than a service she performs.

And verse 6 supplies a line a person can take into a hard morning: *atāriṣma tamasaḥ pāram asya* — we have crossed to the far shore of this darkness. It is said in the plural, by people who have got through a night together, and the same verb, √tṝ, is the one Agni is asked for at [[1.97]].8 and [[1.99]].1 when the crossing is over something worse than a night.
92.disagreements:
Verse 4's *nṛtūr iva* draws Sāyaṇa's most interesting note, and Wilson's oddest translation. Sāyaṇa gives two readings: *nṛtū* as a dancing-girl, so that Uṣas displays her graces like a dancer; or, taking *peśāṃsi vapate* as cutting rather than putting on, an image of shearing. Wilson prints the second and produces "Uṣas cuts off the accumulated (glooms), as a barber (cuts off the hair)"; Griffith takes the first, "She, like a dancer, puts her broidered garments on." The verb *vapate* genuinely carries both shearing and strewing, and the two pictures could hardly be less alike.

Verse 1's plural draws the other substantial note. Sāyaṇa observes, citing Yāska, that *uṣasaḥ* is plural used honorifically for one goddess, and glosses *mātaraḥ* as makers or authors — *bhāso nirmātryaḥ*, authors of light — rather than mothers. Wilson keeps "the radiant and progressing mothers"; Griffith keeps "the Mother Cows".
