On verse 11's *jāra* Sāyaṇa is explicit: the word means the causer of the night's decay, and he identifies it with Sūrya — which turns "the young woman shines with her lover's look" into an astronomical statement. Wilson prints "like the bride of the sun"; Griffith keeps "her lover's splendour" without identifying him.

Verse 12's *aminatī daivyāni vratāni* Sāyaṇa glosses with a cross-reference to [[5.77]].2, that sacrifice is not acceptable to the gods at night or in the evening — so the observances Uṣas does not injure are specifically the rites that require daylight.

93.title: Agni and Soma Together — Their Only Sūkta
93.synthesis:
Twelve verses addressed to a pair, and the pair is named in every one of them. *Agnīṣomā* or *agnīṣomau* stands in all twelve verses and opens nine of them, which is as insistent as the Ṛgveda gets about a dual deity. Two of the tradition's largest powers are being spoken to as one thing with two names.

The first three verses are the ordinary business of a rite, done twice over. Hear this call of mine, you bulls; welcome the well-made words; be *mayas*, joy, to the giver (v1). To whoever honours this speech of yours today, grant *suvīrya*, an increase of cattle, good horses (v2). Whoever gives you the poured offering and the making of *havis* — may he enjoy heroic strength with offspring, through a whole lifetime (v3). Nothing distinguishes these from a hundred other opening verses except that everything is dual: the hearing, the welcoming, the giving.

Then three verses of what the two have done together, and they are startling. *Agnīṣomā ceti tad vīryaṃ vām* — known is that heroic deed of yours, by which *amuṣṇītam avasaṃ paṇiṃ gāḥ*, you stole the cows that were the {{paṇi}}'s food; you sent down the offspring of Bṛsaya; and *avindataṃ jyotir ekaṃ bahubhyaḥ*, you found the one light for the many (v4). The cattle-raid that maṇḍala 1 elsewhere gives to {{indra}} and to the Aṅgirases is here credited to these two, and the finding of the one light for the many is put in the same breath. The fifth verse continues: acting with one *kratu*, you two set these shining lights in the sky, and you released the rivers from curse and from disgrace when they had been seized. The sixth tells where each of them came from: *ā anyaṃ divo mātariśvā jabhāra* — Mātariśvan brought one of you from heaven; *amathnād anyaṃ pari śyeno adreḥ*, the hawk wrenched the other from the rock. Grown great by *brahman*, the sacred word, *uruṃ yajñāya cakrathur u lokam*, you two made a wide space for the sacrifice. Two separate arrivals, and one result: room to perform in.

The last six return to the reciter's own case, and they are quieter. Partake of the offering set forth; take pleasure in it, bulls; be of good shelter and good help, and grant the sacrificer *śaṃ ca yoḥ*, wellbeing and long freedom from harm (v7). Whoever honours you with *havis* and with ghee, with a god-directed mind — guard his observance, protect him from *aṃhas*, distress, and hold out great *śarman* to his clan and his people (v8). Of like wealth, called together by one invocation, accept our songs: *saṃ devatrā babhūvathuḥ*, you two have been together among the gods (v9). To the man who gives you this ghee, shine forth abundantly (v10). Be pleased with these our offerings, and come to us together (v11). And last, the household list: cherish our horses; may our milch-cows, providers of the offering, grow full; place strengths in us and in our liberal patrons; and *kṛṇutaṃ no adhvaraṃ śruṣṭimantam*, make our rite one that is heard (v12).

The hymn's whole argument is in its grammar. Two deities who could not be less alike — one is fire, the other is a drink pressed from a plant, one consumes the offering and the other is the offering — are addressed in the dual, twelve times, and asked for a single set of things. The fourth and sixth verses supply the reason: they act with one *kratu*, and what they made together was space for a rite to happen in.
93.practice:
This is the only sūkta in the entire Ṛgveda dedicated to Agnīṣomau. Across 1,028 hymns the Anukramaṇī names this pair once, here. That is worth knowing before anything else about it: the joint deity is real, it is institutionally important, and it has exactly one hymn.

The pairing is not a poetic conceit. {{agni}} and {{soma}} are the two poles of every offering — Agni that receives and the substance that is given — and Sāyaṇa preserves the tradition's own formulation of it: *rājānau vā etau devānāṃ yad agnīṣomau*, Agni and Soma are the two kings of the gods. The śrauta system has a standing *āgneya* offering and a standing *agnīṣomīya* one; the exact placements differ by sūtra and this hymn does not determine them, but the pair's institutional life is why a single sūkta can carry it.

Verse 7 hands the reader a formula they already recite. *Śaṃ ca yoḥ* — the two syllables of wellbeing and of long freedom from harm — is the phrase that closes countless *śānti* and *svasti* recitations, usually expanded as *śaṃ yor abhi sravantu naḥ*. Here it is what Agni and Soma are asked to grant the *yajamāna*, and *śam* is the same word repeated five times at [[1.90]].9.

Verse 6's two origins are the tradition's account of how each of them came to be available at all. Mātariśvan brought Agni down from heaven; a hawk tore Soma from the rock. Both had to be fetched. Neither was simply here, and the pair's joint act — *uruṃ yajñāya cakrathur u lokam*, they made wide space for the sacrifice — is what fetching them accomplished. A rite requires room, and this verse says the room was made.

And verse 12 asks for something a reader may not have thought to ask for: *kṛṇutaṃ no adhvaraṃ śruṣṭimantam*, make our rite one that is heard. Not larger, not more correct. Heard. The anxiety that a rite might be performed properly and simply not land is old, and it is stated in the last line of the only hymn these two gods share.
93.disagreements:
Verse 4's Bṛsaya draws Sāyaṇa's largest note and the translations do not touch it. *Bṛsayasya śeṣaḥ*, he says, is Bṛsaya's offspring, citing the Nirukta; Bṛsaya he identifies with Tvaṣṭṛ, an asura, whose offspring is Vṛtra. He then explains how {{agni}} and {{soma}} could be the agents of Vṛtra's death by identifying the two with *prāṇa* and *apāna*, the two vital airs, whose separation from Vṛtra was the cause of his dying, citing the Taittirīya Saṃhitā — and adds that with the enveloping cloud destroyed the sun could appear. Neither Wilson nor Griffith goes beyond "the brood of Brsaya".

Verse 5 draws a second legend. Sāyaṇa reports that the imputation the rivers are freed from is the *brahmahatyā* incurred by {{indra}} in killing Vṛtra at [[1.32]], the guilt of which was distributed to rivers, women and trees; and an alternative, that the rivers were defiled by Vṛtra's corpse falling into them and were unfit for sacred use until purified by oblations to fire and libations of soma. Wilson prints only "the notorious imputation"; Griffith gives "From curse and from reproach... ye freed the rivers".

On verse 6 Sāyaṇa names the agents: Vāyu brought Agni from heaven at Bhṛgu's wish, and Gāyatrī in the form of a hawk brought Soma from the summit of Meru — and adds, unusually plainly, that the allusion is to the early use of fire and soma in ceremonies. Griffith keeps Mātariśvan; Wilson translates him as "the wind".

94.title: Agni's Friendship — a Refrain Said Fourteen Times
94.synthesis:
Sixteen verses, and fourteen of them end with the same line: *agne sakhye mā riṣāma vayaṃ tava* — Agni, may we not be harmed in your friendship. Not "protect us", not "give us". May we not come to harm inside a relationship we are already in. The word is *sakhya*, the bond between companions, and everything in the hymn is arranged around it.

The first verse says what the hymn is: *imaṃ stomam arhate jātavedase rathaṃ iva saṃ mahema manīṣayā* — this praise for the worthy Jātavedas we fit together with our insight as a chariot is put together. A hymn is built, part by part, and the maker knows it. Good is our forethought in his assembly. The second states the result: for whom you sacrifice, he succeeds, dwells unassailed, gains heroic strength, prospers, and *na enam aśnoti aṃhatiḥ*, distress does not reach him.

Two verses on the work itself. May we be able to kindle you; *sādhaya dhiyaḥ*, perfect our thoughts; in you the gods eat the offering; bring the Ādityas, for we long for them (v3). We bring the fuel and make the offerings, *citayantaḥ parvaṇā parvaṇā*, attentive at each joint of the year — perfect our thoughts further, that we may live (v4). *Sādhaya dhiyaḥ* twice in two verses: the request is that the mind be brought to completion, made in the same breath as bringing firewood.

The fifth describes his reach — the guardians of the clans move about, and two-footed and four-footed alike are lit by his beams; wondrous is the herald of the dawn, and you are great. The sixth is the fullest office list in the collection: *tvam adhvaryur uta hotāsi pūrvyaḥ, praśāstā potā januṣā purohitaḥ* — you are the *adhvaryu* who performs, the ancient *hotā* who calls, the *praśāstṛ* who directs, the *potṛ* who purifies, and by birth the *purohita* placed in front. Knowing all the priestly functions, you carry them out.

The seventh is about sight: fair-faced on every side, you shine like lightning even when far, and *rātryāś cid andhaḥ ati deva paśyasi*, you see past even the blindness of night. The eighth asks for advantage: let the presser's chariot go first, and let our word prevail over the ill-minded. The ninth is blunt: strike down with your weapons those of evil speech and evil thought, far or near, and then make an easy road for the singer.

Verses 10 and 11 leave the enclosure and describe a fire in a forest. When you have yoked the ruddy red ones, wind-driven, your roar is like a bull's, and *ād invasi vaninaḥ dhūmaketunā*, you attack the trees with a banner of smoke (v10). At your sound even the birds are frightened, when your grass-eating sparks fly out — and then the going is easy for you and your chariots (v11). The refrain follows both. Whatever Agni is in the enclosure, this is what he is in the open, and the hymn asks not to be harmed in the friendship of that too.

The twelfth turns to other gods: this one sustains Mitra and Varuṇa; wondrous is the anger of the descending Maruts — be gracious, and let their mind turn toward us again. The thirteenth names his standing: *vasur vasūnām*, the Vasu among Vasus, wondrous friend of the gods, lovely in the rite; may we be within your widest *śarman*. The fourteenth names his best gift and its place: kindled in your own house, invoked with {{soma}}, you sound most gracious, and *dadhāsi ratnaṃ draviṇaṃ ca dāśuṣe*, you set treasure and substance before the giver. That is the last refrain.

The last two drop it. To whom you grant *anāgāstva*, sinlessness, whole and entire, and whom you urge on with auspicious strength — may we be that man, with bounty that carries offspring (v15). And: knowing what good fortune is, prolong our life here; *tan no mitro varuṇo mamahantām aditiḥ sindhuḥ pṛthivī uta dyauḥ* — may Mitra, Varuṇa, {{aditi}}, {{sindhu}}, Earth and Heaven grant us that (v16).
94.practice:
What this hymn asks for, fourteen times, is worth stating exactly, because it is not what most prayers ask. *Sakhye mā riṣāma vayaṃ tava* — may we not be harmed in your friendship. The relationship is assumed. The worry is that being close to {{agni}} is itself dangerous, and verses 10 and 11 say why: this is the same power that roars like a bull through a forest and drives birds off in terror. The hymn does not resolve the tension. It asks to stand near without being burnt, and it asks fourteen times.

Anyone who keeps a fire in the house — the lamp, the *homa*, the *agnihotra* — is inside the situation the refrain describes. So is anyone whose relation to a teacher, an institution or a power is close enough to be useful and close enough to be costly.

Verse 6 is the most complete statement in the Ṛgveda of the priestly offices, and it is worth learning as a list: *adhvaryu*, who does the physical work of the rite; *hotā*, who calls and offers; *praśāstṛ*, who directs the others; *potṛ*, who purifies; *purohita*, placed in front. Sāyaṇa adds the identification that gives the list its point — Agni is chief of the sixteen priests employed at a solemn sacrifice, and is to men what Bṛhaspati is to the gods, citing the Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa. A householder who has watched a large rite and wondered what each man was for has the answer in one verse.

Verse 3 and verse 4 both say *sādhaya dhiyaḥ* — perfect our thoughts. Not "grant our wishes". The petition is that the {{dhī}}, the formed thought, be brought to completion, and it is made twice, in the same verses that mention bringing firewood and attending to each joint of the year. Material preparation and mental completion are the same request here.

The last verse's closing line is not this hymn's alone. *Tan no mitro varuṇo mamahantām aditiḥ sindhuḥ pṛthivī uta dyauḥ* appears twenty times in the Ṛgveda: nineteen of them in maṇḍala 1, closing this sūkta and nearly every one from here to [[1.115]] — the exceptions being [[1.97]], [[1.99]] and 1.104 — and once more at 9.97.58. It is the seal on a long stretch of the collection, and 1.94 is where it starts.
94.disagreements:
Sāyaṇa's note on verse 6 is the substantial one and it goes well beyond both translations. Agni, he says, is the chief of the sixteen priests engaged at solemn sacrifices: he is the *adhvaryu*, reciter of the Yajus, defined as presenter of the offerings; the *hotā*, invoking priest; the *prastotṛ* or *maitrāvaruṇa*, who directs the other priests what to do and when; and the *potṛ* and hereditary *purohita* or *brahman* of the ceremony — being to men what Bṛhaspati is to the gods, on the Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa's authority. Wilson prints the offices as a list with brackets; Griffith renders them as titles without explanation.

On verse 8 Sāyaṇa makes a large claim in passing: all gods are but portions or members of Agni. Neither translation carries it, and the verse itself only addresses *devāḥ* in the vocative.

Verse 5 divides the translations completely. Wilson has Agni's flames as "the preservers of mankind" and reads the last clause as "you are superior to the dawn"; Griffith has "Mighty art thou, the wondrous herald of the Dawn." The padapāṭha's *citraḥ praketaḥ uṣasaḥ mahān asi* supports Griffith — Agni is the dawn's herald, not her superior.

Sāyaṇa's note on verse 16 is the one that matters for reading forward: this closing line, he says, terminates the following sūktas from 95 to 101, with two exceptions. The padapāṭha shows the line running further than that — through 1.115, skipping [[1.97]], [[1.99]] and 1.104 — so his count is an approximation of a real and much longer pattern.

95.title: Two Mothers, Ten Maidens, Three Births of Agni
95.synthesis:
Eleven triṣṭubh verses, and the first four are riddles. This is the most enigmatic of Kutsa's Agni hymns, and it works by describing {{agni}} entirely through his relations — who bears him, who tends him, where he comes out — without once saying what he is.

*Dve virūpe carataḥ svarthe anyānyā vatsam upa dhāpayete* — two of unlike form move, each toward its own end; one after the other they suckle the calf. In one he is *hari*, golden, *svadhāvān*, self-sustaining; in the other he is seen bright and of fair lustre (v1). Two mothers, one child, and the child looks different in each. The second verse changes the number: *daśa imaṃ tvaṣṭur janayanta garbham* — ten unwearied young women beget this embryo of Tvaṣṭṛ, borne apart, sharp-faced, self-glorious, shining among men; they lead him around. Ten now, and the ten are unmarried, and what they beget is called Tvaṣṭṛ's.

The third counts births rather than mothers. *Trīṇi jānā pari bhūṣanti asya* — three of his births they honour: one in the ocean, one in heaven, one in the waters. And then, without transition, an act of government: ruling over the eastern quarter of the earthly regions, *ṛtūn praśāsad vi dadhau anuṣṭhu*, he ordained the seasons in their proper order. The one who has three births is the one who set the calendar.

The fourth asks the reader directly. *Ka imaṃ vo niṇyam ā ciketa* — which of you has perceived this hidden one? *Vatso mātṝr janayata svadhābhiḥ*: the calf begot his own mothers by his own power. The embryo of many working ones, he goes forth from the lap; great, a *kavi*, self-sustaining. That is the hymn's centre. Whatever else is being said, it is being said about something that produces what produces it.

From verse 5 the riddles resolve into description. Manifest, dear, he grows among them, rising upright in the lap of the crooked waters, self-glorious; both worlds were afraid at his birth, and turning back toward him they welcome the lion (v5). The two auspicious ones tend him like women; like lowing cows they came to him by their own paths; he became lord of powers among the powers, whom they anoint from the right with offerings (v6). Like Savitṛ he stretches up his two arms; terrible, he strives, grasping both borders; he drives a bright garment out of everything, and from his mothers he draws new clothing (v7).

The eighth verse turns technical and then, in its last words, turns theological. He makes for himself a higher, brilliant form, mingling in the seat with the cows and the waters; the *kavi* burnishes the depth — and *dhīḥ sā devatātā samitir babhūva*, that {{dhī}} became the assembly at the worship of the gods. A formed thought is the meeting-place. The ninth asks for protection in the ordinary way: wide is your onrush, going round the depth, the shining station of the buffalo; kindled by us, Agni, protect us with all your self-glorious, undeceived guardians.

The tenth returns to water, and it is the most concrete verse in the hymn. *Dhanvan srotaḥ kṛṇute gātum ūrmim* — in dry ground he makes a stream, a course, a wave; with bright waves he reaches the earth; *viśvā sanāni jaṭhareṣu dhatte*, he puts all old things into his bellies, and moves about within the new shoots. Fire consuming the dry stubble and fire ripening the next crop are the same verse.

The eleventh closes the way this whole stretch of the collection closes: thus, Agni, growing by our fuel, blaze richly, purifier, for renown — and *tan no mitro varuṇo mamahantām aditiḥ sindhuḥ pṛthivī uta dyauḥ*, may Mitra, Varuṇa, {{aditi}}, {{sindhu}}, Earth and Heaven grant us that.
95.practice:
This hymn is where a reader meets the Vedic riddle, and it is worth meeting deliberately. The Ṛgveda has a whole register of hymns built on unanswered questions — [[1.164]] is the great example — and they are not obscurity for its own sake. They are a way of saying that the thing described exceeds any one description, and the technique is to give several accounts that cannot all be literally true at once.

Here the accounts are: two mothers of unlike form who suckle the calf turn about; ten young women who beget him; three births, in ocean, heaven and waters; and a calf who begot his own mothers. Sāyaṇa's readings are worth having because they are concrete rather than mystical: the two of unlike form are night and day; the ten are either the ten directions, which generate lightning in the clouds through the wind, or the ten fingers, which generate fire in the kindling-sticks by friction. Both are true of {{agni}} at once, and neither exhausts him. A reader who has watched a fire drill turned by ten fingers and then watched lightning has seen the two answers.

Verse 4's *vatso mātṝr janayata* — the calf begot his mothers — is the line the later tradition returns to. Fire generates the smoke and vapour that become the clouds that generate the lightning that is fire. Cause and effect are a circuit rather than a line, and the Ṛgveda states it as a puzzle rather than a doctrine.

Verse 3 gives a Hindu reader something practical: *ṛtūn praśāsad vi dadhau anuṣṭhu*, he ordained the seasons in their proper order. The *ṛtu* declared in every *saṅkalpa* — the season named when the occasion of a rite is stated — is here set in place by Agni himself. The one who carries the offering is the one who fixed the calendar the offering is timed by.

And verse 8's last words are worth keeping alone: *dhīḥ sā devatātā samitir babhūva* — that thought became the assembly at the gods' worship. Where the gods gather is not a place. It is a mind that has been properly formed. Anyone who has wondered what is actually happening when a rite is performed with attention has that half-line to work with.
95.disagreements:
Sāyaṇa carries this hymn and both translators lean on him. On verse 1 he identifies the two of unlike form as night and day, and explains the sequence: day is the mother of fire, which is then as if in embryo and not fully born until dark; the sun is in the womb of night and shines in the morning. He supports it with a Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa citation on the evening offering to {{agni}} and the morning offering to Sūrya. Wilson prints "Two periods, of different complexions"; Griffith keeps the riddle — "To fair goals travel Two unlike in semblance."

On verse 2's "ten" Sāyaṇa offers two readings and does not choose: the ten regions of space, which generate lightning as an embryo in the clouds by means of the winds — *agner hi vāyuḥ kāraṇam*, wind is the cause of fire — or the ten fingers, which generate Agni by friction in the kindling-sticks. Wilson prints the first and supplies "through the wind"; Griffith reads *tvaṣṭur* as a genitive of relation and gives "Tvastar's ten daughters", which is a third possibility neither of the others considers.

Verse 4's *upasthāt* Sāyaṇa glosses as *samudrāt*, from the ocean, on the reading that Agni rises in the morning from the sea in the form of the sun. Wilson follows; Griffith has "from the waters' bosom".

On verse 5's *siṃha*, lion, Sāyaṇa gives an unexpected derivation — *sahanaśīlam*, from the capacity to bear or to overcome — so that the epithet names endurance rather than the animal. Neither translation registers it.

96.title: Agni Draviṇodā, Whom the Gods Hold as Wealth-Giver
96.synthesis:
Nine verses, and seven of them close with one line: *devā agniṃ dhārayan draviṇodām* — the gods held {{agni}}, the giver of substance. Not "we praise" and not "may he give". A statement about what the gods did, repeated until it settles, and the last two verses then do something with it.

The first verse gives him his origin and his equipment at once. *Sa pratnathā sahasā jāyamānaḥ* — he, in the ancient manner, being born by force, at once took to himself all the *kāvya*s, the seer-powers; and *āpaś ca mitraṃ dhiṣaṇā ca sādhan*, the waters and Dhiṣaṇā made him their friend. Born of force and immediately in possession of wisdom, and the first thing that happens to him is friendship.

The second makes him a creator. By the ancient *nivid*, by the seerhood of Āyu, he generated these progenies of the Manus; and with a pervading eye, the sky and the waters. An old formula and one man's insight are given as the means. The third is the human response: him the Ārya clans praise as first, *yajñasādham*, the accomplisher of the sacrifice, offered to, straightening things out — *ūrjaḥ putram*, son of nourishment, *bharatam*, the sustainer, *sṛpradānum*, of flowing gifts.

The fourth widens his offices: he, Mātariśvan, nourishing with many choice things, found the path for his offspring, winner of light; guardian of the clans, begetter of the two worlds. The fifth is the loveliest verse in the sūkta and the quietest. *Naktoṣāsā varṇam āmemyāne dhāpayete śiśum ekam samīcī* — night and dawn, exchanging each other's colour, meeting together, suckle one and the same child; golden, he shines between earth and heaven. The image [[1.95]].1 posed as a riddle is here stated plainly, and the child is not named.

The sixth verse is the fullest list of what he is: the root of riches, the meeting-place of goods, *yajñasya ketuḥ*, the banner of the sacrifice, *manmasādhanaḥ*, the accomplisher of formed thought — and then the reason for the refrain, stated at last: *veḥ amṛtatvaṃ rakṣamāṇāsaḥ enam*, guarding him as their own immortality, the gods held him as the giver of substance. Six verses have said "the gods held Agni"; the sixth says why. He is what they are keeping alive by.

The seventh puts him in time: now and formerly the seat of riches; the ground of what has been born and what is being born; guardian of what is and of much that is coming to be. And then the seventh refrain, and it is the last.

The eighth verse abandons the sentence and repeats a single name four times. *Draviṇodā draviṇaso turasya, draviṇodā sanarasya pra yaṃsat, draviṇodā vīravatīm iṣaṃ naḥ, draviṇodā rāsate dīrgham āyuḥ* — may the wealth-giver grant swift wealth; may the wealth-giver grant abiding wealth; may the wealth-giver grant us nourishment with heroes; may the wealth-giver bestow long life. The epithet that has stood at the end of seven verses becomes the subject of four clauses in one. What the gods held is now what is being asked from.

The ninth verse closes with the line that closes this whole stretch of maṇḍala 1: thus, Agni, growing by our fuel, blaze richly, purifier, for renown; and *tan no mitro varuṇo mamahantām aditiḥ sindhuḥ pṛthivī uta dyauḥ* — may Mitra, Varuṇa, {{aditi}}, {{sindhu}}, Earth and Heaven grant us that. It is the same verse that closes [[1.95]], word for word.
96.practice:
*Draviṇodā* is the word to take from this hymn, and it repays being taken exactly. *Draviṇa* is substance — movable goods, the stuff a household actually runs on — and *-dā* is the giver. Verse 8 asks for four kinds of it in four clauses: *draviṇaso turasya*, wealth that moves quickly; *sanarasya*, wealth that stays; nourishment attended by heroes; and long life. Speed, permanence, people and time. It is a more careful list than most prayers manage, and it is worth using as one.

But the refrain says something the petition does not, and the two should be read together. Seven verses end *devā agniṃ dhārayan draviṇodām* — **the gods** held Agni as the wealth-giver — and verse 6 explains it: they did it *amṛtatvaṃ rakṣamāṇāsaḥ*, guarding their own immortality. {{agni}} is not primarily a source of goods for men. He is what the gods themselves depend on, and men are asking from the same channel the gods use. That is the theology behind the ordinary act of pouring ghee.

Verse 5 is the one to keep for its own sake. Night and dawn exchange colours, meet, and nurse the same child between them, and he shines gold between earth and sky. It is what a fire looks like at the turn of the night, and it is also the plainest statement in the collection of why the *sandhyā* junctures matter: the hour where one hands over to the other is where the child is being fed.

Verse 6 names Agni *manmasādhana*, the accomplisher of the formed thought, in the same line that names him *yajñasya ketuḥ*, the banner of the sacrifice. This is the recurring Kutsa concern — [[1.94]].3 and 4 both ask *sādhaya dhiyaḥ*, perfect our thoughts — and it locates the whole enterprise correctly. What the rite completes is a mind.

This is the third of five Agni sūktas by Kutsa Āṅgirasa running from [[1.94]] to [[1.98]], the beginning of a block the Anukramaṇī gives him: twenty sūktas in all, 1.94–1.98 and 1.101–1.115, interrupted only by [[1.99]] and [[1.100]], which belong to other seers.
96.disagreements:
Sāyaṇa's identifications carry the two hardest words. On verse 1, *dhiṣaṇā* — which he takes as speech, so that "the waters and voice make him their friend" in Wilson — Griffith reads instead as a ritual vessel: "The waters and the bowl have made him friendly." The word carries both in the Ṛgveda and neither witness closes it.

On verse 2 Sāyaṇa identifies Āyu with Manu and paraphrases: being hymned by Manu, he created all the offspring of Manu. Wilson prints "the primitive laudatory hymn of Āyu"; Griffith gives "At Ayu's ancient call". The *nivid* named here is the same *pūrvā nivid* invoked at [[1.89]].3, where Sāyaṇa glosses *nivid* as *vāk*, speech or an old formula.

Verse 3 divides them structurally. Wilson makes it an exhortation — "Approaching him, let all men adore Agni" — and reads *bharatam* as "the sustainer of all men"; Griffith reads *viśaḥ ārīḥ* as a vocative, "Praise him, ye Aryan folk", and takes *bharatam* as a proper name in effect, leaving "Son of Strength, the Constant Giver". The padapāṭha's *viśaḥ ārīḥ* is nominative plural and supports Wilson's construction.

Verse 4's *mātariśvā* Wilson translates as a description, "the dweller in the firmament", where Griffith keeps the name. Sāyaṇa elsewhere in this maṇḍala treats Mātariśvan as the agent who brought Agni from heaven — see [[1.93]].6 — which makes the identification of Agni with him here more striking than either translation indicates.

101.title: Indra with the Maruts, Called Seven Times as Friend
101.synthesis:
The hymn has a hinge you can hear before you can explain it. Seven verses in a row close on the same line — *marutvantaṃ sakhyāya havāmahe*, "him, accompanied by the {{marut}}s, we call for friendship" — and what is asked for is not victory and not wealth. It is *sakhya*, companionship. Everything preceding that line in each of the seven is a relative clause: he who, he whose, he who. {{indra}} is being identified rather than addressed, seven times, and each identification arrives at the same request.

The identifications move outward. The first is a deed: he who with Ṛjiśvan struck down the dark brood, the bull whose right hand holds the *vajra*. The second is a list of the beings he has broken — Vyaṃsa, Śambara, Pipru who keeps no *vrata*, and the devouring Śuṣṇa. The third leaves the battlefield entirely: his manhood is Dyāvāpṛthivī; {{varuṇa}} and {{sūrya}} stand inside his *vrata*, his fixed ordinance, and the rivers run according to it. Within three verses the god who kills has become the god whose rule the sun and the water obey, and the same word — *vrata* — does both jobs, once for what Pipru refuses and once for what the rivers keep.

The fourth verse makes him lord of horses and of cattle, *gopati*, steady in act after act, and — flatly — the death of the man who presses no {{soma}}. The fifth widens again: lord of everything that moves and breathes, the one who first found the cattle for the *brahman*, who threw the {{dasyu}}s down. The sixth is the one to keep. He is to be called on by the brave and by the frightened, by those running away and by those winning — *śūrebhiḥ*, *bhīrubhiḥ*, *dhāvadbhiḥ*, *jigyubhiḥ*, four kinds of men in one line, and all four call the same name. Whatever else the hymn claims for Indra, it does not make him the property of the successful. The seventh sets him among the Rudras, far-seeing, while praise, *manīṣā*, rises toward him.

Then verse eight drops the third person and does not return to it. *Yad vā marutvaḥ parame sadhasthe* — whether you take your pleasure in the highest seat or in the lowest enclosure, come from there to our *adhvara*; longing for you we have made the offering, you whose giving is true. The seven verses of description were a way of getting the address right; now the address happens. The ninth presses the point in the first person plural: for you we have pressed the soma, for you made the offering, you whom the *brahman* draws; sit with your teams and your Marut troop on this *barhis*. The tenth is almost physical — rejoice with your bays, part your lips, let the tawny horses bring you, be pleased with what we have set out. A god who has just been called the ordinance behind the rivers is asked to open his mouth.

The eleventh closes with the poet's own claim on the exchange: guardians of the settlement whose praise the Maruts are, may we win *{{vāja}}* through Indra — and then the line that ends nineteen hymns in this stretch of the collection, asking {{mitra}}, Varuṇa, {{aditi}}, {{sindhu}}, Pṛthivī and Dyaus to confirm it. The hymn ends where it began, with a request for company rather than for conquest.
101.practice:
The word to carry out of this hymn is *sakhya*. Of the ten places in maṇḍala 1 where that form appears, seven are the closing line of these first seven verses — the poet has decided what he wants and has said it seven times without variation. It is worth noticing what he did not ask for. Indra is described here as the breaker of forts, the killer of named enemies, the ordinance the rivers obey; and the request attached to every one of those descriptions is friendship. The Ṛgveda's characteristic posture before Indra is not prostration. It is the claim of a companion who has brought something and expects the relationship to work both ways.

Verse 6 is the one to remember in a hard week. Indra is *havya* — to be invoked — by the brave and by the fearful, by those in flight and by those already winning. The verse puts the four categories in a single line and gives them the same god. A tradition that only heard from its winners would not have kept that.

The Maruts, who stand in every one of the seven refrains, are the storm troop, and the corpus treats them as a real presence rather than an ornament: thirty-one sūktas across the collection are addressed to them alone. Here Indra is never invoked without them. *Marutvant*, "accompanied by the Maruts," occurs eight times in maṇḍala 1 and seven of the eight are in this hymn.

For household use, the hymn's own instruction is verse 8: come from wherever you are, the highest seat or the lowest enclosure. The offering does not have to be made in a grand place for the invitation to be valid, and the text says so before it says anything about what it wants in return.
101.disagreements:
The dark brood of verse 1 divides the readers. Sāyaṇa takes Kṛṣṇa as an *asura* slain together with his wives so that no posterity of his should remain, but offers the alternative that Kṛṣṇa, "the black," is {{vṛtra}}, the black cloud; Wilson prints the first ("destroyed the pregnant wives of Kṛṣṇa"), Griffith the second ("drove the dusky brood away"). On verse 5 Sāyaṇa glosses *brahmaṇe* as "for {{aṅgiras}}" — the cattle were recovered for the seer-family, not for a class.

Verse 7 is unsettled. Sāyaṇa reads the Rudras as the Maruts in their character of vital airs, deriving *rudra* from *rud*, to weep, because when the breaths leave the body the kinsmen of the dead weep. Wilson then makes *yoṣā* "speech," which spreads with celerity; Griffith keeps a feminine figure, "with the Rudras through the wide space speeds the Dame." Neither is secure.

At verse 8 Wilson has Indra pleased "in a stately mansion or in a lowly dwelling," a contrast of houses; Griffith reads *parame sadhasthe* as the loftiest gathering-place, a contrast of heights. The padapāṭha's *vṛjane* for the second term means an enclosure or settlement, which favours Griffith's reading of two locations rather than two social stations.

102.title: Indra, Mount Our Chariot: a Hymn Made for Battle
102.synthesis:
This hymn knows what it is: a made thing, offered as a thing made. *Imāṃ te dhiyaṃ pra bhare maho mahīm* — I bring you this *{{dhī}}*, a great one to a great one — and the reason given is that *dhiṣaṇā*, the shaping insight, has been polished for his praise. The gods, it says, have gladdened {{indra}} with power both in the raising and in the setting forth. The hymn begins by declaring the making of the hymn.

Then it takes the largest possible witnesses. The seven rivers carry his fame; Dyāvākṣāmā and the earth carry his visible shape; {{sūrya}} and the moon go by turns *abhicakṣe śraddhe kam* — so that we may see, and so that we may have *śraddhā*. That is a remarkable clause. The alternation of sun and moon is offered not as proof but as the thing that makes trust possible: what returns can be relied on. *Śraddhā* occurs three times in the whole of maṇḍala 1, and all three are in this run of hymns.

From there the request is concrete and stays concrete. Verse 3 asks Maghavan to send that chariot forward for the winning, the victorious car the singers rejoice to see in the clash — and, in the same breath, to give *śarma*, shelter, to those who love him. Verse 4 wants an ally in the plural: with you as yokemate may we conquer what is fenced in, raise our share in fight after fight, make *varivas*, open room, and break the manly strength of the enemy. Verse 5 comes back to the car — many men in many ways call on you, holder of wealth; mount ours, for your mind is fixed on victory. The chariot is asked for three times in this hymn, at verses 3, 5 and 9, and each time the request is different: send it, mount it, put it in front.

Verse 6 is the hymn's portrait. His two arms win cattle; his *kratu*, his effective purpose, has no measure; alone, in act after act, hundred-formed, the maker of the din of battle, Indra is a *pratimāna* by his *ojas* — a counterweight, the thing on the other side of the scale. Verse 8 picks up that word again and multiplies it threefold: three earths, three lights, and he has grown past all of it, without rival from birth. Between the two, verse 7 gives the scale in numbers — your fame exceeds a hundred, exceeds more, exceeds a thousand among the peoples; the great *dhiṣaṇā* has made you blaze, and then you break the obstructions, breaker of forts. The counting is not decoration; it is what a counterweight requires.

The last three verses turn practical. Verse 9 calls him first among the gods, the one who has been the victor in battles, and asks him to make this poet impetuous and this chariot foremost. Verse 10 is honest about the transaction: you conquered and did not keep the spoils back, in trifling fights and in great ones; we whet you, the fierce one, for our help — so urge us on when we call. And verse 11 asks for the office a person actually needs: *viśvāhā indro adhivaktā no astu* — may Indra always be the one who speaks on our behalf. Then the closing line shared with this whole run of hymns hands the request to {{mitra}}, {{varuṇa}}, {{aditi}}, {{sindhu}}, Pṛthivī and Dyaus.
102.practice:
Two words here are worth taking home.

The first is *śraddhā*, in verse 2. The hymn does not ask anyone to believe something unlikely; it points at the sun and the moon going by turns and says that this is what lets a person trust — *abhicakṣe śraddhe kam*, for seeing, and for trust. The word that later carries the whole weight of faith in the Gītā and in the Upaniṣads appears here attached to a regularity you can check. Across maṇḍala 1 it appears three times, at 1.102.2, 1.104.6 and [[1.108]].6, all three in this same short run of hymns, and all three by the same seer.

The second is *adhivaktā* in the last verse — the one who speaks on your behalf. Not the giver, not the protector: the advocate. It is a small word and it names the relation most people actually want with a power greater than themselves.

The hymn is also an unembarrassed war prayer, and it is worth reading as one. It asks for a chariot, for a share of the spoil, for the breaking of the enemy's strength; it says plainly in verse 10 that the god is whetted like a blade for the singer's use. The Ṛgveda does not hide this register, and a reader who has only met the tradition through its later quietism should see it. What tempers it is the vocabulary the same hymn uses: *varivas*, room to move; *śarma*, shelter; *pratimāna*, the counterweight. The god is asked to be the weight on the other side of a scale that is currently tipped — an image of relief rather than of domination.

For a reciter, the opening verse is also a small teaching about what a hymn is. It is *bhṛta*, carried and brought, like the offering; the singer says he brings his *dhī* the way another man brings ghee.
102.disagreements:
Verse 1's *utsave ca prasave ca* is read differently. Wilson makes it a purpose — the gods delight Indra "for the sake of prosperity and wealth"; Griffith makes it two occasions, "at feast and when the Soma flowed." The gloss preserved on this verse in Sāyaṇa's bhāṣya concerns Indra's lustre being one with the sun's — fire combining with the sun by day and the sun with fire by night — rather than the phrase itself.

On verse 2 Sāyaṇa identifies Ahi and Vṛtra as differently-formed clouds and Rauhiṇa, in the parallel at [[1.103]].2, as possibly a red cloud — the naturalistic reading he applies throughout the Vṛtra material.

Verse 7's *dhiṣaṇā* splits the translators badly. Wilson takes it as praise: "great praise has glorified you." Griffith takes it as a vessel: "the great bowl hath inspirited thee boundlessly." The word carries both senses elsewhere in the collection, and neither reading can be excluded here.

Verse 8's *triviṣṭidhātu* is rendered by Wilson as "strong as a twice-twisted rope" and by Griffith as "of thy great might there is a threefold counterpart," which the three earths and three lights named in the same verse support.

103.title: Indra's Highest Power Far Off, the Bolt Near at Hand
103.synthesis:
Eight verses, and the first of them sets a problem the rest of the hymn works on. *Tat te indriyaṃ paramaṃ parācaiḥ* — that highest power of yours is turned away, far off; the *kavis* held it long ago. Then the split: *idaṃ kṣamā, idam anyad divi* — this one is on the earth, that other is in heaven — and the two combine, the verse says, as a banner joins a banner in battle. {{indra}}'s power is described as being in two places at once, one of them out of reach, and the hymn's business is the near one.

Verse 2 is the near one, told in four strokes. He held the earth firm and spread it out; having struck with the *vajra* he let the waters out; he slew the {{ahi}}; he split Rauhiṇa and cut down Vyaṃsa by his *śacīs*, his effective powers. The order matters: the earth is fixed before the waters are released, so that the release lands on something.

Verse 3 turns from cosmos to campaign. Bearing his weapon by nature, trusting his *ojas*, he went about breaking the Dāsa forts; and then the singer instructs him — knowing one, wielder of the bolt, cast your missile at the {{dasyu}}; increase the strength and the splendour of the Ārya. Verse 4 makes the deed into a name: Maghavan, bearing a title worth celebrating, went out to the killing of the Dasyus and took a name for himself for glory. This is one of the places where the Ṛgveda says outright that an epithet is earned rather than given.

Verse 5 is the pivot, and it is short. Look at this, his abundant prosperity — *śrad indrasya dhattana vīryāya*, place your trust in Indra's manly power. And then the evidence, five clauses with the same verb: he found the cattle, he found the horses, he found the plants, he found the waters, he found the trees. Not conquered — found. What the bolt opens turns out to be a world that was there and hidden.

Verse 6 sets the exchange in an image nobody would invent for a god they were flattering. Let us press {{soma}} for the one of many works, the bull, whose fury is true — who, waiting like a highwayman on the road, goes distributing the wealth of the man who does not sacrifice. Indra takes from the one who withholds and hands it on, and the poet says so with a word for an ambusher.

Verse 7 returns to the killing and adds a detail the great telling in [[1.32]] does not have: *yat sasantaṃ vajreṇābodhayo 'him*, when you woke the sleeping *ahi* with the bolt. He was asleep. Then the wives rejoiced after you, and the winged ones, and all the gods — the hymn spends its last line on the celebration rather than on the corpse.

Verse 8 gathers the names into a single list — Śuṣṇa, Pipru, Kuyava, {{vṛtra}}, and the forts of Śambara — and hands the whole hymn over to the closing line shared across this stretch of the collection: may {{mitra}}, {{varuṇa}}, {{aditi}}, {{sindhu}}, Pṛthivī and Dyaus grant us that. Eight verses that began by saying his best power is out of reach end by asking six other powers to confirm what the reachable part has done.
103.practice:
The first verse is the hymn's gift to anyone who has ever felt that the tradition's greatest moments happened to somebody else, long ago. It says exactly that, and does not apologise: the highest power is *parācaiḥ*, turned away; the seers of old held it. Then it spends seven verses on what is still here. That structure — the acknowledgement of loss followed by the inventory of what remains — is a usable shape for a person taking stock of a practice.

Verse 5 is where the hymn puts its weight, and the verb is worth noticing. *Sa gā avindat, so avindad aśvān, sa oṣadhīḥ, so apaḥ, sa vanāni* — he found the cattle, he found the horses, the plants, the waters, the trees. The same verb five times, and it is a verb of finding rather than of making or of seizing. What the bolt accomplishes, in this telling, is that things which existed but were shut away become available. That is the sense in which a reader can hold the Vṛtra story without first deciding whether it is weather, war, or something interior: in all three it is the same event, an obstruction removed and something already there coming into use.

*Śrat ... dhattana*, "place your trust," in the same verse, is the imperative behind the noun *śraddhā*. Of the seven places in maṇḍala 1 where the element *śrat* appears, two are in this hymn and one more in [[1.104]] — the seer of this run of sūktas returns to the idea repeatedly, and always attaches it to something visible rather than to something merely asserted.

The one line to be careful with is verse 3, which asks for the Dasyu to be struck and the Ārya's strength increased. That is a partisan prayer, spoken by one people about another, and the honest thing is to read it as such rather than to allegorise it away.
103.disagreements:
The naturalistic reading runs through Sāyaṇa's treatment of this hymn as it does through [[1.32]]: Ahi and Vṛtra are differently-formed clouds, and Rauhiṇa is possibly a red cloud, an *asura* only by figure. Wilson follows him into English — "having struck the clouds, he has extricated the waters" — while Griffith keeps the narrative surface: "smote with his thunderbolt and loosed the waters."

Verse 4 is genuinely obscure and the two translators do not agree on who is doing what. Wilson has Maghavan offering the human generations to the one who celebrates his name; Griffith has Indra giving himself the name of Son for glory. The padapāṭha's *yad ha sūnuḥ śravase nāma dadhe* leaves both open.

Verse 6's *paripanthī iva śūraḥ* is uncomfortable in both. Wilson softens it — Indra takes wealth from the non-sacrificer "like a foot-pad from a traveller" and then proceeds to give it to the sacrificer; Griffith keeps the menace, "watching like a thief in ambush, goes parting the possessions of the godless." The Sanskrit supplies the ambusher; the redistribution is supplied by Wilson following Sāyaṇa.

At verse 7 Wilson's "the wives of the gods, the Maruts, and all the gods" and Griffith's "Dames divine, the flying Maruts and all Gods" divide over whether *vayaḥ* names birds or the Marut troop.

104.title: A Seat Made for Indra — 'Do Not Harm Our Unborn'
104.synthesis:
The hymn opens with a piece of furniture. *Yonis te indra nisade akāri* — a seat has been made for you to sit in; sit down on it. And then the image that carries the rest: like a horse that has run and is blowing, unyoke, loose the horses that carry you at dusk and at dawn. Before anything is asked, {{indra}} is invited to stop travelling.

Verse 2 says who is asking. These men have come to Indra for help; may he cover the road to them at once; may the gods put down the fury of the Dāsa and bring us through into good standing. From there the hymn becomes hard to follow, and it is honest to say so. Verses 3, 4 and 5 concern Kuyava, and the details are not recoverable with confidence from this evidence. Someone carries off by himself, knowing where the goods are; he carries off the foam on the water; the two wives of Kuyava bathe in milk — may they be drowned in the depth of the Śiphā. Three rivers are named, Añjasī, Kuliśī and Vīrapatnī, sending their milk forward. The hold of the roving one was hidden; the hero goes on with the earlier waters and rules. Then verse 5: since the track to the {{dasyu}}'s dwelling has been seen, as a cow that knows her stall goes to it — remember us, Maghavan, and do not throw us away as a spendthrift throws away wealth.

With verse 6 the hymn changes register entirely, and stays changed. *Sa tvaṃ na indra sūrye so apsv anāgāstve ā bhaja* — give us a share in {{sūrya}}, a share in the waters, a share in blamelessness, and in the good word of the living. Do not injure what we enjoy while it is still within; our trust, *śraddhitam*, is set on your great power. The word for what is unborn has already entered.

Verse 7 makes the trust explicit — now I think it has been placed in him — and asks for great wealth, and then asks something smaller and more urgent: do not set us in a house that has not been made ready; give food and drink to the hungry. And verse 8 is the heart of the hymn, five refusals in four lines. *Mā no vadhīr indra mā parā dāḥ* — do not kill us, do not abandon us; do not steal away the enjoyments dear to us; do not break our eggs, strong Śakra; do not break the vessels with what is inside them. *Āṇḍā*, eggs, is the plainest available word for a thing that is alive and not yet born, and the poet uses it about his own descendants.

Then verse 9, whose effect is in its last three words. Come near; they say you love {{soma}}; here it is pressed, drink it for your rapture; wide-bellied, pour it down inside you; and — *pitā iva naḥ śṛṇuhi hūyamānaḥ* — hear us, when you are called, as a father does. That phrase, *pitā iva*, occurs twice in the whole of maṇḍala 1. The other is the last verse of [[1.1]], where {{agni}} is asked to be easy of approach as a father is to a son. The first hymn of the collection and this one, a hundred sūktas apart and addressed to two different gods, end on the same comparison and the same request.
104.practice:
This is a hymn about children, and it does not arrive there by way of a general benevolence; it arrives by way of fear. Read verses 6 to 8 continuously and the sequence is: give us a share in the sun and the water and in being blameless — do not injure what is still inside — do not put us in an unprepared house — feed the hungry — do not kill us, do not abandon us, do not break our eggs. Whoever composed this had something specific in mind, and the tradition did not tidy it away.

*Mā no vadhīḥ*, "do not slay us," is a formula the reciter will meet again almost immediately: the Rudra hymn ten sūktas further on, [[1.114]], is built on the same negations, verse after verse, about father, mother, son, grandson, cattle and horses. Two different gods, two different seers' subjects, one grammatical shape. When the Ṛgveda is most frightened it stops asking for things and starts listing what must not be touched.

The closing comparison is worth holding beside its twin. [[1.1]].9 asks Agni to be *sūpāyana*, easy to approach, as a father is to a son. Here the request is that Indra should *hear* like a father. These are the only two places in maṇḍala 1 that use *pitā iva*, and both stand in the final verse of their hymn, after everything else has been asked for. A reader who recites the opening of the Ṛgveda daily is already carrying half of this.

On the middle verses, the honest answer is that the Kuyava episode is not clear from this evidence. The rivers named — Añjasī, Kuliśī, Vīrapatnī — do not recur in a way that fixes them, and the traditional gloss supplies the story rather than reading it out of the words. It is a good place to notice how much of what looks like narrative in the Ṛgveda is allusion to something the first audience already knew and we do not.
104.disagreements:
Verse 3 is where the readings part company most sharply. Sāyaṇa supplies an *asura* as the subject and names him Kuyava, so that Wilson prints "the Asura, knowing the wealth of others, carries it off of himself." Griffith declines the identification: "He who hath only wish as his possession casts on himself, casts foam amid the waters." Nothing in the padapāṭha names the actor.

On verse 4 Sāyaṇa glosses *āyu* as an appellative of Kuyava, one who goes about doing mischief to others, which gives Wilson "the abiding-place of the vagrant Kuyava"; Griffith reads the same words as kinship checked in a neighbour.

Verse 5's *sma naḥ maghavan carkṛtād it* is a plea for defence in Wilson ("defend us from his repeated violence") and a plea to be remembered in Griffith ("Now think thou of us, Maghavan"); the second sits closer to the reduplicated form of the verb.

Verse 8's *āṇḍā* is "unborn offspring" for Wilson and "our unborn brood" for Griffith — a rare agreement, and the strongest ground for reading the whole closing movement as being about children. Sāyaṇa's gloss on the same verse extends the protection to those capable only of crawling on their knees.

105.title: Trita's Complaint to the Viśvedevāḥ from the Well
105.synthesis:
Eighteen of this hymn's nineteen verses end on the same four words: *vittaṃ me asya rodasī* — Heaven and Earth, know this of me. Not "grant," not "protect." Know. A man is trapped, and what he asks the two largest witnesses in the world to do is register that it is happening. The nineteenth verse drops the refrain and closes with the formula shared across this whole run of hymns. Nothing else in maṇḍala 1 sustains a single line this way.

The opening three verses set the loss by naming what is out of reach. The moon runs in the waters and the fair-winged one in the sky; you gold-rimmed lightnings — nobody finds your station. Then the ordinary world going on without him: those who want a thing get it, the wife draws her husband close, and from their pressing together the juice is milked. Then the fear stated plainly: may that light never fall from heaven; may we never be without the sweet one who is our joy. Verse 4 turns it into a question the whole hymn is really asking — *kva ṛtaṃ pūrvyaṃ gataṃ, kas tad bibharti nūtanaḥ*: where has the ancient {{ṛta}} gone, and who now carries it? Verse 5 puts the question to the gods directly: you in the three bright realms, what counts with you as *ṛta* and what as *anṛta*, and where is the old offering I made? Verse 6 asks it a third time, by naming the offices that should be working — where is your upholding of *ṛta*, where {{varuṇa}}'s watching eye, where the path of great Aryaman, that we might get past the malicious?

Verses 7 and 8 are the body of the man. I am the one who used to speak at the pressing, he says, and cares eat me as a wolf eats a thirsty deer. Ribs close on me from every side like co-wives; anxieties gnaw me as rats gnaw threads — and he adds, still your praiser, Śatakratu. Two similes, both domestic, both about being worn away rather than struck.

Then the hymn lifts its eyes again. Seven rays, and his navel stretched among them; Trita Āptya knows it and cries out for kinship. Five bulls standing in mid-heaven have turned back together. Fair-winged ones sit at the sky's ascent and drive the wolf from the path as he crosses the restless waters. Verse 12 answers verse 4 without saying so: *ṛtam arṣanti sindhavaḥ, satyaṃ tatāna sūryaḥ* — the rivers run as *ṛta*, {{sūrya}} has stretched out what is true. The order he could not find is still working; it simply is not working for him yet.

Verses 13 and 14 call {{agni}} to sit as *hotā* as he did for {{manu}} and carry the offering; verse 15 has Varuṇa making the *brahman* and unfolding thought in the heart, and asks that *ṛta* be born new. Verse 16 warns that the Āditya's path in the sky cannot be crossed and that mortals do not see it. Verse 17 finally says outright what has been happening: *tritaḥ kūpe 'vahito devān havata ūtaye* — Trita, dropped into a well, calls the gods for help, and Bṛhaspati heard him, making wide room out of the narrow. Verse 18 gives one more glimpse of the road he was on when it went wrong: a ruddy wolf saw me as I walked, and reared up at the sight like a carpenter whose back aches from stooping. Then verse 19 speaks for everyone: by this song may we, having {{indra}}, with all our men, prevail.
105.practice:
This is the hymn to know about when the tradition is accused of having only triumph in it. A man is in a hole. He is not rescued for eighteen verses. He does not stop reciting, and what he says over and over is not a demand but a request to be witnessed: Heaven and Earth, know this of me.

Two things in it are worth carrying. The first is verse 4's question — where has the ancient *ṛta* gone, and who carries it now? That is a question about whether the order one was taught still holds, asked from inside a situation where it visibly does not. The Ṛgveda keeps it. The second is the answer the hymn gives eight verses later without announcing it as an answer: the rivers still run as *ṛta*, Sūrya has still stretched out what is true. Nothing has changed about his position; what has changed is that he can see the order operating elsewhere. That is a very exact description of what it is like to recover a footing.

Verse 8's image of anxiety — *sam mā tapanti abhitaḥ sapatnīr iva parśavaḥ*, ribs pressing on every side like co-wives, and cares gnawing like rats at threads — is one of the plainest descriptions of a mind under pressure anywhere in the collection, and it is not spoken by an outsider. Verse 7 establishes that this is the man who used to lead the singing.

The rescue, when it comes, is a spatial word. Bṛhaspati heard him *kṛṇvann aṃhūraṇād uru* — making wide out of the narrow. *Aṃhas*, the narrow place, and *uru*, the wide, are the corpus's basic pair for distress and relief; the next hymn, [[1.106]], asks in every verse to be lifted out of *aṃhas* like a chariot out of a rut. Read the two together and the pair becomes hard to forget.
105.disagreements:
Sāyaṇa reads the whole hymn as spoken by Trita from the bottom of a covered well — hence verse 1's "nobody finds your station," which he takes to mean that the covering shuts out every visible object. In [[1.106]].6 the same predicament is ascribed to Kutsa, and Sāyaṇa there states simply that Kutsa is Trita. Griffith translates the refrain neutrally, "Mark this my woe, ye Earth and Heaven"; Wilson supplies "(my affliction)" in brackets, which is Sāyaṇa's reading rather than the Sanskrit's.

Verse 3 divides them completely. Sāyaṇa takes it as a fear of having no son, citing the Aitareya Brāhmaṇa that there is no world for one without a son, and Wilson prints that; Griffith reads it as a fear that the light in the sky might fall.

Verse 11's wolf is where Sāyaṇa's naturalism is most visible. He offers a legend — a wolf about to swim the river to devour Trita, deterred by the sun's brightness — and then an alternative in which *vṛka* is the moon and *āpaḥ* the firmament, so that the line means the sun's rays keep the moon from appearing. He extends the second reading to verse 18, taking *mā sakṛt* as *māsakṛt*, the month-maker.

On verse 10's five bulls he lists three possibilities: Indra, Varuṇa, Agni, Aryaman and Savitṛ; or fire, wind, sun, moon and lightning; or the same five distributed by sphere.

106.title: Viśvedevāḥ, Lift Us Out as a Chariot from a Rut
106.synthesis:
Six verses, six different sets of gods, and after each one the identical line: *rathaṃ na durgād vasavaḥ sudānavo viśvasmān no aṃhaso niṣ pipartana* — like a chariot out of a bad place, you good givers, carry us out of every narrowness. The image is exact and unheroic. A cart is stuck; it does not need to be rebuilt, only lifted clear. *Aṃhas*, the word for the trouble, means a narrow place before it means a sin, and the whole hymn is built on the contrast between being wedged and having room.

The first verse assembles the largest names: {{indra}}, {{mitra}}, {{varuṇa}}, {{agni}}, the {{marut}} host, {{aditi}}. Nobody is described; they are simply called, and the refrain follows. The second turns to the Ādityas and asks for *sarvatāti*, wholeness, and for them to be a source of ease in the {{vṛtra}}-fights — the same word for battle that elsewhere in this book carries the great cosmic combat is used here for whatever these men are actually facing.

The third verse is the one a household will notice. May the Fathers help us, whose praise comes readily; and the two goddesses whose sons are the gods, the two who increase {{ṛta}} — heaven and earth, addressed as a pair of mothers. The dead and the world are asked in the same breath as the gods, and the refrain does not change for them.

The fourth calls Narāśaṃsa, "the praise of men," and Pūṣan, who is given the epithet *kṣayadvīra* — the word that will dominate the Rudra hymn eight sūktas further on, at [[1.114]]. It appears eight times in the collection and this is one of only two places outside that hymn in maṇḍala 1. The fifth asks Bṛhaspati for something small and daily: *sadam it naḥ sugaṃ kṛdhi* — always make good going for us — and then for *śaṃ yos*, welfare and safety, "which was set down by {{manu}}." What is asked for is not a new benefit but the restoration of one already established.

The sixth verse names the speaker's own predicament and does it in the third person: *indraṃ kutso vṛtrahaṇaṃ śacīpatiṃ kāṭe nibāḷho ṛṣir ahvad ūtaye* — Kutsa the seer, pressed down in a pit, called Indra the {{vṛtra}}-slayer, lord of powers, for help. One line, and it explains the whole hymn. The chariot in the rut is not a figure chosen for elegance; the man saying it is in a hole. The preceding sūkta, [[1.105]], is nineteen verses of the same predicament with a different refrain.

The seventh verse drops the chariot and closes differently. May the goddess Aditi with the gods guard us; may the god who protects protect without slackening — *aprayucchan*, not letting his attention wander. Then the line that ends this whole stretch of the collection: may {{mitra}}, Varuṇa, Aditi, {{sindhu}}, Pṛthivī and Dyaus grant us that. A hymn that spent six verses asking to be pulled out of a ditch ends by asking for undistracted attention, which is the same request in another form.
106.practice:
The value of this sūkta is its scale. It asks for nothing large. Six times it says: we are stuck in a narrow place; lift us out as you would lift a cart. The gods called are the biggest available — Indra, the Ādityas, the Fathers, Bṛhaspati, Aditi — and the task given them is small and specific.

*Aṃhas* is the word to carry. It is the narrow place, the pinch, and it stands opposite *uru* and *varivas*, room and open going. This pair runs through the Ṛgveda's whole vocabulary of trouble and relief, and it is worth knowing that the tradition's oldest picture of misfortune is not guilt but constriction, and its oldest picture of grace is space. The preceding hymn ends its rescue with the same words: Bṛhaspati heard Trita and made wide out of the narrow.

Verse 5's *śaṃ yos* is the phrase to recognise. It is a paired benediction — welfare and safety — and it recurs in the Rudra hymn at [[1.114]].2, where it is again something Manu obtained and the singer asks to attain in turn. Three verses in the whole collection carry the full form. It is not a wish for something new; it is a request for what an ancestor already secured.

Verse 3 is the one to keep for a household. The Fathers are asked for help in the same breath as Aditi and heaven and earth, and no distinction is made in the asking. A family that performs tarpaṇa is doing something the Ṛgveda already treats as continuous with worship of the gods rather than as a separate department of piety.

And verse 6 is worth reading aloud for its plainness. The seer names himself, states that he is in a pit, and says he called. No shame is attached to the position, and no explanation is offered for how he got there.
106.disagreements:
Verse 3's *devī devaputre ṛtāvṛdhā* is read as heaven and earth by both translators, though Wilson names them and Griffith leaves them as "the two Goddesses, Mothers of the Gods." Sāyaṇa identifies the Fathers of the same verse as the Agniṣvāttas and the other classes named in the Manusmṛti.

Verse 4 is genuinely obscure. The padapāṭha gives *narāśaṃsaṃ vājinaṃ vājayann iha kṣayadvīraṃ pūṣaṇaṃ sumnair īmahe*. Griffith takes it as two gods, Narāśaṃsa and Pūṣan; Wilson dissolves the names into descriptions — "him who is the praised of men and the giver of food" and "him who is the purifier and destroyer of heroes" — which makes *kṣayadvīra* a menace where Griffith makes it "ruler over men." The same disagreement recurs at every occurrence of the word in [[1.114]]. Sāyaṇa's note here identifies the pair as nourishing gods, Agni and Pūṣan.

Verse 5's *śaṃ yor yat te manurhitam* is "implanted in you by Manu" for Wilson and "what boon thou hast for men" for Griffith, reading *manurhita* as "set down for man" rather than "set down by Manu."

On verse 6 Sāyaṇa states without argument that Kutsa is Trita, which is what makes [[1.105]] and this hymn a single episode rather than two.

107.title: Three Verses: the Yajña Goes to the Viśvedevāḥ
107.synthesis:
Three verses. It is the shortest sūkta in this whole stretch of the collection, and its brevity is not an accident of transmission — it is a complete movement, and it does in three steps what the hymns around it take twenty to do.

The first verse states the mechanism: *yajño devānāṃ prati eti sumnam* — the {{yajña}} goes toward the favour of the gods. Not "may it go"; it goes. What is offered travels, and the direction of travel is toward *sumna*, the gods' good will. Then the request built on that: Ādityas, be gracious, be the ones who show mercy; and let your *sumati*, your good thought, turn back this way toward us — the *sumati* which is the better deliverer even out of *aṃhas*, the narrow place. The word that dominates the preceding hymn, [[1.106]], where every verse asks to be lifted out of *aṃhas* like a cart from a rut, is here in the first verse, and the answer offered is not force but a turn of mind on the gods' side.

The second verse is the hymn's centre and its most beautiful line. *Upa no devā avasā gamantu aṅgirasāṃ sāmabhi stūyamānāḥ* — may the gods come near with help, being praised by the sāmans of the {{aṅgiras}}es. The seer of this whole run of sūktas belongs to that family, so the line is both a general claim about which songs bring gods and a specific claim about these songs. Then the arrangement that makes the verse worth memorising: *indra indriyair maruto marudbhir ādityair no aditiḥ śarma yaṃsat* — {{indra}} with his own powers, the {{marut}}s with the Maruts, {{aditi}} with the Ādityas, may she extend shelter to us. Each god is asked to arrive accompanied by what is properly his: Indra with the *indriyas* that carry his name, the Maruts as a troop of themselves, Aditi with the sons who are called after her. Nobody is asked to come alone, and nobody is asked to bring anything foreign. The line is a small statement about how a Viśvedevāḥ hymn works — the gods are not a list but a set of households, each arriving whole.

The third verse asks for one thing and names five givers for it. *Tan na indras tad varuṇas tad agnis tad aryamā tat savitā canaḥ dhāt* — may {{indra}} set that for us, and {{varuṇa}}, and {{agni}}, and Aryaman, and Savitṛ; *canas* is the nourishment, the acceptable food. Five names, one demonstrative repeated five times, one verb at the end. And then the closing line that seals nineteen hymns in this part of the collection: may {{mitra}}, Varuṇa, Aditi, {{sindhu}}, Pṛthivī and Dyaus grant it.

Read in sequence, the three verses are a complete liturgical thought: the offering travels; the gods come, each with his own; five of them are named and asked to set down food. The hymn does not narrate, does not argue, and asks for nothing that could not be given at a single sitting. Its ending is identical to the ending of the nineteen-verse hymn two sūktas back, which is one way the collection shows that length is not the measure of a complete address.
107.practice:
Short hymns are useful, and this one is the shortest in a run of twenty-two. Three triṣṭubh verses can be learned in a morning, and they contain the essential grammar of a Viśvedevāḥ address: the offering goes; the gods come with their own; the named ones set down what is needed.

Verse 2 is the line to keep. *Indra indriyair maruto marudbhir ādityair no aditiḥ* — the same principle three times. A god arrives with what belongs to him. Nothing is borrowed and nothing is asked out of its own nature. In a tradition that later organises worship around the āvāhana of a deity with his retinue and attributes, this is where the pattern is already visible.

The Viśvedevāḥ are the third most frequent addressee in the collection — sixty-three sūktas are given to them alone, behind {{indra}}'s two hundred and eighteen and {{agni}}'s hundred and eighty-six, and ahead of the Aśvinau's fifty-two. That is worth knowing, because the category is often treated as a leftover. It is not: after the two great gods it is the commonest thing a Ṛgvedic poet chose to address, and what it means is that the gods are frequently approached as a company rather than singly.

The word to notice is *sumati* — good thought, in verse 1, asked to turn toward the singer. It is not favour won by force of praise; it is a disposition, and the hymn's request is that it should face this way. When a person prays for someone's mind to soften rather than for an outcome, this is the Vedic word for it.

The last verse's *canas*, the food that is accepted, is the plain thing being asked for. The hymn takes three verses to arrive at bread on the table, and does not pretend otherwise.
107.disagreements:
Verse 1's second half is the crux and the two translators read it in opposite directions. The padapāṭha has *ā vo 'vārcī sumatir vavṛtyād aṃhoś cid yā varivovittarā asat*. Griffith takes it as a plea: "Hitherward let your favour be directed, and be our best deliverer from trouble." Wilson's printed English — "so as to be an abundant source of affliction to the poor" — reverses the sense of *aṃhas* and of *varivovit*, the finder of open room, and is almost certainly a compositor's or a copyist's failure rather than a reading; nothing in the padapāṭha supports it. Where the two diverge this sharply, the morphology is the arbiter: *varivovittara* is a comparative of the agent noun "finder of room," which cannot mean a source of affliction.

Verse 2's *aṅgirasāṃ sāmabhiḥ* is "by the hymns of the Aṅgirasas" in Wilson and "by praise-songs of Angirases" in Griffith — agreement, and a rare instance of the Ṛgveda naming a family's chants as the instrument by which gods are brought.

Verse 3's *canaḥ* is "that food which we solicit" for Wilson and "this laud of ours" for Griffith, who takes the gods as finding the praise pleasant rather than as granting nourishment. Sāyaṇa's gloss on this sūkta is not preserved in the witness consulted here; that is a gap in the witness, not a silence on his part.

108.title: Indrāgnī — Wherever You Are, Come and Drink
108.synthesis:
{{indra}} and {{agni}} are addressed here as a single dual deity, *indrāgnī*, and the hymn's first move is to give them one chariot. That most wonderful car of yours, which looks out on all the worlds — mount it together, come, and drink of the pressed {{soma}}. Twelve sūktas in the collection are given to this pair; two of them stand side by side here.

Verse 2 measures the offering against the world: as wide as all this is in its compass, as deep as it is with its far-stretching surface, so much let this soma be — *araṃ ... manase yuvabhyām*, enough for your mind. Verse 3 explains why the two are addressed as one: you have made a joint name, an auspicious one, and together you are {{vṛtra}}-slayers; so sit together and pour the bull-soma into yourselves. The joint name is treated as an achievement rather than a convenience.

Verse 4 puts the scene in front of the reader: the fires kindled, the ladles lifted and dripping, the *barhis* strewn, the sharp somas poured around — come near for our good-mindedness. Verse 5 gathers everything the pair has ever been: whatever heroic deeds you have done, whatever forms you have taken, whatever bull-powers, whatever ancient auspicious friendships are yours — by all of those, drink. Verse 6 recalls a promise: what I said first, when I chose you — this soma is to be contended for by us against the *asuras* — you came to that true confidence of mine and drank. *Śraddhā* appears here, one of only three occurrences in maṇḍala 1, and all three are by this seer within these few hymns.

Then the hymn does the thing it is remembered for. Six consecutive verses, 7 through 12, end on the identical couplet: *ataḥ pari vṛṣaṇāv ā hi yātam atha somasya pibataṃ sutasya* — come here from there, you two bulls, and then drink of the pressed soma. What changes is only the "there." In your own house, or with a *brahman*, or with a *rājan*. Among the Yadus, the Turvaśas, the Druhyus, the Anus, the Pūrus. In the lowest earth, the middle, the highest. Then — and this is visible only in the word order — in the highest, the middle, the lowest: the same three terms run backwards, so that the pair of verses closes on itself. In heaven, on earth, in the mountains, in the plants, in the waters. At the rising of {{sūrya}}, in mid-heaven, delighting by your own *svadhā*.

Six verses to say that there is nowhere the gods can be that is too far to come from. The list is not random. It runs through the social world first — one's own house, the priest's, the king's — then across the peoples, then down and up the tiers of the cosmos and back, then through the elements, and finally into the sky at the two hours when the sun is most conspicuous. A reader who has ever wondered how the Vedic mind pictured extent has the answer in these six verses: extent is enumerated, not gestured at, and every item on the list is a place someone might actually be.

The thirteenth verse is one line of business and one of formula: having drunk your fill of what is pressed, win us every kind of wealth — and then the closing line shared by nineteen hymns in this stretch, handing the request on to {{mitra}}, {{varuṇa}}, {{aditi}}, {{sindhu}}, Pṛthivī and Dyaus.
108.practice:
Verse 8 is why this hymn is cited outside a seminar. *Yad indrāgnī yaduṣu turvaśeṣu yad druhyuṣv anuṣu pūruṣu sthaḥ* — Yadu, Turvaśa, Druhyu, Anu, Pūru. These are the five peoples whose names the later tradition would build genealogies on, and here they are simply five places the gods might be found, listed without ranking and without hostility. Whatever these names later became, in this verse they are neighbours.

The structural teaching is in verses 7 to 12 as a block. Six times: wherever you are, come from there. It is a form of address worth knowing, because it makes no assumption about where the god is and no claim that the worshipper's own place is central. The last of the six even allows that the pair may be delighting in their own *svadhā*, their own inherent power, needing nothing from anybody — and still says, come.

*Śraddhā* in verse 6 is the third and last of its occurrences in maṇḍala 1; the others are at [[1.102]].2 and [[1.104]].6, both by this same seer. Here it is not belief in a proposition but the keeping of a word: I said this first, when I chose you, and you came to that. Trust, in this hymn, is something a person has already acted on.

For a household, verse 4 is the useful picture — fires kindled, ladles lifted, grass strewn, the pressing poured out — and it is followed immediately by a request for *saumanasya*, good-mindedness. The whole apparatus is there to produce a state of mind, and the hymn says so in the same breath.

The pair itself is worth knowing. Indra and Agni together receive twelve sūktas; the collection treats them as a dual power with a joint name, and verse 3 makes the joint name the reason they can be asked for anything at all.
108.disagreements:
Verse 8 is the divergence that matters most. Sāyaṇa offers the five names as proper names of families — the descendants of Yayāti's five sons — but then gives etymologies for each as a common noun: Yadu the non-injurious, Turvaśa the injurious, Druhyu the tyrannical, Anu the one possessed of breath, Pūru the one to be filled with objects of desire. Wilson prints the etymologies and loses the peoples entirely: "men who are inoffensive, malevolent, or tyrannical." Griffith prints the names: "If with the Yadus, Turvasas, ye sojourn, with Druhyus, Anus, Purus." Here the padapāṭha's plain locatives support Griffith, and Sāyaṇa's own first alternative agrees with him.

On verse 7 Sāyaṇa reads *brahmaṇi rājani* as two hosts, another brāhmaṇa who sacrifices and a kṣatriya, which both translators follow.

Verse 6's *asurair no vihavyaḥ* is a contest for the soma against the *asuras* in Griffith; Wilson turns it into the priests having prepared the soma, dropping the contest. The padapāṭha's *asuraiḥ* is instrumental and favours Griffith.

Verse 4's "the two" who stand anointing with lifted ladles Sāyaṇa identifies as the adhvaryu and his assistant, which is a ritual identification rather than a reading of the words.

109.title: Indrāgnī Sought as Kin — 'No Other Care Is Mine'
109.synthesis:
This hymn begins with a man looking for relatives and not finding any. *Vi hy akhyam manasā vasya icchann indrāgnī jñāsa uta vā sajātān* — I looked all round with my mind, wanting something better, for kinsmen or for people of my own blood. And then the finding: *nānyā yuvat pramatir asti mahyam* — there is no forethought for me other than yours. So, he says, I have fashioned this {{dhī}} for you, the one that seeks *{{vāja}}*. The verb is *atakṣam*, from the root a carpenter uses. The hymn is presented as joinery, and it is offered because the two gods turned out to be the only family available.

Kinship then organises everything that follows. Verse 2 measures {{indra}} and {{agni}}'s generosity against two figures from a wedding: I have heard you give more freely than a son-in-law who has fallen short of what was required of him, or than a bride's brother — the two men in a marriage who are under the heaviest obligation to be open-handed. It is a startling comparison to make about gods, and its force is that it comes from the same world as the first verse's search for relatives. Verse 3 makes the family literal: *mā chedma raśmīn iti nādhamānāḥ* — may we not cut the cords, we say, pleading, holding to the powers of the fathers. The cords are the line of descent, and the fear is of being the place where it stops. Then, immediately, the workshop of the rite: for Indrāgnī the strong drops rejoice; here the two pressing-stones lie in the lap of Dhiṣaṇā.

Verse 4 keeps her there. The goddess Dhiṣaṇā, longing, presses the {{soma}} for your rapture; and then a turn that reads like a slip and is not — you two of blessed hands, of fair hands, Aśvinā, run and mix it with sweetness in the waters. The dual pair is addressed for one line with the name of the other great dual pair of the collection, which is the sort of thing the hymns do when the shape of a relation matters more than the identity of its holders.

Verse 5 recalls a specific occasion: I have heard that you two were the strongest in the dividing of the wealth, at the {{vṛtra}}-slaying. Sit on the *barhis* at this {{yajña}} and take pleasure in the pressing.
