Verse 6 gives the pair their measure, and it is comparative all the way: beyond men where they shout for battle, beyond earth and heaven, beyond the rivers and the mountains in greatness, beyond all other beings whatever. Five terms, one preposition, no image — the hymn's one moment of pure magnitude.

Verse 7 returns to the family and closes the argument the first verse opened. Bring, give, you whose arms hold the bolt; help us with your *śacīs* — and then: *ime nu te raśmayaḥ sūryasya yebhiḥ sapitvaṃ pitaro na āsan*. These are the rays of {{sūrya}} by which our fathers had their fellowship. The cords of verse 3 and the fathers of verse 7 are the same thread, and the sun's rays are where the ancestors are still in company. A man who began by finding no kinsmen ends by naming the light in which his kinsmen are gathered.

Verse 8 is one line of request — breakers of forts, bolt in hand, give, and defend us in the battles — and then the closing formula shared across this whole run of hymns.
109.practice:
The first verse is the hymn's gift. A man says he looked around, with his mind, for family, and found only the gods. That is a sentence a great many people could say, and the Ṛgveda does not treat it as a lament. It is stated as a fact and then acted on: since you are what I have, I have made you something.

*Atakṣam*, "I have fashioned," is the word to keep. Making a hymn is spoken of throughout the collection with the vocabulary of carpentry — cutting, joining, fitting — and the next sūkta, [[1.110]], is addressed to the Ṛbhus, craftsmen who became gods by the quality of their work. Two hymns in a row, by the same seer, treat skilled making as the thing that connects a person to what is above him.

Verse 3 is the verse for a family. *Mā chedma raśmīn* — may we not cut the cords — asked while "holding to the powers of the fathers." The Ṛgveda's dread here is not damnation but discontinuity: being the generation at which a line, a practice, a transmission stops. Anyone who has worried about whether what they were given will pass on has the verse for it.

Verse 2 is worth knowing for a quite different reason. It shows what a wedding looked like from inside: a son-in-law who has not met the expectations placed on him and must make it up in gifts, and a bride's brother who gives out of affection. The gods are said to give more freely than either. That is a domestic simile, not a heroic one, and it tells us that the audience for these hymns knew both figures well.

And verse 7's last line is the one to hold at a śrāddha: the rays of the sun are where the fathers had their fellowship. The path of light by which the ancestors are reached is already here, in eight lines by a seer asking two gods to stand in for the relatives he could not find.
109.disagreements:
Verse 2's *vijāmātuḥ* is where the tradition is most informative. Sāyaṇa reads the prefix *vi-* as marking a son-in-law who lacks the qualifications the Vedas require and who must therefore conciliate his father-in-law with liberal gifts, and he cites the Nirukta's gloss *asusamāpta*, the unaccomplished bridegroom. He then takes some trouble to deny that any bride-price is implied, quoting the Manusmṛti that a father who takes a gratuity for his daughter is a seller of his offspring. Wilson prints "an unworthy bridegroom"; Griffith, "worthless son-in-law."

Verse 3 divides them badly. Wilson turns it into a prayer for descendants — never may we cut off the long line of posterity — following Sāyaṇa; Griffith translates the words and leaves them opaque: "Let us not break the cords: with this petition we strive to gain the powers of our forefathers." The padapāṭha supports the cords being cords.

On verse 4 Sāyaṇa glosses *devī dhiṣaṇā* as divine speech in the form of *mantra*, which lets Wilson write "the sacred prayer, desiring your presence, offers the libation"; Griffith keeps her as a vessel, "the bowl divine."

At verse 7 Sāyaṇa identifies the rays of the sun as the path by which worshippers reach the world of Brahmā, citing the Chāndogya, and glosses *sapitva* as a place to be reached in company.

110.title: The Ṛbhus Make One Cup Four and Win Immortality
110.synthesis:
The {{ṛbhu}}s are three brothers, sons of Sudhanvan, who were born mortal and are addressed here as gods. The hymn is about how that happened, and its answer is unusual enough to be worth stating plainly: they were made immortal because of the quality of their work.

The first verse begins by admitting a repetition. The work I did before is being done again; my sweetest *dhīti*, the thought shaped into speech, is spoken for praise; here is this sea belonging to all the gods — drink your fill of what has been offered with *svāhā*. A poet who returns to a hymn he has made before, and says so, is already talking about craft.

Verse 2 puts the brothers on a road. Seeking their enjoyment, going forward from far off, some kinsmen of mine, sons of Sudhanvan — by the extent of their journeying you came to the house of the liberal Savitṛ. Verse 3 is the turn: *tat savitā vo 'mṛtatvam ā suvat* — then Savitṛ impelled immortality toward you, when you came proclaiming the one who cannot be hidden. And in the same verse, the deed: that cup of the *asura*, the drinking vessel, which was one, you made fourfold.

That is the hymn's central fact and it is stated without ceremony. A single vessel was divided into four and the makers were given deathlessness. Verse 4 says how long it took: *saṃvatsare sam apṛcyanta dhītibhiḥ* — in the course of a year they were joined with the thoughts. Mortals, it says explicitly, *martāsaḥ santaḥ*, they reached immortality by service and by speed. Verse 5 describes the work itself in the flattest possible terms — like a field measured with a rod they measured out the one cup, wide-mouthed — praised by everyone who saw it, asking for the best, wanting fame among the immortals. Wanting fame is not held against them.

Verse 6 is the offering made back. To the leaders in the firmament we will pour our thought as ghee is poured with a ladle, knowingly; the Ṛbhus, who came with the swiftness of that father, climbed by *{{vāja}}* to the region of heaven. Verse 7 puts them beside {{indra}} without apology: Ṛbhu is our Indra, newest in strength; Ṛbhu with his *vājas* and his goods is the giver — gods, by your favour, on the good day may we withstand the attacks of those who press no {{soma}}.

Verse 8 lists the rest of their work, and it is domestic. Out of a hide you shaped a cow; you brought the mother back to her calf; sons of Sudhanvan, by your fine workmanship you made your aged parents young again. Three repairs: an animal restored, a bond restored, a lifetime restored. Nothing here is created from nothing. Everything is mended, divided, or renewed — which is what a craftsman actually does.

Verse 9 asks for help in the winning and for Indra, accompanied by the Ṛbhus, to break open wonderful bounty; then the line shared by nineteen hymns in this stretch of the collection hands the request to {{mitra}}, {{varuṇa}}, {{aditi}}, {{sindhu}}, Pṛthivī and Dyaus. The last request of a hymn about craftsmen is that something closed should be opened — which is the fourth of their repairs, and the one they are asked to perform now.
110.practice:
Ten sūktas in the whole Ṛgveda are addressed to the Ṛbhus, and two of them are this one and the next. It is a small body of text carrying a claim nothing else in the collection makes so directly: three men became gods because of what they made. Not by asceticism, not by descent, not by a boon — by workmanship, assessed and rewarded.

The details are worth holding because they are so ordinary. They divided one cup into four. They made a cow out of a hide and reunited her with her calf. They made their aged parents young. A chariot, in the next hymn. These are a smith's and a wheelwright's jobs, and the hymn treats them as the ground of immortality without any sense of incongruity.

The word to notice is *saṃvatsare*, "in the course of a year," in verse 4. The year is the unit of the work and the unit of the reward, and the Ṛbhus are elsewhere associated with the turning seasons. For a reader, the useful part is that the transformation is dated: it took a year of doing the thing properly.

*Dhīti* in verse 1 and *dhītibhiḥ* in verse 4 are the same word doing two jobs — the poet's shaped thought, and the thoughts with which the Ṛbhus were joined when they became immortal. The hymn's own making and the making it describes are named alike. In a tradition where the hymn is called *takṣita*, fashioned, that identification is not a flourish.

And verse 5 records that they wanted fame among the immortals, *amartyeṣu śravaḥ icchamānāḥ*. The Ṛgveda does not present ambition as an obstacle. It presents it as the ordinary motive of good work, and then grants what was wanted.
110.disagreements:
Sāyaṇa cites the Nirukta for the names — Ṛbhu, Vibhvan and Vāja were the three sons of Sudhanvan, himself a descendant of {{aṅgiras}} — and adds that Kutsa, the seer of this hymn, belongs to the same line, which is why verse 2 calls them his kinsmen of an earlier time. Wilson's English turns the same verse into a retirement to the forest for penance, which the padapāṭha does not supply.

Verse 3's Savitṛ divides them. Sāyaṇa notes that in the preceding hymn *savitṛ* may name the presenter of oblations, from *su*, to offer, while in this hymn the sun is meant. Wilson prints "the worshipper Savitā" in verse 2 and the god in verse 3; Griffith keeps the god throughout.

The cow of verse 8 comes with a story in Sāyaṇa: a seer's cow had died leaving a calf, and the Ṛbhus at his prayer formed a living cow and covered it with the dead one's skin so that the calf took it for its mother. Both translators print the making but only Wilson's bracket carries the deception.

On verse 6 Sāyaṇa glosses *nṛbhyaḥ* as "to the leaders of the sacrifice," since the Ṛbhus lead it, and notes a further identification in which the Ṛbhus are the rays of the sun. Griffith reads the same line as a hymn offered like oil in ladles; Wilson makes the ghee literal.

111.title: The Ṛbhus Who Fashioned — Now Fashion for Us
111.synthesis:
Five verses, and the whole hymn turns on a single verb changing tense. The first verse says *takṣan* four times — they fashioned. The second and third say *ā takṣata* — fashion for us. Everything the {{ṛbhu}}s are is contained in the first word of the hymn, and everything that is asked of them is that word put into the imperative.

What they fashioned, in verse 1: a well-rolling chariot, working with skill; the two bay horses that carry {{indra}}, bringers of good things; for their parents, a young lifetime; and for the calf, a mother to stand beside it. Four objects, one verb, and no two of them of the same kind — a vehicle, a pair of animals, a span of years, a relationship. The Ṛbhus' craft is not confined to things that can be held.

Verse 2 turns the verb round. Fashion for us, for the {{yajña}}, a Ṛbhu-like vigour; for the season, for *dakṣa* — competence, the skill that gets a thing done — food rich in offspring, so that we may dwell with a clan of heroes; set that excellent power in our company. The request is exactly parallel to the making of verse 1: not one thing but a set, some of it material and some of it not. Verse 3 continues in the same grammar and narrows to what a household needs: fashion winning for us, winning for the chariot, winning for the horse; a daily victorious gain, subduing in battle those of our own blood and those who are not. The last phrase, *jāmim ajāmim*, kinsman and stranger, is one of the corpus's unsentimental touches — the fights that matter are as often inside the family as outside it.

Verse 4 opens the invitation outward. I call Ṛbhukṣan Indra for help — Indra under the epithet that makes him lord of the Ṛbhus — and the Ṛbhus, the Vājas, the {{marut}}s, to the {{soma}}-drinking; and both Mitrāvaruṇau, and the Aśvinā. Then the purpose, in three words: *sātaye dhiye jiṣe* — may they speed us to gain, to *{{dhī}}*, to victory. The middle term is the one a reader should not pass over. Between winning and winning again, the poet asks for thought. In a hymn otherwise entirely about acquisition, the thing asked for in the same breath as the spoils is the faculty that shapes.

Verse 5 is two lines of request and one of formula. May Ṛbhu whet gain for the fight; may Vāja, victorious where men meet, help us — and then the closing line that seals nineteen sūktas in this part of the collection, handing everything to {{mitra}}, {{varuṇa}}, {{aditi}}, {{sindhu}}, Pṛthivī and Dyaus. Vāja, one of the three brothers, is here both a name and the ordinary word for the prize; the hymn ends by letting the two meanings sit on top of each other.

Read whole, the sūkta is an argument compressed into a grammatical move. Craftsmen who made a chariot, a team, a lifetime and a mother are asked to make vigour, offspring, competence and a day's winning. The claim is that these are the same kind of work.
111.practice:
Ten sūktas in the collection belong to the Ṛbhus alone. This is the shortest of them and the most usable, because it is built as a single request repeated: you made, now make.

*Takṣ*, to fashion, is the root behind *takṣan*, the carpenter, and it is the root the Ṛgveda uses for the composing of hymns — the seer of the preceding sūkta, [[1.109]], says *atakṣam*, I fashioned, of his own poem. Reading [[1.109]], [[1.110]] and this one in sequence gives a small doctrine of work: the hymn is joinery, the craftsmen who did their joinery well became immortal, and now they are asked to fashion for the man who fashioned for them.

*Dakṣa* in verse 2 is the word for competence — the practical capacity to carry a thing through. It sits beside *ṛtve*, "for the season," in the same line, which is the same idea as the *ṛtvij* of [[1.1]]: doing what belongs to the time, well. A reader who wants a Vedic word for professional excellence has it here.

The line to take away is verse 4's *sātaye dhiye jiṣe* — for gain, for thought, for victory. Three datives in a row, and the middle one is not an instrument for the other two; it stands as a thing to be asked for in its own right, in the middle of a request for spoils. The Ṛgveda does not treat clear thinking as preparation for the real business. It treats it as part of the haul.

For a family, verse 2's ask is exactly the ordinary one: strength for the rite, skill for the season, food and children, a household with capable people in it. There is nothing esoteric about what the Ṛbhus are asked to build.
111.disagreements:
Sāyaṇa is the reason the plurals in verse 4 can be read at all. He glosses *ṛbhukṣaṇam indram* as Indra who is Ṛbhukṣan, the mighty, and takes the accusative plurals *ṛbhūn* and *vājān* as naming the three sons of Sudhanvan — Ṛbhu, Vibhvan and Vāja — on the authority of the Nirukta. Griffith prints the names as a class, "the Rbhus, Vajas"; Wilson prints "the Ṛbhu, Vājas."

Verse 2 shows the two translators pulling apart on the same words. Sāyaṇa derives *ṛbhumat* from *uru* and *bhā*, "having much light," and Wilson accordingly writes "resplendent sacrificial food"; Griffith reads the compound as vigour — "make for us active vital power." The morphology allows both, and the second sits better beside *dakṣāya* in the same line.

Verse 1's *takṣan pitṛbhyāṃ yuvad vayaḥ* is "they gave youthful existence to their parents" in Wilson and "made life young again" in Griffith — agreement, and the clearest of the Ṛbhus' four makings.

Verse 5's *vājaḥ samaryajit* is a proper name in both, one of the brothers, but Wilson glosses him as "victorious in battle" and Griffith as "conquering in the fight," neither noticing in the English that the same word is the ordinary noun for the prize being asked for two words earlier.

112.title: 'With Which Aids' — the Aśvins' Long Roll of Rescues
112.synthesis:
Twenty of this hymn's twenty-five verses begin with the same word, *yābhiḥ* — "with which (aids)." Twenty-three of them end with the same line: *tābhir ū ṣu ūtibhir aśvinā gatam*, "with those, then, with those helps, Aśvinā, come." Between the two clamps, each verse names something the twins once did for somebody. The hymn is a list, and the list is the argument: you have helped before, by name, in these cases; come with the same helps now.

The first three verses set the frame. Verse 1 praises Dyāvāpṛthivī for the first thought and {{agni}}, bright and hot, so that the approach may be prepared; then the first *yābhiḥ*: with the aids by which you speed the cry for the prize in battle. Verse 2 has the offerings standing round the chariot as listeners stand round a teacher's words, and asks for the aids by which the twins protect *{{dhī}}*, thought at work in the rite. Verse 3 gives them lordship over the peoples by the force of what is deathless, and names the first rescue — the barren cow made to yield milk.

Then the roll opens, and it does not close for twenty verses. Rebha and Vandana lifted out of the water to see the light. Kaṇva helped when he was striving. Antaka failing in the pit; Bhujyu brought through; Karkandhu and Vayya comforted. Śucanti given wealth and a seat; the burning pit made bearable for {{atri}}; Pṛśnigu and Purukutsa guarded. Parāvṛj set on his feet, the blind given sight, the lame made to walk, the quail loosed from the jaws that held her. The sweet flood made to run; Vasiṣṭha gladdened; {{kutsa}}, Śrutarya and Narya helped. Viśpalā made able to go into a battle of a thousand spoils. Honey poured from a cloud for Dīrghaśravas the merchant, and {{kakṣīvant}} the praiser protected. The Rasā filled with water; a chariot made to win without a horse; Triśoka's cattle driven out. The sun encircled at a distance; Mandhātṛ upheld in his lordship of lands; Bharadvāja helped. Divodāsa guarded at Śambara's killing; Trasadasyu at the breaking of forts. Vamra, Upastuta, Kali when he took a wife, Vyaśva, Pṛthi. Śayu, Atri, and {{manu}} long ago, shown the way out; arrows shot for Syūmaraśmi. Paṭharvan shining like a kindled fire; Śaryāta held in the great struggle. The {{aṅgiras}}es, whose hearts rejoiced when they went first to open the pen of milk; Manu again, sustained with food. A wife brought for Vimada; the ruddy cows won back; wealth carried to Sudās. Bhujyu again, and Adhrigu, and Ṛtastubh. Kṛśānu where the arrows flew; a young man's horse given speed; honey carried to the bees. The man fighting for cattle, for land, for offspring; his chariots and horses kept. Kutsa the son of Arjuna, Turvīti, Dabhīti, Dhvasanti, Puruṣanti.

Then verse 24 stops listing and asks. *Apnasvatīm aśvinā vācam asme kṛtaṃ naḥ dasrā vṛṣaṇā manīṣām* — make our speech productive, make our thought; and, the detail that dates the hymn's use, *adyūtye avase ni hvaye vām* — in the lightless hour I call you for help. Verse 25 is one line: by days and by nights guard us with blessings undiminished — and then the closing formula shared across this whole run of sūktas.

Fifty-two hymns in the collection belong to the Aśvinau alone. This is the one that shows what their reputation was made of: not a doctrine but a caseload.
112.practice:
The Aśvinau are the physicians of the gods, and this hymn is their record of practice. Read the roll and notice what kind of trouble it covers: a man in a well, a man in a fire-pit, a man at sea, a woman who cannot walk, a blind man, a lame man, a barren cow, a dried river, a bird in a predator's mouth, an old man, a woman without a husband, a merchant far from home. Almost nothing in the list is a battle. What the twins are remembered for is extraction — getting somebody out of a fix that they could not get out of themselves.

Verse 24 tells you when to call them. *Adyūtye*, in the lightless hour — the last watch of the night, before dawn, which is where the tradition's ritual manuals place the Aśvins' worship. That is the brāhma-muhūrta, the hour a great many Hindus still keep for practice, and this is one of the places in the Ṛgveda where a deity is attached to it.

The other half of verse 24 is what the singer actually wants: *apnasvatīṃ vācam*, speech that yields something, and *manīṣā*, the shaping mind. After twenty verses of other people's rescues, the poet asks for his own words to work.

The form is worth imitating. The hymn does not argue that the Aśvins are powerful; it recites what they have done, name by name, and lets the accumulation make the case. That is how memory functions in this tradition — not as nostalgia but as evidence. Anyone who has kept a list of times they were helped knows the mechanism.

Fifty-two sūktas are addressed to the Aśvinau alone, sixteen of them in maṇḍala 1; the six hymns from this one through [[1.120]] are the densest run of them in the collection. If a reader wants to know these gods, this is where to begin, because it is where they are least abstract.
112.disagreements:
Sāyaṇa supplies almost every story behind the names, and without him the list is unreadable. Rebha and Vandana thrown into wells by *asuras*; Atri shut in a cave of a hundred doors with chaff fires at each, quenched with cold water — or, on his alternative, Atri as the eater, Agni himself, renewed by rain. Viśpalā the wife of Khela son of Agastya. Bhujyu the son of Tugra, shipwrecked. Manu taught to sow barley, which he gives as the substance of the help in verse 18. Kṛśānu he identifies with the keepers of the soma, citing the Taittirīya Saṃhitā.

Where the two translators diverge it is usually because Wilson has taken a name as a description or the reverse. In verse 8 Wilson makes Parāvṛj, the blind man and Śroṇa three persons; Griffith keeps Paravrj and reads the others as conditions. In verse 4 Wilson's "circumambient wind" for *parijman* becomes Griffith's "Wanderer," and Sāyaṇa's note on the same word runs to Agni as the son of Vāyu and to *dvimātṛ* as the two fire-sticks.

Verse 21's honey and bees is agreed by both, and is one of the few images in the hymn needing no legend. On verse 24's *adyūtye* Sāyaṇa is precise: the hour without light, the last watch before dawn, at which he says the Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra directs that the Aśvins be worshipped. Both translators lose it — Wilson to "the last watch of the night," Griffith to "in luckless game."

113.title: Uṣas Wakes the World and Outlives All Who See Her
113.synthesis:
*Idaṃ śreṣṭhaṃ jyotiṣāṃ jyotir āgāt* — this has come, the best light of lights. The hymn opens by not naming her. What has arrived is a light, and a bright *praketa*, a far-reaching foresign, has been born; and Rātrī, sent forth for Savitṛ's impelling, has yielded up her womb to {{uṣas}}. The first thing said about the dawn is that the night made room for her.

Verses 2 and 3 hold the two together. The bright one has come with her bright calf and the dark one has given over her seats; kin, immortal, following one another, exchanging colour, the two move across the sky. Their road is one and endless, travelled by turns; of unlike forms and of one mind, Naktoṣāsā neither clash nor stand still. Same road, different colours, one intention, no collision, no pause.

Then three verses that close on the same line — *uṣā ajīgar bhuvanāni viśvā*, Uṣas has awakened all beings. Verse 4: shining, *netrī sūnṛtānām*, leader of true and generous speech, she is perceived; she has opened our doors; stirring the world, she has shown us riches. Verse 5: she sets the man curled asleep on his feet — one for enjoyment, one for wealth, one for the rite, and those who saw little, to see far. Verse 6 counts the waking out: one to power, one to fame, one to greatness, one to his own business, one simply to go — to look upon lives of unlike kinds. Read together, the three verses are a census taken at first light. Every person is going somewhere different, and one event starts all of them.

Verse 7 finally names her in address: this daughter of heaven has been seen, a young woman in bright raiment, mistress of all earthly treasure — shine here today. Verse 8 sets the long axis: she follows the track of the mornings gone and is first of the endless ones to come, rousing the living, waking no one who is dead. Verse 9 says what she has done for the gods: because you made {{agni}} kindled, because you disclosed the world by the eye of {{sūrya}}, because you woke the men who would sacrifice. Verse 10 asks what nobody can answer: how long until they are together, the dawns that have shone and those still to shine? She longs after the earlier ones and goes on gladly with the others.

Verse 11 is the verse. *Īyus te ye pūrvatarām apaśyan vyucchantīm uṣasam martyāsaḥ* — they are gone, those mortals who saw an earlier Uṣas dawning; to us she is now there to be looked at; and they are coming, those who will see her in times after. Nothing is added. The hymn does not console.

Verse 12 gives the epithets that make her more than weather: driver-off of hostility, *ṛtapā* and *ṛtejā* — guardian of {{ṛta}} and born of *ṛta* — urging generous speech, bringing the gods' feast. Verse 13: she shone in the old days, shines today, will shine on days to come, unaging, undying, moving by her own *svadhā*. Verse 14 has her throw off the black robe at the sky's border and come with ruddy horses. Verse 15 makes her the last of those gone and the first of those to shine. Verse 16 is the shout: *ūrdhvaṃ jīvo asur na āgāt* — rise, the living breath has come, darkness has gone; she has left a path for Sūrya, and we have arrived where they lengthen life.

Verse 17 has the singer raising his voice on the thread of speech and asking for life with offspring; verse 18 wants the presser to win the dawns rich in cattle; verse 19 calls her mother of the gods, the face of Aditi, the *ketu* of the {{yajña}}. Verse 20 hands it all to {{mitra}}, {{varuṇa}}, {{aditi}}, {{sindhu}}, Pṛthivī and Dyaus.
113.practice:
Twenty sūktas in the Ṛgveda are addressed to Uṣas alone. This is the longest of them, at twenty verses, and it is the one to know.

Verse 11 is why. *They are gone, those mortals who saw an earlier Uṣas; to us she is now to be looked at; and they are coming who will see her afterwards.* Three clauses: the dead, the living, the unborn, arranged around one recurring event that outlasts all three. The hymn does not offer a doctrine of the soul and does not need one. It observes that the same dawn was watched by people who are no longer here and will be watched by people not yet here, and it says this while the reciter is standing outside at daybreak. That is the whole of the teaching, and it is available every morning without any preparation.

The practical shape of the hymn is verses 4 to 6, the three that close on *uṣā ajīgar bhuvanāni viśvā*, she has awakened all beings. The waking is enumerated rather than generalised: one man rises for enjoyment, one for wealth, one for worship, one for power, one for reputation, one just to go about his business. The Ṛgveda does not rank them. What it says is that all of them get up because of the same thing, and that those who could see little are given far sight.

The hour is the hour the tradition kept hardest. Uṣas has no later temple and no image, but the *saṃdhyā* at daybreak, the Gāyatrī said facing east, the brāhma-muhūrta before it — all of them are practices about this moment, and this hymn is the oldest sustained description of it in any Indian language.

Two of her epithets in verse 12 are worth carrying: *ṛtapā* and *ṛtejā*, guardian of *ṛta* and born from *ṛta*. The daily arrival of light is treated as an instance of the order itself, not merely as an occasion for praising it. And *netrī sūnṛtānām* in verse 4 — she who leads out true and generous speech — occurs twice in the collection, here and in the other great Uṣas hymn of this maṇḍala, [[1.92]].7. What the dawn releases first, in both, is the beginning of honest speaking.
113.disagreements:
The refrain of verses 4 to 6 is the hymn's sharpest divergence. The padapāṭha gives *uṣāḥ ajīgar bhuvanāni viśvā*, and the morphology makes *ajīgar* a reduplicated aorist of √jāgṛ, to wake. Griffith reads it so: "All living creatures hath the Dawn awakened." Wilson, following Sāyaṇa, prints instead "Uṣas gives back all the regions," supplying a bracket that the regions had been swallowed by night. The form does not support it, and the reading followed above is the one the padapāṭha and the grammar give.

Verse 19 divides them again. *Mātā devānām aditer anīkam*: *anīka* is a face or appearance. Griffith has "Aditi's form of glory"; Wilson has "rival of Aditi," and Sāyaṇa explains the rivalry — the gods are woken at dawn by the worship they then receive, so Uṣas may figuratively be called their mother, and in that character she is {{aditi}}'s competitor. It is an ingenious defence of a reading the word itself resists.

At verse 2 Sāyaṇa glosses the bright calf as the sun, saying that dawn precedes and therefore figuratively bears him; Wilson prints "the parent of the sun." Verse 1's night he calls the precursor and therefore the womb of the dawn. On verse 4 he adds a lovely observation: the animals and birds utter their true, natural cries when she appears, which is why she leads *sūnṛtāḥ*. On verse 12 he takes the driven-off hostility as the rākṣasas, who vanish at daybreak, and for verse 8's *pāthaḥ* he cites the Nirukta's gloss, the mid-region.

114.title: Rudra, Best of Healers — Harm Not One of Ours
114.synthesis:
*Imā rudrāya tavase kapardine kṣayadvīrāya pra bharāmahe matīḥ* — these thoughts we bring forward for {{rudra}}, the strong, the one with braided hair, the *kṣayadvīra*. And then, at once, what they are for: *yathā śam asad dvipade catuṣpade viśvaṃ puṣṭaṃ grāme asmin anāturam* — that it may be well with two-footed and four-footed, that everything in this village may be thriving and free from sickness. The first verse of the Ṛgveda's only Rudra hymn outside maṇḍalas 2 and 7 asks for public health.

Verse 2 gives the vocabulary the tradition kept. *Mṛḷā no rudrota no mayas kṛdhi* — be gracious to us, Rudra, and make us gladness; with *{{namas}}* we would serve the *kṣayadvīra*; and what *śaṃ ca yoś ca* — welfare and safety — father {{manu}} won by sacrifice, may we obtain under your leading. Nothing new is requested. What is asked for is what an ancestor already secured, and the paired benediction *śaṃ yoḥ* stands in only three verses in the whole collection.

Verse 3 asks for his *sumati* through the worship of the gods, calls him *mīḍhvas*, the bountiful, and invites him into the settlements: come to us wishing us well, and with our men unharmed we will pour your offering. Verse 4 calls him down from a distance — the blazing one, *yajñasādha*, who brings the rite to completion, *vaṅku*, who goes crookedly, and *kavi*; may he cast the gods' anger far from us; his good thought is what we choose. Verse 5 is the hymn's central image and its most surprising: *divo varāham aruṣaṃ kapardinam* — the boar of the sky, ruddy, braided — we call him down with *namas*, and then the reason: *haste bibhrad bheṣajā vāryāṇi*, carrying in his hand choice medicines. Three words for shelter follow, piled up: *śarma varma cchardiḥ*, covering, armour, roof. A god who arrives with a fistful of drugs is asked for a roof.

Verse 6 names him father of the {{marut}}s, calls this word sweeter than sweet, and asks the immortal for the food of mortals and for grace on the speaker, his child and his grandchild. Then verses 7 and 8 do the thing this hymn is known for. *Mā no mahāntam uta mā no arbhakaṃ mā na ukṣantam uta mā na ukṣitam mā no vadhīḥ pitaraṃ mota mātaram* — not our great one and not our small one, not the one growing and not the one grown, do not kill our father, nor our mother; and do not injure our own dear bodies. Then verse 8 extends the list outward: not in our children or our children's children, not in our lifetime, not in our cattle, not in our horses; do not, when angry, kill our men; bringing offerings we call you always. Eleven separate refusals across two verses, and among them every member of a household and everything it owns.

Verse 9 is quiet after that. I have brought my praises up to you as a herdsman brings his animals; give us your *sumna*, father of the Maruts; your good thought is auspicious, most gracious — therefore we choose your help. Verse 10 asks for the weapon to be set aside: far be your cow-killing and your man-killing; be gracious; speak on our behalf; grant shelter, you who are strong on both sides. Verse 11 closes: we have said *namas* to him, seeking help; may Rudra with the Maruts hear our call — and then the formula shared by nineteen hymns in this stretch of the collection.
114.practice:
Rudra is addressed by only three sūktas in the whole Ṛgveda — this one, [[2.33]], and 7.46 — and this is the one most people meet. That count says something about the Ṛgveda's distribution, not about Rudra: the Yajurveda gives him the Śatarudriya, one of the largest single addresses to any deity anywhere in the Veda, and it is recited daily as the Rudram. Where a deity stands in one saṃhitā is not the measure of where he stands in the Veda.

The continuity is exact and can be heard. Verse 8 of this hymn — *mā nas toke tanaye mā na āyau mā no goṣu mā no aśveṣu rīriṣaḥ*, do not harm our children or our descendants, our lives, our cattle, our horses — is carried in the Rudram, and anyone who has heard the Rudram recited has heard this verse. Within the Ṛgveda it stands in exactly one other place, 7.46.3, also a Rudra hymn. It is the same petition in the same words across the corpus.

What this hymn asks for is worth being plain about, because it is not what a reader expecting devotion might expect. It asks Rudra to withhold. *Mā* — do not — governs the hymn: do not harm, do not be angry, do not take. He is addressed as *jalāṣa-bheṣaja*, the one whose medicine cools, and as the fiercest of the fierce in the same breath, and the worshipper asks for the medicine and the sparing together. That doubleness is not a tension the hymn resolves; it is what the hymn is about.

He is *kapardin*, wearing the coiled hair — a word that occurs twice in the Ṛgveda, here and at 9.67.11. And he is called *bhiṣaktama*, the best of healers, which is why the tradition's approach to him has always run through both fear and cure at once.
114.disagreements:
Sāyaṇa gives five derivations of the name and refuses to choose. Rudra makes all weep, *rodayati*, at the end of the world; or *rut* is the pain of living, which he drives away; or the Upaniṣads by which he is approached; or the divine speech he grants; or the darkness he tears open. He adds the Taittirīya Saṃhitā's account of Agni, who stole the gods' treasure and wept when they recovered it, and was called Rudra from *arudat*.

*Kṣayadvīra*, which stands in verses 1, 2, 3 and 10, is the hymn's real crux. Sāyaṇa offers two constructions — one in whom heroes perish, or one whose sons are the ruling heroes, the Maruts — and keeps both. Wilson prints the first throughout, so that his Rudra is "the destroyer of heroes"; Griffith prints the second, "Lord of Heroes." The whole tone of the hymn turns on which is heard.

Verse 5's *varāha* is a boar in Griffith, "the wild-boar of the sky." Sāyaṇa will not have it: he reads the word as a shortening of *varāhāra*, one who has good food, or as denoting a hard body like a boar's, and Wilson prints "him who has excellent food."

On verse 6 Sāyaṇa recounts the Purāṇic origin of the Maruts as sons of Rudra — the shapeless births given form at Pārvatī's asking. Verse 4's *vaṅku* is "the tortuous" in Wilson, "the wanderer" in Griffith.

115.title: Sūrya, the Ātman of All That Moves and Stands
115.synthesis:
Six verses, and the first of them contains the line that outlived everything else in the hymn. *Citraṃ devānām ud agād anīkaṃ cakṣur mitrasya varuṇasyāgneḥ* — the bright face of the gods has risen, the eye of {{mitra}}, of {{varuṇa}}, of {{agni}}. Then: *sūrya ātmā jagatas tasthuṣaś ca*, {{sūrya}} is the *ātman* of what moves and what stands; he has filled Dyāvāpṛthivī and the mid-air. In one verse the sun is called a face, an eye, and a self, and each of the three is doing different work. A face is what is turned toward you. An eye is what sees you. An *ātman* is what animates you. The hymn moves from being looked at to being lived by, in the space of two lines.

Verse 2 makes him a young man following a woman: Sūrya goes after the shining goddess {{uṣas}} as a youth goes after a girl — and in the same verse, the human world beneath the pursuit, where men who seek the gods stretch out the yokes, going after good for the sake of good. The sky's romance and the ploughing of a field are put in one frame without a seam.

Verse 3 is the horses. Auspicious are the tawny mares of Sūrya, dappled, worthy of the shout of joy; honoured by us, they have mounted the back of the sky and in a single day go round earth and heaven. Nothing is asked. The verse exists to say that the circuit is completed daily, which is the fact the rest of the hymn depends on.

Verse 4 is the one that stops a reader. *Tat sūryasya devatvaṃ tan mahitvaṃ madhyā kartor vitataṃ saṃ jabhāra* — this is Sūrya's godhead, this his greatness: in the middle of the work, he gathers back in what he had spread out. When he has unyoked his mares from their station, then Rātrī spreads her robe over everything. The greatness of the sun is defined by his withdrawal, and the withdrawal is dated to the middle of a job — the moment when the work of the day is unfinished and stops anyway. The tradition's own gloss makes this literal: the farmer and the craftsman put down their tools at sunset whether or not they are done.

Verse 5 gives him two colours and one team. In the lap of the sky he makes his form for Mitra and Varuṇa to see; endless is the one, his gleaming brightness, and the other is black — and his tawny mares carry both. The bright and the dark are not two powers in conflict; they are two aspects of one appearance, drawn by the same horses.

Verse 6 is the only request in the hymn and it is one line: *adya devā uditā sūryasya niraṃhasaḥ pipṛtā nir avadyāt* — today, gods, at the rising of Sūrya, carry us out of the narrow place and out of disgrace. Then the closing formula that seals this whole run of sūktas, handing the request to Mitra, Varuṇa, {{aditi}}, {{sindhu}}, Pṛthivī and Dyaus. Five verses of description, one verse of asking, and what is asked for is release from *aṃhas*, the constriction that the two preceding hymns in this run are also about.
115.practice:
*Sūrya ātmā jagatas tasthuṣaś ca.* If a reader learns one line from this range of the Ṛgveda, it should be this one. The formula occurs twice in the collection — here of Sūrya, and at 7.101.6 of Parjanya, where it is *tasmin ātmā jagatas tasthuṣaś ca*, "in him is the self of what moves and what stands." Its later career is enormous: the pairing of the moving and the standing becomes the standard Sanskrit way of saying "everything whatsoever," and the claim that one thing is the *ātman* of all of it is the seed of a great deal that came after. Here it is said of something a person can walk outside and see.

Six sūktas in the Ṛgveda are addressed to Sūrya alone. That is a small number, and it needs a distinction to be understood: the daily verse most Hindus actually recite, the Gāyatrī, is addressed to Savitṛ, the impeller, not to Sūrya — a related but separate name. What Sūrya carries in this hymn is the eye and the self, and the *arghya* offered to the sun at *saṃdhyā*, the *sūryopasthāna*, the *namaskāra* done facing east, all belong to this address.

Verse 4 is the one to take into a working life. The sun does not finish; he gathers in what he had spread, *madhyā kartoḥ*, in the middle of the work, and then Night covers everything. The Ṛgveda calls that his godhead and his greatness. A day ends when the light ends, not when the task is done, and the hymn treats the ability to stop mid-work as a divine attribute rather than a failure.

And verse 5's two colours are worth holding beside the Uṣas hymn that precedes this one, [[1.113]], where Night and Dawn share one road and one mind. Here the bright form and the black are borne by the same horses. Neither hymn treats darkness as an enemy. It is the other half of the same movement, and both halves are drawn by the same team.
115.disagreements:
Sāyaṇa's reading of the first verse is the most consequential thing preserved on this hymn. He glosses *ātmā jagataḥ* as the soul of the world, from the sun's pervading and animating all things, and takes *jagataḥ* as what moves and *tasthuṣaḥ* as what is fixed; then he grounds it causally — *sa hi sarvasya sthāvarajaṅgamātmakasya kāryavargasya kāraṇam*, he is the cause of the whole class of effects, moving and unmoving. Wilson softens this to "the soul of all that moves or is immoveable"; Griffith softens it further to "the soul of all that moveth not or moveth," losing *ātman* entirely.

Verse 2's *yugāni* is where the two translators separate. Wilson, following the sense of an age, has pious men performing the ceremonies established for ages. Sāyaṇa records the other possibility outright — *yugāni* as yokes for ploughs, so that at dawn men seeking the gods' favour through the profit of agriculture harness their teams — and Griffith prints something between the two, "where pious men extend their generations."

Verse 4's *madhyā kartoḥ* Sāyaṇa fixes by the Nirukta and then makes concrete: the cultivator or artisan leaves off his labour, unfinished, when the sun sets. Wilson prints "the unfinished task"; Griffith, "what spread o'er work unfinished."

At verse 5 Sāyaṇa notes that *haritaḥ* may be either the rays or the horses, and that Mitra and Varuṇa here stand by metonymy for the world.

116.title: The Aśvins' Deeds Told — Bhujyu Brought from the Sea
116.synthesis:
A new seer takes over the collection here, and he announces himself by his craft. *Nāsatyābhyāṃ barhir iva pra vṛñje* — for the Nāsatyā I trim my song as one trims the sacred grass; I send praises up as the wind drives rainclouds. The first thing the poet says about his hymn is that making it is a manual operation.

Then the deeds, and this hymn tells them rather than listing them. Vimada's bride carried off in a chariot swift as an arrow. The ass that won the thousand in Yama's contest. And then five verses on one rescue, told with a persistence nothing else in the collection gives it. Tugra left {{bhujyu}} in the flood of waters as a dying man leaves his wealth; you brought him back in ships that had breath in them, moving through the air, keeping out the water. Three nights and three days you carried him with winged things to the far shore of the sea, in three chariots with a hundred feet and six horses. And then the verse that says what the sea was: *anārambhaṇe tad avīrayethām anāsthāne agrabhaṇe samudre* — in that which offers no hold, no standing-place, nothing to grasp, you did the heroic thing, when you brought Bhujyu home in a hundred-oared ship. Three negations in one line for what open water is like to a man in it.

From there the deeds come one to a verse. The white horse given to Pedu, always a victory. Insight dug out for {{kakṣīvant}} of the Pajras, and a hundred jars poured from a stallion's hoof. Snow held against the burning for {{atri}}, and Atri brought up out of the pit with his whole company. The well turned over for the thirsty Gotama, its bottom put up and its mouth down, so the water ran. Aged Cyavana's skin stripped off like armour, his abandoned life lengthened, and he made the husband of young women. Vandana brought up out of hiding like a buried treasure. Dadhyañc, son of Atharvan, telling them the honey by the head of a horse — a deed the poet says he makes public as thunder makes rain public. A son, Hiraṇyahasta, given to a woman whose husband could not father one. The quail freed from the wolf's mouth; a mourning poet given his sight.

Verse 15 is the one people remember. In Khela's battle in the night, Viśpalā's leg was cut off like a bird's wing, and at once they fitted her an iron leg so that she could run, the prize being already set. Verse 16: Ṛjrāśva, blinded by his own father for slaughtering a hundred sheep for a she-wolf, given eyes by the two who are called *bhiṣajau*, physicians. Verse 17: the daughter of {{sūrya}} mounted your chariot, reaching the goal as a runner reaches it, and all the gods assented in their hearts.

The last stretch is a run of names — Divodāsa and Bharadvāja, the children of Jahnu, Jāhuṣa carried out by night through easy roads, Vaśa helped in a single dawn, Pṛthuśravas's enemies driven off, water raised from the bottom of a well for Śara, milk given to Śayu's barren cow, Viṣṇāpu restored to Viśvaka his father like a lost animal found. Verse 24 returns to Rebha, bound ten nights and nine days, wounded and under water, drawn up like {{soma}} with a ladle.

Verse 25 is the poet's own request, and after twenty-four verses of other men's crises it is startlingly modest: may I be master of this, with good cattle and good sons, and with my sight, and reaching a long life — *astam iva id jarimāṇaṃ jagamyām*, may I come to old age as a man comes home.
116.practice:
The Aśvinau are called *bhiṣajau*, physicians, in verse 16 of this hymn, and everything in the twenty-five verses is consistent with that. What they do is get people out — out of water, out of a pit, out of blindness, out of a wolf's jaws, out of old age, out of childlessness. Not one of the deeds is a conquest.

Verse 15 is the passage most often pointed to, and it deserves it: Viśpalā's leg is severed in a night battle and she is fitted with an iron one *sadyaḥ*, at once, so that she can run while the prize is still in play. Whatever historical weight one gives it, the text plainly imagines a prosthesis and a woman using it to get back into the contest. It is one of the very few places in the collection where a woman is named in a battle.

Verse 5's three negations — *anārambhaṇe anāsthāne agrabhaṇe*, no hold, no standing, no grasp — are the corpus's description of the open sea, and they double as a description of any situation in which there is nothing to take hold of. Read with the ships that have breath in them and the crossing of three days and nights, this is the Ṛgveda's fullest picture of a rescue from something that cannot be fought.

The closing line is the practical one. *Astam iva id jarimāṇaṃ jagamyām* — may I enter old age as one enters his own house. Not may I escape it, not may I be young again; may arriving there feel like arriving home. After a hymn full of people saved from catastrophe, the poet asks for an ordinary end, and asks for it in the language of coming indoors.

Eleven sūktas in maṇḍala 1 belong to this seer, [[1.116]] through [[1.126]], and one more in maṇḍala 9. Five of the eleven are to the Aśvinau, and this is the first. If the twenty-verse litany of [[1.112]] is their case-list, this is the same material told as stories.
116.disagreements:
Sāyaṇa supplies the narrative frames, and the two translators diverge chiefly over how much of them to print. On Bhujyu he gives a full account: Tugra sent his son with an army by ship against enemies on another island; the vessel foundered, and the Aśvins brought him and his troops back in three days in their own ships. Wilson prints the outline; Griffith keeps only the words.

Verse 3's *naubhir ātmanvatībhiḥ* is "vessels of your own" in Wilson and "animated vessels" in Griffith. The padapāṭha's *ātmanvatībhiḥ*, having *ātman*, supports Griffith; Wilson's reading follows a gloss rather than the word.

On verse 12 Sāyaṇa gives the whole Dadhyañc episode: {{indra}} taught him the *pravargya* and the *madhu* knowledge and threatened to cut off his head if he passed it on; the Aśvins persuaded him, removed his own head and replaced it with a horse's; Indra struck off the horse's head, and the twins restored his own. Wilson calls the content "the mystic science"; Griffith reads *madhu* as the sweetness of Soma.

Verse 16's she-wolf Sāyaṇa explains as one of the Aśvins' own asses in disguise, testing Ṛjrāśva's charity — which is why his father's anger is at the exaction of the sheep from his people. Neither translator prints the disguise.

117.title: The Aśvins Restore — Ghoṣā, Cyavana, Dadhyañc's Head
117.synthesis:
The companion piece to [[1.116]], the same length, by the same seer, and it opens by stating its own liturgy. For the rapture of the sweet {{soma}} your ancient *hotā* invites you; the gift is set on the strewn grass, the song is laid out — come with food and with strength, Nāsatyā. Verse 2 gives them the chariot swifter than mind, drawn by good horses, which goes to the house of the man who does right; come on it to us.

Then the restorations. {{atri}}, honoured by the five peoples, freed from the burning pit along with his people, the guiles of the {{dasyu}} baffled. Rebha, sunk in water like a hidden horse and wounded, drawn out — *na vāṃ jūryanti pūrvyā kṛtāni*, your ancient deeds do not grow old. Vandana brought up like buried gold, like a man asleep in the lap of destruction, like {{sūrya}} living in darkness. A hundred jars poured from a stallion's hoof for {{kakṣīvant}} of the Pajras — the poet naming himself in the third person as a man the twins once helped.

Verse 7 is the one to mark. You gave Viṣṇāpu back to Viśvaka son of Kṛṣṇa who praised you — and: *ghoṣāyai cit pitṛṣade duroṇe patiṃ jūryantyai aśvināv adattam*, to Ghoṣā too, growing old in her father's house, you Aśvinā gave a husband. Verse 8 continues in the same vein: a bride for Śyāva, sight for Kaṇva, and glory laid on the son of Nṛṣad. Verse 9 gives Pedu the swift horse, the thousand-winner, unopposed, serpent-slaying. Verse 10 acknowledges the patrons: these are your glories, bountiful ones; prayer and praise are your dwelling in both worlds; when the Pajras call you, come with food.

Verse 11 names Agastya as the one whose *brahman* strengthened them, and Viśpalā as the one they set on her feet. Verse 12 asks where they were going when they raised the buried one on the tenth day like a pitcher full of gold. Verse 13: you made the aged Cyavana young again by your *śacīs*, and the daughter of Sūrya chose your chariot with all her splendour. Verses 14 and 15 return to {{bhujyu}}: brought out of the sea with brown birds that flew, carried to safety on a well-yoked car swift as thought.

Verse 16 has the quail calling and being loosed from the wolf's jaws, and verses 17 and 18 give Ṛjrāśva's blinding and his cure — and then, remarkably, the she-wolf speaks. *Śunam andhāya bharam ahvayat sā vṛkīḥ* — she called out, for the blind man's good: Aśvinā, heroes, Ṛjrāśva has cut up a hundred and one sheep for me like a young lover. The creature the man was punished for feeding intercedes for him.

Verse 19 names what the twins do: your help is great and gladdening, and *srāmaṃ saṃ riṇīthaḥ*, you make the maimed whole. Verse 20 has Śayu's barren cow filled with milk and Purumitra's daughter brought to Vimada. Verse 21 is the widest of them: ploughing and sowing barley, milking out food for {{manu}}, blasting the Dasyu — *uru jyotiś cakrathur āryāya*, you made wide light for the Ārya. Verse 22 returns to Dadhyañc and the horse's head and the honey he told. Verse 23 asks for wealth with children; verse 24 gives Hiraṇyahasta to the childless wife and restores Śyāva, who had been cut into three. Verse 25 closes: these ancient deeds men have told; may we, with good sons, speak in the assembly.
117.practice:
Ghoṣā, in verse 7, is the reason to read this hymn twice. She is growing old unmarried in her father's house, and the Aśvinau give her a husband. Nothing more is said here. But the Anukramaṇī gives 10.39 and 10.40 — two Aśvin hymns, twenty-eight verses between them — to *Kākṣīvatī Ghoṣā*, Ghoṣā the daughter of {{kakṣīvant}}. The man composing this verse is her father, and she becomes a seer in her own right, addressing the same gods. Whatever the tradition means by naming a woman as ṛṣi, this is one of the places it does it, and the two ends of the story sit nine maṇḍalas apart in the same collection.

The verb that runs under the hymn is restoration. *Srāmaṃ saṃ riṇīthaḥ*, verse 19 — you make the maimed whole. Sight given back to Kaṇva and to Ṛjrāśva. Youth given back to Cyavana. A son given back to Viśvaka. Śyāva, cut into three, put together. A leg for Viśpalā. What the Aśvinau are for, in this seer's understanding, is that things which have been broken can be made to work again.

Verse 21 is where they touch ordinary livelihood: ploughing and sowing barley, milking food out for Manu. The gods who fly on falcons are also the gods of the first furrow, and the same verse ends with light made wide for the Ārya.

Verse 18 is worth pausing on for its strangeness. The she-wolf, for whom Ṛjrāśva slaughtered the sheep that cost him his eyes, calls out to the Aśvins on his behalf — *śunam andhāya*, for the blind man's good. The animal that occasioned the punishment asks for the cure. The Ṛgveda leaves it there without comment, and it is one of the few places in the collection where a beast speaks.
117.disagreements:
Sāyaṇa's note on verse 7 is what makes Ghoṣā's story legible: she was the daughter of Kakṣīvat, afflicted with a skin disease and therefore unmarriageable, who prayed to the Aśvins when already advanced in years; they healed her and restored her youth, and she obtained a husband. Wilson prints only "growing old and tarrying in her father's dwelling"; Griffith the same. The affliction is Sāyaṇa's, and it is the reason he reads *ghoṣeva śaṃsam* in [[1.122]].5 as her praise offered for the removal of her whiteness.

Verse 8's Śyāva is treated the same way: Sāyaṇa says he had black leprosy, was cured by the twins, and was consequently able to marry. In verse 24 the same name belongs to a man cut into three pieces and reassembled — Sāyaṇa does not reconcile the two.

Verse 11's *sūnor mānena* Sāyaṇa glosses as Agastya, born from a jar, which gives Wilson "the praises of the son (of the jar)"; Griffith reads it as "the reverence of a son."

Verse 22's *tvāṣṭram apikakṣyam* is Tvaṣṭṛ's secret in Griffith and, in Sāyaṇa's reading, a girdle strengthening the twins for their rites, with Tvaṣṭṛ identified as Indra. Wilson follows Sāyaṇa. The compound is obscure and neither reading can be preferred on the words alone.

118.title: The Aśvins' Falcon-Swift Car, Called at Daybreak
118.synthesis:
Eleven verses, and the first five of them are about a vehicle. *Ā vāṃ ratho aśvinā śyenapatvā sumṛḷīkaḥ svavāṃ yātu arvāṅ* — let your chariot come here, Aśvinā, flying like a falcon, full of mercy, carrying its own goods; swifter than a mortal's mind, three-seated, quick as the wind. Verse 2 names it again — three-seated, threefold, three-wheeled, well-rolling — and attaches the request: fill our cows, quicken our horses, and make the man among us grow.

Verse 3 is the hymn's small piece of impatience. Come down swiftly on your well-rolling car and hear this song of the pressing-stone; and then: *kim aṅga vāṃ prati avartiṃ gamiṣṭhā āhur viprāso aśvinā purājāḥ* — how is it, then, that the seers born before us called you the quickest to come against destitution? A worshipper is holding the tradition's own claim up and asking whether it still holds. The Ṛgveda does not usually let that question be asked out loud.

Verse 4 puts falcons in the harness — swift, winged, water-hastening, like eagles of the sky, bearing you toward the feast. Verse 5 puts a passenger in the seat: the young woman, the daughter of {{sūrya}}, mounted your chariot here, delighted; let your shining, winged, ruddy horses bring you near. The daughter of Sūrya choosing this chariot is told in three consecutive hymns by this seer, at [[1.116]].17, [[1.117]].13 and here.

Then, in verses 6 to 9, the whole roll of rescues compressed to four verses, one deed to a line. You raised Vandana; you raised Rebha by your powers; you carried Tugra's son out of the sea; you made Cyavana young again. To {{atri}}, thrown down into Agni that scorched him, you gave strengthening food and favour; accepting his praise, you gave his eyes back to blinded Kaṇva. For the ancient Śayu, pleading, you made his cow swell with milk; you loosed the quail from her trouble; you fitted a leg to Viśpalā. To Pedu you gave the white horse, serpent-slaying, sent by {{indra}}, loud-neighing, overpowering the enemy, fierce, winner of a thousand, firm-limbed. What the two long hymns before this one tell at length, this one recites at speed, which is what a shorter hymn in the same series is for.

Verse 10 turns from the record to the present: such as you are, well-born heroes, we call you in our need for help; take pleasure in these songs and come on your treasure-laden car to bring us through. And verse 11 fixes the hour. *Ā śyenasya javasā nūtanena asme yātaṃ nāsatyā sajoṣāḥ* — come to us with the falcon's fresh speed, of one accord; *have hi vām aśvinā rātahavyaḥ śaśvattamāyā uṣaso vyuṣṭau* — for I call you, having given the offering, at the shining-forth of the most constant dawn.

That is where the hymn ends: at daybreak, with the offering already made, calling for a chariot faster than the mind. Everything about the sūkta is speed, and its last word is the moment at which speed is asked for.
118.practice:
The last verse tells you when this hymn belongs: *uṣaso vyuṣṭau*, at the breaking of the dawn, with the oblation already given. Taken together with [[1.112]].24, where the twins are called *adyūtye*, in the lightless hour before dawn, the two hymns place the Aśvinau at the hinge of the night and the day — which is where the ritual manuals put them and where the household practice of the first hour still sits.

Verse 3 is the verse for a doubting morning. *How is it, then, that the seers born before us called you the quickest to come against destitution?* The worshipper is quoting the tradition back at the gods and asking whether the reputation is deserved. That the question survives, unanswered, in the middle of a hymn of praise is worth knowing about the Ṛgveda: it does not require its reciters to pretend.

The chariot is the hymn's real subject, and its adjectives are worth keeping: *śyenapatvā*, flying like a falcon; *sumṛḷīka*, full of mercy; *manaso javīyān*, swifter than mind; *trivandhura*, three-seated; *trivṛt*, threefold; *tricakra*, three-wheeled. A vehicle described as merciful is not a common thing. What the Aśvinau bring is presented as a means of arrival, and the arrival itself is what is being asked for.

And verse 2's requests are as ordinary as they come: fill the cows, quicken the horses, let the young man of the house grow strong. This is a family's hymn, and the extraordinary machinery of the first five verses exists to serve those three requests. A reader looking for where the Vedic imagination is anchored can find it in the distance between the falcon-drawn three-wheeled car and what it is being asked to deliver.
118.disagreements:
Verse 3's rhetorical question is read differently in tone. Griffith keeps the challenge: "How then have ancient sages said, O Asvins, that ye most swiftly come to stay affliction?" Wilson turns it into a rhetorical affirmation with a bracket — "do not the ancient sages say that you are most prompt to avert poverty from the worshipper?" The Sanskrit's *kim aṅga* is an interrogative and Griffith is closer to it.

Verse 3's *ślokam adreḥ* is "this hymn recited by one who reveres you" in Wilson and "the press-stone's song" in Griffith; the padapāṭha's *adreḥ*, of the stone, supports the second, and makes the sound of the pressing itself the thing the twins are asked to hear.

Verse 1's *svavān* is "rich" in Wilson and "bringing friendly help" in Griffith. Verse 4's *gṛdhrāḥ* is "vultures" in Wilson and "airy eagles" in Griffith — a difference in register rather than in sense.

Sāyaṇa's gloss is not preserved on this sūkta in the witness consulted here, which is a gap in the witness rather than a silence; the parallel verses in [[1.116]] and [[1.117]] carry his notes on the same episodes, and those are what make the compressed catalogue of verses 6 to 9 readable at all.

119.title: The Aśvins' Car Swift as Thought — a Bride Chooses
119.synthesis:
*Ā vāṃ rathaṃ purumāyaṃ manojuvaṃ jīrāśvaṃ yajñiyaṃ jīvase huve* — I call your chariot here, of many devices, swift as thought, with quick horses, worthy of worship, so that I may live. The purpose clause is the point. Not for wealth, not for victory: *jīvase*, in order to live. Then the chariot's inventory — a thousand banners, hundredfold wealth, obedient, making room.

Verse 2 describes the hymn arriving with the chariot. As it moves, the *dhīti* is raised up to meet it; the quarters gather at the song; I sweeten the hot offering; the helps come near; and Ūrjānī has mounted your chariot, Aśvinā. Verse 3 sets the scene in which such a chariot is wanted: when men have come together contending with one another for glory, countless, eager, keen for victory in the fight — then your car is seen on the slope, when you bring a chosen good to the patron.

Verse 4 is {{bhujyu}} again, told in a single line and with one detail the other hymns do not carry: you went to Bhujyu as he struggled, with self-yoked birds, and brought him down to his fathers. And then, of the same journey, *divodāsāya mahi ceti vām avaḥ*, great and well-known is the help you gave Divodāsa.

Verse 5 is the hymn's centre. For the beauty of it, your two voices held the chariot you had yoked to its course; and *ā vāṃ patitvaṃ sakhyāya jagmuṣī yoṣāvṛṇīta jenyā yuvāṃ patī* — the noble young woman, having come for your friendship, chose you as her husbands. The daughter of {{sūrya}} is not given here; she chooses. The verb is *vṛ*, the same root the tradition uses for the *svayaṃvara*, and it is placed in the middle of a hymn otherwise about speed and rescue.

Verses 6 and 7 return to the roll: Rebha kept from the constriction around him; the burning heat quenched with snow for {{atri}}; milk made to flow in Śayu's cow; Vandana's life extended. Then Vandana again, worn out with age and put back together by skilled workmen as a chariot is repaired — *rathaṃ na dasrā karaṇā sam invathaḥ* — and, in the same verse, a sage brought to birth out of the earth by wonder. The two similes stand side by side: a man mended like a vehicle, and a man born like a plant.

Verse 8 is the loneliest line in the series. *Agacchataṃ kṛpamāṇaṃ parāvati pituḥ svasya tyajasā nibādhitam* — you went to the one lamenting far away, pressed down by his own father's abandonment. Whoever he is, the hymn says that the twins went to him, and that their help was bright with heaven's light and marvellous when they stood by him.

Verse 9 gathers three things that made sounds on their behalf: the honey-seeking bee murmured sweetly of you; the son of Uśij calls you in the rapture of {{soma}}; you drew Dadhyañc's mind toward you, and then the horse's head spoke to you. Verse 10 closes with Pedu's white horse — much-desired, breaker of ranks, unconquerable by arrows in battle, worth celebrating, subduing men like {{indra}}.
119.practice:
The purpose stated in the first word of the hymn — *jīvase*, so that I may live — is the whole address in miniature. Whatever the Aśvinau are being asked for, and however far their chariot has to come, the reason given is survival. This is the register of a person in difficulty, not of a person in ceremony, and it explains why the deeds recited are always extractions.

Verse 5 is the one to keep. *Yoṣāvṛṇīta yuvāṃ patī* — the young woman chose you two as husbands. The act is hers and the verb is the one the later tradition uses for a woman's choice at the *svayaṃvara*. The Ṛgveda tells this of the daughter of Sūrya in four places, three of them in this seer's consecutive hymns; the full account is the marriage sūkta 10.85, which is still drawn on at Hindu weddings. What is worth noticing here is that the choosing is placed among rescues — as though a woman deciding for herself belonged in the same list as a man pulled out of the sea.

Verse 8 is the verse for anyone estranged from a parent. Someone is far away, lamenting, "pressed down by the abandonment of his own father," and the hymn records only that the twins went to him. No blame is assigned and no reconciliation is described. They came.

Verse 7's two images of restoration are worth holding together: a man worn out by age put back together *rathaṃ na*, like a chariot, by skilled hands; and a seer brought to life out of the earth. Repair and birth, in one verse, as two ways of describing the same help.

And verse 9's honey-bee, murmuring sweetly of them, is one of the few places where the Ṛgveda lets a small creature be a praiser. It stands in the same line as Dadhyañc and the speaking horse's head, and the hymn makes no distinction of rank between them.
119.disagreements:
Verse 2's Ūrjānī is unexplained by the words. Wilson supplies "(the daughter of the sun)" in a bracket; Griffith leaves the name bare. Nothing in the padapāṭha identifies her, and the identification with the daughter of Sūrya in verse 5 is an inference from context.

Verse 7's *kṣetrād ā vipraṃ janathaḥ* — you brought the sage to birth from the field or the earth — Sāyaṇa refers to Vāmadeva, who according to the tradition invoked the Aśvins while still in his mother's womb. Wilson prints "the sage (Vāmadeva) from the womb"; Griffith keeps it opaque: "From earth ye brought the sage to life in wondrous mode."

On verse 8 Sāyaṇa takes the abandoned man to be Bhujyu, whose father Tugra had left him — or, on his softer formulation, was unable to rescue him. Wilson prints the identification implicitly, Griffith not at all.

Verse 9's *makṣikā*, the bee, both translators keep. Sāyaṇa's note is not preserved on the verse in the witness consulted here, so the identification of the bee with anything other than a bee has no support in this evidence.

Verse 5's *vāṇī* — the two voices that held the chariot to its course — is "your admirable horses" in Wilson, following a gloss, and "your own two voices" in Griffith, following the word.

120.title: 'How Shall the Ignorant Worship?' — to the Aśvins
120.synthesis:
This is the odd one of the five, and it announces itself in the metre: no other sūkta in this stretch of the collection changes shape so often, running through gāyatrī, kakubh, uṣṇih, bṛhatī and several irregular forms in twelve verses. It also begins with a question no other hymn here asks.

*Kā rādhad dhotrā aśvinā vāṃ ko vāṃ joṣa ubhayoḥ kathā vidhāty apracetāḥ* — which offering will succeed with you, Aśvinā? Who is pleasing to you both? How shall a man without understanding do you honour? A hymn of praise opens by admitting that the speaker does not know how to praise.

Verse 2 does not resolve it; it makes the difficulty a method. Let the one who does not know ask the ones who do about the doors — for nobody else knows, and not a spiritless mortal. Ignorance is not concealed, and the response is to ask the addressee for instruction in addressing him. Verse 3 makes that a request: we call you two who know; being knowers, declare to us today the thought that will be accepted; loving you, your servant sings. Verse 4 puts the asking as plainly as it can be put — *vi pṛcchāmi pākyā na devān*, I ask like a simple person, like a child — about the wondrous thing made with the *vaṣaṭ* call; and then, out of nowhere, the small fear: protect us from what is stronger and fiercer than we are.

Verses 5 and 6 are the poet's credentials, such as they are. The song that shone in Ghoṣā goes forth; this is the speech with which the son of the Pajras worships you. Hear the *gāyatra* of the one who comes hurrying; for I am the one who has praised you — turn your eyes this way, lords of splendour. The line about the eyes is placed just after the tradition's Ṛjrāśva, who was blinded and healed, and the hymn does not say which is meant.

From verse 7 the register changes to household anxiety and stays there. You were near to deal out ample wealth and to give what you had gathered; be good guardians, you good ones, and keep us from the wicked wolf. Verse 8: *mā kasmai dhātam abhy amitriṇe naḥ* — do not hand us over to anyone who hates us; and let not our milch-cows go from our houses without their calves. That second clause is the whole economy of a household in one line. Verse 9 asks the same thing in the language of measure: may those who love you gain you as friends; measure out for us wealth with strengthening food, measure out food that comes with cows.

Then the three closing verses, which are among the strangest in maṇḍala 1. *Aśvinor asanaṃ rathaṃ anaśvaṃ vājinīvatoḥ* — I have got the chariot of the Aśvinau, the horseless one, of the two rich in prizes, and with it I am well content. Verse 11: may it carry me always; may the light-running car go from men to men to the {{soma}}-drinking. And verse 12: *adha svapnasya nir vide abhuñjataś ca revataḥ, ubhā tā basri naśyataḥ* — now I have contempt for sleep, and for the rich man who does not enjoy what he has; both of them vanish quickly.

A hymn that began by asking how an ignorant man is to worship ends by claiming a horseless chariot and despising two things: sleeping late, and hoarding.
120.practice:
The first verse is the most usable line in this whole range for someone who feels unqualified. *Kathā vidhāty apracetāḥ* — how shall a man without understanding do honour? The hymn does not answer it by supplying a technique. It answers it by asking: verse 2 says let the ignorant ask those who know, verse 3 asks the gods themselves to declare what thought will be accepted, and verse 4 says outright, "I ask like a child." Four verses of a twelve-verse hymn are spent establishing that not knowing how to pray is not a reason to stop.

Verse 12 is the one to carry into a morning. *Adha svapnasya nir vide* — I have come to despise sleep — *abhuñjataś ca revataḥ*, and the rich man who does not use what he has; both of them, it says, vanish quickly. Sleeping through the hour and sitting on wealth are put in the same sentence and given the same fate. In a family of hymns whose deities are called at the last watch of the night, that is not a general moralism; it is a remark about the specific hour at which this hymn is said.

Verse 8 is a household's actual prayer: do not give us to anyone who hates us, and do not let our cows leave the house without their calves. The second clause is more than sentiment — a cow separated from her calf stops yielding — and it shows how tightly the ordinary prayers of this collection are tied to the working of a farm.

And verse 10's *anaśvaṃ ratham*, the horseless chariot, is worth sitting with. The poet says he has obtained it and is content. Whatever it names — and the evidence does not settle it — the hymn treats it as something a man can be given and can be satisfied by, and puts it immediately before the two verses about not wasting what one has.
120.disagreements:
Verse 5 is a knot. The padapāṭha has *pra yā ghoṣe bhṛgavāṇe na śobhe yayā vācā yajati pajriyo vām*. Sāyaṇa glosses *ghoṣa* as Suhasti, which produces Wilson's "the hymn that was repeated by the son of Ghoṣā, and by Bhṛgu"; Griffith reads a comparison, "the hymn that shone in Ghosa Bhrgu's like." The name Ghoṣā belongs, in [[1.117]].7, to a woman the Aśvins helped and, in the Anukramaṇī, to this seer's daughter, who composed 10.39 and 10.40 — but nothing in this verse establishes which is meant.

Verse 6's *ṛjrāśva* Sāyaṇa identifies simply as "the blind man," which lets Wilson write "recovering my eyes through you"; Griffith keeps it first-person and general, "I am he who sang your praise."

Verse 7 divides them completely. Wilson has the Aśvins giving great riches and then causing them to disappear; Griffith has them ever near to deal forth and to give what they had gathered. The Sanskrit's *nir atataṃsatam* is obscure and neither can be preferred.

Verse 12 is agreed in substance by both — contempt for sleep and for the rich man who does not enjoy — which is unusual for a verse this compressed, and is the best ground for taking it at face value.

127.title: Agni the Axe, Agni the Guest of Every Clan
127.synthesis:
*Agniṃ hotāraṃ manye* — I hold {{agni}} to be the *hotā*, the one who calls the gods and pours into them what is given. The first verse stacks his titles fast: giving, good, *sūnuṃ sahasaḥ*, son of {{sahas}} — overpowering strength — and *jātavedas*, knower of all that has come to be, said twice in a single line, once plainly and once by comparison, as an inspired singer knows. Then a small exact picture that governs everything after it: when ghṛta is poured, he reaches after its flare with his own flame. He wants what he is given.

The second verse sets him in a lineage. He is *yajiṣṭha*, best at worship, and *jyeṣṭham aṅgirasām*, eldest of the {{aṅgiras}} — a fire carrying a seer's ancestry — and *hotāraṃ carṣaṇīnām*, the one who offers on behalf of the peoples. *Śociṣkeśa*, flame-haired; circling like the sky itself; and the clans press round him to be sped on.

Verses three and four are the hard middle, and they are about force. He blazes with {{ojas}} and is *druhantara*, the one who gets past malice, like an axe among trees; what is solid slackens where he touches it; he holds his ground and does not flinch, no more than a man who can hold a bow flinches. The fourth presses further: firm things give way to him because he knows them; he is rubbed alive out of the hottest *araṇis*, Agni-sticks; he goes deep into many things and hews them like timber, and even hard food he grinds down with *ojas*. Three verses in, this is not a mild god.

The fifth turns him domestic without softening him. His food is set out in the night hours, because he shows more clearly by night than by day, when his life runs thin; his shelter is firm, given as a father gives to a son. And the closing line is quietly enormous: these fires, which do not age, consume what has been apportioned to them and what has not.

The sixth lets him be loud — *śardho na mārutaṃ tuviṣvaṇiḥ*, roaring like the {{marut}} troop — over worked land and unworked, taking the oblations, *yajñasya ketuḥ*, the banner by which a {{yajña}} is known from a distance. Men are glad of his road. In the seventh the {{bhṛgu}}s, bearing {{namas}} and rubbing him into life, address him *dvitā*, in two ways at once; bright, holding these goods, he is asked to win out the dear things that lie hidden.

The eighth is where the hymn arrives. *Viśvāsāṃ tvā viśāṃ patim* — lord of all the clans, the one house-lord who is the same in every house, *atithiṃ mānuṣāṇām*, the guest of men. Through his mouth, as through a father's, all the immortals eat. The god who split and ground in verse three is here the visitor you feed.

The ninth names the thread outright: born from *sahas*, most overpowering, most impetuous, born *devatātaye*, for the service of the gods, in the way {{rayi}} is. His rapture is the brightest and his {{kratu}} the most full of splendour, and men wait on the unaging one as servants wait on a lord. The tenth sends the praise off — to the great one, strong against the strong, awake at dawn, giver of cattle — while the man with the oblation calls him aloud in every dwelling and the singer sings out ahead of him.

The eleventh asks. Seen nearest to us, in accord with the gods, bring great riches with a kind mind; make us large enough to look at what we have and to have the use of it; and stir up *suvīrya*, strength in men, for those who praise — fierce, the hymn ends, as a fierce man is fierce with *śavas*. It closes on force again, but the force has changed hands.
127.practice:
This hymn opens a block that a reciter notices before a reader does. Thirteen sūktas of the Ṛgveda are ascribed to Parucchepa Daivodāsi — [[1.127]] through [[1.139]] — and he has none anywhere else in the collection. His signature is a long line and a doubling: in all eleven verses here, and in almost every verse of the twelve sūktas that follow, a phrase at the end of a line comes straight back, slightly altered or not altered at all. *Jātavedasam … jātavedasam.* *Bhṛgavaḥ … bhṛgavaḥ.* *Sucetunā … sucetunā.* Recited aloud, the hymn keeps catching on its own words. The metre is *atyaṣṭi*, sixty-eight syllables to the verse, and the echo is part of how a line that long is held together in the mouth.

What the hymn is for is stated in its eighth verse. {{agni}} is *viśvāsāṃ viśāṃ patiḥ*, lord of all the clans; *samānaṃ dampatim*, the one house-lord who is the same in every household; and *atithiṃ mānuṣāṇām*, the guest of men. That triple address is the ground the later household treatment of Agni stands on — Agni is not the family's property but its guest, owed what a guest is owed, and the same guest is sitting in the neighbour's house. Anyone who keeps a lamp or a hearth has the verse's situation exactly.

Verse 5 is the one to sit with. *Bhaktam abhaktam avaḥ vyantaḥ* — the ageless fires consume what is apportioned to them and what is not. Nothing moralises this. Fire takes what is offered and it also takes what was never meant for it, and both are said in one breath about the god who is asked seven verses later to be gracious. Agni in the Ṛgveda is never merely benign, and a household that lives with fire knows why.

Note also what the hymn finally asks for. Not victory, not long life: *mahi … naḥ kṛdhi saṃcakṣe bhuje asyai*, make us great for the seeing and for the use of this — the capacity to look at what one has and actually to enjoy it. The Anukramaṇī gives 186 sūktas to Agni alone across the ten maṇḍalas, 44 of them in maṇḍala 1; this is one of the few that ends by asking for the ability to take pleasure in what has already been given.
127.disagreements:
Verse 7's *dvitā* is where the tradition is most generous. Sāyaṇa offers three readings and settles on none: Agni celebrated as twofold because he is recognised in both Śruti and Smṛti; or because he gives happiness in this world and the next; or because "two" here stands for "many", Agni being manifold in the āhavanīya and the other fires. Wilson keeps the ambiguity — "celebrating him in both his forms" — and Griffith drops the word altogether.

On verse 5 Sāyaṇa cites the Taittirīya Āraṇyaka for *aprāyuṣe divātarāt*: Agni "has not prominent or vigorous life through the day, being dimmed or enfeebled by the superior effulgence of the sun." That is an explanation of why the hymn says he is better seen by night.

Verse 4 divides sharply. Sāyaṇa glosses *sthirāṇi* as *pāpāni*, sins — or as enemies — so that what Agni grinds down is wrongdoing, not food; Wilson follows him partway, with Agni maturing "the standing corn" and destroying "whatever things are stationary"; Griffith keeps it literal, "hard and solid food he crunches with his might."

Verse 6 splits the translators outright: Wilson's Agni roars amid "sanctified and selected rites", Griffith's "in fertile cultivated fields … in desert spots adorable." And on verse 9 Sāyaṇa reads *ajara* three ways — undecaying, not causing decay, or the one who praises no other, praise being his alone.

128.title: Agni Seated at Iḷā's Place, House after House
128.synthesis:
*Ayaṃ jāyata manuṣo dharīmaṇi* — this one was born within the ordinance of {{manu}}. {{agni}} arrives in the first verse already bound to two obligations at once: the *vrata* of the Uśijs, those who long for the rite, and his own *vrata*.
