He is all-hearing to the man who wants his friendship and is {{rayi}} itself to the man who wants renown; and then, undeceived, he sits down — *niṣasāda iḷaspade*, in the place of Iḷā, wrapped round on every side. The hymn's whole argument is in that sitting down. A god who could be anywhere takes a marked seat.

The second verse says how he is brought there: *ṛtasya pathā*, by the road of {{ṛta}}, with {{namas}} and with the oblation. Under that carrying-up of strength he does not grow old. And the verse names the older arrival too — Mātariśvan brought him from far away for Manu. He was fetched once, long before; he is fetched again each time by the same road.

The third verse lets him loose across the world. He goes round the earthly at once, swallowing fast, a bull bellowing and bearing the seed, watching with a hundred eyes, winning in the woods, taking his seat on the ridges below and the ridges far off. The fourth then puts him back indoors: *sukratu*, of effective purpose, *purohita*, placed in front, *dame-dame* — house after house — he takes note of the {{yajña}} with {{kratu}}, and as *vedhas*, the one who orders things rightly, he keeps watch on all born things for the man who strives. Out of that he is born as the guest bright with ghṛta. The god ranging over ridges and the priest in the kitchen are the same verse apart.

The fifth is about what his force is spent on. When his powers mix by *kratu*, like the {{marut}}s' good things given to the eager, he speeds the gift on and by the sheer size of his goods rescues us from *duritā*, the bad going, from the curse and from evil. The sixth holds a picture worth keeping: wide-ranging, good, he holds what is precious in his right hand — and, crossing over like the sun, he has not let go. He carries the offering to the gods for anyone who asks; for every *sukṛt*, every doer of good, he grants the wish and swings the doors open.

The seventh brings the placing back once more, and now the place is human: *sa mānuṣe vṛjane śaṃtamo hitaḥ*, he has been set, most benign, in the enclosure where men live, and in the rites he is the loved *viśpati*, the clan's lord, like a prince who wins. The offerings men make at Iḷā's place are his to own. Then the verse turns dark and asks something very specific — that he protect us from the *dhūrti* of {{varuṇa}}, the malice or the crookedness of the great god. It is the only line in the hymn that names another deity, and it names him as a danger.

The eighth closes by describing men doing exactly what the hymn has been doing. They praise Agni as *hotā*, holder of goods, dear, most attentive; they have set him down as *arati*, the one who ranges and rules, they have set him down as *havyavāha*, carrier of the offering; and they name him *viśvāyu*, belonging to all life, *viśvavedas*, knowing all, worshipful, a *kavi*. The verb repeated in that last verse is the one from the first: *ni erire*, they set him down, they set him down. Being seated is what Agni is for.
128.practice:
Twice this hymn locates Agni at *iḷaspada*, the place of Iḷā — in verse 1, where he sits down there, and in verse 7, where the offerings men make there belong to him. Iḷā is at once nourishment, the poured offering, and the daughter of {{manu}} whom the tradition remembers as the first to conduct the rite; the ground of the altar is called the print her feet left. Whatever else is uncertain, the hymn's picture is not: Agni is not addressed as an element at large but as something with an assigned seat, and the seat has a name and a story. That is why one prepares a place before lighting a lamp rather than lighting it anywhere.

The other thing to carry away is verse 4's *dame-dame*, house after house, joined to *purohita*. Agni is the priest placed in front — but in every house separately, not once for the whole people. The Vedic household fire and the domestic priest are named by the same word here, and the *gṛhya* fire, kindled at marriage and kept for a lifetime, is already assumed: each home has its own, and each is the same god.

Verse 7's request repays attention because it is uncomfortable. Agni is asked to protect us *varuṇasya dhūrteḥ*, from Varuṇa's malice. {{varuṇa}} is the god who binds the perjurer and holds men to their word; to ask one god for shelter from another is not a tidy ordering of the gods. The Ṛgveda does not resolve this, and a reader should not resolve it either. The honest description is that the collection lets its gods be genuinely other to each other, and that a man who has broken something is right to feel exposed.

Of the 186 sūktas the Anukramaṇī assigns to Agni alone, 44 stand in maṇḍala 1, and this one belongs to the block of thirteen by Parucchepa Daivodāsi, [[1.127]]–[[1.139]], the only sūktas of his in the collection. His long doubled line is audible here too: *iḷaspade parivīta iḷaspade* — the seat named twice in the same breath, which is the point being made.
128.disagreements:
Sāyaṇa is unusually full on verse 1. He glosses *iḷaspade* as *bhūmyāḥ pade*, a site on the ground — the altar — and cites the Taittirīya Saṃhitā twice: "they call the vedi the utmost end of the earth", and "so much, verily, as is the earth, so much is the vedi." He then gives the other reading alongside it: *pada* is the spot where Iḷā, daughter of Manu, in the form of a cow, set her feet, and he quotes the formula *iḍāyāḥ pade ghṛtavati svāhā*, adding that Iḷā was the first instructor of the rites. Wilson prints "the footmark of Iḷa"; Griffith flattens it to "Ila's holy place".

Verse 7 is the sharpest divergence in the hymn, and it is theological. Sāyaṇa declines to read *varuṇa* here as the Āditya at all: he takes it as *vāraka*, the impeder — the obstructor of rites, "the mighty deity presiding over sin". Wilson follows him ("the malignity of the mighty deity of sin"); Griffith keeps the god and the sense that goes with him, "Varuna's chastisement."

Smaller splits: on verse 6 Sāyaṇa reads *arati* as sovereign or as one not easily pleased, and *taraṇir na* as "like the sun, who conveys across". On verse 2 he makes Mātariśvan's fetching concrete — brought from the far-off sun, set fittingly on earth. In verse 8 Wilson's praisers are priests "desirous of affluence", Griffith's "the Gods when they are fain for wealth".

129.title: Indra's Car Brought Near, Ill-Will Driven Off
129.synthesis:
The hymn opens on a vehicle rather than a god. *Yaṃ tvaṃ ratham indra medhasātaye* — the chariot that you, {{indra}}, bring forward for the winning of the offering, though it stands far off: bring it, and today make it swift for our advantage; let it be a thing of strength. And then, at once, the request that the whole hymn will keep making in different words: hear this speech of ours, the speech of men who arrange the rite. Distance and speech are the two problems, and the hymn works on both for eleven verses.

The second verse gives the reason he should hear. He is the one who must show *dakṣa*, effective competence, in any fight whatever — called with men for the war-cry, called with men for the breaking through. He wins *svar*, the light, alongside heroes; he wins {{vāja}}, the prize, alongside the inspired singers. Those two clauses are matched deliberately: the same god is the fighters' and the poets'. Men who have power want him the way they want a fast horse.

The third turns to rain. He swells and splits the bull-hide that holds the water, and keeps off the grudging mortal. Then the verse widens without warning into a list — this I say to you, and to Dyaus, and to Rudra glorious in himself, and to {{mitra}}, and to {{varuṇa}} far-reaching and kind. A hymn to Indra spends a line handing the praise around.

The fourth is the hymn's plainest sentence: we want our Indra to be here, the friend belonging to all life, the overpowering yoke-fellow in the contests. Guard our {{brahman}}, our formulated prayer, in whatever battles there are; no enemy has ever brought you down, and every enemy you set on, you bring down.

From the fifth the hymn narrows onto one target. Bend down the *atimati*, the overweening thought, of anyone at all — with your fiercest helps, which are like fire-sticks rubbed to their hottest. Lead us as you led before; you are still reckoned blameless; and you carry away everything of Pūru's, bearing it off yourself. The sixth stays with the pressed drop: may I speak this to the *indu* that is coming, which, like one who must be invoked, sets the *manman*, the framed thought, trembling — the demon-killing thought. May he himself drive off with his weapons the scorn and the ill intent aimed at us, and let the man whose speech is evil trickle away downhill like something small.

The seventh gathers what is wanted: may we win {{rayi}} with *suvīrya*, strength in sons, from the lord of riches, soften the ill-minded with well-meant words, and reach Indra with true and splendid callings. The eighth states the office directly: for you and for us, with helps that are his own glory, Indra stands in the driving-off of the ill-minded, in the tearing of them apart — and the weapon flung at us by devourers turns and destroys itself. Struck down it will not arrive; hurled, the brand will not land.

The ninth and tenth ask for company. Come by a path with no harm and no *rakṣas* on it; be with us when we are far away and be with us near home; guard us from a distance and from close by, always. And with wealth that carries a man across — strongest, protector, undying — harm someone else and not us, wielder of the stone, someone else who means harm.

The eleventh closes on the word the last third of the hymn has been circling. *Duḥmati*, ill-mind: it stands in verse 6, again as *duḥmanman* in verse 7, twice in verse 8 and twice here. Indra is the constant averter of ill-minds, the killer of the wicked *rakṣas*, the rescuer of a singer such as I am — and the maker who begot him begot him for exactly that.
129.practice:
What this hymn wants protection from is not an army. It is *duḥmati* — the bad mind, ill intention — and the word arrives six times in the last six verses. Around it sit *atimati*, overweening thought; *nid*, the sneer; *aghaśaṃsa*, the man whose speech is evil; and *arāru*, the one who will not give. The enemy of this hymn is malice, spoken and unspoken, and the request is that it recoil. Verse 8 is exact about the mechanism: *hatā īm asat*, the weapon flung by devourers is itself struck down, and does not reach. Nobody is asked to retaliate.

That makes this a useful sūkta to know, because most people's actual trouble is of this kind. {{indra}} here is not being asked to win a war; he is asked to be present when someone wishes you badly and you cannot answer it. And the answer the hymn gives is not that malice is harmless but that it turns on the one who launched it, which the text states twice and does not argue for.

The other line worth carrying is verse 9. *Sacasva naḥ parāke ā sacasva astamīke ā* — be with us far off, be with us near home. The two halves are not decoration: *parāka* is the distant place a man travels to, *astamīka* is the region of the house he returns to. The Ṛgveda's Indra is a god of expeditions, but the request here is for continuity between the road and the household, which is what anyone who works away from home is asking for.

A note on proportion. The Anukramaṇī assigns 218 sūktas to Indra alone across the ten maṇḍalas — more than to any other deity, and more than the 186 given to {{agni}}. Of the thirteen sūktas of Parucchepa Daivodāsi ([[1.127]]–[[1.139]]) five are Indra's: this one and [[1.130]] through [[1.133]]. Read as a set, they show him from very different sides — the fighter of [[1.130]], the king of [[1.131]], and here the one who stands between a household and the hostility of its neighbours.
129.disagreements:
Verse 3 is the hymn's real crux, and Sāyaṇa reads it as weather throughout. *Vṛṣaṇaṃ tvacam* is the skin that holds the rain; the *martya* whom Indra overtakes is the cloud fleeing like an enemy, and the *martya* he then abandons is the same cloud after it has parted with its water, "like an enemy who has been killed, whom the victor abandons". Wilson prints this as it stands, with the cloud supplied in brackets. Griffith keeps a human wrongdoer — "thou keepest far away, Hero, the wicked man" — so that the verse is about a person, not a rain cloud. Sāyaṇa also identifies that verse's Rudra with Agni, citing the Taittirīya Saṃhitā.

Verse 6 divides the same way at a smaller scale. Wilson makes the subject a libation — "may I be competent to utter praise for the Soma libation" — while Griffith addresses "the present Soma-drop" and lets the demon-slaying prayer be the thing that wakes. Verse 7 splits further: Wilson's worshippers praise a god "whom it is difficult adequately to honour"; Griffith's placate one "who is wroth".

On verse 10 Sāyaṇa allows *mitra* either sense — the god, or simply a friend whom praise fills with attachment — and on *adrivat* he records both derivations, the wielder of the *adri*, the stone or bolt, and, citing the Nirukta, the excessive eater of enemies. On verse 2 he glosses *nṛbhiḥ* as the {{marut}}s, or else as the worshippers.

130.title: Come Drink, Indra — Ninety Forts, the Rivers Freed
130.synthesis:
*Ā indra yāhi upa naḥ parāvataḥ* — come to us, {{indra}}, from far off. He is asked to come the way a *satpati*, a true lord of men, comes to the assemblies, and the way a king comes home; and we call you, the verse says, as sons call a father, at the pressing, with pleasant food ready, for the winning of {{vāja}}. The second verse puts the cup in his hand at once: drink the {{soma}} crushed out with the stones and poured from the vessel, as a bull drinks at a well, a thirsty bull at a well — for your rapture, for your strongest nourishment. Let the bay mares bring you here as they bring Sūrya, as all the days bring Sūrya.

Then the deeds, and they begin with a find rather than a fight. He discovered the treasure of heaven laid away in secret, shut in rock like a bird's brood inside its shell — inside rock without end. Wanting it, most Aṅgiras-like, bolt in hand, he broke open the pen; he flung wide the shut-up stores and the shut-up doors. The fourth verse arms him: gripping the *vajra* in both fists he honed it to an edge for the throwing, honed it for the killing of the *ahi*; wrapped in {{ojas}} and *śavas* and sheer bulk, he cuts things down as a carpenter cuts a tree, cuts them down as with an axe.

The fifth is the release. *Tvaṃ vṛthā nadyaḥ indra sartave* — effortlessly you let the rivers run out toward the sea, like chariots; and going from here they yoked themselves to one unfailing purpose, like milch-cows yielding everything, yielding everything for {{manu}}, for the people. Rivers made to behave like a herd is a homely thing to say about a flood.

The sixth verse stops the deeds dead and turns to the men making the hymn. *Imāṃ te vācam vasuyantaḥ āyavaḥ ratham na dhīraḥ svapā atakṣiṣuḥ* — wanting good things, men have carpentered this speech of yours as a steady, skilled workman carpenters a chariot; they carpentered you for their own welfare. They are grooming you, they say, the way one grooms a racehorse before the contests. It sits at the exact middle of the hymn, and it is the only verse about the poets: between two blocks of smashing, a workshop.

The seventh names names. He broke ninety forts for {{pūru}}, for Divodāsa the giver — *nṛtaḥ*, O dancer, an epithet that will not be softened — with the *vajra*, for the giver, O dancer. For Atithigva he brought Śambara down off the mountain, sharing out great riches with *ojas*, all riches with *ojas*. The eighth extends it into an alignment: Indra helped the *yajamāna*, the man who sacrifices, in the encounters; he has a hundred aids in every contest, in the contests where *svar* is the stake. Correcting things for Manu he made the *avrata*, those who keep no vow, subject; he made the black skin subject; and like a flame he burns down the man who is greedy and thirsty for more, burns down the hurtful one.

The ninth is the strangest. Born with *ojas* he tore the wheel off the sun; ruddy, at the hour of eating, he steals speech away, the master steals it away. And then, without a joint: as you came from far off, *kave*, seer, to the help of Uśanā, so come with every good thing, overcoming as {{manu}} overcomes, overcoming as all the days do.

The tenth stands apart in shape as well as sense — a short *triṣṭup* after nine long verses, and the doubling that has closed every line so far simply stops. With new *ukthas*, bull in deed, splitter of forts, guard us with strong protections; praised by the men of Divodāsa's line, grow great, Indra, as Dyaus grows great with the passing days.
130.practice:
Verse 6 is the one to take away, and it is about the making of hymns. *Atakṣiṣuḥ* — they carpentered it — is used twice of this very sūkta, and the comparison is spelled out: men shape a *vāc* for {{indra}} as a skilled and steady workman shapes a chariot. The root is √takṣ, the root behind *takṣan*, the carpenter, and behind Tvaṣṭṛ, who fashions the gods' equipment and who in [[1.32]] made the *vajra* itself. The Ṛgveda's own account of what a poet does is therefore not inspiration but joinery: measured pieces, fitted, load-bearing, made to carry weight over distance. A reciter is handling a made object, and the hymn says so.

The proper names in verse 7 place this hymn in a history the collection assumes and never narrates. {{pūru}} and Divodāsa are peoples and a chieftain; Atithigva is either Divodāsa's epithet or another man; Śambara holds forts in the mountains and is thrown down from them. Parucchepa, to whom [[1.127]]–[[1.139]] are ascribed, is called Daivodāsi, "of Divodāsa" — so the singer is claiming the patron whose victories he lists, and the last verse asks Indra to be praised "by the Divodāsas". This is a hymn with an address.

Verse 8 needs care, because one phrase in it has carried more modern weight than any other line of the Ṛgveda. *Tvacaṃ kṛṣṇām arandhayat* — he made the black skin subject. The collocation of *kṛṣṇa* with *tvac* occurs twice in the whole Ṛgveda, here and at 9.41.1, and the traditional commentary does not read either as a description of a people's complexion. What the verse pairs the phrase with is *avrata*, those who keep no vow, and *ayajvan*, those who do not sacrifice — the line's contrast is observance, not descent. That is a description of the evidence, not a settlement of the argument; the argument is live and this note does not adjudicate it.

Finally, verse 2's picture is worth keeping for its plainness. Indra drinks soma *avataṃ na vaṃsagaḥ tatṛṣāṇaḥ* — as a thirsty bull drinks at a well. The greatest god of the collection is shown wanting something the way an animal wants water.
130.disagreements:
Sāyaṇa supplies two full legends here, and both are otherwise invisible. On verse 8's black skin he tells of an asura named Kṛṣṇa who advanced with ten thousand followers to the banks of the Aṃśumatī and laid it waste, until Indra with the {{marut}}s was sent against him and stripped him of his skin — so that *kṛṣṇā tvac* is one being's hide, not a population. On verse 9's wheel of the sun he gives two: the asuras had obtained from Brahmā that Indra's bolt should not destroy them, so Indra flung the wheel of the sun's chariot at them instead, which served as well; or the verse is dawn, with Aruṇa the charioteer silencing the clamour and the lord of day scattering the dark. He adds that *vācaṃ muṣāyati*, "steals speech", may mean taking away breath and so life, or merely silencing an outcry.

Verse 7's *nṛtaḥ* is left standing by both translators — Wilson glosses "the dancer with delight in battle", Griffith simply "O Dancer" — and Sāyaṇa confirms *raṇe nartanaśīla*, given to dancing in war. On Śambara he reports the later Purāṇic figure destroyed by Pradyumna, which is a different Śambara from the hymn's.

Verse 5's *vṛthā* splits: Sāyaṇa allows both "without effort" and "fruitlessly, in vain", and Wilson and Griffith both take the first. On verse 10 Sāyaṇa reads *divodāsebhiḥ* as the singers themselves — "by us, the Parucchepas", the plural being honorific — where Griffith keeps "Divodasa's clansmen".

131.title: Dyaus Bows to Indra, Then Husband and Wife Come
131.synthesis:
*Indrāya hi dyaur asuro anamnata* — for {{indra}} Dyaus the *asura* bowed himself down; for Indra the great Pṛthivī with all her expanses, in the winning of splendour. The hymn opens by making the sky and the earth do obeisance, and then adds the assembly: all the gods, of one mind, have put Indra in front. The verse ends with a consequence that sounds like a rule — let all the pressings men make be given over to Indra, all that men offer be his.

The second verse looks at the many people doing this at once. In every pressing they urge him on, *samānam ekam*, the same one and single, but they urge him *pṛthak*, separately, each with the fury of a bull, each wanting the light for himself, separately. One god, many claimants, and no attempt to smooth it: the hymn simply notes that the god everyone shares is wanted by each alone. Then the image the verse settles on — we set you at the pole of our strength like a boat for the crossing — and men make themselves known to Indra by their {{yajña}}s, known by their *stoma*s.

The third verse brings forward a pair of worshippers the Ṛgveda does not often name. *Vi tvā tatasre mithunāḥ avasyavaḥ* — couples, wanting help, have stretched themselves toward you, in the winning of the pen, in the letting-out of the cattle. And when you bring two peoples face to face, both after cattle and both after *svar*, you make visible the bull, the *vajra* that stays always at your side.

The fourth turns to memory. The {{pūru}}s know this heroic act of yours — that you brought down the autumn forts, overpowering, brought them down; that you corrected the mortal who will not sacrifice, lord of *śavas*; that in your joy you took the wide earth for your own and these waters, these waters. The fifth continues the recollection and gives it a voice: then indeed the Uśijs, in the raptures, keep telling this deed of yours, bull — that you helped the men who wanted your friendship. You made a *kāra* for them, a shout that carried them forward in the fighting; and river after river they won, wanting renown, they won.

The sixth is the turn from what was to what is being asked now. May he take pleasure in this dawn of ours; take notice of the song and of the oblation, called with our callings, called in the winning of *svar*. And since you know, thunder-armed bull, how to strike the scorners down — then listen to this *manman*, this framed thought of mine, of a *vedhas* who is new, listen to a newer one. The claim in that last word is deliberate. Verses 4 and 5 have just said that the Pūrus and the Uśijs of long ago knew Indra's deeds; verse 6 asks the same god to hear someone who has arrived late and has nothing but a new poem.

The seventh closes on protection. You, Indra, grown strong and turned toward us, strike with the *vajra* the mortal who behaves as an enemy — strike that mortal, hero. Kill the one who works evil against us. Hear, you who hear best of all. And let *duḥmati*, ill intention, be gone — like an injury met on a journey, let it be gone; let every ill intention be gone. The hymn that began with Dyaus bending down ends with a household asking not to be wished harm.
131.practice:
The verse to know here is the third, because of who is in it. *Mithunāḥ* means a pair, a couple — the two of a household — and the hymn shows them exerting themselves toward {{indra}} together, wanting help and wanting cattle. The Ṛgveda usually shows priests and patrons; here the unit that approaches the god is a married pair, and the tradition took the line seriously enough to hang the whole question of a wife's presence at Agni on it. The *gṛhya* rites still assume that shape: the householder's fire is established by the two of them, and a rite in which the wife is absent is understood to be defective. This verse is one of the places the assumption is anchored in the Saṃhitā itself.

The second thing worth carrying is verse 2's honesty about crowds. Indra is *samānam ekam*, the same and one, and men press toward him *pṛthak*, separately, each after the light for himself. The hymn does not pretend that shared worship makes everyone's wants identical. And the image it gives for what the god is in that situation is neither king nor father but a boat — *nāvaṃ na parṣaṇim*, a boat for the crossing over, set at the pole of one's strength. What one wants from a boat is not affection.

Then verse 6, which is the sort of thing a reader can use directly. After two verses recalling that the Pūrus and the Uśijs of old knew Indra's deeds, the singer asks him to hear *navīyasaḥ manma*, the newer thought of a newer man. He is not claiming ancestry or precedent. He is saying: they had theirs, this is mine, listen to it. Anyone who has felt late to a tradition already fully formed has the verse's exact position.

The Anukramaṇī gives this sūkta, with [[1.127]] through [[1.139]], to Parucchepa Daivodāsi, who has no sūktas anywhere else in the collection; five of his thirteen are Indra's, of the 218 the Anukramaṇī assigns to Indra alone. The long *atyaṣṭi* line with its doubled close runs through all seven verses here without a break.
131.disagreements:
Verse 3 is where Sāyaṇa does his most consequential work in this hymn, and it is not lexical but legal. Reading *mithunāḥ* as "couples consisting of husband and wife", he cites the Mīmāṃsā to establish that a wife may be joined with her husband in the offerings — *jāyāpatī agnim ādadhīyātām*, let wife and husband together establish the fire — and adds from the Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra that the husband, having imparted the Veda to his wife, may have her recite, she joining in the mantra *suprajasas tvā vayam*. Wilson prints "the married couples"; Griffith keeps only "Couples desirous of thine aid", with no comment.

Verse 1's *asura* divides the translators sharply. Wilson, reading it as an epithet of the sky, renders "heaven, that excludes the wicked"; Griffith leaves the word standing — "Dyaus the Asura hath bowed him down" — which preserves the older, unfallen sense of *asura* as lord.

On verse 4 Sāyaṇa explains *puraḥ śāradīḥ*, the autumn forts, as strongholds made secure with wall and ditch for a year at a stretch. On verse 5 he glosses *cakartha kāram* two ways, as a war-cry — the lion-roar — or simply as "you did a deed, you performed a service"; Wilson takes the shout, Griffith "their battle-cry thou madest sound victorious". And on verse 7 he explains the simile of harm on the road as the ill intent of robbers toward a traveller.

132.title: As of Old, So Now — Indra and Parvata Called
132.synthesis:
This is a short hymn built on a single move, and the move is stated three times in three different words. *Pūrvye dhane* in the first verse, *pratnathā* in the third, *pūrvathā* in the fourth: of old, as of old, as before. What {{indra}} did once is the whole argument for what he should do today.

The first verse asks for the transfer directly. With you, *maghavan*, in the old contest — helped by Indra — may we overcome those who draw up against us, may we get the better of those who begrudge us. Then it narrows to the present hour: on this day, which is the nearest one, speak for the man who is pressing; in this {{yajña}} may we come out with the thing that is won in battle, wanting {{vāja}}. Ancient precedent, today's pressing, one sentence.

The second verse sets the scene of that old winning. In the fight that wins *svar*, at the summoning call of the generous man, at the offering of one who wakes at dawn, in his own straight and unconcealed track — Indra killed, as we know. And then a phrase easy to skim: *śīrṣṇā-śīrṣṇā upavācyaḥ*, he is to be addressed head by head, one by one, by each. May your bounties be turned all one way toward us; may the good gifts of the good one be good.

The third verse locates him. That shining food of yours is set out for you as it was long ago, in the rite where they made the choice, made the dwelling — and *ṛtasya vāḥ asi kṣayam*, you possess the dwelling-place of {{ṛta}}. Declare it, the verse asks; and then, twofold, they see within by rays of light. He knows in order, this Indra who searches out the cows for his kin, searches for his kin.

The fourth names the oldest case. Now as before, this must be proclaimed of you: that you opened the pen for the {{aṅgiras}}es, giving them your help, opened the pen. In the same manner, in the same direction, win for us and fight for us, for the men who press. Give over into our hands whoever keeps no vow, whoever rages at us and keeps no vow. The precedent is exact and the request is that it be repeated in the same direction.

The fifth verse is about what happens among people when he acts. When the hero brings men to see, by his *kratu*s, with the prize set down between them, then those who want renown press through, press forward wanting renown. For him they sing, asking long life with children and the strength to hold off pressure; and *dhītayaḥ*, the shaped thoughts, find their settled place in Indra — the {{dhī}}s go out toward the gods. The hymn has been about repeating an old deed, and here it says what the singing is for: the thoughts get somewhere to rest.

The sixth verse changes the address without warning and closes the hymn. *Yuvaṃ tam indrāparvatā purayudhā* — you two, Indra and Parvata, fighters in the front rank: whoever comes at us in force, strike him down, strike him down with the *vajra*. And then a line that is almost gentle in its grimness: far off, let the hiding-place he has reached be pleasant to him. May the render tear our enemies apart on every side, tear them apart everywhere, hero. The hymn ends by wishing the enemy a comfortable distance and no return.
132.practice:
This hymn is a model of how the Ṛgveda argues, and the argument is one a person can use. It does not claim {{indra}} is powerful in the abstract. It says he did a specific thing at a specific time — he broke open the pen for the {{aṅgiras}}es — and then asks for the same act, *ebhyaḥ samānyā diśā*, in the same direction as for them. The reasoning is precedent, not praise: you have done this, and I am in the position they were in. That is also how a *saṅkalpa* works, and how the recollection of a deity's past acts functions in every later stotra. The past is not nostalgia here; it is the ground of the claim.

Verse 2 has a phrase worth keeping. Indra is *śīrṣṇā-śīrṣṇā upavācyaḥ*, to be addressed head by head. Whatever else a collective rite is, the hymn insists the address is individual — every head speaks for itself. That sits oddly and deliberately beside the crowd of [[1.131]].2, where all press toward the same god separately.

Verse 6 introduces the hymn's one surprise. The dual compound *indrāparvatā*, Indra-and-Parvata, occurs exactly three times in the whole Ṛgveda — [[1.122]].3, here, and [[3.53]].1 — and nowhere is a sūkta given to the pair. Parvata is the mountain, or a power over mountains; the pairing is old and rare, and the collection preserves it without explaining it. It is a good example of a thing the evidence underdetermines. What can be said is that the mountain is where forts stand and where Śambara is thrown down from in [[1.130]].7, and that a god of mountains beside Indra in a fighting verse is not arbitrary.

And verse 5 gives the plainest statement in these hymns of what the singing accomplishes: *indre okyaṃ didhiṣanta dhītayaḥ*, the shaped thoughts seek a home in Indra, and go out toward the gods. Not the singer travels; the {{dhī}} does.
132.disagreements:
Verse 3's *ṛtasya kṣayam* draws three readings out of Sāyaṇa, and he keeps all three. Indra possesses the abode of the sacrifice, which is called {{ṛta}} because its reward does not fail; or *ṛta* is water, so that he dwells in the house of the waters and is the giver of rain; or *ṛta* is the sun, and he brings the sacrificer to the sun's region. Wilson prints the first, Griffith avoids the word entirely with "thou choosest the place of sacrifice."

Verse 4's *vraja* splits along the same line as the whole Vṛtra question. Sāyaṇa glosses it first as a cloud and then, on its repetition, as the cattle-pen of the {{aṅgiras}}es raided by the {{paṇi}}s — the two readings, meteorological and narrative, standing side by side within one verse's commentary. Both translators keep the pen.

On verse 6 Sāyaṇa identifies Parvata as a cloud, or as the deity presiding over clouds, "another form of Indra" — which dissolves the pair into one god. Neither translator follows him there; both keep two.

Smaller notes: on verse 1 he glosses *bhare kṛtam* as the maker of victory in battle, citing the Nirukta for *bhara* as a name for battle. On verse 5 he distinguishes the two occurrences of *śravasyu* — the first wanting food or fame, the second wanting to offer food — and explains "in Indra" as meaning in Indra's neighbourhood, by the same figure as calling a village "on the Gaṅgā".

133.title: Both Worlds Purified, the Yātumatīs Crushed
133.synthesis:
This sūkta breaks the pattern of the twelve around it before it says anything. The metre changes from verse to verse — a *triṣṭup*, then three *anuṣṭups*, a *gāyatrī*, then the long *dhṛti* and *aṣṭi* at the end — and with the short verses the doubled line-ending that has run through all of Parucchepa's other hymns simply drops away. The hymn is doing something else and it sounds different while doing it.

It opens in the first person, which is rare. *Ubhe punāmi rodasī ṛtena* — I purify both worlds by {{ṛta}}; I burn up the great ones who are *anindrāḥ*, who have no {{indra}} in them. Not a request that a god act: the speaker himself purifies and burns. And then the aftermath is described as already accomplished — where the enemies, set upon and beaten, lay strewn in the *vailasthāna*, the pit.

The second verse hands the work back to Indra and gets physical. Having trodden them down, O wielder of the stone, break the heads of the *yātumatīs*, the sorceresses, with your broad foot — with your very broad foot. There is no weapon in the line. It is a foot coming down. The third asks the same again in different terms: strike down the massed strength of these *yātumatīs*, *maghavan*, into the small pit, into the great-and-small pit. The fourth then quantifies, and the quantifying is the point: of these you have already flung away thrice fifty with your onslaughts — a thing that seems great to us, and slight to you.

The fifth is the shortest verse in the hymn and the most concentrated. *Piśaṅgabhṛṣṭim ambhṛṇaṃ piśācim indra saṃ mṛṇa* — Indra, grind down the *piśāci*, tawny-tipped and terrible; lay low every *rakṣas*. One line, one target, no qualification.

The sixth opens out again into the long metre and with it comes the hymn's one moment of visible fear. Bring the great ones down; hear us. *Śuśoca hi dyauḥ kṣāḥ na bhīṣā* — the sky has burned as the earth has, out of fear, wielder of the stone; out of fear of the scorching. Then the reassurance, and it is precise: most impetuous, you go out with impetuous men and with fierce weapons — *apuruṣaghnaḥ*, not a killer of human beings, unopposed, hero, with your thrice-seven fighting men. The hymn has spent five verses on crushing, and at exactly this point it says the crushing is not aimed at people.

The seventh closes by naming the only qualification anyone needs. *Sunvan*, the one who presses — the word stands four times in four lines. The presser wins a dwelling of abundance; the presser worships away hostilities, the hostilities of the gods themselves; the presser, holding {{vāja}}, unchecked, means to win in thousands; and to the presser Indra gives *ābhuvaṃ rayim*, wealth that stays and serves. After the pit and the trampling and the burning, the hymn ends on the plainest possible domestic condition: press the {{soma}}, and this is yours.
133.practice:
This is the Ṛgveda's *rakṣoghna* register, and it is worth knowing that the collection contains it. Most of maṇḍala 1 addresses gods; this hymn addresses what is to be got rid of — *yātumatī*, the woman who works *yātu*, sorcery; *piśācī*; *rakṣas*; and the beings called *anindrāḥ*, those with no {{indra}} in them, which is as close as the Veda comes to a definition of the hostile. The vocabulary survives everywhere in living usage: *yātu* stands behind *yātudhāna*, and *piśāca* is still an ordinary word. What a reader should notice is that the hymn does not treat these as metaphors, and neither does the tradition that handed it down.

Verse 6 is the one that fixes the boundary, and it is a boundary a reader should hold onto. *Apuruṣaghnaḥ* — not a slayer of men. Indra comes with fierce weapons and thrice-seven fighters, and the hymn takes the trouble, in the middle of an exorcism, to say that human beings are not what he is coming for. Whatever the *yātumatīs* are, the text distinguishes them from people. Hymns of this kind are the ones most easily turned into permission, and this one closes that door itself.

Verse 1 repays attention for a different reason. The speaker says *punāmi* and *dahāmi* — I purify, I burn — in his own voice, and the instrument is {{ṛta}}, not fire and not a weapon. The claim is that correct order, rightly performed, is itself what cleanses the two worlds. That is the same logic as a *prāyaścitta*: what puts something right is not force but the rite done as it should be.

And then verse 7 dismantles all the ferocity into a household act. Four times in four lines the hymn names the *sunvan*, the man pressing the {{soma}} — he gains a dwelling, he wards off hostility, he wins by thousands, he receives lasting wealth. Nothing is asked of him but that he press. Of the thirteen sūktas ascribed to Parucchepa Daivodāsi, [[1.127]]–[[1.139]], this is the only one that turns outward against demons, and it ends by turning back to the man at the pressing-stones.
133.disagreements:
*Vailasthāna* in verses 1 and 3 is genuinely unsettled, and Sāyaṇa says so. He derives it from *vila*, a hole or cavern, giving "they sleep in a place that is a pit"; then identifies it with the *śmaśāna*, the ground where the dead are burnt or buried — "there corpses are thrown, that is *vailasthāna*, the cremation ground"; then offers a third possibility altogether, that it is *nāgaloka* or *pātāla*, the regions below the earth. Wilson prints "a deep pit"; Griffith, "the pit of death". The word is rare and the readings are not reconcilable.

On verse 2's *yātumatīnām* Sāyaṇa gives three: armies that inflict injury; armies bearing weapons; or hosts made up of *rākṣasas*. Wilson takes the martial sense throughout — "malignant hosts" — while Griffith keeps the feminine and renders "sorceresses", which the grammar supports and which makes the hymn a very different thing.

Verse 5's *piśācī* Sāyaṇa glosses simply as decay, which neither translator follows; both keep the demon.

Verse 6 draws his fullest note. He takes *ghṛṇāt* as fear of the absence of rain, and also as fear of *Ghṛṇā*, a name of Tvaṣṭṛ or of blazing fire personified, telling the legend that when the world was wrapped in thick darkness the gods prayed to {{agni}}, who burst forth from heaven and earth in the form of Tvaṣṭṛ to the dismay of both. He reads *trisaptaiḥ* as "by three or by seven" attendants, suggesting the seven platters offered to the {{marut}}s; Griffith takes it as thrice-seven.

134.title: Vāyu Drinks First — the Dawns Dress for Him
134.synthesis:
Everything in this sūkta turns on one word in its first line. *Pūrvapītaye* — for the first drinking. {{vāyu}} is asked to come not merely to the {{soma}} but to the first draught of it, and the hymn keeps returning to that precedence until it states it flatly in the last verse.

The first verse gets him moving. Let the swift ones, hurrying, bring you here to the food, for the first drinking of the soma. Then a request about his mind rather than his horses: may your *manas* stand upright, attentive and knowing, following the *sūnṛtā* — the speech that is both true and generous. Come with the *niyut*-yoked chariot for the giving; come, Vāyu, for the giving. The team, the *niyuts*, is named at once, and it will run through the whole hymn and through [[1.135]] after it.

The second verse turns to the drops themselves. May the gladdening *indus* gladden you, well made by us, working, turned toward heaven, made with the milk of cows and turned toward heaven. When they are made and ready to be sped on, the helps attend on *dakṣa*, effective skill; the *niyuts* come all one way for the giving; and — the last phrase is the striking one — the {{dhī}}s speak up to him, the shaped thoughts address him. The drink and the thought arrive together.

The third verse harnesses the chariot in front of us. *Vāyur yuṅkte rohitā, vāyur aruṇā* — Vāyu yokes the two red, Vāyu the two ruddy, Vāyu the two quick ones at the pole to draw, the best at drawing. Then the two commands that make the verse: wake up *puraṃdhi*, fullness of thought, as a lover wakes a woman who is sleeping; and light up the two worlds, make the dawns shine out, make the dawns shine out for glory. Wind, thought and daybreak are set in the same motion.

The fourth verse then hands the dawns to him. For you the shining {{uṣas}}es in the far distance spread out their auspicious garments among the working rays, bright among new rays. For you the cow that yields the sweet milks out all good things. And a genealogy in one line: you begot the {{marut}}s out of the wombs, out of the wombs of heaven. Vāyu is here the father of the storm-troop.

The fifth is the hymn's hardest verse and its most personal. For you the bright, pure, hastening ones press on fiercely in their raptures, press on in the churning, in the churning of the waters. Then the picture changes without warning to one frightened man: *tvāṃ tsārī dasamānaḥ bhagam īṭe* — the one who creeps along, exhausted, prays to you for *bhaga*, for a portion, when thieves are about. And the answer is given in a word that carries a great deal: *tvaṃ viśvasmāt bhuvanāt pāsi dharmaṇā* — you protect from every being by *dharman*, by the upholding law; you protect by *dharman*. Not by strength. By what holds.

The sixth verse states the precedence outright and closes. You, Vāyu, who have none before you, are entitled to the drinking of these somas, first, entitled to the drinking of what is pressed — and of the offerings of the clans that pour widely, the clans that have shaken themselves clear. All your cows are milked out for the *āśir*, the milk that is mixed in; they are milked out for ghṛta. The hymn ends where it began, on Vāyu's first cup, having in between made him the yoker of horses, the waker of thought, the dresser of dawns, the father of the Maruts, and the shelter of a man on a dangerous road.
134.practice:
{{vāyu}} is the god of first things in this collection, and the reason is worth knowing because it is not the reason later thought gives. He drinks first because he is fastest — he arrives before the others do. That is the argument in [[1.2]], where he is called before {{indra}} and before {{mitra}} and {{varuṇa}}, and it is the argument here: *apūrvyaḥ*, having none before him, *prathamaḥ pītim arhasi*, first entitled to the drinking. Priority in the rite follows priority in arrival.

He is also rarer as a whole-hymn addressee than his prominence suggests. Across the ten maṇḍalas only four sūktas are ascribed to Vāyu alone — this one, [[4.48]], [[10.168]] and [[10.186]] — though seventeen name him, most of those sharing him with Indra as *indravāyū*. The pattern of [[1.2]] is the collection's habit: Vāyu opens, and then Indra joins him.

Two things here bear directly on practice. The first is verse 3's instruction: *pra bodhaya puraṃdhim*. Wake up *puraṃdhi*, the mind's fullness — and the simile chosen is a lover waking someone asleep, not a master rousing a servant. What the wind is asked to do to a dull morning mind is exactly what a reciter hopes the recitation does. The verse then moves straight from that waking to the lighting of the two worlds and the shining of the dawns, as though they were one act.

The second is verse 5's *dharman*. A man creeping along the road, worn out and afraid of thieves, asks Vāyu for a portion; and the hymn says Vāyu protects him from every being *dharmaṇā*, by what upholds. This is the Ṛgvedic ancestor of the word every Hindu uses daily, and its sense here is concrete: the thing that holds a frightened traveller up is not the god's force but the order he maintains. It is the same claim {{ṛta}} makes elsewhere, in a word that survived into ordinary speech when *ṛta* did not.
134.disagreements:
Verse 5 divides the witnesses more than any other line here, and the trouble is *tsārī* and *takvavīye*. Sāyaṇa reads a timid worshipper who praises Vāyu as *bhaga*, "that which is to be enjoyed", and glosses the phrase as being for the driving-off of thieves — *taskarāṇāṃ yajñavighātinām anyatra gamanāya*, for sending elsewhere the thieves who obstruct sacrifices. Wilson prints that: "the timid and anxious worshipper praises you … for driving away thieves." Griffith reads a different man altogether — "to thee the weary coward prays for luck that he may speed away" — and then takes the last line as protection "from the world of highest Gods", where Wilson has protection "from the fear of evil spirits". The verse's *asuryāt* is doing that work, and neither reading is secure.

On verse 4's *daṃsu raśmiṣu* Sāyaṇa offers three: rays that are doing their work; *daṃsa* as a house, the rays covering the world like one; or the sacrificial chamber where the fires are lit at dawn, so that the flames themselves are the garment offered to Vāyu. He glosses *sabardughā* by taking *sabar* as *amṛta*, the cow who yields the deathless.

Elsewhere the divergences are small. Sāyaṇa derives *dāvane* from *dā*, to give, and allows it both ways — for what we are to give, and for his giving us what we ask — and glosses *bhurvan* as both sacrifice and cloud.

135.title: Come Where the Stone Speaks — Vāyu, Then Indra
135.synthesis:
*Stīrṇam barhiḥ* — the grass is strewn. The sūkta opens with the seat already prepared and asks {{vāyu}} to come to it with a thousand of his *niyuts*, with hundreds of them. The team is the hymn's spine: it is named in six of the nine verses, and the whole poem is organised as an arrival. The first verse also states the standing arrangement — the gods have held themselves back for you, for the first drinking — and the sweet pressed drops have stood up for your rapture, stood up for your {{kratu}}.

The second verse follows the {{soma}} rather than the god. Purified by the stones, wearing splendours worth wanting, it runs round the *kośa*, the vessel; wearing bright things, it runs. *Tava ayaṃ bhāgaḥ* — this is your portion among men, and the soma is being poured among the gods. Then: drive the *niyuts*, come here well disposed toward us, come delighting in us. The third verse repeats the invitation with the numbers reversed and adds a word that fixes the hour: this share of yours is *ṛtviya*, the one belonging to its proper season, and it is *saraśmiḥ sūrye sacā*, sharing rays with the sun. The morning pressing is meant.

From the fourth verse the address becomes dual and {{indra}} is standing beside him. Let the chariot with its team bring you both, to the well-laid foods; drink of the sweet stalk, since the first draught is set aside for you two — come with shining bounty, Vāyu; come with bounty, Indra also. The joining is done without ceremony, and the precedence Vāyu held alone is now shared.

The fifth verse says what brings them. *Ā vāṃ dhiyo vavṛtyuḥ* — may our {{dhī}}s turn you two toward the rites. Men have groomed this drop as one grooms a fast horse before a race; drink of them, well-inclined to us, come here with help — you two who give {{vāja}}. The sixth stays with the pressing and describes the equipment plainly: these somas pressed in the waters, carried and offered by the adhvaryus; poured out for you both through the strainer, swift, wanting you, across the sheep's wool.

The seventh verse is the one to remember. *Ati vāyo sasato yāhi śaśvataḥ* — pass over all the sleepers, Vāyu; *yatra grāvā vadati tatra gacchatam*, where the pressing-stone speaks, go there, go to that house, Indra too. The god is given a criterion for choosing among houses, and the criterion is sound: not who is worthy, but where someone is awake and working. And when he arrives: the *sūnṛtā*, the true and generous speech, is visible; the ghṛta is running; come to the rite with a full team.

The eighth stays in that house and looks around it. Bring the offering of the sweet there, to the *aśvattha* which the victorious men stand about — and may they stay victorious for us. Then the household's own state, in two flat clauses: the cows are calving together, the barley is being cooked. And the promise: your cows will never fail, Vāyu, never be carried off. A hymn that began with a thousand horses ends up counting cattle and grain.

The ninth turns back to the team and lets it run. These bulls of yours, Vāyu, with strength in the arm, fly within the river; great, growing, they are not slow even in waste country; swift, they take no lodging from shouting; like the rays of the sun they are hard to rein in — hard to rein in with both hands. The last image of the hymn is of something that arrives when called and cannot be held once it comes.
135.practice:
Verse 7 is why this sūkta is worth knowing. *Yatra grāvā vadati tatra gacchatam* — where the pressing-stone speaks, go there. {{vāyu}} is told to pass over everyone who is asleep and enter the house where work is audibly being done. The Ṛgveda is often read as though divine favour followed status or lineage; here the test is sound, and the sound is somebody up before dawn doing the thing. The verse pairs naturally with the *ṛtviya* share of verse 3 — the portion that belongs to its own season, co-rayed with the sun. Being awake at the right hour is not a virtue the hymn recommends; it is the condition on which the god arrives.

The eighth verse is the other half of the same picture, and it is unusually domestic. The cows are calving, the barley is cooking, and Vāyu is promised cows that never fail and are never driven off. A reader looking for what these hymns actually want will find it stated here without ornament: the household continuing, its animals safe, its grain on Agni.

On the *niyuts*: the word names Vāyu's team specifically, and it runs through this sūkta and [[1.134]] before it as a signature. It is worth registering that the Ṛgveda gives its gods distinguishable transport — Indra's *harīs*, {{pūṣan}}'s goats in [[1.138]], Vāyu's *niyuts* — and that the arrival, not the residence, is what the hymns describe. These are gods who come.

The join in this sūkta is also a fact about the collection's habits. Verses 1–3 and 9 are Vāyu's; 4–8 belong to *indravāyū* as a pair. Of the seventeen sūktas that name Vāyu, only four are his alone; the standing arrangement, set out already in [[1.2]], is that Vāyu comes first and {{indra}} comes with him. The pairing is old enough that the Anukramaṇī has a single word for it.
135.disagreements:
Sāyaṇa's most useful note here is technical. On verse 6's *pavitra* he explains that the word covers both the bundle of kuśa grass thought to purify what is poured on it and the woollen strainer through which the soma passes, and he takes *avyaya* two ways in the same verse — first as made of sheep's wool, *avimayāni*, and on its repetition as "unexpended, unexhausted", so that the same syllables name the fleece and then the inexhaustibility of the drink. Wilson prints both senses; Griffith keeps only "the wether's fleece".

On verse 2 he glosses *ṛjīṣa* as soma that has lost its strength, and explains *pari kośam arṣati* as the soma reaching the ladle that stands in place of a vessel.

Verse 8's *aśvattha* is the real divergence. Griffith keeps the tree — "the holy Fig-tree which victorious priests surround" — while Sāyaṇa explains it away, taking *aśvattha* here as the soma plant found growing across mountainous country; Wilson follows him with "the rock-born plant". A sacred tree standing in the middle of the rite, or a name for the soma stalk: the two readings give very different pictures of what the men are gathered round.

On verse 9 Sāyaṇa glosses *agiraukasaḥ* as horses that take no lodging from speech: not to be halted by abuse or by shouting, nor by pulling on the reins.

136.title: Mitrāvaruṇā Joined by Aryaman and Bhaga
136.synthesis:
The sūkta is addressed to {{mitra}} and {{varuṇa}} and it keeps failing to stay with only two. Aryaman enters in the second verse and is named again in the third and the fifth; Bhaga stands beside him in the second and the sixth; by the last two verses {{indra}}, {{agni}} and the {{marut}}s have been drawn in as well. The movement from a pair to a company is what this hymn does.

It opens on offering rather than on the gods. Bring forward the greatest, the highest {{namas}}, the oblation, the shaped *mati* — bring it to the two watchful ones, the two who are gracious, and bring the sweetest to them. They are *samrājā*, joint sovereigns, with ghṛta poured for them, praised at every {{yajña}}; and their *kṣatra*, their power to rule, cannot be assailed from any quarter — their godhead cannot be assailed.

The second verse is the hymn's finest. *Adarśi gātur urave varīyasī* — a way has come into view for the broad one, a wider way; *panthā ṛtasya sam ayaṃsta raśmibhiḥ*, the path of {{ṛta}} has been held together by rays, the eye of Bhaga by rays. And then the seat: *dyukṣaṃ mitrasya sādanam aryamṇo varuṇasya ca*, the dwelling of Mitra, of Aryaman and of Varuṇa is fixed in heaven; and from it they give great *vayas*, vigour worth praising. The path of order is not an idea here but something the light physically holds in place, and the three who live at the far end of it are named in one breath.

The third verse brings in Aditi. Attend on her — luminous, upholding the settled lands, possessed of *svar* — attend day after day, you two who never sleep, day after day. You have won a shining *kṣatra*, Ādityas, lords of the gift; and of those two, one is Mitra and one is Varuṇa *yātayajjana*, who sets the peoples in their places, and Aryaman too is *yātayajjana*. That epithet, given twice in a line, is the closest the hymn comes to saying what these gods do: they assign people their stations and hold them to them.

The fourth is the offering. May this {{soma}} be most kindly to Mitra and Varuṇa, having its share among the drinkings — a god having his share among gods. Let all the gods take pleasure in it today, of one accord. And then the request, made to them as kings: therefore do what we ask, you who possess ṛta, do what we ask.

The fifth states the covenant plainly. Whoever has served Mitra and Varuṇa — guard that man untouched from *aṃhas*, from the narrow place a person gets caught in; guard the giving mortal from *aṃhas*. And Aryaman watches over the man who goes straight along the *vrata*, the observance — who dresses their *vrata* with *ukthas*, who dresses it with *stomas*. The protection is conditional and the condition is stated: straightness, and observance kept.

The sixth widens fully. *Namo dive bṛhate rodasībhyām* — homage to great Dyaus, to the two worlds; to Mitra I speak, and to Varuṇa the generous, gracious, generous. Praise Indra, praise Agni, praise heaven-dwelling Aryaman and Bhaga. And the thing wanted, when it finally comes, is ordinary: living long, may we be joined with our children, joined by the help of Soma.

The seventh is short where every verse before it was long — the metre drops from *atyaṣṭi* to *triṣṭup*, and the doubled line-ending stops with it. By the gods' help, with Indra beside us, may we be reckoned self-glorious among the Maruts; may Agni, Mitra and Varuṇa stretch shelter over us; may we and our patrons obtain it.
136.practice:
Two of the Ādityas can be met here who are rarely met elsewhere. Aryaman is named four times in this short sūkta and given the whole business of protection in verse 5 — he guards the man who goes straight along the *vrata* — yet not one sūkta in the entire Ṛgveda is ascribed to Aryaman alone. Bhaga, whose name is simply "portion, share", stands beside him twice and has no sūkta of his own either. What both survive in is the name a person carries: *aryaman* is remembered in the marriage rites and in offerings to the fathers, and *bhaga* is the root of *bhāgya*, one's portion in life, and of *bhagavat*. These are gods whose vocabulary outlived their hymns.

The counted background is worth having. Thirty-six sūktas of the collection name *mitrāvaruṇau*; eighteen are theirs entire, eleven of those standing consecutively in maṇḍala 5. In maṇḍala 1 the pair holds this sūkta, [[1.137]], and the three at [[1.151]]–[[1.153]], and exactly one sūkta in the Ṛgveda, [[3.59]], is addressed to Mitra by himself.

The line to carry away is verse 2. *Panthā ṛtasya sam ayaṃsta raśmibhiḥ* — the path of {{ṛta}} has been held together by rays. Order is not described as a decree here but as something being physically held in position by light, day after day, by gods who are called *jāgṛvāṃsā*, wakeful, in the very next verse. The reason sandhyā is kept at the junctures is the same claim in practice: the order holds because it is attended to, and the attending has to be repeated.

And verse 5 states the terms of the relationship as clearly as anywhere in the collection. What is asked for is protection from *aṃhas* — narrowness, the strait a person is squeezed into — and what is required is *ṛjuyantam anu vratam*, going straight, along the observance. Mitra and Varuṇa are the gods of the kept word, and this verse is the plainest form of their bargain.
136.disagreements:
Verse 2's list of names splits the readings completely. Sāyaṇa treats Mitra, Aryaman and Varuṇa here as designations of the sun — "several names are used to multiply his praises" — so that the shining dwelling is the firmament lit up, and Wilson prints exactly that: "the brilliant mansion of Mitra, of Aryaman, of Varuṇa, has been lighted up by his rays." Griffith keeps three distinct gods with a shared house: "Firm-set in heaven is Mitra's home, and Aryaman's and Varuna's. Thence they give forth great vital strength." One reading has a single solar power under several names; the other has a family.

The third verse's *yātayajjana* is where Sāyaṇa is at his most severe. He glosses it as the one by whom men are impelled to exertion, urged to discharge their proper functions — and then, on its repetition for Aryaman, adds the darker sense: the one by whom the irreligious, those who perform no worship, are cast down into the infernal regions. Neither translator carries that second reading; Wilson has "the animator of mankind", Griffith "Movers of men".

Verse 1's *samrājā* he allows twice over, as joint sovereigns or as "thoroughly shining". On verse 6 he notes that *mīḷhuṣe* is properly an epithet of Rudra, and takes the words after it as applying to Mitra, Varuṇa and Rudra together — a third god in a line that does not name him.

137.title: Milk-Blent Soma at Dawn for Mitrāvaruṇā
137.synthesis:
Three verses, and no argument in any of them. This is an invitation and nothing else: the {{soma}} is pressed, it is mixed, the hour is right, come and drink. The whole sūkta is in *atiśakvarī*, a very long metre that the collection uses for a complete hymn only here, and the effect of such a line carrying so slight a content is that the same few facts come round again and again with the wording barely shifted — pressed with stones, blent with milk, come to us.

*Suṣuma ā yātam adribhiḥ* — we have pressed with the stones; come. These somas, *gośrīta*, mixed with the milk of cows, are *matsara*, the drinks that carry a mind away; these are the ones that carry it away. Come here to us, you two kings, *divispṛśā*, touching heaven — a single epithet that does the work of a paragraph, since it makes {{mitra}} and {{varuṇa}} the pair who reach as far as the sky and are yet being asked to sit down at a household's pressing. These are yours, Mitrāvaruṇā, blent with milk, bright, blent with milk.

The second verse changes the mixture and fixes the hour. Here are the drops: come — somas mixed with *dadhi*, with curd, pressed and mixed with curd. And yours at the waking of {{uṣas}}, together with the rays of Sūrya. The pressing is a morning act, done as the light comes, and the verse says so twice over. Then the closing line turns the drinking itself into an offering: *sutaḥ mitrāya varuṇāya pītaye, cāruḥ ṛtāya pītaye* — pressed for Mitra and for Varuṇa to drink; the lovely one pressed for {{ṛta}} to drink. Ṛta is put in the place a god's name occupied one clause earlier. Whatever the two of them are, the order they keep can be given a cup.

The third verse describes the work. *Tāṃ vāṃ dhenuṃ na vāsarīm aṃśuṃ duhanti adribhiḥ* — that stalk they milk for you two with stones, as one milks a cow in the morning; they milk the soma with stones. The verb is *duh*, the same used of a cow, and it is used twice: the plant is not crushed but milked, and the stones are the hands. Then, once more, the invitation — come to us, turned this way, for the soma-drinking — and the last line adds the only new information in the hymn: *ayaṃ vāṃ mitrāvaruṇā nṛbhiḥ sutaḥ*, this one has been pressed for you by men. Pressed by men, for gods who touch heaven, and offered as the drink of ṛta.

What the three verses hold, taken together, is a complete small rite rather than a thought about one. Someone got up before the sun. The stones were used. The juice was mixed once with milk and once with curd. The sun came up while this was happening. And the two gods who between them keep the day and the night, and hold men to what they have said, were asked to come and take the first of it. The hymn does not explain why they should, and it does not praise them for anything. It reports the preparation and repeats the request, which is what an invitation is.
137.practice:
This is the shortest sūkta in this stretch of the collection — one of five in maṇḍala 1 with only three verses — and it is almost pure procedure. That makes it useful in a way the grand hymns are not: it shows what the ordinary morning looked like.

The technical vocabulary here is exact and has stayed exact. *Gośir* and *gavāśir* name {{soma}} mixed with milk; *dadhyāśir*, soma mixed with curd; and both appear in these three verses as distinct preparations, not as poetic variation. *Adribhiḥ*, with the stones, names the pressing-stones, the *grāvan* that [[1.135]].7 says the god listens for. The Ṛgveda is often approached as poetry with ritual behind it; a hymn like this is the other way round, and shows how much of the collection is a description of what hands were doing.

The verb in verse 3 is worth keeping. *Duhanti* — they milk the stalk. The same word is used of a cow, and the verse says so in its simile: like a cow in the morning. The plant gives what it has the way an animal does, willingly and on schedule, and the pressing-stones are treated as hands rather than as a mill. That is a small thing, and it tells you what kind of relation the rite understood itself to be in with the thing it used.

The line to hold is the close of verse 2: *cāruḥ ṛtāya pītaye* — the lovely one pressed for {{ṛta}} to drink. Half a line earlier the same juice was pressed for {{mitra}} and {{varuṇa}} to drink. The hymn puts an abstract noun where a god's name stands, without marking the substitution, and this is one of the clearest places in the collection where the order of things is treated as something that can receive an offering. The two gods and the order they maintain are not being carefully distinguished, and the reader should not distinguish them more sharply than the text does.
137.disagreements:
There is little to divide here, which is itself worth recording: on a hymn this bare, Wilson and Griffith agree almost line for line, and Sāyaṇa's surviving note is a single remark.

That remark is on verse 1's *matsarāḥ*, the exhilarating drops, and it concerns the repetition rather than the word. Sāyaṇa takes the doubling to carry a competitive sense — the somas of this rite as *envious* or emulous of those offered at other ceremonies. Neither translator follows him; Wilson has simply "these Soma are exhilarating; these Soma are exhilarating", and Griffith "these Soma-drops which gladden you". The suggestion is a small window onto how the tradition handled Parucchepa's doubled line-endings: rather than treat the echo as metrical filling, the commentary looks for a difference of sense between the two occurrences, and here manufactures one.

The one substantive divergence is in verse 3. Wilson takes *vāsarīm* with the cow — "that succulent creeper, like a productive cow"; Griffith reads the adjective as colour, "as 'twere a radiant-coloured cow", where the sense of morning is at least as well supported. It changes a cow milked at daybreak, matching verse 2's dawn, into a bright-coloured one.

Neither translator remarks on *ṛtāya pītaye* in verse 2. Wilson gives "for their drinking at the sacrifice" and Griffith "fair juice for drink, for sacrifice", both quietly resolving {{ṛta}} into the rite. The harder reading, which leaves ṛta itself as the drinker, is what the case ending gives.

138.title: Pūṣan Goat-Drawn — a Friendship Not Denied
138.synthesis:
Four verses to {{pūṣan}}, and the hymn is about friendship with him — asked for in the second verse, described in the third, and refused to be let go of in the fourth.

It opens with praise that will not stop. *Pra-pra pūṣṇaḥ tuvijātasya śasyate mahitvam* — forth and forth is the greatness of Pūṣan, strong-born, proclaimed; the praise of him who is powerful does not slacken, his praise does not slacken. Then the singer says what he is doing and why: wanting favour, I sing to the one whose help is close at hand, who is *mayobhu*, maker of ease — and who has drawn to himself the mind of everyone; he, the *makha*, the god, has drawn it. The first thing said about this god is that his help is *antyūti*, near help, help that is nearby. That is his whole character in one compound.

The second verse puts him in motion. I drive you forward with *stoma*s, Pūṣan, like a swift one on a journey, so that you may drive off the *mṛdhaḥ*, those who scorn and obstruct — so that you may carry us over the *mṛdhaḥ* as a camel carries a load. The comparison is not decorative: what a pack animal does is get things across ground that would otherwise stop them, and that is what is wanted. Then the relationship is named for the first time: I, a mortal, call you, a god who makes ease, *sakhyāya*, for friendship. And make our song full of splendour; in the contests for {{vāja}}, make it full of splendour.

The third verse looks back at what that friendship has already produced. Those who praise, being possessed of {{kratu}}, have had the use of your help in your friendship — by *kratu* they have had the use of it. Following that, we ask you for a newer team of riches. And then the two words that give this god his particular tone: *aheḷamānaḥ*, not becoming angry, and *uruśaṃsa*, widely praised — be our runner, our companion who goes alongside, in every contest for *vāja*, be our runner. What is asked of him is not power. It is that he keep pace and not take offence.

The fourth verse asks the same two things again and names him. Be near for our winning, not angry, generous — *ajāśva*, whose horses are goats; be so for those who want renown, *ajāśva*. May we turn you here with *stoma*s that work, wonder-worker. And then the closing line, which is unlike the endings of the hymns around it: *nahi tvā pūṣan atimanye, āghṛṇe, na te sakhyam apahnuve* — I do not think slightingly of you, Pūṣan, glowing one; I do not deny your friendship.

That last verse is a denial of two things a person might be doing, and both are ordinary. *Atimanye* is to hold someone in low regard, to think past them; *apahnuve* is to disown, to deny a connection one actually has. The hymn's final gesture is not a request but a disclaimer: whatever else, I have not looked down on you and I have not pretended you are not my friend. Of all the closings in Parucchepa's thirteen sūktas this is the most personal, and it is addressed to the smallest of the gods he treats — the one with goats for horses, whose help is near, who does not get angry.
138.practice:
{{pūṣan}} is the god of the road, and everything in the hymn follows from that. He is asked to carry us across the obstructors "as a camel does"; to be a *sarī*, one who runs alongside; and his help is *antyūti*, close at hand. Where the great deities of the collection are asked for victory and wealth, Pūṣan is asked to accompany. That is the office the later tradition kept for him: the guardian of paths and of what travels on them, of herds on the move and of the roads themselves.

Two places a Hindu reader still meets him are worth naming. He is invoked three times in the marriage sūkta [[10.85]] — the rite in which a bride is conducted from one house to another, which is a journey before it is anything else — and he is a god of the passage at the end of life. His epithet here, *ajāśva*, "whose horses are goats", is preserved in the tradition unchanged; the goat-drawn car is his and no one else's, and it fits a god whose work is hill paths rather than battlefields.

He is also, by the collection's own count, a minor deity with a durable presence: eight sūktas are his alone and fifteen name him, against 218 for {{indra}}. Five of the eight stand in one run in maṇḍala 6, [[6.53]] to [[6.58]], with [[6.57]] given to Indra and Pūṣan together; this sūkta and [[1.42]] are his in maṇḍala 1.

What to take from the hymn is its last line. *Nahi tvā pūṣan atimanye, na te sakhyam apahnuve* — I do not think slightingly of you; I do not deny your friendship. The two verbs describe the ordinary ways a small helper gets treated: overlooked because there are bigger gods, and disowned when the connection is no longer convenient. The singer says he has done neither. It is a sentence about how one holds a relationship with something modest and reliable, and it does not need translating into doctrine to be useful.
138.disagreements:
Verse 1's ending is where Sāyaṇa is most interesting and least literal. *Mana āyuyuve makho devo āyuyuve makhaḥ* he reads first mystically — the text means to identify {{pūṣan}} with both the performer of the worship and the performance itself — and then offers a plainer alternative: *makha* as *yajñavān*, the one who receives the sacrifice and grants what the sacrificer asks, "mixing with" his mind by giving quickly; and on the repetition he takes *makha* as the sacrifice itself, which Pūṣan mingles with until it is complete. Wilson prints the second, with the god "blending with the thoughts of all his worshippers"; Griffith flattens it to "hath drawn to him the hearts of all".

On the camel of verse 2 both translators keep the animal, and Sāyaṇa confirms the sense — *uṣṭro na*, as a camel bears a burden. His note on *dyumninaḥ kṛdhi* is that *dyumna* may be brilliance, or fame, or food, and that on its second occurrence the sense is what conquest brings.

*Ajāśva* in verse 4 is left standing by everyone. Sāyaṇa reports it on Yāska's authority as "he who is drawn by goats, or has goats for horses"; Wilson simply keeps the name, Griffith renders "Goat-borne".

The one real split is verse 3's *sarī*. Wilson takes it as leadership — "be our leader in every encounter" — where Griffith has only "come thou to us in every fight". The sense of running alongside, which the word supports, is in neither.

139.title: From Agni to Bṛhaspati — and the Thirty-Three
139.synthesis:
This is the last of Parucchepa's thirteen sūktas and it takes them all in at once: nine deities in eleven verses, each given a verse or three, and then a closing verse that counts the whole company.

*Astu śrauṣaṭ* — may there be a hearing. The opening words are the call sent up when the offering is poured, and the verse follows it by putting {{agni}} in front *dhiyā*, with the thought engaged; then choosing the heavenly troop, choosing Indravāyū. When the new song has been fastened at the navel, then — the verse ends — may our {{dhī}}s go forward, may our shaped thoughts go out toward the gods.

The second verse is one of the hardest in the maṇḍala and it belongs to {{mitra}} and {{varuṇa}}. What they do is take up *anṛtam*, the untrue, from beyond {{ṛta}}, by their own *manyu*, which is also their *dakṣa*'s own. Then the seeing: in your seats we looked upon the golden one — not with our thoughts, not with the mind, but with our own eyes, the eyes that {{soma}} gives.

Three verses go to the {{aśvin}}s. In the third, men who want the gods send the *śloka* up to them with somas, and the rims of the golden chariot scatter sweetness as they turn. In the fourth their intent is recognised: you two open the *nāka*, the vault; your yokers harness for the *diviṣṭi*s, the morning rites; we have set you on the seat of the golden car, and you go by a path that leads straight through the middle air. The fifth is short — the metre drops to *bṛhatī* — and asks the plainest thing in the hymn: by your powers, rich in power, favour us by day and by night; let your giving never run out, and never ours.

The sixth is {{indra}}'s. These drops, pressed with the stones, bursting out, are for the bull to drink; may they gladden you into giving great and wonderful *rādhas*; praised in our songs, come, and come gracious to us.

The seventh returns to Agni and tells a story in half a verse. Hear us and speak for us to the gods worthy of the rite, to those kings. And then: when you gods gave that cow to the {{aṅgiras}}es, they milked her — Aryaman was the doer, working with them — and he knows her, along with me.

The eighth turns to the {{marut}}s, and it is a request not to be harmed. Never let these manly deeds of yours be turned against us; let our splendours not wear out, and not before our time. Whatever of yours is bright, new in age after age, deathless, sounding out — set that among us, and whatever is hardest to come by, set that among us too.

The ninth is the singer's own genealogy. Dadhyañc, Aṅgiras of old, Priyamedha, Kaṇva, Atri, {{manu}} — they know my birth; those of old and Manu know it. Their line reaches to the gods; *asmākaṃ teṣu nābhayaḥ*, our navels are in them. By their footstep I bow low with song; I bow to Indrāgnī with song.

The tenth is Bṛhaspati's, and it is all ritual sound. Let the *hotā* offer; let those who long for it obtain the desirable; Bṛhaspati, longing, sacrifices with oxen, with oxen much desired. We have caught the *śloka* of the pressing-stone from far off — and by himself the one of good *kratu* held up the waters, held up many dwellings.

The eleventh counts. *Ye devāso divi ekādaśa stha* — you gods who are eleven in heaven; eleven upon the earth; eleven who dwell in the waters by your greatness: take pleasure in this rite. After ten verses of naming gods one at a time, the hymn stops naming and simply totals them.
139.practice:
The last verse is the one every reader should carry: eleven gods in heaven, eleven on earth, eleven in the waters. That is the thirty-three, the standard total the tradition keeps for the Vedic gods — stated as a single number at [[1.45]].2 and distributed here across the three worlds. What the verse actually does is close a hymn that has been naming gods individually for ten verses by refusing to name any of them. Whatever the list, the count holds.

Verse 9 is the other one that touches a reader's own practice directly. The singer names his forebears — Dadhyañc, {{aṅgiras}}, Priyamedha, Kaṇva, Atri, {{manu}} — and says *asmākaṃ teṣu nābhayaḥ*, our navels are in them; their reach extends to the gods. This is the logic that every *pravara* still recites: before making an offering a person names the ṛṣis of his line, because the line is the connection. The Ṛgveda states the reason here in one image. You are joined to the gods at a distance, through people, and the joint is a navel — a cord, not a claim.

The opening is worth noticing too. *Astu śrauṣaṭ* is not ordinary speech; it is a ritual call belonging to the moment of offering, and Parucchepa begins his final hymn with it. Whatever else the sūkta is doing, it starts by behaving like a liturgy.

And verse 5 is the one to keep for its modesty. The {{aśvin}}s are asked to favour us by day and by night, and then: *mā vāṃ rātir upa dasat kadā cana, asmat rātiḥ kadā cana* — may your giving never fail, and may ours never fail either. Both halves are asked for. The worshipper does not only want the god's generosity to continue; he wants his own to.

This closes the block of thirteen — [[1.127]] to [[1.139]] — that is all the Ṛgveda has of Parucchepa Daivodāsi. It is fitting that the set ends with a hymn that gives one verse each to Agni, Mitrāvaruṇā, the Aśvins, Indra, the Maruts, Indrāgnī and Bṛhaspati, and then counts the gods.
139.disagreements:
Verse 2 is where the witnesses part most sharply, and the issue is what Mitra and Varuṇa do with *anṛtam*. Griffith reads it as a taking-in: "above the true have taken to yourselves the untrue with your mind" — the gods absorbing falsehood. Wilson, following Sāyaṇa, does not read *anṛtam* as untruth at all but as water, and produces "bestow upon us abundantly that unenduring water which you obtain from the sun." The same line yields either a statement about the gods and falsehood or a request for rain, and nothing in the Sanskrit forces a choice.

On verse 1 Sāyaṇa records that *śrauṣaṭ* is "an exclamation uttered when the butter is poured upon the fire", and explains "the navel" by citing the Taittirīya Saṃhitā — "they have called the sacrifice the navel of the world" — while allowing that the accompanying word may instead name Vivasvat, the sun. Griffith takes it as Vivasvān, Wilson as the altar.

Verse 7 he expands into a legend: the {{aṅgiras}}es, having propitiated the gods, were given the cow of plenty but could not milk her, until Aryaman drew from her the milk that could be turned to butter for the fire.

On verse 9's *nābhayaḥ* he offers two: the vital airs, bound up with life, or sacrifices bound to their rewards. On verse 10 he glosses the holding of the waters as rain produced by worship. His note on verse 11 is a single phrase, *tisraḥ eva* — three only.

140.title: Agni Twice-Born, Eating and Growing Again
140.synthesis:
This is the first sūkta of Dīrghatamas, and it is a physiology of fire. Almost nothing is asked for until the last three verses; the rest watches {{agni}} eat, move, mate, age, and be born again, and reports what it sees.

The first verse prepares the place. Bring forward a womb for Agni as one brings the offering — for him who sits on the *vedi* and loves his own station, brightly shining. Clothe the pure one with the *manman*, the framed thought, as with a garment: him whose chariot is light, bright of colour, killer of darkness. The song is treated as cloth, and the seat is treated as a birthplace.

The second verse states the hymn's central fact. *Dvijanmā* — twice-born — he reaches for the threefold food; in the course of the year what he has swallowed grows again.
