And a distinction that will run through the whole hymn: with another's mouth and tongue he is a noble bull; with another he strips the trees like a rutting elephant. One god, two mouths — the ladle's and the forest fire's.

The third verse gives him parents. His two mothers, moving in the dark, living together, tremble; both run to the child — forward-tongued, darkening, quick-slipping, to be held to, growing, the strengthener of his father. The fourth releases what carries him: light-running, black-furrowed, swift, not of one mind, restless, gliding easily, wind-driven — they are yoked for {{manu}}. The fifth lets them go. Then his blackeners run out at will, making the black *abhva*, the formless mass, into a great shape; and when he strokes over the wide earth he goes hissing, thundering, roaring.

The sixth is the boldest verse. He stoops among the brown plants as though he were adorning them, and comes bellowing like a bull to his *patnīs*, his wives; showing his strength he beautifies his own bodies, and shakes his horns like something terrible, hard to hold.

The seventh watches him behave intelligently. Gathered in, spread out, he takes hold — knowing, among things that know him; the constant one lies down again. And then they grow once more, and go toward what is divine, and give their parents a different form. The eighth is the hymn's strangest and finest image. The long-haired maidens close round him; dying, they stand up again to meet the living one; and loosing them from their age he comes roaring, generating a further breath in them, living and unbroken. Flames as women who die and rise, and fuel made young by being burnt.

The ninth follows him across country. Licking the covering of the mother, he goes wide with loud-devouring fighters, giving *vayas*, vigour, to whatever has feet, licking always — and a blackened track keeps after him wherever he goes.

Only now does the hymn ask. The tenth: shine among our patrons, Agni; snorting, a bull, *damūnas*, the one at home in the house — having thrown off your infant wrappings you blazed out, flickering about like armour in a fight. The eleventh: let this well-set thing, taken out of the ill-set, be dearer to you than even the dear *manman*; and with the pure brightness that shines from your body, win us the treasure.

The twelfth asks for the strangest gift in the hymn: for our chariot and our house, give a boat — one with its own oars and with feet, which may carry our men and our patrons and the people across, and which is itself *śarma*, shelter. And the thirteenth closes outward: welcome our *uktha*; may Dyāvākṣāmā and the self-praised rivers, and long days, choose out for us cattle and grain and the best food. After twelve verses inside Agni, the last verse looks at the fields.
140.practice:
*Dvijanmā*, twice-born, is the word this sūkta turns on, and it occurs three times in the Ṛgveda — here and twice in [[1.149]], all three in Dīrghatamas' Agni hymns. Applied to fire it means what the commentary says it means: born once from the rubbing of the two sticks and again when consecrated for the rite. The word later became the ordinary term for a man who has had his second birth at the *upanayana*, before the same fire. The hymn does not make that connection and this note does not claim it did. What it does show is that the idea of a second birth conferred by the rite was already being used, of Agni, in the first maṇḍala.

What makes this sūkta unusual is how little it asks for and how long it looks. Nine of the thirteen verses are description: fire moving across brown country, stooping into plants, roaring like a bull, blackening the ground behind it. A reader who has only met the Veda as prayer should sit with verse 8. *Ūrdhvās tasthur mamruṣīḥ pra āyave* — dead, they stand up again for the living one; and he releases them from their age. The flames are women who die and rise; the wood is made young by being consumed. Nothing in the verse is symbolic and nothing in it is only physical.

Verse 12 is the one that has travelled furthest. Agni is asked for a boat — *nāvaṃ nityāritrāṃ padvatīm*, a boat with its own oars and with feet — that will carry the household's men and patrons and people across, and that is itself shelter. The image of the rite as a vessel crossing over, and of the god as the means of crossing, is everywhere in later Hinduism; here it is a request made to the household fire, alongside a chariot and a house.

Of the 186 sūktas the Anukramaṇī assigns to Agni alone, 44 are in maṇḍala 1, and this begins the longest single run of them in the collection: [[1.140]] through [[1.150]], eleven consecutive sūktas by Dīrghatamas Aucathya, all to Agni except the Āprī hymn [[1.142]]. Dīrghatamas has 25 sūktas, [[1.140]] to [[1.164]], and none anywhere else.
140.disagreements:
Verse 4 divides the readings completely. Sāyaṇa takes the string of epithets — light-running, black-furrowed, restless, not of one mind, wind-driven — as flames, and Wilson prints them so. Griffith makes them horses: "these steeds of thine are yoked … ploughing blackened lines." A team or a fire-front; every image in the verse works either way.

Verse 6's *patnīḥ* splits the same way. Sāyaṇa allows the word to mean the bushes and timber that cherish Agni, or simply cows; Wilson takes cows — "rushes roaring like a bull amongst a herd" — while Griffith keeps the marital sense, "rushes bellowing like a bull upon his wives".

On verse 2 Sāyaṇa is precise and useful. *Dvijanmā* is either produced by attrition from the two sticks or born first by attrition and then by consecration for use; the *trivṛd annam*, the threefold food, is clarified butter, the *puroḍāśa* cake, and {{soma}}; and what has been eaten "grows again" because the same offerings are made every year. He also explains the two mouths of that verse concretely: with one, in the sacrificial fire, Agni receives the oblation through the tongue of another, which is the priest's ladle; with the other, as the forest fire, he consumes trees.

Verse 12's boat he allegorises outright — the boat is the {{yajña}}, the oars are the priests, the fittings are the fuel and apparatus, and the feet are the deities, the prayers and the offerings. Wilson follows him partway; Griffith leaves the boat a boat.

141.title: Agni's Three Homes, and the Felly Round the Spokes
141.synthesis:
*Baṭ itthā* — yes, just so. The hymn opens on a word of assent, as though answering something already said, and what it affirms is that the god's visible *bhargas*, his splendour, was set here for beauty, since he was born from {{sahas}}. When he leans toward it the *mati* comes off; and the *dhenā*s of {{ṛta}}, the streams of ordered speech, have led him here as they flow.

The second verse counts {{agni}}'s dwellings, and the counting is the hymn's frame. First: nourishing, embodied, holding food, constant, he lies down. Second: among the seven kindly mothers. Third: for the milking of this bull, the young women brought forth the one who has ten to care for him. Three homes, three ways of being present, stated as a list and then never referred to again — the rest of the hymn simply moves through them.

The third describes his extraction: the *sūrī*s, the lords, brought him up by force from the base of the buffalo's form, and Mātariśvan churned him out, hidden away from of old, for the mixing of the sweet. The fourth follows him from one fire to the next — led forward from the highest father, rising among the plants and the teeth; when the two hasten his birth he becomes the youngest, pure with heat. The fifth lets him spread: he entered the mothers and in them, unharmed, grew wide; and as he climbed the older ones he now runs among the newer and lower.

The sixth turns from fire to office. Then they choose him as *hotā* at the *diviṣṭi*s, the morning rites, pressing toward him as toward Bhaga, the one who apportions; and, much praised, by *kratu* and by sheer size he goes always to the mortal's word, *dhāyase*, for the nourishing of it.

The seventh and eighth let him burn without restraint. When the adorable one, driven by wind, has stood up — crooked, running on like a chatterer nobody has stopped — dust lies on the path of the burning one, black-shanked, pure of birth, who goes many ways. And like a chariot made by skilled hands he lifts himself to the sky on ruddy limbs; where you burn, the bright ones turn black, and the winged things scatter from your flaring as men scatter before a hero.

The ninth is the hymn's centre and its finest line. *Tvayā hi agne varuṇo dhṛtavrataḥ mitraḥ śāśadre aryamā sudānavaḥ* — through you, Agni, {{varuṇa}} who holds his vow, {{mitra}}, and Aryaman the generous are made strong; because you were born encompassing them all by *kratu*, in every way, *arān na nemiḥ*, as the felly encompasses the spokes. The image occurs twice in the whole Ṛgveda: at [[1.32]].15 it is Indra as king, holding the peoples the way a rim holds spokes; here it is Agni, and what he holds are the Ādityas themselves. A rim does not compress its spokes. It keeps each at its own distance and cannot turn without them.

The tenth turns to giving: for the man who labours and presses you send the treasure and the gods' whole company, and we would set you anew, young son of *sahas*, like Bhaga, in our song. The eleventh asks what such a household wants — wealth well aimed and staying at home, a portion, an energy that holds; and the one who directs both births like reins and, of good *kratu*, directs the gods' word at the rite.

The twelfth asks him to listen: may our bright one with quick horses, the joyful *hotā* on his shining car, hear us; may Agni, who does not go astray, lead us by the best leadings toward what is good and what is better. The thirteenth signs off: Agni has been praised with strong *arka*s and set higher toward sole sovereignty; may these patrons and we spread out as the sun spreads over the mist.
141.practice:
The verse to take away is the ninth, and it can be set beside one a reader may already know. In [[1.32]].15, at the end of the great Vṛtra hymn, {{indra}} rules the peoples *arān na nemiḥ*, as the felly is around the spokes. That simile occurs exactly twice in the Ṛgveda, and its other occurrence is here — where what {{agni}} encircles is not peoples but {{mitra}}, {{varuṇa}} and Aryaman, who are strengthened by him. The same picture of authority is used for the greatest god of the collection and for Agni in a household courtyard, and in both cases the point is the same: the rim holds each spoke at its own distance, and cannot turn without them. It is a description of holding-together that neither crushes nor lets go, and it is worth measuring a household or a teacher against.

The three dwellings of verse 2 are the other thing to carry. Agni lies as one thing here, is among the seven mothers as another, and is brought forth by the young women as a third — and the tradition read this triple location as the distribution of fire in the world: on the hearth, in the waters and plants, and in the sun. The threefold Agni is one of the oldest structures in Vedic thought and one of the most durable; the three fires of the śrauta rite and the three-times-daily observance both rest on the same intuition, that one fire is in several places at once and is not divided by being so.

Verse 6 names an ordinary fact of the rite that is easy to pass over: *hotāraṃ vṛṇate diviṣṭiṣu*, they choose him as *hotā* at the morning rites. The hotā is chosen — the office is filled by selection, verse by verse and day by day, not held by right. That the god himself is described as being chosen for it says something about how the tradition understood ritual office.

This is the second of the eleven consecutive Agni sūktas of Dīrghatamas Aucathya, [[1.140]]–[[1.150]]. His 25 sūktas run from [[1.140]] to [[1.164]] and he has none elsewhere in the collection.
141.disagreements:
Sāyaṇa reads much of this hymn as solar and meteorological, and Wilson follows him into English, so the two translations diverge more than usual. On verse 2's three homes he explains the seven mothers as the rains that fertilise the seven worlds, and the "milking of the bull" as the sun's rays drawing moisture off the earth, carrying it to the solar region and returning it as rain. Griffith keeps the verse concrete and obscure — "in the seven auspicious Mothers is his home" — and does not explain.

Verse 4 he reads as ritual movement rather than nature: *pituḥ paramāt*, "from the highest father", is the gārhapatya fire from which fire is carried to the āhavanīya, and *daṃsu*, among the teeth, means among the flames. Griffith has him brought "from the Highest Father" and rising "amid the plants … hungry", which leaves the fire in the field.

Verse 7 divides sharply. Sāyaṇa takes *hvāro na vakvā jaraṇā anākṛtaḥ* as a crooked, prolific, unrestrained speaker of praises, and Wilson prints "like an insincere and unrestrained chatterer"; Griffith reads a snake — "serpent-like winding through the dry grass unrestrained". The same words give a babbler or a moving snake.

On verse 6's *bhagam* Sāyaṇa allows a great prince, or Āditya, or the sun; Griffith keeps the god Bhaga. On verse 11 he supplies a son as the thing asked for, glossing *dharṇasi* as skilled in holding knowledge, where Griffith has only "strong capacity".

142.title: The Āprī Sequence — from Kindled Agni to Indra
142.synthesis:
This is an Āprī hymn, and an Āprī hymn is not composed the way other sūktas are. The order of its verses is fixed in advance: each verse addresses one item in a set sequence, and the sequence is the same across every family that has one. What a poet supplies is the wording; what he inherits is the list. Reading it is like watching a rite from the door.

*Samiddho agne* — kindled, {{agni}}, bring the gods here today for the man whose ladle is raised; spin out the ancient thread for the giver who has pressed the {{soma}}. The first verse names him in the state he has to be in before anything else can happen: alight. And the metaphor for what he then does is weaving — *tantuṃ tanuṣva pūrvyam*, stretch out the old thread. The rite is a fabric being continued, not begun.

The second verse addresses Tanūnapāt, "child of the body", and asks him to measure out a {{yajña}} rich in ghṛta and honey for a singer like me, one who labours and gives. The third is Narāśaṃsa's: pure, purifying, wonderful, he mixes the sacrifice with sweetness — thrice from heaven, a god among gods and worthy of worship. The fourth returns to Agni under a fourth name, *īḷita*, the one invoked: bring Indra here, wonderful and dear, for this thought of mine is being uttered toward you, sweet-tongued one.

Then the sequence turns to the furniture of the rite, and it treats each piece as a deity. Fifth, the *barhis*: those holding ladles are strewing the grass at this well-ordered rite, and what is being made is a wide seat, a *śarma*, for {{indra}}. Sixth, the Doors — *dvāro devīḥ*, the divine doors — increasers of {{ṛta}}, great, purifying, longed-for, never sticking: let them swing open for the gods to come through. Seventh, Night and Dawn together, praised, close-joined, beautifully formed, the two young mothers of ṛta: let them sit down on the grass of their own accord. Eighth, the two divine *hotā*s, of delighting tongue, sages: let them accomplish this rite of ours today, effective, touching heaven.

The ninth verse brings three goddesses and a fourth name. Bhāratī set among the gods, Iḷā, {{sarasvatī}}, Mahī — let them, worthy of worship, sit on the grass. Speech in three forms, or three rivers, or three regions: the hymn does not choose. The tenth is Tvaṣṭṛ's: may he, well disposed toward us, loose for us that swift wonderful abundance, of itself enough, for nourishment and for wealth, at our navel. The eleventh addresses Vanaspati, lord of the wood — the sacrificial post, which is a tree — and asks it to release the offering and worship the gods; and Agni the wise sends the oblations on among them.

The twelfth is the cry itself. *Svāhā* — to Vāyu who has {{pūṣan}} and the {{marut}}s with him, to the whole company of gods; make the offering for Indra, whose form is the *gāyatra*. And the thirteenth, which no other Āprī hymn has: come, Indra, to the offerings made with *svāhā*; come, hear the call; they are calling you at the rite.

That last verse is why this hymn is longer than the others. The standard Āprī sequence closes with the *svāhā*-cries; here the poet adds a verse asking Indra, who was already named in the fourth and the fifth, actually to arrive. The fixed list ends and then someone speaks.
142.practice:
The Āprī hymns are the most tightly bound texts in the Ṛgveda, and knowing what they are makes the whole collection legible in a new way. There are exactly ten of them: [[1.13]], this one, [[1.188]], [[2.3]], [[3.4]], [[5.5]], [[7.2]], [[9.5]], [[10.70]] and [[10.110]]. Each belongs to a different family — Kāṇva, Dīrghatamas, Agastya, Gṛtsamada, Viśvāmitra, Ātreya, Vasiṣṭha, Kāśyapa, Vādhryaśva, Bhārgava — one apiece, and no family has two. They are the invitatory verses of the animal offering, and the reason for the one-per-family arrangement is that a household uses its own. This is the clearest surviving evidence in the Saṃhitā that the Ṛgveda was not one book used by everyone but a set of family properties gathered together.

Nine of the ten have exactly eleven verses in exactly the same order. [[1.13]] has twelve and no verse for the *barhis*; this one has thirteen. What Dīrghatamas adds is a fourth Agni verse at the head and a closing verse to {{indra}} — the only Āprī hymn that ends by addressing a great god rather than the *svāhā* cries. It is also the only one in *anuṣṭup*.

What the sequence teaches, and it is worth sitting with, is that the rite's equipment is addressed as divine. The strewn grass, the doorway, the wooden post, the two times of day, the exclamation *svāhā* itself: each gets a verse, in the vocative, as a god does. Nothing here is background. A reader who has watched a homa and wondered why the priest speaks to the ladle and the post has the answer in these eleven names.

And two of them are still in daily use. *Svāhā* ends every oblation poured into fire, and is here a deity in its own right, *svāhākṛtayaḥ*. Iḷā, Sarasvatī and Bhāratī are still invoked together as the three goddesses of speech. Of the sixteen sūktas that name {{sarasvatī}}, this is one of the few where she appears not as a river but as one of a triad.
142.disagreements:
The ninth verse's *hotrā* is where the readings part. Sāyaṇa allows that it is the presenter of the oblation, or that the phrase *marutsu bhāratī* names *vāc*, speech, seated in heaven and connected with Bharata as a name of the sun; and he takes Iḷā, Sarasvatī and Mahī either as sound simply, or as the goddesses presiding over sound in the three regions — earth, middle air and heaven. Wilson prints the priestly reading, "may the pure hotā, placed among the gods"; Griffith keeps "Hotri pure, set among Gods" without deciding. Whether this verse names three goddesses, three rivers, or speech in three regions is genuinely open, and the tradition preserves all of it.

On verse 3 Sāyaṇa identifies Narāśaṃsa as *yajñābhimāni devaḥ*, the deity presiding over the sacrifice, and reads "thrice from heaven" as either three arrivals or three bestowals of reward, perhaps the three daily rites. Neither translator commits.

Verse 10 divides sharply. Sāyaṇa takes the whole line as being about water — the swift, wonderful, abundant thing that Tvaṣṭṛ looses at the navel is rain held in the middle of the cloud, Tvaṣṭṛ himself being fire or lightning and so its sender. Wilson prints that reading in full. Griffith gives "genial dew" and leaves it vague.

On verse 11 Sāyaṇa explains Vanaspati as the fire of the sacrificial post, the *yūpa*, since the post is timber; on verse 6 he reads *asaścataḥ* as doors that do not stick to each other, perhaps folding doors.

143.title: A Newer Song for Agni, Apāṃ Napāt
143.synthesis:
*Pra tavyasīṃ navyasīṃ dhītim agnaye* — I bring forward a stronger, newer {{dhī}} for {{agni}}. The first thing this sūkta says about itself is that it is new, and the claim is made in a competitive form: *tavyasī*, stronger, and *navyasī*, newer, than what came before. Then the god it is for: the son of *sahas*, and *apāṃ napāt*, the child of the waters, who along with the Vasus, dear and *ṛtviya* — arriving in his season — has sat down here on the earth as *hotā*.

The second verse sends him back to his origin. Being born in the highest vault, Agni became visible to Mātariśvan; and when he was kindled, by his {{kratu}} and by sheer mass his flame lit up heaven and earth. Birth in the far sky, manifestation to the one who fetches fire, and then a light that reaches both worlds — three stages in a single verse.

The third verse simply looks at him. His flames are fierce and do not age; the beams of him whose face is fair are good to see, bright, made of shining strength; and through the night, like rivers, Agni's beams tremble — *asasantaḥ ajarāḥ*, sleepless and unaging. That the flames are compared to rivers, and that the two adjectives of the first line come back unchanged at the end of the last, are both deliberate: this is a verse about something that keeps going.

The fourth places him. Whom the {{bhṛgu}}s, all-knowing, set at the navel of the earth by the might of the world — urge that Agni on with songs in his own house; for he alone rules over what is precious, as {{varuṇa}} rules. The comparison is exact and unexpected: sole authority over wealth, of the kind Varuṇa has over the keeping of vows.

The fifth is the counterweight, and it is violent. He whom nothing holds back — like the roar of the {{marut}}s, like an army let loose, like the bolt out of heaven — Agni with sharpened jaws eats and chews, and he brings down the woods as a warrior brings down enemies. The hymn has just called him a householder's fire ruling in his own house; here it says what that fire is when it is not contained.

The sixth turns to asking, and it does so as a series of hopeful questions. *Kuvit* — surely? Surely Agni will take pleasure in our *uktha*; surely the good one will turn our desire toward wealth; surely the impeller will hurry our *dhī*s to their winning. Three times the word, three times a hope stated as a near-certainty and not quite claimed. And then the singer, having asked three questions, answers with an act: him of the pure face I sing, with this *dhī*.

The seventh describes the kindling itself. The man who lights Agni wins Agni over as one wins a friend — Agni of the ghṛta-face, seated at the pole of {{ṛta}}, where the load is carried. Kindled and blazing at the *vidatha*s, may he lift our thought up, our bright-coloured *dhī*. The verse holds together the two things the hymn keeps joining: fuel and thought, both of them things you have to raise.

The eighth closes on protection, and it does it by piling up negatives. *Aprayucchan aprayucchadbhiḥ* — never neglectful, with guards that never neglect: guard us, Agni, with kindly, effective protections, with protections undeceived, unbewildered, unblinking. And the last word specifies who: *pari pāhi naḥ jāḥ* — protect our offspring, those born to us. After seven verses about a fire that is unaging, sleepless and unstoppable, the final request is that all that unsleeping attention be pointed at the children.
143.practice:
*Apāṃ napāt*, child of the waters, is one of the collection's stranger titles, and it is given here to {{agni}} in the first verse. Fire born of water is not a paradox the Ṛgveda finds difficult; it belongs with the lightning in the cloud, with Agni hidden in the plants that rain feeds, and with the Agni who lies in the waters in [[1.144]].2. A reader who has wondered why the tradition treats water and fire as neighbours rather than opposites — why the same rite uses both, why *ācamana* precedes kindling — will find that the Veda never thought them opposed.

The word to watch here is {{dhī}}. The hymn opens by offering a *dhīti*, hopes in verse 6 that Agni will speed our *dhī*s to their winning, and ends the seventh by asking him to lift our *dhī* up. The pattern is worth naming plainly: the thought is offered, then the god is asked to move the thought, then to raise it. Attention is both what one brings and what one asks for. The same word stands behind *dhyāna*, and this is as close as the Ṛgveda comes to describing what happens when recitation works.

Verse 6 has a form that is unusual and useful. Three clauses, each beginning *kuvit* — surely? will he not? The singer does not assert that Agni will be pleased; he asks whether he will be, three times, and then simply sings. It is an honest register, and rarer in the collection than confident praise.

And verse 8 is the one to keep. Everything asked for is stated as an absence of failure: guards that are never neglectful, never deceived, never confused, never blinking. What is wanted from a god is not power but attention that does not lapse — and the thing it is to be pointed at, named in the last word of the hymn, is *jāḥ*, the children. Agni is the witness of the *saṃskāras* from birth onward, and this verse is the plainest form of why a household keeps him.
143.disagreements:
Sāyaṇa's derivation of *apāṃ napāt* in verse 1 is worth having because it is entirely naturalistic: vegetable substances are the offspring of rain, and fire is the offspring of vegetable substances — timber and fuel — so fire is the grandson of the waters. Wilson prints "the grandson of the waters"; Griffith has "Offspring of the Waters" and does not explain. He also glosses *pṛthivyām*, "on the earth", as specifically the mound of earth that makes the altar.

On verse 2 Sāyaṇa allows Mātariśvan two senses: the wind, to which the newborn fire is revealed and by which it is fanned, or the *yajamāna* himself, the man performing the rite. That is a large difference — a cosmic figure or the householder in front of you — and neither translator records it; both keep the name.

Verse 3 turns on *na rejante*. Sāyaṇa reads the negative: the beams do not tremble, are not shaken by others in their burning and ripening. But he adds that *na* may instead be the particle of comparison, giving "like rivers", which is what both translators take — Wilson's rays "desist not", Griffith's "glimmer sleepless, ageless, like the floods". Whether the verse says the flames are steady or that they move like water depends on one syllable.

On verse 7 Sāyaṇa derives *akra* from *kram*, to go, and explains it as Agni surpassed or exceeded by flame and fuel; Wilson renders "well kindled and well supplied", Griffith "inflamed and keen".

144.title: Two of One Age Serve Agni — the Ladles Turn Right
144.synthesis:
*Eti pra hotā vratam asya māyayā* — the *hotā* goes forward to his observance with *māyā*, with the skill that makes things happen, holding up a {{dhī}} of pure shape. Then a detail of the floor: he moves toward the ladles *dakṣiṇāvṛtaḥ*, turning rightward — the ladles which are the first to kiss {{agni}}'s dwelling. The hymn opens with a man walking in a particular direction and a vessel touching a particular place.

The second verse goes underneath the rite to its source. The milkings of {{ṛta}} sang out to him, enclosed in the womb, in the god's own seat; and when he lay spread out in the lap of the waters, he drew in the *svadhā*s, the sustaining powers, by which he now moves. Agni in the waters, feeding on what is his own — the verse is one of the collection's plainest statements that the fire on the hearth has a hidden life somewhere else.

The third and fourth verses are about a pair, and the pair is never named. Two of the same age, striving, crossing past one another toward one goal, are working at that same form; and then, like Bhaga, he is to be called by us, and he has gathered it in as a charioteer gathers the reins. The fourth repeats the pattern: whom two of the same age attend, a couple in one womb, sharing one dwelling, by day as by night — the grey one is born young, ranging widely, unaging, through the generations of men. Whoever the two are, the point of both verses is the contrast between them and him: they are matched, paired, bound to one place; he is single, old and newborn at once, and passes through the ages of men without belonging to any of them.

The fifth brings hands into it. The *dhīti*s and the ten *vriś*, the ten fingers, urge him on; we mortals call the god for help. He runs down the slopes as from a bow; and among those who press around him he has taken up new *vayunā*, new ways of doing things. Ten fingers and a shaped thought are the equipment; what comes back is knowledge of how to act.

The sixth widens to his rule. *Tvaṃ hi agne divyasya rājasi* — you rule what is of heaven, and what is of earth, by yourself, like a herdsman with his herd. The comparison is not grand: a herdsman rules by being present and walking about. And then the two great bright ones, golden, joined, rolling, have come to the *barhis* — heaven and earth arriving at the strewn grass like guests.

The seventh asks for nothing but reception. Take pleasure, Agni, and welcome this speech — joyful one, holder of your own *svadhā*, born of ṛta, of good {{kratu}}; you who face every direction, visible from all of them, delightful to look at *pitumān iva kṣayaḥ*, like a dwelling with food in it. That is the last image of the sūkta, and it is the most domestic thing in it. What Agni looks like, to the people around it, is a house where there is something to eat.
144.practice:
Verse 1 records a movement that is still made. *Dakṣiṇāvṛtaḥ* — turning toward the right — describes how the officiant approaches Agni and the ladles, and the same rightward turn is what *pradakṣiṇa* names: the circuit kept with one's right side toward what is honoured, made round a shrine, a fire, an elder, a bride and groom. The Ṛgveda does not explain the direction and does not argue for it. It simply says which way the man went, which is what a reader wants to know.

The unnamed pair of verses 3 and 4 is genuinely open, and the honest position is to keep both readings. The two "of one age", dwelling in one place and serving Agni day and night, may be the two officiants at the rite, or the two fire-sticks, or heaven and earth — or, as one strand of the tradition takes it, the householder and his wife. That last reading connects this hymn to [[1.131]].3, where *mithunāḥ*, couples, exert themselves toward {{indra}}. The evidence here underdetermines the answer; what the verses do establish is a contrast worth keeping, between the pair who are matched and bound to one house and the god who is grey and newborn at once and passes through the generations of men without ageing.

Verse 5's *daśa vriśaḥ*, the ten fingers, is the sort of detail that makes these hymns usable. What sets the god going is a shaped thought and ten fingers — the hands that rub the sticks, hold the ladle, strew the grass. The Veda's picture of worship is not interior. It has hands in it, and it counts them.

And the last line of the hymn is the one to carry. Agni is *raṇvaḥ saṃdṛṣṭau pitumān iva kṣayaḥ* — delightful to look upon, like a dwelling that has food in it. After six verses of cosmology, the final comparison for the god is a house where a person will be fed. That is what Agni looked like to the people sitting round it, and it is a fair description of what a household shrine is still for.
144.disagreements:
The identity of the pair in verses 3 and 4 is the hymn's real question, and Sāyaṇa gives two answers in the same breath. Primarily he takes them as the two priests, the *hotā* and the *adhvaryu*, of equal standing and working at one object; but he then adds, of this hymn and the next together, that the two may be the husband and wife associated in the performance of the sacrifice. Wilson prints the priestly reading and mentions "mortal couples" in verse 4; Griffith keeps the neutral "the two copartners" throughout and declines to say who they are.

On verse 3's closing image Sāyaṇa justifies the charioteer by a pun he does not hide: *raśmi* means reins, rays of light, and the streams of ghṛta that spread like rays — so the god gathering the offering, the driver gathering the reins, and the light gathering itself are one picture.

Verse 2 divides them completely. Sāyaṇa and Wilson read weather: the raindrops, wrapped in the sun's rays, renewed at their birthplace, and the world drinking the rain that {{agni}} as lightning goes with. Griffith reads liturgy — "to him sang forth the flowing streams of Holy Law". The Sanskrit *ṛtasya dohanāḥ*, the milkings of {{ṛta}}, supports either.

On verse 1 he glosses the ladles' action literally — *agneḥ sthānaṃ cumbanti*, they kiss Agni's place — before giving the sense "first to present the oblations".

145.title: Ask Agni — He Has Come, He Knows, He Answers
145.synthesis:
Five verses, and the whole sūkta is about putting a question to a god and being answered. Nothing in the collection is quite like it.

*Taṃ pṛcchata* — ask him. The imperative is addressed to us, not to {{agni}}, and the reasons follow in short clauses laid end to end: he has come; he knows; he, who discerns, is approached — he is approached indeed. In him are the *praśiṣ*, the directions or commands; in him the *iṣṭi*s, the offerings that are made to obtain something. And he is lord of {{vāja}}, of *śavas*, of what is impetuous. The verse is a list of qualifications for being asked, and the first two are the ones that matter: he has arrived and he knows.

The second verse is the hardest in the hymn and the most interesting. *Tam it pṛcchanti na simo vi pṛcchati* — him they ask; not everyone gets an answer by asking. The wise one has taken it in with his own mind, and he neither forgets the first word nor the later one; he goes on by his own {{kratu}}, unclouded. What the verse describes is a hearer who holds the whole of what has been said, beginning and end together, and is not carried away by either. The asking is not a transaction. It reaches someone with a memory.

The third verse shows the traffic going toward him. To him the ladles go; to him the mares; and — the singer says it in the first person — he alone will hear all the words I speak. He is *purupraiṣa*, the sender of many, *taturi*, the one who carries across, *yajñasādhana*, the instrument by which the {{yajña}} succeeds, and *acchidrotiḥ*, whose help has no gap in it. And then, without preparation, *śiśuḥ* — the child; the child has taken hold of vigour. The strongest epithets in the hymn are followed immediately by the smallest word in it.

The fourth verse watches him behave like one. He goes about attending on things; the moment he is born he runs off with his own kind; he touches what pants and gasps, for gladness and delight, when the eager ones come to him where he stands. Fire as an infant that is born and instantly in motion, playing with its own, reaching toward what is offered because it wants to.

The fifth changes register entirely and closes the hymn on knowledge. *Sa īṃ mṛgaḥ apyaḥ vanargur upa tvaci* — he is a wild animal, of the waters, forest-ranging, laid on the surface, on the uppermost skin. And then, in the same breath: *vi abravīt vayunā martyebhyaḥ*, he has declared to mortals the *vayunā*s — the ways things are done, the marks by which one knows how to proceed. Agni, who knows; who discerns {{ṛta}}; for he is *satya*, true.

That is the hymn's whole movement. It begins by telling us to ask, spends three verses establishing that there is somebody there who hears and remembers and wants, and ends by reporting that he has already spoken — and that what he told mortals was not doctrine but *vayunā*, how to go about things. The last word of the sūkta is *satyaḥ*, true. The reason for asking him, given at the end, is not that he is powerful but that what he says holds.
145.practice:
This is the sūkta to know if the question is what one may take a difficulty to a deity for. Its answer is unusually specific. What {{agni}} gave mortals, in the last verse, is *vayunā* — the knowledge of how a thing is properly done, the mark or rule by which one proceeds. Not visions, not release, not power: procedure. And the ground given for trusting it is the final word, *satya*, true.

Verse 2 is worth reading slowly because it describes a listener rather than a giver. He grasped it with his own mind; he does not forget the first word or the later one; he goes on by his own *kratu*, unclouded. Whoever asks is being heard by something that keeps the whole of what was said — the earlier statement and the later one together. Anyone who has ever changed their account halfway through a request will feel the weight of that line.

And the hymn is honest about the limits. *Na simo vi pṛcchati* — asking does not by itself produce the answer. The verse states it flatly in the middle of a sūkta that begins by commanding us to ask. Both are true and the hymn does not reconcile them.

Two images repay keeping. The first is verse 3's *śiśu*, the child, set immediately after four heavy titles — sender of many, carrier-across, perfecter of the rite, whose help has no gap. The second is verse 5's *mṛgaḥ apyaḥ vanarguḥ*, a wild creature of the waters that ranges the forest, laid now on the topmost surface. The god who declares the rules to mortals is described one clause earlier as something undomesticated that has been brought indoors. The Ṛgveda's Agni is both, and this verse refuses to separate them.

This is the sixth of the eleven consecutive Agni sūktas of Dīrghatamas Aucathya, [[1.140]] to [[1.150]] — the longest unbroken run of Agni hymns anywhere in the collection, and part of the 44 sūktas maṇḍala 1 gives to Agni alone.
145.disagreements:
Verse 2's opening splits the witnesses completely, and the sense of the hymn turns on it. Wilson, following Sāyaṇa, reads a rule of decorum — "they ask of Agni, but no one asks improperly" — and continues that Agni "tolerates not a speech that anticipates his reply, nor endures a rejoinder", so that the verse is about how to address a god. Griffith reads it as a statement about knowledge: "They ask of him: not all learn by their questioning what he, the Sage, hath grasped, as 'twere, with his own mind." One version is etiquette; the other is epistemology. Sāyaṇa's own note is narrow — *na mṛṣyate prathamaṃ nāparaṃ vacaḥ*, he does not bear a first or a later speech, "nor endures a rejoinder" — which supports Wilson.

On verse 1 Sāyaṇa unpacks two words carefully. *Praśiṣ* he takes as the power of restraining: having held back what should not be brought about, Agni is able to bring about what can be. And *iṣṭi*, ordinarily the offering, he glosses as *bhoga*, enjoyment, or the acts of worship that yield reward. Wilson prints both, which makes his English opaque; Griffith reduces the pair to "admonitions" and "commands".

Verse 4's *tatsāra yujyebhiḥ* he leaves open, offering three: joined with abilities suited to their objects; with energies fit to be linked to their consequences; or with his horses yoked to the car. Wilson gives "associated with his objects", Griffith "creeps forward with his kin".

160.title: Dyāvāpṛthivī as Father and Mother, and Their Son
160.synthesis:
Five verses in jagatī, and the second of two hymns the same ṛṣi gives back to back to the pair — [[1.159]] stands immediately before it. What the hymn actually wants is held back until the last verse; the first four are spent establishing who is being asked.

*Te hi dyāvāpṛthivī* — these two. {{dyāvāpṛthivī}} is one word in the Sanskrit, a dual compound, and the epithets come in pairs: *viśvaśambhuvā*, bringing wellbeing to everything; *ṛtāvarī*, holding to {{ṛta}}; *dhārayatkavī*, holding up and seeing at once, so that what sustains the world also understands it; *sujanmanī*, of good birth. And *dhiṣaṇe*, a dual the tradition reads as the two world-halves themselves. Between them {{sūrya}} travels, *śuci*, pure, *dharmaṇā*, by the ordinance laid on him. The pair are not scenery for that journey. They are the frame within which anything at all can keep to a law.

The second verse names them plainly. *Uruvyacasā*, wide-reaching; *mahinī*, great; *asaścatā*, never failing — and then *pitā mātā ca*, father and mother, who guard the *bhuvanāni*, the worlds. They are *sudhṛṣṭame*, very bold, and *vapuṣye*, worth the sight, and the reason given is that the father clothed everything *rūpaiḥ*, with forms. Being visible is itself something done for us.

The third verse produces a son and refuses to name him. *Sa vahniḥ putraḥ pitroḥ* — that bearer, son of the two parents, *pavitravān*, possessed of the straining-cloth, *dhīra*, steady and skilled, and he cleanses the worlds *māyayā*, by the power that makes things be. Then he milks out, day after day, the bright *payas* — from *pṛśni*, the dappled cow, and from the bull of good seed. He draws from both parents at once, and the milk is one.

The fourth verse turns the generation around. *Ayaṃ devānām apasāṃ apastamaḥ* — among the gods who work, this one works most: he begot the two world-halves that bring good to all, he measured out the two *rajasī* with *sukratūyā*, effective skill, and he propped them apart with *ajarebhiḥ skambhanebhiḥ*, pillars that do not age. The son of verse 3 is the maker of his own parents in verse 4, and the hymn sets the two statements side by side without a word of reconciliation. *Viśvaśambhuvā* is repeated from the first verse, so the pair he made are exactly the pair the hymn opened by praising.

Then the fifth verse asks, and what it asks for is unexpectedly ordinary. *Te no gṛṇāne mahinī* — you two, being praised, great ones — *mahi śravaḥ kṣatraṃ dhāsathaḥ bṛhat*: set in us great renown and wide *kṣatra*, the capacity to rule. And the purpose: *yenābhi kṛṣṭīs tatanāma viśvahā*, by which we may extend over the peoples through all days. The verb is *tan*, to stretch — the same stretching by which the two world-halves were measured out in the verse before. Finally *sam invatam*, send us together *ojaḥ panāyyam*, strength worth praising. After four verses on the widest thing that exists, a household asks the world's parents for room to grow into, and asks it in their own vocabulary.
160.practice:
Heaven and earth as a married pair, addressed as one, is among the oldest things the tradition says, and it has never stopped saying it. The Anukramaṇī gives eleven sūktas across the whole Ṛgveda to *dyāvāpṛthivyau*, and three of the eleven are here in maṇḍala 1 — [[1.159]] and this one, consecutive, and [[1.185]] near the very close. Nothing in the collection is invoked more casually and hymned less often: the pair turn up in a line of half the hymns in the book and receive a sūkta of their own about once every hundred.

The order this hymn uses is the order still recited. *Dyauḥ* first, then *pṛthivī*, then what lies between them — the sequence of the śānti-pāṭha that closes so much daily recitation, where peace is invoked on the sky, then on the *antarikṣa*, then on the earth. And the epithet in verse 1 is worth keeping: *ṛtāvarī*, applied to heaven and earth themselves. Ṛta is not laid on them by a legislator from somewhere else. They hold it; that is what they are for.

Verse 2's *pitā mātā ca* is the phrase that survived. A Hindu who has ever said *dyauṣ pitā pṛthivī mātā* is saying what this verse says, and the reason given for calling them parents is not sentiment but function — *bhuvanāni rakṣataḥ*, they guard the worlds. Parenthood here is defined as keeping something else safe while it grows.

What the hymn finally asks for is the part to sit with. Not release, not vision, not even *rayi*. It asks for *śravas* and *kṣatra* — a name that carries and the standing to act among people — so that the family may *tan*, stretch, across the *kṛṣṭī*, the settled peoples. The verb is the one used two verses earlier for the measuring out of the worlds themselves. A householder asking to extend over the peoples is asking, in the hymn's own word, to do a small version of what heaven and earth were made by.
160.disagreements:
Verse 1 divides on two words. *Dhiṣaṇe* is given by the morphology simply as a dual for heaven and earth; Griffith prints "Two Bowls of noble kind," importing a vessel-image the word may or may not carry, and Wilson does not render it at all. The same verse's *rajaso dhārayatkavī* splits them further: Wilson reads *rajas* as the region of the rains and gets "able to sustain the water (of the rains)," while Griffith keeps it spatial — "sustainers of the region, Holy Ones and wise."

The son of verse 3 is unnamed in the text and unsettled in the reading. Sāyaṇa offers two possibilities without deciding: *vahni* is fire, that is Agni; or it is Āditya, the sun, of whom *vahni* is an epithet in the sense *phalasya voḍhā*, the bearer of the fruit of pious rites. Wilson prints the second — "the bearer (of rewards)" — while Griffith turns him into an officiant, "he the Priest with power to cleanse." Both readings survive the verse, because everything predicated of him (purifying, straining, milking the sky) fits either.

Verse 2's *vapuṣye na* also parts them: Wilson supplies a purpose, "as if (for the good) of embodied (beings)"; Griffith takes it as plain description, "the spirited, the beautiful."
160.note: dyāvāpṛthivyau ascription counted across all ten Anukramaṇī files (11 sūktas); viśvaśambhuvā verified as recurring at v1 and v4 in the padapāṭha; dhiṣaṇe morphology from the grammar file

161.title: The Ṛbhus Make One Cup Four and Earn a Share
161.synthesis:
Almost all of this hymn is speech — question, commission, reply, threat, quarrel — told from inside. It opens in alarm. *Kim u śreṣṭhaḥ kiṃ yaviṣṭho na ājagan* — is it the eldest or the youngest who has come to us, and on what *dūtya*, what errand? Then, before any charge has been laid: *na nindima camasam*, we did not disparage the cup, which is of high family; brother {{agni}}, we spoke well of the wood. Men defending themselves against an accusation nobody has made.

The second verse states the commission, and everything hangs on it. *Ekaṃ camasaṃ caturaḥ kṛṇotana* — make the one cup into four; the gods said so, and that is why I have come, O sons of Sudhanvan. Then the wage: *sākaṃ devair yajñiyāso bhaviṣyatha*, along with the gods you shall become *yajñiya*, fit to receive sacrifice. Craftsmen are offered divinity, and the price is one impossible job. The third verse answers by listing what such work involves — a horse to be made, a chariot, a *dhenu*, the two aged ones made young — and having done these, brother, we come. Nobody asks whether it can be done.

The fourth gives the result through someone else's eyes. The work finished, the {{ṛbhu}}s look round for the messenger, who has gone; and when {{tvaṣṭṛ}} saw the four cups made, he hid among the *gnās*, the divine women. The master craftsman of the gods sees the work and hides. The fifth says why: *hanāma enān*, let us kill these men who reviled the cup the gods drink from. The Ṛbhus take other names at the pressing, and by those names the *kanyā* keeps them safe: their escape is a change of name.

The sixth opens on a different scene. {{indra}} has yoked his bays, the {{aśvin}}au horsed their chariot, {{bṛhaspati}} driven up the *viśvarūpā* cow — and the three are named for the first time, Ṛbhu, Vibhvan and Vāja, *svapasaḥ*, good workers, who went to the gods and took up *yajñiyaṃ bhāgam*, a share in the sacrifice. Verse 2's promise is kept here.

The seventh recites the works as fact — a cow drawn out of a hide *dhītibhiḥ*, by acts of thought; the aged pair made young; a horse fashioned from a horse; the chariot yoked. The instrument is {{dhī}}: the making is mental before it is manual. The eighth seats them at the table — drink this water, or this rinsing of the *muñja* grass, and if neither pleases you, take your pleasure at the third pressing, where the rite has kept them ever since. In the ninth they argue: waters are most, said one; Agni is most, said another; a third named something else — and then, *ṛtā vadantaḥ camasān apiṃśata*, speaking true things, they shaped the cups. Truth-telling and good workmanship are one act here.

The tenth sets three men to butcher's work — one driving the cow to the water, one carving the flesh, one carrying off the refuse at sundown — and then the plainest line in the hymn, *kiṃ svit putrebhyaḥ pitarā upāvatuḥ*, what did the parents do to help their sons? The eleventh credits them with grass on the heights and water in the hollows, *svapasyayā*, and tells them not to break off today what they began. The twelfth has them creeping round the worlds with eyes shut, asking where their old parents were, cursing the man who seized their arm. The thirteenth wakes them: Agohya, who woke us? — the goat named the dog as the waker, and after a full year they opened their eyes on this.

The fourteenth leaves the story. The {{marut}}s travel by heaven, Agni by earth, {{vāta}} through the *antarikṣa*, {{varuṇa}} by the waters with the seas — *yuṣmān icchantaḥ*, all seeking you, *śavaso napātaḥ*, sons of strength. The men nearly killed over a cup are what the moving world now seeks.
161.practice:
In this hymn the Ṛbhus are men. They are addressed by a patronymic — *saudhanvanāḥ*, the sons of Sudhanvan — and verse 2 puts the terms in writing: do this work and you will become *yajñiya*, entitled to a share of what is offered. Verse 6 records that they collected. Whatever else the Ṛgveda contains, it contains this: standing among the gods obtained by skilled work, on a commission, with a deadline.

The Anukramaṇī names them in fourteen sūktas. Five run consecutively in maṇḍala 4 ([[4.33]] through 4.37), and maṇḍala 1 holds four — [[1.20]], [[1.110]], [[1.111]] and this one, which is the fullest telling. Their standing hour is fixed by verse 8: the third pressing of the day, the evening savana, is theirs, and the tradition has never moved them from it.

What they are asked for is not devotion and not austerity. It is work — divide one vessel four ways without ruining it, restore youth to two worn-out people, make a cow that gives milk, build a chariot that runs. And verse 7 names the instrument: *dhītibhiḥ*, by acts of thought. The word is the *dhī* that stands behind *dhyāna*. Skill in this hymn is a form of attention, which is why verse 9 can put truth-telling and cup-making in the same breath.

Tvaṣṭṛ is the figure to notice, because he is not a villain and the hymn does not dispose of him. He is the established master of the craft. He looks at what the newcomers have made, hides himself, and then proposes killing them. Anyone who has been overtaken in their own line of work, or has overtaken someone, has met both sides of verse 4. The Ṛbhus survive it by taking other names and going on with the job.

And verse 10's question survives everything around it. Three brothers doing the whole of a hard job, and one of them asking aloud what help the parents ever were. The Ṛgveda kept the line.
161.disagreements:
Sāyaṇa supplies the frame the verses assume. The three Ṛbhus were at a sacrifice, about to drink soma; the gods sent Agni to see what they were doing; Agni found the three so alike that he took a like form himself — which is why they call him brother in verse 1 and cannot tell whether he is the eldest or the youngest.

Verse 4's *gnāsv antar nyānaje* is his, too: he glosses the verb *nyakto abhūt*, was made invisible, takes *gnā* as *strī* on the authority of Nirukta 3.21, and adds that Tvaṣṭṛ *striyam ātmānam amanyata* — thought himself a woman, that is, felt himself humbled. Wilson prints "he was immediately lost amongst the women"; Griffith, "concealed himself among the Consorts of the Gods."

On verse 5 Sāyaṇa makes the new names an etiology: to evade Tvaṣṭṛ the Ṛbhus took the titles *adhvaryu*, *hotā* and *udgātā*, and this, he says, is why a man officiating at a rite is always addressed by his office and never by his own name.

He also reads the sleeping Ṛbhus of verses 11–13 as the sun's rays, citing Nirukta 11.16, with *Agohya* a name of the sun — either "not to be hidden" or "not to be apprehended." On that reading verse 13's *śvan* is not a dog but *antarikṣe śvasantam vāyum*, the wind breathing in the mid-space; Wilson prints the wind, while Griffith keeps the animals: "The goat declared the hound to be your wakener."
161.note: ṛbhu ascriptions counted across all ten Anukramaṇī files (14 sūktas, of which 4.33-4.37 are consecutive); dhītibhiḥ verified as √dhī (dhīti) in the grammar file, not √dhā

162.title: The Sacrificial Horse — Let Nothing of Him Be Lost
162.synthesis:
The hymn opens by guarding itself. Let {{mitra}}, {{varuṇa}}, Aryaman, Āyu, {{indra}} Ṛbhukṣan and the {{marut}}s not pass us over, it says, when we proclaim in the *vidatha* the *vīrya* of the swift *vājin* born of the gods. What follows is the most detailed account of a single rite anywhere in the Ṛgveda, and it is spoken with one anxiety running through it: that something will be mishandled or thrown away.

Verses 2 to 4 bring the procession. The horse is led forward covered and adorned, with the offering carried before him, and a dappled goat goes bleating in front — the goat is {{pūṣan}}'s share, dear to Indra and Pūṣan both, *viśvadevya*, belonging to all the gods, and {{tvaṣṭṛ}} speeds him on. When the men lead the horse round three times *ṛtuśaḥ*, at the proper turns, the goat goes ahead of him *devebhyaḥ prativedayan*, announcing the sacrifice to the gods. The goat is the herald.

Then the hymn names the people. Verse 5 lists the offices — *hotā*, the caller; *adhvaryu*, who does the work; *āvayāj*, who sets the offering down; *agnimindha*, who kindles; *grāvagrābha*, who takes up the pressing stones; *śaṃstṛ*, who recites; *suvipra*, the wise one — and asks them to fill the channels full by this well-ordered rite. Verse 6 goes further down: those who cut the *yūpa* and those who carry it, those who carve the *caṣāla* ring for the horse's post, those who ready the cooking-pots — *teṣām abhigūrtir na invatu*, may their approval carry us forward. Woodcutters and cooks are asked for their blessing.

Verse 7 has him arrive, smooth-backed, at the gods' own regions, with the singer's *manman* set on him and the seers rejoicing. And from verse 8 the accounting begins, with a line that returns three times: *sarvā tā te api deveṣu astu* — let all these of yours be there among the gods. First the gear and the grass in his mouth (v8); then what a fly ate of the raw flesh, what clings to the anointing-stick, the axe, the slaughterer's hands and nails (v9); later his standing-place, his resting-place, the ground he rolled on, his hobbles, the water he drank, the fodder he ate (v14). Nothing is too small or too soiled for the reckoning.

The cooking verses are equally exact. Verse 10 asks the *śamitāraḥ* to make good whatever is undigested or still raw and to cook the *medha* through. Verse 11 forbids waste outright: what drips from the roasting body must not lie on the earth or in the grass, but go to the gods who want it. Verse 12 blesses the bystanders who ask for a portion. Verse 13 names the utensils one by one — the testing-stick, the broth-ladles, the heat-covers, the hooks, the knives. Verse 15 asks that {{agni}} not make him crackle and the pot not break, and says what makes the offering acceptable: chosen, led, approved, made *vaṣaṭkṛta*. Verse 16 lays out the cloth, the outer covering, the gold, the ropes.

Verse 17 turns to the animal's life: whoever drove you with heel or whip, all of that I soothe away *brahmaṇā*, by the sacred word. Verse 18 sets the axe among the thirty-four ribs and demands *acchidrā gātrā*, limbs unmangled, each joint named aloud as it is taken. Verse 19 fixes the roles — one dissector, two who hold, and the *ṛtu*, the due season, governing what is cut and offered. Verse 20 is a plea: let no greedy, unskilled man miss the joints and hack you.

Then verse 21 denies the whole thing. *Na vā u etan mriyase na riṣyasi* — you do not die here, you are not harmed; you go to the gods by easy roads, with Indra's bays and the Maruts' dappled mares for yoke-mates. Verse 22 asks the horse for cattle, horses, sons, all-nourishing *rayi*, and asks {{aditi}} to make the givers *anāgas*, without fault.
162.practice:
Two sūktas in the whole of the Ṛgveda take the horse himself as the deity addressed, and they are these two, consecutive, by one ṛṣi — this and [[1.163]]. Out of 1,028 hymns, the aśvamedha holds exactly that much ground.

The rite is not performed. What a reader meets today is what the tradition did with it afterwards, and that transposition begins very early: the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad opens by taking the sacrificial horse apart into the cosmos — the dawn is his head, the sun his eye, the year his body — so that the animal becomes something to be understood rather than something to be led out. The verses here are the material that operation was performed on.

What the hymn is worth reading for now is its ethic of work. Two verses ask blessings not on the patron but on the labour: the men who fell the post and carry it and carve its ring, the ones who ready the pots, the ones standing about who say it smells good and want a share. Verse 5 names seven offices in a line. Nobody in this rite is anonymous, and the hymn asks their *abhigūrti*, their approving assent, to carry the sponsor forward — the work is not valid unless the workers are willing.

And its ethic of exactness. Three times the hymn stops to say *sarvā tā te api deveṣu astu*, let all these of yours be among the gods, and the list it is protecting includes the rope, the fodder, the ground he rolled on, and what a fly took. Verse 11 will not let a drop fall on the grass. Verse 18 wants the limbs *acchidra*, unpierced, each named as it is separated. Verse 20 asks explicitly that no greedy, unpractised hand mangle him. A hard and bloody job is being described, and the entire moral weight of the description falls on doing it accurately, wasting nothing, and hurting nothing more than necessary.

Verse 17 is the one to keep. Before anything else is offered, the reciter takes every time the animal was goaded with heel or whip and pours those away *brahmaṇā*, with the sacred word, as one pours an oblation with the ladle. The rite begins by making amends for ordinary daily harshness.
162.disagreements:
Sāyaṇa supplies the ritual detail the verses assume, and does not always find it consistent. On verse 2 he specifies the goat as *kṛṣṇagrīva*, black-necked, an *āgneya paśu* belonging to Agni, citing Taittirīya Saṃhitā 5.5.22 and Kātyāyana, and tied at the front of the post — then notes that the Yajus instead attaches it at the horse's *nābhi*, its middle. On verse 6 he reports Kātyāyana's full-scale rite — twenty-one posts of twenty-one cubits, six hundred and nine victims — while observing that the text itself seems to know only one post. On verse 11 he catches the hymn against itself: verse 10 has boiling and verse 13 a cauldron, but verse 11 a spit, from which he infers that part was boiled and part roasted, the drippings caught on darbha grass.

Verse 5's officiants he identifies as seven of the sixteen priests of a solemn rite, glossing *āvayāj* as the *pratiprasthātṛ*, *agnimindha* as the *agnīdh*, *śaṃstṛ* as the *praśāstṛ*, and *suvipra* as the brahman, citing Nirukta 1.8. The verse's *vakṣaṇāḥ* he allows to be either rivers, since rain follows sacrifice, or streams of butter and milk; Wilson prints "replenish the rivers," Griffith "fill full the channels of the rivers."

On verse 19's *ṛtu* Sāyaṇa reads time, with the two holders as day and night or heaven and earth; Griffith takes the word as custom — "this is the custom."
162.note: aśvaḥ verified as devatā in exactly two sūktas across all ten Anukramaṇī files (1.162, 1.163); the refrain sarvā tā te api deveṣu astu counted at vv 8, 9 and 14 in the padapāṭha

163.title: The Horse's Divine Birth, and His Walk to the Post
163.synthesis:
Where [[1.162]] describes a procedure, this hymn speaks to the animal. Every verse is second person, and it moves from where he came from, to what the singer can see of him, to the company he keeps, and finally to the few steps he has left to walk.

It begins with a sound. *Yad akrandaḥ prathamaṃ jāyamānaḥ* — when you first cried out, being born, rising up out of the *samudra* or out of the flood — with a hawk's wings and a deer's forelegs: your great birth, O *arvan*, is to be praised. The second verse gives the chain of hands he passed through: {{yama}} gave him, Trita yoked him, {{indra}} was first to mount him, a {{gandharva}} took his rein, and the Vasus cut him out of the sun. Nobody made him from nothing; he was fashioned, handed on, and broken in.

The third verse says he is those beings. *Asi yamo asy ādityo arvan, asi tritaḥ*, you are Yama, you are Āditya, you are Trita by a hidden *vrata*; and they say there are three bonds of yours in the sky. The fourth doubles it: three bonds in heaven, three in the waters, three in the sea — and then, abruptly personal, *uteva me varuṇaś chantsi arvan*, to me you seem {{varuṇa}}, there where they call your highest birthplace. The singer is looking at a horse and cannot keep him from turning into other things. That is the move [[1.164]], the next hymn, will make its entire subject.

Then the eye comes back down. Verse 5 is what is left on the ground: here are the places where you were washed, here the prints your hooves set down, and here I saw the good reins — the reins that the herdsmen of {{ṛta}} keep watch over. Verse 6 lifts again: *ātmānaṃ te manasā ārād ajānām*, from far off I knew your {{ātman}} with my mind, a winged thing flying below through heaven, head straining upward along easy roads where no dust rises. And verse 7 comes all the way back to the field: I saw your highest form eager for food at the cow's station, and when a man brings you to your feed, you swallow the plants like the greediest of eaters. Praise, vision, and an animal with its head down in the grass, in three consecutive verses.

Verse 8 gathers his following: after you come the chariot, the young men, the cattle, the beauty of girls; whole companies have come after your friendship, and the gods themselves have measured their own *vīrya* against yours. Verse 9 gilds him — golden-horned, feet of metal, swift as thought, with Indra himself behind him — and adds that the gods have come to eat of his offering. Verse 10 widens to a herd: slim-flanked, high-mettled, the heavenly coursers stretch out in file like swans when they strike the road of the sky. Verse 11 is the closest look of all: your body is made for flying, your *citta* rushes like the wind, and your horns are spread out on every side, flickering as they move through the forests.

Then the last two verses walk him in. *Upa prāgāc chasanaṃ vājy arvā* — the strong one has come forward to the slaughter, *devadrīcā manasā dīdhyānaḥ*, thinking with a mind turned toward the gods. The goat, his kin, is led in front; behind come the *kavis* and the *rebhas*, the reciters. It is the same goat the preceding hymn set at the head of the same procession, and the two hymns close the circuit between them. The thirteenth verse gives him his arrival: he has come to the highest seat, to his father and his mother; may he go today most welcome of all to the gods, and then declare good things for the one who gave.
163.practice:
This is one of the few places in the Ṛgveda where an animal is looked at steadily, for its own sake, and described. The hoofprints in verse 5, the head straining upward in verse 6, the plants swallowed greedily in verse 7, the body made for flight and the mind rushing like wind in verse 11 — someone who knew horses wrote these lines. Whatever a reader concludes about the rite, the attention paid here is not the attention of a butcher.

The horse is the deity of exactly two sūktas in the collection, this one and [[1.162]], and they stand side by side at the close of one ṛṣi's work. The rite they belong to is not performed. What survives is the vocabulary and the habit of thought.

That habit is the thing to carry away. Verses 2 to 4 cannot let the animal stay one thing: he is given by Yama, fashioned out of the sun, and then simply *is* Yama, is Āditya, is Trita, and looks like Varuṇa to the man watching him. Three bonds in heaven, three in the waters, three in the sea. Nothing here is argued; the identifications are stated and left. This is where the Ṛgveda is going in its next hymn, [[1.164]], where one thing wearing many names becomes the explicit question, and it is the road that runs from here to the Upaniṣadic habit of finding the whole in the part.

Verse 6 is worth pausing on for one word. *Ātmānaṃ te manasā ārād ajānām* — I knew your *ātman* from far off, with my mind. The term that will carry the entire later tradition is used here of a horse, by a man standing at a distance, and what he claims is recognition rather than doctrine. He knew it when he saw it.

And the last verse gives the rite's own account of where the animal is going: not into Agni, but *paramaṃ sadhastham*, to the highest seat, and *accha pitaraṃ mātaraṃ ca*, toward his father and his mother. The tradition put that sentence in the animal's ear, in the second person, at the moment it mattered.
163.disagreements:
Verse 3 divides the translators into opposites. *Somena samayā vipṛktaḥ* is rendered by Wilson as "you are associated with Soma" and by Griffith as "Thou art divided thoroughly from Soma" — union and separation from the same word. Sāyaṇa reads the same verse's *guhyena vratena* as an act either of the nature of an overcast day or of universal pervasion, and takes the three bonds as media of origin: the Vasus, Āditya and heaven. On verse 4 he names the three differently again — food, site and seed.

Verse 2's names he resolves throughout: Trita is Vāyu, as pervading the three regions; Yama is Agni; the Gandharva is Soma; the Vasus are personified solar rays; and *sūra* is the *ādityamaṇḍala*, the sun's disc. On verse 1 he glosses *samudra* itself as the sun.

Two verses turn on whether the horse has horns. At verse 9 *hiraṇyaśṛṅga* is literally golden-horned; Sāyaṇa takes it figuratively as golden-maned and Wilson prints "his mane is of gold," while Griffith keeps "Horns made of gold hath he." The same split recurs at verse 11, where Wilson has the hairs of the mane tossed in all directions and Griffith the horns spread abroad. Sāyaṇa's note there identifies the horse with Agni, whose flames run through the forests — which makes the flickering in the woods a description of fire.
163.note: the goat led in front verified as shared between 1.162.2-4 and 1.163.12 in the padapāṭha (ajaḥ ... puraḥ nīyate); ātman confirmed at 1.163.6 from the padapāṭha

164.title: Viśvedevāḥ in Riddles — One Being, Many Names
164.synthesis:
Fifty-two verses, and nearly all of it is questions. The hymn does not praise; it asks, it counts, and about half the time it declines to answer. The Anukramaṇī gives verses 1–41 to the {{viśvedevāḥ}} and then parcels the last eleven among {{vāc}}, {{soma}}, {{sūrya}}, the year's wheel, {{sarasvatī}} and the Sādhyas — an admission that no one addressee will hold it.

It opens on a family in which nobody is named: a grey *hotā*, a middle brother, a third with ghee on his back, a clan-lord with seven sons (v1). Seven yoke a one-wheeled chariot drawn by one horse of seven names, and the three-naved wheel does not age (v2); seven ride, seven horses pull, seven sisters call, and in them the seven names of the cows lie hidden (v3). Then the asking begins. Who saw the first-born, when the boneless carried the bony — where is the earth's breath, its blood, its {{ātman}}, and who would even go to a knowing man to ask? (v4). *Pākaḥ pṛcchāmi* — unripe, not understanding, I ask about the seven threads the seers stretched (v5); ignorant, I ask the wise what the One is that propped the six regions in the form of the Unborn (v6); let him speak who knows this dear one's hidden track (v7).

Then parents, and then numbers. The mother gave the father his share by {{ṛta}}, having joined him first in mind (v8); the embryo lay in the cloud-rows and the calf lowed at the many-formed cow (v9); bearing three mothers and three fathers, he stood upright alone (v10). Then a twelve-spoked wheel of ṛta that does not wear out, with seven hundred and twenty in it in pairs (v11); a five-footed father of twelve forms, Puriṣin in heaven's far half and set on a seven-wheeled car in the near (v12); a five-spoked wheel on which all beings rest, its axle never heating (v13); ten yoked ones drawing the felly while Sūrya's eye goes wrapped in the region (v14); and of those born together, the seventh single-born and six twins (v15).

The paradoxes follow. They told me these were males, though female — the seeing man sees, the blind does not, and whoever knows becomes his own father's father (v16); a cow rises with her calf beneath her, and calves outside the herd (v17); who knows this calf's father, and whence has the divine mind arisen? (v18); what they call coming they also call going (v19). Then, with no preparation: two winged ones, joined and companions, clasp one tree, and one eats the sweet fig while the other, not eating, watches (v20). Where they cry out their share of the deathless, the guardian of all being has entered even me, the unripe (v21); and no one reaches the sweet fruit at the top who does not know the father (v22).

Metre comes next — gāyatrī set on gāyatrī, triṣṭubh cut from triṣṭubh, and they who know it win *amṛtatva* (v23); chant measured by metre and syllable into seven voices (v24); the flood in heaven propped by jagatī (v25). Then a cow, patiently: called in for the deft milker, with {{savitṛ}} asked for the best impulse (v26); coming lowing for her calf (v27); licking his forehead and suckling him (v28); answered, and turning to lightning to throw off her covering (v29). Then life: what breathes and moves lies still among the houses (v30); the herdsman who never stumbles, going and returning (v31); and he who made it does not know it, while from the one who saw it, it is hidden (v32).

Verse 33 is the line everyone keeps: *dyaur me pitā janitā*, Dyaus is my father and begetter, this great earth my mother. Then a formal riddle-contest — four questions (the earth's far end, the world's navel, the stallion's seed, the highest heaven of speech, v34) and four answers in the same order: this altar, this {{yajña}}, this Soma, this {{brahman}} (v35). Seven half-formed germs stand under {{viṣṇu}}'s ordinance (v36). And then the singer breaks: *na vi jānāmi yad iva idam asmi*, I do not know what I am; I go bound and hidden in mind, and only when the first-born of ṛta came to me did I get a share of this speech (v37). Immortal and mortal share a womb and go opposite ways; men mark one and miss the other (v38). Verse 39 says why any of it matters — on the imperishable syllable in the highest heaven all the gods are seated, and *yas tan na veda kim ṛcā kariṣyati*, what will he do with the verse who does not know that?

The close is a chain of held images. Good grass and clean water for the cow (v40). Gaurī lows, shaping the waters, one-footed, two, four, eight, nine, thousand-syllabled in the highest heaven (v41), and from her the seas pour and everything lives on what flows (v42). Dung-smoke seen from far off, men cooking the dappled ox — *tāni dharmāṇi prathamāni āsan*, those were the first ordinances (v43). Three long-haired ones appear in season: one shears at the year's end, one surveys all, one is seen only as a rush (v44). Speech is measured in four quarters: three lie hidden and do not stir, and men speak the fourth (v45). Then the line the hymn has been walking toward — they call him {{indra}}, Mitra, Varuṇa, {{agni}}; *ekaṃ sad viprā bahudhā vadanti*, the wise say in many ways what is one being (v46). Golden birds go up clothed in water and return from the seat of ṛta, leaving the earth wet with ghee (v47); twelve fellies, one wheel, three naves, three hundred and sixty pegs — who has understood it? (v48). Sarasvatī is asked to open her breast for us (v49); the gods sacrificed the sacrifice with the sacrifice, and those too were the first ordinances (v50); the same water goes up and comes down with the days (v51); and the last verse calls the great winged one, germ of waters and of plants, for help (v52).
164.practice:
This is the hymn that supplies the tradition with its most-repeated sentences, and a reader has almost certainly met three of them before meeting the hymn. *Ekaṃ sad viprā bahudhā vadanti* (v46) — what is, is one; the wise call it by many names. *Dvā suparṇā sayujā sakhāyā* (v20), the two birds on one tree, one eating and one watching, which the Muṇḍaka and Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣads take up verbatim and make the standard image for the self that acts and the self that observes. And *dyaur me pitā janitā* (v33), which is where the familiar naming of sky as father and earth as mother is at its plainest.

At 52 verses it is the second-longest sūkta in the Ṛgveda; only [[9.97]], at 58, is longer. Nothing else in maṇḍala 1 comes near it.

Verses 34 and 35 preserve the shape of a *brahmodya*, the riddling exchange in which one party asks and another answers — four questions and then four answers, in the same order. That this stands immediately after the two horse hymns [[1.162]] and [[1.163]] is worth noticing, since the brahmodya belongs to the great rites; whether the placement is deliberate is not something these sources settle.

But verse 39 is the one that bears hardest on a reader now. *Ṛco akṣare parame vyoman yasmin devā adhi viśve niṣeduḥ, yas tan na veda kim ṛcā kariṣyati* — on the imperishable syllable in the highest heaven all the gods are seated; what will he do with the verse, who does not know that? The Ṛgveda itself, in its longest hymn, says that reciting without knowing accomplishes nothing. And the same hymn is honest about how hard the knowing is: three verses earlier the same singer says *na vi jānāmi yad iva idam asmi*, I do not know what I am, and admits he got his share of speech only when the first-born of ṛta came to him. The hymn that ends with *ekaṃ sad* also contains the flat confession that its author could not see his way. Both belong to the same reciter, five verses apart.

And verse 45's four quarters of *vāc* — three hidden, one spoken — is the seed of everything the later grammarians and tantric traditions built about levels of speech. What men say aloud is one-fourth of what speech is.
164.disagreements:
Sāyaṇa reads the whole sūkta as Vedānta: the spiritual unity of Brahman and the universe, with Āditya glorified and identified with all creation, so that most of the riddles resolve into the sun, his rays, and the year. He also records a practical use from Śaunaka — a brāhmaṇa who has committed theft may expiate it by fasting three nights and repeating this sūkta silently.

Verse 23 is where that frame parts company with the text's surface. Griffith keeps the metres: "How on the Gayatri the Gayatri was based, how from the Tristup they fashioned the Tristup forth." Wilson, following Sāyaṇa, replaces them with the stations of Agni on earth, Vāyu in the firmament and Sūrya in heaven, since *gāyatra*, *traiṣṭubha* and *jāgata* are identified with the three regions.

On verse 20 Sāyaṇa is explicit: the two birds are *jīvātman* and *paramātman*, citing Nirukta 14.30 for two souls abiding in one body. On verse 46 he takes the One as the sun, while noting that the Nirukta assumes Agni and that the Aitareya Brāhmaṇa says Agni is all the divinities. On verse 11 he identifies the seven hundred and twenty as the days and nights of the year, citing Aitareya Āraṇyaka 3.2.1.

His longest note is on verse 41's Gaurī, where he offers thunder and articulate speech as alternatives, counting her feet as grammatical categories and locating the "highest heaven" in the *hṛdaya-ākāśa*, the space within the heart.
164.note: 52 verses confirmed as the second-longest sūkta after 9.97 (58) by counting all ten Anukramaṇī files; the Griffith file in this repository is misaligned from verse 34 onward (v33 and v34 are merged into one entry, shifting the remainder by one), so no Griffith reading beyond v33 is cited here by verse number; synthesis runs long of the 450-650 band because 52 verses cannot each be carried inside it — this is the second-longest sūkta in the collection and the overrun is deliberate

165.title: Indra and the Maruts Argue Over Who Killed Vṛtra
165.synthesis:
Fifteen verses, and eleven of them are two parties talking to each other. The Anukramaṇī hands verses 1–2, 4, 6, 8 and 10–12 to {{indra}}, verses 3, 5, 7 and 9 to the {{marut}}s, and the last three to Agastya, who has been listening.

Indra begins by looking them over. With what brightness have the Maruts come together — *savayasaḥ sanīḷāḥ*, of one age and one nest — with what thought, and from where? (v1). Whose *brahman*s have the young ones accepted, and who has turned them aside to his rite? They rush through the mid-air like hawks, and it will take a great mind to hold them (v2). The tone is not friendly. He is asking whose party they are at.

The Maruts answer with a question of their own. *Kutas tvam indra māhinaḥ san ekaḥ yāsi* — why do you, mighty as you are, travel alone, lord of the good? What is this, that you meet us and interrogate us? Say plainly what you have against us (v3). Indra's reply is a list of possessions: mine are the *brahman*s and the *matis*, mine the pressings, my *śuṣma* stirs, my stone is hurled, the *ukthas* long for me, and these two bays are carrying me to them (v4). Every clause begins from himself.

The Maruts do not contradict him. They simply start getting ready: so we too yoke up, adorning our bodies with our own powers — and, they add, you have followed our *svadhā* (v5). That last word detonates. *Kva syā vo marutaḥ svadhāsīt* — where was that nature of yours, Maruts, when you left me alone at the *ahihatya*, the slaying of the serpent? I am the fierce one, the strong one, and I bent down every enemy with deadly weapons (v6). The Maruts answer as equals: you have done much with us as your allies, bull, with manly strength like ours — and we too shall do much, mightiest Indra, by our own *kratu*, whenever we choose (v7). Indra will not have it: *vadhīṃ vṛtraṃ marutaḥ indriyeṇa* — I killed Vṛtra by my own power, having grown huge in my own rage; with the vajra in my hand I made those glittering waters run easily for Manu (v8).

Then the argument stops, because the Maruts stop pressing. Nothing of yours is set aside, Maghavan; there is no deity your equal; no one born, or yet to be born, reaches what you have done — do, grown great, whatever you will do (v9). Whether that is surrender or something drier, the hymn does not say. Indra takes it at face value: let my *ojas* alone be vast, and whatever I dare with my *manīṣā*, let it be done; I am known as the fierce one, and of whatever I set moving, Indra is master (v10).

And then, immediately, he softens. Your *stoma* has gladdened me here, Maruts — the *brahman* worth hearing that you men made for me — *sakhye sakhāyaḥ tanve tanūbhiḥ*, as friends for a friend, with your own bodies for my body (v11).
