They shine toward him, taking on blameless *śravas*; having seen you, moon-bright Maruts, I was pleased — now please me again (v12). Nobody has conceded anything. The quarrel simply ends in company.

Agastya closes. Who here has magnified you, Maruts? Go forward to your friends as friends; bright ones, quickening these thoughts, be *navedāḥ me ṛtānām*, knowers of my truths (v13). Since the *medhā* of Mānya's son has worked on our behalf as a poet works for the one he honours, turn toward the *vipra*: the singer chants these *brahman*s for you (v14). And the seal: this *stoma* is yours, Maruts, this song of Māndārya the son of Māna — may we know *iṣam vṛjanaṃ jīradānum* (v15).
165.practice:
This is the hymn to read when credit is in dispute. [[1.32]] gives the killing of Vṛtra to Indra alone and never mentions the Maruts; here they are standing in front of him, and the argument that follows is about exactly that. Indra's charge in verse 6 is that they abandoned him at the moment it mattered; their answer in verse 7 is that he has done much *with us as allies* and that they can act on their own account whenever they choose. The Ṛgveda preserved a hymn in which a god is accused of taking all the credit and defends himself, at length, sounding exactly like someone who is not sure.

What it does not do is adjudicate. No verdict is handed down. Verse 9 concedes his supremacy in terms so absolute they could be read either as praise or as the end of a conversation, and verse 11 has Indra, two lines later, pleased and warm again — *sakhye sakhāyaḥ tanve tanūbhiḥ*, as friends for a friend, with your bodies for mine. The relationship survives the quarrel without the quarrel being settled. Most of them do.

The Anukramaṇī calls the deity here *marutvān indraḥ*, Indra accompanied by the Maruts, and that compound heads exactly two sūktas in the collection — this one and [[1.171]], both Agastya's. The Maruts themselves are named in forty-six.

Verse 15 is worth knowing on its own, because it will recur. *Vidyāma iṣaṃ vṛjanaṃ jīradānum* closes twenty-one of Agastya's sūktas in this maṇḍala — every hymn from 1.165 to [[1.190]] except six — and once more in the whole rest of the Ṛgveda, at [[9.97]].17. A reader working through the last twenty-seven hymns of maṇḍala 1 will hear that line land again and again. It is the seal of one household of singers, and hearing it is how you know whose work you are inside.
165.disagreements:
The speaker assignments are not in the verses; they come from the Anukramaṇī, which gives 1–2, 4, 6, 8 and 10–12 to Indra, 3, 5, 7 and 9 to the Maruts, and 13–15 to Agastya. Wilson prints these attributions in his text and the whole reading of the hymn follows from them.

Verse 5's *svadhām anu hi no babhūtha* is the hinge, and it is unsettled. Sāyaṇa offers three senses of *svadhā* — the sacrificial food, or *bala*, strength, or *udaka*, water — so that Indra has come after "the oblations generated either by our strength or by the water we have created." Wilson takes the food: "verily, Indra, you appropriate our sacrificial food." Griffith reads *svadhā* as inherent nature and gets something quite different: "thou hast learnt and understood our Godlike nature." On the first reading the Maruts are asserting a claim; on the second they are being gracious.

Verse 9 splits the same way. Sāyaṇa glosses *anuttam* as an exclamation of assent — whatever you say, Indra, is true; Wilson prints "nothing done by you is unavailing"; Griffith, "Nothing, O Maghavan, stands firm before thee."

On the closing refrain Sāyaṇa gives *jīradānu* as *jayaśīlaṃ dānam*, a gift bound up with victory — and then, where the identical verse closes the next sūkta, explains it instead as *cirakāla jīvanam*, long life.
165.note: the closing refrain vidyāma iṣam vṛjanam jīradānum counted across all ten padapāṭha files: 21 occurrences in Agastya's block 1.165-1.190 and one at 9.97.17; 1.165.15 and 1.166.15 are word-for-word identical in the padapāṭha; marutvān indraḥ verified as devatā of exactly two sūktas in the Anukramaṇī

166.title: The Maruts Roar, and Spare the Man Who Offers
166.synthesis:
A portrait rather than a story, and it works by holding two things about the {{marut}}s together for fifteen verses: they are frightening, and they are careful.

It opens by announcing itself — let us now proclaim to the impetuous company the ancient greatness of the bull's *ketu*, his sign; as if with fire on your road, loud-voiced Maruts, do your mighty works as though it were battle (v1). Then, at once, the other side. They carry the honey *nityaṃ na sūnum*, like their own son; playful, they play at the *vidatha*s; the Rudras come with help to the man who brings *namas*, and though they are self-strong they do no harm to the one who has made the oblation (v2). Gods who are described as playing, and as carrying something the way a father carries a child, are not common. The third verse continues it: to the giver they have granted wealth and increase, and for him the Maruts, like friends who have set their minds on it, sprinkle the many regions with milk.

Then the storm. They have wrapped the regions in their powers, their self-driven horses have rushed out, and every world and every dwelling is afraid, for *citro vo yāmaḥ*, wonderful is your coming, with the spears held out (v4). When their glittering course makes the mountains roar and shakes the back of heaven, every lord of the forest is afraid at your onset, and the plant scrambles aside as if it were riding a chariot (v5). The sixth verse asks them, in the middle of that, to be kind: fierce Maruts, whose troop is never broken, fulfil our good thought with your kindness — even where your lightning digs with its cutting teeth and cuts down the cattle like a well-placed blow.

Verses 7 and 8 give the reasons they can be trusted. They are *skambhadeṣṇāḥ*, whose giving is a prop under a man; their bounty cannot be stripped away; they are *alātṛṇāsaḥ*, not abusive; they chant the *arka* for the drinking of the exhilarating one, and they know the hero's first manly deeds (v7). And then the promise: with hundredfold strongholds guard the man you have favoured from ruin and from harm; whom you protect from slander, in the thriving of his children (v8).

Verses 9 to 11 are an inventory. All good things are in your chariots, and strengths are set on your shoulders as if competing with each other; on your journeys you wear the *khādi* rings, and your axle turns both wheels together (v9). Good things in your manly arms, gold discs on your breasts, glittering ointments, dappled skins on the shoulders, knives set on the wheel-rims — they spread out their splendours as birds spread wings (v10). Great by their greatness, wide, visible from far off like the sky with its stars, delightful, fair-tongued, ringing clearly out of their mouths, mingled with {{indra}}, shouting all round (v11). It is the closest look the collection takes at how a divine troop is equipped, and every detail belongs to men on the move.

Verse 12 makes the hymn's strongest claim. This is your greatness, well-born Maruts: your gift is *dīrgha*, long-lasting, *aditer iva vratam*, like the standing law of {{aditi}} — and not even Indra, by turning away, undoes what you have granted to the man who did well. A promise made by the troop outlasts the favour of the greatest of the gods.

Verse 13 grounds it in the past: this is your kinship, that in the far age you immortals so often heeded our call, and gave Manu a hearing through this {{dhī}}. Verse 14 asks for the ordinary continuation of it — that we may long thrive on your abundance and spread out among the people. And verse 15 is the seal, word for word the same verse that closed [[1.165]].
166.practice:
The Maruts are the storm as a company — never one, always a troop, all of one age, all born together — and this hymn is where their character is set out most fully. Forty-six sūktas across the Ṛgveda name them, more than any deity except {{indra}} and {{agni}}, and eight of those stand consecutively here in Agastya's block, [[1.165]] through [[1.172]].

What the hymn offers a reader is a picture of force that knows what it must not damage. The mountains roar, the trees are afraid, the shrubs scatter — and in the same breath *na mardhanti svatavasaḥ haviṣkṛtam*, self-strong as they are, they do not injure the man who has made the offering. Verse 6 asks them, in the very act of describing their lightning tearing into cattle, to fulfil a good thought kindly. Nothing here pretends the power is safe. It asks that it be aimed.

Verse 12 is the one to keep. The Maruts' gift is described as long-lasting *aditer iva vratam*, like Aditi's standing ordinance, and then the claim is pushed further: not even Indra, by withdrawing, cancels what the Maruts have given to a man who did well. A promise made collectively is treated as more durable than the goodwill of the single greatest power. Anyone who has watched an institution outlast the person who ran it will recognise the thought.

And verse 2 is the one to enjoy. *Krīḷanti krīḷāḥ* — the playful ones play. They carry sweetness the way a man carries his own son. A tradition that pictures the thunderstorm as a band of young men in gold discs and deerskins, showing off their gear and playing at the assembly, is not a tradition that finds nature frightening in principle. It finds it magnificent, and asks it to be considerate.
166.disagreements:
Verse 9's *prapatheṣu khādayaḥ* divides the reading of the whole equipment sequence. Sāyaṇa takes it as provision for travellers — shelter and food ready along the road — and Wilson follows: "at your resting-places on the road refreshments (are ready)." Griffith reads *khādi* as the ornament it is elsewhere: "Rings are upon your shoulders when ye journey forth." Verse 10's *etāḥ* parts them the same way, Wilson giving garlands on the shoulders and Griffith deerskins.

Verse 5's closing image is unsettled. Wilson has the bushes waving "as a woman in a chariot"; Griffith has the shrubs flying "swift as whirling wheels." The Sanskrit *rathiyantī iva pra jihīte oṣadhiḥ* will bear either.

On verse 6 Sāyaṇa attaches *paśvaḥ* to the lightning's cutting teeth and explains it by ordinary weather — when the wind blows, animals are withered — which turns a violent line into a description of cold. Wilson keeps a hunting image, "as a well-hurled weapon wounds the deer"; Griffith keeps the violence, "it crunches up the cattle like a well-aimed dart."

On verse 12's *aditer iva vratam* Sāyaṇa allows Aditi to be either the mother of the gods or the earth, which changes the comparison from a divine ordinance to the plain reliability of the ground.
166.note: 1.166.15 verified word-for-word identical with 1.165.15 in the padapāṭha; marut ascriptions counted across all ten Anukramaṇī files (46 sūktas)

167.title: Rodasī Climbs the Maruts' Car of Her Own Will
167.synthesis:
Eleven verses, of which the Anukramaṇī gives the first to {{indra}} and the rest to the {{marut}}s — and the middle of it is taken up by someone who appears almost nowhere else at this length.

It opens by counting. A thousand helps of yours, Indra; a thousand refreshments most praised; a thousand kinds of wealth to gladden with; may thousandfold *vāja*s come to us (v1). Then the Maruts are asked to come with their helps and their highest heaven-born gifts, *sumāyāḥ*, good at contriving, since their farthest teams win wealth *samudrasya cid pāre*, even on the far shore of the sea (v2).

The third verse turns to the figure who clings to them. She is *ghṛtācī*, ghee-bearing, well-fitted among them, *hiraṇyanirṇik*, gold-gleaming, like a spear carried at the back; she moves *guhā*, in concealment, like the wife of a man; and she is, in the assembly, like {{vāc}} herself. Two comparisons in one verse, and they pull in opposite directions — a woman kept in private, and speech that carries a hall. The hymn does not choose.

The fourth verse names her position among them. The bright untiring Maruts have joined with the young one *sādhāraṇyā iva*, as with something held in common; and the fierce gods did not push Rodasī away — *juṣanta vṛdhaṃ sakhyāya devāḥ*, they wanted her to grow, for friendship. The fifth gives her the initiative: when she chose — *joṣat yad īm* — to go with them, undying, with her hair loose and her mind on the men, she climbed the chariot of her worshipper like Sūryā, her face flashing, coming like the cloud. The verb is hers. She was not put on the chariot; she got on it.

Then the sixth verse says the young men set her there, wedded to brilliance, strong in the assemblies, when the singer with his oblation and his pressed soma sang the *arka*. Both statements stand — she climbed up, they seated her — and the hymn is not embarrassed by the doubling. The seventh declares what is worth declaring about the Maruts' greatness, and it turns out to be her: that with them she, *vṛṣamanāḥ*, bull-minded, *ahaṃyuḥ*, saying I, and *sthirā*, firm, carries the fortunate wives. The greatness of the storm-troop is stated through the woman who rides with them.

The eighth verse widens out to guardianship — Mitra and Varuṇa protect from what is shameful, Aryaman pays out the unpraised, things that were never shaken are overthrown, and the man who gives choice offerings prospers. The ninth returns to the Maruts and admits defeat in measuring them: *nahi nu vo marutaḥ anti asme ārāttāc cit śavasaḥ antam āpuḥ* — none of us, near or far, has ever reached the limit of your power; grown bold, they stand round hostility as a flood stands round.

The tenth verse asks for the ordinary thing: let us be Indra's dearest today, and tomorrow speak up in the contest, as we did before; let greatness follow us day after day, and let Ṛbhukṣan stay with us among men. Verse 11 is the seal — this *stoma* is yours, Maruts, this song of Māndārya the son of Māna — the same closing line that ends [[1.165]] and [[1.166]].
167.practice:
This is where a reader meets Rodasī. Elsewhere the word is the dual for the two world-halves; here it is a person who does things, and this hymn gives her more room than anywhere else in the collection. Her verses are worth reading carefully, because what they describe is unusual.

She is not abducted and not bestowed. Verse 5's verb is *joṣat*, she chose; and she climbed the chariot herself, hair loose, mind on the men. Verse 4 says the fierce gods did not push her away but *wanted her to grow*, for friendship. Verse 7, declaring the Maruts' true greatness, states it through her — *ahaṃyuḥ*, one who says "I", firm, bull-minded. Those adjectives are feminine, and they are not the vocabulary of a subordinate. Whatever else the Vedic world was, it produced this picture: a company of young men on a chariot with a woman who joined them because she decided to, and whose self-assertion is named as their glory.

Verse 3 sets the tension out plainly and refuses to resolve it. She moves *guhā*, in concealment, like a man's wife — and she is, in the assembly, like *vāc*, speech itself. Kept in and carrying the room, in one verse. That contradiction has stayed in the tradition, and a reader who has watched it play out in their own family will recognise the shape of it here, unresolved, at the beginning.

Verse 9 is the other keeper. *Nahi nu vo marutaḥ... śavasaḥ antam āpuḥ* — no one among us, near or far, has ever reached the limit of your strength. It is an honest confession from a singer whose whole business is praising: the thing being praised has not been measured, and the praise knows it.

Verse 11 seals the hymn with the line that closes twenty-one of Agastya's sūktas in this maṇḍala. By the third hymn in a row a reciter is hearing it as a signature.
167.disagreements:
Rodasī is the whole question. Sāyaṇa states the ambiguity outright: *rodasī* ordinarily means heaven and earth, but here it signifies the lightning, or else *marutpatnī*, the wife of the Maruts. Wilson keeps her a person — "Rodasī, the associate of the scatterers (of the clouds), with dishevelled tresses" — while glossing her elsewhere as the lightning; Griffith simply prints "immortal Rodasi."

Verse 4's *sādhāraṇyā iva* is where the translators' registers separate most sharply. Wilson writes that the Maruts "have mingled with (their) associate, like (youths) with common women," following Sāyaṇa, who glosses the word as a public woman. Griffith renders it neutrally: the Maruts "cling to the young Maid as a joint possession." The Sanskrit supports both, and the difference in tone is considerable.

On verse 3 Sāyaṇa gives both halves of the comparison and their tension: she goes in the darkness of the sky as though in private, like a wife who, however finely dressed, stays within the inner apartments — and then, on *sabhāvatī*, either the lightning showing itself as if in an assembly, or a woman who is not always confined and does appear in public.

He also notes that the epithets of verse 7 — *vṛṣamaṇā*, *ahaṃyu*, *sthirā* — are feminine and belong to Rodasī, which is what fixes that verse as being about her.
167.note: speaker/devatā split (1) indraḥ, (2-11) marutaḥ taken from the Anukramaṇī; 1.167.11 verified identical with 1.165.15 and 1.166.15 in the padapāṭha

168.title: Every Rite, Every Thought — the Maruts of Pṛśni
168.synthesis:
Ten verses, and the first of them makes a claim that governs the rest. *Yajñā-yajñā vaḥ samanā tuturvaṇiḥ* — at rite after rite your onrush is the same; *dhiyaṃ-dhiyaṃ vo devayāḥ dadhidhve*, you take up thought after thought of the god-seeking man. Not the great rite and the great thought: each one, every time. The verse ends by asking to turn the {{marut}}s this way with well-worked hymns, for the great help of the two worlds.

The second verse describes their coming into being: self-born and self-strong, shakers, born toward *iṣ* and *svar*, refreshment and light; thousandfold like the waves of the waters; to be praised when they are present, like cattle. The third is the strangest in the hymn. They are like pressed somas with well-fed stalks, drunk down *hṛtsu*, into the hearts — and there they sit like men who have attached themselves. The storm is described as something swallowed that stays. Then, in the same verse, back to the gear: something clings on their shoulders, and in their hands the *khādi* ring and the *kṛti* blade are held together.

The fourth has them descend. Self-yoked, they came down easily from heaven; drive yourselves on with the whip, immortals; dustless, strong-born, the Maruts with flashing spears have shaken loose even the things that were fixed. The fifth asks the obvious question about a self-yoked troop: who among you moves you, *hanvā iva jihvayā*, the way the jaws are moved by the tongue? And the answer is not given — instead the image goes on, of them shaken loose from the dry land, travelling as though hunting food, on many errands, like the horse that runs the day.

The sixth pushes the question outward. Where is the far limit of this great *rajas*, and where the near one, into which you have come — you who shake what is fastened as if it were loose and fly with the stone across the glittering flood? The hymn has stopped describing and started admitting that it cannot find the edges.

The seventh verse turns to what they give, and every word of it is double-edged: your winning is forceful and sun-bright, dazzling, ripening, crushing; your gift is auspicious, *pṛṇato na dakṣiṇā*, like the fee of a man who gives freely — wide-sweeping, and roaring like an *asurya* power. Bounty described in the vocabulary of an assault.

The eighth is the finest picture in the hymn: the rivers roar back at the wheel-rims when the clouds lift their voice, and *ava smayanta vidyutaḥ pṛthivyām*, the lightnings smile down at the earth, when the Maruts sprinkle the ghee. Lightning smiling is not a metaphor the collection uses twice.

The ninth gives their birth. *Asūta pṛśnir mahate raṇāya* — Pṛśni bore, for a great battle, the glittering front of the untiring Maruts; fed together, they begot the *abhva*, the shapeless overwhelming thing, and then looked around for the *svadhā* that gives vigour. And the tenth is the seal: this *stoma* is yours, Maruts, this song of Māndārya son of Māna — the same closing verse that ends [[1.165]], [[1.166]] and [[1.167]], the fourth time in four hymns.
168.practice:
Verse 1 is what to take from this hymn. *Yajñā-yajñā... dhiyaṃ-dhiyam* — rite after rite, thought after thought. Each word is doubled in the Sanskrit, which is how the language says "every single one." The Maruts are not being praised for grand interventions; they are being praised for turning up with the same energy at every rite, and for picking up every thought a god-seeking person has. That is an unglamorous kind of divinity and it is exactly the kind a householder needs. Reliability, repeated.

Verse 9 gives their mother. Pṛśni bore the Maruts for a great battle, and the tradition kept that: they are the *pṛśnimātaraḥ*, the sons of Pṛśni, and the Taittirīya Saṃhitā puts it in a line the commentators quote — the Maruts were born of Pṛśni's milk. The storm has a mother, and she is spotted like a rain-cloud and like a cow.

Verse 3 is the one to sit with. The Maruts are compared to soma that has been pressed and drunk *hṛtsu*, down into the hearts, where they then settle and stay like men who have attached themselves to a household. The gods of the outside weather are described as taken inward and lodged. It is a small verse and it does a great deal: whatever moves the sky is also something that can be swallowed and kept.

And verse 8 is the one to enjoy. *Ava smayanta vidyutaḥ pṛthivyām* — the lightnings smile down on the earth, when the Maruts sprinkle their ghee. The first rain after the dry months, seen from below, described by someone who was glad.

This is the fourth consecutive Marut hymn in Agastya's block and the fourth to close with *vidyāma iṣaṃ vṛjanaṃ jīradānum*. Eight Marut sūktas stand together here, [[1.165]] to [[1.172]]; forty-six name them across the whole Ṛgveda.
168.disagreements:
Verse 3 leaves unsaid what hangs on the Maruts' shoulders, and Sāyaṇa says so, offering either a *śakti*, a lance, or *bhujalakṣmī*, the beauty of the arms. Wilson prints "upon their shoulders hangs (a lance) like a youthful female"; Griffith, "Upon their shoulders rests as 'twere a warrior's spear."

Verse 7's *asuryā iva jañjatī* divides them further. Sāyaṇa explains it by the behaviour of the asuras, who take from one to give to another, and applies it to the winds, which plunder the clouds in order to enrich the earth; Wilson follows with "the all-subduing force of the asuras." Griffith takes *asurya* in its older, non-hostile sense and gets the opposite tone: the gift is "victorious, spreading far, as of immortal Gods."

On verse 9 Sāyaṇa supplies the authority for the Maruts' descent from Pṛśni by citing Taittirīya Saṃhitā 2.2.11.4, *pṛśnyai vai payaso maruto jātāḥ* — of Pṛśni's milk the Maruts were born.

Verse 6's *rajas* he allows to be either *loka*, the region, or *udaka*, water, so that the unfindable limit is either the edge of space or the edge of the rains. Wilson takes the rains; Griffith keeps "this mighty region's farthest bound."
168.note: the doubled yajñā-yajñā and dhiyam-dhiyam verified in the padapāṭha at 1.168.1; 1.168.10 identical to 1.165.15, 1.166.15 and 1.167.11

169.title: Indra Asked to Release the Maruts' Blessings
169.synthesis:
Eight verses to {{indra}}, in which the {{marut}}s are named in six of them. This is not a hymn about Indra alone; it is a hymn asking Indra for something the Maruts hold.

The first verse states the request outright, and the argument it uses is affection. Even from great *tyajas* — abandonment, the being left in the lurch — you are the shelter, Indra; so, you who dispose the Maruts and know them, win their kindnesses for us, *tava hi preṣṭhāḥ*, for they are your dearest. The petitioner does not ask Indra to overrule the Maruts. He asks him to intercede, on the grounds that they are the ones he loves best.

The second verse sets the scene of a campaign: all the peoples are yoked to you, and the Marut host goes out rushing to win the prize that bestows light. The third puts everything in place at once — *amyak sā te indra ṛṣṭir asme*, that spear of yours sat firm for us; the Maruts drive on the whole *abhva*, the shapeless mass; {{agni}} blazes in the scrub; and the offerings stand round him as waters stand round an island. Four things happening simultaneously, and the island image is the only still point in the verse.

The fourth asks for wealth in the language of fee and return: give us that *rayi*, Indra, as a gift won by the strongest *dakṣiṇā*; and let the praises that pleased you swell as the sweet breast swells with milk. The fifth widens it: in you are the most bounteous riches, and they lead forward anyone at all who seeks {{ṛta}} — no lineage requirement, no precondition beyond that. May the Maruts be gracious to us, they who long ago went ahead making the way passable.

The sixth verse sends Indra out to them. Go forward, Indra, toward the men who shed bounty; exert yourself in the great earthly seat — for their broad-based dappled ones stand like the manly powers of a chief drawn up at the crossing. The seventh is pure sound: the tramp of the terrible, glittering, untiring Maruts is heard as they come on, they who swoop on the mortal who makes war on those they protect, and settle with him as with a man who owes them.

The eighth returns to the request and finally names the family making it. *Tvaṃ mānebhyaḥ indra viśvajanyā rada marudbhiḥ śurudhaḥ goagrāḥ* — you, Indra, with the Maruts, cut open for the Mānas the all-benefiting streams that have cattle at their head. God, you are praised together with the gods who are praised. And then the seal: *vidyāma iṣaṃ vṛjanaṃ jīradānum*. The word *mānebhyaḥ* is the same family name that the refrain itself carries in the neighbouring hymns, Māndārya the son of Māna — the singers ask for themselves, by name, in the last verse, and then sign it.
169.practice:
The hymn is a lesson in how to ask through a third party. Agastya's household wants what the Maruts give — rain, cattle, the streams with cattle at their head — and rather than approach them directly, the first verse goes to {{indra}} and appeals to his affection for them: win their kindnesses for us, *for they are your dearest*. Anyone who has had to get something from one person by going to another they love will recognise the manoeuvre, and the Ṛgveda does not treat it as beneath the dignity of prayer.

It sits inside a quarrel. [[1.165]] had Indra and the Maruts arguing over credit for Vṛtra; [[1.170]] will have Indra and Agastya arguing over whether the Maruts get a share of the offering; [[1.171]] will have Agastya apologising for withdrawing their oblations. This hymn is one move in that sequence, and it moves by conciliation — six of its eight verses name the Maruts, and the last one asks Indra to act *marudbhiḥ*, together with them.

Verse 5 is the line worth keeping. Indra's riches are *pranetāraḥ kasya cid ṛtayoḥ* — they lead forward *anyone at all* who seeks ṛta. Not the wealthy patron, not the established lineage: whoever is oriented toward the order of things. It is one of the collection's plainest statements that the qualification for divine help is a disposition rather than a status.

And verse 8 is where the singers stop being anonymous. They ask Indra to cut open the streams *mānebhyaḥ*, for the Mānas — their own family, the same name the closing refrain carries in the surrounding hymns. Twenty-one sūktas in this maṇḍala end with *vidyāma iṣaṃ vṛjanaṃ jīradānum*; here the family that says it puts its own name in the verse just before.
169.disagreements:
Verse 1 is read in two quite different ways. Wilson makes Indra's greatness derive from those he protects — "you, Indra, are mighty from the might of those of whom you are the protector against abandonment" — and turns *vedhaḥ* into "creator of the Maruts." Griffith keeps *tyajas* as treachery and reads the protection as protection of the petitioners: "As, Indra, from great treason thou protectest… these who approach us." Both end at the same place: grant us the Maruts' blessings, for they are thy dearest.

Verse 4's second half divides them completely. Wilson has the priests nourishing Indra as one cherishes the breast with sweet milk; Griffith names a god the Sanskrit does supply — "May hymns that please thee cause the breast of Vayu to swell as with the mead's refreshing sweetness."

On verse 6 Sāyaṇa offers two constructions of *tīrthe na aryaḥ pauṃsyāni tasthuḥ*. Taking *arya* as *ari*, enemy, and *tīrtha* as the way of battle, the standing powers are an enemy's; taking *arya* as *svāmin*, a lord, and *tīrtha* as the royal road, they are a prince's armies drawn up on it. Wilson prints the first, Griffith the second.

On verse 7's *ṛṇāvānam* Sāyaṇa allows both a contemptible foe and a literal debtor — as though the cloud owed the winds its contents.
169.note: mānebhyaḥ at 1.169.8 verified in the padapāṭha and matched to māndāryasya mānyasya in the refrain verses of the surrounding sūktas

170.title: Indra and Agastya Quarrel Over the Maruts' Share
170.synthesis:
Five verses, two speakers, and no narrator. The Anukramaṇī gives verses 1, 3 and 4 to {{indra}} and verses 2 and 5 to Agastya; the tradition also allows verse 4 to Agastya, and on that reading the man speaks last three times. What is at issue is whether the {{marut}}s are to receive a portion of an offering that was meant for Indra.

Indra opens, and his opening is one of the strangest things in the collection. *Na nūnam asti no śvaḥ* — there is no now, there is no tomorrow. Who knows what is wonderful? Another's mind is a thing one has to go along with, and what has been well thought out perishes. A god begins the argument by saying nothing is settled, including what he himself expects to receive. Whether that is bitterness, resignation or genuine bewilderment the hymn does not say, and it is worth resisting the urge to decide.

Agastya answers in the second verse and answers frightened. *Kiṃ na indra jighāṃsasi* — why do you want to kill us? The Maruts are your brothers; arrange it well with them; do not strike us down in the encounter. He does not argue about entitlement. He points out a relationship — *bhrātaraḥ marutas tava*, the Maruts are your brothers — and asks the stronger party to settle it inside the family.

Indra's reply is sulking, and it is unmistakable. *Kiṃ na bhrātar agastya sakhā san ati manyase* — why, brother Agastya, when you are my friend, do you think past me? And then the accusation, flat: *vidma hi te yathā manaḥ, asmabhyam in na ditsasi*, we know your mind; you do not mean to give us anything. He calls the man brother and friend in the same breath in which he accuses him of holding out. Two verses earlier he had said that another's mind must be gone along with; now he claims to know one.

The fourth verse does not answer the accusation. It changes the subject to work. Let them get the *vedi* ready; let them kindle Agni in front; and there — *yajñaṃ te tanavāvahai* — let the two of us stretch out the sacrifice, the awakening of what is immortal. The verb is dual. Whoever is speaking, the proposal is that the two parties stop settling the question and do the rite together.

The fifth verse closes it with titles and an instruction. You rule the *vasus*, lord of the *vasus*; you, lord of friends, are the best establisher of friends; Indra, *marudbhiḥ saṃ vadasva* — speak together with the Maruts — and then eat the oblations *ṛtuthā*, at their proper season. The last word of the argument is not a ruling on who deserves what. It is: talk to them, and then eat, on time.
170.practice:
This is the Ṛgveda at its least ceremonious. A god accuses a man of stinginess; the man says, in effect, please do not kill me, and points out that the people being excluded are the god's own brothers; and the matter ends with somebody saying let us just light Agni and do it together. Nobody is proved right. Nothing is conceded. The rite is performed anyway, and the last instruction is *saṃ vadasva*, speak with them.

It belongs to a run. [[1.165]] has Indra and the {{marut}}s disputing the credit for Vṛtra; [[1.169]] has Agastya asking Indra to release the Maruts' blessings; and [[1.171]].4 has Agastya confessing that he fled in terror of Indra and set the Maruts' oblations aside. Read in order, these are four hymns about one household's difficulty in honouring two powers at once without offending either — which is a problem any family that keeps more than one observance will recognise.

Verse 1 is the one to carry away, and it is remarkable that it is spoken by a god. *Na nūnam asti no śvaḥ* — there is no now and no tomorrow; who knows what is wonderful? Another's mind must simply be gone along with, and even what was carefully thought through comes to nothing. If a reader wants a verse for the state of not knowing how something will turn out, the Ṛgveda supplies one, and puts it in Indra's mouth rather than a mortal's.

And verse 5's last word is *ṛtuthā*, at the due season — the same root as the *ṛtu* declared in every saṅkalpa. Even at the end of a quarrel, what is asked for is not victory but timeliness: settle it, then eat when it is time to eat.

This is one of only six sūktas in Agastya's twenty-seven that does not close with his household's refrain.
170.disagreements:
The speaker assignments carry the whole hymn and they are supplied from outside it. The Anukramaṇī gives verses 1, 3 and 4 to Indra and 2 and 5 to Agastya. Sāyaṇa notes that verse 4 is also attributed to Indra, and on the dual verb *tanavāvahai* he offers two readings of who the two are: the sacrificer and his wife, or the instituting patron and the officiating priest.

Sāyaṇa also supplies the occasion, without which the exchange is opaque: Agastya intended to sacrifice to Indra and proposed to make offerings to the Maruts as well, and Indra objected. He reads it as reflecting an actual dispute among worshippers of Indra about admitting the Maruts to a share.

On verse 2's *bhrātaro marutas tava* he explains the brotherhood as descent — the Maruts being, like Indra, sons of Aditi — and adds that the affinity is one of function. On verse 3's "brother Agastya" he takes the kinship term differently again, as a relationship founded on exchange: one party presents the oblations, the other returns the reward.

Verse 1 itself is unsettled in tone. Wilson makes it a general observation about the unsteadiness of mind; Sāyaṇa makes it Indra's complaint that he does not know whether he will receive an offering today or tomorrow at all.
170.note: speaker split from the Anukramaṇī; 1.170 verified as one of six sūktas in 1.165-1.191 that lack the closing refrain vidyāma iṣam vṛjanam jīradānum (the others are 1.172, 1.179, 1.187, 1.188, 1.191)

171.title: The Maruts' Offerings Withdrawn — Agastya Apologises
171.synthesis:
Six verses. The Anukramaṇī gives the first two to the {{marut}}s and the last four to *marutvān indraḥ*, Indra accompanied by the Maruts — a compound deity that heads only this sūkta and [[1.165]] in the whole collection. And in the middle of it stands one of the frankest verses in the Ṛgveda.

It opens with an approach made carefully. *Prati va enā namasā aham emi* — I come toward you with this *namas*, and with a well-made hymn I beg the favour of the swift ones. Then two requests that are really one: *ni heḷo dhatta, vi mucadhvam aśvān* — put down your anger, and unyoke your horses. Unharnessing is how you know the anger is finished; a guest whose team is still standing in the yoke has not decided to stay.

The second verse describes the offering being made in place of the one that was withdrawn. This *stoma* of yours is *namasvān*, full of homage, *hṛdā taṣṭaḥ*, carved with the heart, and set down with the mind. Come, taking pleasure in it — *yūyaṃ hi stha namasa id vṛdhāsaḥ*, for you are the ones who make homage grow. A hymn is being substituted for a meal, and the singer says as much by describing it as something worked with tools.

The third verse asks for the future in modest terms: may the praised Maruts be gracious, may Maghavan praised be most kindly, and may all our days to come stand upright, be lovely, and be worth winning.

Then the fourth verse says what happened. *Asmād ahaṃ taviṣād īṣamāṇaḥ indrād bhiyā marutaḥ rejamānaḥ* — fleeing from this mighty one, trembling with fear of {{indra}}, O Maruts: the oblations that had been made ready for you were there, and *tāni āre cakṛma*, we put them far away. Forgive us. The singer confesses to having taken back an offering already prepared, names the reason as fear of a stronger god, and asks the wronged party to be merciful. There is no attempt to justify it. He was frightened, he took back what he had promised, and he says so.

The fifth verse turns to Indra with the family's own name in it: he by whom the Mānas become aware at the dawnings, by the power of the unbroken succession of mornings — give us *śravas*, bull, together with the Maruts, fierce among the fierce, firm, giving the strength to prevail. The sixth asks for exactly the settlement the whole sequence has been working toward: *bhava marudbhir avayātaheḷāḥ* — be one whose anger has been turned away, along with the Maruts; overcoming, with those of good discernment, bestowing. And then the seal: *vidyāma iṣaṃ vṛjanaṃ jīradānum*.

The hymn ends with the same word it opened by asking for. The first verse asked the Maruts to set down their *heḷas*; the last asks Indra to be *avayātaheḷāḥ*, his anger turned aside. Both parties are asked to stop being angry, in the first line and the last, and the man who caused the trouble stands between them.
171.practice:
This is the hymn of the broken promise, and it is short enough to read whole in a minute.

Verse 4 is why it exists. Offerings had been prepared for the {{marut}}s; the singer became frightened of {{indra}}; the offerings were taken away; and rather than let the matter lie he says so to the injured party, in the second person, with the reason attached. *Bhiyā rejamānaḥ* — trembling with fear. He does not claim the Maruts were unworthy or that the offering was needed elsewhere. He says he was afraid of someone stronger, and asks to be forgiven.

What he offers instead is the hymn itself, and verse 2 describes it as a made object — *hṛdā taṣṭaḥ*, chiselled by the heart, set down by the mind. When there was no longer anything to pour, there was still something to construct. That is a workable account of what praise is for.

The request in verse 1 is worth keeping as an image. *Ni heḷo dhatta, vi mucadhvam aśvān* — put your anger down, and unyoke the horses. You cannot tell whether a guest has forgiven you by what they say at the door; you can tell by whether they unharness. The hymn asks for the second kind of sign, and asks the same thing of Indra at the close in the compound *avayātaheḷāḥ*, having-had-his-anger-turned-away.

The deity named is *marutvān indraḥ*, Indra with the Maruts — a combination the Anukramaṇī records for only two sūktas in the whole Ṛgveda, this one and [[1.165]], both Agastya's. The first of the pair is where the two powers quarrel; the last is where they are asked, together, to be done with it. Between them stand [[1.169]] and [[1.170]]. Anyone who has been caught between two people they cannot afford to offend has the shape of these four hymns already.
171.disagreements:
Sāyaṇa reads the unyoking of verse 1 as a practical request rather than an image: take the horses out of your chariot, so that you do not come back to the sacrifice angry. On that reading it is not a sign of forgiveness but a condition of it.

Verse 1's *rarāṇatā* is otherwise handled differently by the two translators. Wilson attaches it to the Maruts' state — "with minds pacified by our praises" — while Griffith attaches it to the hymn: "A hymn that truly makes you joyful, Maruts."

Verse 3's *ūrdhvā naḥ santu komyā vanāni* is read by Wilson as the days to come proving "gratifying and full of enjoyment," and by Griffith as "very pleasant, lovely and triumphant." Neither is confident, and the Sanskrit is compressed.

Verse 5 is where the two diverge most. Wilson makes the subject the rays of the recurring mornings, which "confer consciousness as they shine," and reads the whole as a request for food; Griffith keeps the family name in the verse — "By whom the Manas recognize the day-springs" — and reads the request as one for glory shared with the Maruts. The padapāṭha has *mānāsaḥ*, which supports naming the family.
171.note: marutvān indraḥ verified as devatā of exactly two sūktas across all ten Anukramaṇī files (1.165, 1.171); heḷas at v1 and avayāta-heḷāḥ at v6 verified in the padapāṭha

172.title: Three Verses to the Maruts — Keep the Stone Away
172.synthesis:
Three verses in gāyatrī, and one word holds them together. *Sudānavaḥ* — good givers, generous ones — stands in every verse, and each time it is used to ask for something different.

The first verse asks for the arrival. *Citro vo astu yāmaḥ* — let your coming be wonderful, wonderful in its help, O generous ones, {{marut}}s *ahibhānavaḥ*. The word *citra* is repeated inside the line: the journey itself wonderful, and the protection wonderful. Nothing is asked for except that they come, and come well.

The second verse asks for the opposite, and repeats its key word too: *āre* stands at the head of both halves. Far from us, generous ones, be that *śaru* of yours, the arrow described as *ṛñjatī*, going straight — an epithet of praise used of a weapon the singer wants nowhere near him. And far from us the stone you throw. Nothing here denies that the Maruts aim well. The whole request is that they aim elsewhere. The same beings, addressed with the same epithet, in the same breath in which their weapons are being warded off. This is the whole problem of the storm stated in nine words: the ones who bring the rain are the ones who throw the stone, and there is no separating them.

The third verse asks for people. *Tṛṇaskandasya nu viśaḥ pari vṛṅkta sudānavaḥ* — the settlements of Tṛṇaskanda: pass them by, generous ones. The verb is *pari vṛj*, to go round something rather than through it, which is what is actually being asked of a storm. And then *ūrdhvān naḥ karta jīvase*, make us upright, that we may live. It closes on the most ordinary petition there is. Not wealth, not renown, not sons — set us on our feet, so that we can go on living. Being upright is treated as the whole of what survival looks like.

The metre is gāyatrī, three feet of eight syllables, the shortest the Ṛgveda commonly uses, and the hymn does not waste any of it: three verses, three requests — come; do not strike; let us live. And *sudānavaḥ* three times, so that the beings who are being begged to withhold their weapons are called generous each time they are begged. The hymn does not resolve that. It simply keeps saying it, and stops.

This is one of only six sūktas in maṇḍala 1 of three verses or fewer, and it stands at the end of eight consecutive Marut hymns, [[1.165]] through 1.172. After the quarrel with {{indra}}, the long portraits, the inventory of gear, the apology for withdrawn offerings — this. Three lines, and the last thing said to the Maruts in the whole run is *jīvase*, so that we may live.
172.practice:
The shortest hymns are often the most usable, and this one is three lines long and asks for exactly three things: come well, do not strike us, let us live.

Its honesty is in the epithet. *Sudānavaḥ*, good givers, is repeated in all three verses — including the verse that asks their arrow and their hurled stone to stay far away. The Ṛgveda does not solve this by splitting the {{marut}}s into a kind aspect and a cruel one. The same generous ones bring the rain that fills the tanks and the lightning that kills the cattle, and the hymn addresses that single set of beings with a single name while asking them to give one thing and withhold another. Anyone who has prayed for a monsoon and then prayed for it to stop knows the position this hymn is written from.

The third verse names a group of people — the settlements of Tṛṇaskanda — and asks that they be passed over. It is worth noticing that the request is for a community rather than for the singer. Whatever Tṛṇaskanda is, the last thing asked of the storm in this run of hymns is that a village be spared.

And the last word is the plainest in the collection: *jīvase*, to live. Set us upright, that we may live. After eight hymns of thunder, gold discs, spears, chariots and a quarrel among gods, the sequence ends with a request that would be intelligible to anyone in any century.

This sūkta does not carry Agastya's closing refrain — it is one of six in his twenty-seven that does not — and at three verses it is one of six in the whole maṇḍala that short. Both facts point the same way: it is a small, practical prayer, and it was kept because it was used.
172.disagreements:
Both of the hymn's difficult words are unsettled, and between them they decide what the hymn is about.

Verse 1's *ahibhānavaḥ* is taken by Wilson as "of inseparable splendour," reading the first element as *a-hi*, an unbroken or unfailing brightness. Griffith takes *ahi* as the serpent it usually is and renders "who gleam as serpents gleam" — which puts the shimmer of a snake's back into a hymn that will, in the next verse, ask the same beings not to strike.

Verse 3's *tṛṇaskandasya* divides them more consequentially. Griffith reads a proper name and prints "Trnskanda's folk," so that the hymn is asking protection for an identifiable group of people. Wilson dissolves the compound into its parts — *tṛṇa*, grass, and a root for leaping or falling — and gets a self-deprecation instead: "protect my people, (although I be) as insignificant as grass." On the first reading a village is being named; on the second the singer is calling himself worthless. The word occurs here and the padapāṭha treats it as a single compound, *tṛṇa-skandasya*, which slightly favours reading it as a name.

The Sāyaṇa material available for this sūkta is silent on both.
172.note: su-dānavaḥ verified in all three verses of the padapāṭha; tṛṇa-skandasya appears as a single compound there; 1.172 confirmed as one of six sūktas of three verses or fewer in maṇḍala 1 (1.98, 1.99, 1.107, 1.137, 1.150, 1.172)

173.title: Heaven and Earth Too Small for Indra's Girth
173.synthesis:
Thirteen verses in triṣṭubh, and the hymn takes its time. Four verses on the rite, four on the size of the god, four on what kind of relation the two are in, and one to close.

It opens with the chant. Let him sing out the *sāman* that bursts forth like a bird, and let us chant that swelling, light-bearing thing; the milch-cows on the *barhis*, unhindered, that they may bring the divine seat near (v1). The second verse sets the singers to work: the bull sings with the bulls whose oblations are their own labour, roaring like a hungry wild beast — and the *hotā*, a mortal, honoured, brings a twofold offering (v2). The third is the finest in the hymn. The *hotā* goes round the measured stations, carrying the earth's autumn fruit; the horse cries out as it is led, the ox bellows — and *dūto na rodasī carat vāk*, {{vāc}} moves between the two worlds like a messenger. Everything in the rite makes a noise, and the noise is the courier. The fourth asks {{indra}} to accept: the god-seekers bring their strongest deeds to him; may he of wondrous lustre take pleasure, standing in his chariot, easy in his going like the {{aśvin}}au.

Then the size of him. Praise that Indra who is really a fighter, who is a hero, who is Maghavan, chariot-borne, better in war than those who come against him, breaker of the darkness that shuts things in (v5). And then verse 6, which is the reason to read this hymn: he passes the men in greatness, and *rodasī kakṣye na asmai sam vivye* — heaven and earth are not enough to serve him for a girth; he wraps the earth round himself like a belt, and, having *svadhā*, wears the sky as one wears a headpiece. A god too large to be belted by the world.

Verse 7 puts the peoples around him: chosen by the good in the contests, foremost on the road, and the assembled folk rejoicing in his exhilaration after the patron who gives *vāja*s. Verse 8 says his pressings are a blessing in the sea itself, where the divine waters delight in them, and that every cow is his to enjoy when he seeks out patrons and peoples with {{dhī}}.

Then the relation. May we be your good friends by this, well-helped, as men are helped by the praise of chiefs; may Indra stand within our praise, like a swift one brought to the work by our *ukthas* (v9). Verse 10 makes the comparison political and explicit: as men who want friendship approach the *pūrpati*, the lord of a city that is well governed, so our intermediaries win Indra with sacrifices. Prayer is being described as the approach of citizens to a good administration.

Verse 11 then says something unexpectedly generous. *Yajño hi sma indraṃ kaś cid ṛndhan* — any sacrifice at all makes Indra prosper, even one performed by a man going about crooked in his mind; and the two similes are a ford to a thirsty man, and a long road that still brings the traveller to his end. The rite is not voided by the state of the one performing it. It may be a longer road; it still arrives.

Verse 12 returns to the quarrel that runs through this whole stretch: do not stand with the gods against us here in the fighting, Indra, for there is your own share set aside, mighty one — and the song, it says plainly, praises the {{marut}}s. The last verse asks Indra to find the way by this *stoma* and turn the singers toward wellbeing, and seals it with *vidyāma iṣaṃ vṛjanaṃ jīradānum*.
173.practice:
Two verses in this hymn have a long reach.

Verse 3 says what speech is for. *Dūto na rodasī carat vāk* — speech travels between the two worlds like a messenger. Everything else in the verse makes noise as well: the *hotā* walking his circuit, the horse crying out as it is led, the ox bellowing. The hymn's picture of a rite is a place full of sound, and the sound is not decoration; it is the traffic between here and there. For a reader recovering the sense of what they recite, this is the Ṛgveda's own account of why the words matter.

Verse 11 is the one to keep for the days when the mind will not settle. Any sacrifice at all makes {{indra}} prosper — *kaś cid*, whichever it may be — even from a man going round crooked in mind. And the images are honest about the difference: to one it is a ford right there for a thirsty man, to the other a long road, which still brings him where he was going. The rite is not cancelled by distraction. It simply takes longer. Nothing here excuses inattention; it just declines to make attention a precondition.

Verse 10's simile is worth noticing for what it assumes. Approaching Indra is compared to men seeking the friendship of a *pūrpati*, the lord of a city, and the qualification attached is *suśiṣṭau*, under good governance. The comparison only works because the audience knew the difference between a well-run town and a badly run one, and the hymn takes the well-run one as the natural figure for a god.

And verse 6 is the image the hymn is remembered by: heaven and earth will not go round him for a belt, so he wears the earth for a girdle and the sky on his head. Nothing in it is invented by the translators — the words are *rodasī kakṣye*, the two worlds as a saddle-girth.
173.disagreements:
Verse 6's *opaśam iva* is the hinge of the hymn's best image, and Sāyaṇa gives two senses without deciding: *opaśa* as "near to," so that the sky is upheld as a thing contiguous, or *opaśa* as a horn, so that Indra bears the sky as easily as a bull carries his horns. Wilson takes the first and has him upholding the sky; Griffith takes an ornament and has him wearing heaven "as 'twere a frontlet."

Verse 11 divides them completely. Wilson reads two kinds of worshipper — one who propitiates Indra by sacrifice, another who is insincere and worships "with mind averted" — and applies the ford to the first and the long road to the second. Griffith makes the subject Indra himself: every sacrifice strengthens him "yea, when he goes around angry in spirit." Sāyaṇa notes only that the comparisons may refer to the sacrificers.

On verse 2's *mithunā*, the twofold thing the *hotā* brings, Sāyaṇa allows either praise and oblation together, or the instituting patron and his wife as a pair.

On verse 1 he glosses *dhenavaḥ* by *adabdhāḥ*, unimpeded, and adds that the cows here may stand for the rains — which converts a picture of cattle at the strewn grass into a picture of rainfall, and is a good example of how far the naturalistic reading reaches into ordinary verses.
173.note: dūtaḥ na rodasī carat vāk verified in the padapāṭha at 1.173.3; the Marut reference at v12 read against the quarrel sequence 1.165-1.171

174.title: Indra Breaks the Seven Forts and Ferries Turvaśa
174.synthesis:
Ten verses in triṣṭubh, and unlike the hymn before it this one is almost entirely names — peoples helped, enemies broken, men carried across.

It opens with titles. *Tvaṃ rājā indra* — you are king, and the gods are yours; protect the men, guard us, *asura*; you are *satpati*, lord of the true, Maghavan, our deliverer; you are true, wealth-abiding, and giver of the power to prevail (v1). *Asura* is used here as an honour, which is worth registering: at this stage of the language it is a word for a lord.

Verse 2 gives the first deed. You subdued the peoples of *mṛdhravāc*, insulting speech, when you broke down the seven autumn forts that sheltered them; blameless one, you set the floods running; and you gave Vṛtra over to young Purukutsa. Seven strongholds, and a young man handed his enemy. Verse 3 turns to protection: drive the troops whose lords are heroes, and the daylight with them, much-invoked one, and guard {{agni}} — ravening, overpowering — as a lion guards, so that his work is done at daybreak in the house.

Verse 4 has the enemies laid to rest in one place by the greatness of his weapon, while he loosed the floods, went down into battle for the cows, mounted his bays and boldly took the prizes. Verse 5 names Kutsa: carry Kutsa, Indra, in whom you delight, with the ruddy obedient horses of Vāta; let {{sūrya}} tear off the wheel at the encounter, and let the vajra-armed go against the rivals. It is one of the strangest fragments in the collection — the sun's chariot wheel wrenched loose during a fight, told in half a line, with no explanation offered before or after.

Verse 6 says whom he killed: those who harm friends, and the ones who give nothing; those who looked past Aryaman among the living were flung aside as they rode. Verse 7 gives the second named enemy: the *kavi* cried out at the winning of the chant, and you made the earth a covering for the Dāsa; Maghavan made the three gleam with moisture, and laid Kuyavāca low in the fray at his own door. Verse 8 draws the ledger together: your ancient deeds have come to new singers now; you broke the godless forts as one breaks strongholds, and bent down the deadly weapon of the godless scorner.

Verse 9 is the one the hymn is remembered for. *Tvaṃ dhunir indra dhunimatīr ṛṇor apaḥ* — you, the roarer, set the roaring waters running like streams; and then, hero, when you cross the sea, *pāraya turvaśaṃ yaduṃ svasti*: bring Turvaśa and Yadu over safely. After eight verses of breaking things, the request is for two men to be got across water without loss.

Verse 10 asks for the ordinary continuation. Be ours at all times, Indra, *avṛkatamaḥ*, most free of the wolf, guardian of men, giver of the strength to prevail over all rivals — and closes with the household's seal, *vidyāma iṣaṃ vṛjanaṃ jīradānum*.
174.practice:
This is a hymn of names, and the names are the point. Purukutsa, Kutsa, Kuyavāca, the Dāsa, Turvaśa and Yadu — the Ṛgveda is remembering particular people and particular fights, and it expects the listener to know who they were.

Two of those names went furthest. Turvaśa and Yadu appear together in the same verse eight times in the collection, at [[1.36]].18, [[1.54]].6, here, and five times more; they are almost never spoken of apart. Yadu is the name the later tradition carries hardest — the Yādavas, and so Kṛṣṇa's own line, are traced back to him. What is asked here on their behalf is not conquest: *pāraya turvaśaṃ yaduṃ svasti*, carry them across, safely. The oldest thing said about that lineage in Sanskrit is a request that they get over the water in one piece.

Kuyavāca in this exact form occurs once in the whole Ṛgveda, in verse 7 of this hymn; a related name, Kuyava, turns up six times elsewhere. Purukutsa appears five times. These are not stock figures. Somebody's grandfather is in this hymn.

Verse 1 repays attention for one word. Indra is addressed as *asura*, and it is plainly a compliment — lord, possessor of power — beside *rājā*, *satpati* and *maghavan*. A reader who knows *asura* only as the opponent of the *deva*s is meeting the word before that hardening happened. The Ṛgveda uses it of Varuṇa and of Indra without embarrassment.

And verse 10 is what a household actually wants at the end of a war hymn: *avṛkatamaḥ*, most wolfless — the most thoroughly free of predation. Not victory. The absence of anything circling.
174.disagreements:
Verse 2's opening is read three different ways. Sāyaṇa's first gloss makes it a request rather than a conquest — *dānamanaso manuṣyān mṛduvācaḥ kuru*, make men of liberal mind soft-spoken. His second, which he attributes to current usage, turns the whole line meteorological: you made the rain descend, rending the gliding world-filling clouds, and opened the chief cloud for young Purukutsa. Wilson prints a third — the peoples humbled and suing for pardon — while Griffith keeps the insult in *mṛdhravāc*: "thou humbledst tribes that spake with insult."

Verse 3 parts the translators completely. Sāyaṇa reads *vṛtaḥ śūrapatnīḥ* as cities held by rākṣasas and explains the lion simile as a lion protecting the forest where his own lair is; Wilson follows him. Griffith reads troops whose lords are heroes, and brings the protection home: Agni is to dwell "in our tilled fields and in our homestead."

On verse 7's *tisraḥ*, three of something, Sāyaṇa has to supply the noun. He offers earth in three aspects — the *darśa* rites, the victim, and the soma — or simply earth, firmament and heaven. Wilson prints "the three (regions)"; Griffith declines to name them, "the three that gleam with moisture."

On verse 9 Sāyaṇa allows *sīrā* to be a particular river or rivers in general, and *pāraya* to mean either protect or carry across.
174.note: kuyavācam counted as a single occurrence across all ten padapāṭha files (kuyava- forms appear at 1.103.8, 1.104.3, 2.19.6, 4.16.12, 6.31.3, 7.19.2); turvaśa and yadu counted as co-occurring in one verse at 1.36.18, 1.54.6, 1.174.9, 6.20.12, 6.45.1, 8.4.7, 9.61.2 and 10.49.8

175.title: Indra Exhilarated, and Sūrya's Wheel Carried Off
175.synthesis:
Six short verses — one in bṛhatī, four in anuṣṭubh, the last in triṣṭubh — and they move fast, because the metre is short and the subject is a god who has just drunk.

*Matsi* — be glad. The first verse says the drink has been taken: your greatness has been drunk down, lord of bays, as a bowl takes it; for you, the bull, there is the bull {{soma}}, the *indu*, gladdening, intoxicating, *vājī*, winner of a thousand. Every word in the line is doing the same work, and the effect in the short metre is of something coming on quickly.

The second verse asks for that state to reach the singers too. Let your bull-like *mada* come to us — *vareṇya*, choice; *sahavān*, overpowering; *sānasi*, winning; *pṛtanāṣāṭ*, conquering armies; *amartya*, undying. Five epithets in one short verse, and every one of them belongs to a warrior rather than to a drink. The exhilaration is not being described from outside; it is being asked for, in the vocabulary of a fight.

The third turns it toward work. *Tvaṃ hi śūraḥ sanitā* — you are the hero and the winner; drive on the chariot of Manu; and burn the Dasyu who is *avrata*, without observance, as flame burns a wooden vessel. The description of the enemy is worth reading exactly: what is named is not a people or a colour but the absence of *vrata*, of kept observance.

The fourth verse is the one that stops a reader. *Muṣāya sūrya kave cakram* — you carried off the wheel of {{sūrya}}, sage that you are, being master by your *ojas*; take up the weapon for Śuṣṇa, and bear Kutsa with the horses of Vāta. Three clauses, three separate stories, no connective tissue at all. The theft of the sun's chariot-wheel is stated as a known thing and dropped.

The fifth verse weighs the two sides of him: your *mada* is the most impetuous and your *kratu* the most brilliant — the intoxication and the effective skill named in the same breath, in the same grammatical shape, so that neither is subordinate. And with these, Vṛtra-slaying and room-finding, you thought yourself the greatest winner of horses.

The sixth verse changes register entirely, lengthens into triṣṭubh after four short verses, and closes on memory. *Yathā pūrvebhyo jaritṛbhyaḥ indra mayaḥ iva āpo na tṛṣyate babhūtha* — as you were joy to the ancient singers, as water is to a thirsty man, so I call out this *nivid* after you. Then the seal: *vidyāma iṣaṃ vṛjanaṃ jīradānum*.

That last verse is word for word the last verse of [[1.176]], and both hymns begin with the same word, *matsi*. Two six-verse hymns to {{indra}}, standing side by side, opening alike and closing identically — the pair is deliberate, and reading either one alone loses half of it.
175.practice:
The verse a reader will stop at is the fourth, and it deserves to be left as strange as it is. Indra carries off a wheel of Sūrya's chariot; he takes up the weapon meant for Śuṣṇa; he bears Kutsa away behind the horses of Vāta. Three fragments of a story the singers plainly knew and never bothered to set out, and the Ṛgveda contains many such. The honest response is not to reconstruct the whole account from these three clauses. It is to notice that the collection assumes a listener who already knows, and that we are reading somebody else's shorthand.

Verse 5 is the one with something to say about a life. *Śuṣmintamo hi te madaḥ, dyumnintamaḥ uta kratuḥ* — your intoxication is the most impetuous, and your effective skill the most brilliant. The two are set side by side in identical form. The Veda does not make the god of the soma-drink apologise for the drink, and it does not let the drink stand in for the competence either. Both are named as superlatives in one verse. The *kratu* is not what he has instead of the *mada*.

Verse 3 is the one to read carefully rather than quickly. The enemy Indra is asked to burn is the *dasyu avrata* — the Dasyu who keeps no *vrata*. The next hymn, [[1.176]].4, uses the parallel term *asunvant*, the one who presses no soma. In this pair of hymns, whatever else the word Dasyu carried, the charge that is actually made is non-participation: no observance kept, nothing pressed, nothing given. That is the collection's own vocabulary, and it is worth knowing before importing any later one.

And the sixth verse is a good thing to say. As you were to the ancient singers, so be to me. It asks for nothing new — only for what an earlier generation already received.
175.disagreements:
Sāyaṇa's shortest note on this hymn is his strangest: on verse 4 he glosses *Kutsa* as the thunderbolt. On that reading Indra does not carry a man to Śuṣṇa at all; he carries his own weapon, and the sentence has no second person in it. Both Wilson and Griffith keep Kutsa a person — Wilson has Indra proceed "to Kutsa," Griffith has him bear "Kutsa with the steeds of Wind to Susna as his death," which are themselves two different arrangements of the same words.

Verse 5's superlatives Sāyaṇa reads as a dual pair, referring to the *mada*, the intoxication, and the *kratu*, Indra's effective acts. Wilson accordingly turns the verse into an argument — the intoxication and the beneficence are both means of destroying enemies and distributing riches — while Griffith leaves them as two separate praises, "most mighty is thy rapturous joy, most splendid is thine active power."

Verse 1 divides them on what was drunk. Wilson supplies the soma and makes Indra the vessel that receives it; Griffith reads *mahaḥ* as Indra's own glory — "thy glory hath been quaffed" — so that what is consumed is the god rather than the drink.
175.note: 1.175.6 verified word-for-word identical with 1.176.6 in the padapāṭha, and both sūktas open with matsi; dasyum avratam at 1.175.3 and asunvantam at 1.176.4 verified in the padapāṭha

176.title: Soma Enters Indra — Strike the One Who Harms Us
176.synthesis:
Six verses, the first five in anuṣṭubh and the last in triṣṭubh — the twin of [[1.175]], which opens with the same word and ends with the same verse.

*Matsi naḥ vasyaïṣṭaye* — be glad, for our seeking of the better. And then the drink is addressed directly: *indo*, {{soma}}, enter {{indra}} as a bull enters, raging; when you have gone in, you drive on and find no enemy standing near. The whole logic of the hymn is in that first verse: something is poured into a god, and what comes out the other side is a cleared field.

The second verse asks the songs to go the same way. Make our *giras* enter into him who is *ekaḥ carṣaṇīnām*, the one of the peoples, for whom the *svadhā* is strewn — and then a farmer's image drops into the middle of it: as the bull turns the barley in, ploughing. Praise entering a god is compared to seed being worked into soil by an animal that pulls.

The third verse says what he holds. In whose two hands are all the goods of the five settlements — *pañca kṣitīnām*, the five peoples, which is the Ṛgveda's way of saying everyone there is. Then the request, and it narrows abruptly from all mankind to one man: *spāśayasva yaḥ asmadhruk* — mark the one who does us harm, and kill him like the bolt out of heaven. The verb is from √spaś, to spy out; the god is asked first to identify, then to strike.

The fourth verse widens the target and states its criterion plainly. *Asunvantaṃ samaṃ jahi* — strike down the one who presses no soma, whoever he is, however hard to get at, who is no joy to you; give us the knowing of his wealth; even the patron looks for that. The enemy here is defined by what he does not do: he does not press. Whatever else lies behind these words, the charge the hymn actually makes is non-participation.

The fifth returns to Soma and to the one being helped. You have helped the man of double strength, *dvibarhas*, in whose *arka*s there was no break — *sānuṣak*, unbroken, uninterrupted, which is the quality being rewarded. And then, in the contest, *indo*, you helped Indra himself, the *vājin*, in the winnings. The drink is credited with the god's own performance, and the hymn neither remarks on the reversal nor takes it back.

The sixth verse ends where the twin hymn ends, in the same words. As you were joy to the ancient singers, Indra, as water is to a thirsty man, so I call out this *nivid* after you; *vidyāma iṣaṃ vṛjanaṃ jīradānum*. After five verses of pressing, entering, striking and seizing, the hymn closes with a man saying he is thirsty and that this has worked before.
176.practice:
This is a short, hard hymn and it should be read as what it is: a request for a specific person to be dealt with. Verse 3 does not generalise — *yaḥ asmadhruk*, the one who does us harm; mark him, and strike him. Anyone who imagines Vedic prayer as uniformly serene has not read verse 3.

What is worth attention is the criterion in verse 4. The one to be struck is the *asunvant*, the man who presses no soma — and in the twin hymn, [[1.175]].3, the *dasyu avrata*, the one who keeps no observance. In this pair the category of enemy is drawn by participation: not by descent, not by where a man lives, but by whether he presses, offers, and keeps to what he has undertaken. That is the Ṛgveda's own account of the line it is drawing, and it is more useful to a reader than any later gloss on either side of the argument.

The image in verse 2 is the one to keep, because it says something exact about praise. Our songs are to go into Indra the way the ploughing bull works the barley into the ground. Not delivered to him, not laid before him — worked in, by an animal that pulls, into ground that will hold it. The Ṛgveda's picture of what a hymn does to a god is agricultural.

Verse 3's *pañca kṣitīnām*, the five settlements, is the collection's standard way of saying all the peoples there are. Everything anyone owns is described as sitting in Indra's two hands.

And the pairing itself is the practical lesson. [[1.175]] and this hymn open with the same word, run to the same length, and close with the same verse. Whoever arranged this part of maṇḍala 1 put twins next to each other and expected them to be heard together.
176.disagreements:
Verse 1 is read in two incompatible ways. Wilson makes Soma the object throughout — "Soma, exhilarate Indra… pervade him, showerer of benefits, for when imbibed you are the annihilator of enemies" — so that the drink is the agent that clears the field. Griffith addresses the whole verse to Indra and gives the drink to him instead: "Cheer thee with draughts to win us bliss: Soma, pierce Indra in thy strength. Thou stormest trembling in thy rage." The padapāṭha's vocative *indo* supports the address to Soma at least in the first half.

Verse 2's farming image divides them further. Wilson has Indra causing every desire to bud like barley; Griffith keeps the ploughing steer — "as the steer ploughs the barley in" — which makes the songs, not the desires, the thing worked into the ground.

Verse 5's *dvibarhasaḥ*, of double strength, is applied by Wilson to the worshipper's prayers, "in whose prayers, doubly devout, there is the combination of praise and oblation," and by Griffith to the man himself, "him the doubly strong whose hymns were sung unceasingly."

The Sāyaṇa material available for this sūkta is silent throughout, which is a limit of this witness and not evidence that he passed over it.
176.note: 1.176.6 identical with 1.175.6 in the padapāṭha; both sūktas open with matsi; asunvantam verified at 1.176.4; no Sāyaṇa gloss is present for this sūkta in the available witness

177.title: Indra the Bull Called Down to Sit and Unyoke
177.synthesis:
Five verses in triṣṭubh, and the first three of them do something a reader can hear before understanding it: they say *bull* over and over, more times in each verse than in the one before.

The first verse calls him. *Ā carṣaṇiprāḥ vṛṣabho janānām* — filler of the peoples, bull of men, king of the settlements, {{indra}} called by many; praised and seeking renown, yoke your two bull-like bays and come down here toward me. Two words on the root *vṛṣ*, the root of showering and of virility.

The second raises it to three. Those bulls of yours, Indra, those bull-like stallions, *brahmayujaḥ* — yoked by the sacred word — harnessed to the bull-chariot: mount them, come here with them; we call you, the soma pressed. The horses are bulls, the chariot is a bull-thing, and the harness is *brahman*. Nothing physical fastens this team. The compound says that what holds the god's horses in the yoke is the formula being spoken, which makes the reciter the harness.

The third raises it to four. Mount the bull-chariot; the bull {{soma}} has been pressed for you, the sweet drinks are poured round; having yoked the two bulls, O bull of the settlements, come with the bays, downhill, toward me. Two, then three, then four — nine forms of the one root across three consecutive verses, rising by one each time. The hymn is doing with sound what it is asking for in sense: an approach that builds.

Then the fourth verse stops, and everything becomes concrete and near. *Ayaṃ yajño devayāḥ* — here is the god-seeking rite; here is the *miyedha*, the offering; here are the *brahman*s; here, Indra, is the Soma; the *barhis* is strewn. Come, Śakra, quickly; sit down; drink; and *vi muca harī iha*, unyoke the two bays here. Five demonstratives in a row — this, this, these, this — and then the four imperatives of hospitality: come, sit, drink, unharness. After three verses of accelerating bulls, the hymn asks for the horses to be taken out of the yoke. The unyoking is how you know the visit is not a passing one.

The fourth verse is also where the hymn changes what it is doing with the metre: the first three build, and this one lists. Then the fifth verse names the singer's own family and asks for one more thing besides. Well praised, Indra, come here toward the *brahman*s of Mānya's son, the poet; and *vidyāma vastoḥ avasā gṛṇantaḥ*, may we know, at daybreak, with your help, as we sing. Then the seal, *vidyāma iṣaṃ vṛjanaṃ jīradānum* — and the two clauses beginning *vidyāma*, may we know, stand one after the other in the last two lines.
177.practice:
Read this hymn aloud and the point arrives without commentary. In verse 1 the root *vṛṣ* — the bull, the shower, the one who pours out — appears twice; in verse 2, three times; in verse 3, four. Nine occurrences in three verses, increasing each time. Then verse 4 drops the word entirely and says, five times over, *here*: here is the rite, here the offering, here the prayers, here the Soma, here the strewn grass.

That is a shape worth carrying into any practice. The build is not the point; the arrival is. Everything the first three verses do with mounting, harnessing and speed exists to reach a verse in which the guest is asked to sit down.

And the last request of that verse is the one to keep. *Vi muca harī iha* — unyoke the two bays here. It is what you say to someone you want to stay. A visitor whose horses are still standing in harness has not really arrived, and the Ṛgveda knows the difference. The same request is made of the {{marut}}s a few hymns earlier, at [[1.171]].1, in the same words — put down your anger, unyoke your horses — where it is a test of whether a quarrel is over. Here it is simple hospitality.

Verse 4 also supplies a word a reader may meet elsewhere: *miyedha*, the offering, which the commentators connect with *medha*. The vocabulary of the great rites is not far away in these hymns.

Finally, verse 5 asks twice in two lines with the same verb: *vidyāma vastoḥ*, may we know at daybreak, and then *vidyāma iṣaṃ vṛjanaṃ jīradānum*. Whatever the household refrain means in detail — and the tradition does not agree — the request the singer makes twice at the end of his hymn is to *know*.
177.disagreements:
Sāyaṇa's note on verse 2 is the useful one: he points out that the words built on *vṛṣ* are being repeated deliberately — the horses are *vṛṣaṇa*, the chariot *vṛṣaṇa*, Indra himself *vṛṣabha*, and Soma *vṛṣan*. The translators handle this differently. Wilson mostly converts the root into a formula, "showerer of benefits," "bounty-shedding car," which preserves the sense and loses the drumbeat. Griffith keeps the animal — "Thy mighty Stallions… thy Coursers to thy mighty chariot harnessed" — which keeps some of the force and blurs which word is which.

On verse 4's *miyedha* Sāyaṇa glosses it as an epithet of the *yajña*, derived from *medha* in the sense of the victim. Wilson accordingly prints "this is the offering of the victim"; Griffith gives simply "here the victim."

Verse 1's *carṣaṇiprāḥ* also parts them: Wilson takes it as "cherisher of men," a filler in the sense of one who satisfies; Griffith renders the phrase as "who cherishes all people" but attaches the bull to the men rather than the filling. The compound will bear either, and nothing in the verse decides it.
177.note: vṛṣ- forms counted directly in the padapāṭha: 2 at v1 (vṛṣabhaḥ, vṛṣaṇā), 3 at v2 (vṛṣaṇaḥ, vṛṣabhāsaḥ, vṛṣa-rathāsaḥ), 4 at v3 (vṛṣaṇam, vṛṣā, vṛṣa-bhyām, vṛṣabha), none at vv4-5

178.title: Indra's Hearing — Do Not Burn Away Our Desire
178.synthesis:
Five verses in triṣṭubh, and the hymn turns on a single word in the first line: *śruṣṭi*, the readiness to hear.

*Yad ha syā te indra śruṣṭir asti* — if that hearing of yours is there, {{indra}}, the one by which you have been a help to singers. The condition is stated openly. The singer does not assume he is being listened to; he begins with an if. And then the request, which is unlike almost anything else in the neighbourhood: *mā naḥ kāmaṃ mahayantam ā dhak* — do not burn away our desire, the desire that makes us great. Not do not deny it; do not *burn* it. The verb is √dah. And the verse ends open-handed: may I obtain, through you, all that comes round to a man.

The second verse asks him not to spoil what is already under way. Let king Indra not damage us in what the two sisters bring about in the womb; the swift waters have run to him; may Indra come to us with friendship and with *vayas*, vigour. Who the two sisters are the verse does not say, and the tradition has not settled it.

The third verse describes the god the first two have been addressing, and it is a portrait made entirely of what he does for other people. Conqueror alongside the men in battles, a hero; *śrotā havaṃ nādhamānasya kāroḥ*, a hearer of the call of the poet who is pleading; one who brings his chariot right up beside the giver — if, that is, he himself is holding the songs up. The condition of verse 1 comes back in the last clause of verse 3, and both times the hymn leaves it standing rather than resolving it.

The fourth verse puts the whole thing in a crowd. Indra, with the men, out of love of good repute, consumes the strong food of those who are his friends; and in the *samarya*, the meeting, *vivāci*, amid the clash of voices, the song of the sacrificer is sung — he being *satrākara*, one who carries a thing through to the end. The rite is not pictured in a quiet place. It is pictured in an argument, with several people talking at once, and the singer's praise being sung in the middle of it.

The fifth verse asks for the thing all this was for. *Tvayā vayaṃ maghavan indra śatrūn abhi syāma mahato manyamānān* — with you, Maghavan, may we get the better of enemies who think themselves great. You are the protector; be for our increase. And then the seal, *vidyāma iṣaṃ vṛjanaṃ jīradānum*.

The enemies are not described as great. They are described as *manyamānāḥ*, thinking themselves so — which is a precise thing to say and a different claim from the one a boast would make.
178.practice:
The line to take from this hymn is verse 1's, and it is unusual enough to be worth learning: *mā naḥ kāmaṃ mahayantam ā dhak* — do not burn away the desire that would make us great.

Two things are remarkable about it. First, the prayer is not that a desire be granted but that it not be destroyed — the fear is of losing the wanting itself. Second, the desire is described approvingly. *Mahayantam*, magnifying, making great. A tradition that later develops an elaborate vocabulary for the discipline of desire begins, here, with a man asking a god not to scorch his ambition out of him.

And it is asked conditionally. The hymn opens *yad ha... asti*, if that hearing of yours is there — and verse 3 puts the same condition on Indra's coming: he brings his chariot up to the giver *yadi ca tmanā bhūt*, if he himself is upholding the songs.
