Twice the singer declines to assume he is being heard. That is not doubt in the modern sense; it is accuracy about a relationship in which the other party is free.

Verse 4 is worth noticing for where it puts the rite. Not in solitude — in the *samarya*, the meeting, *vivāci*, in the clash of voices, with the sacrificer's song being sung inside the noise. Whoever composed this expected a rite to be performed among people who were talking, competing and interrupting, and did not think that a problem. And the epithet given to Indra there is *satrākara*, the one who carries a thing all the way through, which is exactly the quality such a setting requires.

Verse 5's phrasing is the last thing to keep. The enemies are *mahato manyamānān*, ones who consider themselves great. The hymn does not concede that they are.
178.disagreements:
Verse 2's *svasārā*, the two sisters, is undetermined, and Sāyaṇa gives three candidates without choosing: day and night; the instituting patron and the officiating priest; or the fingers used in the ritual manipulations. Wilson prints the first, glossing "(Day and Night)"; Griffith declines to interpret and gives "what shall bring both Sisters to our dwelling," which leaves them a different kind of pair altogether.

Verse 1's imperative divides them sharply. Wilson softens the verb into disappointment — "disappoint not the desire (that would raise us) to greatness" — while Griffith keeps the burning: "Blast not the wish that would exalt us." The Sanskrit has √dah, to burn.

Verse 3's closing condition is read two ways. Wilson attaches it to Indra's mood — he will drive his chariot near "when disposed to accept his praises… of his own accord" — whereas Griffith makes it a stated condition, "if he himself upholds the songs that praise him." On the first reading Indra is spontaneous; on the second something is required of him.

One practical note on the witnesses: the Griffith text available here runs verses 4 and 5 of this sūkta together in a single entry, so no reading of his can be cited by verse number for the last two verses.
178.note: the Griffith file in this repository merges 1.178.4 and 1.178.5 into one entry and leaves v5 empty; mā naḥ kāmam mahayantam ā dhak verified in the padapāṭha at 1.178.1

97.title: Apa Naḥ Śośucad Agham — Agni Burns the Fault Off
97.synthesis:
Eight gāyatrī verses, and the same line closes every one of them: *apa naḥ śośucad agham* — may it burn our fault away from us. The first verse says it twice, at the start and at the end, so the hymn opens and closes on the identical words and the reciter says them nine times in eight short verses. Nothing else in this part of maṇḍala 1 is built so tightly around one request.

*Apa naḥ śośucad agham agne śuśugdhy ā rayim* — burn our fault away from us, {{agni}}; blaze wealth toward us; may it burn our fault away. Two imperatives from the same root, √śuc, in one verse: the burning that removes and the blazing that brings are the same act of the same fire. That is the hymn's entire argument and it is made in the first line.

The second verse says what the sacrifice is for, and the list is unexpectedly plain: *sukṣetriyā sugātuyā vasuyā ca yajāmahe* — we sacrifice out of desire for good fields, for good paths, and for goods. Fields and roads. Not visions, not deliverance. Then the refrain.

The third and fourth are about the people. May he be the most praiseworthy among these, and our own patrons foremost (v3); and *pra yat te agne sūrayo jāyemahi pra te vayam* — that your patrons, Agni, and we ourselves may be propagated onward (v4). The verb is from √jan, to be born, and the tradition reads it as being born onward in one's descendants — which makes the fourth verse a prayer for continuance through a line rather than for personal survival.

The fifth turns to Agni itself: since the beams of powerful Agni go out in every direction — refrain. The sixth draws the consequence and gives him the name the hymn has been working toward: *tvaṃ hi viśvatomukha viśvataḥ paribhūr asi* — you, whose face is turned every way, are the encompasser on every side. Agni that removes fault can do it because there is no direction it does not face.

Then the last two verses change the image entirely and become the best-known thing in the hymn. *Dviṣo no viśvatomukha ati nāveva pāraya* — you of faces everywhere, carry us past our haters as if in a boat (v7). *Sa naḥ sindhum iva nāvayā ati parṣā svastaye* — carry us across, as over the {{sindhu}} in a boat, for *svasti*, wellbeing (v8). And the refrain once more.

A hymn about burning has ended in water. The fault is not argued away or expiated by any procedure; it is burnt off, and then the person carrying it is ferried over. Both verbs — *pāraya* and *parṣa*, from √pṛ, to carry across — belong to the vocabulary of getting someone to the far side, and the same root is what [[1.99]].1 uses two sūktas later when it asks Agni to carry us past all hard passages *nāveva sindhum*, as over a river in a boat. Read together, 1.97.8 and 1.99.1 are the same request in nearly the same words, and the boat is in both.
97.practice:
This is one of the most usable sūktas in maṇḍala 1, because it is short, it is in gāyatrī, and it asks for one thing.

*Agha* is the word. It is not sin in a juridical sense and not karmic residue in the later technical sense; it is the fault, the harm, the wrong that has attached to a person and is now doing damage. What the hymn asks is that it be burnt off — *śośucat*, an intensive of √śuc, to burn or to grieve — and Sāyaṇa records two ways of taking it: let our fault pass away from us and light upon our adversaries, or let our fault, afflicted by grief, perish. He does not choose between them, and the ambiguity is worth preserving: the second is straightforwardly a purification, the first is a transfer.

Verse 1's construction is what makes the hymn coherent. *Apa naḥ śośucad agham agne śuśugdhy ā rayim* — burn the fault away, blaze wealth in. One fire, one root, two directions. A Hindu who lights a lamp in the evening is performing exactly that double act and this verse names it.

Verses 7 and 8 give the tradition one of its permanent images: being ferried across. The verb √pṛ, to bring over, is the same one behind *pāra*, the far shore, and behind the *tāraka* language of later devotion. Here the crossing is not of *saṃsāra*; it is over enemies and over a river, for *svasti*. But the shape of the request — you carry, we are carried, there is a far side — is fixed already, and [[1.99]].1, two sūktas later, uses the identical boat image for a crossing over every hard passage.

Verse 2 is worth setting against any impression that the Veda's dharma is chiefly otherworldly. *Sukṣetriyā sugātuyā vasuyā ca yajāmahe*: we sacrifice because we want good fields, good roads, and goods. That is the whole stated motive, in the second verse of a hymn about the removal of fault, and the two sit together without embarrassment.

Note also that this is one of three sūktas in the run from [[1.94]] to [[1.115]] that does not carry the *tan no mitro varuṇo mamahantām* closing — the others being [[1.99]] and 1.104. Its own refrain occupies that position instead.
97.disagreements:
Sāyaṇa's note on the refrain is the hinge, and it is the only place in the hymn where a real choice is offered. *Apa naḥ śośucad agham*, he says, may be taken two ways: "let our sin pass away from us, and light upon our adversaries", or "let our sin, afflicted by grief, perish." The first makes the verse a transfer of harm to an enemy; the second makes it an inward destruction. He records both without deciding. Wilson translates neither directly, printing the oddly passive "may our sin be repented of" throughout — which follows the *śuc*-as-grieve sense and loses the burning. Griffith takes the burning: "May his light chase our sin away", eight times.

Verse 3 is where Wilson supplies most. He prints "(in like manner as, among these your worshippers, Kutsa) is the pre-eminent panegyrist" — the ṛṣi's name is not in the padapāṭha, and the Anukramaṇī supplies it. Griffith translates the bare words: "Best praiser of all these be he."

On verse 4's *prajāyemahi* Sāyaṇa is specific: from √jan, to be born — "may we be born successively in the persons of our posterity." Wilson prints "may we obtain posterity", Griffith "in our sons may live". The verse is about continuing through a line rather than about acquiring one.

98.title: Agni Vaiśvānara — in Sky, Earth, and Every Plant
98.synthesis:
Three verses. It is one of the shortest sūktas in maṇḍala 1, and it says one thing three ways: that {{agni}} under the name {{vaiśvānara}} is not in one place.

*Vaiśvānarasya sumatau syāma* — may we be in the good favour of Vaiśvānara; *rājā hi kaṃ bhuvanānām abhiśrīḥ*, for he is king, the crowning glory of all that exists. Then two clauses that put him in two states at once: *ito jāto viśvam idaṃ vi caṣṭe*, born from this, he looks out over all this — and *vaiśvānaro yatate sūryeṇa*, Vaiśvānara ranges alongside Sūrya. "From this" is the kindling in front of the speaker. He is born out of a piece of wood on the ground and he keeps pace with the sun.

The second verse states the distribution flatly, and it does so by repeating one word four times. *Pṛṣṭo divi pṛṣṭo agniḥ pṛthivyām, pṛṣṭo viśvā oṣadhīr ā viveśa, vaiśvānaraḥ sahasā pṛṣṭo agniḥ* — present in the sky, present on earth, present he has entered into all the plants; Vaiśvānara, present in force. Sky, ground, and every growing thing, in one line each. And then the request, which is the only thing the hymn asks for: *sa no divā sa riṣaḥ pātu naktam* — may he guard us from harm by day and by night. The verse has just said he is everywhere; the request is for cover at all times. The form of the claim and the form of the petition match exactly.

The third verse is one line of its own and one line shared. *Vaiśvānara tava tat satyam astu, asmān rāyo maghavānaḥ sacantām* — Vaiśvānara, let that of yours be true; let riches and liberal patrons attend us. *Satyam astu* is not a request for a new thing; it asks that what has already been said hold. And then the seal that closes nearly every sūkta in this stretch of the maṇḍala: *tan no mitro varuṇo mamahantām aditiḥ sindhuḥ pṛthivī uta dyauḥ* — may Mitra, Varuṇa, {{aditi}}, {{sindhu}}, Earth and Heaven grant us that.

It is worth noticing what the three verses do not contain. There is no narrative, no legend, no epithet beyond the name and the word *rājan*, no request for wealth until the last line, and no praise of the kind that fills the surrounding Kutsa hymns. Three verses is enough for the whole argument because the argument is simple and does not need developing. A king of all beings (v1) who is present in sky, earth and plant (v2) can be asked to protect by day and by night (v2), and what remains is to ask that the claim be true (v3). The brevity is not truncation. It is a complete piece of reasoning, and the name it turns on — *vaiśvānara*, belonging to all men — is doing the work the argument needs, since a fire that belongs to everyone is by definition not confined to one hearth.
98.practice:
*Vaiśvānara* is the name to understand here, because it outlives the hymn by a very long way. Sāyaṇa gives three derivations without choosing: he who rules over all (*viśva*) men (*nara*); or he who conducts men to another region, to heaven, through the oblations; or, possibly, he who conducts them to a future life through the funeral fire. All three read the compound as *viśva* + *nara*, all-men, and all three are about a fire that is not any one person's.

The name is not rare, but neither is it everywhere. Across the whole Ṛgveda *vaiśvānara* and its forms occur 53 times in the padapāṭha, spread over eight maṇḍalas — most densely in the sixth and seventh — and the nominative *vaiśvānaraḥ* itself twenty times. What is worth knowing is that the Anukramaṇī does not use the name at all in its dedications: this sūkta is assigned simply to Agni. Vaiśvānara is a form the hymns name, not a deity the index separates out.

Where a Hindu reader will meet the name again is in two quite different places, and both are prefigured here. Vaiśvānara becomes the standing name for the digestive fire — the Bhagavadgītā's *ahaṃ vaiśvānaro bhūtvā prāṇināṃ deham āśritaḥ*, I having become Vaiśvānara dwell in the body of the living — which is a straight development of verse 2's claim that he has entered into all the plants. And in the Māṇḍūkya Upaniṣad Vaiśvānara is the name of the waking state, the first of the four quarters of the self, because it is the condition in which one is turned outward toward everything. Verse 1's *viśvam idaṃ vi caṣṭe*, he looks out over all this, is where that comes from.

This is the last of Kutsa Āṅgirasa's first five Agni sūktas, running from [[1.94]] through [[1.97]] to this one, and it is by far the shortest. What it asks for is small and worth keeping small: *sa no divā sa riṣaḥ pātu naktam*, may he guard us from harm by day and by night. A three-verse hymn establishing that a god is everywhere ends by asking him to be on duty around the clock. The reasoning is not devotional. It is practical, and it is complete.
98.disagreements:
There is little to divide here, and the divergences are small but instructive.

Sāyaṇa's three derivations of *vaiśvānara* — ruler over all men; conductor of men to heaven through oblations; conductor to a future life through the funeral fire — are given as alternatives, and the third is the only one that ties the name to the cremation fire. Neither Wilson nor Griffith renders the name at all; both keep "Vaiśvānara" untranslated, so the reader who does not have Sāyaṇa has no access to the etymology the hymn depends on.

On verse 1's *yatate sūryeṇa* Sāyaṇa offers two accounts and does not choose: either terrestrial heat is combined with solar radiance, or the rays of the earthly fire ascend and mix with the descending rays of the sun, citing the Nirukta. Wilson renders it "he accompanies the rising sun"; Griffith makes it a contest — "Vaisvanara hath rivalry with Surya" — which is a real difference, since √yat can mean to range alongside or to strive against.

On verse 2's *pṛṣṭaḥ* Sāyaṇa glosses *saṃspṛṣṭa* or *nihita*, in contact with or placed in, and specifies where: in the sun in the sky; on earth in the sacred and domestic fires; and in the plants as the cause of their coming to maturity. That last identification — fire as what ripens a crop — is his, and neither translation carries it.

On verse 3's *rāyaḥ* he notes the sense is wealth in family rather than in goods.

99.title: One Verse to Jātavedas — Past Every Hard Place
99.synthesis:
One verse. This is the only sūkta in the Ṛgveda with a single verse — 1,027 others run from three verses to fifty-eight, and this one stops after four lines.

*Jātavedase sunavāma somam* — for Jātavedas let us press the {{soma}}. The name comes first, before the verb, before the offering, and it is the name that carries the whole verse: {{agni}} as the one who knows all that is born, or in whom all that is born is known. What is proposed is the ordinary act. Let us press.

Then the second line, and it turns on a play the English cannot hold. *Arātīyato ni dahāti vedaḥ* — may he burn down the *vedas*, the property and substance, of the one who acts without giving. *Arātīyat* is formed on *arāti*, ungenerosity, the refusal to give: the enemy here is defined not by hostility but by withholding. And the word for what is burnt, *vedaḥ*, is the same stem that stands in *jātavedas* three words earlier. The one whose knowing is total burns away the having of the one who will not give. Whoever composed the line put the two forms in one verse deliberately.

The second half is the reason the verse survived. *Sa naḥ parṣad ati durgāṇi viśvā* — may he carry us across all the *durgāṇi*, the hard places, the passages difficult to get through. And then the image, in five words: *nāveva sindhuṃ duritāty agniḥ* — as over a river in a boat, Agni (carries us) past the ill-goings. *Durgāṇi* and *duritāni* are near neighbours built the same way, *duḥ*- prefixed to a word for going: the hard passage and the bad passage. The verse names the trouble twice with two words for the same idea, and answers both with one boat.

That boat is not new here. Two sūktas earlier, at the close of [[1.97]], Kutsa asked Agni twice in succession to ferry him — *ati nāveva pāraya*, carry us past as in a boat, and *sa naḥ sindhum iva nāvayā ati parṣā svastaye*, carry us across as over the {{sindhu}} in a boat, for wellbeing. The same verb √pṛ, the same *sindhu*, the same vessel. Whether 1.99 was placed here because of that echo or the echo produced the placement cannot be told from the evidence; what can be seen in the padapāṭha is that three of the Ṛgveda's thirty-eight verses containing a word for boat stand within three sūktas of one another, at 1.97.7, 1.97.8 and 1.99.1.

What the single verse does, then, is complete: it names the god, proposes the offering, states what he does to those who hold back, and asks for the one thing wanted — passage. There is no praise in it and no epithet beyond the name. A hymn that had gone on longer would have had to add something, and the verse is exactly as long as its request.
99.practice:
This verse is almost certainly the most-recited line of the Ṛgveda that most people cannot place. It is the opening of the *Durgā Sūktam*, which stands in the Taittirīya Āraṇyaka and is recited at Navarātri, in Durgā *homa*, and in the Caṇḍī observances — usually chanted together with the verses that follow it there, addressed to a goddess *agnivarṇā tapasā jvalantī*, of the colour of fire, blazing with *tapas*.

Two honest points follow, and they matter.

First, the Ṛgvedic verse addresses {{agni}} Jātavedas, and no goddess. The identification with Durgā comes from the word *durgāṇi* in the third line — the hard passages — and from the Āraṇyaka's placing of this verse at the head of a sequence to a goddess. The name Durgā means what *durgāṇi* means: hard to go through. The connection is real and it is etymological, but it is a later liturgical development, not something 1.99 states.

Second, the verse works perfectly well as what it is. Anyone facing something genuinely hard to get through has a four-line Ṛgvedic prayer for exactly that, with a river-crossing for its image and no theological requirement beyond lighting a fire.

Three structural facts are worth having. This is the only single-verse sūkta in the entire Ṛgveda. Its ṛṣi is Kaśyapa Mārīca, whose four other sūktas — 9.91, 9.92, 9.113 and 9.114 — are all in the Soma maṇḍala; he appears in maṇḍala 1 exactly once, here. And it sits inside another man's block: [[1.94]] to [[1.98]] and [[1.101]] to [[1.115]] all belong to Kutsa Āṅgirasa, and 1.99 and [[1.100]] are the two interruptions. It is also one of only three sūktas in that whole range — with [[1.97]] and 1.104 — that does not carry the closing line *tan no mitro varuṇo mamahantām*.

A single verse by a seer who otherwise wrote for Soma, dropped into the middle of Kutsa's Agni series, and it became one of the most widely chanted verses in living Hindu practice.
99.disagreements:
There is no Sāyaṇa gloss on this verse in the witness available here, which means only that this witness does not carry one — his bhāṣya covers 933 of maṇḍala 1's 2,006 verses, and absence is a fact about the manuscript, not about him.

Wilson and Griffith agree almost exactly, which is unusual and is a sign of how little the verse leaves open. Wilson: "We offer oblations of Soma to Jātavedas, may he consume the wealth of those who feel enmity against us; may he transport us over all difficulties; may Agni convey us, as in a boat over a river, across all wickedness." Griffith: "For Jatavedas let us press the Soma: may he consume the wealth of the malignant. May Agni carry us through all our troubles, through grief as in a boat across the river."

The one real divergence is the last word. Wilson renders *duritā* as "wickedness", making it moral fault; Griffith gives "grief", making it misfortune. The word is *duḥ* + *ita*, ill-going, and covers both — the bad step and the bad outcome — and the parallel with *durgāṇi*, hard passages, in the previous line suggests the sense is closer to trouble gone through than to sin committed. Neither translator renders *arātīyataḥ* by its root sense of ungenerosity; both give hostility, which loses the specific charge that the enemy is the one who does not give.

Neither renders the wordplay between *jātavedase* and *vedaḥ*, which is not translatable into English and is visible only in the padapāṭha.

100.title: Marutvān Indra Fifteen Times — Then Five Brothers
100.synthesis:
Nineteen verses, and the first fifteen end identically: *marutvān no bhavatv indra ūtī* — may {{indra}} with the {{marut}}s be our help. Then the refrain stops, three verses name a family and its horses, and the last verse closes with a different formula entirely.

The opening five build him out of comparatives. He is the bull housed with bull-powers, *samrāṭ* of the great heaven and earth, of real substance, to be called in battles (v1). His course is unattainable, like Sūrya's; in every fight he is the Vṛtra-slaying force, moving with his own swift friends (v2). His paths go on, unassailed, as though milking the seed of heaven; he overcomes hatred and prevails by manly powers (v3). Then the verse built entirely on the figure of the superlative: *so aṅgirobhir aṅgirastamo bhūd, vṛṣā vṛṣabhiḥ sakhibhiḥ sakhā san, ṛgmibhir ṛgmī gātubhir jyeṣṭhaḥ* — among the {{aṅgiras}}es he became most Aṅgiras, a bull among bulls, a friend among friends, a singer among singers, foremost in the paths (v4). Five terms, each of which makes him the extreme case of the company he keeps rather than something apart from it. And the fifth: with the Rudras as with his own sons, skilful, conquering enemies in the men's fight, winning glories with his own kin.

Verses 6 to 11 turn to what he does for a side. Crusher of wrath, maker of the fight, with our men *sūryaṃ sanat asmin ahan* — may he win the sun this day (v6). His helps make him rejoice in the winning of heroes; the peoples make him guardian of their security; he alone rules over every act (v7). Men seek him at the risings of strength, a man among men, for help and for wealth — and *so andhe cit tamasi jyotir vidat*, he found light even in blind darkness (v8). With the left hand he restrains even the strong; with the right he gathers what has been won; even with the humble man he wins riches (v9). He wins with troops and with chariots; he is known today among all peoples (v10). With kinsmen or without kinsmen, invoked by many, he drives to the prize — for the winning of waters, of offspring, of descendants (v11).

Verses 12 to 15 raise him past measure. Bolt-bearer, *dasyuhā*, fearsome, of a thousand thoughts and a hundred devices, and by strength *pāñcajanya*, belonging to the five peoples (v12). His bolt roars, winning the sun; his roar is terrible as heaven's; gifts and riches attend him (v13). His measure, through strength, is unceasing; his hymn encompasses the two worlds on every side; delighted by our acts, may he carry us across (v14). And *na yasya devā devatā na martā, āpaś cana śavasaḥ antam āpuḥ* — neither the gods by their godhead, nor mortals, nor the waters have reached the limit of his strength; he surpasses earth and heaven by his force (v15). That is the last refrain.

Then the hymn becomes a particular family's. A red and dark mare, blaze-marked, of good rays, heavenly, bearing the chariot at the pole for the enrichment of Ṛjrāśva — she was noticed, gladdening, among the Nāhuṣa peoples (v16). And the signature: *etat tyat ta indra vṛṣṇe uktham, vārṣāgirā abhi gṛṇanti rādhaḥ, ṛjrāśvaḥ praṣṭibhir ambarīṣaḥ, sahadevo bhayamānaḥ surādhāḥ* — this hymn the Vārṣāgiras sing to you as their bounty: Ṛjrāśva with his companions, Ambarīṣa, Sahadeva, Bhayamāna, Surādhas (v17). Five names, all of them the seers of the sūkta. Then the deed that the hymn was for: having slain the {{dasyu}}s and the Śimyus, he laid them low on the earth with his arrow; with his white-complexioned friends he won the field, won the sun, won the waters (v18).

And the nineteenth: *viśvāhā indro adhivaktā no astu* — may Indra always be our advocate; may we, undeflected, win *vāja*. Then the seal that closes almost every sūkta in this part of the maṇḍala: may Mitra, Varuṇa, {{aditi}}, {{sindhu}}, Earth and Heaven grant it.
100.practice:
Verse 4 is the one to keep, and it says something about excellence that is easy to miss. *Aṅgirobhir aṅgirastamo* — among the {{aṅgiras}}es, most Aṅgiras; a bull among bulls, a friend among friends, a singer among singers. {{indra}} is not praised for being of a different order from the company he keeps. He is praised for being the fullest instance of it. That is a model of pre-eminence a person can actually use: not apartness, but being more thoroughly what everyone around you is.

Verse 8 gives the line that outlasts the battle it was written for: *so andhe cit tamasi jyotir vidat* — he found light even in blind darkness. Sāyaṇa reads *tamas* here as the darkness of understanding and *jyotis* as the light of knowledge, which is a move beyond what the verse literally says and worth knowing as his.

Verse 9 is a small piece of practical observation: the left hand restrains, the right hand gathers. The god who holds off the strong is the same one collecting what has been won, at the same moment, with two hands. And the verse ends *sa kīriṇā cit sanitā dhanāni* — even with the humble man he wins riches. Verse 7 says the peoples made him guardian of their *kṣema*, their secure possession, which is the word that pairs with *yoga* in the standing phrase *yogakṣema*: acquiring and keeping. What this hymn asks Indra for is both.

The signature at verse 17 is unusual enough to be worth stating. The Anukramaṇī gives 1.100 jointly to five named brothers of the Vārṣāgira family — Ṛjrāśva, Ambarīṣa, Sahadeva, Bhayamāna and Surādhas — and they name themselves inside the hymn. Across all 1,028 sūktas this is the only one ascribed to five co-authors of the whole text rather than divided verse by verse among several seers. The family appears once more, at 9.98, under Ambarīṣa alone.

Read with [[1.99]], which precedes it, this sūkta marks the second of the two interruptions in Kutsa Āṅgirasa's long block from [[1.94]] to [[1.115]]. Two sūktas by other hands sit inside it: a single verse by Kaśyapa Mārīca, and nineteen verses by five brothers who put their names in the text.
100.disagreements:
Sāyaṇa supplies this hymn's occasion and it is a specific one. On verse 6 he explains that the appeal is for daylight in which to attack the enemies of the Vārṣāgiras and to recover cattle that had been stolen — or, alternatively, that the light be withheld from their opponents. Nothing in the padapāṭha names cattle or a raid; the reading comes from him, and it makes verse 18's winning of field, sun and waters the account of a real engagement rather than a cosmic one.

On verse 8 he makes his most consequential move. Where the text has *andhe cit tamasi jyotir vidat*, he glosses *tamas* as the darkness of thought and hopes that {{indra}} will give the light of knowledge to a darkened understanding. Neither translator follows: Wilson has "the light (of conquest) in the bewildering darkness (of battle)", Griffith "He hath found light even in the blinding darkness." The verse in its own terms is about a battle; Sāyaṇa reads it about a mind.

On verse 18's *sakhibhiḥ śvitnyebhiḥ* he offers two readings without choosing — the winds or {{marut}}s, or earthly friends and worshippers of Indra who were white. Wilson prints "his white-complexioned friends", Griffith "his fair-complexioned friends"; the alternative that they are the Maruts, which the refrain of the previous fifteen verses would support, is left out of both.

On verse 16's *nāhuṣīṣu vikṣu* Sāyaṇa glosses *viś* as people in the specific sense of an army, *senālakṣaṇāsu prajāsu*, which neither translation carries.

121.title: Indra Hears the Aṅgirases — Śuṣṇa Broken for Kutsa
121.synthesis:
This is the most difficult hymn in this stretch of the collection, and it is honest to say so at the start: several of its fifteen verses cannot be construed with confidence from the evidence available, and the two English versions frequently do not agree about who is acting.

It opens as a question about hearing. *Kad itthā nṝn pātraṃ devayatāṃ śravad giro aṅgirasāṃ turaṇyan* — when, then, will the protector of men hear, hastening, the songs of the {{aṅgiras}}es who seek the gods? When he comes to the people of the house, he strides wide at the *adhvara*, the one worthy of worship. The hymn's premise is a delay: the songs have been sung and the god has not yet arrived.

Verses 2 and 3 build him. He propped the sky and poured out the support; as Ṛbhu he made the cow's wealth for *{{vāja}}*. He reached the ancient call of the Aṅgirases' clans day after day; he fashioned the bolt and the team; he propped the sky for the four-footed and the two-footed man. Verse 4 is the deed: in the rapture of this you gave back, for {{ṛta}}, the lowing herd that was shut away; when the three-crested one comes down in onslaught he opens the doors of the deceitful. The cattle are released *ṛtāya*, for the sake of the order — not for profit.

Verse 5 turns to the offering: for you the milk your two parents brought, a strengthening gift for conquest, the pure treasure, the milk of the cow that streams. Verse 6 is his appearing: then he is born, the swift one; may he shine like the sun out of this dawn — the *indu* by which those who pour with a ladle reached him. Verse 7 is a working morning: when the pile of good logs is ready, when the enclosure of the cow is bound at the sun's rite, when you shine through the days of work — for the man with the cart, the man after cattle, the quick man. It is one of the few glimpses in this range of who is actually present at a dawn sacrifice.

Verse 8 has eight bays brought down from great heaven and a fight for the well that gives splendour, so that men might press the gladdening tawny drink with stones. Verses 9 and 10 are the hymn's centre, and they are the reason it is remembered. *Tvam āyasaṃ prati vartayo gor divo aśmānam upanītam ṛbhvā* — you turned back the iron stone, brought from heaven by the skilled one, for {{kutsa}}, when, much-invoked, overcoming Śuṣṇa, you encompassed him with endless weapons. And then: before darkness overtook the sun, wielder of the stone, you cast your weapon at the enclosing one; you tore open, out of heaven, the well-knotted might of Śuṣṇa that had been thrown around him. Kutsa is the seer of the twenty hymns immediately preceding this one in the collection. His name arrives here in a hymn by his successor, in the middle of the fight the older seer's own sūktas are full of.

Verse 11 has heaven and earth, the two great wheel-less masses, rejoicing at the deed, and {{indra}} putting {{vṛtra}} to sleep in the channels with the bolt. Verse 12 asks him to mount his horses and names the bolt's donor: Kāvya Uśanā gave it, gladdening, Vṛtra-slaying, decisive. Verse 13 stops the sun's horses, says Etaśa did not draw the wheel, and drives the non-sacrificers beyond ninety navigable rivers into the pit. Verses 14 and 15 come back to the household: save us from this hard destruction, bolt-bearer, from the misfortune at close quarters; give us prizes founded on horses, for food, for fame, for true speech. And: may that good thought of yours not fail us; give us a share among the cattle; may we be your most bountiful companions at the feast.
121.practice:
Read this hymn beside the twenty that come before it and one thing stands out. Kutsa — the seer of [[1.94]] through [[1.115]], every hymn in this book from the Agni run through the Rudra and Sūrya hymns — appears here as a *character*, the man for whose sake Indra broke Śuṣṇa. The composer is a different seer, and he is treating his predecessor's name as part of the material. The Ṛgveda's own memory of its makers is visible in a single word.

The verse to keep is 4, and its keyword is a dative. The shut-in cattle are released *ṛtāya*, for the sake of *ṛta*. It is worth pausing on. The same act — forcing an enclosure and letting out what was held — is told elsewhere as a raid and as a rescue; here the reason given is the order of things itself. The Ṛgveda keeps all three descriptions and does not rank them.

Verse 7 is the practical one, because it names who is at the sacrifice: the man who has driven the cart for the firewood, the man who has gone after the cattle, and the quick man. A rite at daybreak is not only priests. There is a pile of logs, and someone brought it.

The closing two verses are the plainest speech in the hymn. Save us from the misfortune that is close at hand — *duritād abhīke* — and let your good thought not fail us. After thirteen verses of cosmology and combat, the request is for protection from what is near, and for a disposition that does not lapse.

For a reader, this hymn is also a useful corrective. Not all of the Ṛgveda is legible. Several verses here resist construction, the translators contradict each other about the actors, and the honest position is that the evidence underdetermines the reading. That is a finding about the corpus, not a failure of attention.
121.disagreements:
Verse 2 is where the readings separate furthest. Wilson has Indra manifesting himself after his own daughter, the dawn, and making the mare unnaturally the mother of a cow — a construction Sāyaṇa supports with the remark that Indra is said, apparently in jest, to have made a mare bring forth a calf. Griffith declines the whole thing: "The Mighty One his self-born host regarded, the horse's mate, the mother of the heifer." Nothing in the padapāṭha decides it.

Verse 7's *pari rodhanā goḥ* has no verb, and Sāyaṇa says so; he supplies the adhvaryu's competence to bind the victim to the stake, and offers an alternative in which *vanadhiti* is a body of clouds ready to rain and *go* is water, so that Indra removes the obstacle to the shower. Wilson prints the first, Griffith the first as well; the second is Sāyaṇa's own and is not visible in either English.

At verse 9 Sāyaṇa identifies the Ṛbhu who brought the bolt from heaven with Tvaṣṭṛ, its fabricator, and glosses Śuṣṇa as drought, so that the whole episode becomes the ending of a dry season. Griffith keeps the demon.

Verse 12 attributes the bolt to Kāvya Uśanā, which Sāyaṇa notes sits awkwardly beside verse 9's attribution to the Ṛbhu; he records the discrepancy without resolving it. Verse 13's Etaśa he glosses both as a horse of the sun and as the name of a seer.

122.title: Viśvedevāḥ Called One by One — and the Gifts Counted
122.synthesis:
Fifteen verses that begin among the gods and end among named patrons and their sons, and the movement between the two is the hymn.

Verse 1 offers the drink to {{rudra}} the bountiful, addressing the priests as *raghumanyavaḥ*, those of light anger; and praises the {{marut}}s of heaven and earth as the heroes of the *asura* of the sky, sent out as arrows from a quiver. Verse 2 puts Uṣāsānaktā, Dawn and Night, together as one pair known in many forms, coming to strengthen the early invocation like a wife; the barren one clothes herself in wide-woven raiment, and {{uṣas}} shines with {{sūrya}}'s splendour and with gold. Verse 3 asks three powers for delight — the one who goes around, the wind who showers the waters, {{indra}} and Parvata — and then, *tan no viśve varivasyantu devāḥ*, may all the gods make room for us.

Verse 4 brings in the poet by his descent: *auśijo huvadhyai*, the son of Uśij calls; make the child of the waters yours, and the two mothers of the living one who shines. Verse 5 names Ghoṣā — I call as Ghoṣā called, for the winning of Arjuna's assent — and asks for Pūṣan's bounty and for {{agni}}'s wealth to be proclaimed. Verse 6 turns to Mitrāvaruṇā: hear these calls of mine, and hear those from every side in the seat of worship; and let {{sindhu}} hear, the giver of good fields, with all his waters. Sindhu is asked to listen along with the gods.

Verse 7 begins the counting. Praised is your gift, {{varuṇa}} and {{mitra}} — a hundred cows to the Pṛkṣayāmas and to the Pajra; brought by the man famed for chariots, they came at once. Verse 8 continues: I praise the bounty of that very wealthy one; may we, men with heroic sons, enjoy it together; he it is who gives to the Pajras and has made me rich in horses and chariots.

Verse 9 is the hymn's hardest sentence and its best. *Jano yo mitrāvaruṇāv abhidhrug apo na vāṃ sunoty akṣṇayādhruk, svayaṃ sa yakṣmaṃ hṛdaye ni dhatta* — the man who wrongs you two, Mitrāvaruṇā, who presses no libation for you, who deceives crookedly, himself lays a wasting sickness in his own heart; whereas the one who keeps {{ṛta}} attains by his offerings. *Yakṣma*, consumption, occurs once in maṇḍala 1, and this is it. Nobody sends the disease. The man puts it there himself.

Verses 10 to 13 praise the patron and his company: strong, urged on, famed among men, liberal, undaunted in every encounter; kings of the immortal, listen to the caller's summons; the gods have declared that they set vigour on the worshipper; we rejoice at the tenfold draught when the twice-five come bearing the food. Verse 14 asks all the gods for a son with golden earrings and a jewelled neck, and for the dawns hastening to the praises of the pious to be pleased with both givers and singers. Verse 15 ends abruptly and personally: four young sons of Maśarśāra and three of the victorious king Āyavasa are troubling me — let your long-shaped, splendour-reined chariot shine like the sun, Mitrāvaruṇā. A hymn to all the gods ends with a specific complaint about seven named men.
122.practice:
Verse 9 is why this hymn matters outside its own occasion. The man who withholds his offering and deals crookedly *lays a yakṣma in his own heart*. Not a curse, not a punishment sent down: he places it there himself, and the verb is reflexive. *Yakṣma* is the corpus's word for wasting sickness, and its only appearance in maṇḍala 1 is here; the hymn devoted entirely to driving it out of a body is 10.163. What this verse claims is that stinginess and crooked dealing are not merely wrong but pathogenic — that they settle in the chest of the person who practises them. The traditional gloss softens it toward the mortification such a man feels when he sees what devotion is rewarded with, which is a psychological reading of a physical word, and a good one.

The second half of the same verse is the balance: *āpa yad īṃ hotrābhir ṛtāvā*, the one who holds to *ṛta* obtains it by his offerings. The two halves make one sentence about where a life ends up, and neither half requires a court.

The other thing to take is structural. This hymn is a Viśvedevāḥ address that turns, halfway through, into a reckoning of who gave what — a hundred cows, horses, chariots — and finishes with a grievance against seven named men. That mixture is characteristic of this seer, and it is worth seeing, because it shows that a hymn to all the gods and a record of a household's patrons and its enemies were not felt to be different kinds of speech.

And Sindhu asked to listen in verse 6, "with all his waters," is worth marking. The river is addressed alongside Mitra and Varuṇa as one of the hearers, not as scenery.
122.disagreements:
Verse 9 is where Sāyaṇa's gloss is most valuable and most interpretive. He explains *akṣṇayā dhruk* as offending "by a wheel or a way," which he resolves to "in another manner," and then reads the *yakṣma* in the heart as sickness in general, adding that the reference may be to the mortification felt by those who neglect the gods when they see the blessings devotion brings. Wilson prints the sickness; Griffith prints "a wasting sickness" and keeps it literal.

Verse 5's Ghoṣā divides everything. Sāyaṇa's reading of her in [[1.117]].7 as a woman cured of a whitening skin disease produces Wilson's "in like manner as Ghoṣā praised you for the removal of her white-tinted skin," a whole clause with no basis in the padapāṭha of this verse. Griffith reads simply "as, to win Arjuna's assent, cried Ghosa."

Verse 13's *daśatayasya dhāseḥ* Sāyaṇa glosses in two ways — the ten *indriyas*, the organs of sense, whose vigour the food increases; or Soma offered in ten ladles — and Wilson prints both in brackets. Griffith keeps "the tenfold present."

Verse 15's names both translators keep, and neither can say who Maśarśāra and Āyavasa were. Sāyaṇa glosses only *śiśvaḥ* as childish. This is a place where the evidence simply runs out.

123.title: Uṣas Comes First, House by House, Never Breaking Ṛta
123.synthesis:
*Pṛthū ratho dakṣiṇāyā ayoji* — the broad chariot of Dakṣiṇā has been yoked; the immortal gods have mounted it; and the noble, wide-reaching one has risen up out of the black, *cikitsantī mānuṣāya kṣayāya* — seeking to heal the human dwelling. That participle, from the root that gives *cikitsā*, medicine, occurs once in the whole Ṛgveda, and it is here, in the first verse of an {{uṣas}} hymn. The dawn is described as a physician making a call.

Verse 2 states her precedence: she has woken before all the world, the lofty one who wins *{{vāja}}* and gathers; ever young and reborn, she looks out from on high; Uṣas has come first to the morning invocation. Verse 3 turns that into a request with a legal shape — if today you apportion a share among mortals, well-born goddess, then may Savitṛ of the house declare us free of offence before {{sūrya}}. The day's distribution is made at dawn, and what the singer asks is to be certified blameless before the sun sees him.

Verse 4 is her circuit. *Gṛhaṃ-gṛham ahanā yāti acchā*, house by house she goes, taking on a name day after day; wanting to win, she has come shining always, and she takes for herself the foremost of the goods. Verse 5 gives her a family: sister of Bhaga, kinswoman of {{varuṇa}}, *sūnṛtā* — she of true and generous speech — be praised first; let the one who makes evil fall behind; may we overcome him with the chariot of Dakṣiṇā. Verse 6 is the morning itself: let true words rise up, let full thoughts rise; the kindled fires have stood; and the desirable goods that darkness had hidden the shining dawns make plain.

Verse 7 is the pair of days: one goes off and the other comes; the two unlike days move together; one of them hides the darkness of the surrounding two; Uṣas has shone with her blazing chariot. Verse 8 measures her: the same today, the same tomorrow, they follow the long ordinance of Varuṇa; blameless, thirty *yojanas* apiece, each goes round its purpose in a moment. Verse 9 says what she does not do: knowing the name of the first day, white she is born from the black, and *ṛtasya yoṣā na mināti dhāma* — the maiden does not diminish the ordinance of {{ṛta}}, coming day by day to the place appointed.

Verses 10 and 11 are the hymn's frankest. Like a girl proud of her body you go, goddess, to the god who desires you; smiling, young, from the east, you make your breast manifest as you shine. Fair as a bride adorned by her mother, you make your body plain to be seen; be auspicious, Uṣas, shine wider still — no other dawns have reached what you reach. Nothing is euphemised, and nothing is leered at; the description is of a woman who knows she is beautiful and of a light that is not hiding.

Verse 12 is the plural again: rich in horses, rich in cattle, all-desirable, contending with Sūrya's rays, they go away and come back, carrying an auspicious name. And verse 13 is the request the whole hymn has been building toward: *ṛtasya raśmim anuyacchamānā bhadraṃ-bhadraṃ kratum asmāsu dhehi* — holding to the rein of *ṛta*, place in us good purpose upon good purpose; shine on us today, easily invoked; may wealth be with us and with those who give.
123.practice:
The last verse is the one to learn. *Ṛtasya raśmim anuyacchamānā, bhadraṃ-bhadraṃ kratum asmāsu dhehi* — she who holds to the rein of *ṛta*, put good purpose in us, good upon good. The image is of a driver keeping to a rein, and what is asked for is not wealth first but *kratu*, the resolve that gets things done rightly. The wealth comes in the last line, after.

Verse 9 is the pair to it: the maiden *does not diminish the ordinance of ṛta*, coming day by day to the appointed place. Between the two verses the hymn says the same thing twice — she keeps to the order, and please put in us whatever it is that lets her do that. This is the most direct statement in the Uṣas material of what a person is supposed to learn from watching a sunrise. Not awe. Regularity.

*Cikitsantī* in verse 1 is worth carrying too, because it is the only occurrence of the form in the collection: she rises out of the darkness *seeking to heal the human dwelling*. The word behind it is the same one behind *cikitsā*, the ordinary Sanskrit word for medical treatment. Darkness is treated as a condition and daylight as its remedy.

Verse 4's *gṛhaṃ-gṛham* — house by house, day by day — is the hymn's picture of how a large power meets an ordinary life: not once and impressively, but repeatedly and at everybody's door. Twenty sūktas in the Ṛgveda are addressed to Uṣas alone, five of them in this maṇḍala, and no other deity is so consistently described as arriving where people live rather than being visited.

And verses 10 and 11 are worth reading without flinching. The tradition's oldest picture of a goddess includes a young woman conscious of her beauty, adorned by her mother, uncovering herself to be seen. It is a description of daybreak, and it is also, plainly, a description of a woman.
123.disagreements:
Verse 1's Dakṣiṇā is where the readings diverge first. Sāyaṇa reads *dakṣiṇāyāḥ* as "of the skilled one," she who is expert in her own work, and Wilson accordingly writes "the spacious chariot of the graceful dawn"; Griffith keeps Dakṣiṇā as a name, "the Daksina's broad chariot." The word means both the priestly fee and skill, and the hymn returns to it in verse 5, where the chariot of Dakṣiṇā is the means of overcoming the evildoer.

Verse 8's thirty *yojanas* drew from Sāyaṇa the longest astronomical note in this part of the bhāṣya: Varuṇa is the sun, circling Mount Meru daily, with the dawn always thirty yojanas ahead of his appearance; he then computes the duration of dawn in *ghaṭikās* and *paras* and cites the Purāṇas for the sun's daily journey. Wilson prints the thirty yojanas as a measure of distance; Griffith turns them into "thirty regions."

Verse 4's *ahanā* Sāyaṇa identifies with Uṣas herself on the authority of the Nirukta; Wilson prints "Ahana" as a name, Griffith dissolves it.

Verse 2's *jayantī vājam* Sāyaṇa reads either as conquering the departing darkness or as winning food, citing the Śatapatha that *vāja* is food. Both translators take the second.

124.title: Uṣas: Wake the Giver, Let the Paṇis Sleep On
124.synthesis:
The hymn begins with three things happening at once. {{uṣas}} shining out as {{agni}} is kindled; {{sūrya}} rising and spreading his light wide; and Savitṛ — *devo naḥ atra savitā nu arthaṃ pra asāvīt* — impelling us to our business, two-footed and four-footed, to get going. The first verse of the sūkta is a household at daybreak: a fire lit, light in the sky, and everybody sent to work.

Verse 2 sets the long view in a single line that is one of the most quoted in the Uṣas material: not violating the divine ordinances, though wearing away human generations, she shines — *īyuṣīṇām upamā śaśvatīnām āyatīnāṃ prathamā*, the last of the endless ones that have gone, the first of those that come. She is doing two contradictory things — keeping the divine law and using up human lives — and the verse does not soften either.

Verse 3 has her seen in the east, clothed in light, going straight along the path of {{ṛta}}, and — the detail that matters — *prajānatīva na diśo mināti*, like one who knows, she does not confuse the directions. Verse 4 heaps up similes: seen near, like the breast of the bright one; like Nodhas she has made dear things manifest; like a housewife she wakes the sleepers; of all who return, the most constant. Verse 5 has her in the east half of the watery region, mother of cows, raising her banner, spreading wider and wider, filling the laps of both her parents.

Verse 6 is the ethical one and it is simply stated: she is very great to look on, and *na ajāmiṃ na pari vṛṇakti jāmim* — she excludes neither the stranger nor the kinsman; proud of her spotless body, shining, she does not shrink from the small or from the great. Nothing else in the range says as plainly that light is not distributed by merit.

Verse 7 is a run of four comparisons for the same movement. Like a woman with no brother, going toward the men of her family; like one mounting the stand for the winning of wealth; like a wife eager for her husband, well-dressed; and Uṣas, as if smiling, uncovers her beauty. Verse 8 is the handover: the sister has given up her place to the elder sister, and having looked at her, goes away; shining with Sūrya's rays she paints herself, like women going in a company to a festival. Verse 9 makes it a sequence: of all the sisters who have gone before, a later follows the earlier day by day; so, new like the old, may the dawns shine on us richly with good days.

Verse 10 is the hymn's most famous line and its hardest. *Pra bodhaya uṣaḥ pṛṇato maghony abudhyamānāḥ paṇayaḥ sasantu* — wake up the givers, wealthy Uṣas; let the {{paṇi}}s, the withholders, sleep on unwoken. Shine richly for the liberal, richly for the singer, you who are true speech and who wear life away. Twice in maṇḍala 1 the withholders are named in the plural, and here they are simply left asleep.

Verse 11 has her harnessing her team of ruddy oxen from the east; she will shine, the light will hurry, and Agni will be present in every house. Verse 12 watches the world get up: the birds have flown from their nests and the men who need food are on their feet at her shining — and to the one who stays at home and gives, goddess, you bring much good. Verse 13 closes with thanks rather than a request: you have been praised, you praiseworthy ones, and you have increased us by my *brahman*; goddesses, by your favour may we win by hundreds and by thousands.
124.practice:
Verse 10 is the verse this hymn is known by, and it is worth being exact about what it says. Uṣas is asked to wake the givers and to leave the Paṇis asleep. Nothing is asked against them — no harm, no punishment. They simply do not get the morning. In a collection that is often very direct about wanting enemies broken, this is a different kind of severity: the withholders are excluded by being allowed to go on sleeping.

Set that beside verse 6, four verses earlier, where the same goddess *excludes neither stranger nor kinsman* and does not shrink from the small or from the great. The two verses sit in one hymn without contradiction, and the difference is instructive. The light falls on everyone; what a person does with the hour is his own business, and the man who has nothing to give also has no reason to get up.

Verse 1 is the household verse: Agni is kindled, the sun rises, and Savitṛ impels *dvipat* and *catuṣpat*, the two-footed and the four-footed, to their work. The morning is not described as a devotional interval; it is described as the start of the day's labour, with the animals included.

Verse 2 gives the double truth about time that the Uṣas hymns keep returning to: she does not violate the divine ordinances, and she wears away human generations. Both clauses are in one line. She is regular and she is consuming. In verse 10 she is even addressed as *jarayantī*, the one who ages things, in the same breath as she is asked to shine on the singer.

And verse 12's last clause is a small kindness worth noting: to the mortal who stays at home and gives, she brings much good. A hymn that has just sent the birds out of their nests and the men out after food finishes by saying that the one who did not go anywhere is not forgotten.
124.disagreements:
Verse 7's four similes are where Sāyaṇa's social knowledge is most on display and most disputed. *Abhrāteva puṃsa eti pratīcī* he takes as a woman with no brother, turned away from her own house and dependent on her male relatives — or, on his second thought, one who must herself offer the funeral cakes to her ancestors. For *gartārug iva sanaye dhanānām* he glosses *garta* as a house, and then as the board on which dice are thrown, and reports a practice by which a childless widow seeks support from her husband's relatives at a gambling house. Wilson prints "one ascending the hall of justice for the recovery of property"; Griffith reads simply "mounting her car, as 'twere to gather riches." None of this is settled.

Verse 4's *śundhyuvo na vakṣaḥ* Sāyaṇa gives three ways: the collective rays of the sun; a white water-bird whose plumage the morning light resembles; or, on the Nirukta, the waters. Griffith prints "the Bright One's bosom"; Wilson, "the breast of the illuminator."

Verse 6's *jāmi* and *ajāmi* Sāyaṇa reads as of the same species and of another — gods and men — rather than as kin and stranger, and adds that she lights everything from an atom to a mountain. Both translators keep the human reading.

Verse 10's Paṇis Wilson renders as "niggard traders" and Griffith as "niggard traffickers," both importing the commercial sense the word carries elsewhere.

125.title: The Gift Given at Dawn, and What Comes of Giving
125.synthesis:
This sūkta is not addressed to a god. The Anukramaṇī gives its deity as *svanayasya dānastutiḥ*, the praise of Svanaya's gift, and all seven verses are about what happens when one man gives something to another. Of the nineteen sūktas in the collection whose entries name a *dānastuti*, only two are a *dānastuti* from beginning to end; this is one of them, and it stands first in the collection's order.

Verse 1 states the transaction in the third person, as a general law. *Prātar ratnaṃ prātaritvā dadhāti* — the one who comes early in the morning sets down a treasure; the discerning man, receiving it, takes it in; and thereby, increasing his offspring and his lifetime, he lives with brave sons in the fullness of wealth. Two people, neither named yet, and a benefit that flows to both.

Verse 2 turns to the giver's side: may he be rich in cattle, in gold, in horses; {{indra}} sets great vigour on him — on the man who stops you as you come, early-comer, with his wealth, as game is caught in a net. The image is startling and affectionate. The patron detains the guest with gifts the way a hunter takes an animal in a snare; being caught is the good outcome.

Verse 3 puts the speaker into it. *Āyam adya sukṛtaṃ prātar icchan* — I have come today at dawn seeking the well-doer, the son of the sacrifice, with a chariot heavy with goods. Give him the pressed stalk of the exhilarating one to drink; increase the *kṣayadvīra* with true and generous speech. Everything in the hymn happens at daybreak, and the poet's own arrival is the same arrival the first verse described.

Verses 4 and 5 leave the two men and describe what surrounds a giver. The rivers flow toward him, bringing ease; the milch-cows yield for the one who has sacrificed and for the one who is about to; streams of ghee come from every side toward the man who fills and satisfies. And then the largest claim: *nākasya pṛṣṭhe adhi tiṣṭhati śritaḥ* — he stands established on the back of the firmament; the one who gives goes among the gods; for him the waters run ghee; for him this *{{dakṣiṇā}}* swells always.

Verse 6 is the hymn's centre and one of the most concentrated verses in maṇḍala 1. *Dakṣiṇāvatām id imāni citrā, dakṣiṇāvatāṃ divi sūryāsaḥ, dakṣiṇāvanto amṛtaṃ bhajante, dakṣiṇāvantaḥ pra tiranta āyuḥ.* Four times in four lines: for those who give the *dakṣiṇā* are these bright things; for those who give, the suns in heaven; those who give have a share in the deathless; those who give lengthen their life. The word appears ten times in the whole Ṛgveda and four of the ten are in this one verse.

Verse 7 turns it round and closes. May those who give never come to harm or to sin; may the patrons of good vows not wither; may some other be the enclosing defence around them — and may griefs fall on the man who does not give. The last line is a curse, and it is the only harsh thing in the hymn.
125.practice:
*Dakṣiṇā* is the gift made at the close of a rite, and it is the ancestor of everything from the fee handed to a priest at a wedding to what is put in the hand at a house-blessing. Verse 6 is the tradition's oldest and most emphatic statement of what it does. Four clauses, one subject repeated four times: the bright things, the suns in heaven, a share in the deathless, and a longer life — all of them *dakṣiṇāvatām*, of those who give.

That the word occurs ten times in the entire Ṛgveda and four of those are in this single verse tells you something about how the hymn works. It is not arguing. It is hammering.

Verse 5 is the claim that carries furthest: *yaḥ pṛṇāti sa ha deveṣu gacchati* — the one who fills up, who satisfies, goes among the gods. Giving is described as a means of transit, and the destination is not a reward stored up but a place already reached, *nākasya pṛṣṭhe*, on the back of the firmament. Whatever later Hinduism does with *dāna*, it does not have to invent the idea.

The hour matters. Everything in this hymn happens *prātar*, at daybreak — the giver comes early, the receiver receives early, the poet arrives at dawn seeking the man who does well. This is the same hour as the surrounding Uṣas hymns, [[1.123]] and [[1.124]], and the last of those asks the dawn to wake the givers and let the withholders sleep. Read consecutively, the three make one statement: the day begins, the generous get up, and this is what follows for them.

The one thing to be honest about is that this is a poet praising his own patron and hoping to be paid again. The hymn does not conceal it. What is worth noticing is that the tradition kept a poem of that kind in the collection and gave it a deity slot of its own.
125.disagreements:
Sāyaṇa supplies the occasion, and without it verse 3 has no referent. Kakṣīvat, having finished his studies and taken leave of his teacher, fell asleep by the roadside on the way home; Rājā Svanaya, son of Bhāvayavya, passing with his retinue, disturbed him, was struck by the young brāhmaṇa, married ten of his daughters to him, and gave him a hundred *niṣkas* of gold, a hundred horses, a hundred bulls, a thousand and sixty cows and eleven chariots. Kakṣīvat took the whole of it home to his father Dīrghatamas. Every one of those figures is itemised in the next sūkta, [[1.126]].

Verse 4's *pṛṇantaṃ ca papuriṃ ca* Sāyaṇa distributes: the first he applies to the Fathers, the one who satisfies his ancestors; the second to all living beings. Wilson prints the distinction — "propitiates his progenitors, and benefits mankind" — where Griffith keeps one giver, "him who freely gives and fills on all sides."

Verse 5's *iyaṃ dakṣiṇā* Sāyaṇa reads as the earth, deriving it from *dakṣa*, able, the earth being able to bear crops. Griffith keeps the gift: "to him this guerdon ever yields abundance."

Verse 7's *anyas teṣāṃ paridhir astu kaścit* is opaque, and Sāyaṇa offers four fillings for the "some other" — another man, or a divinity, or a particular merit, or Svanaya himself as the type of the protector. Neither translator chooses.

126.title: Kakṣīvān Counts Svanaya's Gift — then Romaśā Speaks
126.synthesis:
Seven verses, and the Anukramaṇī divides them among three voices: verses 1 to 5 to {{kakṣīvant}}, verse 6 to Svanaya Bhāvayavya, and verse 7 to Romaśā. That is unusual enough on its own; the last two verses are also in a different metre from the first five, and they are about something else entirely.

Verse 1 sets the hymn as praise offered with the mind: I bring forth unstinting praises of Bhavya, who dwells upon the {{sindhu}} — an unconquered king seeking fame, who measured out a thousand pressings for me. Verse 2 begins the counting and puts the poet's name in the middle of it. *Śataṃ rājño nādhamānasya niṣkān, śatam aśvān prayatān sadyo ādam, śataṃ kakṣīvān asurasya gonām* — a hundred *niṣkas* from the beseeching king, a hundred horses offered, I took at once; a hundred of the lord's cattle — I, Kakṣīvān; and he has stretched his imperishable fame to heaven. The *niṣka*, a weight of gold, is named once in the whole Ṛgveda, and this is it.

Verse 3 continues the inventory with a detail that changes its character: dusky horses given by Svanaya stood beside me, ten chariots *vadhūmantaḥ* — with women in them; and sixty thousand cattle followed after; Kakṣīvān won them at the closing of the days. The wives come with the herds, in the same list, counted the same way. Verse 4 has forty bays of the master of the ten chariots leading the procession in front of a thousand, and the Pajras, the poet's own kin, rubbing down the spirited horses decked with pearl. Verse 5 accepts an earlier gift on behalf of the family — three yoked and eight cows of great price — and hopes that the kindly Pajras, like clans bound by mutual affection, may seek fame with their carts.

Then the hymn stops, and two people speak. Verse 6, in the husband's voice: clinging, closely clinging, she who has hidden herself like a mongoose gives me a hundred joys. Verse 7, in Romaśā's: *upopa me parā mṛśa, mā me dabhrāṇi manyathāḥ, sarvāham asmi romaśā gandhārīṇām ivāvikā* — come close, come closer, touch me; do not think there is little of me; I am all over hairy, like a ewe of the Gandhāris.

The two verses are an exchange between a wife and her husband about her body, and she has the last word and the better line. Her name, Romaśā, is the ordinary adjective for "hairy" made into a name, and her reply plays on it. The Anukramaṇī records her as the ṛṣi of the verse — she is not being quoted, she is credited with composing it.

Nothing in the hymn prepares for this and nothing follows it. The collection sets a scrupulous accounting of gold, horses, chariots and sixty thousand cattle beside two verses of a married couple in bed, and gives them the same sūkta number. Read as a whole, the effect is not incongruity but completeness: what a great gift finally amounts to is a household, and this is what a household sounds like from inside.
126.practice:
Two things here are unusual enough to be worth knowing, and both are countable.

Romaśā is one of the small number of women the Anukramaṇī names as *ṛṣi*, and in the order of the collection she is the first. The others come later — Lopāmudrā at [[1.179]], Viśvavārā in maṇḍala 5, Apālā in 8, and in maṇḍala 10 Ghoṣā, Yamī, Urvaśī, Indrāṇī, Śraddhā, Śacī, Sūryā Sāvitrī and Vāc Āmbhṛṇī. Ghoṣā, who composes 10.39 and 10.40, is this same seer's daughter, named in his own hymns at [[1.117]].7 and [[1.122]].5. A single family in this book therefore contains a father who is a major ṛṣi, a woman he names in his verses, and a daughter credited with two hymns of her own.

The second is Gandhāra. The name appears once in the entire Ṛgveda, in Romaśā's verse, as the source of a particularly woolly sheep. The one occurrence of a region that will matter enormously later is a woman's simile for her own body.

For a reader, the hymn's value is in refusing to be embarrassed. The Ṛgveda is often received as either a liturgical or a philosophical document, and it is both; it is also a record of people who counted their cattle carefully and who talked to their spouses at night. That the collection kept these two verses, in a different metre, attached to a receipt for sixty thousand cows, is worth more than any argument about how wide the tradition's range is.

The counting itself is worth reading as a document. A hundred gold *niṣkas*, a hundred horses, a hundred bulls, sixty thousand cattle, ten chariots with the brides in them, forty bay horses at the head of a thousand. This is what a royal gift looked like, itemised by the man who received it, and it is the concrete backing for the general claims made in the preceding sūkta, [[1.125]], about what giving does for the giver.
126.disagreements:
Sāyaṇa's account is what makes the numbers legible: Kakṣīvat, returning from his teacher, slept by the road; Svanaya son of Bhāvayavya passed, was impressed, gave him ten daughters in marriage and made over a hundred *niṣkas*, a hundred horses, a hundred bulls, one thousand and sixty cows and eleven four-horse chariots. The verse itself says sixty thousand cattle, which the gloss does not match; Wilson prints "a thousand and sixty," Griffith "sixty thousand."

Verse 1's *sindhau adhi kṣiyataḥ* Sāyaṇa allows to be either the river Sindhu or the sea-shore. Verse 2's *niṣka* he sizes at four *suvarṇas* on the Manusmṛti and at a hundred and eight on the Amarakośa, recording the discrepancy rather than settling it. On verse 5 he suggests that the three and the eight may be a way of saying eleven.

Verses 6 and 7 are the one place in this range where a translator refused the job. Griffith prints both in Latin rather than English; Wilson prints them in English but with the sense blunted. The Latin is a Victorian decision, not a textual one.

On verses 6 and 7 Sāyaṇa identifies the speakers as Bhāvya and his wife Lomaśā, and glosses the mongoose as a female that has just borne young. He then remarks that the two verses are brought in abruptly and in a different metre, and suggests they may echo an older popular song — an observation that concedes the strangeness rather than explaining it away.

179.title: Lopāmudrā Tells Agastya the Waiting Is Over
179.synthesis:
Six verses and three speakers. The Anukramaṇī gives the first two to Lopāmudrā, the next two to Agastya, and the last two to a *brahmacārin*, a student of his — and names the deity of the whole as *rati*, the pleasure of union, which it does for no other sūkta in the Ṛgveda.

Lopāmudrā speaks first, and she opens with a count of time. *Pūrvīr ahaṃ śaradaḥ śaśramāṇā* — for many autumns I have worn myself out, through nights and daybreaks and the dawns that bring on age. Then the observation that everything follows from: *mināti śriyaṃ jarimā tanūnām*, old age diminishes the beauty of bodies. And then the request, put in the third person and the plural, so that it is a statement about how things should be rather than a personal demand: *api nu patnīr vṛṣaṇo jagamyuḥ*, let husbands, then, come to their wives.

Her second verse is an argument, and it is a theological one. *Ye cid hi pūrve ṛtasāpaḥ āsan* — even those of old who kept to {{ṛta}}, who spoke the truths *sākaṃ devebhiḥ*, together with the gods: *te cid avāsuḥ, nahi antam āpuḥ*, even they left off, and they did not reach the end. The point is exact and hard to answer. Austerity has no terminus. The greatest of the ancients stopped, and stopping was not failure, because there was nothing there to arrive at. Therefore, she repeats, let wives come together with their husbands.

Agastya answers, and his first word is a concession dressed as doctrine. *Na mṛṣā śrāntam* — the toil is not wasted, since the gods favour it. Then he shifts entirely into the first person dual: let us two overcome all rivals, let us win this contest of a hundred stratagems, since we two, going together as a matched pair, drive it forward. Everything from here is *āvām*, we two. Whatever the years of austerity were, they were his; the victory he now proposes is shared.

His second verse is candid to a degree that later translators could not print. Desire has come upon me, he says — from here, from there, from wherever it was born — and then, of his wife: *lopāmudrā vṛṣaṇaṃ niḥ riṇāti*, Lopāmudrā draws the bull out; *adhīrā dhayati śvasantam*, the unsteady one drinks down the steady, panting one. He names her, and the naming is the only occurrence of her name in the whole Ṛgveda.

The last two verses belong to the student, and they change the subject to conscience. This Soma, drunk close at hand within the hearts, I address: whatever fault we have committed, let it be forgiven — *pulukāmo hi martyaḥ*, for a man is full of many desires (v5). It is not clear from the text what the fault was, and the honest thing is to say so.

The sixth verse closes the whole thing as a life rather than an episode. *Agastyaḥ khanamānaḥ khanitraiḥ* — Agastya, digging with digging tools, wanting progeny, offspring and strength: the fierce ṛṣi nourished *ubhau varṇau*, both classes, and his true wishes went home among the gods. The hymn ends by saying that the man in the middle of it got what he asked for, and that he did not have to give up either half of his life to get it.
179.practice:
No other hymn in the Ṛgveda is as directly about a marriage, and none is as directly about the collision between austerity and a household. A woman says she has spent many autumns waiting, that bodies do not stay beautiful, and that even the greatest ascetics of old stopped short of any end. Her husband agrees, in public, in a hymn that was preserved.

Verse 2 is her argument and it is worth having in full. Those who kept ṛta and spoke with the gods *did not reach the end* — *nahi antam āpuḥ*. She is not saying austerity is worthless; she is saying it has no finish line, and that a life spent waiting for one is a life spent. Anyone who has postponed a marriage, a child, or a life for a discipline that keeps receding will find their own position stated here, in the oldest book the tradition has, and answered.

Verse 6 is the tradition's own resolution, and it is why this hymn matters beyond its frankness. Agastya *ubhau varṇau pupoṣa* — nourished both classes. The commentators read the two as *kāma* and *tapas*, the obligations of the householder and those of the ascetic, and the verse says he fed both and that his prayers were answered. The four-āśrama scheme is not in the Ṛgveda; but this verse is where the tradition later pointed when it wanted to say that the two lives are not rivals.

The name Lopāmudrā occurs once in the entire Ṛgveda, in verse 4 of this hymn. She is the ṛṣi of two of its verses. And the deity the Anukramaṇī assigns is *rati* — again, once in the whole collection.

And verse 5 is a good thing to know by heart, whatever the fault behind it was: *pulukāmo hi martyaḥ*, a mortal is full of many desires. The Ṛgveda offers it as a reason for mercy rather than as an accusation.
179.disagreements:
The most informative fact about how this hymn has been read is what Griffith did with it: he rendered verses 3 and 4, and the extra material his text carries at the end, into Latin rather than English, the Victorian convention for passages held unfit to print. A reader in 1896 could not learn what Lopāmudrā and Agastya said to each other unless he had Latin. Wilson translates but softens: his verse 2 has the ancient sages "begot (progeny), nor thereby violated (their vow of continence)," which supplies both the begetting and the excuse. The Sanskrit says only *te cid avāsuḥ, nahi antam āpuḥ* — even they desisted; they did not reach the end.

Sāyaṇa handles verse 5 by removing the drink. *Antito hṛtsu pītam*, he says, means drunk mentally and not actually; and he identifies the fault being confessed as the students' having overheard their teacher's conversation with his wife. Nothing in the verse says this; it is a reading rather than a datum — but it is the tradition trying to explain why a pupil is apologising in the middle of somebody else's marriage.

On verse 6 Sāyaṇa glosses *ubhau varṇau* as *kāma* and *tapas*, the duties of domestic and of ascetic life, and reads *khanamānaḥ khanitraiḥ*, digging with digging tools, as achieving one's ends by the appropriate means. On verse 4's "from here, from there" he offers your wife's company, the influence of a season such as spring, or the promptings of this world or the next.
179.note: lopāmudrā verified as occurring once in all ten padapāṭha files, at 1.179.4; ratiḥ verified as devatā of exactly one sūkta across all ten Anukramaṇī files; the Griffith text in this repository prints vv3-4 in Latin and its verse divisions for this sūkta do not align with the padapāṭha

180.title: Atri's Heat Cooled, Milk Restored — the Aśvins' Car
180.synthesis:
The first of five consecutive hymns to the {{aśvin}}au that close out this stretch of maṇḍala 1. Ten verses in triṣṭubh, and most of them are about a chariot and the things it has been used for.

It opens in motion. Your well-guided horses cross the regions when your chariot flies round the floods; *hiraṇyayā vām pavayaḥ pruṣāyan*, your golden felly-rims scatter drops as they turn; and drinking the sweet, you keep company with the dawns (v1). Wheels that throw off moisture as they go — the image will return in the fourth verse and in the last.

The second verse has them overtaking a swift flier, the manly and much-worshipped one, while their sister, praised everywhere, carries for them; and the prayer is made *vājāya iṣe ca*, for strength and for refreshment. The third gives the first of the miracles: *yuvaṃ payaḥ usriyāyām adhattam* — you placed milk in the cow; you set the ripened, the ancient, down inside the raw. Something already finished is put back into something not yet ready. The pure offerer worships you, whose very forms are {{ṛta}}.

The fourth names a man. *Yuvaṃ ha gharmaṃ madhumantam atraye* — you made the burning heat honey-sweet for Atri when he wished it, like a rush of water; therefore Agni-offering is yours, Aśvin men, and your chariot wheels come toward us like springs of honey. The heat that was killing a man is turned into sweetness, and the same wheels that scattered drops in verse 1 now arrive as wells.

The fifth verse names another, obliquely: may I turn you toward giving, *dasrā*, by praise, as did the worn-out son of Tugra. Earth and heaven attend your greatness, and *jūrṇo vām akṣur aṃhasaḥ*, the net of distress is worn out for you. The sixth asks for the ordinary version of all this: when you yoke down your teams, good givers, you let *puraṃdhi*, abundance of thought, loose by your own powers; let the patron be quick as the wind to serve you, and take his *vāja* like a man who keeps his vows.

The seventh is a small piece of theatre: we singers, truthful, praise you in many ways; the *paṇi* is set aside; and now, blameless ones, bulls, protect the man who has a god close by. Whatever *paṇi* means here — the vessel, or the trader who gives nothing — something has been put out of the way to make room.

The eighth verse names the poet himself. Day after day, Aśvins, Agastya — renowned among men — roused you with thousands, *kārādhunīva*, like a thing that makes sound, for the winning of the great outflowing torrent. The ninth asks that when they drive on in the chariot's greatness, and go speeding like the *hotā* of Manu, they give the patrons horses, so that the singers may be attended by wealth.

And the tenth calls the chariot itself. *Tam vāṃ rathaṃ vayam adya huvema* — that chariot of yours we call today with our *stoma*s, new, for our wellbeing, *ariṣṭanemim*, whose felly is unbroken, going round the sky. Then the seal: *vidyāma iṣaṃ vṛjanaṃ jīradānum*. The hymn ends where it began, on the wheel — but now the wheel is asked for by name, and the quality asked of it is that nothing on it be damaged.
180.practice:
The {{aśvin}}au are the rescuers, and this hymn is a short list of rescues. Sixty-eight sūktas name them across the Ṛgveda — more than any deity except {{indra}}, {{agni}} and the {{marut}}s — and five of them stand consecutively here, this one through [[1.184]].

What is being remembered in verses 3 to 5 is a particular kind of help. Milk put back into a cow that had none. A killing heat made sweet for Atri when he asked. The worn-out son of Tugra, who in the fuller tellings elsewhere is pulled out of the sea. These are not victories over enemies. They are reversals of situations that had already gone wrong — the barren made to yield, the burning made bearable, the drowning brought up. The tradition kept the Aśvins as *devānāṃ bhiṣajau*, the physicians among the gods, and this is the material that stands behind it. Where the concern is illness, exhaustion or a body that has stopped doing what it should, these are the verses.

Verse 4's *gharma* is worth knowing as a word. It is the heat, and it is also the name of the heated milk-offering of the pravargya rite. What the Aśvins do for Atri is described in a term that is at once his suffering and an oblation — the heat that was destroying him becomes the sweet thing that is poured.

Verse 8 is where Agastya signs his own name in the middle of the hymn, and describes his praise as *kārādhunī iva*, like something that makes a sound — the commentators think of a conch. He is not claiming eloquence. He is claiming to have made a noise, daily, until they came.

And the last verse asks for exactly the right thing from a vehicle: *ariṣṭanemi*, an unbroken rim. Not a faster chariot. One that will not fail on the way.
180.disagreements:
Verse 7's *vipaṇir hitāvān* is genuinely unsettled and Sāyaṇa lays out the options. *Paṇi* may be the *droṇakalaśa*, the vessel into which the pressed soma is strained — in which case the line says the jar has been set in place, which is how Wilson prints it. Or *paṇi* may be the trader, the niggard, with *vi* read as "let him be separated": let the stingy rich man who offers no worship be cast out. Griffith takes that second road — "the niggard trafficker is here excluded" — so that one translator has a vessel being made ready and the other a man being thrown out.

Verse 3's simile parts them just as far. Wilson has the offerer worshipping "as a thief (in the midst) of a thicket"; Griffith has him "shining like a serpent mid trees." The word behind it is *hvāra*, and neither reading can be ruled out.

On verse 4 Sāyaṇa explains *paśvaḥ iṣṭi* by identifying the *paśu* with Agni, citing the formula that Agni was the victim, and concludes that the oblations reach the Aśvins through fire. Wilson follows him and prints "the fire-offering."

On verse 8's *kārādhunī* Sāyaṇa derives it from *kārā*, sound, and *dhuni*, generating — something that produces noise, such as a conch. Wilson gives "an instrument of sound"; Griffith, "like sounds of music."
180.note: agastyaḥ verified in the padapāṭha at 1.180.8; aśvinau ascriptions counted across all ten Anukramaṇī files (68 sūktas), of which 1.180-1.184 are consecutive

146.title: The Three-Headed Agni and His Two Mothers
146.synthesis:
Five verses, and the sūkta is held together by a family. {{agni}} has parents, he has two mothers who are cows, he is their calf, and by the last verse he is himself the father of a great many.

*Trimūrdhānaṃ saptaraśmiṃ gṛṇīṣe* — I sing the three-headed, seven-rayed Agni, who is *anūna*, lacking nothing, seated in the lap of his two parents. The numbers come first and without explanation: three heads, seven beams. And then the reach: he has filled all the shining spaces of heaven that belong to what moves and what stands still. A god sitting in his parents' lap and filling the sky is the first thing this hymn asks a reader to hold together.

The second verse grows him. The great bull swelled toward these two; unaging, he stood — lofty, his help coming from here. He sets his foot down on the ridge of the wide earth, and his ruddy ones lick the udder.
