The last clause is the hymn in miniature: flames described as calves at the teat, feeding on what is above them.

The third verse gives us the two cows themselves, and it is the strangest verse in the sūkta. Coming together toward one common calf, the two well-shaped *dhenu*s range apart in every direction — measuring out roads that cannot be dodged, and holding all the *keta*s, all the marks by which things are known, in the great one. Whoever the two are, what they do is lay out paths nobody can avoid and deposit knowledge in the calf. They meet at him and spread from him.

The fourth verse brings people in for the only time. *Dhīrāsaḥ padaṃ kavayo nayanti* — the steady ones, the *kavi*s, lead his footprint; guarding the unaging one variously in the heart. Wanting to win him, they looked all round for the {{sindhu}}, for the stream; and Sūrya became visible to them, to those men. What they were searching for was water, and what appeared was the sun. The hymn does not connect the two clauses, and neither should a reader — except to note that the seeking and the appearing are put in one verse, and that what they had in their hearts was already the god they were looking for.

The fifth closes on his fatherhood. He is *didṛkṣeṇya*, worth wanting to see, in all the quarters; victorious; to be invoked; and he is there for the life of the great and of the small alike. Because in many places at once he became the begetter — the *maghavan*, visible to everyone, of these that come from the womb. The calf of verse 3 is the sire of verse 5, and the hymn has not troubled to explain how; it simply reports that fire is both, everywhere, and that its light is for large and small on the same terms.

What holds the five verses is not an argument but a set of relations. Two parents, two cows, one calf, many offspring; three heads, seven rays; a footprint led by men who already carry him in their hearts. The sūkta is short and its terms are all family terms, and its one general statement is the one worth taking away: *mahaḥ arbhāya jīvase*, for the living of the great and of the small.
146.practice:
The numbers in the first verse are the durable ones. Three heads and seven rays have stayed attached to {{agni}} throughout the tradition, and the readings the commentary gives for the three are all live: the three daily rites; the three household fires — *gārhapatya*, *āhavanīya* and *dakṣiṇāgni*, which are three fires and one Agni; or the three regions, earth, middle air and heaven. Nothing here forces a choice, and the reason the image survived is probably that all three are true at once. The seven are the flames, and the later tradition fixed them into a numbered list; the hymn simply says seven.

The two cows of verse 3 are read by the tradition either as the two officiants at the rite or as the householder and his wife — the same open pair that stands behind [[1.144]].3–4. What they do is worth keeping whichever they are: they come together at the calf, spread out in all directions, and measure out *anapavṛjyān adhvanaḥ*, roads that cannot be got round. That is a description of what a rite does to a life. It lays out a path that is not optional.

Verse 4 is the one a reader can use. The *kavi*s guard him *nānā hṛdā*, variously in the heart, and then go looking outside for him — and what becomes visible is Sūrya. The Ṛgveda does not usually put the inward and the outward in one sentence like this, and this note will not resolve it into a doctrine. What the verse says plainly is that the men had him in their hearts before they found him in the sky.

And the phrase to carry is verse 5's: *mahaḥ arbhāya jīvase* — for the living of the great and of the small. Agni is not described as favouring either. That is a claim about fire and about the rite that uses it, and it belongs beside the ninth verse of [[1.1]], where the god who mediates everything is finally asked to be easy of approach.
146.disagreements:
Sāyaṇa reads the first verse's numbers as a set of options rather than a puzzle. *Trimūrdhan*, the three-headed, is either the three daily sacrifices, or the three household fires, or the three regions — heaven, earth and mid-air. *Saptaraśmi*, seven-rayed, he takes as the seven flames of fire, noting that *raśmi* can also carry the sense of rule or reign. Wilson prints the epithets bare; Griffith does the same and adds no note. That the tradition itself offers three readings for one epithet, and settles on none, is the most useful thing in the commentary here.

On verse 3's two cows Sāyaṇa gives the same alternatives he gives at [[1.144]]: either the *yajamāna* and the officiating priest, or the sacrificer and his wife, with {{agni}} as the calf. Wilson keeps "two well-disposed cows"; Griffith "both Cows, fairshaped". Neither commits, and the padapāṭha's *dhenū* — two milch cows — does not decide it either.

The last clause of verse 3 is genuinely obscure. Sāyaṇa reads *viśvān ketān adhi maho dadhāne* as the two holding knowledge that increases every kind of highest wisdom, which Wilson turns into "possessing more than the great intelligence necessary for his development". Griffith goes the other way — "entrusting all desires to him the Mighty" — reading *keta* as wish rather than insight.

On verse 5 Sāyaṇa explains the "progeny" of which Agni is father as the priests themselves, who take their character from performing his worship.

147.title: Agni's Guards Saved Blind Māmateya
147.synthesis:
This sūkta has a man in it, and knowing that changes how the five verses read.

The first verse asks a question rather than making a claim. *Kathā te agne śucayanta āyor dadāśuḥ* — how have your bright ones given to Āyu, striving with prizes? — when, holding both in offspring and in what comes after, the gods take delight in the *sāman* of {{ṛta}}, in the melody of the order kept. The hymn opens not by praising {{agni}} but by wondering how his giving actually works.

The second verse is personal and blunt. Mark this speech of mine, youngest one, most generous, brought here to you, holder of your own power. And then a line that is unusual in the collection for its flatness: *pīyati tvaḥ anu tvaḥ gṛṇāti* — one man reviles you, another sings your praise. I, who honour you, praise your body, Agni. The hymn admits, in the middle of a hymn, that not everyone is doing this.

The third verse names the case. *Ye pāyavo māmateyaṃ te agne paśyanto andhaṃ duritād arakṣan* — those guards of yours, Agni, which, seeing the blind son of Mamatā, protected him from harm. He who knows all things protected those who acted rightly, and the enemies who meant to injure did not injure. The guards see; the man does not. That is the whole force of the verse: the protection was given to someone who could not watch out for himself, by something that could.

The fourth turns outward against a specific kind of person: the one who gives nothing, who wants harm, who is ungenerous, and who damages us *dvayena* — by doubleness, by saying one thing and meaning another. May his *mantra*, the formula he used, come back heavy on him; may he wear down his own body with his ill speech. Nothing is asked of Agni here except that the thing return to its sender.

The fifth repeats the case in general terms and asks for the plainer thing. Or when a mortal, knowing what he is doing, damages another mortal *dvayena* — by that same doubleness — then, praised one, protect the man who praises you; Agni, do not set us down into harm. The two verses are matched, and the second is the more careful: the first speaks of an enemy who is ungiving and godless, the second only of a man who knows what he is doing to another man. The offence is the same either way, and it is named twice by the same word.

So the shape of the sūkta is this. It begins by asking how Agni's giving reaches people; it observes that some people revile him; it recalls one occasion when his guards saw a blind man and kept him from harm; and it asks that the same seeing be turned now against duplicity — against the neighbour who deals doubly and knows it. The blindness of verse 3 and the doubleness of verses 4 and 5 are the hymn's two problems, and Agni's *pāyavaḥ*, his watchers, are the one answer offered to both.
147.practice:
The *māmateya* of verse 3, the blind son of Mamatā, is the ṛṣi of this hymn. Dīrghatamas Aucathya — to whom the Anukramaṇī gives 25 consecutive sūktas, [[1.140]] through [[1.164]], and none anywhere else in the collection — is remembered by the tradition as Māmateya and as blind, and his name means "long darkness". A reader coming to this stretch of maṇḍala 1 is therefore reading the work of a man who, on his own account here, was kept from harm by guards he could not see; and the same man composed [[1.164]], the great riddle-hymn, which asks more questions about seeing and knowing than any other sūkta in the Ṛgveda.

That is worth holding without over-reading it. The hymn does not moralise the blindness or make a lesson of it. It states, in one line, that Agni's watchers saw a man who could not see and kept him out of trouble. What a reader can take is the direction of the seeing: protection in the Ṛgveda is not usually described as strength but as attention — *pāyavaḥ*, guards, watchers — and here it is explicitly attention supplied to someone who lacked it.

The other half of the sūkta bears on something ordinary. *Dvayena* — with doubleness — names the injury done by a person who speaks one way and means another, and it appears in both of the last two verses. The response asked for in verse 4 is not that the man be struck but that his own formula come back on him and that he wear himself out with his own bad speech. In verse 5 even that is dropped, and what is asked is only: protect the one who praises you; do not put us into trouble. Two verses on the same offence, and the second is gentler than the first — which is itself a thing to notice.

Verse 2's admission is the line most worth keeping. *Pīyati tvaḥ anu tvaḥ gṛṇāti* — one reviles, another praises. The Ṛgveda does not assume a world where everyone worships.
147.disagreements:
Sāyaṇa's note on verse 3 is the most consequential in this sūkta because it converts a person into an allegory. Mamatā, he says, was the wife of Utathya; her son was Dīrghatamas, "long darkness", the blindness or ignorance that is the natural offspring of *mamatā*, mine-ness or selfishness. That reading treats the ṛṣi's own name and parentage as a moral figure rather than a biography. Wilson prints the story as story — "the blind son of Mamatā" — and Griffith keeps "blind Mamateya" without comment. Both a man and an allegory are available, and the tradition holds them at once.

Verse 4 divides on who is being described. Sāyaṇa notes that the hostile epithets — *araru*, *aghāyu*, *arātivan* — attach to the man, not to the *mantra*, and that the reference is to maledictory prayers, imprecations used against others. Wilson makes the whole line a curse turned back: "may his prayer be heavy on him, and involve his person in the consequences of his evil words." Griffith reads a sentence passed rather than a curse rebounding: "Be this in turn to him a heavy sentence."

Verse 1 splits oddly. Wilson has Agni's "shining and evaporating rays" supporting life and supplying food; Griffith reads a question about the worshippers — "how have the radiant ones, aspiring, endued thee with the vigour of the living" — so that the giving runs from men to the god. The Sanskrit *dadāśuḥ*, they have given, supports Griffith.

148.title: Mātariśvan Churned Him Out — Agni Kept Unharmed
148.synthesis:
Most hymns ask {{agni}} for protection. This one is largely about protecting Agni, and that inversion is what makes it worth reading.

*Mathīd yad īṃ viṣṭo mātariśvā* — when Mātariśvan, having entered in, churned him out: the *hotā* of every form, belonging to all the gods, whom they then set down among the human clans, dappled like the light itself, shining out for beauty. The first verse gives the whole sequence in one breath — the churning, the extraction, the placing among people — and ends on the word *vapuṣe*, for beauty, or, as the tradition takes it, for the accomplishing of the rite.

The second verse turns to the man who is speaking and to what he is afraid of. They shall not harm the one who gives; my *manman*, my framed thought — Agni is my shelter, and he has taken pleasure in it. They welcome all the acts of this *kāru*, this maker, who brings the praise forward. The verse is a poet's verse: what he has to offer is a made thing, and what he wants is for it not to be spoiled.

The third verse describes a movement that is precise and physical. Him whom the worshipful ones have taken hold of in his constant seat, and settled there with their praises — let them lead him forward, holding him, at the moment of the offering, the way swift horses harnessed to a chariot carry it forward. A fire is picked up in one place and carried to another, and the hymn treats the carrying as the god's own hurrying.

The fourth verse lets him be what he is. The wondrous one grinds many things down with his jaws; then he shines wide in the wood; and the wind blows along after his flame, driving it like the arrow shot from an archer's bow, day after day. Two comparisons in two lines, and both are about something released and travelling.

The fifth returns to the anxiety of the second and states it fully. *Na yaṃ ripavo na riṣaṇyavo garbhe santaṃ reṣaṇā reṣayanti* — whom no cheats, no harm-wishers, no injurers injure while he is still in the womb; whom the blind and the sightless do not spoil by looking at him; for his own constant ones, those who go before him, have kept him safe. Agni is at its most vulnerable before it has caught. What guards it, the verse says, is not power but people who stay with it — *nityāsaḥ*, the constant ones, the same word used of his seat in verse 3.

That is the sūkta's spine. Agni is churned out of hiding and set among human households; he is at risk while still unformed; the people who tend him are constant; and once he is out he grinds down forests and rides the wind like a loosed arrow. The god who will be asked in every other hymn for shelter is here shown needing shelter first, for the length of time between the friction and the flame.
148.practice:
Verse 3 describes an act still performed. Fire is taken hold of in its *nitya sadana*, its constant seat, and led forward at the moment of offering — and the tradition identifies this as the carrying of fire from the *gārhapatya*, the household hearth, to the *āhavanīya*, Agni into which the offering goes. One fire, moved. That is why the Vedic rite has more than one hearth and yet only one {{agni}}, and it is the practical form of the "three heads" of [[1.146]].1. Anyone who has lit one lamp from another has performed the same act and knows why it does not make two fires.

The more useful thing here is the reversal. This hymn is about Agni being kept safe. He is *garbhe santam*, still in the womb, and the enemies who might spoil him are named — cheats, harm-wishers, injurers, and then, oddly, "the blind and the sightless", who do not spoil him by looking. What protects him is *nityāsaḥ pretāraḥ*, the constant ones who go before: not force, just people who stay. For a household that keeps a lamp or a fire, this is the plainest description in the collection of what tending actually is. The vulnerable stretch is at the beginning, and the answer to it is constancy rather than strength.

Verse 2 is the poet's own worry, and it will be familiar. What he brings is a *manman*, a thing he has made, and what he asks is that it not be harmed and that it be received. He calls himself *kāru*, a maker. As in [[1.130]].6, where men carpenter a hymn as a wright carpenters a chariot, the Ṛgveda's picture of composition is workmanship, and its fear is that the work will be spoiled.

This is the ninth of the eleven consecutive Agni sūktas of Dīrghatamas Aucathya, [[1.140]]–[[1.150]], the longest run of Agni hymns in the collection.
148.disagreements:
The most useful note here is Sāyaṇa's on verse 3, which turns metaphor into procedure: *praṇayanta* is the solemn conveyance of fire from the *gārhapatya*, the household fire, to the *āhavanīya*, the fire of the offering. Wilson keeps it vague — "convey him diligently to the sacrifice" — Griffith vaguer still. Without the commentary the verse is a figure of speech; with it, it describes men carrying fire across a ritual ground.

Verse 2 divides the translators completely on who is being protected. Wilson reads it as the singer's own defence — "let not my enemies prevail against me, when presenting acceptable oblations" — while Griffith turns it outward: "They shall not harm the man who brings thee praises: such as I am, Agni my help approves me." The Sanskrit *dadānam it na dadabhanta* supports either the giver in general or the speaker in particular.

Verse 5's blindness is genuinely unclear in both witnesses. Wilson makes it intellectual — "the blind of intellect, or those who see not physically, detract not from his glory" — while Griffith reads the blindness as caused by Agni himself: "Men blind and sightless through his splendour hurt not." One has the blind failing to harm him; the other has them blinded by him. Nothing in the line settles it.

On verse 1 Sāyaṇa glosses *vapuṣe*, ordinarily "for beauty", as *yajñasiddhaye*, for accomplishing the sacrifice — an aesthetic word made functional. Griffith keeps "shining forth for beauty".

149.title: Twice-Born Agni Where the Waters Gather
149.synthesis:
Five short verses in *virāj*, and they move very quickly. This is the most compressed of Dīrghatamas' Agni hymns, and each verse is a single image without connectives.

*Mahaḥ sa rāya ā īṣate patiḥ* — he, the lord of great riches, comes speeding, the mighty one of what is mighty, to the place where the treasure is. And then, in the last clause, something small and concrete: the pressing-stones attend on him as he hurries near. Wealth arrives, and stones get to work.

The second verse makes him a source. He who is a bull for men as he is for the two worlds, by his renowns; whose stream everything alive has drunk; who, having run forward, has settled himself in the womb. Three relative clauses and no main verb: the verse simply keeps naming him. What is claimed in the middle clause is large — that every living thing has drunk what comes from him — and it is stated in passing.

The third verse lights something up. He who has kindled the *nārmiṇī* stronghold: a swift *kavi*, of the cloud or the springing water, like a courser, shining like Sūrya, *śatātmā*, of a hundred selves. The name of that fort is not explained anywhere and the tradition does not agree on it; what the verse gives is a fire in a high place, seen at a distance, and a god counted in hundreds.

The fourth is the hymn's centre. *Abhi dvijanmā trī rocanāni* — twice-born, he has stood shining across the three luminous realms and across all the regions: the *hotā* who sacrifices best, *apāṃ sadhasthe*, where the waters gather. Twice-born, standing in three worlds, seated where the waters meet: the verse holds his whole distribution in one line and argues for none of it.

The fifth turns the same words toward a household. This is the *hotā*, the one who is twice-born, who through desire of renown holds all things worth choosing; and the man who gives to him readily — the verse breaks off with the reward left to be understood, and both witnesses supply good offspring. What matters is the join: after four verses of cosmology, the hymn ends by naming a mortal who gives, and gives promptly.

The word to follow is *dvijanmā*, twice-born, which stands in verses 4 and 5. It occurs three times in the whole Ṛgveda — twice here and once at [[1.140]].2 — all three in this poet's Agni hymns, and it is the closest the collection comes to a technical term for {{agni}}'s double origin. The commentary offers three explanations and does not choose between them: born from the two fire-sticks; born first by the rubbing and again by the oblation that makes him a ritual fire; or born of earth and of heaven, his two parents. Each gives a different account of what the second birth is — mechanical, ritual, or cosmic — and the hymn puts the word in two consecutive verses without hinting which it means.

What holds the sūkta is that everything in it is stated as accomplished. He comes; he is a bull; he has lit the fort; he has stood across the three realms; he holds what is worth choosing. Nothing is asked for anywhere in the five verses except in the implication of the last line — that a man who gives readily gets something. It is a hymn of description that ends in a transaction, and the transaction is left half-said.
149.practice:
*Dvijanmā* is the word this short sūkta puts in the reader's hands, and it is worth being exact about it. Its three occurrences in the Ṛgveda are all in Dīrghatamas' Agni hymns — here in verses 4 and 5, and at [[1.140]].2 — and all three are said of {{agni}}. The tradition gives three accounts of the two births: from the two fire-sticks; from the rubbing and then from the consecration that makes a fire ritual; or from earth and from heaven. The second of these is the one that matters for a reader, because it says that a thing becomes what it is by being taken up into the rite. That is the same logic the *upanayana* applies to a boy, in front of this same god, using this same word; this note does not claim the Ṛgveda intended that application, only that the word and the logic are already here.

The other phrase to keep is *apāṃ sadhasthe*, where the waters gather, in verse 4 — fire seated at the meeting-place of water. On one reading this is the ritual ground itself, where the water for the sprinklings is set out; on another it is the middle air, where Agni is lightning. Both are old. Together with *apāṃ napāt* in [[1.143]].1, they show how thoroughly the Ṛgveda declines to treat fire and water as opposites.

Verse 1's last clause is the sort of detail that keeps these hymns honest. The lord of great riches hastens to the place of treasure — and what greets him is the pressing-stones getting to work. The grandest sentence in the hymn ends with equipment.

And verse 5 states the terms of the exchange in as few words as the collection ever uses: the man who gives to him *sutuka*, readily, promptly. Not the man who gives most. The man who does not delay.
149.disagreements:
*Dvijanmā* draws Sāyaṇa's fullest note here, and he keeps three readings without ranking them: born from the two pieces of stick; born from attrition and again from the oblation; or born of earth and heaven, the two parents of {{agni}}. On the same verse he takes *trī rocanāni*, the three luminous realms, as either heaven, earth and mid-air or the three ritual fires. Neither translator records the alternatives; Wilson gives "the twice-born" and "the three bright regions", Griffith "doubly born" and "the three luminous realms".

*Apāṃ sadhasthe* he reads two ways: the place of sacrifice where the waters are collected for the purificatory sprinklings, or the *antarikṣa*, the middle air, in which Agni exists as lightning. The choice determines whether verse 4 describes a courtyard or the sky.

Verse 2's central claim divides the translations sharply. Sāyaṇa explains it through the rain cycle — Agni carries the offerings to the sun, is identified with the solar rays, and generates the rain on which all life depends. Wilson prints that chain in full; Griffith keeps the image bare, "he whose streams all life hath drunken."

Verse 3's *nārmiṇī* is unsettled in every witness. Wilson takes it as an epithet, "the delightful spot", meaning the altar; Griffith keeps a building, "the joyous castle". Sāyaṇa notes that this hymn and the one before it stand in the Sāmaveda, and preserves a rendering from there in which Agni springs in the air like a bright sun full of life.

150.title: Agni Passes By the Rich Man Who Gives Nothing
150.synthesis:
Three verses in *uṣṇih* — one of only five sūktas in maṇḍala 1 this short — and it says one thing clearly.

*Puru tvā dāsvān voce* — with much to give, I speak to you. The speaker names himself twice over in the first line: he is *dāsvān*, the giving one, and he is *ari*, a word that is genuinely double-edged and that the tradition here bends toward service — the one who brings, who comes before you as a dependant does. And the position he takes up is stated by a comparison: in your keeping, {{agni}}, as in the shelter of a great driver, a master who urges his people on. The relation asked for is not friendship. It is a man placing himself under someone who both protects and pushes.

The second verse says who is left outside that shelter, and it is the reason to know this sūkta. You never go forward — *kadā cana prajigataḥ* — to the man who is *anina*, without vigour or drive, though he is *dhanin*, possessed of wealth; who is *araru*, ungiving, even when the offering is at hand; who is *adevayu*, not turned toward the gods. Three descriptions in three words: he has money, he has no impulse, and he does not give. And the verb governing them is a negative one. Agni does not come.

That is a hard verse and it should be read for what it is. It does not say the rich man is punished, and it does not say he is cursed. It says the god does not arrive at his house. The refusal is not a judgement passed but an absence of movement — the same movement the rest of the collection spends hundreds of verses asking for. Everything in the Ṛgveda that turns on Agni coming near turns, here, on his not bothering.

The third verse takes the other case. *Sa candro vipra martyaḥ* — that mortal is bright, O inspired one; greatest among the great in heaven. The man being described is the opposite of the one in verse 2: not richer, but giving, and what happens to him is that he shines and takes a place among the great in the sky. And then the hymn ends where a short hymn should, in the first person plural: *pra-pra id te agne vanuṣaḥ syāma* — may we, Agni, be forward, forward among those who are yours.

The whole sūkta is therefore an arrangement of three positions. The speaker, who gives much and stands like a servant under a demanding master. The wealthy man who gives nothing and whom the god does not visit. And the mortal who gives and becomes bright in heaven. It is three verses long and it contains the entire economy of the collection: not what you have, but whether it moves.
150.practice:
Verse 2 is one of the most useful things in maṇḍala 1 and it takes ten seconds to learn. {{agni}} does not go to the wealthy man who has no impulse and makes no offering. Not "will punish", not "is displeased with" — simply does not go. Three words describe him: *dhanin*, rich; *anina*, without drive; *araru*, ungiving. Wealth is not the problem and is not treated as one anywhere in the verse. What is named is the combination of having and not moving.

That reading has a long afterlife in Hindu practice, where the obligation of *dāna* is not tied to amount and where the offering poured into fire is small by design. The Ṛgveda's position, here, is that what makes a household one the god visits is that something leaves it. It is worth setting beside [[1.149]].5, one sūkta earlier in this same poet's sequence, where the man rewarded is the one who gives *sutuka*, promptly — again not the largest giver but the one who does not delay.

The third verse contains a claim the later tradition took a long way. The mortal who gives becomes *candra* — bright, or the moon — and greatest among the great in heaven. The commentary reads it both as a comparison and as a destination, connecting it to the doctrine of the path that leads through the region of the fathers to the moon. That is a genuine thread from this verse to the *pañcāgni-vidyā* of the Upaniṣads, and it is recorded here as a reading the tradition made, not as the hymn's plain sense. The plain sense is that a giving man becomes luminous.

And the first verse gives the posture. The speaker calls himself *ari* and puts himself in Agni's keeping as in the shelter of a *toda*, one who drives or goads. He is asking for the protection of somebody who will also push him. That is an unsentimental picture of what it is to be under a god, and it is stated in the opening line without any softening.

This closes the eleven consecutive Agni sūktas of Dīrghatamas Aucathya, [[1.140]]–[[1.150]]; from [[1.151]] he turns to {{mitra}} and {{varuṇa}}.
150.disagreements:
The whole hymn turns on one word in verse 1, and Sāyaṇa's handling of it is remarkable. *Ari* ordinarily means enemy or stranger — he cites the Nirukta for exactly that — and yet he takes it here as *artā*, a servant, one who brings the oblation into the god's presence, glossing: "since I, Agni, going verily into your presence for the purpose of conveying oblations, I am a servant." Wilson prints the servant. Griffith arrives at the same result by another route, "thy faithful servant I call upon thee". That a word for adversary should be pressed into meaning dependant shows how much interpretive work the tradition does.

The same verse's *toda* Sāyaṇa glosses as a master who instructs, literally a tormentor or goader; Wilson gives "a mighty master", Griffith "the great inciting God", which shifts the epithet from the human master of the simile to Agni himself.

Verse 3 is where the readings part most consequentially. Sāyaṇa offers both a simile and a destination for *candro maryaḥ*: the man becomes *like* the moon, the delighter of all — or he becomes the moon outright, and for this he cites the Chandogas on the passage from the world of the fathers to the ākāśa and thence to the moon, "this is Soma the king". Wilson follows the strong reading, "becomes a moon in heaven". Griffith declines it: "Splendid, O Singer, is that man." A lunar destination, or a compliment.

151.title: Mitra and Varuṇa Proclaim Ṛta Aloud
151.synthesis:
The sūkta opens on something being born and the two worlds shaking at it. *Arejetāṃ rodasī pājasā girā* — heaven and earth trembled at his bulk and at his voice: at him whom men of good intent, wanting cattle, brought to birth by their exertion at the *vidatha*, in the waters — dear, worthy of worship, the help of things born, and *mitraṃ na*, like a friend. The Anukramaṇī gives this one verse to {{mitra}} by himself and the eight that follow to {{mitra}} and {{varuṇa}} together, and the verse it singles out is the one in which the god is present only as a comparison.

The second verse turns to the pair. Since men, like friends, have set out that pressing of Purumīḷha who offers {{soma}} — now find a {{kratu}}, a way forward, for the singer, and hear, bulls, the master of this house. The third widens: the peoples make much of your birth from the two worlds, a thing to be proclaimed, for great *dakṣa*; you bring it for {{ṛta}} and for the racehorse, and by the *hotrā* and by hard work you take pleasure in the rite.

The fourth is the hymn's declaration, and it puts *ṛta* at the centre of what these two do. That dwelling is great and dear, *asura*; and you, possessors of ṛta, *ṛtam ā ghoṣathaḥ bṛhat* — you proclaim ṛta aloud, at the top of your voices. Then an image that grounds it: you yoke to the pole the *dakṣa* of lofty heaven, effective and serving everything, as one yokes a cow to a load. What holds the world is put in harness like a working animal.

The fifth verse comes down to the ground. Here on the great earth you throw open with your might what is wanted; free of dust, hurrying, the milch-cows call out in their stall; and close by they cry toward Sūrya at his setting and at dawn, like birds of prey. Cattle bawling at both ends of the day, at the two junctures the pair presides over.

The sixth returns to the rite and makes an unexpected claim. The long-haired ones — the flames — have sung to you for ṛta, where you two, Mitra and Varuṇa, sing out the path. Release of your own will; make our {{dhī}}s swell. And then: *yuvaṃ viprasya manmanām irajyathaḥ*, you two have command over the thoughts of the inspired man. What the singer is offering is described as already under the gods' authority.

The seventh states the terms. Whoever, toiling with {{yajña}}s, gives to you two — the *kavi*, the *hotā*, the man who brings a *manman* to completion — to him you come; you enjoy his rite; come to our songs with a favourable mind, well disposed toward us. The eighth watches the anointing: you two are the first they anoint with sacrifices and with the produce of cows, holders of ṛta, as the mind is set going toward its objects; they bring you songs held together by thought, and with an unarrogant mind you have attained wealth.

The ninth closes with a comparison nobody expects. You hold rich *vayas*, vigour; you have reached wealth, O men, by your *māyā*s. And then: *na vāṃ dyāvo ahabhir na uta sindhavo na devatvaṃ paṇayo nānaśur magham* — not the days with the nights, not the rivers, not the {{paṇi}}s have reached your godhead or your bounty. The hymn ends by naming three things that keep going without stopping — daylight and dark, the rivers, and the hoarders who never let anything go — and says that none of them has got as far as these two.
151.practice:
{{mitra}} and {{varuṇa}} are the gods of the kept word, and this sūkta gives the plainest description in maṇḍala 1 of what that means as an activity. Verse 4: *ṛtam ā ghoṣathaḥ bṛhat* — you proclaim {{ṛta}} aloud, loudly. They do not merely uphold the order; they announce it, which is what a witness does. The word occurs in four of the nine verses, and every time it is something the pair either carry, hold, or say out.

Verse 4's other half is the image to keep. The *dakṣa* of lofty heaven — the effective power by which things get done — is yoked *dhuri*, to the pole, "like a cow". What runs the universe is put in harness and made to pull. That is a working household's picture of cosmic order, and it is nearer to a rope and a yoke than to a throne.

There is a counted fact worth having about the first verse. The Anukramaṇī assigns it to Mitra by himself, and this is one of only two places in the entire Ṛgveda where Mitra stands alone: the other is [[3.59]], the single sūkta addressed to him without Varuṇa. Thirty-six sūktas of the collection name *mitrāvaruṇau* as a pair. Mitra alone gets one sūkta and one verse.

And verse 6 says something that changes how a reciter should hold the whole exercise. *Yuvaṃ viprasya manmanām irajyathaḥ* — you two rule over the thoughts of the inspired man. The song being offered is not the singer's property that he brings to a god; the god already has authority over it. The verse asks, in the same breath, that the *dhī*s be made to swell. Both halves are worth keeping together: the thought is asked for and is already theirs.

Three sūktas here in a row, [[1.151]] to [[1.153]], are Mitrāvaruṇā's; the longest such run in the collection is the eleven consecutive sūktas at [[5.62]]–[[5.72]].
151.disagreements:
The first verse is the hymn's real crux and Sāyaṇa's reading of it goes against the Anukramaṇī. Where the index gives verse 1 to {{mitra}}, Sāyaṇa reads *mitraṃ na* as a simile — "like a friend" — and takes the subject to be {{agni}}, identified with the Agni of the firmament, that is, lightning. Wilson prints that reading in full: heaven and earth terrified by the god generated "amidst the waters of the firmament … as a friend". Griffith keeps the ambiguity, "a Friend, mid waters, at the sacrifice", without naming Agni. Whether the opening verse addresses Mitra, or Agni under a comparison to a friend, is genuinely unsettled inside the tradition itself.

Verse 2's *purumīḷhasya sominaḥ* divides the same way. Sāyaṇa gives both an adjectival reading — the abundantly flowing soma — and a proper name, Purumīḷha the soma-offering prince. Wilson prints the first, Griffith the second, and nothing in the line decides it.

On verse 4 Sāyaṇa unpacks the yoking: what is joined to the pole is the *apas*, the work, able to bear heaven's burden, and the cow either bears a load matched to her strength or gives milk. Griffith reduces it to "ye bind unto the work, as to the pole an ox." On verse 9 he spells out the triple negative: no one in the three worlds can overcome these two.

152.title: The Footless Goes First — Mitrāvaruṇā's Riddles
152.synthesis:
Seven verses, and four of them are riddles. This is the hymn in which Dīrghatamas begins doing what he will do at length in [[1.164]]: stating something plainly true and impossible in the same breath, and asking who has understood it.

The first verse is not a riddle but a statement of office, and it is the ground for everything after. You two wear garments thick with fat; your thoughts are unbroken and so are your streams. *Ava atiratam anṛtāni viśvā ṛtena mitrāvaruṇā sacethe* — you have driven down all the untruths, and you cleave to {{ṛta}}. That is {{mitra}} and {{varuṇa}} in a single line: what they do to *anṛta* and what they hold to.

The second verse turns hard. Not one among them makes this out. True is the *mantra* the *kavi* has spoken, and crushing. *Triaśriṃ hanti caturaśrir ugraḥ* — the fierce four-cornered kills the three-cornered; and the revilers of the gods were the first to wear out. Four against three, without further comment. The verse says in its own first line that this is not generally understood.

The third is the famous one. *Apād eti prathamā padvatīnām* — the footless one goes first among those that have feet. Who has understood this of yours, Mitra and Varuṇa? *Garbho bharaṃ bharati* — the unborn thing carries the load; it fulfils *ṛta* and puts *anṛta* down. Three impossibilities in three lines, and the middle line is a question about them.

The fourth and fifth answer without saying they are answering. We see him going on ahead, the lover of the young women, never lying down, wearing raiment that cannot be taken off and is spread wide — the dear *dhāman* of Mitra and of Varuṇa. And then: *anaśvo jāto anabhīśur arvā* — a courser born without horses and without reins, neighing, flying, with his back lifted. The young men have taken pleasure in the *brahman* that thought cannot get hold of, praising in Mitra and in Varuṇa their *dhāman*. Whatever moves across the sky, unharnessed, ahead of the dawns and never resting, is what the earlier riddles were about; and the hymn declines to name it.

The sixth drops out of the riddles into a plain domestic request, and the man asking is named. May the milch-cows, favouring Māmateya who loves the *brahman*, swell in this udder. Knowing the *vayunā*s, the ways things are done, let him beg for food; and with his mouth, seeking to serve, let him make Aditi wide. After five verses of unanswerable questions the poet asks that the cows give milk and that he be allowed to eat.

The seventh closes with three requests of ordinary size. May I turn your enjoyment of the offering toward us, divine Mitrāvaruṇā, with {{namas}} and with help. May our *brahman* prevail in the fights. And may our rain come from heaven, *supārā* — carrying us well across.

What holds the sūkta together is the pairing of *ṛta* against *anṛta* in the first verse and again in the third, at the bottom of the deepest riddle. Whatever it is that goes without feet and carries a burden while unborn, what the hymn says it does is exactly what the two gods do: it makes the true stand and puts the false down.
152.practice:
Verse 3 is one of the lines every reader of the Ṛgveda eventually meets. *Apād eti prathamā padvatīnām* — the footless goes first among the footed. The tradition reads the footless one as Uṣas, who moves ahead of everything that walks and does not walk on her own feet; the *garbha* that carries the burden is then the sun, still unborn below the horizon. That reading is old and it is good. But the verse itself asks *kaḥ tad vāṃ ā ciketa*, who has understood this of yours — and the honest position is that the hymn frames its own image as something not yet grasped. It is worth keeping as a question rather than converting into an answer.

Verse 5 is where a reader should stop longest. *Acittaṃ brahma jujuṣur yuvānaḥ* — the young men have taken delight in a *brahman* that thought does not reach. This is among the earliest places in the collection where the sacred formulation is described as being beyond the mind that handles it, and the whole later career of the word {{brahman}} — the formulation, then the power in the formulation, then what the Upaniṣads mean by it — has this line somewhere behind it. What the verse actually says is modest and worth honouring: they enjoyed it; they did not comprehend it.

The first verse is the practical one. {{mitra}} and {{varuṇa}} drive down *anṛta* and cleave to {{ṛta}}. Everything a Hindu associates with these two — the witness of oaths, the binder of the perjurer, the observance of the two junctures at dawn and dusk — follows from that one clause. It is worth memorising in its own words, because it is the shortest definition of them the Veda gives.

And verse 6 names the poet. *Māmateya*, the son of Mamatā, is Dīrghatamas himself, who is remembered as blind and who composed the 25 sūktas from [[1.140]] to [[1.164]]. He asks here for milk and for permission to beg his food. A man who has just posed four cosmological riddles ends by asking to be fed.
152.disagreements:
The riddles divide the witnesses more than anything else in this stretch of the maṇḍala. On verse 3 Sāyaṇa is explicit and Wilson follows him: Mitra and Varuṇa preside over day and night — he cites the Taittirīya Saṃhitā, *ahorātre vai mitrāvaruṇau* — so daybreak and the sun's course are their work; and the dawn is called *apād*, footless, because she does not move by her own steps but depends on the motion of the sun. Wilson accordingly supplies "the sun" for the *garbha*. Griffith translates the riddle and leaves it standing: "The Footless Maid precedeth footed creatures … The Babe Unborn supporteth this world's burthen."

Verse 2 is worse. Sāyaṇa reads *eṣām* as "one of you two", the plural honorific — if one can do this, how much more the two together — or else as their followers; and he explains the four-cornered killing the three-cornered prosaically, as the better-armed defeating the less well armed. Wilson builds an elaborate sentence about a warrior weighing his means; Griffith keeps the weapon and the mystery.

On verse 5's *acittaṃ brahma* Sāyaṇa glosses *acitta* as not an object of thought and *brahman* as the act declared very great — the rite, not an absolute. Wilson writes "the inconceivable mystery of sacred rites"; Griffith, "mystery thought-surpassing".

On verse 6 Sāyaṇa explains the cows concretely: their milk supplies the offerings proper to Mitra and Varuṇa, and *pitvo bhikṣeta* means the poet begs for what is left over after the oblations.

153.title: Aditi the Milch-Cow Swells for Mitrāvaruṇā
153.synthesis:
Four verses, the shortest of the three Mitrāvaruṇā sūktas here, and unlike [[1.152]] it contains no riddles at all. It is an offering hymn: what is brought, how it is brought, who brings it, and what should come back.

*Yajāmahe vāṃ mahaḥ sajoṣāḥ* — we worship you two, the great ones, being of one mind with you, with oblations, {{mitra}} and {{varuṇa}}, with acts of {{namas}}, with ghṛta. And then the epithet that fixes the physical scene: *ghṛtasnū*, you whose backs stream with ghṛta. The gods are pictured wet with what has been poured for them. The verse closes on the men doing the pouring — when the *adhvaryu*s bring these to us with their {{dhī}}s. Ladle and thought arrive in the same clause.

The second verse is about the praise itself and is oddly self-conscious. Your *prastuti*, the praise offered ahead, is like a *dhāman*, like an impulse sent out; a well-turned hymn has been brought to you, Mitrāvaruṇā. When the *hotā* adorns you at the *vidatha*s, then the *sūri*, the patron, seeking to worship you, bulls, wants your favour. Three parties are named in one verse — the song, the priest who fits it out, and the man paying for the rite — and each is doing a different part of the same act.

The third verse is the one to remember. *Pīpāya dhenur aditir ṛtāya* — Aditi the milch-cow has swollen with milk, for {{ṛta}}, for the people, for the man who gives the oblation, Mitrāvaruṇā. Aditi, the boundless one, mother of the Ādityas of whom these two are chief, is here simply a cow whose udder has filled. And the verse ends by naming a man: when he serves you at the rite, he, Rātahavya, like a human *hotā*. Whether that is a name or a description — "he whose oblation is given" — the effect is the same: a particular person is standing there doing the work.

The fourth verse asks for the flow to continue and then, in its last line, tells the gods to eat. Among the gladdening clans, may the cows and the divine waters swell your drink. And may the ancient lord of this house give us of it. Then: *vītaṃ pātaṃ payasa usriyāyāḥ* — eat, drink of the milk of the ruddy cow. The hymn ends with an imperative that would be at home at any table.

The shape of the four verses is a single circuit and it is worth following. Ghṛta is poured over the two gods; the *adhvaryu*s bring it with thought; the praise is fitted out and the patron pays; Aditi's udder fills for the man who gave; the cows and the waters swell what the gods drink; the householder gives a share back to us; and the gods are told to drink the milk. Nothing in the hymn is asked for that is not already moving. What a reader is watching is a loop — milk, ghṛta, song and food going round between a household and two gods — and the only request in it is that the loop keep turning.
153.practice:
Aditi as *dhenu*, a milch-cow whose udder has filled, is the image to take from this sūkta. She is the mother of the Ādityas, and {{mitra}} and {{varuṇa}} are the two chief of them; her name means the unbound, the boundless. And in verse 3 what she does is give milk *ṛtāya janāya haviṣde* — for {{ṛta}}, for the people, for the man who brought the offering. The Veda's largest abstractions keep resolving into cattle, and this is one of the clearest cases: what boundlessness does, in practice, is feed the household that made the offering.

The fourth verse is worth knowing because of its last line. *Vītaṃ pātaṃ payasa usriyāyāḥ* — eat, drink of the milk of the cow. That is the imperative one would use to a guest. The hymn has spent three verses on {{ṛta}}, on Aditi, on the men who fit out the praise; and it closes by telling two gods to have some milk. The register of Vedic offering is hospitality, and this verse states it without ornament — which is also what the household lamp and the daily *naivedya* are.

Verse 2 names the three roles at any rite and is useful for that alone: the *hotā*, who dresses the praise; the *sūri*, the patron who wants the god's favour and pays for the occasion; and the *prastuti*, the praise itself, sent out ahead like an impulse. A reader attending a modern homa will see the same three.

Of the collection's thirty-six sūktas that name *mitrāvaruṇau*, eighteen are theirs entire; this is the third of three consecutive ones by Dīrghatamas, [[1.151]] to [[1.153]]. From [[1.154]] he turns to {{viṣṇu}}, and one of the most quoted hymns in the Ṛgveda.
153.disagreements:
This short hymn produces one large divergence and several small ones. The large one is verse 3's *rātahavya*. Sāyaṇa takes it as a proper name, a king; Wilson prints "Rātahavya, glorifying you"; Griffith dissolves it into a description, "he who worships moves you, like to a human priest, with gifts presented". Whether the verse names a patron or merely describes any giver changes what kind of document this is.

Verse 2 divides the translations almost past recognition. Sāyaṇa reads the opening as a disclaimer — the praise offered is not itself the fulfilment; the singer comes to the god's abode detached from what he might grasp at — and Wilson builds an involved English sentence out of it: "the purpose of worshipping you is not the performance, but even by so much I may attain to your glory". Griffith reads no disclaimer at all: "Your praise is like a mighty power, an impulse: to you, Twain Gods, a well-formed hymn is offered." One version is about renouncing the fruit of the praise; the other is a straightforward compliment.

On verse 1's *ghṛtasnū* Wilson gives "dispensers of butter", making the gods the source, where Griffith has "ye Twain whose backs are sprinkled with oil", making them the recipients. The compound supports the second more naturally.

On verse 4's imperative Sāyaṇa notes that "eating" the milk may refer to it in its coagulated forms — curds or butter — as against drinking it fresh, which is why the verse uses two verbs.

181.title: One Aśvin and the Other — Twins Told Apart
181.synthesis:
The {{aśvin}}au are a dual deity: two who are almost always spoken of as one thing with two bodies. This hymn keeps pulling them apart. Four times in nine verses it says *the one* and *the other*, and each time the two turn out to be doing something different.

It opens with a question. What is this, dearest pair, of refreshments and riches that you, acting as *adhvaryu*s, are bringing up out of the waters? This *yajña* has made your praise, you holders of goods, helpers of the peoples (v1). The second verse asks their horses to bring them: pure, milk-drinking, wind-swift, born of heaven, quick as mind, bulls, fair-backed, self-ruling. The third asks for the chariot, and compares it to running water — like a stream going downhill, broad-seated, may it come for our wellbeing; swifter than the mind, *ahaṃpūrva*, one that would be first.

Then the fourth verse divides them. *Iheha jātā* — born here and here — with stainless bodies and with their own separate names: one of you is the victorious patron of the good rite; the other is reckoned the fortunate son of Dyaus. Two births, two names, two descriptions. The fifth verse continues it: may your best chariot, tawny, gliding down, come to our dwellings at will — and let them feed *anyasya harī*, the bays of the other one, with *vāja*s, while the Aśvins churn the regions with their shouting. The sixth does it again: forward goes the *śaradvān* bull, overpowering, sending abundant sweetness; and again, *anyasya*, let them feed the other with strength; the risen rivers have come to serve us.

Nothing is explained. The hymn never says which is which, and it never says why one has bays to be fed while the other is a bull going forth. It simply keeps insisting that there are two.

Verse 7 turns to the song. The steady hymn has been let loose for you, ordainers — *tredhā kṣarantī*, flowing threefold — and the request is small and exact: help the man who is pleading, and, *yāman ayāman*, whether you are travelling or standing still, hear my call. The eighth places the singing: this song of your bright shapes swells in the men's hall where the grass is strewn three deep; your bull-cloud has swelled, and honours men as with a pouring out of milk. Verse 9 names the hour and does it by association rather than by clock: the offerer with his oblation praises you as he wakes {{agni}} and {{uṣas}} — which is to say, at first light, at the hour when the Aśvins are in fact invoked. And it ends with the singer describing himself at work, *huve yad vāṃ varivasyā gṛṇānaḥ*, calling you while singing and making room. Then the seal, *vidyāma iṣaṃ vṛjanaṃ jīradānum*.
181.practice:
The {{aśvin}}au come as a pair and are named in the dual, and most hymns treat them as a single addressee. This one does not, and that is what makes it useful. Four times — in verses 4, 5 and 6 — it separates them: *anyaḥ* and *anyaḥ*, one and the other; and then *anyasya*, of the other, twice more. Two births, two names, two different things being done.

The tradition has read that division in more than one way, and the readings do not agree. What the hymn itself says is only that they were born *iheha*, here and here, in two places, and that they have *nāmabhiḥ svaiḥ*, their own separate names — which it does not give. A reader who has been told confidently what the two Aśvins stand for should know that the text is more reticent than the explanations of it.

What is not reticent is the hour. Verse 9 puts the praise of the Aśvins alongside the waking of {{agni}} and {{uṣas}}, and the tradition has always kept them there: the Aśvins belong to the first light, to the morning pressing, to the moment when Agni is stirred and the dawn is named. Anyone who keeps a morning observance is keeping their hour.

And verse 7 has the phrase to take away. *Yāman ayāman śṛṇutaṃ havaṃ me* — travelling or not travelling, hear my call. The singer does not ask them to come. He asks them to hear him whether or not they are on the move — which is a more modest and more usable request than most in the collection. He would like to be heard in transit.

Verse 8's detail is worth keeping too: the hall where the *barhis* is *tribarhis*, strewn three deep. The rite in these hymns is a physical place with a floor you can describe.
181.disagreements:
Sāyaṇa identifies the two of verse 4 with the sun and the moon, so that one Aśvin is the son of the middle region and the other the son of the sky. He also attaches to the same verse's *arepasā*, stainless, the legend of the beheading of Dadhyañc — the point being that no sin attached to the Aśvins for that act. Neither translator brings the legend into the verse.

Verse 3's *ahaṃpūrva* is normally the word for a warrior who means to be first into the fight. Sāyaṇa declines that here and offers *manasvin*, intelligent, or *atyudāra*, exceedingly generous. Wilson prints "cumulative," Griffith "that ever would be foremost" — which keeps the martial sense Sāyaṇa set aside.

Verse 6's *śaradvān* gets three readings from Sāyaṇa alone: blighting, as autumn withers leaves; or *bahusaṃvatsara*, of many years, hence ancient; or simply autumnal, applied to one Aśvin as the moon. Wilson chooses none of them and prints "the disperser (of the clouds), like Indra"; Griffith gives "your strong Bull like a cloud of autumn."

On verse 5's *kakuha* Sāyaṇa allows either an epithet of the chariot, meaning best, or the points of the horizon — which changes whether the verse describes a vehicle or a direction of travel.
181.note: anyaḥ/anyasya counted in the padapāṭha at 1.181.4 (twice), 1.181.5 and 1.181.6

182.title: Four Ships for Tugra's Son — the Aśvins' Rescue
182.synthesis:
Eight verses, and the last four of them tell one story — the fullest account in this maṇḍala of the rescue that the {{aśvin}}au are best remembered for.

The first four verses clear the ground. *Abhūd idaṃ vayunam* — this has come about; be ready, you who think; here is the bull-drawn chariot; be glad. The Aśvins are called *dhiyaṃjinvā*, quickeners of thought, *dhiṣṇyā*, attentive, sons of Dyaus, of pure *vrata*, and good to the man who does well (v1). Then the chariot is asked for, with a stack of superlatives: most Indra-like, most Marut-like, *dasrā*, most wondrous in deed, best of charioteers — bring it heaped full of sweetness, and come with it to the one who gives (v2).

The third verse is impatient and rather rude. *Kim atra dasrā kṛṇuthaḥ kim āsāthe* — what are you doing here, and why are you sitting about, where any man at all who brings no oblation is held in honour? Step over them; wear away the life of the *paṇi*; and make light for the *vipra* who is trying to speak. The fourth keeps the tone: crush on every side the dogs that bark at us; kill the scorners — you know how; make every word of the singer rich in *ratna*; and accept, both of you, this praise of mine.

Then the story. *Yuvam etaṃ cakrathuḥ sindhuṣu plavam* — you two made that raft in the waters for the son of Tugra, *ātmanvantam pakṣiṇam*, breathing and winged; by it, with a god-devoted mind, you brought him up, and flew with easy flight out of the great surge (v5). A boat that breathes and has wings, in five words, and no further explanation.

The sixth verse gives the situation he was in. Flung down, the son of Tugra, in the middle of the waters, thrown into a darkness with nothing to take hold of, *anārambhaṇe tamasi* — and four ships, welcome, urged on by the Aśvins, bring him across. The precision is what strikes: not the sea, but a dark with no handhold; not a rescue, but four ships.

The seventh verse asks a question and does not answer it. *Kaḥ svit vṛkṣo niḥṣṭhito madhye arṇasaḥ* — what was that tree, standing out in the middle of the flood, that the pleading son of Tugra clung to? The comparison offered is of leaves grasped by a falling creature. And then: you, Aśvins, bore him up, to your own renown. The hymn does not know what the tree was. It says so, in the middle of a hymn of praise, and moves on.

The eighth verse returns to the present: may what the Mānas have said be after your mind, Nāsatya men; be gladdened today from this seat of soma. Then the household's seal, *vidyāma iṣaṃ vṛjanaṃ jīradānum*.
182.practice:
The rescue of Tugra's son is the {{aśvin}}au's signature deed, told in fragments all across the Ṛgveda and told here at length. What is worth noticing is the shape of it. A man is thrown into water, in darkness, with nothing to hold; something is made for him; he is carried out. Every element of the story is about being brought back from a place where nothing could be done.

That is what these two gods are for. They are the ones the tradition keeps as *devānāṃ bhiṣajau*, physicians among the gods, and the reason is the pattern in this hymn rather than any one miracle: their department is situations that have already become hopeless. Illness, drowning, night, an old body, a barren cow. Where the concern is rescue rather than victory, this is the address.

The most useful verse for a reader is the seventh, and it is useful because of what it admits. *Kaḥ svit vṛkṣaḥ* — what was that tree? The singer is praising a rescue and stops to say he does not know what the drowning man was holding on to. A hymn is allowed to contain a question it cannot answer, and that is a better model for reading the Veda than any confident reconstruction of the legend.

Verse 3 is worth knowing for its bluntness. The complaint is not that the gods are absent, but that they are hanging about somewhere a man who gives nothing is being honoured. The singer's grievance is against a world where the wrong people are respected, and his prayer is that the gods walk past that house and come to his. It is unedifying and entirely recognisable.

And verse 5's *plavam ātmanvantaṃ pakṣiṇam* — a raft that breathes and has wings — is one of the images the collection simply hands over without explanation. It is meant to be strange.
182.disagreements:
Verse 1's *viśpalāvasū* is the sharpest divergence in the hymn, because one translator finds a person in it and the other does not. Griffith reads a proper name and prints "succourers of Vispala," pointing to the woman for whom, in another hymn, the Aśvins are said to have made a metal leg. Wilson dissolves the compound and gets "rich in benevolence to mankind," taking *viś* as the people and *pala* as cherishing. Sāyaṇa records both: he gives the etymological reading and then notes that the reference may be to the Viśpalā legend.

On verse 2's *maruttamā*, most Marut-like, Sāyaṇa offers an unexpected alternative — reading it as *mitarāgiṇau*, of moderated passions, mild; or *mitarāviṇau*, not noisy. The Maruts being what they are, this turns a superlative of storm into its opposite. Both translators keep the Maruts.

Verse 7's comparison defeats everyone. Sāyaṇa works at *parṇā mṛgasya patatoriva ārabhe* at length, taking *mṛga* as a sweeper or cleaner and the leaves as something sufficient to hold on to when falling. Wilson prints "as leaves (are caught hold of) for the support of a falling animal"; Griffith, "Like twigs, of which some winged creature may take hold." The verse is difficult and no witness pretends otherwise.
182.note: taugryāya and taugryam verified in the padapāṭha at 1.182.5, 1.182.6 and 1.182.7; Bhujyu is not named in this sūkta, which speaks only of the son of Tugra

183.title: Three-Wheeled Car — the Aśvins Cross the Darkness
183.synthesis:
Six verses, five of them about a vehicle and the last one about what it was for.

The first verse builds the chariot out of threes. Yoke that thing which is swifter than mind — *trivandhura*, with three seats; *tricakra*, with three wheels; and, by the end of the verse, *tridhātu*, of three substances, in which you fly like a bird on its wings. Three "three"s in four lines, and the vehicle described is one no wheelwright could make.

The second verse brings it down to the ground. *Suvṛd ratho vartate yann abhi kṣām* — the easy-rolling chariot turns as it goes toward the earth, when you two, full of *kratu*, mount it for the food. May this song, itself a marvel, keep company with your marvellous form; and you keep company with {{uṣas}}, the daughter of Dyaus. The word for wonder is used twice in one line, once of the hymn and once of the gods, which is the singer putting his own work on the same shelf as the thing he is describing.

The third verse asks them to get in. Mount the easy-rolling car — the one that turns *anu vratāni*, according to the observances, of the man with the oblation; the one in which, Nāsatya men, you make your round to give refreshment, *tanayāya tmane ca*, for the offspring and for oneself. That last phrase is what a householder wants: something for the children, and something for himself.

The fourth verse is the strange one. *Mā vāṃ vṛko mā vṛkīr ā dadharṣīt* — let not the wolf, let not the she-wolf overpower; do not pass by, and do not hand over. Then, immediately: this is your portion, set down; this is the song; these are your stores of sweet things, *dasrau*. A fear and a table, in the same verse, with nothing between them.

The fifth calls the roll of everyone else who has called. Gotama, Purumīḷha and Atri — three names from three different singing families — each with his oblation, invoke you for help — and then a plain simile: like someone who goes straight to the quarter he has been pointed toward, come, Nāsatyas, to my call. The request is for directness. No detours, no other houses first.

And the sixth verse says what all the travel was in aid of. *Atāriṣma tamasaḥ pāram asya* — we have crossed to the far shore of this darkness; the *stoma* has been set toward you; now come here by the *devayāna*, the paths the gods travel. Then the seal, *vidyāma iṣaṃ vṛjanaṃ jīradānum*.

That last verse is repeated exactly as the last verse of [[1.184]], which follows immediately. Two consecutive Aśvin hymns end on the same sentence about having got through the dark.
183.practice:
*Atāriṣma tamasaḥ pāram asya* — we have crossed over to the far side of this darkness. It closes this hymn and it closes [[1.184]] as well, and it is the line to carry out of both.

It is spoken in the past tense. Not may we cross, not carry us across: we have crossed. Whatever the darkness was — a night, an illness, a season, the interval before dawn when the {{aśvin}}au are invoked — the hymn's position is that the far bank has been reached and the praise is what is offered on arriving. Anyone who has come through something and wanted words for the morning after has them here, and the tradition put them at the end of two hymns in a row.

The chariot verses repay a slower reading than they look as though they need. Verse 1 gives it three seats, three wheels and three substances, and verse 3 says it turns *anu vratāni*, following the observances of the man who has brought the oblation. The vehicle's course is set by somebody's kept practice. It is not summoned; it goes where the *vrata*s are being kept, and stops there.

Verse 5 is the one that places the reader in company. Gotama, Purumīḷha and Atri are named as men who have called these gods before — three families, not one — and the request that follows is for the Aśvins to come as directly to this call as they came to those. The argument for being heard is that others were.

And verse 3's *tanayāya tmane ca*, for the offspring and for oneself, is the most ordinary and most honest formulation of what a household asks for. Something for the children. And something for me.
183.disagreements:
Verse 1's *tridhātu* is where the readings part. Sāyaṇa fixes it as three metals — gold, silver and copper — and Wilson prints "embellished with three metals." Griffith declines the metals and keeps the word abstract: "whereon, threefold, ye fly like birds with pinions." On one reading the chariot is described materially; on the other the threefoldness is a property of the flight.

Verse 4 is the more consequential divergence, and here the padapāṭha decides it. Wilson translates "let not the wolf, let not the she-wolf, harm me safe (in your protection)," making the singer the endangered party. Griffith has "let not the wolf, let not the she-wolf harm you" — and the word division supports him: the verse reads *mā vām*, with the dual pronoun for the two Aśvins, so it is the gods who are being warded, not the man. The oddity of a worshipper warning gods against wolves is in the Sanskrit, and Wilson's version removes it.

The same verse's second half then divides them again on who is being asked not to be abandoned. Wilson supplies the singer — "abandon me not, nor deliver me (to another)"; Griffith keeps it plural and open, "nor pass me by or others."

Sāyaṇa's note on verse 5 explains the simile as applying to the man who invokes, the straight path being the direct route to what he wants.
183.note: 1.183.6 verified word-for-word identical with 1.184.6 in the padapāṭha; tri-vandhuraḥ, tri-cakraḥ and tri-dhātunā all confirmed at 1.183.1; mā | vām at 1.183.4 read from the padapāṭha

184.title: The Aśvins at Sūryā's Wedding, and Agastya's Song
184.synthesis:
The last of five consecutive hymns to the {{aśvin}}au, six verses in triṣṭubh, and it closes with the same sentence that closed [[1.183]].

*Tā vām adya tau aparaṃ huvema* — those two of you we call today, and those same two another day. The verse is careful about repetition: the same pair, this morning and the next. At the shining out of {{uṣas}}, the *vahni* calls with *ukthas*; Nāsatyas, wherever you may be, sons of Dyaus, on behalf of the man who gives more freely than the one who gives nothing (v1).

The second verse asks them to be glad among us and, in the same breath, to strike down the *paṇi*s — the ones who hold back what should be given. The two requests sit in one line without any sense that they need reconciling: be happy here, and deal with them. Then a request about attention that is unusually specific: hear me with the callings of my thoughts, for you are seekers and you are *nicetārā karṇaiḥ*, ones who notice with the ears. The singer is not asking to be granted anything yet. He is asking to be listened to properly.

The third verse is the one that carries furthest. *Śriye pūṣan… nāsatyā vahatuṃ sūryāyāḥ* — for glory, you gods arranged the *vahatu*, the bridal procession, of Sūryā. The wedding of the sun's daughter is being referred to as a known event, with the Aśvins in it as the ones who brought the bride. And then a comparison for their tall horses, born in the waters: they move like the worn yokes of great Varuṇa.

The fourth verse asks for the household's own portion of all that. Let that gift of yours be ours, sweet ones; speed the *stoma* of Mānya's poet — for when they hear of your renown, the peoples rejoice, wanting heroic strength. The fifth names the family and the man. *Eṣa vāṃ stomo aśvinā akāri mānebhiḥ* — this praise, Aśvins, has been made for you by the Mānas, with fair working; come on your round *tanayāya tmane ca*, for the offspring and for oneself, taking your pleasure in Agastya, Nāsatyas. Agastya names himself here in the third person, in the last full verse of his last Aśvin hymn.

And the sixth is the repeated close. *Atāriṣma tamasaḥ pāram asya* — we have crossed to the far shore of this darkness; the *stoma* has been set toward you; come here by the *devayāna*, the paths the gods travel. Then the seal, *vidyāma iṣaṃ vṛjanaṃ jīradānum*.

Five hymns to the Aśvins end here, and the last thing said in all of them is that the dark has been got through and that the way in is the road the gods use.
184.practice:
Verse 3 is why this hymn matters beyond its own six verses. The {{aśvin}}au are said to have arranged the *vahatu* of Sūryā — the bridal procession of the sun's daughter — and that is the event around which the whole Hindu wedding liturgy is built. The long telling stands at [[10.85]], the sūkta from which the mantras of the vivāha are drawn, and where the Aśvins appear as the two who came for the bride. What is stated here in half a line is the reason they are remembered at weddings at all.

Verse 5 is where Agastya signs off. The praise was made *mānebhiḥ*, by the Mānas, and the Aśvins are asked to come *agastye… madantā*, taking their pleasure in Agastya. He is named in the third person by his own household. Of the twenty-seven sūktas the Anukramaṇī gives him in this maṇḍala, this is the last that names him in its verses.

And what he asks for, in the same line, is what he asked for in [[1.183]].3: *tanayāya tmane ca*, for the offspring and for himself. It is worth setting that beside [[1.179]], where his wife tells him that the years have gone and that even the ancients who kept ṛta never reached the end of their austerity. The man in these hymns asks the gods, twice, for children and for his own life — and elsewhere in his own collection there is a verse in which he says he nourished both the householder's obligations and the ascetic's.

Verse 2's phrase is the one for a reader who finds prayer difficult. *Nicetārā karṇaiḥ* — you notice with your ears. What is asked first is not a gift but attention: hear me with the callings of my thoughts. Everything else in the hymn comes after that.
184.disagreements:
Verse 3 is the most heavily worked verse in the hymn and the translators end up in different places. Griffith takes it straightforwardly as the wedding: "Nasatyas, Pusans, ye as Gods for glory arranged and set in order Surya's bridal." Wilson turns *vahatu* into an abduction — the Aśvins "darting like arrows to acquire glory, and to carry off Sūryā" — and then reads the second half as being about the sacrifice rather than about horses, giving "the uninterrupted, sin-removing (sacrifice)." Sāyaṇa is the source of that: he glosses *varuṇasya bhūreḥ* as the unbroken rite which removes the sin that blocks the reward, and he explains the verse's *Pūṣan* as connoting both Aśvins, one as the sun and the other as the moon. He also attaches to this verse a legend of a prize of a thousand-stanza hymn, which the Aśvins won and then gave portions of to Agni and the other competitors at their request.

Verse 1's last word divides them too. Wilson makes *aryaḥ* the pious reciter and has him invoke on behalf of the liberal donor; Griffith reads a contrast and gets "for him who is more liberal than the godless." The two readings put the beneficiary in quite different company.

On verse 2's *ūrmyā* Wilson finds the libations and Griffith "our stream of Soma," while the word is more usually the night.
184.note: agastye verified in the padapāṭha at 1.184.5; 1.184.6 identical with 1.183.6; vahatum sūryāyāḥ confirmed at 1.184.3

154.title: Viṣṇu's Three Strides and the Well of Honey
154.synthesis:
*Viṣṇor nu kaṃ vīryāṇi pra vocam* — now I will proclaim the *vīrya*s of {{viṣṇu}}. Anyone who has read [[1.32]] will hear it at once: that hymn opens *indrasya nu vīryāṇi pra vocam*, and those are the only two verses in the whole Ṛgveda that begin this way. The formula that announces the killing of Vṛtra is used here to announce something with no fighting in it at all. What follows the announcement is not a battle but a measuring: he measured out the earthly regions, he propped up the upper *sadhastha*, the seat where things dwell together — *vicakramāṇas tredhā*, striding out threefold, the wide-going one.

The second verse says why the praise is offered and does it with an image nobody expects. *Mṛgo na bhīmaḥ kucaro giriṣṭhāḥ* — like a beast, dread, roaming where it will, keeping to the mountains. The god who holds the worlds up is compared to something wild that lives in high country and moves without asking. And then the claim the hymn will keep returning to: in whose three wide strides all the worlds have their dwelling.

The third verse sends the song after him. Let the strengthening *manman* go forth to Viṣṇu — mountain-dwelling, wide-going, the bull — *yaḥ idaṃ dīrghaṃ prayataṃ sadhasthaṃ eko vimame tribhir it padebhiḥ*: who alone measured out this long, far-stretched common dwelling with three steps and no more. Two words carry the verse: *ekaḥ*, alone, and *tribhiḥ*, with three. No helper and no fourth stride.

The fourth verse is where the strides stop being a feat and become a place. *Yasya trī pūrṇā madhunā padāni* — whose three steps are full of *madhu*, honey; *akṣīyamāṇā*, never running out; and they rejoice *svadhayā*, by their own power, needing nothing from outside. Then, again, the single-handedness: who alone upheld the threefold, and earth, and heaven, and all beings. The strides are not marks left behind. They are full of something, and what fills them does not diminish.

The fifth verse is the one the tradition never let go of. *Tad asya priyam abhi pātho aśyām* — may I reach that dear place of his, where men who go toward the gods take their delight. He is *bandhu*, the bond, the kinsman, of exactly that; for *viṣṇoḥ pade parame madhva utsaḥ* — in Viṣṇu's highest step is a spring of honey. Everything in the first four verses has been enormous and impersonal: regions measured, worlds propped, three steps across everything. Here a single person says *aśyām*, may I reach it — and what is there when he arrives is not power or knowledge but a well that runs sweet.

The sixth widens the wish from one man to two and gives the place a landscape. *Tā vāṃ vāstūny uśmasi gamadhyai* — we want to go to those dwellings of yours, where the cows are many-horned and swift-moving. And there, it says, that highest step of the wide-going bull shines down abundantly. The hymn ends looking upward at something that is shining down; the cows in that country are the only furniture it gives us.

What the sūkta does, then, is this. It borrows the opening of the Ṛgveda's greatest battle hymn and spends it on a god who does not fight. It states four times, in four different words, that the world is contained in three paces. It fills those paces with inexhaustible honey. And then it stops describing and starts wanting — *may I reach that*; *we want to go there* — so that the last two of its six verses turn a cosmological fact into a destination. That turn is why this hymn outlived almost everything around it.
154.practice:
Read by the numbers, {{viṣṇu}} in the Ṛgveda is a minor god. He is named in six sūktas of the 1,028 — [[1.22]] in its last six verses, this one, [[1.155]], [[1.156]], [[7.99]] and [[7.100]] — and only three are wholly his: [[1.154]], [[1.156]] and [[7.100]]. Against that stand 218 sūktas for {{indra}} and 186 for {{agni}}. Two of Viṣṇu's six are in this poet's stretch of maṇḍala 1. And yet this is the god who becomes, for one of the two great later streams of Hinduism, the whole of what there is. Nothing in the collection's arithmetic predicts that; this hymn is a large part of the reason it happened.

The phrase that did the work is in verse 6 and again, in reversed order, in verse 5: *paramaṃ padam*, the highest step or place. It occurs four times in the whole Ṛgveda — twice in [[1.22]], once here, once at [[4.5]].12 — and the most familiar of those is [[1.22]].20, *tad viṣṇoḥ paramaṃ padaṃ sadā paśyanti sūrayaḥ*, the seers always see that highest step of Viṣṇu. That line is recited daily by Vaiṣṇavas, and *paramapada* becomes the standard word for the final state. Its Ṛgvedic sense is concrete: the place where his third stride came down.

The three strides themselves became the Trivikrama story and, in the Purāṇas, the Vāmana avatāra — the dwarf who asks Bali for three paces of ground and takes the universe. It is worth being exact about what is and is not here. This hymn has the three strides, the measuring of the worlds, and the unreachable third step ([[1.155]].5 says even birds cannot follow it). It has no dwarf, no Bali, no request, no deception. The story grows later, out of these verses; the verses do not tell it.

And verse 5 is what to carry away from the sūkta itself. *Viṣṇoḥ pade parame madhva utsaḥ* — in Viṣṇu's highest step is the spring of honey. What is asked for is not to understand the three strides but to arrive where the third one landed, in the company of *devayavaḥ*, people who are moving toward the gods and are glad there. The Ṛgveda's usual request is for cattle, sons and safety. Here, for once and in one line, it is for somewhere to end up.
154.disagreements:
The hymn turns on how much is being measured, and Sāyaṇa opens it out rather than narrowing it. *Pārthivāni rajāṃsi* he takes not as "the earthly regions" but as the three worlds together, arguing that *pṛthivī* names all three — citing [[1.108]].9 and the Taittirīya Saṃhitā for Indra and Agni standing "in the lowest, the middle and the highest *pṛthivī*" — or else the three named in every invocation, *bhūḥ bhuvaḥ svaḥ*. Wilson prints "the three worlds"; Griffith keeps "earthly regions". For the *uttaraṃ sadhastham* propped in the same verse he offers four possibilities: the firmament; the seven regions above the earth; the highest region of all, from which there is no return; or *satyaloka*.

*Tridhātu* in verse 4 he reads as the three elements — earth, water, light — or the three divisions of time, or the three *guṇa*s. Griffith gives simply "the threefold".

Verse 2's wild beast draws the most from him. *Mṛga* he takes as a lion, {{viṣṇu}} hunting out his enemies; and *giriṣṭhā*, mountain-standing, he allows to mean one who abides in speech, in the form of the *mantra*. Wilson prints that second sense at verse 3 — "who abides in prayer" — where Griffith keeps mountains throughout.

His note on verse 6 is the most surprising here. He takes *vām*, "of you two", as the sacrificer and his wife, and records that the Yajurveda alters this pāda and applies it to the *yūpa*, the sacrificial post, while it is being trimmed to shape.

155.title: Indra and Viṣṇu: Two Strides Followed, One Not
155.synthesis:
The first three verses belong to {{indra}} and {{viṣṇu}} as a pair, the last three to Viṣṇu alone, and the hymn's best line is in the fifth.

*Pra vaḥ pāntam andhaso dhiyāyate* — bring forward your drink of the stalk to the one who sets his mind on it, to the great hero, and to Viṣṇu; sing to them. And the picture given of the two: undeceivable, they stood on the ridges of the mountains as though carried there by a good horse. It is an odd, exact image — two gods arriving on high ground the way a rider arrives.

The second verse names a danger and a rescue in the same breath. The meeting of you two vigorous ones is a blazing thing, Indra and Viṣṇu; the man who has drunk the pressed juice keeps clear of it. And then: *kṛśānor astur asanām uruṣyathaḥ* — the shot aimed at a mortal by Kṛśānu the archer, you two turn wide.
