Kṛśānu appears here and rarely elsewhere as the bowman who guards the {{soma}}; what the verse asks is that the arrow already loosed should go somewhere else.

The third verse is the hardest in the hymn. These offerings increase his great manhood; he brings the two parents down for the seed and for the enjoying. And then: *dadhāti putro avaraṃ paraṃ pituḥ nāma tṛtīyam adhi rocane divaḥ* — the son holds the father's lower name and his higher one, and a third up in the shining of heaven. Three names, one below, one above, one in the light: the verse plants the number three before the strides are mentioned, and does it in the vocabulary of a family rather than of space.

The fourth verse states the deed plainly. That manhood of his we sing — of the strong one, the protector, the one who does not injure, the generous — *yaḥ pārthivāni tribhir id vigāmabhiḥ uru kramiṣṭa urugāyāya jīvase*: who strode wide across the earthly regions with three paces, for a life that has room in it. That last phrase is the point of the strides in this hymn. They are made *jīvase*, for living, and the space they open is what living needs.

The fifth verse is the one to keep. *Dve id asya kramaṇe svardṛśo abhikhyāya martyo bhuraṇyati* — a mortal, catching sight of two of the strides of the one who looks on the sun, bestirs himself after them. *Tṛtīyam asya nakir ā dadharṣati* — but nobody dares approach his third; not even the winged birds that fly. The hymn does not say the third stride is forbidden or hidden. It says two of them can be seen and followed and the third cannot be reached, and it measures the failure by the flight of birds, which is the highest thing the poet could point at.

The sixth closes on a wheel and a count. With ninety names together with four, like a wheel set turning, he has set the passing ones in motion; vast of body, measuring himself out along with the singers, a youth who is no longer a child, he comes to our call. Whatever the ninety-four are — the tradition reads them as divisions of the year — the verse ends by bringing the god who cannot be followed to the third stride back down to a household that has called him.
155.practice:
Verse 5 is the verse to know, and it is one of the most useful things in the Ṛgveda for a reader who wants to know what these hymns think a person can and cannot do. Two of {{viṣṇu}}'s strides a mortal can see and go after; the third nobody reaches, and birds do not reach it either. There is no complaint in the line and no promise attached to it. It states a limit and leaves it standing.

Set beside [[1.154]].5 — *may I attain that dear place of his* — the two verses give the tradition's whole tension in miniature: the highest step is asked for and is out of reach, and the collection puts both statements next to each other without resolving them. That pairing is worth more to a reader than either verse alone.

The other line to carry is verse 4's. The three strides are taken *urugāyāya jīvase* — for a wide-going life, for living that has room in it. This is the plainest statement in the collection of what the strides are for. Viṣṇu does not measure the worlds to demonstrate anything; he does it so that there is space to live in. That is why he is invoked in later thought as the one who pervades and thereby makes room, and the sense of the root √viś behind his name is doing some of that work.

The pairing with {{indra}} in the first three verses is also worth registering. Of the six sūktas in the Ṛgveda that name Viṣṇu, two give verses to *indrāviṣṇū* as a dual — this one and [[7.99]] — and the compound occurs in only three verses of the whole collection. In the Ṛgveda Viṣṇu is most often Indra's ally: he stands beside him in the fight, and [[1.156]].4 has the two of them opening the cattle-pen together. The relative positions of these two gods in later Hinduism are the exact reverse of their positions here, and knowing that makes both the Veda and what came after it more legible.
155.disagreements:
Verse 3 is where every witness struggles. Sāyaṇa gives the family reading first — the son of the father has an inferior name, that of grandson, and a superior, that of son — then supplies a quite different explanation: the oblations rise to the solar region and nourish {{indra}} and {{viṣṇu}} as two of the Ādityas, who send down rain, by which the earth is made fruitful and fathers, sons and grandsons are successively begotten. Wilson prints the first and gestures at the second. Griffith reads a contest of rank: "He lowers, though a son, the Father's highest name."

Verse 2's Kṛśānu also divides. Sāyaṇa does not keep him as an archer at all, glossing *kṛśānu* as fire, the scatterer of good things or the disperser of enemies; Wilson builds from that an elaborate sentence about a reward distributed through fire. Griffith keeps the bowman — "bow-armed Krsanu's arrow, ye turn far aside" — which is the older figure, the guardian of the {{soma}}.

Verse 6's count is unexplained in the hymn. Sāyaṇa takes Viṣṇu here as time and enumerates the ninety-four: the year, two solstices, five seasons, twelve months, twenty-four half-months, thirty days, eight watches and twelve signs. Griffith declines the identification and makes them horses.

On verse 5 Sāyaṇa explains the limit concretely — the strides on earth and in the firmament fall within mortal sight, the one in heaven does not — and reads the flying things as the {{marut}}s, or as Garuḍa, or as the winds.

156.title: Viṣṇu, Germ of Ṛta, Opens the Pen with Indra
156.synthesis:
Five verses, and unlike the two hymns before it this one is not about the strides. It is about {{viṣṇu}}'s standing among the other gods and about what a man gets for addressing him.

*Bhava mitro na śevyo ghṛtāsutiḥ* — be kindly, like a friend, you who are poured with ghṛta; of manifest splendour, *evayā*, going your own way, and wide-extending. And then a claim about the hymn itself: even by a man who knows, Viṣṇu, your *stoma* is still to be increased, and your {{yajña}} still to be accomplished by the one who holds the offering. Knowing is not finishing. The praise has to be added to and the rite carried out.

The second verse describes the man who does it. He who gives to Viṣṇu — the ancient ordainer and the newest of all, *sumajjāni*, well accompanied by his wife — and who speaks greatly of the birth of this great one: he indeed, by his renowns, goes past even his equal. The reward named is not wealth but standing among peers, which is a very specific thing to want.

The third verse turns to the singers and gives Viṣṇu the epithet that matters most in this sūkta. Him, O praisers, since you know him — the ancient one, *ṛtasya garbham*, the germ of {{ṛta}}, the embryo carried by the order itself — fill him by your very birth. Knowing his name, speak it out. And then the first person plural, quietly: may we share in your good favour, great Viṣṇu. The instruction is to name him and the request is to be included.

The fourth verse places him in company. King {{varuṇa}} attends on this {{kratu}}, and so do the {{aśvin}}s — the *kratu* of the ordainer of the {{marut}} troop. Viṣṇu holds *dakṣam uttamam aharvidam*, the highest effective power, the power that finds the day; and, having a friend beside him, he uncovers the pen. That last clause is the one to catch. Opening the cattle-pen is {{indra}}'s deed, told in [[1.32]] and [[1.130]]; here it is Viṣṇu who does it, and the friend at his side is Indra.

The fifth verse says why he was there. Viṣṇu, the divine one, came *sacathāya*, for fellowship, to Indra — a doer of good coming to a doer of good, and being the better doer. The ordainer, *trisadhastha*, occupying three seats, quickened the *ārya*; and he gave the man performing the rite *ṛtasya bhāge*, a share in ṛta. The hymn ends on a distribution. What the god who has three seats hands out to the householder is a portion of the order itself.

Read together the five verses make a single argument, and it is not the argument of [[1.154]]. There the strides open a place a man might want to reach. Here Viṣṇu is described entirely by association and effect: he is friendly like Mitra, he is both the oldest and the newest, he is carried in ṛta, Varuṇa and the Aśvins wait on his purpose, he opens the pen with Indra beside him, and he gives the sacrificer a share. *Trisadhastha*, three-seated, is the only trace in this hymn of the three strides — and the hymn does not stop to explain it, because by now nobody needs telling.
156.practice:
The epithet to take from this sūkta is verse 3's: *ṛtasya garbham*, the germ or embryo of {{ṛta}} — {{viṣṇu}} as the thing the order carries. Set beside the identification the Brāhmaṇa tradition makes, that Viṣṇu is the sacrifice itself, this is the root of everything later Vaiṣṇava thought does with him as *yajña-puruṣa*, the person who is the rite. The Ṛgveda does not say that in so many words. What it says is that he is what {{ṛta}} is carrying, which is a stranger and better image.

The other thing here that changed the shape of Hinduism is in verse 4, and it is easy to read past. *Vrajaṃ ca viṣṇuḥ sakhivān aporṇute* — and Viṣṇu, having a friend, uncovers the pen. That is {{indra}}'s signature deed, the opening of the cattle-enclosure told in [[1.32]] and [[1.130]] and again at [[1.132]].4. Here Viṣṇu performs it with Indra as the companion. In the Ṛgveda Viṣṇu is Indra's ally and the junior of the two; by the time of the epics and Purāṇas that relation has inverted completely. This verse is one of the places where the inversion can be seen beginning: the deed is being shared.

Verse 2's *sumajjāni*, "having a good wife", is worth flagging honestly because it is often over-read. It is one of very few places in the collection that suggests a consort for Viṣṇu at all, and the Ṛgveda gives her no name. The identification with Śrī or Lakṣmī belongs to later texts, and the Śrī-sūkta is a *khila*, an appended hymn, not part of the Śākala collection proper. What is here is a single compound.

And verse 1 is the practical one. Even for the man who knows, the *stoma* has still to be increased and the {{yajña}} still to be accomplished. Understanding does not discharge the obligation to perform. That is the reason the tradition keeps reciting texts it has already understood, and this hymn states it in its first verse.
156.disagreements:
Verse 3's *ṛtasya garbham* is the hymn's crux, and Sāyaṇa gives two readings that pull in opposite directions. On the first, {{ṛta}} is the sacrifice and {{viṣṇu}} is born as one with it — for which he quotes the Aitareya Brāhmaṇa, *yajño vai viṣṇuḥ*, Viṣṇu verily is the sacrifice. On the second, *ṛta* keeps its sense of water, and the phrase makes Viṣṇu the cause of the waters, for which he cites Manu, "in the beginning he created water". A god identical with the rite, or a god who made the waters. Wilson prints "the germ of sacrifice"; Griffith, "primeval germ of Order".

The same verse's *januṣā pipartana* he glosses as propitiating him "by your birth", explaining it as spontaneously, from no interested motive, not because a boon is expected. Wilson follows with "of your own accord"; Griffith reads only "as well as ye know".

Verse 4 divides on who is described. Sāyaṇa allows *mārutasya vedhasaḥ* to mean either the rite offered to Viṣṇu attended by the {{marut}}s, or *māruta* as a name for {{indra}}. Wilson makes the verse about the sacrifice and inserts the priests; Griffith keeps it about the god and keeps the pen literal, "with his Friend unbars the stable of the kine".

On verse 5 Sāyaṇa records the Nirukta's derivation of *indra* as the one who pours out the food, allowing the word here to mean the *yajamāna* — Viṣṇu coming for fellowship with the man, not the god. Neither translator takes it.

157.title: The Aśvins Yoke at Dawn — Physicians with Medicines
157.synthesis:
The sūkta opens with four things happening at once, in four clauses, in one verse. *Abodhi agnir jma ud eti sūryaḥ* — {{agni}} has woken; Sūrya is rising from the earth; great shining {{uṣas}} has opened the dark with her light; the {{aśvin}}s have yoked their chariot to travel. And then a fifth clause that sets everyone else moving: god Savitṛ has impelled the world, each thing to its own. It is a description of a morning, and the gods in it are doing what a household does at first light — waking, getting up, harnessing, going out to work.

The second verse asks for the chariot to be loaded. When you yoke the bull-chariot, Aśvins, sprinkle our *kṣatra*, our power to act, with ghṛta and with *madhu*; quicken our {{brahman}}, our formulated prayer, in the fights; may we take our share of the winnings in the contest of heroes. Two liquids and a word, poured on the same thing.

The third verse describes the chariot itself, and it is the finest inventory in the hymn. *Tricakraḥ madhuvāhanaḥ rathaḥ* — three-wheeled, honey-carrying; drawn by quick horses, well praised, three-seated, rich, bringing every good fortune. May it come near, and bring welfare *dvipade catuṣpade*, to our two-footed and our four-footed. The Aśvins' vehicle is counted in threes and the thing it carries is honey, and what is asked of it is the health of the people and the animals in one phrase.

The fourth verse is the one to hold, because everything asked for is bodily. Bring us *ūrj*, nourishment; *madhumatyā naḥ kaśayā mimikṣatam* — sprinkle us with your whip that is full of honey; *pra āyus tāriṣṭam*, carry our lifespan further; *nir rapāṃsi mṛkṣatam*, wipe the blemishes off us; drive away hatred; and be *sacābhuvā*, those who are alongside. A longer life, a body cleaned of what is wrong with it, and company.

The fifth verse states their reach. *Yuvaṃ ha garbhaṃ jagatīṣu dhatthaḥ* — you two place the germ within the creatures that move; you are inside all beings; and you, bulls, sent forth Agni and the waters and the trees of the wood. From the seed in a womb to fire, water and forest, in one verse: the Aśvins are named as the ones who put life into things and then as the ones who released the elements.

The sixth closes on the office everybody remembers them for. *Yuvaṃ ha stho bhiṣajā bheṣajebhiḥ* — you two are physicians, with medicines; and you are charioteers, with the skill of driving. And then the exchange: you set *kṣatra* upon the man who has given to you with the offering and with his mind. The last verse names their two trades side by side — healing and driving — and both are practical crafts requiring equipment and training. Neither is described as a power.

The thread running the whole sūkta is *madhu*. It is in the second verse as what should be sprinkled on our power, in the third as what the chariot carries, in the fourth as what coats the whip. The Aśvins arrive at dawn with a load of honey, and everything they are asked to do — strengthen, prolong, cleanse, heal — is done by putting it on.
157.practice:
The {{aśvin}}s are the physicians, and this hymn is where the Ṛgveda says so most plainly. *Yuvaṃ ha stho bhiṣajā bheṣajebhiḥ* — you two are healers, with remedies. The word *bhiṣaj* appears in only five verses of the whole collection, and this is one of them; the tradition's standing description of the twins, *devānāṃ bhiṣajau*, physicians of the gods, rests on lines like this one. When the concern is illness, surgery, recovery or a body that has stopped working, the Aśvins are the door the Veda opens, and the later prestige of Āyurveda's divine descent runs back through them.

Verse 4 is the one to keep for that purpose. What it asks for is exactly what a sick person asks for: *pra āyus tāriṣṭam*, extend the span of life; *nir rapāṃsi mṛkṣatam*, wipe off the flaws — *rapas* is bodily defect, injury, the thing wrong with you; and *bhavatam sacābhuvā*, be the ones who stay alongside. Long life, a body put right, and not being left alone.

The first verse repays being read as a clock. Agni wakes, Sūrya rises, Uṣas opens the light, the Aśvins harness, Savitṛ sets everyone to their separate work. That is the order of a Vedic morning and the reason the Aśvins belong to the dawn: they are the pair who arrive as the light does. Their pressing in the rite is the early one, and their hymns are full of the words for first light.

They are also, after {{indra}} and {{agni}}, among the most frequently addressed deities in the collection: 69 sūktas name them, against 86 for the *Viśvedevāḥ* and 36 for *mitrāvaruṇau*. Sixteen sūktas are theirs alone in maṇḍala 1 — more than in any other book — and twenty-two name them here.

And verse 5 accounts for a use that is still made of them. *Yuvaṃ ha garbhaṃ jagatīṣu dhatthaḥ* — you two set the germ in creatures that move. Where the concern is conception and childbirth, this is the verse behind the tradition's habit of turning to the twins.
157.disagreements:
The honey is where the witnesses differ most, and the difference is about what kind of substance is meant. On verse 2 Sāyaṇa gives three possibilities for *madhu*: citing the Nirukta, it is a name for water, so the phrase means sweet water; or it is *amṛta*, so the sense is trickling nectar; or it is simply honey — and he supports the last by pointing forward to the next verse, where the {{aśvin}}s' chariot is *madhuvāhana*, honey-carrying, a compound that occurs nowhere else in the Ṛgveda. Wilson prints "trickling honey"; Griffith, "honey and … oil".

Verse 4's whip divides them completely. Sāyaṇa glosses *kaśā*, whip, as *vāc*, speech, so that the Aśvins sprinkle us with their honeyed *words*; Wilson prints exactly that — "animate us with your honied speech". Griffith keeps the object: "sprinkle us with your whip that drops with honey-dew." A whip that drips honey is one of the collection's strangest images, and one of the two witnesses has removed it.

On verse 2 Sāyaṇa reads *brahman* not as prayer but as *anna*, food, and *pṛtanā* not as battles but, citing the Nirukta, as men — children and dependants. Wilson follows into "bestow abundant food upon our people", where Griffith keeps both words in their usual senses. The two English versions of that half-verse have almost nothing in common.

Verse 5's *jagatīṣu* is left open: Wilson has "all moving creatures", Griffith "female creatures". The word supports the first, the context the second.

158.title: The Aśvins and Dīrghatamas Cast in the Waters
158.synthesis:
This is the strangest of Dīrghatamas' sūktas, because most of it happened to him.

The first verse calls the {{aśvin}}s by two group names that do not belong to them — *vasū rudrā*, you Vasus, you Rudras — and adds *purumantū*, of much counsel, and *vṛdhantā*, increasing. Favour us, bulls, in your presence; since Aucathya sets wealth before you, and since you have come forward with aids that are not stingy. The poet names himself in the first verse by his patronymic and will name himself outright in the last.

The second verse asks the question a man asks when he cannot repay. *Kaḥ vāṃ dāśat sumataye cid asyai* — who could give you enough for this good favour of yours, when with {{namas}} you set something down at the place of the cow? And then what he wants: wake up rich *puraṃdhi*s for us — fullness of mind, abundance — you two who move about with a mind that means to fulfil what is wanted.

The third verse recalls the rescue everyone knew. *Yuktaḥ ha yad vāṃ taugryāya peruḥ* — when your crossing-vessel, harnessed and strong, was set for the son of Tugra in the middle of the flood. Bhujyu, abandoned at sea, is the Aśvins' standing case, told again and again across the collection; here it is named in half a verse and then turned into a wish: may I come to your shelter and your protection, as a hero comes back to his army with flying speed.

The fourth verse turns to the poet's own danger, and it is difficult. May this praise protect Aucathya. Let not these two winged ones drain me dry; let not the ten-layered pile of wood burn me; when the bound man, of himself, bites the earth. Something is threatening to consume him, something is stacked and ready to be lit, and someone is tied and face down on the ground.

The fifth says who did it. *Na mā garan nadyo mātṛtamāḥ* — let the rivers, the most motherly of all, not swallow me: since the Dāsas threw down the well-bound man. And when Traitana would cut his head off, the Dāsa cut into his own breast and shoulders instead. A man bound and thrown into water, an attempted beheading that goes wrong, and rivers addressed as mothers by the man they are about to drown. The Ṛgveda does not narrate this anywhere else, and the verse assumes we know it.

The sixth verse, in a shorter metre, closes with the poet's name and a claim about his age. *Dīrghatamā māmateyo jujurvān daśame yuge* — Dīrghatamas, son of Mamatā, grown old in the tenth *yuga*; and he becomes the *brahmā* and the charioteer of the waters as they strive toward their goal. Whatever the tenth *yuga* means — a decade, a generation, an age of the world — the verse claims great age; and what an old blind man becomes, in the last line, is the one who directs something moving toward where it is going.

The sūkta is therefore built as a single argument from precedent to case. You saved Bhujyu out of the sea. Here I am, bound and thrown into a river, with fire stacked beside me. Let the water not take me. And when it is over, the man who was in the water is the one who steers.
158.practice:
This is one of the few places in the Ṛgveda where a poet describes what happened to him. Dīrghatamas — named here in the last verse, and named again only at [[8.9]].10 in the whole collection — says he was bound, cast down by the Dāsas, threatened with fire and with a blade, and nearly drowned. The tradition remembers him as blind, as the son of Mamatā ([[1.147]].3), and as the author of the 25 consecutive sūktas from [[1.140]] to [[1.164]], including the great riddle-hymn. This sūkta is the biographical note attached to that body of work, and it is worth knowing that the man who composed [[1.164]] is on record as having been thrown in a river.

What he does with it is the instructive part. He does not curse anyone. He recalls a precedent — the {{aśvin}}s bringing Bhujyu, son of Tugra, out of the open sea, which is their standing deed across the collection — and asks to be in the same position as the man who was saved. That is how the Ṛgveda argues, and [[1.132]] does the same with {{indra}}. A person in trouble names a case where the god acted and asks for the same act.

The phrase to carry is in verse 5: *nadyo mātṛtamāḥ*, the rivers, most motherly of all — said by a man asking them not to swallow him. Nothing in the tradition's reverence for rivers is inconsistent with that verse. What is holy is not therefore safe, and the hymn holds both at once without embarrassment.

And the last verse gives an image worth keeping for old age. Grown old, in the tenth *yuga*, the poet becomes *brahmā* and *sārathi* — the one who holds the formulation and the one who drives — of the waters striving toward their end. The man who could not save himself from the water in verse 5 is steering it in verse 6. Whether *yuga* here means a decade or an age of the world, neither witness can say, and neither should a reader.
158.disagreements:
Verses 4 and 5 are obscure in every witness, and the divergences are large. Sāyaṇa reads verse 4's *tmani khādate kṣām*, "he eats the earth by himself", as an old man too infirm to walk who crawls or rolls on the ground, which Wilson prints. Griffith takes the same clause of the stacked wood — "when fixed for you it bites the ground it stands on" — so that the subject is a pyre, not a person. In one reading a decrepit man is on the ground; in the other, timber is.

Verse 5's Traitana is unexplained by anyone. Wilson has Traitana wound the poet's head and then, in parallel, the slave wound his own; Griffith reads a single failed attack — "When Traitana would cleave my head asunder, the Dasa wounded his own breast and shoulders." Sāyaṇa makes the verb an imperative: therefore let that Dāsa of his own accord wound his own head. A completed act, a botched attempt, or a curse.

Sāyaṇa attaches an unusual use to the sūkta: silent repetition of it protects against a murderer, a wolf or a tiger, and a traveller is to repeat it three times until sunrise.

On verse 6 he reads *brahmā* as "like Brahmā", the chief; and *apām* as either those who must make water-offerings to the ancestors or, taking the word as *apas*, rites in general — making Dīrghatamas chief of those performing rites rather than of the waters. Griffith keeps the waters.

159.title: Dyāvāpṛthivī, Whose Children Are the Gods
159.synthesis:
Five verses to {{dyāvāpṛthivī}}, Heaven and Earth as a single dual deity, and the sūkta treats them throughout as parents — of the gods, of everything alive, and of the men saying the hymn.

*Pra dyāvā yajñaiḥ pṛthivī ṛtāvṛdhā* — with {{yajña}}s I praise Heaven and Earth, increasers of {{ṛta}}, great, wise at the *vidatha*s. And then the phrase that gives them their standing: *devebhir ye devaputre sudaṃsasā*, who have the gods for their children, and who, with {{dhī}}, with the thought engaged, bring forward what is worth choosing. A hymn to a pair older than the gods it usually addresses is a rare thing in this collection, and this one begins by saying so.

The second verse divides them by role. *Uta manye pitur adruho manaḥ* — I think on the mind of the father, who does not deceive, and on the great self-standing power of the mother, with my callings. The father has a *manas*, a mind, and the epithet given him is negative and moral: *adruh*, without treachery. The mother has *svatavas*, strength that is her own and needs no source. And then what they made: *pitarā bhūma cakratuḥ*, the parents made the world of life, and by their expanses, wide deathlessness for their offspring.

The third verse turns to the children. These sons of yours, skilled in work and of wondrous power, brought the two great mothers to birth for the first perceiving; and for the truth of what stands and the ordering of what moves, they guard the *pāthas*, the station, of the son who has no duplicity in him. The verse is hard and both witnesses read it differently, but its shape is clear enough: the children of Heaven and Earth are doing something to Heaven and Earth in return, and what they keep in place is the truth of the standing world and the *dharman* of the moving one.

The fourth verse is the finest here. *Te māyino mamire supracetasaḥ* — those possessors of *māyā*, very wise, measured out the twins, born of one womb, paired, dwelling together. And then: *navyaṃ-navyaṃ tantum ā tanvate divi samudre antaḥ kavayaḥ sudītayaḥ* — ever new, ever new, they stretch out a thread in the sky and within the sea, the seers, brightly shining. The verse gives the collection's own image of what a poet does: weaving is going on continuously, in heaven and in the deep, and the thread is new every time. Set beside the Āprī hymn [[1.142]].1, where {{agni}} is asked to *spin out the ancient thread*, the two together say the whole thing — the same weaving, always old and always new.

The fifth verse ends by asking, and it does so in words a Hindu reader will recognise instantly. *Tad rādho adya savitur vareṇyaṃ vayaṃ devasya prasave manāmahe* — that choice bounty of Savitṛ today, at the god's impulsion, we bring to mind. Then the request to the pair: Dyāvāpṛthivī, with a kindly mind, place with us wealth full of goods and counted in hundreds. The hymn began with the parents of the gods and ends with a household asking for cattle.
159.practice:
The last verse of this sūkta contains a phrase that almost every Hindu says daily without knowing where else it stands. *Tat savitur vareṇyam* — that choice thing of Savitṛ — occurs in exactly two verses of the entire Ṛgveda: here at [[1.159]].5, and at [[3.62]].10, which is the Gāyatrī. The two verses share more than the phrase: this one has *devasya prasave*, at the god's impulsion, where the Gāyatrī has *devasya dhīmahi* and then *dhiyo yo naḥ pracodayāt*, may he impel our thoughts. The same god, the same syllables, the same idea of being set in motion. Anyone who recites the Gāyatrī at the junctures has, in this verse, its nearest relative in the collection.

{{dyāvāpṛthivī}} themselves are worth knowing as a form. Eleven sūktas of the Ṛgveda name them; six are theirs alone — this one, [[1.160]] immediately after it, [[1.185]], [[4.56]], [[6.70]] and [[7.53]]. They are always dual, always a pair, and the tradition's habitual line about them is that Dyaus is the father and Pṛthivī the mother. That division survives in ordinary speech: *pṛthivī mātā* is a phrase a child still learns, and touching the ground before beginning something rests on the same instinct.

Verse 2 is the one to sit with. The father is *adruh*, one who does not deal falsely; the mother is *svatavas*, strong of herself. Those are not decorative epithets — they are the two things one would most want to be able to say of a parent, and the Veda assigns one to each. And what the pair are said to have made is *uru amṛtam prajāyai*, wide deathlessness for their offspring, by their sheer extent.

And verse 4 gives a working image for recitation itself. *Navyaṃ-navyaṃ tantum ā tanvate* — they stretch out a thread that is new and new again. The Ṛgveda's word for its own composition is weaving, and the thread it describes is simultaneously the oldest thing there is and made fresh every morning. That is a fair description of what a reciter is doing.
159.disagreements:
Verse 3 is where the two translations part company entirely, and the disagreement is about who made whom. Griffith reads the sons as producing their parents: "These Sons of yours well skilled in work, of wondrous power, brought forth to life the two great Mothers first of all." Wilson, following the commentary, reverses the direction — the children "recognize you as their great parents, through experience of former kindness" — and turns the second half into a request that stability be preserved in the functions of the offspring. One version has the gods generating Heaven and Earth; the other has them acknowledging them.

The same difficulty runs through verse 1. Sāyaṇa glosses *devaputre* two ways: having the gods for children, or reverenced by the gods, taking *deva* as the *yajamāna*. Wilson prints the second — "cherishing their worshippers as children" — Griffith the first, "having Gods for progeny".

On verse 2 Sāyaṇa records the standing formula *dyaur vaḥ pitā pṛthivī mātā*, and adds the Nirukta's alternative that the mother here is the *antarikṣa*.

Verse 4 he treats as a grammatical problem. Some epithets there are plural — *māyinaḥ*, *supracetasaḥ*, *kavayaḥ* — and some dual, *sayonī*, *samokasā*. He concludes that the plurals need another subject, the rays of light, while the duals belong to Heaven and Earth. Wilson accordingly makes the verse about rays; Griffith about the two.

185.title: Which of the Two Is Elder — Dyāvāpṛthivī, Guard Us
185.synthesis:
Eleven verses, and seven of them end with the same line: *dyāvā rakṣataṃ pṛthivī no abhvāt* — Dyāvā and Pṛthivī, guard us from the *abhva*, the shapeless overwhelming thing. It runs from verse 2 through verse 8 without a break. Whatever else the hymn is doing, it keeps coming back to the same fear.

It opens with a question that is never answered. *Katarā pūrvā katarā aparā* — which of these two is the earlier, which the later? How were they born? Who knows it, you *kavi*s? The hymn asks the seers, and moves on: by themselves they carry everything that is, and the two days turn over as though on wheels. A hymn to {{dyāvāpṛthivī}} that begins by admitting nobody knows which came first is a different kind of praise from most.

The second verse states the paradox they hold. *Bhūri dve acarantī carantam* — the two, not moving and without feet, sustain the moving and footed offspring, as parents hold their own son in their lap. Then the refrain begins.

Verse 3 asks for a specific gift: the faultless, unassailable, sun-bright, undying, homage-worthy giving of {{aditi}} — generate that for the singer, Rodasī. Verse 4 asks for nearness rather than gifts: unwearied, helping with help, having the gods for their children — may we keep close to those two, with both halves of the days. Verse 5 describes them as a pair of women: going always together, of the same age, with their edges meeting, sisters and kin, lying in their parents' lap, breathing upon *bhuvanasya nābhim*, the navel of the world. Whose parents' lap two world-halves lie in the hymn does not say.

Verse 6 calls them *urvī sadmanī bṛhatī ṛtena* — the two wide seats, lofty, by {{ṛta}} — the mothers, of fair face, who hold the *amṛta*. Verse 7 piles up the dimensions: wide, broad, abundant, with their ends far off, auspicious, well-advancing; and says what the singer is doing about it — *upa bruve namasā yajñe asmin*, I address them with *namas* at this rite.

Verse 8 is the confession. Whatever fault we have committed against the gods, or against a friend, or at any time against the *jāspati* — may this {{dhī}}, this very thought, be the turning-aside of it. The hymn itself is offered as the expiation. Then the refrain, for the last time.

The last three verses drop the refrain and change tone. May both, praise-worthy and friendly to men, favour me and stay with me as helpers; may we be refreshed and glad, gods, for the sake of the one who gives more (v9). Then verse 10: *ṛtaṃ dive tad avocaṃ pṛthivyai* — that truth I have spoken to Dyaus and to Pṛthivī, first, so that it may be heard, being of good understanding; may they guard us from blame and from misfortune close at hand; may father and mother protect us with their helps.

And verse 11 asks for the one thing left. *Idaṃ dyāvāpṛthivī satyam astu* — let this be true, father, mother, what I say here to you two; be the nearest of the gods with your helps. Then the household's seal. A hymn that began by asking which of them is older ends by asking that what has just been said should turn out to be so.
185.practice:
This is the third and last hymn to {{dyāvāpṛthivī}} in maṇḍala 1 — [[1.159]] and [[1.160]] are the other two — out of eleven in the whole collection. All three sit near the end of the book.

Its most usable verse is the eighth, which is a confession with a specific list. Offences against the gods; offences against a friend; offences at any time against the *jāspati*, the head of the family. Three parties, in that order, and the third is domestic. And the remedy offered is not a payment or a penance: *iyaṃ dhīr bhūyā avayānam eṣām* — may this thought be their turning-aside. The hymn is put forward as the expiation. That a Vedic household's formula for setting things right names a friend and a family head alongside the gods, and offers a well-made act of attention as the amends, is worth knowing.

The refrain is the second thing to take. Seven verses in a row end *rakṣataṃ pṛthivī no abhvāt*, guard us from the *abhva* — a word for something huge and without shape, the formless overwhelming. Nothing is specified. A reader who has ever been frightened of something they could not name has the Vedic word for it, repeated seven times, in a prayer to the two most solid things there are.

And verse 1 is worth sitting with precisely because it fails. Which of the two is older? How were they born? *Kaḥ vi veda* — who knows it? The question is put to the seers and never taken up again. Praise in the Ṛgveda is compatible with saying plainly that the thing being praised is not understood.

Verse 5 gives the image the tradition kept: heaven and earth as *svasārā jāmī*, sisters and kin, of the same age, their borders meeting, lying together in a lap. Not a hierarchy. Two who are the same age and touch along an edge.
185.disagreements:
Verse 8's *jāspatim* is where the family in this confession changes shape. Sāyaṇa parses it as *jāḥ*, daughters, plus *pati*, husband — a son-in-law — and Wilson prints exactly that. Griffith reads the compound as the head of the house and gives "our house's chieftain." On one reading the offence is against the man who married your daughter; on the other, against your own father.

Sāyaṇa also fills in what the refrain leaves blank. *Abhva* is glossed by supplying a noun: *mahato bhayahetoḥ pāpāt*, from sin, as the cause of great danger. Wilson accordingly prints "from great (danger)" and Griffith "from fearful danger," but neither names sin. The refrain in the Sanskrit is bare.

On verse 5's *bhuvanasya nābhim* Sāyaṇa offers *udaka*, water, as what binds all beings together, and notes it may be regarded as the child of heaven and earth since both contribute to producing it; or the two things meant may be water and the oblation. Wilson keeps "the navel of the world"; Griffith gives "the centre of the world."

On verse 3 Sāyaṇa glosses Aditi as the firmament, which converts an appeal to a goddess into a description of the sky. Wilson keeps her a giver of wealth; Griffith keeps the name and the gift: "Aditi's unrivalled bounty." On verse 11 Sāyaṇa reads *devānām* as *stotṛṇām*, of the praisers, which Wilson follows and Griffith does not.
185.note: the refrain dyāvā rakṣatam pṛthivī naḥ abhvāt counted at vv 2-8 in the padapāṭha (seven consecutive verses); dyāvāpṛthivyau ascriptions counted across all ten Anukramaṇī files (11 sūktas, of which 1.159, 1.160 and 1.185 are in maṇḍala 1)

186.title: Viśvedevāḥ Summoned in Turn, from Savitṛ to Pūṣan
186.synthesis:
A hymn to the {{viśvedevāḥ}} is a hymn that has to get everybody in, and this one does it by naming them in turn over eleven verses, with four consecutive verses beginning on the same two words.

It opens with {{savitṛ}}. May the god Savitṛ, *viśvānara*, belonging to all men, come to our *vidatha* with the *iḷā*s and with good praise; and may you, ever young, gladden us and the whole moving world at your arrival (v1). The second verse calls the group: may all the gods come to us together, {{mitra}}, Aryaman, {{varuṇa}} of one mind, so that all may be our strengtheners and make our force firm where it was slack. The third names {{agni}}: I praise with hymns your dearest guest, Agni, the swift, well-pleased along with you — so that Varuṇa, of good renown, praised even by the stranger, may carry refreshment across to us.

The fourth verse is the one where the imagery starts. I come to you with *namas*, Uṣāsānaktā, night and morning, seeking to win, like a good milch-cow — measuring out the *arka* on the same day, with milk of many forms in one udder. The whole rite is described as one udder giving several kinds of milk, and the chant is what is being measured out of it.

Then four verses in a row begin *uta naḥ*, and us too. Verse 5: and for us, may Ahi Budhnya make joy; may Sindhu come like a swelling mother to her young, by whom we may urge on Apāṃ Napāt, the child of the waters, whom the bulls swift as thought convey. Verse 6: and for us, may {{tvaṣṭṛ}} come, of one mind with the patrons at his visit; and may {{indra}} the Vṛtra-slayer, filler of the peoples, the strongest, come here to our men. Verse 7: and for us — and here the subject changes from gods to the singer's own thoughts — our *mati*s, yoked like horses, lick him as cows lick a young calf, and the songs come to him like wives to a husband, most fragrant of the men. Verse 8: and for us, may the {{marut}}s of the grown army sit down with heaven and earth, of one mind, with their dappled horses, like chariots, devourers of foes, like gods yoked in friendship.

Verse 9 stays with the Maruts and their arrival: their greatness is known when they set their teams to work, and their host sprinkles every barren place. The tenth returns to summoning and gets through the remainder in a line: bring forward the {{aśvin}}au for help, and Pūṣan, for they are self-strong; friendly are {{viṣṇu}}, Vāta and Ṛbhukṣan — may I turn the gods this way for our happiness.

The eleventh verse is about the hymn itself. *Iyaṃ sā vo asme dīdhitir yajatrāḥ* — this is that thought of ours for you, worshipful ones; may it be *apiprāṇī ca sadanī ca*, both filling with breath and taking a seat, this thought which strives among the gods, wanting good. Then the household's seal, *vidyāma iṣaṃ vṛjanaṃ jīradānum*.

The last thing the hymn asks for is that its own thought should breathe and sit down — that the words should live and stay.
186.practice:
The Ṛgveda gives eighty-six sūktas to the {{viśvedevāḥ}}, and their difficulty is always the same: how do you address everyone without addressing no one? This hymn's answer is the phrase that opens verses 5 to 8 — *uta naḥ*, and for us too. Each verse adds another power and each verse repeats that we are still here. It is closer to a household's list of everyone who must be remembered than to a theology.

What such lists preserve is the small deities. Ahi Budhnya, in verse 5, has almost no hymns of his own; Apāṃ Napāt, the child of the waters, is named alongside him; {{sindhu}} is asked to come like a mother with milk to her young. Verse 10 sweeps in the {{aśvin}}au, Pūṣan, {{viṣṇu}}, Vāta and Ṛbhukṣan in a line and a half. A Viśvedevāḥ hymn is where the tradition kept the names that would otherwise have been lost.

Verse 7 is the one worth carrying. It gives two pictures of what a hymn does when it reaches a god, one after the other. First: *śiśuṃ na gāvas taruṇaṃ rihanti* — the thoughts lick him as cows lick a newborn calf. Then: *taṃ īṃ giro janayo na patnīḥ* — the songs go to him as wives to a husband. Animal tenderness and married intimacy, in one verse, describing the same thing. The Ṛgveda does not think of praise as formal.

And verse 4's image is the one for a reader who wonders what a rite is doing. One udder, many kinds of milk, the *arka* measured out of it on the appointed day. The material is single; what comes from it varies with what is drawn.

The last verse asks that the singer's *dīdhiti*, his considered thought, should be *apiprāṇī*, filling with breath, and *sadanī*, taking a seat. Both together: live, and stay.
186.disagreements:
Verse 5's Ahi Budhnya is the most consequential name here and the readings differ on whether it is one being or two. Sāyaṇa allows *ahir* who is also *budhnya*, and glosses both elements as *antarikṣa*, so that the compound names a deity presiding over the firmament; he adds that the Purāṇas count Ahirbradhna among the Rudras and that the name belongs to Śiva. Wilson prints "Ahirbudhnya" as a name; Griffith translates it away entirely — "the great Dragon of the Deep."

Verse 1's *iḷābhiḥ* divides them at the outset. Sāyaṇa offers both *iḷā* as food and *iḷābhiḥ saha* as "with the divinities whose place is earth." Wilson takes the second and has Savitṛ arrive "together with the divinities of earth"; Griffith takes the first — "through praises offered as sacred food."

Verse 3 parts them on who Varuṇa is. Wilson keeps Varuṇa a separate god who fills the singers with food; Griffith reads Agni as being addressed throughout — "that he may be our Varuna rich in glory" — turning the name into an epithet.

Verse 9 is the widest divergence in the hymn. Wilson makes it rain: their host "pours rain upon every arid soil, as light spreads on a fine day." Griffith makes it weaponry: "As on a fair bright day the arrow flieth o'er all the barren soil their missiles sparkle." Water and arrows, from the same line.
186.note: uta | naḥ verified as opening vv 5, 6, 7 and 8 in the padapāṭha; viśvedevāḥ ascriptions counted across all ten Anukramaṇī files (86 sūktas)

187.title: Pitu, the Food — the One Hymn to What We Eat
187.synthesis:
Eleven short verses, alternating anuṣṭubh and gāyatrī, addressed to *pitu* — nourishment, the food that is eaten. The Anukramaṇī names the deity *annam*, and does so for no other sūkta in the Ṛgveda.

*Pituṃ nu stoṣam* — now I will praise Pitu, the great upholder, the strength by whose power Trita tore Vṛtra apart, joint from joint (v1). The hymn opens by crediting a victory over the serpent not to the god who struck but to what he had eaten. The second verse is the choosing: *svādo pito madho pito* — savoury Pitu, honeyed Pitu, we have chosen you; be our helper. The vocative is repeated twice in one line, which is how the whole hymn talks.

Verse 3 asks it to come, in the language usually reserved for a deity arriving at a rite: come to us, Pitu, auspicious, with auspicious helps, *mayobhū*, bringing gladness, not to be hated, a friend, very kind, *advayāḥ* — not double. Verse 4 spreads it out: your saps, Pitu, are laid out through the regions, resting in the sky like winds. Verse 5 watches people eat: these are your givers, sweetest one; the sweetnesses of your saps rouse men as though they had thick necks.

Verse 6 makes the largest claim in the hymn. *Tve pito mahānāṃ devānāṃ mano hitam* — in you, Pitu, the mind of the great gods is set; under your sign a fine thing was done, and *tava ahim avasā avadhīt*, with your help he killed Ahi. The subject is not named; the hymn does not need to name him. Verse 7 asks for delivery: when you have gone off to the shining of the mountains, even from there, honeyed Pitu, come to us, fit for our eating.

Then three verses in a row end on the same line. Whatever mouthful of the waters and the plants we take — *vātāpe pīva id bhava*, may it grow fat (v8). Whatever of {{soma}} we share, mixed with milk or with barley — the same close (v9). *Karambha oṣadhe bhava pīvo vṛkka udārathiḥ* — O barley-cake, be substantial, wholesome, strengthening — and the same close again (v10). The hymn moves from the abstraction of nourishment to what is actually on the ground: water, plants, milk, barley, and a lump of parched meal.

Verse 11 closes by describing what the hymn has just done. *Tvāṃ vayaṃ pito vacobhir gāvo na havyā susūdima* — you, Pitu, we have made sweet with our words, as cows are made ready for the offering; you, who feast together with the gods; you, who feast together with us. The last line is the point of the whole thing, and it is said twice, once for each party: *devebhyas tvā sadhamādam, asmabhyaṃ tvā sadhamādam*. The same food is the god's companion at table and ours.
187.practice:
There is exactly one sūkta in the Ṛgveda whose deity is *annam*, food, and this is it. That should be enough to make a reader stop. Out of 1,028 hymns, the thing eaten every day gets one, and it is placed near the very end of the first maṇḍala.

What it does with that one hymn is treat food as a guest. Verse 3 invites it in the terms a deity is invited — come to us, auspicious, with auspicious helps, a friend, very kind. Verse 2 chooses it: *vayaṃ tvā vavṛmahe*, we have chosen you. And verse 11 seats it at both tables at once: the same nourishment feasts with the gods and feasts with us. Nothing here separates the offering from the meal.

That is the seed of a great deal that came later. The Taittirīya Upaniṣad's *annaṃ brahmeti vyajānāt* — he understood food as brahman — is the same recognition worked out philosophically; the household discipline of offering before eating, and the treatment of *annadāna* as the highest giving, are the same recognition worked out in practice. For a Hindu who says a word over food before touching it, this hymn is where the habit is first visible.

Verse 6 is worth keeping for what it implies about strength. The mind of the great gods is set in food, and Vṛtra was killed *tava avasā*, with its help. The Ṛgveda's most celebrated act of power is here attributed to nourishment. Whatever else the singer thought heroism was, he thought it rested on having eaten.

And the last three verses are the practical ones. They name water, plants, soma mixed with milk or barley, and *karambha*, a lump of parched meal — and ask each of them to be nourishing. It is a blessing said over ordinary food, not over a rare offering. The Ṛgveda contains a grace, and this is it.
187.disagreements:
The refrain of verses 8 to 10 is where the readings part completely. *Vātāpe pīva id bhava* is understood by Sāyaṇa as an address to the body: *vātāpi* is *śarīra*, that which is sustained by *vāta*, the breath. Wilson follows and prints "Body, do you grow fat." Griffith keeps the word as a name and addresses it — "Vatapi, grow thou fat thereby" — and at verse 8 he substitutes Soma for it altogether. On Sāyaṇa's reading the hymn is asking one's own body to thrive on what is eaten, which is a different prayer from asking a being called Vātāpi to do so.

Verse 9 is where Sāyaṇa notices the subject change. The addressee, he says, is no longer food in general but a particular preparation of soma, mixed with *gavāśira* and *yavāśira*, boiled milk and boiled barley.

On verse 5's *tuvigrīvāḥ iva* Sāyaṇa offers two senses of *tuvi*: many, so that the eaters are like men with many throats, that is great eaters; or grown, so that when men eat they stand firm-limbed, and when they go without their necks bend down. Wilson prints the stiff necks; Griffith gives "creatures that have mighty necks."

On verse 3's *advayāḥ*, not-twofold, Sāyaṇa allows either a food with no incompatible property in it, or a friend who does not differ in mind and act.
187.note: annam verified as devatā of exactly one sūkta across all ten Anukramaṇī files; the refrain vātāpe pīvaḥ it bhava counted at vv 8, 9 and 10 in the padapāṭha

188.title: Agastya's Āprī — from Kindled Agni to Svāhā
188.synthesis:
An Āprī hymn is not a hymn to a god. It is a hymn in which the rite itself is addressed, item by item, in a fixed order, and the items answer to names. Eleven verses in gāyatrī, one deity each, and the Anukramaṇī lists them all.

It begins with Agni already lit. *Samiddho adya rājasi* — kindled, today you shine, a god among gods, winner of thousands; messenger, *kavi*, carry the oblations (v1). Then Tanūnapāt, self-born: the *yajña* going toward {{ṛta}} is anointed with honey, bestowing thousandfold refreshments (v2). Then, in the third verse, {{agni}} again as the one invoked — being called on, worthy of praise, bring here the gods who are worthy of sacrifice; you are winner of thousands. Between verse 2 and verse 3 the sequence has skipped a station that other Āprī hymns keep.

Verse 4 addresses the strewn grass. *Prācīnaṃ barhir ojasā sahasravīram astṛṇan* — eastward, with power, they have strewn the *barhis* that holds a thousand heroes, on which, Ādityas, you shine forth. Verse 5 addresses the doors, and does it in a rush of feminine plurals: *virāṭ samrāṭ*, wide, mighty, many and more — the doors, which have poured out streams of ghee. The entrance to the enclosure is spoken to as a queen.

Verse 6 calls the two who divide the day: *surukme supeśasā*, fair-golden and fair-shaped, they shine forth in beauty — let the two Uṣases sit down here. The pair are Night and Morning, named in the dual as a single thing, and what is asked of them is only that they take a seat. Verse 7 calls the two divine *hotā*s: the first, well-speaking, divine, *kavī* — let them perform this sacrifice of ours. Verse 8 calls the three goddesses by name: *bhārati iḷe sarasvati* — Bhāratī, Iḷā, {{sarasvatī}}, all of you I address; impel us toward *śrī*.

Verse 9 is {{tvaṣṭṛ}}: the master of forms, who has anointed all the animals — offer us their increase. Verse 10 is Vanaspati, the tree that becomes the sacrificial post: of your own accord send the offering to the gods, and let Agni make the oblations sweet. And verse 11 closes with the cries: Agni, who goes before the gods, is anointed with the gāyatrī, and he blazes among the *svāhākṛti*s, the utterances made with *svāhā*.

The shape is a walk through a rite. Fire lit; the offering anointed; the gods called; the grass laid down; the doors opened; the two halves of the day seated; the two priests set to work; the three goddesses invoked; the forms of creatures blessed; the post consenting; and Agni, at the end, blazing as the cries go up. The hymn's twelve or so stations are the rite's own furniture, and every one of them is spoken to in the second person.
188.practice:
The Āprī hymns are a family's property. Nine of them stand in the Ṛgveda — [[1.142]], this one, [[2.3]], [[3.4]], [[5.5]], [[7.2]], [[9.5]], [[10.70]] and [[10.110]] — and each belongs to a different line of singers, each keeping the same sequence of stations with its own wording. Two of the nine are in maṇḍala 1: Dīrghatamas has 1.142, and Agastya has this one. A reader who wants to see what a tradition means by a fixed form with room inside it should read the two together.

What is worth carrying is what the sequence addresses. The doors of the enclosure. The grass laid down on the ground. The tree that will become the post. The two halves of the day. Nothing in the rite is treated as mere equipment: the barhis is spoken to, the doors are called *virāṭ samrāṭ*, sovereign and imperial, and the wood is asked to send the offering *tmanyā*, of its own accord — consent rather than use.

Verse 8 is the one that has stayed in living speech. Bhāratī, Iḷā and Sarasvatī are invoked together in every Āprī hymn, and Sarasvatī is the only one of the three the later tradition kept as a goddess in her own right. Here she is one of three, named last, and what the three are asked for is *śrī*.

And verse 11 names the moment a reader performs whenever they offer anything into a fire: *svāhākṛtīṣu rocate*, he shines among the utterances made with *svāhā*. The word every household offering ends with is the last word of Agastya's Āprī, and the hymn says what happens when it is said — Agni brightens.
188.disagreements:
The most informative point about this hymn is an omission, and Sāyaṇa catches it. The Āprī sequence normally has Narāśaṃsa standing before the *īḍya* station; here, he notes, Narāśaṃsa is left out and verse 3's *īḍya* stands alone. The fixed form has been varied, and the commentator says so rather than smoothing it over. He also records the ritual placement of the whole set: the Āpris, he says, are the *prayāja*s, the fore-offerings.

Verse 5 divides the translators on how much of the line is a name. Sāyaṇa observes that the last two epithets are epithets of number and the rest are names, so that *virāṭ* and *samrāṭ* are titles of the doors rather than adjectives. Wilson turns them all into adjectives — "variously and perfectly radiant, manifold, excellent, many, and numerous" — while Griffith keeps the titles: "The sovran all-imperial Doors."

On verse 8 Sāyaṇa distributes the three goddesses across the three regions: Bhāratī presiding over heaven, Iḷā over earth, Sarasvatī over the firmament, and adds that all three are held to be particular manifestations of the sun's majesty. Neither translator brings that scheme into the verse.

On verse 9 he notes that a verb has to be supplied for Tvaṣṭṛ's forms, and offers the tradition that Tvaṣṭṛ shapes what has been begotten while it is still in the womb.
188.note: Āprī sūktas counted across all ten Anukramaṇī files by the presence of the svāhākṛtayaḥ station: 1.142, 1.188, 2.3, 3.4, 5.5, 7.2, 9.5, 10.70, 10.110; 1.188 is one of six sūktas in 1.165-1.191 without Agastya's closing refrain

189.title: Agne Naya Supathā — Agni Asked for the Good Road
189.synthesis:
Eight verses in triṣṭubh, and the first line of the first one has outlived every other line in this maṇḍala.

*Agne naya supathā rāye asmān* — {{agni}}, lead us by a good road to *rayi*; god, knowing all *vayunāni*, all the ways things are done; *yuyodhy asmaj juhurāṇam enaḥ*, keep away from us the crooked *enas*, the fault that makes us swerve; and *bhūyiṣṭhāṃ te nama-uktiṃ vidhema*, may we offer you the fullest utterance of *namas* (v1). The request is not for wealth directly but for the road to it, and the obstacle named is not an enemy but a crookedness in oneself.

The second verse asks for passage and for shelter in one breath. Carry us across, Agni, anew, with *svasti*, past all the hard places; and be for us a stronghold, wide, broad, ample — and then, in the last line, *tokāya tanayāya śaṃ yoḥ*, welfare and remedy for our children and our children's children. A road, a fort, and the grandchildren, in three lines.

The third verse turns to sickness. Keep the diseases far from us, Agni; let them go against the peoples who are *anagnitrāḥ*, without Agni to guard them; and make the ground favourable for us again, worshipful one, with all the immortals. The fourth asks for constancy rather than rescue: guard us with unfailing guardians, blazing in the seat you love; let no fear find your singer, youngest one, today or afterwards.

The fifth verse names what it is afraid of, and the list is unexpectedly precise. Do not give us over to the evil one, greedy, hostile, bringing ruin; not *datvate daśate*, to the fanged that bites; nor *adate*, to the one without teeth; nor to the injurer — do not hand us over, powerful one. Both the toothed and the toothless are named. Whatever is meant by each, the singer wants the whole range covered.

The sixth verse says what a man like Agni does for the man who praises him: *ṛtajāta*, born of {{ṛta}}, he stretches a shelter over the body against everyone who would injure or revile — for you, god, are the splitter of the crooked. The word for crooked is the same root as verse 1's *juhurāṇa*: the thing that makes us swerve, and the god who cuts it apart.

The seventh verse places him in the day. Knowing both kinds of men, you come at the morning to them, worshipful Agni; and at evening be teachable for man, to be groomed, like a swift horse, by those who want you. A god described as something to be curried down at nightfall.

The eighth verse signs off: we have spoken these *nivacanāni* to the conquering Agni, I the son of Māna; may we win a thousand along with the ṛṣis. Then the household's seal, *vidyāma iṣaṃ vṛjanaṃ jīradānum*. It is the last sūkta in maṇḍala 1 whose deity is Agni — the book that opened with *agnim īḷe* closes its Agni hymns here.
189.practice:
Verse 1 of this hymn is the closing verse of the Īśāvāsya Upaniṣad, and it is also the verse the tradition says over a body at the last rite. *Agne naya supathā rāye asmān* — lead us by the good road. Whatever a reader knows of the Upaniṣads, they have very likely met this line there without knowing it was Agastya's, and without knowing it stands at the head of the last Agni hymn of the Ṛgveda's first book.

What it asks for is worth attending to word by word, because it is not what a request for prosperity usually looks like. Not give us wealth — *lead us by a good road to* wealth. Not destroy our enemies — *keep away from us the crooked fault*, the *enas* that is *juhurāṇa*, that makes a man swerve off his line. And not I will praise you — *may we offer the fullest utterance of namas*, as though even the praising had to be asked for.

The rest of the hymn is a householder's list and can be read as one. Verse 2: get us across the hard places, be a broad fort, and let the children and grandchildren be well. Verse 3: keep illness off. Verse 4: no fear for the man who sings, today or later. Verse 5: not to the fanged, not to the toothless. Verse 6: a shelter over the body.

That fifth verse is the one to notice for its realism. Danger is enumerated in two categories, the thing with teeth and the thing without — snakes on one side and, on the commentators' reading, whatever harms with horns or claws or with nothing at all. Nobody is asking to be made invulnerable. They are asking that the list be complete.

And the last verse asks for something in company: *vayaṃ sahasraṃ ṛṣibhiḥ sanema*, may we win a thousand along with the seers. Not instead of them.
189.disagreements:
Verse 1's *vayunāni* is the word the translators handle differently and it changes what Agni is being credited with. Wilson gives "knowing all kinds of knowledge"; Griffith, "God who knowest every sacred duty." One makes him omniscient, the other makes him the one who knows what is to be done — and the second sits closer to the word's use elsewhere for a marked-out way or observance.

Verse 5's two categories are glossed by Sāyaṇa with more specificity than the verse supplies: the fanged that bites he takes as snakes and venomous creatures, and the toothless as those that do harm by other natural weapons, horns and claws; *rīṣate* he explains as one who injures, like thieves and rākṣasas. Both translators keep the categories bare, as the Sanskrit does.

Verse 6 is where they separate most. Wilson reads it as a transformation of the worshipper — a man praising Agni "becomes such as you are" and exempts himself from those who would harm him. Griffith reads it as protection from outside: "Such as thou art… when lauded give protection to our bodies." The difference is whether the singer takes on Agni's quality or merely stands behind it.

Verse 7's close divides them again: Wilson makes Agni compliant like an officiant directed by the priests' wishes; Griffith keeps the horse — "to be adorned, as keen, by eager suitors." The word behind it is *marmṛjenya*, to be groomed.
189.note: 1.189 verified as the last sūkta in maṇḍala 1 with agniḥ as devatā, from the Anukramaṇī file; juhurāṇam at v1 and viṣpaṭ / abhihrutām at v6 read from the padapāṭha

190.title: Bṛhaspati, Whose Śloka Travels Heaven and Earth
190.synthesis:
Eight verses in triṣṭubh to Bṛhaspati, and it is a difficult hymn — several of its lines are compressed to the point where the witnesses cannot agree what they say. What holds throughout is the subject: this is the god of the formulated word, and the hymn is about what a word does once it has been made.

Strengthen with your *arka*s the unassailable bull, the one of gladdening tongue, Bṛhaspati, anew — he of the bright chants, whom the gods and the thoughts of the singer listen for (v1). The second verse describes his release: the words of the season attend him, who was let loose like a stream for the god-seeking men; and Bṛhaspati became, spreading wide, the anointer of open spaces, in {{ṛta}} a Mātariśvan.

The third asks him to hold out the praise: may he extend the *upastuti*, the raising of *namas*, and the *śloka*, as Savitṛ extends his two arms; by whose *kratu* the daily one exists; who is terrible like a wild animal, and *arakṣasa*, without any demon in him, and strong. A god whose effective power is what makes the day recur.

The fourth verse is the one that says what the hymn is about. *Asya ślokaḥ divi īyate pṛthivyām* — his *śloka*, his sounded verse, travels in heaven and on earth; like a steed it is stretched out by the discerning bearer of the mystery. And then, without transition: like the weapons of hunters, these of Bṛhaspati go day after day against those whose wiles are a serpent's. The verse holds a made word travelling between the worlds and a volley of arrows in the same four lines, and does not explain the join.

The fifth is the hymn's ethical centre and it is unmistakable. *Ye tvā deva usrikaṃ manyamānāḥ* — those who, thinking you a poor milch-cow, wicked and grasping, live off what is good in you: to the ill-minded you do not hand over anything desirable; Bṛhaspati, you settle with the reviler. People who feed on a thing while treating it as worthless is a recognisable species, and the hymn names it.

The sixth verse gathers contrasts: one who is easy of approach, like a path with good grazing; ill to control; like a friend fully loved; unassailable — and those who watch us, covered over, stood there uncovering themselves. The seventh sets out the traffic in praise: he to whom the *stubh*s come as streams come, as rivers with banked channels go to the sea — he, knowing, looks at both from within, Bṛhaspati, the crossing and the waters, eager.

And the eighth closes: thus the great, strong-born, powerful Bṛhaspati, the bull, the god, for our upholding — praised by us, may he grant us wealth in heroes and in cattle. Then the seal, *vidyāma iṣaṃ vṛjanaṃ jīradānum*. It is the last time the refrain is heard: after this hymn only [[1.191]] remains, and it does not carry it.
190.practice:
Bṛhaspati is the lord of the *brahman* — the formulated, effective word — and this hymn is where a reader can see what that meant before it meant anything else. The commentators gloss his name as the protector of the mantra, and the hymn's fourth verse gives the picture: *asya ślokaḥ divi īyate pṛthivyām*, his sounded verse travels in heaven and on earth. A word properly made goes somewhere. That is the whole claim, and everything else in the hymn depends on it.

Fourteen sūktas across the Ṛgveda name Bṛhaspati, two of them in maṇḍala 1. The tradition afterwards made him the *devaguru*, the teacher of the gods, and gave his name to the planet Jupiter and to Thursday; a reader who keeps *bṛhaspativāra* is keeping his name without necessarily knowing this hymn exists.

Verse 5 is what to take away, and it needs no translation into modern terms. *Ye tvā deva usrikaṃ manyamānāḥ pāpā bhadram upajīvanti* — those who, reckoning you a scrubby little cow, live off your goodness. They are described exactly: not enemies, not deniers, but dependants who despise what they are dependent on. The hymn does not ask for them to be destroyed. It says only that nothing desirable will be handed to the ill-minded, and that Bṛhaspati settles accounts with the man who sneers.

The seventh verse gives the image for a life of praise: songs going to him the way rivers with cut banks go to the sea, and the god standing in the middle, watching both the water and the crossing. Whatever is being said is going somewhere whether the speaker sees it arrive or not.

And this is the last hymn in Agastya's twenty-seven to carry the family seal *vidyāma iṣaṃ vṛjanaṃ jīradānum*. Twenty-one sūktas in this maṇḍala end on that line, and this is the twenty-first.
190.disagreements:
This is one of the hardest hymns in the maṇḍala and the two translations diverge so widely that they cannot both be describing the same lines. Verse 4 is the clearest case: Wilson has Bṛhaspati's glory spreading through heaven and earth and his weapons falling daily on "the workers of guile," while the Griffith text available here gives a verse about worthless bullocks and wealthy sinners. Verse 5 shows the same displacement — Wilson's poor men who reckon Bṛhaspati an old ox, against Griffith's fair path where the grass is pleasant. The cause is mechanical: the Griffith file here is offset by one verse throughout this sūkta and has no entry for verse 8, so his renderings cannot be cited by verse number.

Where Sāyaṇa can be consulted he is careful. He defines Bṛhaspati at verse 1 as *mantrasya pālayitāram*, the protector of the formulated word. On verse 5's *usriya* he offers a cow that gives little milk, or an old draught ox; and on *cayase piyārum* he gives both "you go to favour the one who presses soma" and, citing the Nirukta, "you destroy the malevolent" — two opposite readings of the same half-line, kept side by side.

On verse 7 he glosses *gṛdhra* as one longing for rain and *taras* as a crossing or an increase of waters, and adds that if Bṛhaspati is identified with Indra, the "both" he looks at from within are heaven and earth, with the rain-region between them as his proper station.
190.note: bṛhaspatiḥ ascriptions counted across all ten Anukramaṇī files (14 sūktas); 1.190.8 is the last of the 21 occurrences of the refrain vidyāma iṣam vṛjanam jīradānum in maṇḍala 1; the Griffith file in this repository is offset by one verse across this sūkta and lacks an entry for v8

191.title: A Charm Against Poison — Sūrya and the Unseen Ones
191.synthesis:
Sixteen verses, and nothing else in maṇḍala 1 resembles them. No chariot, no pressing, no patron, no *stoma*. A man has been bitten, or thinks he has, and this is what he says.

One word runs through the first nine verses and stops dead: *adṛṣṭa*, the unseen — ten times in nine verses, and not once in the last seven. The stinger and the non-stinger and the water-stinger, and two like fleas — *ny adṛṣṭā alipsata*, the unseen ones have smeared me (v1). The remedy, coming, kills the unseen; going, it kills; striking down, it kills; grinding, it grinds them (v2). Then the places they live: śara, kuśara, darbha, sairya, muñja, vīraṇa — six kinds of long grass named one after another, and among them all the unseen ones together have smeared me (v3). A man just bitten lists the grasses.

Verse 4 is the hour. *Ni gāvo goṣṭhe asadan* — the cows had settled in the byre, the wild animals had gone down to their lairs, the *ketavaḥ* of men had gone out — and then the unseen ones smeared me. It is the most exact picture of nightfall in the maṇḍala, and it is here because that is when this happens.

Verse 5 turns on them: these have been made out, like thieves at dusk — *adṛṣṭā viśvadṛṣṭāḥ*, unseen ones who see everything, you have been noticed; be watchful. The paradox stands in two words side by side, and it is the hymn's whole problem: what cannot be seen sees you.

Then verse 6, which is not what anyone would expect. *Dyaur vaḥ pitā pṛthivī mātā somo bhrātā aditiḥ svasā* — Dyaus is your father, {{pṛthivī}} your mother, {{soma}} your brother, {{aditi}} your sister. Unseen ones, all-seeing: *tiṣṭhata ilayata su kam*, stand still, be quiet, and be at ease. He does not curse the creature. He tells it who its family is, and then asks it, gently, to settle down.

Verse 7 goes back to being direct: those at the shoulder, those on the body, the needle-stingers, the fore-stingers, whatever you are — all together, be gone. And then the sun comes up. *Ut purastāt sūryaḥ eti viśvadṛṣṭo adṛṣṭahā* — the all-seen {{sūrya}} rises in the east, the killer of the unseen, crushing the unseen ones and every *yātudhānī* (v8); he has flown up, burning through everything, Āditya from the mountains, all-seen, killer of the unseen (v9). The word said ten times is undone by its own opposite, and never returns.

The next four verses share a closing line. *Sūrye viṣam ā sajāmi* — I hang the poison on the sun, like a wineskin in a liquor-seller's house; *sa cin nu na marāti no vayaṃ marāma*, he does not die, and neither shall we; his yoking is far off; *madhu tvā madhulā cakāra*, the honey-maker has made you honey (v10). Then the same reasoning with a smaller witness: this tiny little bird has eaten your poison, and she does not die, and neither shall we (v11). Then the thrice-seven *viṣpuliṅgaka*s, who ate the flower of the poison and did not die (v12); then, of the ninety and nine that undo poison, I have taken hold of every name (v13). Four times the same last line, three times the same argument — something has already swallowed this and lived.

The last three verses carry it off. Thrice-seven peahens and seven unmarried sisters have taken your poison away, *udakaṃ kumbhinīr iva*, as girls carry water in jars (v14). This tiny *kuṣumbhaka* — I split it with a stone, and from there the poison turned away into far-off regions (v15). And the closing verse of maṇḍala 1: the *kuṣumbhaka*, coming out from the mountain, said this — *arasaṃ vṛścikasya viṣam*, the scorpion's poison has no sap in it; scorpion, your poison has no strength.

A book that began *agnim īḷe purohitam* ends with a sentence spoken to a scorpion.
191.practice:
This is the last hymn of maṇḍala 1 and it is a snakebite charm. After a hundred and ninety sūktas to {{agni}}, {{indra}}, the {{marut}}s and the {{aśvin}}au, the book closes with a frightened man in the dark reciting over his own body. Whoever arranged the collection kept it, and put it last.

It belongs, in kind, with the Atharvaveda rather than with its neighbours, and the commentators point that out by citing Atharvan parallels for two of its verses. This is one of the places where the two collections visibly touch. Of the fifteen occurrences of *viṣa*, poison, across the whole Ṛgveda, eight are in this one hymn.

Verse 6 is the one to keep. Having been bitten in the dark by something he cannot see, the singer says: Dyaus is your father, Pṛthivī your mother, Soma your brother, Aditi your sister — now be still, and be at ease. He does not damn the creature or deny it a place. He recites its lineage, which is the same lineage as his own, and on that basis asks it to stop. It is the oldest instinct in the tradition, applied at the worst possible moment: the thing harming you is inside the same family as you.

Verse 10 supplies the other half of the method, and it is not destruction either. *Madhu tvā madhulā cakāra* — the honey-maker has made you honey. The poison is not annihilated; it is turned into its opposite and hung up in the sun. The commentators call the discipline behind these verses the *viṣavidyā*, the knowledge of poisons, and note that it goes by a second name — *madhuvidyā*, the knowledge of honey. One science, two names, depending on which end of the transformation you are standing at.

And the argument of verses 10 to 12 is worth having on a bad night. The sun took this and did not die. A small bird took it and did not die. Twenty-one sparks took it and did not die. *No vayaṃ marāma* — and we shall not die. It is not a proof. It is a man reciting every survival he can think of until the fear lets go.
191.disagreements:
Sāyaṇa gives the occasion plainly: the sūkta is an antidote against poison, recited by Agastya in the apprehension of having been poisoned. On verses 10 to 13 he identifies the source discipline as the *viṣavidyā*, also called *madhuvidyā*, and quotes its procedure — the poison taken up in the solar orb with the fourth finger, made into *amṛta*, and blended, so that it becomes poisonless. He adds the lineage of that knowledge: the *madhuvidyā* was taught by Indra to Dadhyañc, who passed it to the Aśvins and lost his head for it. He also refers verses 8 and 9 to Atharvaveda parallels at 5.23.6 and 6.52.1.

The last two verses turn on one word, and the witnesses split. Sāyaṇa reads *kuṣumbhaka* as *nakula*, the mongoose — proverbially the snake's enemy — and Wilson follows, so that a mongoose is threatened with a stone and then speaks from the hillside. Griffith reads a poison-insect, so that the creature crushed in verse 15 is the same creature that speaks in verse 16. Neither is comfortable, and the hymn is stranger than either.

Verse 12's *viṣpuliṅgaka* is equally open. Sāyaṇa offers the seven tongues of fire multiplied by three colours — red, white and black — or else a female sparrow, of which he says there are twenty-one varieties that eat poison with impunity. Verse 13's ninety-nine are unnamed in the Sanskrit; Wilson supplies rivers, and Griffith prints "ninety rivers and nine."
191.note: adṛṣṭa- forms counted in the padapāṭha at vv 1-9 (ten occurrences, two at v8) and none at vv 10-16; viśva-dṛṣṭa- at vv 5, 6, 8, 9 (the v5 token is spelled viśva-dṛśṭāḥ in this file); the refrain āre asya yojanam ... madhu tvā madhulā cakāra counted at vv 10-13; viṣa forms counted across all ten padapāṭha files: 15 in the Ṛgveda, of which 8 are in 1.191; the Anukramaṇī devatā aptṛṇaḥ does not itself occur anywhere in the padapāṭha

69.title: Agni Father of the Gods While Being Their Son
69.synthesis:
*Uṣo na jāraḥ* — like the lover of {{uṣas}} — opens this hymn and returns in its ninth verse, and the two occurrences hold everything between them. Outside these two lines the phrase appears only once more in the whole Ṛgveda. It is this poet's signature for {{agni}} at daybreak: the one who comes to Uṣas, who is there when she is, whose arrival and hers cannot be pulled apart.

The first verse: bright, blazing, like her lover, he has filled *samīcī*, the two that face each other, as the light of heaven fills them. The second is the sharpest sentence in the sūkta. *Pari prajātaḥ kratvā babhūtha* — born round about, by *kratu* you have come to exceed; *bhuvo devānāṃ pitā putraḥ san*, you became the father of the gods while being their son. It is not a paradox offered for admiration. Agni is produced by the gods' own rite and carries up what they are given; he is generated, and he generates them. The relation runs both ways and the verse simply says so.

The third turns domestic. He is *vedhāḥ*, an ordainer, and *adṛptaḥ*, without arrogance — a rare thing to say of a god — and discerning; and then a kitchen comparison, that as the udder is to cows, so he is the sweetness of foods. What makes milk in a cow is what makes food good.

Verses four and five settle him into the house, and repeat themselves doing it. *Raṇvo duroṇe*, delightful in the dwelling, closes the fourth and opens the fifth. In the fourth he is kindly as one is kindly among his own people, someone to be invited in, seated in the middle. In the fifth the comparison sharpens: delightful in the dwelling *like a son newly born* — and then, like a horse well pleased, he carries the clans across. A newborn and a warhorse in two short lines.

The sixth is the poet in his own voice: when I called the clans, kin with the men, *sanīḍāḥ*, of one nest — may Agni attain all the states of godhood. The seventh says what secures it. *Nakiṣ ṭa etā vratā minanti*, nobody transgresses these *vrata*s of yours, because you made *śruṣṭi*, ready hearing, for these men. His observances hold because he first made himself audible to them.

The eighth is the one martial verse and it is compressed almost to obscurity: that is your *daṃsas*, your feat, that on the day, with your equals, yoked with men, you drove off the *rapas* — the injuries, the infirmities. Then the ninth comes back to the opening line with a request folded inside it: like the lover of Uṣas, shining, of the morning, *saṃjñātarūpaḥ*, his form recognised — may he take notice of this man.

The tenth ends in movement. *Tmanā vahanto duro vy ṛṇvan* — carrying of their own accord, they threw the doors open; all cried out, *svar dṛśīke*, in the sight of the sun. Those last two words close [[1.66]] as well and occur nowhere else in the Ṛgveda. Two of this poet's hymns end on the same phrase: everything opened, everyone calling out, and the daylight there to be seen.
69.practice:
The second verse is the one to sit with, and it is not a riddle. *Devānāṃ pitā putraḥ san* — father of the gods while being their son. {{agni}} is kindled by men and by gods and so is produced by them; he carries what is offered and so sustains them. Anyone who has raised children and then been looked after by them has the shape of it. The Veda states the double relation without softening it, and moves on.

*Adṛpta* in the third verse deserves attention because it is so unusual. The word means unintoxicated, not carried away, not full of oneself — and it is said of a god, as praise. The Ṛgveda's Agni is repeatedly *kavi* and *vedhas*, one who sees and one who ordains; here he is also the one who does not get above himself.

For a daily fire, verses 4 and 5 set the tone. *Raṇvo duroṇe*, delightful in the dwelling, twice over — once with him seated in the middle of the house, once with him as a newborn son. A fire kept in a home is described in the vocabulary of a child in a home. That is the register of the *aupāsana*, the domestic fire a married householder tends morning and evening: not awe, but the pleasure of a presence in the room.

And the opening phrase is worth knowing before dawn. *Uṣo na jāraḥ* occurs three times in the Ṛgveda — twice in this sūkta, once at 7.10.1 — and both occurrences here frame the hymn. {{uṣas}} and Agni belong to a single moment. The *agnihotra* offered at daybreak and the *sandhyā* said facing east are not two observances that happen to fall at the same hour; the Veda's own language treats Agni and the dawn as a pair who arrive for each other.
69.disagreements:
