Ten verses in the Anukramaṇī, *dvipadā virāj*; both translators halve them and print five units, so their fifth covers verses 9 and 10. Verse numbers here are the Anukramaṇī's.

*Uṣo na jāraḥ* is the hymn's real dispute. Sāyaṇa derives *jāra* from *jarayitrī*, the causer of wasting: the dawn is obliterated by the sun's superior radiance, so Agni is the *extinguisher* of Uṣas. Wilson prints exactly that — "like the extinguisher of the dawn". Griffith takes the ordinary sense of the word and gives "Dawn's lover". The morphology offers only *jāra*, a paramour; the reading turns on whether the poet meant the word plainly or the commentator is preserving an older physical explanation.

At verse 2 Sāyaṇa softens the paradox: Agni is father to the gods as bearer of oblations, and their son as the priests' messenger, going at their command. At verse 5 he adds a rule with wide reach — *tvam agne varuṇo jāyate tvaṃ mitro bhavasi*, you are born as {{varuṇa}}, you become {{mitra}} — Agni taking the form of whichever deity is being served. At verse 8 he identifies the *samānair nṛbhiḥ*, the equal men, as the {{marut}}s; Wilson makes them followers like Agni himself repelling intruders, where Griffith reads a boast, "thou smotest with thy peers".
69.note: uṣo na jāraḥ frames vv. 1 and 9; three occurrences in the Ṛgveda (1.69.1, 1.69.9, 7.10.1). svaḥ dṛśīke ends this sūkta and 1.66 and occurs nowhere else — both verified across all ten padapāṭha files. Numbering is the Anukramaṇī's (10 ṛcs) against 5 units in both translations

65.title: Agni Tracked Like a Thief, Found in the Waters
65.synthesis:
{{agni}} has gone into hiding, and this hymn opens in the middle of the search for him. *Paśvā na tāyuṃ guhā catantam* — as men track a thief who has made off with a beast, so they tracked him fleeing into concealment. The first verse gives no verb and no subject, only the one being hunted, described by what he does even while hidden: *namo yujānaṃ namo vahantam*, yoking *namas* and carrying *namas*. Homage harnessed to him, homage borne by him. Two short lines to a verse in this metre, and the sentence simply runs on.

The second verse says who was searching. *Sajoṣā dhīrāḥ* — of one accord, the discerning ones — went after him *padair anu*, along his footprints, and *viśve yajatrāḥ*, all who are fit for worship, sat down close to you. The hunt ends in the second verse; the rest of the hymn is about what was found. The third widens the same motion into a law: *ṛtasya devā anu vratā guḥ*, the gods went along the *vrata*s, the fixed courses, of {{ṛta}} — and an encompassing arose, measured against heaven and the earth. Following a track and following ṛta are made one movement across two consecutive verses. The fourth puts him where the search ended: the waters make him grow, the well-nourished one, *ṛtasya yonā garbhe sujātam*, well born in the womb, in the seat of ṛta.

From the fifth verse the hymn stops narrating and starts comparing, and does not stop. Delightful as *puṣṭi*, nourishment; broad as the earth people live on; sustaining as a mountain; kindly as rushing water — four likenesses in one two-line verse. The sixth adds two more and a question: like a steed loosed on the course, like the flood of the {{sindhu}} — *ka īṃ varāte*, who shall hold him back? The seventh sets kinship beside appetite in a single breath: he is *jāmiḥ sindhūnām*, kin of the rivers, a brother among sisters, and *ibhyān na rājā vanāny atti*, he eats the woods as a king eats the wealthy. The eighth drops comparison for one verse and states the plain fact underneath it: wind-driven, he has spread through the forests, and Agni shears the hair of the earth.

The ninth returns him to the water where he was found. *Śvasity apsu haṃso na sīdan* — he breathes in the waters, sitting like a *haṃsa*; and *kratvā cetiṣṭho viśām uṣarbhut*, most awake by *kratu*, the one who wakes at dawn for the clans. The one nobody could find is now the one who wakes everybody. The tenth closes with two more likenesses and a birth: an ordainer like {{soma}}, *ṛtaprajātaḥ*, born out of ṛta; like a beast with its young, wide-reaching, shining from far off.

The hymn is held at both ends by the same animal. The first verse tracks him as one tracks a stolen *paśu*; the last shows him as a *paśu* with its own young beside it. What was hunted turns out to be what feeds. And ṛta is named three times along the way — as the courses the gods follow, as the womb he is born in, as the origin he comes out of — so that the search, the birth and the nature all rest on one word.
65.practice:
A fire is not made; it is found. That is the ordinary fact this hymn is built on, and anyone who has watched an *araṇi* turned knows it — the wood is not producing something new, it is releasing something already there. {{agni}} *guhā catantam*, fleeing into hiding, is the same Agni who appears when the drill is worked, and the picture of gods on their knees reading footprints is a description of what kindling is: attention paid to where Agni already is.

The word to carry out of it is *uṣarbudh* in the ninth verse — awake at dawn, waker of the clans. It is the Ṛgveda's standing description of Agni and the reason the *agnihotra* is offered at the joining of night and day rather than at some convenient hour. Agni is not being asked to wake. It is the thing that is awake first.

Verse eight is worth keeping for its plainness. *Roma pṛthivyāḥ* — the grasses and shrubs are the hair of the earth, and Agni, driven by the wind, shears them. No moral is attached. The hymn has just called him kin of the rivers and sweet as nourishment, and in the next breath says he burns the countryside bare. Both are true and the Ṛgveda does not choose.

The poet is worth knowing as a poet. Parāśara Śāktya has nine sūktas in the whole collection — 1.65 through [[1.73]], every one of them to Agni — and fourteen verses of 9.97 to {{soma}} Pavamāna. Nine hymns, one deity, no other subject. Read in order, as they stand, they are a single sustained attempt on one god, and this is where it begins.

The third verse is the one to sit with. The gods find Agni by walking *anu vratā ṛtasya*, along the fixed courses of {{ṛta}} — not by force and not by cleverness, but by going the way things already go. That is the Veda's oldest instruction on how anything divine is located, and here it is given as a hunting story.
65.disagreements:
First, the numbering. This sūkta is in *dvipadā virāj*, in which each ṛc is only two short pādas, and the Anukramaṇī counts ten of them. Wilson and Griffith both merge them in pairs and print five units, so a reader comparing by number will find the translations running at half the count. Numbering here follows the Anukramaṇī. Sāyaṇa states the rule himself at the head of this hymn: in *dvipadā virāṭ chandas* each hymn is divided in half, and every two pādas are taken to form a complete unit.

On the hiding place he is specific. *Guhā* means the depth of the waters and the hollow of the aśvattha, and Agni had hidden in both for a season. For the search he cites the Taittirīya account — he concealed himself and entered the waters, the gods wanted a messenger to him, and a fish disclosed where he was. Neither translator carries this.

Verse 3's *pariṣṭir dyaur na bhūma* divides them: Wilson has "the search spread everywhere, and earth became like heaven"; Griffith, "there was a gathering vast as heaven itself." On verse 10's *somo na vedhāḥ* Sāyaṇa supplies an equation from the Vājasaneyi text — soma is the food and Agni the eater — so that Agni is a maker in the way soma is, drawing out of plants what nourishes.
65.note: verse numbering follows the Anukramaṇī (10 ṛcs); both translations run at 5 merged units. paśu frame (v1 paśvā, v10 paśuḥ) and ṛta ×3 verified from the padapāṭha

68.title: Agni Unveils the Nights, Then the Doors of Wealth
68.synthesis:
This is the one hymn of its six in which {{agni}} is almost never compared to anything. Its neighbours run on similes; this one has exactly one in ten verses, and where the poet puts it decides the shape of the whole.

It opens with an uncovering. *Śrīṇann upa sthād divaṃ bhuraṇyuḥ* — blending as he goes, restless, he stood up toward heaven — and *sthātuś carathaṃ aktūn vy ūrṇot*, he unveiled what stands and what moves and the nights themselves. The verb is *vṛ*, to cover; with *vi* it means to strip the cover off. Firelight does not create the world at night, it takes the lid off it. The second verse states his position: when he alone came to surround all these, he became a god among gods by sheer greatness.

The third and fourth tell what happened to the other gods because of him. *Ād it te viśve kratuṃ juṣanta* — then all of them took pleasure in your *kratu*, your effective resolve, when you, born living out of dry wood, came forth. And then: *bhajanta viśve devatvaṃ nāma*, all of them received a share in the very name of godhead, *ṛtaṃ sapantaḥ*, tending {{ṛta}}, tending the immortal, each by his own ways. Divinity is described here as something the gods came into by service, not something they arrived holding.

The fifth gives the two things ṛta produces. *Ṛtasya preṣā ṛtasya dhītiḥ* — the impulse that comes from ṛta and the *dhīti*, the formed thought, that comes from ṛta; and he in whom all life sits, *viśvāyu*; and all of them performed the works. Impulse and thought traced to one source, and then labour.

The sixth turns to the worshipper, and its verb is exact. *Yas tubhyaṃ dāśād yo vā te śikṣāt* — whoever gives to you, or merely tries to serve you — *tasmai cikitvān rayiṃ dayasva*: to him, discerning one, deal out *rayi*. Not grant, not pour: *dayasva*, apportion a share. The man who only attempts is named alongside the man who gives. The seventh seats Agni where that sharing happens — *hotā niṣatto manor apatye*, the *hotā* settled among the offspring of Manu — and says it is he who is master of these riches.

The eighth is about human continuance and is unusually plain: desiring seed in one another's bodies, undeluded, they came to agreement by their own *dakṣa*s, their own competence. The ninth then delivers the hymn's single comparison, and it is a family one. *Pitur na putrāḥ kratuṃ juṣanta* — like sons a father's, they take pleasure in his *kratu*, those quick ones who listen to his command. That phrase, *kratuṃ juṣanta*, occurs twice in the entire Ṛgveda and both times in this hymn: in the third verse it was the gods who took pleasure in his kratu, and here it is men. The poet has said one sentence twice, six verses apart, and changed only who is doing it.

The tenth ends by opening things again. *Vi rāya aurṇod duraḥ* — he threw back the doors of wealth, rich in provision — and *damūnāḥ*, the one at home in the house, studded the vault of heaven with stars. The verb that unveiled the nights in the first verse unbars the doors in the last, and between them a fire in a house has been made answerable for the night sky.
68.practice:
*Damūnas*, in the last verse, is the word to take away. It names {{agni}} as the one who belongs to the house — the household's own, not a visitor. And the tenth verse hands that domestic god the decoration of the night sky, in the same line as the doors of wealth being thrown open. Whatever the tradition built later, the Vedic conviction is already here in one verse: Agni on your hearth and the order of the heavens are the same person's work.

The hymn's most usable claim is in verses 3 and 4. The gods came to *share in* the name of godhead, *ṛtaṃ sapantaḥ* — by tending {{ṛta}}, by service, each in his own way. Divinity is a thing arrived at. That is worth holding against the assumption that the Veda's gods are simply born superior; here they are described as having gained what they hold by keeping to order. And the verb used of them, *sap*, to tend or serve, is the same one used two verses earlier in [[1.67]] of human worshippers. Gods and men are doing the identical thing, and the poet uses the identical word for it.

Verse 6 is the one to remember when an offering feels inadequate. *Yas tubhyaṃ dāśād yo vā te śikṣāt* — the one who gives, or the one who only tries to. Both are named, and the same *rayi* is dealt out to both. The Veda is exacting about ritual precision, and this line is in it too.

And the phrase repeated at verses 3 and 9 is the teaching, carried in the structure rather than asserted. The gods took pleasure in Agni's *kratu*; men take pleasure in Agni's *kratu*, as sons in a father's. It occurs nowhere else in the Ṛgveda. That a household stands in the same relation to him as the gods do is never claimed outright — it is done by saying the same sentence a second time.
68.disagreements:
The Anukramaṇī gives ten verses in *dvipadā virāj*. Wilson and Griffith each print five, merging them two by two, so their unit 3 covers the Anukramaṇī's verses 5 and 6. Numbering here is the Anukramaṇī's.

Sāyaṇa's surviving coverage of this sūkta is thin, and where it exists it is corrective. On verse 1 he records an alternative to what Wilson prints: rather than Agni comprehending the virtues of all these, he alone *surpasses* the greatness — *mahitva* — of all these gods. On verse 7 he glosses the offspring of Manu simply as mankind.

Verse 1's *śrīṇan* is unsettled. Wilson takes it of the oblations, "mixing them with other ingredients"; Griffith reads it of Agni himself, "commingling, restless". The verb means to cook or to blend and no object is supplied.

Verse 5 divides them further. Wilson distributes it between praise and offering — "praises are addressed to him who has repaired to the solemnity; oblations to him who has gone" — where Griffith keeps the two genitives together: "strong is the thought of Law, the Law's behest." The padapāṭha has *ṛtasya preṣāḥ* and *ṛtasya dhītiḥ* standing in parallel, which favours Griffith's construction. On verse 8's *icchanta reto mithas tanūṣu* Wilson makes it a request to Agni for procreative vigour; Griffith reads it of the men themselves, "men yearn for children to prolong their line".
68.note: kratum juṣanta occurs twice in the whole Ṛgveda, at 1.68.3 and 1.68.9 — verified across all ten padapāṭha files. Exactly one comparison particle in the sūkta (pituḥ na, v9). vi + √vṛ frames vv. 1 and 10. Numbering is the Anukramaṇī's (10 ṛcs) against 5 units in both translations

67.title: Mantras Made in the Heart Find Agni in Hiding
67.synthesis:
*Guhā* — in hiding, in secret — occurs three times in these ten short verses, and the whole sūkta turns on it. {{agni}} is somewhere he cannot be seen, and the hymn is about what finds him.

It opens by placing him in two worlds at once. *Vaneṣu jāyur marteṣu mitraḥ* — victorious among the woods, a friend among mortals — and he claims *śruṣṭi*, ready obedience, as an ageless king claims it. The second verse asks him to be what he is: secure as *kṣema* is secure, auspicious as *kratu* is auspicious, *svādhī*, well-intentioned, *hotā*, the one who offers and calls, *havyavāṭ*, the carrier of what is given.

The third hides him. Holding every *nṛmṇa*, every manly power, in his hand, he put the gods into *ama*, dread — *guhā niṣīdan*, sitting in concealment. The gods are frightened by an absence they cannot account for. And then the fourth says who finds him, and it is not the gods. *Vidantīm atra naro dhiyaṃdhāḥ* — the men who hold {{dhī}}, thought at work, find him here; and the means is stated exactly: *hṛdā yat taṣṭān mantrān aśaṃsan*, when they recited *mantra*s chiselled by the heart. *Takṣ*, the verb behind *taṣṭa*, is what a carpenter does to timber. The verse before had the gods in fear. This one has men reciting something they made, and it works.

The fifth then does something with those same mantras that should stop a reader. Like *aja*, the unborn, he holds the earth firm — and *tastambha dyāṃ mantrebhiḥ satyaiḥ*, he propped the sky apart with true mantras. The word for what found him in verse 4 is the word for what holds up the sky in verse 5, with nothing in between.

The sixth returns to the hiding and to something homelier: guard the dear tracks of the cattle, *viśvāyu*, you in whom all life is — and *guhā guhaṃ gāḥ*, you have gone from one concealment into the next. The seventh and eighth describe whoever gets through. He who has discerned him while he is hidden, who has come and sat at *dhārām ṛtasya*, the flowing stream of {{ṛta}}; those who work him loose while *ṛtā sapantaḥ*, tending ṛta — to such a one he then declares aloud where the good things are.

The ninth widens him into everything that grows: he swells in the plants by his greatness, and in the offspring, and *prasūṣv antaḥ*, inside the mothers that bear them. And the tenth ends where the searching stops. *Cittir apāṃ dame* — the awareness of the waters, in the house; and the wise, having measured him out, made him, *sadmeva dhīrāḥ saṃmāya cakruḥ*, the way one lays out a seat.

That last verb is the hymn's quiet answer. Agni is not caught; he is built a place. The hidden one is found by mantras made in the heart, and is then given a measured seat to sit in — which is what an altar is.
67.practice:
The fourth verse is why this hymn matters to anyone who recites. *Hṛdā taṣṭān mantrān* — mantras chiselled by the heart. The verb is the carpenter's, the same one the tradition uses for the shaping of a chariot; a *mantra* here is not received passively, it is worked. And what these worked mantras do, in the very next verse, is hold up the sky. A tradition that preserved recitation to the syllable for three thousand years has in these two verses its own account of why: the recited word is treated as load-bearing.

*Viśvāyu*, appearing twice here and again in [[1.68]], is a name worth carrying. It says that all life, the whole span of it, is in {{agni}}. That is the ground of the fact that a Hindu life is punctuated by fire from the *jātakarma* to the last rite — not because fire is a symbol of life, but because in the Veda's own vocabulary he is the one in whom the whole span sits.

The sixth verse asks him to protect *priyā padāni paśvaḥ*, the dear tracks of the cattle. It is a small, specific prayer: keep the grazing safe, keep the herd's paths from harm. The Ṛgveda's household concerns are not abstract, and the hymn that has him propping up heaven asks him in the next breath to mind where the animals walk.

And the closing image is the one to hold at any fire. The wise did not capture Agni. They measured, and made — the words used for laying out a dwelling. Every *vedi* marked out and every hearth set is that verse being performed. He stays hidden until somebody prepares a place precise enough for him to sit in. The work is not persuasion; it is preparation, done accurately.
67.disagreements:
Ten verses in the Anukramaṇī, *dvipadā virāj*. Wilson and Griffith both merge them two by two and print five, so their fourth unit is the Anukramaṇī's verses 7 and 8. Numbering here is the Anukramaṇī's.

On verse 2's *havyavāṭ* Sāyaṇa supplies the tradition's threefold division of Agni: *havyavāhana*, who carries offerings to the gods; *kavyavāhana*, who carries them to the pitṛs; and *saharakṣas*, who receives what is offered to the rākṣasas. Neither translator mentions it.

Verse 5 divides them sharply. Sāyaṇa reads it against a Taittirīya passage in which the gods, alarmed that the sun's region might fall, propped it up with the metres of the Veda — the act here credited to Agni, and the reason *mantrebhiḥ satyaiḥ* is to be taken literally. Wilson prints "props up the heaven with true prayers"; Griffith weakens it to "with effective utterance fixed the sky".

Verse 6's *guhā guhaṃ gāḥ* is unresolved. Sāyaṇa takes *guha* as arid or rugged ground unfit for grazing, a tract Agni may scorch, which gives Wilson his "repair to the spots where there is no pasturage". Griffith reads the words plainly — "thou hast gone from lair to lair" — which the padapāṭha supports at least as well. The two are not reconcilable, and nothing in the verse decides between them.
67.note: guhā ×3 (vv. 3, 6, 7) verified from the padapāṭha; mantra in vv. 4 and 5; viśvāyu in vv. 6 and 10. Numbering is the Anukramaṇī's (10 ṛcs) against 5 units in both translations

70.title: Agni the Garbha of Waters, Woods, All That Moves
70.synthesis:
Eleven verses — one more than each of the five sūktas before it — and the odd verse changes how the run ends.

The first is a wish in the first person plural: *vanema pūrvīr aryo manīṣā*, may we win many things by *manīṣā*, by the mind's own devising; and may {{agni}}, fair of flame, attain all. The second says what he attains by. *Cikitvān*, discerning, he takes in the *vrata*s of the gods and the *janma*, the birth and lineage, of the human folk. Two orders held in one act of knowing, and the hymn returns to it twice more.

The third verse is the one people remember. *Garbho yo apāṃ garbho vanānāṃ garbhaś ca sthātāṃ garbhaś carathām* — the germ of the waters, the germ of the woods, the germ of what stands and the germ of what moves. Four occurrences of *garbha* in two short lines, and no other verse in the Ṛgveda repeats the word four times. He is not in the waters and in the wood; he is what is unborn inside them, waiting. The fourth follows him into the two places anyone would look: *adrau cid*, even in the rock, and *antar duroṇe*, inside the house — immortal, well-intentioned, like one who belongs to all the clans.

The fifth names him *kṣapāvān*, lord of the night, and states the exchange: he is the Agni of riches for the man who serves him *araṃ sūktaiḥ*, fittingly, with well-made hymns. The sixth turns the second verse's knowing into a command: *etā cikitvo bhūmā ni pāhi* — you who discern, guard these creatures of earth — *devānāṃ janma martāṃś ca vidvān*, knowing the birth of gods and of mortals both. What he knows is exactly what he is asked to protect.

The seventh puts him in time. Many nights, *virūpāḥ*, unlike one another, strengthen him — no two the same, and he is grown by all of them — along with what stands still, and the chariot *ṛtapravīta*, driven forward by {{ṛta}}. The eighth reports the outcome as already accomplished: *arādhi hotā*, the *hotā* has been won, seated in *svar*, making all works *satyā*. Not successful. True.

The ninth and tenth are about what people bring and what they take. He sets renown in the cattle and in the woods, and *bharanta viśve balim*, all bring tribute; may there be *svar* for us. Then: in many places men served you, and they bore away the portion as sons divide the goods of an aged father. It is an ordinary domestic picture of what a shared fire is — the property of someone old enough that his sons are dividing it.

Then the eleventh, standing alone where every other verse in these six hymns has a partner. It has no main verb at all, only three comparisons: like one skilled and eager, like a hero who is an archer, like an avenger terrible to meet — *tveṣaḥ samatsu*, a glare in the clashes. The run that began at [[1.65]] by likening Agni to a hunted animal ends on three likenesses and nothing else, unfinished, mid-gesture; and with the next sūkta the metre goes back to triṣṭubh and the sentences get their verbs again.
70.practice:
*Garbha* is the word this hymn puts into a reader's hands, and it is one an educated Hindu already carries — it is the word in *garbhādhāna*, the rite at the beginning of a life. Here {{agni}} is called the *garbha* of the waters, of the trees, of everything standing and everything moving. Not their ruler, not merely present in them: the unborn thing inside them. It is the Veda's most economical statement of why the same fire is looked for in wood, in water, in the body's heat and in the sun — one thing gestating everywhere, brought out by different means.

The ninth verse contains *bali*, and the word repays notice. It occurs four times in the whole Ṛgveda — here, and at 5.1.10, 7.18.19 and 8.100.9 — and it means the tribute a people brings to the one who rules them. That is the same word as the *bali* offered in daily household worship, the portion set aside before the family eats. Its first sense is what is owed to the one who protects. Anyone who sets that portion down is doing what this verse describes, with the older meaning still inside the word.

Verse 5 gives the condition attached to all of it. Agni is lord of riches for the one who serves *araṃ sūktaiḥ* — fittingly, adequately, with well-made hymns. *Aram* is a measure word: enough, and to the point. Not more offering, and not louder. Apt.

And verse 10 is the image to keep. Men served him in many places, and took their share of him as sons take the property of an aged father. Every household that carries fire from a parent's hearth, every lamp lit from another lamp, is inside that sentence. Nothing is lessened by the division — which is precisely why the poet reached for an inheritance rather than a gift.
70.disagreements:
The Anukramaṇī counts eleven verses, *dvipadā virāj*. Wilson and Griffith both merge them in pairs and print six units — five pairs, then verse 11 standing alone, which makes their last unit the only one in these six sūktas that corresponds one-to-one with a numbered ṛc. All numbering here is the Anukramaṇī's.

Sāyaṇa's surviving note on this sūkta is a single gloss, on verse 5, and it preserves two senses of *kṣapāvān* without choosing between them: capable of destroying the rākṣasas, or possessed of the night — for which he cites the Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa, *āgneyī vai rātriḥ*, night belongs to Agni, and the *agnyādheya* formula *agnir jyotiḥ jyotir agniḥ svāhā*. Wilson prints "lord of night"; Griffith drops the word and writes only "Agni is Lord of riches".

Verse 1's *aryaḥ* separates the translators: Wilson gives "we solicit abundant food" and Griffith "may we, the pious, win much food by prayer", neither rendering the genitive, which in the padapāṭha points to goods belonging to a stranger or a rival.

Verse 9's *goṣu praśastiṃ vaneṣu dhiṣe* Wilson makes a petition — confer excellence on our cattle — where Griffith reads a statement, "thou settest value on our cows and woods". The verb is an aorist and both constructions are open.
70.note: 1.70.3 is the only verse in the Ṛgveda with garbha four times (10.184.2 has three) — verified across all ten padapāṭha files. balim occurs at 1.70.9, 5.1.10, 7.18.19, 8.100.9 only. kṣapāvān five times in the collection. 11 ṛcs in the Anukramaṇī against 6 units in both translations, the sixth being v11 alone

66.title: Agni in Nothing but Similes, Then Named Yama
66.synthesis:
Nine of this sūkta's ten verses tell you what {{agni}} resembles. One tells you what he is, and it is placed where a reader would least expect it.

The first verse is four comparisons and nothing else: various and bright as *rayi*, wealth; like the sun's own look; like *prāṇa*, the breath that is a life; like a son of one's own body. No verb, no request — a man reaching for the four nearest things he values and finding all four insufficient. The second continues without a pause: restless as a hunting bird he attends the woods, and as a *dhenu* holds her milk, so he holds his brightness, *śucir vibhāvā*, pure and shining out.

The third lets a verb through at last. *Dādhāra kṣemam* — he has held security in place; delightful as a house is delightful, like ripened barley, conqueror of men. The fourth compares him to two kinds of excellence at once: praised among the clans like a *ṛṣi* who chants, and, like a horse well pleased, he confers *vayas*, the vigour proper to an age of life. The fifth is the strangest. *Durokaśociḥ*, his flame hard to dwell beside — a word that occurs nowhere else in the collection — and then, in the same two lines, constant as *kratu* is constant, and like a wife in the house, *araṃ viśvasmai*, adequate to everyone. Unapproachable heat and domestic sufficiency, stacked without apology.

The sixth and seventh turn martial. When he blazed out he was white among the clans, like a gold-decked chariot, fierce in the clashes; and then, like an army let loose he puts *ama*, dread, into them, like the flashing missile of an archer, his very face a glare.

Then the eighth, alone in the hymn, drops the word *like*. *Yamo ha jāto yamo janitvam* — Yama is what has been born, Yama is what is yet to be born; *jāraḥ kanīnāṃ patir janīnām*, lover of maidens, husband of wives. After seven verses of approximation the poet stops approximating and makes an identification, and it is with the god who holds what is born and what is still to come. Everything in a life that has begun and everything that has not is put into one hand.

The last two verses come home. *Astaṃ na gāvo* — as cattle reach the byre, we approach him kindled, bringing what moves and what stays. And the tenth: like the flood of the {{sindhu}} he drove his flames downward, and the cows lowed, *svar dṛśīke*, in the sight of the sun. The hymn that began with wealth, the sun, breath and a son ends with animals calling under an open sky.

The device is not decoration. In a metre of two short lines a comparison is the largest thing a verse can hold; the poet has almost nothing else available, and he uses it until the technique becomes the argument. Nothing in ordinary experience is enough — so here are all of them, and then one verse that stops trying.
66.practice:
This is the hymn to give someone who asks what the Ṛgveda actually sounds like. Nearly every line is a comparison drawn from what a household could see: wealth, the sun, breath, a son, a hunting bird, a milking cow, a house, ripened barley, a chanting *ṛṣi*, a horse, a wife, a chariot, an army, an arrow, cattle coming home, a river in flood. Eighteen comparisons in ten short verses. Measured against every sūkta of eight verses or more in the collection — 596 of them — this one stands fourth in the density of the comparison particles *na* and *iva*, and its neighbour [[1.65]] fifth. The two are the concentrated centre of this way of speaking about {{agni}}.

The eighth verse is where it bears on a life. Agni is called *yama*, and *jāraḥ kanīnāṃ patir janīnām* — the one the maidens love, the husband of wives. Behind that lies the plain fact that a Hindu marriage is completed at Agni: the circling is done around Agni, the vows are spoken before him, and the household fire begun on the wedding day is the one carried on in the *aupāsana*, tended by the couple morning and evening. The hymn is not making a startling claim. It is describing the position Agni actually occupies between a woman and the household she enters.

And *durokaśociḥ*, in the fifth, is a word to keep. The flame it is hard to live next to — and in the same breath, *araṃ viśvasmai*, enough for everyone, like a wife in her own house. Whoever tends a fire knows both, and the verse makes no attempt to reconcile them. Neither should a reader. The Veda is content to say that the thing at the centre of the house is also the thing that will burn you.
66.disagreements:
The Anukramaṇī counts ten verses of *dvipadā virāj*, two short pādas each. Wilson and Griffith both merge them in pairs and print five units, so their third covers the Anukramaṇī's verses 5 and 6. Numbering here is the Anukramaṇī's throughout.

*Yama* in verse 8 is where the readings part. Sāyaṇa offers two derivations and keeps both: from *yam*, to give — *yacchati dadāti kāmān stotṛbhyaḥ*, he who gives worshippers what they want, making Yama a name of Agni — or, following Yāska, that Agni is one of a pair of twins, born together with {{indra}}. He takes *jāta* and *janitva* as all beings now existing and all yet to exist. For "husband of wives" he tells a legend: {{soma}} obtained a maiden and gave her to the Gandharva Viśvāvasu, who passed her to Agni, who gave her to a mortal husband along with wealth and offspring. Wilson prints "as Yama, all that is born"; Griffith flattens it to "Master of present and of future life", losing the name.

Verse 9's *carātha* and *vasati* Sāyaṇa reads as moving and unmoving offerings — animals and rice — and Wilson follows him; Griffith takes them as movement and rest, "to him lead all your ways". Verse 5's *durokaśociḥ* has no parallel anywhere in the collection, and neither translator is confident: Wilson "of unattainable brightness", Griffith "with flame insatiate".
66.note: 18 comparison particles (na ×16, iva ×2) in 97 padapāṭha tokens — 4th densest of the 596 Ṛgvedic sūktas of 8+ verses; verse 8 is the only one without a comparison. durokaśociḥ is a hapax. Numbering is the Anukramaṇī's (10 ṛcs) against 5 units in both translations
